Mayor Howard called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m.
Alderman Coring gave the welcome and pronounced the invocation.
Mayor Howard stated the purpose of the meeting was to receive the City of
Southport’s proposed operating budget for FY 2012-2013.
City Manager Thomas presented the proposed operating budget for FY 2012-2013
which includes no tax or fee increases. The budget message and summary of
revenues and appropriations included. A copy of the budget is placed on file
with the City Clerk and available for public inspection at the James and
Margaret Harper Library.
ANNUAL BUDGET MESSAGE FY 12-13
CITY OF SOUTHPORT
To: The Honorable Mayor and Board of Aldermen
From: Patrick Thomas, City Manager
Overview
Since the budget process did not begin until the arrival of a new city manager
on April 16, its preparation this year has been a very challenging process.
Department have had to rapidly respond to a late-starting timetable, a new city
manager had to rapidly familiarize himself with city operations and projects, a
relatively new finance director has had to accelerate his familiarization with
his department, and we experienced significant difficulty in tracking some
previous accounting practices and actions. This challenge has also been
increased by the need to accomplish several improvements in budget development.
These have included the following:
∙   The need to increase department heads’ familiarity with the details and
building blocks of their financial plans;
∙   The need to re-visit the basic details from which line item and
departmental are constructed and to question traditional assumptions;
∙   The need to achieve significantly greater consistency in the classification
of expenditures;
∙   The need to shape the budget in manner that clearly reflects any goals
clearly expressed by the governing board;
∙   The need to re-shape certain portions of the budget to increase budget
management accountability.
Despite these challenges, the department heads have tried hard to respond to
the demands of a re-vamped budget process, and the finance director has
attempted to respond to a significant volume of requests for detailed budget
information. Their efforts to help produce a sound budget for FY 12-13 are
deeply appreciated.
Preparation of the fiscal 2012-13 budget has also occurred against a back-drop
of other issues that present significant – and sometimes increasing – financial
challenges to municipal governments. These issues include, for example:
∙   A still-recovering economy that has adversely affected revenue growth and
has negatively affected some rates of revenue collections;
∙   New, severe restrictions on municipal annexation, affecting cities and
towns’ abilities to maintain a balanced and fair revenue base;
∙   Actions of the legislature that have significantly slashed programs – such
as the Clean Water Management Trust Fund, the Parks and Recreation Trust Fund,
and the Public Beach and Waterfront Access Program – that have historically
played an important role in community improvements in coastal areas.
Budget Structure
Despite the very limited time available in which to prepare the budget, several
changes in budget structure have been made that are designed to make the budget
(a) more understandable, (b) more goals-focused, and (c) easier to use and
manage. These changes and additions include the following:
1.   Information about the mission of each department, its human resources, and
its goals for the coming year;
2.   More specific information about costs within line items and the basis of
those costs (although this process could not be developed as thoroughly as
desirable due to the time constraints);
3.   Much more consistent assignment of costs to line item categories;
4.   The separation of costs related to Administration and Finance, in order to
allow more specific budget management;
5.   The re-establishment of a budget division for the maintenance of
cemeteries (last included in the budget in FY 08-09), and the re-assignment of
one significant maintenance responsibility – the city dock – to Parks and
Recreation;
6.   The creation of a Non-Departmental budget division to reflect costs that
are not specific to an operational department, principally transfers to other
funds (such as capital project funds and future capital needs);
7.   The very modest beginning of Capital Reserve funds to set aside funds for
identified future capital needs;
8.   The tightening of budget allocations where possible, coupled with the
inclusion of contingency allocations in each budget, so that management can
respond to any genuine needs that may develop.
Revenue Outlook
The outlook for major revenues (the City receives almost 90% of its annual
revenues from just eight sources) is somewhat mixed. Improving retail sales are
expected to produce healthy growth in sales tax revenue, and franchise tax
revenue, which had slumped somewhat, is also expected to stage a modest
recovery. On the other hand, the still-struggling construction industry has
weakened building inspections revenue, and there remains no sign of increases
in some revenue sources, such as county support for the rescue squad. Ad
valorem taxes are expected to produce a modest increase, but we have concerns
about the collection rate, and a successful challenge to the county’s
revaluation of boats has resulted in a substantial reduction in the levy
related to boats. The budget does not propose any change in the existing
$0.2456/$100 rate in the ad valorem tax levy, but, if the scale of desired
community improvement projects increases in the near future, the tax rate will
need to be reconsidered at that time.
In the enterprise funds, the revenue trends are decidedly different. Warmer
temperatures in the last year led to a major decline in electric system
revenue, which, fortunately, was largely offset by reduced purchases of
wholesale power. Temperatures are expected to be more normal in the coming
year, which should lead to some degree of recovery in these revenues.
The Water and Sewer Fund, on the other hand, experienced a six percent-plus
surge in sales revenue in FY 2011-12. Its overall revenue picture was clouded,
however, by receipts of sewer impact fees that were far below expectations –
expectations that may have been based, in part, on the now-cancelled
annexations. A significant amount of fund balance is being used to balance the
Water and Sewer Fund budget in FY 12-13. However, this is tempered by the facts
that (a) the majority of the cause is one-time expenses – the local share of a
Corps of Engineers project to protect a lift station and the last reimbursement
payment for a Clean Water grant – and (b) the City received (this fiscal year)
over $1.3 million in sewer impact fee reimbursements from the South Brunswick
Sanitary District. No change in water and sewer rates is proposed at this time,
but there could always be a need to re-visit this issue if the county increases
wholesale water costs or sewer treatment costs above the levels anticipated in
the budget.
Operational Costs
Department heads have been helpful in efforts to re-shape the budget process,
and this has led to a General Fund budget in which seven of the twelve current
budget divisions have recommended budgets that are lower than FY 11-12 and
three other departments are essentially unchanged. The only two budgets that
are higher contain relatively modest increases. The one new operational budget
division – Cemeteries – is under $18,000.
The budget includes a two percent pay level adjustment for full-time employees
and anticipates that a salary and wage study will be undertaken during the year
to determine whether any additional pay level changes are needed in specific
positions. Funds have been set aside in an Administration contingency
allocation to pay for any needed adjustments, as well as to fund any
appropriate merit increases. The same management contingency will also be the
“safety valve” for any needs that arise that were not anticipated in slimmed-
down recommendations for many line items.
Southport, a community of less than 3,000, starts each fiscal year facing a
substantial cost related to former employees – over $150,000 in annual costs
related to its generous retiree health care insurance program. Over 15 former
employees participate in the program, and the premiums for their coverage
–which are equivalent to about 2.4 cents on the tax rate – are, in many cases,
significantly higher than those for active employees. The City has received one
bit of good news with respect to benefit costs: its group health insurance
costs for active employees will drop about 8% in the coming year (the result of
decisions regarding the League of Municipalities insurance pool). On the other
hand, workers compensation insurance rates are expected to rise by about 26
percent.
The amount of capital equipment being recommended in the budget is fairly
modest this year – two police patrol vehicles, a fire brush truck, a cardiac
monitor to support emergency medical services, and a trailer-mounted generator
for sewer pump station back-up. However, transfers to a new Capital Reserve
fund are recommended for future vehicle and equipment needs in Streets, Rescue,
Electric, and Water and Sewer, as well as for a document retrieval system for
official records. In addition, provisions have been made to replace existing
radio equipment with new narrow-band radios and to improve technology resources
– replacement of outdated computer equipment in several departments and a new
software system for management of building inspection records. One ambulance
will be replaced to support emergency medical services, but payments on the
vehicle are not expected to begin until the following fiscal year.
Services and Projects
The Board’s desire to see grounds and rights-of-way better and more
consistently maintained has been reflected in the specific allocation of
resources – partly in the form of part-time workers and partly in the form of
contract services funding – to maintain rights-of-way, parks, and cemeteries.
This should sustain this spring’s Board initiative to place more emphasis on
these services.
The recommended Parks and Recreation budget contains allocations for upgrades
to facilities at several parks and buildings, as well as the resurfacing of the
Ft. Johnston tennis courts and additional improvements to the city dock (for
which some repairs are already scheduled this spring). A stepped-up program of
street resurfacing and sidewalk construction is planned, using Powell Bill
funds.
One of the most important projects for the coming year, of course, will be the
planned improvements to the City Hall and to work spaces for other city
departments, such as Police, Rescue, and Code Enforcement. The budget contains
a $500,000 transfer to a capital project fund to support this project. Also
included is the estimated $180,000 City share of the Lord Street pump station
revetment, various upgrades to 13 different sewer collection facilities, and
continuation of the electric system pole replacement and meter replacement
programs.
Funding has already been set aside in a project budget for one initiative
planned during the upcoming year – the preparation of a waterfront access and
development plan, including an action plan for implementation.
Fund Balances
A summary of projected fund balances at June 30 for the various major funds is
included as an enclosure with this message. The estimated fund balances are
considered sufficient, after reservations of minimum balances under city
policy, to fund the amounts appropriated to balance the budget.
Summary
This budget represents our management team’s best effort to prepare a financial
plan that is thrifty and efficient, while still providing funding to help
implement Board goals and initiatives. We pledge to work diligently to achieve
your goals, to provide community services as economically as possible, to
accomplish more with less whenever possible, and to continuously seek
additional resources to help accomplish community improvements. I commend this
budget to you as a sound and reasonable financial plan for the operation of
City government in the coming fiscal year.
Yours in public service,
Pat Thomas
City Manager and Budget Officer

JUNE 4, 2012
SPECIAL MEETING (BUDGET)
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN             SPECIAL MEETING (BUDGET)
JUNE 4, 2012                  6:00 P.M.
CITY HALL (ALDERMEN CHAMBERS) SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:      Mayor Robert D. Howard
         Aldermen Todd Coring, Ken Karn,
         Mary Ellen Poole, Buddy Barnes,
         Nelson Adams, Jim Powell
 
STAFF PRESENT:   Pat Thomas, City Manager
         Regina W. Alexander, MMC-City Clerk
         Jim Philyaw, Finance Director
I.   Call to Order - 6:00 p.m.
   Mayor Howard called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. and gave the
invocation.
II.   Budget Work Session
   City Manager Thomas presented additional information upon request of Board
members for their review in budget deliberation. The following matters were
discussed:
·   History of pay increases for employees from prior year(s).
·   Position allocations including employee benefit package.
·   Spreadsheet showing impact of 2% increase on salaries and benefits, which
equate to approximately $40,000.
·   The financing for the new fire station and payment arrangements from fire
fees and the general fund was referenced by Mayor Howard. City Manager Thomas
will review this further.
·   City Manager Thomas noted that the proposed operating budget is reduced
approximately $180,000 down from last year including some departmental budgets.
·   Mr. Thomas reported that the Corp of Engineers’ calculations for the Bay
Street Revetment Project did not include real estate cost. Mr. Thomas explained
that there may be added cost to the project if property owners are not willing
to grant easements to the City. Matching funds for this project will be
allocated from the Water & Sewer Fund.
·   Mr. Thomas stated that insurance benefits for 17 retired employees total
$152,726.16.
·   Alderman Karn asked about raising rent on City boat slips. Mr. Thomas
stated that the work being performed is structural and safety, however it his
belief that the dock should be upgraded before implementing a rate increase.
Mayor Howard suggested this issue be referred to the Rate Review Committee.
·   Alderman Karn expressed concern about allocating monies from fund balance.
Mr. Thomas explained that revenues are budgeted conservatively and he does not
anticipate spending all monies budgeted. Of the $1.2 million budgeted, $700,000
with sound management practices will possibly be expended. He informed the
Board that $562,000 will be paid back to the general fund from the Water and
Sewer Fund that was borrowed to pay the Clean Water Management Trust Fund
Grant.
·   Alderman Adams suggested that a portion of the unused $70,000 budgeted for
overtime    last year be used to adjust employees pay. Mr. Thomas noted that he
will conduct a    salary and pay study this year with some funds to be
allocated for merit.
·   Other budgeted items referenced were monies for City Hall Renovations,
Capital Projects, Waterfront Study and resurfacing of tennis courts at Ft.
Johnston.
·   Mayor Howard expressed concern about the City growing internally and
providing incentives to attract people to live within the City limits.
Apprehension was expressed over limitations placed on Cities by the General
Assembly and not being able to expand through annexation.
·   City Manager Thomas informed the Board that there are some legal questions
concerning an opt out plan for health insurance for employees 65 years of age
and older; he will continue to look into this.
·   Electric Fund – The Board questioned the policy on hanging banners in the
City, who should be allowed, the cost and who authorizes banners. All agreed
that a Policy should be established by the City because the cost to hang
banners is included in Brunswick Electric’s contract.
·   Master plan for undergrounding discussed. Brunswick Electric will provide a
cost estimate.
·   Mayor Howard stated the City needs to maintain it parks, but noted the
Parks and Recreation budget is over $500,000. He asked about cost sharing some
of the programs with Brunswick County.
·   The Department of Tourism budget was discussed, Community Building and
projected revenues and the cost of part-time employees to maintain the
facility. For information, it was asked if the building could be contracted to
a private company.
·   Alderman Karn asked about public rest rooms and Mr. Thomas noted that these
are being considered in the capital project fund during renovation of city
buildings.
·   Alderman Coring stated the City Dock is among many needs in the City and
encouraged the Board to begin filling in the gaps. He cited sidewalk
connections as a problem particularly for disabled citizens with motorized
wheelchairs. Alderman Coring questioned the need for a new trailer mounted 25
kw generator for water and sewer for lift stations. He stated that the City has
an 80 kw that was initially purchased for emergencies located on a trailer
behind the old fire station.
   Mayor Howard asked the Board to continue review of the budget for further
comments during the next budget work session. Public Hearing on the budget will
be held June 14, 6:00 p.m. and after the meeting, a budget workshop.
   Meeting adjourned upon motion of Alderman Barnes, seconded by Alderman
Adams, vote carried.

   A. UDO Amendment – Ice Vending Machines
   Alderman Karn moved to adopt the resolution amending the Unified Development
Ordinance to add self service vending machines as a conditional use in the
Highway commercial and Business District, seconded by Alderman Powell. Motion
passed with 4 ayes, Alderman Karn, Coring, Powell and Mayor Howard. 3 noes,

AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE CITY OF SOUTHPORT
UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE, WITH RESPECT TO BASIC DEFINITIONS AND
INTERPRETATIONS, THE TABLE OF PERMITTED USES, AND CONDITIONAL USES, TO PERMIT
SELF SERVICE ICE VENDING MACHINES
WHEREAS the Planning Board of the City of Southport has considered and
communicated in writing its determination that the proposed amendment of the
Unified Development Ordinance to permit self-service ice vending machines is
consistent with the city’s comprehensive plan and any other applicable official
plans and has recommended approval of said amendment; and
WHEREAS the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport finds, pursuant to North
Carolina General Statute 160A-383 that the proposed UDO amendment is consistent
with an adopted comprehensive plan; and
WHEREAS the Board of Aldermen considers the proposed amendment to be reasonable
and in the public interest because it will promote orderly growth and
development and because appropriate regulation of the proposed use will promote
the public welfare; and
WHEREAS a public hearing on the proposed amendment of the Unified Development
Ordinance has been conducted, after proper notice as required by law;
BE IT ORDAINED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport, North
Carolina, that the Unified Development Ordinance of the City of Southport is
amended as follows:
Section 1. ARTICLE 2: BASIC DEFINITIONS AND INTERPRETATIONS
Section 2-2 “Definitions of Basic Terms” is amended by adding the following
definition in alphabetical sequence:
Self-Service Ice Vending Machine: A stand-alone ice production machine that may
operate without full time service personnel. These units are activated by the
insertion of money, credit cards, check cards, token, or similar means; ice is
bagged automatically or dispensed in bulk outside to the consumer. In addition
to site plan review by the Zoning Administrator, several permits and approvals
are required, including but not limited to electrical, plumbing, sewer
connection, and city business license. Health Department certification may be
required.
Section 2. ARTICLE 10: TABLE OF PERMITTED USES:
The Table of Permitted Uses is amended by adding “Self-Service Ice Vending
Machine”, and by placing a “C” entry in the BD (Business District) and HC
(Highway Commercial) columns.
Section 3. ARTICLE 12: ZONING & CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT APPROVAL
Section 12-19: Supplemental Regulations
“Regulations for Conditional Uses”, is amended by adding a new section, to be
inserted in alphabetical sequence, to read as follows:
Use: Self-Service Ice Vending Machine, Conditional Use, District: BD and HC
Self-Service Ice Vending Machine and Other Similar Uses. Where permitted, self-
service ice vending units, or other similar uses, shall comply with the
following minimum standards.
(a)    Self-service ice vending machines or other similar uses shall be an
accessory to an existing business or commercial entity in the Business District
(BD). Machines may be located as an accessory for convenience stores, car
washes, and marinas of twenty (20) boat slips or more.
(b)    Self-service ice vending machines or other similar uses may be located
in the Highway Commercial (HC) District as a stand-alone business.
(c)    Said units shall not be located in a residentially-zoned district.
(d)    No self-service ice vending machine or other similar use shall encroach
into the minimum required setback. Except where directly abutting an existing
business or commercial establishment, additional setbacks may be required if
deemed appropriate.
(e)    Architectural features of any self-service ice vending machine or other
similar
   use shall be complementary to existing development in the immediate area.
Building elevations shall be submitted with each application considered for
approval.
(f) The foundation of each unit shall be screened by skirting, lattice or
landscaping.
(g) Roof-mounted or other equipment on top of the unit shall be screened by a
parapet wall.
(h) Within 30 (thirty) calendar days of the closure or ceasing of operations of
any self-service ice vending unit or other similar use, all equipment and
incidentals shall be removed from the premises.
(i) Landscaping: Where a self-service ice vending machine or other similar use
is proposed as an accessory to an existing business location that has an
approved site plan on record with the Planning Director, skirting, lattice or
landscaping shall be provided around the foundation of the unit. If the
landscaping option is chosen, the planting of vegetation indigenous to the
immediate natural coastal ecosystem is preferred to promote proper plant life
development and maturation. A list of plants provided by the Brunswick County
Agricultural Extension Services as compatible to this planting zone and climate
are kept in the office of the Planning Director. While not all-inclusive, it
should be used as a guideline in selecting predominately coastal North Carolina
native species. Requirements of Article 18, Buffer Strips and Landscaping,
provisions of the City of Southport Unified Development Ordinance shall apply.
(j) Where a self-service ice vending machine or other similar use is proposed
adjacent to residentially zoned property, a buffer shall be installed according
to Article 18-1, Buffer Strips, in the City of Southport Unified Development
Ordinance.
(k) Access: Ingress and egress shall be located where such will not impede
pedestrian or vehicular traffic flow. The existing access or driveway of the
primary business shall be utilized, unless deemed inappropriate.
(l) Vehicle Parking and Stacking Lane. Four (4) standard parking spaces shall
be available on the site. In the design of the area around the self-service ice
vending machine, a provision will be made for the stacking of vehicles on the
property. The stacking area will be designed to avoid a backup of vehicles on
to the public right of way. The design standard for the stacking requirements
will include:
   (i) Required stacking lane shall be a minimum of eight feet wide by one
hundred fifty (150) feet long in total length with a vertical clearance of
fifteen (15) feet in order to accommodate full-size pickup trucks with boats on
trailers.
   (ii) The stacking lane shall be located on private property and as much as
possible to the rear or side of the lot. In no case shall a stacking lane be
arranged or located in any way that impedes off-site traffic movements on
adjacent public roadways.
 
Section 4. When provisions of this ordinance call for addition of new sections
in alphabetical sequence, the new provisions shall be numbered in sequence with
previous numbers and all succeeding provisions of a section shall be re-
numbered accordingly.
Section 5. This ordinance shall be effective upon its adoption.
   Adopted by the City of Southport Board of Aldermen in regular session, June
14, 2012.

                  Robert D. Howard, Mayor

sufficient notice.
   Alderman Adams moved to authorize the City Manager and City Attorney to work
with the State to draft a lease for five years with the option for automatic
renewal, seconded by Alderman Barnes, the vote of approval was unanimous.
   Grant Award: The City received notification of a grant award for a
pedestrian comprehensive plan in the amount of $24,800 with local match of
$6200. The grant will pay for the study of sidewalks and repairs.
   Summer Intern: City Manager Thomas introduced Mr. James Trey Burke, a
graduate student in the Master’s of Public Administration program at
Mississippi State University who has volunteered as a summer intern with the
City.
   Public Services Director: Mr. Robert Tucker was introduced as the new Public
Services Director and comes with extensive experience and background in
government.
XIV. Board Comments
    Proclamation: Alderman Poole moved, seconded by Alderman Barnes to adopt a
proclamation in recognition of the annual celebration held at the Alvin C.
Caviness Park June 16, 2012. Vote unanimous.
   Alderman Barnes welcomed Trey Burke, summer intern, and Robert Tucker, new
Public Services Director.
   Alderman Poole reiterated support for Southport Beat and commended Alderman
Karn for his work with the N.C. 4th of July Committee.
   Alderman Adams and Powell welcomed the summer intern and Public Services
Director.
   Alderman Coring welcomed the new employees and congratulated Officer Hinnant
on her advanced certificate. He commended the emergency services responders
over the weekend for their support and commended the response of the Rescue,
Fire and Police Department i.e. other volunteers during the fire this past
weekend.
   Alderman Karn encouraged the citizens’ indulgence during the filming of two
movies in the City. (Safe Haven, Mary & Martha)
RECESS – 7:47 p.m.
   Mayor Howard called the meeting back to order at 8:02 p.m. and proceeded to
open discussion on the proposed FY 2012-13 budget. Supplemental information was
presented by the City Manager. Mayor Howard reading from a prepared statement
asked the Board to join with him in directing the City Manager to reduce his
proposed budget by 15-16%. Mayor Howard stated using 16.6% ($674,650) from the
reserve funds, which is generally set aside for emergencies, major
infrastructure, repairs and replacement, does not present a balanced budget. He
proposed that the commitment be honored for waterfront improvements, City Hall
renovations and ambulance services. In order to accomplish this, the proposed
general operating budget requires some reductions. He noted that the citizens
would not tolerate a tax increase, therefore; cuts must occur in the general
fund operating costs.
   City Manager Thomas stated if the city was not undertaking a major building
renovation program; the budget would be close to zero because the remainder of
the amount that makes up the $674,650 of fund balance is primarily
contingencies and capital reserves. If the Board looks at balancing current
revenues against current operations, the budget is balanced. Major projects the
City may undertake would come from fund balance if other reserves are
maintained.
   Alderman Karn stated that the proposed budget include some contingency,
capital reserve funds, and capital projects. After reviewing the budget, it
will be a challenge to reduce 16%. Fund balance is used for major capital
projects as proposed. However, he does share concerns that the City continues
to spend from fund balance.
   Alderman Powell expressed his concern about the fund balance.
   Alderman Barnes stated the City should operate like a business and some cuts
are needed.
He cited the private sector making cutbacks and referenced the generous
employee benefit package i.e. insurance and the cost of providing this, which
equates to 40% in the budget.
   Mayor Howard expressed appreciation to staff and commended the City Manager
for compilation of the budget. He reiterated the need to streamline operations
and programs.
   Alderman Powell referenced aging buildings and non-compliance with ADA
regulations, the need for an elevator at City Hall, and possibly eliminating
positions to balance the budget.
   Alderman Adams questioned the Parks & Recreation budget totaling $500,000.
   Mayor Howard asked staff to revisit the budget. City Manager Thomas asked if
the Board was directing him to reduce the proposed budget by 15%. Mayor Howard
explained that this was a challenge from the Board and staff needs to know the
Board’s desire to cut the budget.   
   Alderman Adams stated the City Manager knows what the Board’s desire is and
directed the City Manager to make the cuts, Alderman Poole agreed.
   Alderman Coring stated cutting the budget 15% is too much and cautioned the
Board against reducing the budget. Alderman Coring asked Alderman Barnes to
explain how the City’s benefits are too generous. Alderman Barnes stated that
Brunswick County does not provide the level of benefits to its employees and
the City should be more in line with other municipalities and private
businesses.
   Alderman Adams stated that this should have been mentioned before the budget
was compiled, and this is the first time that he has heard about insurance
since the Board’s Retreat. Mayor Howard stated that this is possible because of
the time it takes to review documents after submittal by the City Manager.
   No further business, it was the consensus of the Board that the City Manager
revisits the budget and submit his recommendations at the June 21st meeting.
(5:30 p.m.)
   Meeting was adjourned upon motion of Alderman Barnes, seconded by Alderman
Adams. Vote unanimous.
                     _________________________________
                      Mayor

the invocation.

Lord Street satellite campus is expected to start June 25 with completion
within 180 days according to contractual obligations.

occupancy tax; no resolution at this time.

committee could affect the budget.

Ft. Johnston Museum Store.
Unanimous vote; motion carried 6-0.
IV.   New Business
Ft. Johnston Museum Store
   City Manager Thomas explained the operation of a Ft. Johnston Museum Store;
various products formerly sold at the Visitors Center from multiple non-
profits, individuals, etc. will be purchased at wholesale prices, put into
inventory and sold at a slight markup. Consistent with a recommendation from
the Ft. Johnston committee, Manager Thomas recommended appropriation of up to
$10,000 to purchase inventory. He estimated a $15,000 revenue.
   Alderman Barnes suggested establishing a separate fund for revenues of the
Museum Store to be used for improvements to the Garrison House. Alderman Karn
pointed out the agreement between the City and the National Parks Service
require any money generated be put back into the property. Manager Thomas
indicated the City exceeds the agreement requirements.
   Alderman Barnes moved, seconded by Alderman Karn to accept staff
recommendation for up to $10,000 to purchase inventory for the Museum Store.
Unanimous vote; motion carried 6-0.

responsibility of the Board.

presented and as submitted with a 15% reduction.

opinion cuts need to be made.

identify areas that could be cut.

City employees.

Manager.

SECTION X. TAX RATE
There is hereby levied, for fiscal year 2012-2013, a tax at the rate of $0.2456
on each one hundred dollars ($100) of assessed valuation of property located
within the Town of Southport for the purpose of raising revenue in the General
Fund.
SECTION XI. BUDGET OFFICER AUTHORITY
The City Manager (Budget Officer) is hereby authorized to transfer
appropriations within a fund and between funds under the following terms:
 
A.   He may transfer amounts between objects of expenditures (line items)
within a departmental appropriation.
B.   He may transfer amounts between appropriations within the same fund,
provided that a report of such transfers shall be made no later than the next
regular financial report to the Board of Aldermen.
C.   He may approve un-budgeted inter-fund transfers, up to $5,000, provided
that a report of such transfers shall be made no later than the next regular
financial report to the Board of Aldermen.
D.   He may transfer and/or utilize appropriations contained in contingency
appropriations within a fund (except for contingency amounts within the
governing board appropriation) or in emergency fund appropriations.
E.   He may authorize temporary transfers of cash among funds as necessary to
meet cash flow needs.
F.   He may transfer funds from capital reserve funds, up to $20,000 per
purpose, to meet current needs for the purpose for which such funds are being
held in reserve, provided that a report of such transfers shall be made no
later than the next regular financial report to the Board of Aldermen.
 
All other transfers of funds between appropriations or budget funds shall be
accomplished by Board amendment of this ordinance.
SECTION XII. CONTINUING AUTHORIZATION
Previously-adopted capital project budgets, grant project budgets, and special
reserve funds are hereby re-authorized, and revenues and appropriations made
for all such funds shall remain authorized on an ongoing basis until such
projects are completed and/or all funds are utilized. At the conclusion of such
capital projects or grant projects, any residual, unexpended local funds shall
be transferred to the general government or enterprise fund with which the
project is associated.
SECTION XIII. BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION
This ordinance and the supporting budget document shall be the basis of the
financial plan for the City of Southport municipal government for the 2012-2013
fiscal year. The budget officer shall administer the budget and shall insure
that the finance officer and department heads of the city are provided with
sufficient guidance to properly implement this plan. Copies of the budget
ordinance shall be furnished to the city manager and the finance officer for
their use and direction in the disbursement of funds and to the city clerk for
the official records of the city.
SECTION XIV. ADOPTION
This ordinance has been adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in special
session on June 25, 2012, upon the motion of Alderman Nelson Adams and the
second of Alderman Mary Ellen Poole , with a vote of 5 ayes and 1 no and shall
be effective July 1, 2012.

IV. Risk Management Policy – Cannon Firing
   Mayor Howard informed the Board of a complaint from a Wilmington resident
that the cannon shooting over Memorial Day Weekend damaged his hearing. The
cannon belongs to the Southport Historical Society and the City Manager is
determining if in fact, this would come under the City’s liability insurance
since it was discharged from City property. Mr. Thomas developed proposed
policies for review regarding future cannon firings to protect the City.
   Alderman Karn called for a point of order stating that this matter was not
on the agenda. Mayor Howard noted that the Clerk posted a special meeting
notice, which included this item, and he will allow the matter to be heard for
information.   
   Alderman Coring asked if the Board would receive public comments. Mayor
Howard stated the Board would receive information because this could result in
a lawsuit.
   Alderman Adams cautioned the Board to be careful regarding statements until
consultation with the City Attorney.
   Alderman Barnes asked if the Southport Historical Society was contacted. Mr.
Thomas stated since the alleged incident occurred on City property, the
Historical Society was not contacted by the individual.
   City Manager Thomas told the Board after Memorial Day, the City received a
claim of injury from an individual who said his hearing was damaged because of
proximity to the cannon “Thor” and his injury has been medically verified. Upon
learning of this, he researched risk management policies of other organizations
for use of muzzled loading artillery. There are at least three different civil
war artillery organizations with public information about safety procedures.
The State of North Carolina has a policy for state park sites. The North
Carolina League of Municipalities’, which is the City’s Insurance Carrier, does
not cover this type of situation. Mr. Paul Miller, the NCLM Risk Management
Specialist, discussed various measures to protect the City’s interest and made
recommendations.
·   Permit/permission for firing weapons on city property
·   Weapons discharged at specified locations
·   Visible and marked safety perimeter around the cannon
·   General liability insurance provided by those involved with the cannon,
minimum of $1 million dollars with the City named as an additional insured.
·   Desirable to have hold harmless indemnification agreement
·   Audible and posted warnings of an impending firing around the location
   Mr. Thomas affirmed that he contacted a member form the Historical Society
to inquire about insurance and procedures. He produced a draft policy for Board
consideration, which incorporate some of the recommendations from the Risk
Management Specialist.
   Alderman Adams stated that the City should be notified of any cannon firings
and permits required.
   Mayor Howard asked that this matter be placed on the July agenda and the
City Manager to report on insurance.
V.   Safe Haven Movie Production
   Mayor Howard told the Board about concerns addressed to him from residents
in the Yacht Basin area about plans by the movie Safe Haven to burn the general
store. He stated that they are supportive of the movie, but concerned about the
proximity of a large oak tree and some of the homes. He realize that
representatives from the special effects department met with the Fire Chief and
other City officials to discuss their plans; however, he asked that a
representative from the Film Company attend the July 12 meeting to discuss this
issue.
VI. Adjournment – 7:00 p.m.
   Meeting adjourned upon motion of Alderman Powell, seconded by Alderman
Poole. Vote unanimous.

RESOLUTION OF APPRECIATION
WHEREAS, Southport, North Carolina is the official home of the N.C. Fourth of
July Festival; and
WHEREAS, Independence Day is the anniversary of the day on which the
Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Continental Congress on July 4,
1776; and
WHEREAS, the community of Southport has celebrated our nation’s independence
for over 200 years, and
WHEREAS, the community festival was incorporated in 1972 as the N.C. Fourth of
July Festival; and
WHEREAS, the festival has grown from a community affair to be recognized over
the State of North Carolina; and
WHEREAS, it is estimated that the North Carolina Fourth of July Festival brings
in approximately 50,000 visitors annually, and
WHEREAS, staging a festival of this magnitude could not be accomplished without
the Fourth of July Executive Committee, President, Committee Chairpersons and
the hundreds of volunteers, support of businesses, government and the
community.
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED,  I, Mayor Robert D. Howard, and the Southport
Board of Aldermen commend the N. C. 4th of July Festival Committee and its many
volunteers for its dedicated work for an outstanding 2012 Fourth of July
Celebration with parade, games, veteran’s recognition, naturalization ceremony,
flag retirement, freedom run/walk, craft shows firemen’s competition and
fireworks.
ADOPTED, this 12th day of July.

VIII.   Old Business
   1) Maritime Museum Lease Extension
   City Manager Thomas stated at the Board’s June 14 regular meeting, he
reported that the two-year concession agreement for the use of city property
for the Maritime Museum was expiring. The Friends of the Museum asked that the
agreement be renewed for a ten-year period, and the NC Department of Cultural
Resources expressed support for a ten year extension. The National Park Service
has also indicated that it has no objection to the ten-year extension of the
agreement.
   The Board voted to authorize the City Manager and the City Attorney to work
with the State to prepare a proposed new lease for five years with an option
for automatic renewal for an additional five years.
   Following the Board’s action, the City received a letter from the Friends of
the Museum asking that the Board reconsider its decision and allow a ten-year
lease extension.
   Mr. Thomas advised that State law provides that property owned by a City may
be leased for up to ten years if the governing board determines that the
property will not be needed by the city for the term of the lease (GS 160A-272
(a)). Leases of property must be authorized by a governing board resolution at
a regular board meeting following ten days published public notice. The notice
must describe the property, state the proposed lease payments, and announce the
board’s intent to authorize the lease at its meeting.
   Alderman Adams moved, seconded by Alderman Poole to grant the ten-year lease
extension to the Maritime Museum. The vote of approval was unanimous. (Copy of
Lease Incorporated, Attachment #1)
IX.   New Business
   1) Rescue Squad Ambulance Acquisition
    City Manager Thomas in his overview to the Board stated approval of the
Emergency Services Committee report regarding the Rescue Squad included the
acquisition of a new ambulance in FY 2012, with the acquisition to be financed
that would delay the initial payments until FY 13-14 and financing over a five-
year period.
   The Rescue Squad reviewed different options for purchase of a new ambulance
and believe the most cost-effective and expeditious option for acquiring a new
quality ambulance is to utilize the “piggy-backing exception.”
   State law (GS 143-129(g)) allows a local government to waive the bidding
process if determined, that it is in its best interests to do so and if another
unit of federal, state, or North Carolina local government has conducted a
public, formal bid process substantially similar to the process normally
required for the purchase of apparatus, supplies, materials, or equipment that
costs $90,000 or more. This “piggybacking exception” may be used if the
supplier is willing to furnish the item at the same or more favorable prices,
terms, and conditions as those provided to the other unit or agency.
   In order to utilize this bidding process exception, the purchase must be
approved by the governing body at a regularly scheduled meeting after at least
10 days published notice that a waiver of the bid procedure will be considered.
   The Rescue Squad Auxiliary has indicated its willingness to cover the cost
of transferring the radio equipment to the new unit and of purchasing and
installing a new Marvlis communications system in the ambulance.
   The Rescue Squad inspected the Taylor Made equipment and recommends that the
City purchase a Type III ambulance from Taylor Made – a 170-inch module on a
GMC G4500 diesel chassis – as set forth in the base bid, specifications, terms,
and conditions in the Davidson County bid, as well as the configuration options
specified by the Southport squad (which are detailed in the company’s
proposal).
   Alderman Coring moved, seconded by Alderman Barnes to accept the
recommendation of the Emergency Services Committee and to (a) advertise the
prospective acquisition of a Type III ambulance from Taylor Made Ambulance
based on waiver of the bid process as permitted by North Carolina law, (b)
authorize the finance director to pursue financing options for purchase of the
ambulance, and (c) and authorize the budget officer to prepare the necessary
budget amendment to appropriate funding (from the financing) for the purchase.
Vote: Unanimous.
   (Approval of the purchase and budget amendment will be on the August agenda)

RISK MANAGEMENT AND SAFETY POLICY
MUZZLE-LOADING ARTILLERY
CITY OF SOUTHPORT, NORTH CAROLINA
A. Purposes
The purposes of this policy are (a) to protect the safety of persons and
property and (b) to minimize the financial risk to the residents and taxpayers
of the City of Southport from the use of muzzle-loading artillery on municipal
property.
B. Application
This policy applies to the use of muzzle-loading artillery on all properties
owned or under the control of the City of Southport, including municipal
rights-of-way and easements (all, hereinafter, “city property”).
C. Requirements
Any person or organization that wishes to discharge muzzle-loading artillery on
a municipal property, right-of-way, or easement shall comply with the following
requirements.
1. Permission. Permits for use and discharge of the artillery must be granted
in writing by a municipal staff member with responsibility for supervision of
the site. The approving city official shall be responsible for providing these
requirements in writing to the owner of the artillery or his/her/its
representative and shall be responsible for insuring that the insurance and
indemnification requirements of this policy are met. No fees shall be charged
for such permits unless approved by the Board of Aldermen, and permits may be
issued at one time to covered multiple specific dates and locations.
2. Locations. Use and discharge of muzzle-loading artillery may take place only
in locations approved by a municipal staff member with responsibility for the
affected site. Locations selected and approved for this purpose shall be
selected to minimize the risk to spectators and bystanders.
3. Qualifications and Procedures. Persons involved in the discharge of muzzle-
loading artillery on city property must have received appropriate education,
training, and certification from the National Civil War Artillery Association,
the American Artillery Association, The American Civil War Society, the
Continental Line, or a similar nationally-recognized organized association that
issues operating procedures and safety standards for the use of muzzle-loading
artillery. The instructions and operating procedures of the applicable
organizations shall be used at all times in preparation for- and the firing of
muzzle-loading artillery on city property, provided that, if any provisions of
this policy establish more stringent requirements, they shall prevail.
4. Spectator Safety. The crew of the muzzle-loading artillery shall be
responsible for the following safety measures in association with the discharge
of the gun:
a. Safety Zone. A spectator safety zone shall be established that does not
allow spectators within 50 feet of the gun on any side and which extends at
least 100 feet wide for a distance of 100 yards in front of the muzzle. The
safety perimeter shall be clearly and visibly marked by cones, rope, or tape,
or similar delineation, and a safety officer or officers associated with the
gun crew shall police the perimeter to prevent spectator entry within the
safety zone prior to the discharge of the gun. No persons except members of the
gun crew shall be allowed within the safety zone during the discharge of the
gun.
b. Warning. The gun crew shall issue a clearly audible warning to spectators
and other persons around the safety perimeter, indicating that loud noise may
accompany the discharge, immediately prior to the discharge of the gun.
5. Insurance and Indemnification. The owner of the muzzle-loading artillery
shall provide the City with evidence of general liability insurance, covering
damage to persons or property, for the use of the muzzle-loading artillery,
with coverage of at least $1 million per incident and with the City listed as
an additional insured. The owner shall also provide the City with a written
statement, provided or approved by the City, indemnifying and holding harmless
the City from any responsibility or liability for allowing the discharge of the
muzzle loading artillery on city property.
Adopted by the City of Southport Board of Aldermen, July 12, 2012.

   1.   North Howe Street Rezoning

receive public comments on rezoning North Howe Street from 12th Street and the
area between 1427 and 1430 North Howe from highway commercial to business
district upon recommendation of the Planning Board. He stated that the Planning
Board believes the character of this area is related to that of the business
district. Alderman Barnes, Planning Board liaison stated support of the
rezoning because it will allow more diversity and consistency. Alderman Poole,
Planning Board liaison acknowledged that the Planning Board did a good job and
suggested a Public Hearing be held in September to receive additional public
input. Alderman Adams concurred. Mayor Howard asked the City Manager to
advertise for a Public Hearing at the September meeting.
   2.   Transportation Planning – Regional Affiliation
   City Manager Thomas briefed the Board on the city’s transportation planning
affiliation and whether or not the city wishes to remain with the rural
planning organization that is staffed by a COG member or to affiliate with one
of the Metropolitan Planning Organizations, Grand Strand (Myrtle Beach) or
Wilmington. He explained that after the 2010 census, boundaries of metropolitan
areas changed and the Federal Highway Administration planning areas for urban
transportation planning. Southport is situated between two Transportation
Management Areas (urbanized with population of 215,000+) Grand Strand and
Wilmington, but not in the boundaries of either. He stated if the Board wishes
to affiliate with one of the Metropolitan Planning Organizations, there is no
guarantee that they will accept the City. Rural Planning Organizations were
created by the State to encourage transportation planning for rural areas, but
receive no State or Federal funding. He stated that the Transportation
Management Areas and Metropolitan Planning Organizations receive direct funding
for planning and construction through the Federal Highway Administration. In
discussion with the Board, he stated Southport and other communities in the
“optional” areas would need to advise the nearby Transportation Metropolitan
Organizations (Grand Strand or Wilmington) whether the City is interested in
joining them. If the urban clusters in the “optional areas” do not express an
interest in becoming a part of a Transportation Metropolitan Area, they will
remain members of the Rural Planning Organization. City Manager Thomas stated
in attending a meeting with the southeastern towns and the Grand Strand MPO,
the towns were leaning towards the Wilmington Metropolitan Planning Area if NC
211, 133 and 87 could be included. If not, they will remain with the Rural
Transportation Planning Organization. Mayor Howard stated the communities
should join together, if not, it might not be feasible. Alderman Powell stated
Southport should make its own decision, and in his opinion; Southport should
lean towards Wilmington because the greater the population, the more money to
be received. City Manager Thomas explained that the TMA is based on the
population from the 2010 census and if Southport is added as an optional area,
they will not get additional funding until the next census. Alderman Barnes
asked if the City joins an MPO, is funding guaranteed. Mr. Thomas stated that
he was advised that any member of the MPO would be given equal consideration.
Alderman Coring encouraged the City to be cautious before making a decision.
Alderman Adams stated that Southport should be a leader and make a decision
based on the best interest of Southport. Mayor Howard stated in this situation,
it is all or none, because they do not have to accept Southport; he wanted to
get input from the Board on what direction to proceed. The Board agreed that
City staff continue to attend meetings, work with other communities and report
to the Board.
   3.   Community Recycling Program – Potential Service Changes
   City Manager Thomas explained that the City currently provides recycling bi-
weekly for $2.20 per month. The current container capacity is eight gallons,
which is too small for some households. He communicated that several towns in
the County have converted to the 96-gallon roll out carts and Waste Industries
has offered to convert recycling in Southport for an additional $1.45 per month
for each residence. The Board agreed to hold a Public Hearing at the September
meeting because there is additional cost and some households do not recycle.
(Possible action to be taken after the hearing)
   4.   Legislative Policy Proposals (NCLM)
   The North Carolina League of Municipalities requested proposals from
municipalities to include in their legislative policy program, which is a guide
that the League uses to advocate in the General Assembly. City Manager Thomas
presented the following for consideration: 1) Legislation to amend G.S. 160A-
299 to allow retention of easement rights other than utility easements if it
elects to close a street. 2) If the League elects not to include the proposed
statutory revision in its advocacy program, the City should seek sponsorship
from its own legislators to amend G.S. 160-299, procedures for permanently
closing streets and alleys. Mr. Thomas explained currently, if a dead end
street is closed, the right of way is divided 50/50 between adjoining property
owners at no cost to them. The general assembly provided for only utility
easements. City Manager Thomas used for an example green space, bike paths, on
closed streets and under the law, the City would not be allowed to keep the
street. The proposal is to request the General Assembly to seek an amendment of
G.S. 160A-299 to allow cities to retain easements other than utility easements
if a street or a portion thereof is closed. Mayor Howard stated there is a need
for greenways and walking trails. The current law gives advantage to property
owners who may be on either side of a public right of way and he supports the
recommendation. Alleys were referenced including the situation on Hankinsville
Road. The Board concurred to add this item to the September agenda .
   Mayor Howard referenced the bill discussed with Senator Rabon to add an
additional two cents occupancy tax to be earmarked for waterfront improvements.
   5.   Waterfront Improvement Plan – Project Development
   City Manager Thomas requested the Board consider a plan of action for
waterfront development and gave each member a copy of a project design for
review. He asked the Board for objectives; formulate a plan, with an approach
for development. The process he presented included public input from a Plan
Advisory Committee, which would be made up of stakeholders with knowledge of
the waterfront while giving the entire community the opportunity to have some
input. Mayor Howard noted that previous plans have been developed, but not
implemented. The Board appropriated $50,000 in this year’s budget for a
waterfront improvement plan, contingent upon a dollar for dollar grant match,
which he said should be announced soon. Mayor Howard appointed a committee
comprised of Aldermen Poole as
Chair, Aldermen Adams, Coring, City Manager and himself to serve on a
Waterfront Committee to develop an implementation plan for the September
meeting.
Alderman Barnes stated that the City should move forward with a plan because of
the waterfront being one of the City’s best economic resources. Alderman Poole
referenced the ecological and erosion concerns. Alderman Karn stated that the
groundwork is needed to develop a final plan for grant review. Alderman Coring
questioned the area for improvements. Mayor Howard acknowledged that no formal
areas were identified, but Kinglsey to the Yacht Basin (including the Bay
Street bank property) will be considered.
   6.   Building Improvements Program – Project Development
   City Manager Thomas in a handout to the Board presented a schematic design
while stating that a structural cost analysis is needed i.e. estimates. He
presented cost estimates performed by Stewart Mulford Cost Estimating.
Estimates were also presented from Clancy & Theys. He stated due to the several
roof lines of the fire/rescue building on Nash Street, it was suggested that
the City might consider some new construction, which would be cheaper than some
of the renovations. Mr. Thomas explained that the cost estimates are
preliminary. (Cost estimates on file with the City Manager) He recommended
proposals be submitted for architectural services, while recognizing the work
of Connie Keller’s design of floor plans. He explained that the City needs
architectural expertise to move forward with the design development and
construction administration. He recommended that the Board tour the buildings
to get a sense of the condition of the facilities and encouraged flexibility
about decisions through the process i.e. adjustments and engineering. City
Manager Thomas recommended request for proposals be submitted for architectural
services i.e. securing financing for the project. The City Hall roof, window
replacements, public restrooms were cited as projects that the City could begin
while securing financing. Mayor Howard appointed Alderman Powell, Chair and
Alderman Adams to work with the City Manager to move the project forward and a
work session scheduled in September.

PROCLAMATION
WHEREAS, the City of Southport has been a major fishing village and a center
for recreational boating since being chartered as Smithville in 1792; and
WHEREAS, the Southport Wooden Boat Show is a celebration of our heritage and
community pride bringing people of all ages together for festivities from the
Greater Southport area and throughout the Southeastern United States; and
WHEREAS, Southport and Brunswick County were home to many wooden boat builders
which provided employment and revenue to their communities, and which created
boats many of which endure today; and
WHEREAS, Downtown Southport, Inc. and the SWBS Committee will host the 3rd
annual Southport Wooden Boat Show at the Old Yacht Basin in Southport on
Saturday, September 29, 2012
WHEREAS, boats will be displayed in and around the historic Old Yacht Basin;
and
WHEREAS, visitors can meet and talk with wooden boat builders and owners.
NOW THEREFORE, I, Robert D. Howard, Mayor of the City of Southport and on
behalf of the Southport Board of Aldermen do hereby proclaim Saturday,
September 29, 2012 as
SOUTHPORT WOODEN BOAT DAY
in Southport, North Carolina.
S/Robert D. Howard, Mayor

   3) Resolution – Surplus Property Disposition
   City Manager Thomas presented a resolution prescribing procedures for
disposal of surplus property. He explained that State law allows cities to use
an administrative process to dispose of items by private sale that can be
handled locally or by the use of online sites such as govdeals.com. Items of
higher value will be disposed of by sealed bids or auctions, and those items
valued $10,000 or higher will be reported to the Board. Alderman Karn moved to
adopt the resolution, seconded by Alderman Powell.  Discussion: Alderman Adams
asked about the status of the case backhoe and the cost to re-furbish. Mr.
Tucker stated the backhoe is in poor condition, and has been stripped of parts
to use on other equipment. Due to the age and condition, he does not believe
that it is a worthy venture to repair. The vote of approval was unanimous.
A RESOLUTION PRESCRIBING PROCEDURES
FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS PERSONAL PROPERTY
   WHEREAS North Carolina General Statute 160A-266(a) and (b) authorizes cities
to dispose of personal property valued at less than $30,000 for any one item or
group of similar items by private negotiation and sale; and
   WHEREAS North Carolina General Statute 160A-266(c) provides that a city
governing board may adopt regulations prescribing procedures for disposing of
personal property valued at less than $30,000 for any one item or group of
similar items, provided that such regulations are designed to secure for the
city the fair market value of the property and accomplish the disposal
efficiently and effectively; and
   WHEREAS NCGS 160A-266(c) further provides that the governing board may
authorize one or more city officials to declare surplus any personal property
valued at less than $30,000, to set its fair market value, and to convey title
to the property for the city, provided that such official shall maintain proper
records of such transactions; and
   WHEREAS NCGS 160A-266(d) allows cities to discard any personal property that
is determined to have no value, that remains unsold or unclaimed after the city
has exhausted efforts to sell the property, or that poses a potential threat to
public health or safety;
WHEREAS the City of Southport has, from time to time, personal property for
which it no longer has a need and considers to be surplus, as well as personal
property that has been determined to have no value, that remains unsold or
unclaimed after sale efforts, or that may pose a threat to public health or
safety;
BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport as follows:
1. The city manager is authorized to declare surplus any personal property
valued at less than $30,000 for any one item or group of similar items, to set
its fair market value, and to convey title to the property for the city, by
public or private sale or exchanges. Surplus property is (a) property that is
no longer needed for the conduct of City business and/or (b) property whose
disposal would, based on sound property management principles and financial
considerations, be in the best interests of the City.
2. Prior to disposition of any individual item of property valued at more than
$10,000, the city manager shall report such proposed disposal to the Board of
Aldermen.
3. The city manager may employ any method or methods that he/she considers to
be the most appropriate, effective means of soliciting fair market offers for
the surplus personal property, and that will accomplish the disposal
efficiently and economically. Such methods may include on-line, electronic
listings or auctions of property.
4. The surplus property shall be sold to the party who tenders the highest
offer or shall be exchanged for any property or services useful to the City, if
greater value may be obtained in that manner.
5. The city manager shall maintain or cause to be maintained proper records of
such transactions, including a general description of the property, the name of
the person to whom it was sold or with whom it was exchanged, and the amount of
money or other consideration received.
6. If no offers are received within a reasonable time, the city manager may
retain the property for the City, may obtain any reasonably available salvage
value, or may cause the property to be disposed of as waste material.
7. The city manager may approve the discarding of any personal property that is
determined to have no value, that remains unsold or unclaimed after the city
has exhausted efforts to sell the property, or that poses a potential threat to
public health or safety;
8. This policy shall become effective upon its adoption.
   Adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in regular session, August 9,
2012.
                                           S/Robert D. Howard, Mayor

S/Regina Alexander, City Clerk

very activities which are attracted to it. The numerous events which create a
fairground atmosphere with tents, vendors, and masses of visitors have stressed
the Live Oaks and other trees, shrubs and what little grass is left by
compacting the soil, badly damaging the tree roots, and in general, trampling
the park. After meeting with Alderman Potter and Heather Hemphill, Director of
Southport Parks and Recreation, it was determined that immediate action needs
to be taken to relocate the large events to another location in Southport.”
   RECOMMENDATIONS:
   a.   SOLUTION - The solution is twofold.
      ·   Immediate actions need to be taken to relocate the large events to
another location in Southport.
      ·   The park needs to be brought back to its use as a quiet retreat
during the large events, and a park for smaller events such as musical
performances, plays, movies, weddings, and to be used by individuals and
families.
   b.   EXECUTION - Execution is twofold
      ·   Determine which new location is best. Two options are across the
sidewalk and around the Franklin Square Gallery or down on Bay Street between
Atlantic and Howe Streets, along with Waterfront Park, and even carefully on
the Garrison lawn. People come to Southport because of the waterfront. Utilize
it to its fullest potential.
      ·   Develop a plan for Franklin Square utilizing the band shell and
benches, re-establish the original walks, emphasize the natural beauty, add
azaleas and camellias where needed, create a plan to protect and preserve the
live oaks. Emphasize small gatherings and events, individual visitors and
families.

Recreation Department determine what must be done to accomplish this. Then each
event organizer must be contacted and explained why the location of their event
has changed.

assist and direct this are Southport Tourism and Economic Development, Downtown
Southport Inc., Southport Forestry Committee and Southport Beautification
Committee

      AN ORDINANCE REZONING 39 PARCELS IN THE N. HOWE STREET AREA
FROM HIGHWAY COMMERCIAL (HC) to BUSINESS DISTRICT (BD)
WHEREAS North Carolina General Statute 160A-383 requires that zoning
regulations shall be made in accordance with a comprehensive plan; and
WHEREAS NCGS 160A-383 requires that, when adopting or rejecting any zoning
amendment, the governing board shall approve a statement describing whether its
action is consistent with an adopted comprehensive plan and any other
officially adopted plan that is applicable, and briefly explain why the board
considers the action taken to be reasonable and in the public interest; and
WHEREAS the Planning Board recommended at its May 17, 2012, meeting that the
zoning classification of a 39-lot area along both sides of Howe Street between
Twelfth Street and 1427/1430 N. Howe Street should be changed from Highway
Commercial (HC) to Business District (BD); and
WHEREAS the Planning Board conducted on July 19 a public meeting, with notice
to affected property owners, regarding the proposed rezoning in order to
provide information and solicit comments regarding the proposed rezoning; and
WHEREAS a public hearing on the proposed zoning has been conducted on the
proposed zoning changes, after published notice and mailed notice to property
owners as required by law; and
WHEREAS the proposed rezoning is partially consistent with the City’s CAMA Core
Land Use Plan (2007), which projects future Heavy Commercial, Office &
Institutional, and Multi-Family use of the affected area; and
WHEREAS the Board of Aldermen find the proposed rezoning to be reasonable and
in the public interest because the character of the area is more closely
related to that of the Business District (BD) than to the Highway Commercial
district and the dimensional requirements of the Business District will allow
greater utilization of lot areas;
      NOW, THERFORE, BE IT ORDAINED by the City of Southport:
Section 1. The Official Zoning Map of the City of Southport, an element of the
Unified Development Ordinance of the City, is amended by changing the zoning
classification of the below-described properties, as well as the immediately
abutting street rights-of-way areas, from Highway Commercial (HC) to Business
District (BD).
Thirty-nine parcels along the east and west sides of the Howe Street from 12th
Street north to 1427/1430 North Howe Street identified by the following
Brunswick County property numbers, and as shown on Attachment A, “Howe Street
Rezoning”:
Properties along the East side of Howe Street:

   D. Waste Container Placement License
        1. License Approval
   City Manager Thomas informed the Board of complaints related to a dumpster
in the City right of way on the north side of Bay Street which is used by a
restaurant and motel, but is in a highly visible location adjacent to
pedestrian routes that could serve as parking.
   The City Code (Section 16-8) prohibits creation of hazardous conditions and
safety hazards that interfere with persons or vehicle passage in rights-of-way,
as well as the obstruction of “lawful parking” within the public right-of-way.
This provision does not necessarily limit the City in designating which
portions of the right-of-way are available for parking and which portions will
be used for other purposes (such as sidewalks, drainage, signs, landscaping,
utilities, or other purposes).
   Discussions were held with the property owners and the dumpster (a) had been
placed in at least two locations in the past, which also proved to be
undesirable. (b) There were no reasonable and desirable locations for placement
of the dumpster on private property, and (c) the only potential location for
the dumpster that would likely be less objectionable, is on municipal right-of-
way in another location. The property owners agreed that they would be willing
to properly enclose the dumpster if the City permitted the dumpster to be
placed in that location which is on the west side of the motel in the corner of
the area near the pilot’s tower. Manager Thomas recommended the following:
1)       Amend Section 16-8 of the City Code to allow approval of right-of-way
use licenses.
2)       Approval of a license (in writing) to place the dumpster in the
selected location, provided that an enclosure for the dumpster is constructed
in accordance with requirements specified by the City.
3)       The adoption of a policy that would establish a framework for
consideration of similar situations in the future.
   Alderman Barnes questioned the proposed location of placing the dumpster in
front of another person’s property. Mr. Thomas stated that it is unoccupied
residential property which is on city right of way, but would eliminate a
parking space.
1) Amendment to Section 16-8 of the City Code.
   Mayor Howard asked for comments on the proposed amendment to the City
Ordinance and asked that the words “or as authorized by a license issued by the
Board of Aldermen”  be included.
   Alderman Powell moved to amend Section 16-8 of the City Code, Obstruction of
public rights of way and add in subsection “b” “or as authorized by a license
issued by the Board of Aldermen.” The motion died for the lack of a second.
   Alderman Karn stated that it is the responsibility of the property owner to
place dumpsters in a place that is out of public right of way and he does not
believe that the Board should set a precedent in helping businesses solve their
problems.
   Mayor Howard stated that the City should assist businesses and he requested
the City Manager and staff look at this situation with property owners to
determine if there was a suitable location on private property that would
accommodate the dumpster. He acknowledged his support of the recommendation and
stated only the Board of Aldermen can allow an exception.
   In answer to a question posed by Alderman Karn, City Manager Thomas
acknowledged that he looked at other areas along Bay Street, which is needed
parking. The area at the end of the motel, which was used in the past resulted
in an undesirable situation with customers being in close proximity to the
dumpster. The area at the east of the restaurant places the dumpster in the
water view, and will take up parking. He looked for the least objectionable
location. Alderman Powell noted that the location was changed because of large
trucks needing access to dump the container.
   Alderman Coring stated that people live across the street and questioned the
proposed location and if the tenants had been contacted. He also noted that the
current dumpster has an impact on the live oak tree. Alderman Barnes stated his
support of wanting to help businesses, but taking a dumpster from someone’s
property to place it in front of another’s property would be setting a
precedent, and questioned why it cannot be placed in front of the motel in an
enclosure where it was previously. Mayor Howard asked if the Board wished to
take further action on this matter.
   Alderman Karn suggested staff look for an alternative location. City Manager
Thomas stated parking spaces are on city right of way and permission will be
required from the city.
   Attorney Isenberg stated in order to grant a license, the right of way use
policy and amendment to Section 16-8 should be adopted. If adopted, this does
not require the Board to grant a license.
Alderman Powell restated the motion to amend Section 16-8 of the City Code and
to adopt the right of way licensing policy, motion seconded by Alderman Barnes.
The votes were 2 ayes, Aldermen Powell, Barnes and 3 nays, Aldermen Karn,
Coring and Poole. Motion failed.

   F. Regional Transportation Planning Affiliation
   City Manager Thomas explained that following the 2010 census, the Federal
Highway Administration’s planning areas for urban transportation planning have
changed. Southport now lies between two Transportation Management Areas
(urbanized areas with populations of 215,000+), but not actually within the
boundaries of either. Instead, Southport and its adjoining communities are in
an area called an “urban cluster” that could potentially be included in one of
these TMAs by mutual consent of the transportation planning organization and
the affected community. The TMA that is closest to Southport includes
Wilmington and the rest of New Hanover County, the Leland-Belville-Navassa
area, and southern Pender County.
   Southport and a number of other small communities in Brunswick County are
currently members of a Rural Planning Organization (RPO) for transportation
that is coordinated by the Cape Fear Council of Governments. RPOs were created
by the State to encourage transportation planning for rural areas, but receive
limited state funding (about $100,000 in the Pender-Brunswick-Columbus region).
Transportation Management Areas receive significantly greater funding for both
planning and construction through the Federal Highway Administration. The
Wilmington Transportation Management Area is expected to receive a major boost
in funding – to about $3 million per year – after being upgraded from an MPO to
a TMA.
   Southport and other communities in the southeastern Brunswick urban cluster
will need to advise the Wilmington TMA whether they desire to be included in
the TMA or remain within the RPO. If affiliation with the TMA is desired, the
TMA would decide whether to accept the community. If the urban clusters in the
“optional areas” do not express an interest in becoming part of a TMA and/or
are not accepted, they would remain members of the Rural Planning Organization.
   At the August 6 meeting, the Southport Traffic and Transportation Committee
recommended that the City pursue potential affiliation with the Wilmington TMA.
   Alderman Powell moved, seconded by Alderman Karn to adopt the succeeding
resolution to pursue participation in the Wilmington Metropolitan Planning
Organization (soon to be designated the Wilmington Transportation Management
Area), provided that NC 133 and NC 87 are included in the planning area
boundary. Vote unanimous.
A RESOLUTION SUPPORTING PARTICIPATION
IN THE WILMINGTON TRANSPORTATION MANAGEMENT AREA
WHEREAS the Federal Highway Administration designates urban transportation
planning areas and provides significant funding to support transportation
planning within those areas; and
WHEREAS the 2010 Census will result in the Wilmington Metropolitan Planning
Organization being upgraded to a Transportation Management Area and will
significantly increase its resources; and
WHEREAS Southport and several other southeastern Brunswick County
municipalities are located within an “urban cluster” that lies in very close
proximity to the boundaries of the Wilmington Transportation Management Area;
and
WHEREAS Southport and its neighboring municipalities have close economic,
cultural, and transportation connections to the Wilmington area; and
WHEREAS the Wilmington Transportation Management Area must resolve, in the near
future, the boundaries of its planning area; and
WHEREAS the Southport Traffic and Transportation Committee has recommended that
the City of Southport pursue inclusion in the Wilmington Transportation
Management Area; and
WHEREAS participation in the Wilmington Transportation Management Area is
appropriate only if the two principal transportation arteries – NC 87 and NC
133 – that connect southeastern Brunswick County to the Wilmington area are
included within the planning area;
BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport that the City
should request inclusion and appropriate representation in the Wilmington
Transportation Management Area, provided that the boundary of the
transportation planning area includes NC 87 and NC 133.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the City of Southport invites and encourages the
City of Boiling Spring Lakes, the Town of Oak Island, the Town of Caswell
Beach, the Village of St. James, and the Village of Bald Head Island to join
Southport in requesting affiliation with the Wilmington Transportation
Management Area.
Adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in regular session, September 13,
2012.
