Hearing on the consideration of locating a maritime memorial on Ft. Johnston
Garrison lawn and consideration of large events held in Franklin Square Park.
   Alderman Poole gave an overview of the process to locate a maritime memorial
on the Fort Johnston Garrison lawn. She stated that the “concept design for the
memorial calls for an area approximately 32 feet in diameter not including
extensions or connecting walkways. The central portion of the memorial would
consist of a brick octagon about 9-10 feet in diameter, containing an anchor
and a 36 foot nautical style flagpole with multiple flags and pennants, as well
as a surrounding walkway, a planted border area, and a post and chain fence
about three feet high.
   The Committee desired that the City of Southport provide a location on
municipal property for the proposed memorial and requested that the City
consider five different sites for possible placement. The five sites were (a) a
property in the Yacht Basin owned by First Bank, (b) Waterfront Park, (c)
Garrison House lawn, (d) Atlantic Street waterfront access, and (e) Kingsley
Park.
   An analysis of the five sites was conducted by City staff. The Garrison
House lawn site outside of the roped border was deemed the most suitable site
because it had high visibility and accessibility, the site was proximate to
other attractions, amenities and support facilities, the land area was suitable
in size and level, there were no flooding or CAMA regulatory issues. The area
had limited alternative use potential and the proposed use would complement the
other historical uses and activities that take place in and around the Garrison
House and the Maritime Museum. The use of the location will require State
Historic Preservation Office approval.
   The analysis was provided to the Parks and Recreation Committee, the private
Maritime Memorial Committee and the Board of Aldermen Committee. All three
committees concluded that the south side of the Garrison House lawn was the
most suitable potential location for the memorial.” As Chair of the Board
appointed committee, she asked for a Public Hearing to receive public comments
on the potential site.
III.   Public Hearing – Maritime Memorial
   Alderman Poole moved to enter Public Hearing, seconded by Alderman Barnes,
the vote was unanimous
   Mrs. Cheryl Daniels, a member of the Maritime Memorial Steering Committee
thanked the Board for its consideration and accepted the site selected by the
city to locate the maritime memorial monument on the Garrison lawn at Fort
Johnston. She asked that the location be moved farther to the right so that it
would be equal distance from the weather tower. She stated that the Committee
does not wish to see any memorials moved and does not want the weather tower
taken down because all the memorials are important. It is their belief, that
the right side of the Garrison lawn towards the Community Building would be
less intrusive and give the memorial a proper setting because of the aesthetic
value.
   The following persons spoke in support of the maritime memorial, but some
citizens supporting the memorial believed that it should be located some place
other than the Garrison lawn because of the historical significance of Fort
Johnston.
   Garrison Lawn                  Kingsley Park or Other Location

   Ms. Mary Eversole of Wilmington asked that the integrity of the history be

the following:
Street Banner Recommendation:
In City applicant for in city event         $400
Outside city applicant and doing in city event   $500
Outside event with event outside of city      $600
Beginning FY 13/14 for any events the Board elects during the budgetary process
to provide city sponsorship or co-sponsorship for a banner installation,
sufficient funds should be budgeted in the general fund at $300 per banner to
pay the electric fund for the banner installation.
Banners should be installed only for non-profit events (not for commercial or
political purposes) and request for installation should be handled on a first
come, first serve basis, and city sponsored/ co-sponsored events will have
priority.

GOVERNING BOARD POLICY               CITY OF SOUTHPORT, NC
USE OF CITY FACILITIES
A. Purpose  
The purposes of this policy are (a) to identify those facilities under the
supervision of the Administration Department that are available for use and (b)
to establish fees for the rental of those facilities that are available for
use.
B. Eligible Facilities
The following facilities are not available for use or rental:
   ·   Board of Aldermen Chambers
The following facilities are available for rental if not in use or planned for
use for municipal purposes:
   ·   Former Visitors Center, 113 East Moore Street
C. Applications and Permits
Any person or organization that requests the use of a municipal facility under
the supervision of the Administration Department shall make application for
same in a form provided by the Administration Department, which shall review
and approve all applications.
D. Cost of Facilities Use
Fees for the use of the former Visitors Center facilities shall be as follows:
In-City residents:         $160 for up to four hours (minimum)
                  $40/hour after four hours
                  Reservation and clean-up deposit: $160 (in advance)
Non-City residents:         $240 for up to four hours (minimum)
                  $60/hour after four hours
                  Reservation and clean-up deposit: $240 (in advance)
Deposits and minimum fees shall be paid in advance at the time of application.
Based on action by the Board of Aldermen, September 24, 2012.

B. Resolution – Fire Prevention Week
   The Board adopted a resolution proclaiming October 7-13, 2012 as Fire
Prevention Week  upon motion of Alderman Poole, seconded by Alderman Adams,
vote unanimous
Resolution
Fire Prevention Week
October 7 - 13, 2012
WHEREAS, the Southport Fire Department is committed to ensuring the safety and
security of all those living in and visiting our Fire District; and
WHEREAS, fire is a serious public safety concern both locally and nationally,
and homes are the locations where people are at the greatest risk of fire; and
WHEREAS, the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) has documented through
its research a significant increase in home fires, and due to this fact, it is
important that everyone know two ways out of your home in case of a fire; and
WHEREAS, the Firefighters of the Southport Fire Department are dedicated to
reducing the occurrence of residential and commercial structural fires and fire
related injuries through prevention and protection education; and
WHEREAS, the residents of the Southport Fire District are responsive to public
education measures and are able to take personal steps to increase their safety
from fire; and
WHEREAS, being prepared in the event of a home fire will have a positive effect
on the home fire problem; and
WHEREAS, each home fire that is prevented in the Southport Fire District is an
opportunity to prevent painful injury and costly property damage; and
WHEREAS, the 2012 Fire Prevention Week theme, KNOW 2 WAYS OUT – WHEN YOU GET
OUT STAY OUT!, effectively serves to remind us all of the simple actions we can
take to stay safer from fire every day.
THEREFORE, I Robert D. Howard, Mayor of the City of Southport, do hereby
proclaim October 7-13, 2012 as Fire Prevention Week throughout this City.  I
further encourage all citizens of Southport to heed the important safety
messages from the Southport Fire Prevention Team, and the Office of the City
Fire Marshal, and to support the many public safety activities and efforts of
the Southport Fire Department.
ADOPTED, October 11, 2012.
                  S/ Robert D. Howard
                Mayor
Attest:
S/ Regina W. Alexander, Clerk
   Resolution – County Delegation of Pyrotechnics Permit Authority approved
under consent agenda.
 A RESOLUTION REQUESTING DELEGATION
OF PYROTECHNICS PERMITTING AUTHORITY
WHEREAS North Carolina General Statute G.S. 14-410 sets forth the conditions
under which pyrotechnics may be exhibited, used, or discharged; and
WHEREAS these conditions include a requirement that the exhibition, use, or
discharge of pyrotechnics may occur only after issuance of written permission
from the board of commissioners of the county – or, if appropriately
authorized, the city in which the pyrotechnics are to be exhibited, used or
discharged; and
WHEREAS G.S. 14-413(a1) provides that a board of county commissioners may
authorize the governing body of any city in the county to issue permits for the
exhibition, use, and discharge of pyrotechnics in association with concerts and
public exhibitions; and
WHEREAS the City of Southport possesses the administrative capacity to ensure
compliance with the requirements of G.S. 14-410 and the technical expertise to
ensure that appropriate measures are undertaken to permissible exhibitions,
uses, and discharges of pyrotechnics take place in a safe manner;
   BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport that the
City requests that the Board of Commissioners of the County of Brunswick adopt
a resolution authorizing the City of Southport to issue permits for the
exhibition, use, and discharge of pyrotechnics within the corporate limits of
the city in connection with the conduct of concerts or public exhibitions.
   Adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in regular session, October 11,
2012.

AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE CITY CODE REGARDING OBSTRUCTIONS OF RIGHTS-OF-WAY
BE IT ORDAINED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport, North
Carolina:
Section 1. The Code of Ordinances, City of Southport, North Carolina, is hereby
amended by addition of the language underlined below.
Sec. 16-8. - Obstruction of public rights-of-way.
(a) Except as specifically set forth in subsection (b) herein or as authorized
by a license issued by the Board of Aldermen, it shall be unlawful for any
person to place or cause to be placed on any public street, road, alley,
sidewalk or other public right of way within the city any wall, fence, gate,
brick, stone, wood, rock, vegetation or other structure, material or substance
above the horizontal plane of the existing ground. In addition, it shall be
unlawful for any person to take any action whatsoever within any public right
of way which creates a hazardous condition or safety hazard or which otherwise
interferes with or obstructs in any manner the passage of persons or vehicles
upon or within said public rights of way or which obstructs, interferes with or
hinders lawful parking within any public right of way.
(b) Nothing herein shall prevent any business or other legal entity located in
areas zoned CBD and BD from (i) placing objects which are not otherwise
prohibited under the Southport Code of Ordinances on that portion of a sidewalk
which is directly abutting the building occupied by such business or entity,
provided that said items do not extend more than thirty-six (36) inches into
the sidewalk and do not violate section 16-7 of the Code of Ordinances
prohibiting the display of goods, or (ii) placing A-frame signs on a sidewalk
or right of way where specifically allowed under the Southport Unified
Development Ordinance. Notwithstanding this, however, no business or other
entity may place or cause to be placed any object on a sidewalk so as to
violate the provisions of the ADA regarding unobstructed clearance.
Section 2. This ordinance shall be effective upon its adoption.
Adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in regular session, October 11,
2012.
                     S/ Robert D. Howard, Mayor

S/Regina W. Alexander, City Clerk
CITY OF SOUTHPORT POLICY
RIGHT-OF-WAY USE LICENSES
A. BACKGROUND
While the City desires to avoid the placement of obstructions in the public
right-of-way, the City acknowledges that special circumstances may sometimes
warrant consideration of allowing use of a right-of-way area or municipal
property for limited private purposes. Such circumstances may arise due to the
significant width of some rights-of-way, the absence of private land to
accommodate essential facilities, unique physical circumstances, a desire to
preserve trees, landscaping, or the environment, or other special situations in
which the City desires to make reasonable and fair accommodations of business
or resident needs.
B. PURPOSE
The purpose of this policy is set forth the reasons, conditions, and
administrative guidelines for allowing – in certain limited circumstances and
under specific conditions – private use of municipal right-of-way or property
areas. When permission is issued pursuant to this policy, the permission shall
be in the form of a written license.
C. POLICY
1. Qualifying Circumstances. The City of Southport may elect to grant
permission for use of a portion of a municipal right-of-way or property when
the Board of Aldermen of the City finds (a) that there will be no significant
adverse effect on essential uses of the municipal right-of-way or property and
(b) that one or more of the following conditions exists:
a. Private property is not reasonably available to accommodate the proposed
land use; or
b. Unique physical circumstances prevent the use of private property for the
proposed land use; or
c. Natural resources would be better protected by the use of the city property
or right-of-way; or
d. Public safety, health, or welfare would be better protected by the proposed
license for use.
2. Form of Permission. Approval to use a portion of a municipal right-of-way or
property shall be in the form of a written license issued to the applicant. A
license is permission granted by a competent authority to exercise a certain
privilege that, without such authorization, would constitute an illegal act.
3. Conditions. The City may impose, in association with any license provided
for the use of municipal right-of-way or property, any conditions that it
considers necessary or prudent to protect the public safety, health, or welfare
or to mitigate any potential adverse effects.
4. Term and Termination. The term of any license for use of a municipal right-
of-way or property shall be as specified by the Board of Aldermen, or, if not
specified, until terminated by the City. The City may terminate a license for
use of municipal right-of-way or property at any time upon 30 days’ notice.
5. Compensation. The Board of Aldermen may require, when it considers it to be
necessary or appropriate, compensation in association with the issuance of a
license or reimbursement of any costs associated with issuance of the license.
D. ADMINISTRATION
1. Applications. Persons who desire consideration for a license for limited use
of a municipal right-of-way or property area shall make application for same in
a form required by the city manager and shall pay any required application fee.
The application fee shall, unless otherwise prescribed by the Board of
Aldermen, be $100. The application shall provide any necessary documents or
maps needed to adequately describe and depict the proposed license.
2. Review. The city staff shall review and investigate the application and
shall bring to the attention of the Board of Aldermen any information or
observations related to the required findings for issuance of licenses.
3. Approval. All licenses must be approved by the Board of Aldermen, after
consideration in a regular or special meeting of the Board and action to make
the findings required by this policy. Any approved licenses shall be in a form
approved by the Board, including any conditions imposed in association with the
approval.
Adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen, October 11, 2012.
                        S/Robert D. Howard, Mayor

   Sewer – East 11th Street (Mrs. Vernell Salmon)
   Mayor Howard briefed the Board on a sewer situation on East 11th Street. He
communicated that staff inadvertently discovered that the resident was not
connected to the City’s sewer system but had been paying for sewer since 1996.
   Alderman Powell, Chair of the Utility Committee stated that he spoke with
the resident and discovered that she did not move into the house until 1996
upon relocating to North Carolina. A realtor was handling her affairs and she
paid through the realtor’s office for city sewer connection. She thought that
she was connected because there is a sewer manhole in her front yard. When the
City was contacted because of a sewer problem, it was discovered that the house
was on a septic system. He stated the resident is a senior citizen and has an
invalid husband and wished to be reimbursed. She paid the sewer bill for
fifteen years at a total cost of $7,768.53 and is asking for a refund. She has
since hired a plumber and was connected to city sewer on September 20, 2012.
The Utility Committee recommends that the monies be reimbursed.
   City Manager Thomas stated since the matter was not on the agenda, he did
not have the information readily available pertaining to this situation.
However, the City has a board-adopted policy dated in 1997 indicating that when
sewer is extended in front of a house whether or not it is connected, it will
be billed for sewer. He explained that this is a common policy in
municipalities because the city pays the upfront capital costs to extend sewer
while making capacity available, people pay whether or not they are physically
connected. At this time, staff does not know, but there may be others in the
City with the same problem. The Board needs to consider whether it is prepared
to refund money to everyone covered by the policy and what to do about billings
going forward under the same policy.
   Alderman Adams, member of the Utility Committee supported the recommendation
to reimburse the resident and start over because the realtor is deceased.
   Alderman Barnes questioned the number of people in the same situation and
was told by City Manager Thomas that a house-to-house audit would need to be
conducted. Alderman Barnes acknowledged the city’s policy but stated it is his
belief that the right thing to do
is to refund the money. Alderman Poole agreed.
   Mayor Howard referenced the issue with the hospital using the wrong
multiplier on electricity for several years, but the city negotiated with them
and could only go back two years to collect because of the statute of
limitation.
   Attorney Isenberg stated that the Board has an adopted policy, which states
that a citizen shall be charged the minimum sewer fee even if not physically
connected if the line is extended by their house. In his opinion, if the Board
is not going to follow policy, it will be in violation of its own policy. There
is also a two-year statute of limitation for claims against the city.
It was noted that the resident has paid more than minimum fee in the amount of
one million, seventy eight thousand, two hundred and fifty gallons worth of
sewer (1,078,250) which is more than minimum. Attorney Isenberg stated with
this scenario, they might be entitled to the difference between the minimum
sewer/water bill.
   Mayor Howard requested that this item be considered at the November Board
meeting as “unfinished business.” Alderman Adams asked that a copy of the
policy be provided to the Board, and the city work to find if other residents
are affected by the same situation.
X.    City Manager Comments
   Resolution – The insurance industry has proposed an increase to homeowners’
insurance rates across the state, with an average increase of 17.7% and 30% for
coastal towns. A Public Hearing will be held in Raleigh on October 17 and
comments can be made on line at 2012homeowners@ncdoi.gov. (Resolution approved
as to form under consent agenda).
A RESOLUTION OPPOSING PROPOSED INCREASE IN COASTAL HOMEOWNER INSURANCE RATES
WHEREAS a robust housing market and sound, sustainable economy depends on the
availability of affordable and accessible property insurance; and
WHEREAS coastal area homeowners already pay – in addition to the separate cost
of wind and hail coverage – homeowner insurance premiums up to five times the
rates charged for inland properties; and
WHEREAS  the North Carolina Rate Bureau has asked the North Carolina Department
of Insurance to approve a major increase in homeowners insurance rates – an
increase that will have a seriously adverse effect on coastal counties,
including Brunswick county; and
WHEREAS the proposed 30 percent increase for the coastal counties closely
follows a 17.5 percent increase for coastal counties in 2009, on top of rate
increases in every rate cycle in the last 20 years; and
WHEREAS actual loss experience indicates that, in many instances, central and
western counties in North Carolina have had more losses per premium dollar than
has been paid in eastern NC counties; and
WHEREAS the steep proposed overall increases and the proposed severe
disparities in insurance rates would place an unfair and unwarranted burden on
homeowners in coastal counties; and
WHEREAS the North Carolina Department of Insurance plans to conduct a public
hearing on the proposed rate increase on October 17, 2012, less than three
weeks following the rate request filing;
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the City of Southport strongly oppose the
radical rate increase requested by the insurance industry for property owners
in Brunswick County and other coastal counties. The Southport Board of Aldermen
also encourages citizens to submit their own comments to the Department of
Insurance before the October 19, 2012 deadline.
Unanimously adopted by the City of Southport Board of Aldermen, October 11,
2012.
                              
                     S/ Robert D. Howard, Mayor
Attest
S/Regina W. Alexander, City Clerk

DECEMBER 4, 2012
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN            SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
DECEMBER 4, 2012             3:00 P.M.
ALDERMEN CHAMBERS, CITY HALL SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:       Mayor Robert D. Howard
          Aldermen Mary Ellen Poole
          Buddy Barnes
          Todd Coring
          Jim Powell
          Ken Karn
    Nelson Adams
STAFF PRESENT:   Pat Thomas, City Manager
         Michele Windham, Deputy City Clerk
         Mike Isenberg, City Attorney
         Robert Tucker, Public Services Director
I.   Call to Order – 3:00 p.m.
   Mayor Howard called the meeting to order at 3:00 p.m.
II.   Invocation
   Alderman Powell welcomed everyone to the meeting.
   Pastor Charles Drew, Lighthouse Pentecostal Church, delivered the
invocation.
   ETHICS STATEMENT: Mayor Howard stated, “if any member of the Board knows of
any conflict of interest or the appearance of a conflict of interest with
respect to matters on the agenda, to please so state it at this time.”
III.   Mayor Howard announced the purpose of the special meeting was to receive
an update and recommendation from the Building Improvement Committee.
Mayor Howard read a statement detailing the background for establishing the
committee, the process taken, studies and evaluations conclusions and the
committee’s recommendation:
   Background:
   “The Board’s charge to the Building Improvement Committee (BIC) was to
determine the most cost effective option of providing affordable solutions for
work space for city employees in the City Hall and Code Enforcement office
buildings. Over the years our administration and prior administrations have
allowed the City’s buildings and workplaces to deteriorate in favor of saving a
few bucks in the moment.
   During the past 18 months, our Board recognized the necessity to maintain
and upgrade City owned properties throughout City government and to provide
sufficient and feasible workspace for our staff, as a result last year we
engaged the services of John Sawyer Architects to assist the Board in producing
a “Long Range Facilities Study Plan.”
    Since that time two separate committees made up of council members and
staff have studied the issue and concluded that the City Hall and Code
Enforcement buildings do not meet the municipal government needs of the City.
   We learned from the initial study that both buildings are in deteriorating
condition, with antiquated operating systems and are functionally obsolete.
   Currently many City employees are working in woefully inadequate and
overcrowded conditions, to include but not limited to the Police, Finance and
Code Enforcement Departments.
   We assume the reason our predecessors deferred maintenance was because the
fact of the   matter is when you look at our existing buildings where we house
our City employees you know it’s just a temporary solution predicting that
other deterioration in the buildings would occur over time.
This Board, as a result of the study, began implementing some of the acceptable
recommendations to include upgrading the Parks & Recreation, Visitors Center,
Tourism and the Fire Department. Now it is time to continue to move forward in
accordance with the Long Range Facilities Plan.
   The BIC has conducted its studies and evaluation in consideration of the
City’s goal for energy
   conservation and energy use; sustainable design and construction including
life cycle cost
   evaluations and the application and suitability of these goals for the City
Hall Renovation and
   Retrofit project.
    The $2.2 million proposal we will recommend this afternoon will replace the
deteriorating City Hall building on Moore Street and the Code Enforcement
Office on Nash Street.
   Process:
   Your (Aldermen’s) difficult decision will be deciding on spending three plus
million dollars to patch-up and maintain a perpetually eroding City Hall
building and constructing a small facility to house police, planning,
inspections and code enforcement or instead constructing or acquiring a new
facility either at a lesser cost to taxpayers.
   At the Board’s direction and with its authorization, the BIC undertook a
feasibility study on the old Fire Department building and the Code Enforcement
building. The evaluation was lead by City Manager Pat Thomas and Project
Architect John Thompson and his associates. This study determined it is not
feasible to use existing Nash Street buildings to accommodate our needs.
   Additionally, City Manager Thomas contracted with Stewart Mulford’s firm who
are professional construction cost estimators. The result of their study
indicated that the cost would approximate $1,750,000.00 to perform the
additions, renovations and retrofit to the City Hall building and $1,350,000 to
construct a facility to house the Police, Code Enforcement and Planning
Departments.
   After looking at the potential cost to renovate and retrofit City Hall, the
committee pondered (i) what if we take down or replace the three buildings and
start over or (ii) what if we find ways to renovate some portions of the
existing buildings, with some substantial changes for making them seismically
functional and energy & operating efficient.
   What are the options?
   1.   Renovate City Hall and construct an annex building on Nash Street. This
approach will be the largest cost to the taxpayers; or
   2.   We could sell the building & property to a private contractor, who
could renovate the building and then sell it back to the City (the hope is it
would cost less than the previous option, but this may be a slippery slope to
travel; or
   3.   We could renovate as a community project through both private and
public funding (an ideal choice that could take a long time to complete - maybe
too long; or
   4.   We could build a facility or acquire an existing facility to house all
of the affected employees under one roof.
   Study and Evaluation Conclusions:
   We believe the most prudent and cost effective approach for the tax payers
is a new facility to replace the existing City Hall which is outdated and
deteriorating; in fact, the building systems including plumbing, electrical,
HVAC are deteriorating and are functionally obsolete. When City Hall was built,
the most a person would have to plug in was a desk lamp. The old City Hall
cannot effectively support our new technological needs. In arriving at our
recommendation, the committee cautions about throwing money away on the current
City Hall building if ultimately it would not be functionally or economically
feasible.
   In considering replacement we evaluated purchasing land if we could find an
appropriate location at an affordable price vs. going into the market to
determine if there is an existing facility that would accommodate our needs.
   The Committee asked City Manager Thomas and Project Architect John Thompson
to project the cost of a new facility. The results will be shared with you in a
few minutes.
   Additionally, City Manager Thomas looked at the market to determine if there
was a suitable option. He located a suitable building located at 1029 N. Howe
Street on the market which we have determined will effectively fit our space
needs.
   It is our opinion that the cost to renovate City Hall and construct a small
annex facility at the combined cost in excess of $3,000,000 is cost
prohibitive; consequently, we came to the conclusion that the City should
seriously consider abandoning those facilities and either construct or obtain a
replacement facility.
   Recommendation:
   The Building Improvement Committee is recommending a new city hall to house
all the city departments (Administration, Finance, Police, Planning,
Inspections and Code Enforcement) under one roof.
   The BIC, after considering (i) site options (ii) land purchase and
construction, and (iii) acquisition of the 1029 N. Howe Street building
concluded that the 1029 N. Howe Street building which is on the same block
directly north of the Fire Department facility is the best alternative.
   Another attractive observation is that with the very functional two story
building on the north end of the block and the fire department on the south end
of the block will create a great public presence with the potential (as
property becomes available) of creating a municipal complex to include
facilities with sufficient parking spaces along Lord and 11 th street.
   The building will house our staff with minimal upfit and retrofits; however
it will require that we construct a small addition to accommodate the Council
Chambers. We have studied variable options considering available property at
that site determining there are several options.
   One proposal has the Council Chambers on the east end of the building, near
N. Howe Street, while another moves Council Chambers to the west end of the
building.”
   Mayor Howard displayed detailed cost projections of the options via a
PowerPoint presentation. He indicated a purchase contract for 1029 N. Howe
Street for $1.8 million has been negotiated, pointing out the purchase listing
was $2.2 million. He stated the total cost of $2,128,000.00 would include a
$50,000 up fit allowance, $250,000 for addition of a Council Chambers and
$25,000 for deferred maintenance.
   Mayor Howard pointed out there are currently two leases for 1029 N. Howe
Street; the first floor lease runs through 2013 and the lease with Wells
Financial for the second floor runs through 2016. He expressed his opinion the
lease for the first floor could be negotiated out to accommodate an expeditious
occupancy of the Police Department and Code Enforcement departments. He added
his belief the second floor lease can be negotiated as well resulting in a
reduced total cost of the structure to $1,926,382.09.
   Manager Thomas went through multiple views of 1029 N. Howe Street
emphasizing the close proximity to the Public Services Department, Fire
Department Headquarters and the potential to create a future municipal campus.
He highlighted specifics of the building;
•      Built in 2006
•      In good condition with the exception of exterior painting needed
•      10,008 heated sq. ft.
•      Meets all space planning needs articulated in previous plans for City
Hall and Nash Street offices
•      Has an elevator and two stairwells
•      Has 30 parking spaces
•      First floor plan mirrored on each end with separate lobbies would allow
for two departments with two distinct entrances
•      Second floor comprised of excellent office space
•      Wired for phone and data
•      The site lends itself to addition of Council meeting space
   Alderman Powell expressed his support of the recommendation to purchase 1029
N. Howe Street noting the age of the building, start of a municipal campus and
that City departments would not be displaced multiple times in the case of
renovations to City Hall.
   Alderman Adams concurred with Alderman Powell stating he sees the Board as
visionaries doing what is best for the City at the least cost.
   Mayor Howard discussed the purchase agreement, copies of which to be
provided to each Board member; anticipated closing date and the period for due
diligence.
   Attorney Isenberg indicated he had reviewed the purchase agreement. He
emphasized the City can cancel the contract any time prior to December 20. He
stated he could have title searches and closing documentation ready for the
December 27 scheduled closing date. He pointed out the means to pay for the
purchase would need to be determined by the closing date and the seller is
anxious to sell before the end of 2012 .
   City Manager Thomas outlined three ways for the City to borrow money:
•      Obligation bonds; normally for amounts $10 million or more
•      USDA loan
•      Installment purchase financing
   City Manager Thomas discussed a short-term alternative strategy for payment
of the proposed purchase:
•      Use of unrestricted fund balances in Water/Sewer/Electric funds
•      Use of unrestricted fund balances in General Fund
•      Exclusive of desired reserve balance available for disasters
•      Replenish fund balances by disposing of assets; i.e. former site of the
wastewater treatment facility
   Mayor Howard discussed four (4) separate statements of interest to purchase
the wastewater treatment facility. He added the Building Improvements Committee
would like to discuss, at some time in the future, appointment of a committee
or foundation to look at options for the future use of the current City Hall.
   Responding to a question by Alderman Karn, Mayor Howard estimated 30 to 60
days after closing for transition of the Police, Code Enforcement and Building
Inspections offices into 1029 N. Howe Street. He stated the relocation of
Administrative offices onto the second floor could be as late as 2016 but a
significant amount of money would be realized for the City through lease
payments by Wells Financial during that interval.
   Alderman Barnes questioned if future needs of the City had been considered.
Mayor Howard displayed an overhead view of the area and discussed potential
future purchase of surrounding properties when they become available.
   Mayor Howard and Alderman Adams both emphasized the recommendation of the
Building Improvement Committee was on the table for consideration of the Board
but a vote was not expected until all members had sufficient time to review the
purchase agreement.
   Alderman Poole thanked the Committee and staff for the detailed information
presented. She expressed her opinion the Board has an opportunity to improve
working conditions for city employees and a decision should be made as soon as
possible.
   Mayor Howard asked for questions from the audience. No one had any questions
or comments. Further consideration of the recommendation was scheduled for a
workshop December 6, 2012.
IV.   Alderman Poole moved, seconded by Alderman Coring to add consideration of
holiday bonuses for city employees to the agenda. Vote unanimous.
   Alderman Poole moved, seconded by Alderman Karn to give City employees a
holiday bonus; full-time employees $175, part-time employees $125.
Discussion:
   City Manager Thomas questioned if a minimum hourly threshold for part-time
employees would apply for receipt of the bonus. Alderman Poole indicated
applicable employment laws would govern issuance of the bonuses.
   Vote unanimous.
   Alderman Powell moved, seconded by Alderman Coring to give a holiday bonus
to the part-time employees that worked through the summer cleaning up the city.
Vote unanimous.
V.    Adjournment – 4:17 p.m.
   Alderman Coring moved to adjourn the meeting, seconded by Alderman Barnes.
Vote unanimous.

Discussion of Potential Capital Projects
   The Board in discussion with City Manager Thomas reviewed a list of
potential capital projects and factors relating to projects as a preliminary
goal and priority setting that will occur in the FY 13-14 budget process.
   Mayor Howard suggested if there are unfinished items, a workshop is held to
discuss these items in addition to the January Retreat.
   Discussed were the following projects by City Manager Thomas
   ·   Workspace Improvements for several departments i.e. Rescue Squad
   Project Description:  Acquisition or construction of modern, adequate
workspace for the operation of the Police, Planning/Code Enforcement, Finance,
Administration and Rescue Departments. Mr. Thomas stated that the Building
Committee discussed capital improvements of the Rescue Squad. The Rescue Squad
needs to be in a central location because most of their calls are from Dosher
Hospital northward. If the Rescue Squad remains in the current location for an
indefinite period, then the committee would consider a phased or complete
approach for improvements to their building or relocation. In speaking with the
Rescue Squad Chief, they would be better off in a more central location. It was
agreed upon with the existing building and adjoining space, that it would be
sufficient with some interior improvements until the City can relocate the
squad. Improvements can be made at a lesser cost than originally estimated.
   City Manager asked if the Board wished to discuss other aspects of the space
improvements plan. It was discussed briefly the prioritization for the space
study.
·   Waterfront Improvements
City Manager Thomas stated in order to develop a feasible plan; the city will
need to consider stakeholder participation, will the affected people buy into
the proposal, and riparian rights will need to be considered. He explained that
the unprotected river frontage is limited for some uses due to wave action and
current, consideration may need to be given on how to conserve the waterfront
due to erosion issues. The waterfront improvements will need to be accompanied
by a waterfront conservation plan due to erosion and waterfront improvement
projects will be subject to regulations and permitting under CAMA, US Army Corp
of Engineers and Division of Water Quality. He asked that the Board consider
specific objectives for waterfront improvements i.e. improved recreation for
residents, promotion of tourism, economic development, water quality, etc.
which will assist in developing the process. Mayor Howard recommended an
execution plan with time line. Mayor Howard questioned whether a study would be
done in house or will the Board consider hiring someone that can lead the
process in order to have stakeholder involvement i.e. citizens and businesses.
Mayor Howard noted that staff is capable of getting this project accomplished,
but the question is whether or not staff has the time. He asked that a timeline
be developed for January and allow staff to look at outside sources to assist
with the project. Alderman Karn and others agreed that execution of the plan is
important.
Yacht Basin Property Acquisition
       Board members have been meeting with First Bank in discussion about
acquisition of 2.02 acres of property in the Yacht Basin for future
development. Acquiring this property is related to potential waterfront
improvement initiatives and would potentially improve the City’s ability to a)
improve public waterfront access in the Yacht Basin, b) resolve storm-water and
tidal flooding issues, and c) encourage appropriate development on adjoining
properties. If the city acquires this property, Mr. Thomas noted that it could
be a significant boost in the Yacht Basin for future development, which would
be an important adjunct to the downtown area. Some possible funding sources:
   ·   CAMA Access Grants (local match)
   ·   Occupancy tax revenue
   ·   Partnership with community organizations
   ·   EDA Grants
   ·   Clean Water Management Grants
   ·   Assessment of storm water improvements benefiting properties
   Mayor Howard requested staff and the Planning Board look at the area and
insure that it is properly zoned to insure that surrounding properties are
protected, possibly look at an overlay area.
   Alderman Karn asked if a tidal study had been performed in the yacht basin
area. No Board member was aware of a previous study. Alderman Karn conveyed
that it is a difficult issue to solve, City Manager Thomas agreed while stating
that is not impossible. Alderman Karn asked if it would make it easier to
acquire only the waterfront property. City Manager Thomas recommended acquiring
it all.
   ·   Underground Electrical Facilities
   Mr. Thomas reported that the City is working with Brunswick Electric
Membership Corporation (BEMC) on its new multi-year plan for improvements to
the electrical system. Emphasis has been placed on the conversion of the
municipal electric distribution system from overhead to underground to a)
improve reliability, b) reduce storm related outages and c) improve community
appearance. The Plan will be presented to the Board in January. The goal is to
shift emphasis from pole replacement and begin to move facilities underground.
The six-year plan proposes allocation of capital funds from electrical system
revenues. The Board will need to consider some policy decisions such as when
the city converts to underground, will the resident or City pay to alter the
service to the building, which will cost approximately $1200. Who pays, the
City, the customer or is the cost shared. He communicated that pad mount
transformers will have to be considered for commercial areas in order to
service underground in the downtown area and location placement. In discussion,
Alderman Poole noted if the City does not have mandatory hook-up,
undergrounding will not succeed. Proposed cost for undergrounding:
2012-2013     $106,700
2013-2014 $126,604
2014-2015 $209,538
2015-2016 $228,598
2016-2017 $209,942
2017-2018 $160,805
   ·   Pedestrian Transportation Improvements
   The objectives of this project is to improve pedestrian access to key
destinations, safety for pedestrians and users of handicapped mobility devices
and eliminate obstacles to use existing sidewalks by handicapped persons. There
are some places in the city where ramps were not constructed to modern
standards and handicapped individuals get stuck. The City did get a grant for a
pedestrian plan, funding will be received to implement safe routes to school
sidewalks project, appropriate Powell Bill funds annually for pedestrian
improvements and request NCDOT installation of sidewalks on all, new or
improved facilities. Some key issues for consideration is whether the city
should have more input in review process insisting that pedestrian connections
between neighborhoods and key destinations. Should the City consider developing
off road pedestrian routes in areas where on-road facilities may be not
feasible or more expensive, which may be easier in some situations. Potential
funding sources: a) safe routes to school grants, b) Powell bill funds, and c)
assessments to adjoining properties
   ·   City Dock Facilities Improvements
City Manager Thomas showed an area photograph outlining the city dock. Some
areas appear to be outside of the City’s deed boundaries, which could
complicate the permitting process for improvements to reconstruct or expand the
dock facilities. Additions to the dock will require acquisition of riparian
rights or partnership with the State department that controls the track of land
on the marsh side of the City dock. This could result in collaborative rights
with the State to make improvements to the yacht basin. Alderman Barnes
recommended the City Manager speak with former Alderman Donnie Potter because
he once had maps and information on the Yacht Basin.
Mr. Thomas noted safety and maintenance issues, which need to be addressed to
minimize risk for boat slip renters and the public, improve the quality of
facility and usability by upgrading, and offer hospitality to transient
boaters. He suggested possibly the following sequence:
   ·    safety improvements,
   ·    dredging of the dock area,
   ·    addition of transient docks spaces,
   ·    reconstruction of dock, possibly to a floating dock.
The deed issue will have to be addressed with possible collaboration with the
State.
   Mr. Thomas told the Board that some of the key issues are:
   a) Does the facility generate sufficient revenue for major capital
expenditures, b) how important is the need to provide additional transient
docking facilities. Funding sources are: a) boat slip rentals which bring in
$23,200 annually, b) boating infrastructure grants for transient docking of
large vessels, c) occupancy tax for waterfront improvements, if obtained
   Other issues cited were: a) the long waiting list for dock rentals and the
need for a policy decision whether city residents should be given priority in
assignment of available boat slips, b) should unauthorized dock attachments be
removed, and c) should measures be taken to limit abuse of limited parking
areas. He cited possible funding sources such as boat slip rental fees which
totals $23,200 annually, boating infrastructure grant (BIG) for transient
docking of large vessels (26 feet), or occupancy tax for waterfront
improvements, if authority obtained through special legislation.
   Alderman Adams asked for clarification about the rate differential for city
residents and assumed that priority was given to city residents for dock rental
during budget workshops. City Manager Thomas noted only rates were addressed
during the budget meetings. He stated that the waiting list will be reviewed
and cleaned up.
   Alderman Barnes motioned, seconded by Alderman Poole to give priority to
city residents for city boat slips. Discussion: Alderman Adams stated no
commitments should be made without at least a 2 day study, and he does not wish
to act spontaneous, because there are other actions that may need to be
considered. Alderman Barnes withdrew the motion.
   Mayor Howard asked the Committee comprised of Aldermen Poole, Barnes and
Coring to meet with the City Manager to develop a written policy and present to
the Board for consideration at the next regular scheduled meeting.
   Alderman Barnes stated the city dock is for small boats, and he will not be
in favor of upgrading the city dock to the point that it dramatically increases
rent. The City dock does not have the amenities as other marinas and improving
revenue potential is not one of his priorities, while believing that $23,200 is
sufficient to spend annually for maintenance improvements.
   Alderman Coring asked about some of the docks being sub-leased. City Manager
Thomas noted that this is being monitored and changes have been made.
   Alderman Barnes addressed same cars parking continuous near the city dock.
Alderman Poole noted that the docks are for public access and not limited to
usage by people that rent boat slips.
   Alderman Karn suggested before improvements are made to determine if the
City proposes to upgrade for current users or to increase revenue source. Mayor
Howard stated after the committee makes it recommendation, this can be
discussed further.
9th Street Park
   City Manager Thomas reported that the property is smaller than the former
Steven’s Park property and is divided by another property, which limits the
city’s potential use design. However, there is a possibility the city can talk
with the property owner of the surrounding property (Bald Head Island Ltd.) for
property exchange or joint development of a park facility. The school system
has also expressed a desire for park facilities for use by the school, but
funding is not known at this time. The city has not set aside funds for park
development or grant matches. He stated that operation and maintenance of
another park will increase operating expenses and the city has not developed a
comprehensive park and recreation plan or a park master plan to support grant
applications. Potential funding sources are a PARTF Grant which requires 50%
match, contributions in lieu of park land dedication by sub-dividers and
participation by Bald Head Island and/or school system.
   Mayor Howard stated that he communicated with owners of the property and
they are aware of the city’s desire to get the property connected. The city is
working on their schedule and asked for diligence by the Board before forcing
the issue.
   Alderman Adams stated his understanding and the sensitivity of the request,
but there is a mandate from citizens wanting ball park and encouraged the Board
not to drop the ball. Mayor stated this is another area of tax duplication,
where the county may be considered for a source of funding.
Cemetery Improvements
   City Manager Thomas asked the Board if they wished to continue driveway
paving in Northwood Cemetery, replacement of older fencing and wooden row
markers with more durable markers. He explained that there is no fund or other
source of revenue to continue this work and the only source of funds is the
general fund. The City Manager asked the Board to what extent should the City
conduct maintenance or make capital improvements on properties that are not
municipally owned, which would be a policy decision.
   Alderman Barnes asked if the city has responsibility to mow property that it
does not own. Mayor Howard stated that the cemeteries house the City’s heritage
and it is a moral obligation. In his opinion, the City needs to do what it has
to legally to maintain the cemeteries. Alderman Powell stated that this was
decided in February. Alderman Adams stated that it is a City practice to take
care of the cemeteries. He also suggested paving another road in Northwood
Cemetery. Mayor Howard stated that establishing a Foundation would be a good
source of funds and possibly appointing a committee to look into this at a
later date. Alderman Coring asked that the wooden poles in the cemetery be
removed or changed because some have fallen over and car doors are bumped when
opened. He recommended getting input from Greg White, owner of Newnam & White
Funeral Home.
Adjournment – 12:38
   No further business, Alderman Coring motioned for adjournment, seconded by
Alderman Karn, vote unanimous.

   ·   Resolution in support of Clean Water Management Trust Funding
A Resolution Supporting 2013-2015 Funding for the North Carolina Clean Water
Management Trust Fund
Whereas the 1996 General Assembly established the Clean Water Management Trust
Fund to provide an innovative and non-regulatory approach to the protection and
restoration of the surface waters all across the state; and
Whereas the Clean Water Management Trust Fund is a non-regulatory program
established to help meet infrastructure needs of municipalities and counties,
restore degraded surface water, protect watersheds, increase recreational
opportunities, and enhance quality of life in this state, all critical
components for communities to obtain a competitive edge in their economic
development; and
Whereas the Clean Water Management Trust Fund has funded 452 infrastructure
projects to assist North Carolina communities balance infrastructure needs with
environmental protection and to help struggling communities become self reliant
with future infrastructure needs; and
Whereas infrastructure needs across the state addressing drinking water,
wastewater, and storm water are estimated at $16.6 billion between 2005 and
2030; and
Whereas  the Clean Water Management Trust Fund has leveraged more than
$1billion of private, local and federal funds to support projects; and
Whereas the General Assembly has reduced funding for the Clean Water Management
Trust Fund by 78 percent since 2010; and
Whereas  limited funding for the Clean Water Management Trust Fund left 88
percent of 2012 critical local needs unmet; and
Whereas our economic vitality, health and ability to sustain ourselves and the
natural environment all rely on clean water; and
Whereas surface water must be protected to ensure sufficient drinking water
supply for the state’s growing industrial base and population; and
Whereas, Clean Water Management Trust Fund has provided grants to the City of
Southport to do one or more of the following: to protect, restore or enhance
surface water quality for the benefit of the state’s agriculture, military,
recreation and tourism economies and to protect our natural heritage for the
benefit of all North Carolinians;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE BOARD OF ALDERMEN OF THE CITY OF
SOUTHPORT THAT THE CITY OF SOUTHPORT SUPPORTS THE CLEAN WATER MANAGEMENT TRUST
FUND AND URGES THAT THE FUND RECEIVE AN INCREASE IN RECURRING FUNDING FROM THE
GOVERNOR AND THE NORTH CAROLINA GENERAL ASSEMBLY FOR THE 2013-2015 BIENNIAL
BUDGET.
Adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in regular session, December 13,
2012.
S/ Robert D. Howard
Attest:
S/Regina Alexander, City Clerk

A RESOLUTION HONORING CONTRIBUTIONS TO THE COMMUNITY BY DOWNTOWN SOUTHPORT,
INC.
   WHEREAS Downtown Southport, Inc. is a non-profit organization dedicated to
preserving the heritage and charm of Southport; and
   WHEREAS Downtown Southport, Inc. (DSI) encourages and supports preservation
projects, cultural activities, educational programs, tourism, and responsible
economic growth in the downtown area; and
   WHEREAS Downtown Southport, Inc. has, since its inception in 2005, been a
major contributor to making Southport a vital and vibrant year-round community
for Southport citizens and guests, through programs and actions such as:
·   Co-sponsorship and coordination, with the Kiwanis Club, of the annual
Southport Spring Festival,
·   Sponsorship and coordination of the Southport Waterfront Market,
·   Co-sponsorship with the Cape Fear Yacht Club of the annual Christmas
Flotilla
·   Sponsorship and coordination of the annual Winterfest Craft Festival,
·   Provision of funding for the advertising and marketing of Winterfest,
·   Co-sponsorship with the Wooden Boat Show Committee of the Southport Wooden
Boat Show each fall,
·   Co-sponsorship with the Southport Garden Club of the bi-annual tour of
Southport gardens
·   Co-sponsorship with City of Southport Tourism of the annual Pyrates
Invasion,
·   Provision of funding to support other tourism development projects in
Southport;
WHEREAS Downtown Southport, Inc. has become a strong, vital, and sustaining
contributor to the quality of life in Southport and to the prosperity of the
community, especially Southport’s downtown area;
BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen that the volunteer leaders and members
of Downtown Southport, Inc. are hereby commended and recognized for DSI’s
strong and sustained commitment to the vitality and uniqueness of Southport and
for Downtown Southport, Inc.’s outstanding and excellent contributions to the
betterment of the community; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Board of Aldermen offers its deepest
appreciation and thanks, on behalf of a grateful community, for Downtown
Southport, Inc.’s generous and outstanding performance as a Community
Institution of Excellence in Southport.
                           s/Robert D. Howard, Mayor

s/Regina Alexander, City Clerk

RESOLUTION
OF APPRECIATION TO THE BRUNSWICK COUNTY
ARTS COUNCIL
“Charles Dickens Festival”
WHEREAS, the historic and beautiful City of Southport hosted the Brunswick
County Arts Council November 30-December 1, 2012, and
WHEREAS, the Brunswick County Arts Council presented the production of “Charles
Dickens Christmas Festival,” and
WHEREAS, the festival attracted local residents, neighboring communities and
visitors to historic downtown Southport to celebrate the 200th birthday of this
beloved English novelist, considered one of the greatest literary giants of the
Victorian era, and
WHEREAS, the eclectic productions and activities educated visitors about the
traditional Old English Victorian Christmases; and
WHEREAS, staging a festival of this magnitude could not be accomplished without
hundreds of volunteers who inspire, educate and promote the arts and cultural
interests of Brunswick County.
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED,  I, Mayor Robert D. Howard, and the Southport
Board of Aldermen commend the Brunswick County Arts Council and its many
volunteers for an outstanding production of “Charles Dickens Christmas
Festival,” and wish much success for future productions.

   C.   Proposed Policy – Fort Johnston Property Uses
   The following resolution was presented for Board consideration and will be
placed on the January agenda regarding proposed uses of Fort Johnston property.
A RESOLUTION REGARDING
PROPOSED USES OF FORT JOHNSTON PROPERTY
   WHEREAS the Fort Johnston property was donated to the City of Southport with
the intention that it be used for public park and recreational purposes; and
   WHEREAS the City’s use and management of the property remains subject to
general oversight by the U.S. Department of Interior and the North Carolina
Department of Cultural Resources; and
   WHEREAS the central and attractive location of Fort Johnston makes it an
attractive location for a wide variety of potential uses, both temporary and
permanent; and
   WHEREAS the City of Southport has a responsibility to give thorough and
deliberate consideration to all potential uses of the Fort Johnston property,
especially those that involve the installation of structures or structural
additions on the site;
   BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport that the
following policy shall normally apply to any proposed uses of the Fort Johnston
property that involve the installation of- or additions to permanent structures
on the site:
1. First Reading. The proposed use shall be provided, described, and/or
illustrated in detail and in written form, to the satisfaction of the Board of
Aldermen, and the requested use shall be presented at a regular meeting (or a
special meeting called for that purpose) of the Board. This presentation and
description, which may be required to be presented in a form prescribed by the
Board or City Manager, shall constitute the first reading of the proposed use.
If the Board agrees by majority vote, upon first reading, that it desires to
further consider the proposed use, the proposed use shall then be sent to any
appropriate agencies – including the State Historic Preservation Office – for
review and comment.
2. Second Reading. After receipt of any agency comments, the proposed use of
the property shall be scheduled for second reading by the Board of Aldermen,
which shall take place at a regular meeting unless otherwise advertised. The
second reading shall normally take place at least three weeks following the
first reading. On the occasion of the second reading, the proposed use shall be
advertised for public comments. After receipt of public comments, the Board
may, if it desires, discontinue consideration of the proposed use or may give
preliminary approval, by majority vote, to the proposed use and schedule the
proposal for third reading.
3. Third Reading. After its initial decision to give further consideration to
the proposal, the receipt of agency and public comments, and a second decision
to give preliminary approval to the proposed use, the Board may give final
consideration to the proposed use at a third reading, which shall take place at
a regular meeting unless otherwise advertised. The third reading shall normally
take place at least three weeks after the second reading. On that occasion, the
Board may elect to discontinue consideration of the proposed use, carry the
matter over for further consideration, or give final approval to the proposed
use.
4. General. This policy is intended to describe the minimum process that should
be followed in considering permanent uses of the Fort Johnston property and is
not intended to inhibit any additional information requests, reviews,
investigations, opportunities for comment, or other measures considered
necessary by the Board of Aldermen in order to give thorough and deliberate
consideration to proposed uses of the property. In rare or extraordinary
circumstances involving opportunities or emergencies with deadlines beyond the
Board’s control, the Board may vary this policy as needed, while making every
effort to preserve its overall purpose and intent.
Adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in regular session, December 13,
2012.
               S/Robert D. Howard, Mayor
Attest:
S/Regina Alexander, City Clerk
   Mayor Howard recommended that this matter be placed on the agenda for the
next workshop.

Restaurant; they also propose to build an enclosure for the dumpster.

   H. Sale of Municipal Property – former Wastewater Treatment Plant Site
   The Board at its December 6 meeting, requested the Building Improvements
Committee develop a proposal for disposition of the former wastewater treatment
plant property. As explained by Mayor Howard, there are three standard methods
under general statutes to dispose of real property: 1) sealed bids, 2)
negotiated offer, advertisement, and upset bids, and 3) public auction. Mayor
Howard presented from the Building Improvements Committee to the Board of
Aldermen the recommendation under G.S. 160A-269, Negotiated offer,
advertisement, and upset bids to dispose of City property. Alderman Adams
motioned to accept the recommendation of the Building Improvements Committee,
seconded by Alderman Powell. Discussion: Alderman Barnes asked the City
Attorney if only one bid is received, can the Board accept a minimum offer.
Attorney Isenberg stated that the Board can accept or reject any bid offer. The
vote of approval was unanimous.
   I. Proposed Policy – Order of Priority, Boat Slip Leases
   Alderman Barnes, Chair of the Rate Review Committee presented the following
policy for consideration. Alderman Barnes moved to adopt the Order of Priority,
Boat Slip Lease Policy, seconded by Alderman Powell, vote of approval was
unanimous.
ORDER-OF-PREFERENCE POLICY
CITY DOCK BOAT SLIP RENTALS
A. Registration. All persons who are interested in renting slips at the
Southport City Dock may register their interest in a log maintained by the
City, in a department designated by the city manager. The registrant, who must
be the actual owner of the boat and who must be at least 21 years of age, shall
provide the following information to the person maintaining the registration
log: his or her name, address, telephone number, e-mail address (if available),
and information regarding any real property owned in Southport. Applications
may not be made in the name of corporations.
B. Order of Preference for Available Boat Slips. Any available boat slips shall
be offered to registrants on the waiting list in the following order of
preference:
   1. Southport residents who also own real property in Southport.
   2. All other residents of Southport
   3. Non-residents who own real property in Southport.
   4. All other non-residents.
   Within the categories of preference, preference for boat slip leases shall
be given in chronological order of registration (earliest first).
C. Accessibility of Registrants. Any person who registers in order to be
considered for a boat slip rental is responsible for keeping his or her contact
information and real property ownership status up to date with the custodian of
the registration list. When a boat slip becomes available, the city staff will
make a reasonable – but not exceptional – effort to contact the person that
should have preference. If the person who should have preference cannot be
contacted readily or does not respond in a timely manner when offered a lease
opportunity, their name will be removed from the list and the next person in
order will be contacted.
D. No Retroactivity. This policy shall not retroactively affect any person who
is already a boat slip lessee in good standing.
E. Effective Date. This policy shall be effective upon its adoption.
   Adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in regular session, December 13,
2012.

DECEMBER 26, 2012
MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN MINUTES
December 26, 2012
                  SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
   The Southport Board of Aldermen met Wednesday, December 26, 2012, in a
session recessed from December 13 and December 20, 2012. The meeting was called
to order by Mayor Robert Howard at 5:30 p.m. In addition to Mayor Howard, those
present included Mayor Pro Tem Mary Ellen Poole, Aldermen Nelson Adams, Buddy
Barnes, Todd Coring, Ken Karn, and Jim Powell, and City Manager Patrick Thomas.
Also attending was Ed Harper of the State Port Pilot.
   Mayor Howard provided the following updates regarding the property under
consideration for purchase at 1029 North Howe Street:
·   Novant Medical, which had a first-floor lease that would expire December
31, 2013, was willing to terminate the lease February 1 and had offered to pay
50 percent of the remaining lease amount for early termination of the lease;
·   Wells Fargo Financial, which had a lease expiring December 31, 2016 plus
two five-year options, had verbally expressed a willingness to early
termination of its lease, but had not thus far offered buy-out compensation;
·   Due to the holidays, the Building Committee had had difficulty meeting
together on various issues – including the lease termination possibilities –
but had met individually on some matters throughout the holidays;
·   All of the due diligence matters related to the property had been
completed, except that a report on the condition of the roof was not in hand.
The Mayor also reported that, shortly after the December 4 recommendation with
respect to the 1029 N. Howe Street property was made public, Security Savings
Bank (SSB) representatives came forward regarding their property at 300 North
Howe Street, as well as the former PJ’s Restaurant property on West West
Street. The former was offered for sale at $1.5 million and the latter at
$475,000. Initially advised that the cost would not be viable for consideration
by the City at $1.5 million, SSB then lowered, on December 20, its asking price
for the 300 North Howe building t to $1.2 million. More recently, SSB’s Board
had agreed to offer the building for sale to the City at $1,125,000, including
all of the high-quality furniture in the building, which its representative
said had originally cost $1 million.
Due to the significant difference in cost between the 1029 North Howe building
and the 300 North Howe Building, reported the Mayor, speculative conversations
had been held between him and the city manager about the viability of placing
three departments in the 300 North Howe building and using part of the cost
savings to perform improvements to the City Hall and provide another department
with expanded space within the City Hall building. He said that a preliminary
comparison of options had been prepared, but the committee had not met to
consider that information.
The Mayor reported that he had also inquired whether the owner of the 1029
North Howe building was willing to provide a 30-day extension of the
examination and closing period, and the realtor had responded that the owner
was willing to agree to an extension.
In discussion, Aldermen Powell indicated that he liked the 1029 North Howe
building because of the greater floor space (10,000 vs. 8,300) and the
potential for developing a municipal campus. Alderman Adams agreed, citing the
benefit of placing facilities closer to the center of town. Ms. Poole reminded
that the use of public monies was involved, and said she felt an in-depth
analysis should be done on the Security Savings building, and said the Board
should maintain its focus regarding the various goals that it had for the
future. Alderman Barnes said that, since a time extension was available, the
Board owed it to the public to give fair consideration to both options.
Alderman Karn said he agreed, but thought that the objective was to locate all
of the departments in one building.
Alderman Coring asked to see the preliminary comparison that had been prepared,
and the Mayor showed several slides that provided financial information and
other information regarding the two options.
Mayor Pro Tem Poole moved (a) that the Building Improvement Committee review
and analyze information regarding the two alternatives and bring that
information and a recommendation back to the whole board for consideration and
(b) that the City obtain a 30-day extension of the examination and closing
periods for the 1029 North Howe building. The motion was seconded by Alderman
Barnes and was approved with six aye votes and no noes.
The meeting was unanimously adjourned at 6:13 p.m. on the motion of Ms. Poole
and the second of Mr. Barnes.

had been working with Brunswick Electric Membership Corporation (BEMC) to
develop a multi-year work plan for the City’s electric system, with emphasis on
converting to underground service.
   Ms. Debra Fish, BEMC, made a PowerPoint presentation of the Six Year Work
Plan FY 2012/13 - FY 2017/18 (On file in the Clerk’s Office). The presentation
detailed the service area, distribution system, power supply, existing
conditions, load and customer growth projections, conversion of the electrical
system from overhead to underground, pole replacement, right-of-way trimming,
streetlight replacement, peak load, projected energy usage, system outages,
recommended improvements, and a cost summary for the six year plan. Ms. Fish
went through each budget year’s priority and cost estimates. She displayed maps
depicting the City’s substation, poles, switches, reclosers, and feeder lines.
   Year 1      $ 340,300
   Year 2      $ 329,160
   Year 3      $ 343,875
   Year 4      $ 309,537
   Year 5      $ 318,806
   Year 6      $ 319,141
    Mr. Lewis Shaw, BEMC, discussed the City’s commitment to replace high-
pressure sodium (HPS) and metal halide (MH) streetlights with light-emitting
diode (LED) streetlights which use approximately 30% fewer watts, require less
maintenance and provide a more uniform dispersion of light.
   Mayor Howard asked staff to provide cash flow forecasting to provide the
Board with a comfort level for commitment of the funding over time.
   Responding to Alderman Karn, Mr. Tucker indicated the City does not have a
policy requiring customers to hook up to underground electrical service when it
becomes available. He advised enacting a policy. Alderman Poole agreed it
should be mandatory to hook up. Ms. Fish pointed out the cost would be $1,250
for an individual customer to hook up. When asked by Alderman Karn, Ms. Fish
speculated a payment schedule could be set up for customers to pay over time.

Motion passed.   
A RESOLUTION REGARDING
PROPOSED USES OF THE FORT JOHNSTON PROPERTY
   WHEREAS the Fort Johnston property was donated to the City of Southport with
the intention that it be used for public park and recreational purposes; and
   WHEREAS the City’s use and management of the property remains subject to
general oversight by the U.S. Department of Interior and the North Carolina
Department of Cultural Resources; and
   WHEREAS the central and attractive location of Fort Johnston makes it an
attractive location for a wide variety of potential uses, both temporary and
permanent; and
   WHEREAS the City of Southport has a responsibility to give thorough and
deliberate consideration to all potential uses of the Fort Johnston property,
especially those that involve the installation of structures or structural
additions on the site;
   BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport that the
following policy is adopted with respect to proposed uses of the Fort Johnston
property that involve the installation of- or additions to permanent structures
on the site:
FORT JOHNSTON INSTALLATIONS POLICY
The following policy shall normally apply to any proposed uses of the Fort
Johnston property that involve the installation of structures or additions to
permanent structures on the site:
1. First Reading. The proposed use shall be provided, described, and/or
illustrated in detail and in written form, to the satisfaction of the Board of
Aldermen, and the requested use shall be presented at a regular meeting (or a
special meeting called for that purpose) of the Board. This presentation and
description, which may be required to be presented in a form prescribed by the
Board or City Manager, shall constitute the first reading of the proposed use.
If the Board agrees by majority vote, upon first reading, that it desires to
further consider the proposed use, the proposed use shall then be sent to any
appropriate agencies – including the State Historic Preservation Office – for
review and comment.
2. Second Reading. After receipt of any agency comments, the proposed use of
the property shall be scheduled for second reading by the Board of Aldermen,
which shall take place at a regular meeting unless otherwise advertised. On the
occasion of the second reading, the proposed use shall be advertised for public
comments. After receipt of public comments, the Board may, if it desires,
discontinue consideration of the proposed use or may give preliminary approval,
by majority vote, to the proposed use and schedule the proposal for third
reading.
3. Third Reading. After its initial decision to give further consideration to
the proposal, the receipt of agency and public comments, and a second decision
to give preliminary approval to the proposed use, the Board may give final
consideration to the proposed use at a third reading, which shall take place at
a regular meeting unless otherwise advertised. On that occasion, the Board may
elect to discontinue consideration of the proposed use, carry the matter over
for further consideration, or give final approval to the proposed use.
4. General. This policy is intended to describe the minimum process that should
be followed in considering permanent uses of the Fort Johnston property and is
not intended to inhibit any additional information requests, reviews,
investigations, opportunities for comment, or other measures considered
necessary by the Board of Aldermen in order to give thorough and deliberate
consideration to proposed uses of the property. In rare or extraordinary
circumstances involving opportunities or emergencies with deadlines beyond the
Board’s control, the Board may vary this policy as needed, while making every
effort to preserve its overall purpose and intent.
Adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in regular session, January 10,
2013.
                        s/Robert D. Howard, Mayor
Attest:
s/Regina W. Alexander, Clerk
