   Ms. Karen Mosteller, 310 N. Atlantic Avenue, read comments pertaining to the
proposed resolution opposing seismic surveying and oil and gas exploration and
drilling offshore the coast of North Carolina.
My name is Karen Mosteller and I am so very proud to live in Southport, North
Carolina.
In 2014, the Aldermen of the City of Southport passed a resolution in
opposition to the use of seismic airguns in our ocean, our Aldermen, stood up
for our community…stood up for a fundamental belief in our way of life, belief
in our responsibility as sound stewards of our unique coastal environment
…honoring our connection to the environment sitting here at the mouth of the
Cape Fear…
This evening our Aldermen are considering another resolution. This resolution
confirms our community’s position against the use of Seismic Airguns and speaks
out against Offshore Oil and Gas Exploration and Drilling off the North
Carolina Coast.
The National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) lists impulsive sound
sources such as airguns and impact pile drivers as having the greatest
potential to affect hearing sensitivity in marine mammals.
For those of us that may not be familiar with what the proposed seismic
surveying and the use of seismic airguns looks like…it’s a boat that can drag
as many as 20 to 30 seismic airguns with microphones strung out as far as 12
miles behind it; firing the airguns approximately every ten seconds, for days,
weeks and months on end. Each burst, from each gun is about 250 decibels, a jet
engine is 150 decibels. The human eardrum ruptures at 140 decibels. The sound
from air guns is not merely twice as loud, it is exponentially greater, each
guns’ release is louder than detonating a stick of dynamite, or a grenade.
The reason the explosive sound is so very loud is they are on the surface of
the ocean shooting through the water to create a map of the area over 2 miles
below the ocean floor.
Sound travels farther, faster and is amplified in water. Sounds this loud have
the potential to travel for hundreds and even thousands of miles through ocean
water according to Duke University Marine Lab Professor Dr. Doug Nowacek.
Earlier this year, when the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, BOEM, whose job
it is to manage the sale of the oil and gas leases, made their presentation in
Wilmington, I spoke directly with their staff Marine biologist. I asked her
what their plan was for guaranteeing the safety of our whales and dolphins.
And she said BOEM’s mitigation plan is to have spotters on the boats while they
are conducting seismic testing. And if one of their spotters sees an animal in
the area they will stop shooting the air guns. So the animal has to surface
within the sightline of the spotter to be detected. If the animal is close
enough to be seen before the powerful explosions under the water are stopped,
given the strength of the sound, this seems to be a flawed mitigation process.
And this does not even address the potential effects on other marine life, some
of which lives on the ocean floor and cannot move away from the sound.
In March of this year, 75 leading marine scientists, several from North
Carolina, signed a letter sent to President Obama stating that, “the magnitude
of the proposed seismic activity is likely to have significant, long-lasting,
and widespread impacts on the reproduction and survival of fish and marine
mammal populations in the region.”
Studies have proven that there’s only 10% of the big fishes left in our oceans
that were here 50 years ago. Hunted almost into extinction, there are only
about 450 North Atlantic Right Whales left on the planet and our Brunswick
County coast is part of their calving area.
Fisheries experts and both the Mid-Atlantic and South Atlantic Fishery
Management Councils have expressed grave concerns and opposition to the use of
seismic airguns and the potential effects on commercial and recreational fish
species in the area. The survival of much of our marine life depends on sound
and I think sometimes we forget that they are wild animals and for us to think
we can predict their exact migration patterns, locations and behaviors is
presumptuous at best.
The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management currently has 4 different applications
for permits to do seismic surveying in the Mid-Atlantic. These permits are for
overlapping areas and if these permits are granted they will be allowed to
begin seismic testing 3 miles off our shore.
If we reduce it to dollars, last year our Aldermen recognized that without
healthy marine life our economy would cease to exist. The resolution being
considered tonight supports our successful tourism and recreation and our
commercial and recreational fishing economies.
In 2014, North Carolina had a record 21.3 billion dollars spent in tourism. In
2014, North Carolina was the sixth most visited state in the nation. In 2014
Brunswick County was in the top 10 North Carolina counties for tourism.
Approximately 204,800 persons are employed in direct tourism jobs in North
Carolina and representing a 2014 tourism payroll of $4.9 billion.
Visitors to North Carolina generated more than $3.2 billion in federal, state
and local taxes. Because of North Carolina’s tourism industry, each North
Carolina household in 2014 saved $455 in state and local taxes as a direct
result of visitor spending in the state. In 2014 The NC Division of Marine
Fisheries (NCDENR) reported 2014 commercial fish landings in North Carolina to
be worth $93,843,254.
The jobs and the money estimates the American Petroleum Institute lobby group
and our state government, Governor McCrory, even North Carolina’s Secretary of
the Department of Environment and Natural Resources Donald van der Vaart are
quoting… come from a report, paid for by the American Petroleum Institute and
written by Quest Offshore Resources, who are according to their own website are
and I quote, “Quest Offshore is a boutique strategic advisory and consulting
firm to the global offshore Oil & Gas industry.”
The Quest report is not based on the current Bureau of Ocean Energy
Management’s (BOEM’s) proposal to sell one lease and drill 50 miles offshore
…No, the Quest Report is based on the premise that drilling will be allowed
closer to our shores, that BOEM will be allowed to sell 350 leases, and that
North Carolina will get revenue sharing that doesn’t even exist and would
require federal legislation to make it possible.
To put this idea of revenue sharing in perspective…Currently the Gulf States
have a revenue sharing plan. They get 37.5% of the leases, royalties and bonus
bids but it has a 500 million dollar cap…and in 2017 the cap will drop to 375
million dollars. This money is split between 4 states.
We all know results depend on who’s doing the math. In spite of the fact that
the Gulf States have a Revenue Sharing plan in place, in the past three years,
the Federal government received over 22 billion dollars and the Gulf States got
about 4 million to share among themselves.
Why would we here in North Carolina consider risking a successful 21.3 billion
dollar tourism industry for this; by anyone’s definition…it’s not smart
business.
According to NOAA’s website, spill accidents are caused by weather, human error
or equipment failure; not the lack of technology. And when something happens
that hasn’t happened before, then the oil and gas industry has to throw the
kitchen sink at it. Like the dispersant they used in the BP Deep Horizon spill…
Within a week after the spill, tens of thousands of gallons of the dispersant
Corexit were dumped into the Gulf from C-130 airplanes and blasted into the
gushing wellhead by subsea robots. Officials at the time judged that the
consequences were worth the risk.
A few weeks after the BP accident in May 2010,” Jane Lubchenco, director of the
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration NOAA, told reporters at a news
conference, “It’s a tradeoff decision to lessen the overall environmental
impact” she went on to say, “When an oil spill occurs, there are no good
outcomes.” The decision to use this dispersant made in those first panic-filled
weeks after the BP well blew has had catastrophic health effects on the
countless people that worked around it, even death, harmed animals and
ecosystems exposed to it, and may have undiscovered consequences for future
generations.
The onshore infrastructure, rail lines, tractor trailers, port expansion,
dredging to accommodate the tankers and the industrialization of our coastline
required to support offshore drilling will impact our coastal communities in
ways that will make us unrecognizable to ourselves.
The Alaskan Senator…Senator Murkowski has introduced a bill in Congress to
allow drilling structures as close as 12 miles to shore. The time is now for us
to speak out, to hold our Governor and our representatives in Raleigh and
Washington accountable. They need to represent us, they need to protect our
economy and our environment.
After tonight, with your leadership, your willingness to take a stand, I hope
each of us here carries this message out into our community and beyond. It’s
going to take all of us to stop this.
I stand before you grateful for your commitment, your willingness to consider
the importance of the things that make our Southport community so very special.
Thank you.

6.   Presentation of Electrical Rates & Rate Committee Recommendation
   City Manager McDuffie gave a presentation about a proposed new electric rate
structure. He explained the cost to the city to purchase electricity from the
North Carolina Eastern Municipal Power Agency (NCEMPA) which included the
kilowatt cost, operations and maintenance, billing, personnel, insurance,
transformers, and line and infrastructure costs. He further gave details to:
   ∙   An increase occurs during peak hours for which the city pays a “demand
cost,”
   ∙   Annual cost of $900,000 for 2,810 customers,
   ∙   The potential to lower costs for customers by using Load Management
switches,
   ∙   The proposed base rates match the rate of Brunswick Electric Membership
Corp. (BEMC),
   ∙   Customers will see savings in their per kilowatt/hour cost,
   ∙   The City will receive $800,000 annually from the sale of assets,
   ∙   The City will realize an annual reduction in revenue of $220,000,
   ∙   BEMC metering and billing will cost $425,000
   ∙   1,000 Load Management switches will be provided free of charge to
customers.
   City Manager McDuffie indicated that the commercial demand rates were not
recommended for change but did need to be reviewed in the future.
   City Manager McDuffie advised that the Rate Committee recommended adopting
the new rates, allowing BEMC to undertake billing for electricity and the city
to begin providing Load Management switches.
   Alderman Barnes motioned, second by Alderman Poole to approve the new rates
as recommended with the bills effective September 1 and to give away load
management switches right away and stop the rebate program.
Discussion
   Alderman Adams stated his support for the Rate Committee recommendation. He
suggested tabling the issue to allow citizens time to review the information
presented.
Ayes:   Aldermen Barnes, Poole, Powell, Humphreys
Abstain: Alderman Adams
Motion passed 5-0

10.   Traffic & Transportation Committee Recommendations
   Mr. Allen explained the recommendations from the Traffic & Transportation
Committee:
      1.   Remove four (4) parking spaces on the north side of Moore Street
immediately west of Caswell Avenue, and replace with two (2) parallel parking
spaces. This will improve the existing sight distance issue at that
intersection.
      2.   Paint crosswalks on Moore Street, immediately east of Caswell Avenue
and on Caswell Avenue, immediately north of Moore Street.
      3.   Make Yacht Basin Drive one way, northbound, between Bay and Moore
Streets.
      4.   “No Parking” signs be placed on the south side of W. West Street,
along the eastern half of the area between the third and fourth entrances to
Southport Marina, in order to alleviate ingress issues for customers of the
business located across West Street from the marina.
   Alderman Barnes motioned, second by Alderman Powell to approve removing four
(4) parking spaces on the north side of Moore Street immediately west of
Caswell Avenue, and replace with two (2) parallel parking spaces. Unanimous
vote; motion carried.
   Alderman Barnes motioned, second by Alderman Poole to paint crosswalks on
Moore Street, immediately east of Caswell Avenue and on Caswell Avenue,
immediately north of Moore Street. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   Alderman Powell recommended, and Board consensus was, for the City Manager
to change the speed limit on Brunswick Street to 10 mph, put up one-way signs,
increase enforcement, and study the area for improving conditions for
pedestrians.
   Alderman Poole motioned, second by Alderman Barnes not to accept the
recommendation to make Yacht Basin Drive one way. Unanimous vote; motion
carried.
   City Manager McDuffie reported that the manager of Southport Marina shared
his opposition to the recommendation to place “no parking” signs between the
entrances to the marina.
   Alderman Barnes, referencing his years on the Planning Board, noted that
when a business is being established, it must provide adequate ingress/egress
to the property without using the public right of way. He questioned if the
area needs to be better patrolled and enforced for illegal parking on the right
of way. He suggested the storage facility could improve access with one way in
and one way out.
   Alderman Powell pointed out that a fire truck would be unable to get into
the storage area if a boat was on fire.
   It was noted that W. West Street is a State road. The recommendation failed
due to lack of a motion.
11.   Police Chief Position
   Mayor Howard pointed out that the City Personnel Policy did not reflect the
practice of the City Manager and Police Chief living within the city limits.
   Alderman Poole motioned, second by Alderman Barnes to adopt the Resolution
Amending Article V of the Southport Personnel Policy with a 90 day period to
secure housing in the City and up to 90 additional days. Unanimous vote; motion
carried.
RESOLUTION AMENDING ARTICLE V OF THE SOUTHPORT PERSONNEL POLICY
   THAT WHEREAS, the positions of City Manager and Chief of Police are
extremely important and critical administrative positions within city
government and require the respect and confidence of the community; and
   WHEREAS, it is important that the persons holding these positions be a part
of the Southport Community and a resident of the City;
   NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT HEREBY RESOLVED as follows:
   1.   That Article V, Section 6 of the Southport Personnel Policy, entitled
“Qualification Standards”, is hereby amended by adding the following language
at the end of the present section:
      In addition, the City Manager and Chief of Police shall be and remain
residents of the City of Southport. In the event that the persons hired for
these positions do not reside within the City at the time of appointment, said
persons shall have 90 days to locate within the city limits. In the event of
unforeseen hardship, this period of time may be extended for up to 90
additional days by the Board of Aldermen.
   This the 13th day of August, 2015.            City of Southport

AN ORDINANCE AMENDING CHAPTER 10, ARTICLE III, OF THE SOUTHPORT CITY CODE
   BE IT ORDAINED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport that
section 10-63 of the Code of Ordinances is hereby amended to read as follows:
Sec. 10-63. Restrictions.
Except as may be specifically permitted or allowed by the City for special
events and activities, the following restrictions apply to those businesses and
activities regulated under this article:
   (a)   All permits hereunder shall be effective and valid only between the
hours of 8:30 a.m. to 9:00 p.m., except during July second through July sixth
when such licenses shall be valid between 8:30 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.
   (b)   The duration of sales for a peddler within any one block in any one
day shall be limited to thirty (30) minutes.
   (c)   Peddling shall not be permitted at any time within the rights of way
of Bay Street or Yacht Basin Drive.
   (d)   All sales are prohibited within marked fire zones, handicapped spaces
or other areas which prohibit parking.
   (e)   No peddler or itinerant merchant shall block or otherwise prevent the
public from using parking spaces when not in use by the vendor.
   (f)   No peddler shall leave a pushcart, wagon, vehicle or other conveyance
unattended on a city right of way or street.
   (g)   No pushcart, wagon, vehicle or other conveyance may be located within
fifty (50) feet of the principal public entrance to any food service business
area not owned by the peddler or vendor selling the merchandise approved for
sale under this Article.
   (h)   An itinerant merchant shall locate for the purpose of selling
merchandise only in the following zoning districts: Business District (BD) and
Highway Commercial (HC). It shall be unlawful to locate in any other zoning
district.
   (i)   Noise-making devices such as, but not limited to, bells, whistles,
gongs and recordings, may not be used to advertise or announce the sale of
products or merchandise.
   (j)   Itinerant merchants shall not locate within the right of way of any
public street in the city.
Adopted this 13th day of August, 2015.         City of Southport
                     By: /s/ Robert D. Howard, Mayor
ATTEST: /s/ Michele Windham, Clerk

AN ORDINANCE AMENDING CHAPTER 10, ARTICLE VII, OF THE SOUTHPORT CITY CODE
         BE IT ORDAINED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport that
Chapter 10, Article VII, of the Southport City Code is hereby amended to read
as follows:
ARTICLE VII. FOR-HIRE TOURS
DIVISION 1. GENERALLY
Sec. 10-156. Purpose and authority.
It is the purpose of this division to require that all walking and vehicle
tours operated in the city for profit be licensed and regulated as set forth in
this article. This article is not intended to regulate walking and vehicle
tours conducted by nonprofit organizations such as the Southport Historical
Society, the North Carolina Maritime Museum at Southport or schools.
Furthermore, the provisions of this article shall not apply to tours conducted
entirely off the public streets, sidewalks, rights-of-way or municipal
property.
Sec. 10-157. Definitions.
   The following words, terms, and phrases when used in this article shall have
the meaning described to them in this section, except where the context clearly
indicates a different meaning:
   Amplifying device shall mean any equipment or apparatus that broadens or
magnifies the human voice, music or any sound.
   Charter routes shall mean the approved route of travel for any tour.
   Person shall mean a natural person, corporation, company, partnership,
limited liability company, or other organization operating for profit.
   Public right-of-way shall mean any street, highway, sidewalk, parking lot or
alley that is owned, controlled, maintained or operated by the "city" or State
of North Carolina.
   Tour or touring shall mean the conducting of or the participation in
sightseeing on foot or in a vehicle in the "city" for hire or in combination
with a request for donations.
   Tour guide shall mean any person who acts or offers to act as a guide for
hire or compensation through any part of the "city" to pedestrians or vehicle
passengers.
   Tour guide permit shall mean the written authority granted by the tourism
commission for an individual to conduct a sightseeing tour on foot or by
vehicle within the "city".
   Vehicle shall mean bicycles, pedicabs, animal drawn or motorized vehicles
used to transport members of a sightseeing tour.
LICENSES AND BUSINESS REGULATIONS
DIVISION 2. TOUR GUIDE PERMIT
Sec. 10-158. Required Permit; Number of Permits.
   No person shall offer a for-hire tour within the corporate limits of the
"city" unless such person shall have first applied for and obtained from the
City a tour guide permit. It shall be unlawful for any person to operate a tour
in any manner contrary to the provisions of this article or without first
having obtained said permit. No more than 3 walking tour permits, 4 low-speed
vehicle tour permits and 1 animal-drawn vehicle permit may be issued and in
effect at any time.
Sec. 10-159. Application.
   Each applicant for a tour guide permit shall submit in writing an
application to the Tourism Commission containing the following information and
documentation: (Application forms available at the Southport Visitors Center)
   (1)   The name, address and telephone number of the owner and operator of
the business. If the applicant is a partnership, the names and addresses of the
general partners; if a corporation the names and addresses of the directors and
officers; if a limited liability company, the names and addresses of the
members and managers.
   (2)   A copy of a valid North Carolina driver’s license.
   (3)   A criminal record check of the previous 5 years which includes
criminal and driving record.
   (4)   The address and phone number from which the applicant will conduct
business operations.
   (5)   A description of the charter route to be used by the applicant
including starting point and stopping points along the route.
      (The tourism commission may alter starting location to prevent traffic
congestion).
   (4)   A description of the hours of operation of the proposed business and
the proposed hours during which the tours will be conducted.
   (5)   A detailed description of the information to be given to the members
of the tour related to those sights to be viewed within the "city", including a
copy of any published literature proposed to be provided by the tour guide to
any members of the tour.
   (6)   A statement showing that the tour guide has sufficient knowledge,
skill and information to conduct said tours.
   (7)   A schedule of the rates and charges proposed by the applicant in the
operation of the business.
   (8)   A certificate of general liability insurance in a minimum amount of
one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000.00) which specifically provides that the
same many not be cancelled without thirty (30) days written notice to the
"city".
   (9)   Proof of City of Southport Privilege License.
   (10)   Application fee of fifty dollars ($50.00) payable at the time of
application and annually thereafter as a renewal fee.
Sec. 10-160. Handicap accessibility.
   All proposed charter routes must follow handicap accessible public rights-
of-way appropriate to tours where walking is utilized by a walking tour or
exiting a tour vehicle.
Sec. 10-161. Hearing; approval.
   (a)   Upon receipt of the complete application for a tour guide permit, the
Tourism Commission shall conduct a hearing on the application within seven (7)
business days. The applicant shall be notified of the time, date and place of
the hearing at least forty-eight (48) hours in advance of the said hearing. The
Tourism Commission may recommend approval of the application to the Board of
Aldermen if it determines that:
      (1)   The applicant is able and sufficiently knowledgeable about the
history of the city to perform the proposed service.
      (2)   The applicant has not within five (5) years of the date of the
application been convicted of a felony, driving while impaired or any crime of
moral turpitude.
      (3)   The application is complete and sufficient with all necessary
documentation.
      (4)   The applicant meets all of the minimum qualifications for the tour
guide permit.
      (5)   The applicant is solvent and financially able to furnish adequate
service on a continuing basis and have the necessary insurance required.
      (6)   The proposed service will be carried out in a reasonably safe
manner so as not to interfere with the health, safety and welfare of
pedestrians, motor vehicles and the general public and the proposed tour will
not unreasonably interfere with the use of the streets, sidewalks, parking
lots, alleys, parks and other public properties within the "city".
      (7)   The maximum number of permits have not already been issued and in
effect.
      (8)   The tour, including any vehicle or conveyance, will be compatible
with the history and area of the City where the tour is conducted.
   (b) The Tourism Commission shall recommend approval or non-approval of the
application to the Board of Aldermen within 5 days of the hearing. The Tourism
Commission may recommend conditions to the tour guide permit as deemed
necessary in the interest of the health, welfare and safety of the public. The
Board of Aldermen shall consider the recommendation of the Tourism Commission
at the next regular meeting of the Board of Aldermen held more than 10 days
from the date of receipt of the Tourism Commission’s recommendation. At said
time, the Board of Aldermen may issue or deny the permit.
   (c)   Each tour guide permit granted by the Board of Aldermen shall be valid
for a period of one year and must be renewed annually. The permit shall include
the charter route and specific hours of operation. The Board of Aldermen shall
have the authority to set other conditions to the tour guide permit as deemed
necessary in the interest of the health, welfare and safety of the public.
Sec. 10-162. Prohibited acts.
   It shall be unlawful and a violation of this article and a violation of a
tour guide permit for any tour guide or any tour guide permit holder to:
   (1)   Fail to follow the approved charter route or move in a manner blocking
entrances to stores, homes, public parks, cemeteries or other places of
business or interfere with street traffic.
   (2)   Fail to follow the lawful commands of a law enforcement officer.
   (3)   Move on a sidewalk in excess of a column of two (2) persons abreast.
   (4)   Solicit members of the public verbally while such member of the public
is on any public street, public sidewalk of public property.
   (5)   Operate an amplifying device during the course of the tour without
specific written tourism commission approval.
   (6)   Fail to comply with all the conditions of the tour guide permit.
   (7)   Place a sign in a public space to promote the business except as
allowed below.
   (8)   Conduct a tour within the confines of a cemetery after dusk.
A temporary sign may be placed one (1) hour before the operating hours of the
tour, within one (1) block of the starting location of the tour and must be
removed at the end of the business day of the permit holder. Both the starting
location of the tour and the location of the temporary sign must be approved by
the Tour Commission.
Sec. 10-163. Revocation.
   The Board of Aldermen may revoke a tour guide permit after a hearing
conducted with forty-eight (48) hours' notice to the permit holder upon the
following grounds:
   (1)   A violation of the terms and conditions of this ordinance or the
conditions of the tour guide permit.
   (2)   Upon determining that false information was given on the application
for a tour guide permit.
   (3)   The cancellation or revocation of the tour guide permit holder's
liability insurance coverage.
   (4)   The business closing of the holder of a tour guide permit.
   (5)   Conviction of a felony, driving while impaired or crime involving the
moral turpitude by a tour guide or permit holder.
   (6)   Failing to operate the tour business for 90 consecutive days.
Sec. 10-164. Transfer.
   The tour guide permit issued pursuant to this article shall not be
transferred by the permit holder.
Sec. 10-165. Violations.
   In addition to revocation of a tour guide permit, the violation of any of
the provisions of the ordinance shall subject the offender to a civil penalty
in the amount of fifty dollars ($50.00) per violation to be collected by the
"city" in the nature of a debt. Each day a continuing violation shall be deemed
a separate violation.
Sec. 10-166.  Exemptions.
   Exempt from this article are walking and vehicle tours conducted by non-
profit organizations such as the Southport Historical Society, The North
Carolina Maritime Museum at Southport and schools. Exempt, non-profit
organizations are subject to the provisions of this article in all matters
related to health and safety, right-of-way and public access concerns.
DIVISION 3. TOURISM COMMISSION
Sec. 10-167. Tourism Commission.
   A Tourism Commission is hereby established to study issues relating to for-
hire tours within the City of Southport, to make recommendations after a review
and study and to execute the provisions of this article regulating for-hire
tours. The Tourism Commission shall consist of three (3) members and shall
include the director of tourism for the City of Southport, the chief of police
of Southport and the code enforcement officer for the City of Southport. The
administrative activities of the Tourism Commission will be placed with the
department of tourism for the City of Southport. The Tourism Commission will
report to the Board of Aldermen and make recommendations when necessary related
to the ordinance.
This the 13th day of August, 2015.         City of Southport
                     /s/ Robert D. Howard, Mayor
ATTEST: /s/ Michele Windham, Clerk
15.   Discussion/Resolution Opposing Off Shore Exploration/Production of Oil/
Gas Resources off the Coast
   Alderman Poole shared her personal sentiments; “I want to speak from the
heart. I am passionate about this. All of us have acknowledged that we are at
the mouth of the Cape Fear River, the jewel that keeps people coming back and
moving here. Many of us come from families that made their living on the water.
I want to preserve that. I was always taught to respect the ocean.”
   Alderman Poole motioned, second by Alderman Barnes to approve the Resolution
in continued opposition of seismic surveying and stated opposition to oil and
gas offshore exploration and drilling on the continental shelf off the coast of
North Carolina. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
RESOLUTION IN CONTINUED OPPOSITION OF SEISMIC SURVEYING AND STATED OPPOSITION
TO OIL AND GAS
OFFSHORE EXPLORATION AND DRILLING ON THE CONTINENTAL SHELF OFF THE COAST OF
NORTH CAROLINA
WHEREAS, the City of Southport is committed to being a sound steward of the
unique coastal environment, including the rare maritime forest, estuaries,
marshes, and pristine beaches on and around our regional coastal communities;
and
WHEREAS, the Aldermen of the City of Southport recognize that Southport’s
economic survival solely depends on the sustainability of the existing
environment; and
WHEREAS, on March 5, 2015, a letter was sent to President Obama signed by 75
leading marine scientists expressing their concern over the significant threat
to marine life posed by the introduction of seismic oil and gas exploration
along the U.S. Mid-Atlantic and South Atlantic coasts. The letter further
states, “Opening the U.S. East Coast to seismic airgun exploration poses an
unacceptable risk of serious harm to marine life at the species and population
levels, the full extent of which will not be understood until long after the
harm occurs.” The scientists’ letter serves as additional confirmation of the
City of Southport’s previous resolution in opposition of the use of seismic
airguns.
WHEREAS, exploratory and commercial drilling, extraction, and transportation of
offshore oil and gas resources pose a significant risk of spill; and
WHEREAS, offshore drilling requires substantial onshore infrastructure, such as
pipelines and/or refineries, which will further risk the health and safety of
the environment, character and natural beauty of North Carolina’s coast; and
WHEREAS, it is known that the 20 counties that comprise North Carolina’s
coastal region generate more commercial and personal income, public revenues,
and employment opportunities than the petroleum and natural gas industry is
estimated to generate for the State, specifically,
   1.   In 2014, a record $21.3 billion in domestic visitor/tourism spending
was realized in North Carolina; and
   2.   In 2014, North Carolina was the sixth most visited state in the nation.
Out of the 100 counties in the State of North Carolina, in terms of travel
expenditures, three of the top 10 counties were coastal counties; and
   3.   In 2014, direct tourism employment in North Carolina is approximately
204,800 persons, with direct tourism payroll of $4.9 billion; and
   4.   Visitors to North Carolina generated more than $3.2 billion in federal,
state and local taxes in 2014; and
   5.   The NC Division of Marine Fisheries (NCDENR) reported 2014 commercial
fish landings in North Carolina to be worth $93,843,254; and
   6.   Because of North Carolina’s tourism industry, each North Carolina
household in 2014 saved $455 in state and local taxes as a direct result of
visitor spending in the state; and
WHEREAS, visitors from all over the world come to enjoy the natural beauty of
our clean beaches, salt and freshwater marshes, inlets, estuaries and
tributaries; and
WHEREAS, the City of Southport and her surrounding coastal communities are rich
in natural areas that provide sanctuary, nesting and breeding grounds for
diverse groups of migratory birds, turtles, dolphin, whales, fish and other
wildlife, some of which are on the endangered species list; and
WHEREAS, North Carolina’s coastal waters and natural habitats provide the world
with some of the best wild-caught seafood, renowned for its freshness and
exceptional quality; and
WHEREAS, the inherent risks to North Carolina’s 320 miles of valued coastline
from seismic surveying, offshore oil and natural gas exploration and drilling
have the potential to irrevocably harm our natural environment, our economic
well-being and our overall quality of life; and
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, the Aldermen of the City of Southport reaffirm
the resolution passed in 2014 in opposition to seismic surveying and are
opposed to the exploration and development of oil/gas resources on the
continental shelf or elsewhere off the coast of North Carolina; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED the Aldermen of the City of Southport stand in
solidarity with North Carolina coastal communities and communities who may be
affected by the onshore infrastructure supporting offshore exploration and
drilling and who may suffer long-term social, economic and environmental
impacts from offshore exploration and production of petroleum resources on the
continental shelf off the coast of North Carolina.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED the Aldermen of the City of Southport call upon all
North Carolina municipal and county governing bodies of North Carolina to pass
similar resolutions to this one and that the League of Municipalities joins in
this effort.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED the Aldermen of the City of Southport urge the Governor
McCrory and the entire North Carolina General Assembly to oppose offshore
petroleum production policies that risk the health, safety and sound
environmental stewardship of North Carolina’s coastline whose natural beauty
attracts a proven tourism-driven economy.
On Behalf of the City of Southport Board of Aldermen:
                         /s/ Robert D. Howard, Mayor
Attest: /s/ Michele Windham, City Clerk

A RESOLUTION REQUESTING THE NORTH CAROLINA DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION
UNDERTAKE A STUDY OF AN
ADDITIONAL TRAFFIC LIGHT ON NORTH HOWE STREET
WHEREAS, the citizens of the City of Southport and all those who visit,
appreciate and enjoy the unique history, charm and appeal that the Southport
area offers; and
WHEREAS, the safe use of roads and highways is of utmost importance to not only
the citizens of Southport, but also to our visitors from this great State and
other states and countries; and   
WHEREAS, Howe Street is a state-maintained road and has only three signalized
intersections and thirteen unsignalized intersections; and
WHEREAS, this creates a dangerous situation for drivers attempting to turn left
onto Howe Street from these numerous unsignalized intersections.
BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport, North
Carolina, that the City of Southport requests that the North Carolina
Department of Transportation undertake a feasibility study for adding a traffic
light on N. Howe Street in the area between 9th & 12th Streets.

SOUTHPORT
RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF INTERNATIONAL DAY OF PEACE
WHEREAS, The United Nations in 1981 established a yearly International Day of
Peace, a day devoted to strengthening the ideals of peace both within and among
all nations and people; and
WHEREAS, The International Day of Peace is now observed around the world each
year on September 20 to put aside all that separates us and to experience
peace; and
WHEREAS, in 1984, the General Assembly adopted the Declaration on the Right of
Peoples to Peace; and
WHEREAS, the theme of the 2015 International Day of Peace is “Partnerships For
Peace - Dignity For All”; and
WHEREAS, Southport residents are coordinating a celebration of the
International Day of Peace on a local level; and
WHEREAS, the Celebration of Peace will be held and will include songs, dances,
art, informational booths and exhibits, a Peace Circle discussion, chidren
crafts, and a Peace Pilgrim film; and
NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Mayor and Southport Board of Aldermen
on this the 1st day of September 2015, hereby proclaim Sunday, September 20,
2015 as “Peace Day” in the City of Southport and urge all citizens to join in
the festivities of this day and promote peace among all peoples.

5.   Resolution of Support for Southport-Oak Island Area Economic Development
Committee
   Alderman Poole motioned, second by Alderman Barnes to adopt the Resolution
of Support for Southport-Oak Island Area Economic Development and to appoint
John Allen to the committee. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
Resolution of Support For Southport Oak Island Area Economic Development
Committee
WHEREAS, the Southport-Oak Island Area Chamber of Commerce has faithfully
served the needs of the Southport-Oak Island area for over 35 years, including
Bald Head Island, Boiling Spring Lakes, Bolivia, Caswell Beach, Oak Island, St.
James, Southport, Sunset Harbor and Supply; and
WHEREAS, the Southport-Oak Island Area Chamber of Commerce is a viable,
thriving organization, providing effective leadership; and
WHEREAS, the Southport-Oak Island Area Chamber of Commerce continues to work on
issues and needs important to our area and business community; and
WHEREAS, the Southport-Oak Island Area Chamber of Commerce supports existing
small businesses in the area with programs such as Business Connections,
Business Networking After Hours, Shop Small Saturday, Gift Local and
recognitions such as the Golden Pineapple Awards, Small Business Person of the
Year and Small Business Customer Service of the Year; and
WHEREAS, the Southport-Oak Island Chamber of Commerce remains committed to
promote businesses in the Southport-Oak Island and surrounding areas; and
WHEREAS, the goal of the Southport –Oak Island Area Chamber of Commerce is to
remain responsive to the unique opportunities and challenges of its service
area and Brunswick County as the Southport-Oak Island Area Chamber of Commerce;
and
WHEREAS, the Southport Oak Island area has seen tremendous population growth as
indicated from the U.S. Census Bureau which indicates the Town of Oak Island
realized a 6% growth in its population from 2010-2013, with the State of North
Carolina only showing 3% growth, and at the same time a recent traffic count
showed an average of 30,000 vehicles a day on Rt 211 west of Rt 87 – second
highest in Brunswick County; and
WHEREAS, the Southport-Oak Island Area Chamber of Commerce recognizes a need
for industrial, commercial and small business recruitment efforts in the
Southport Oak Island area to support this growing population; and
WHEREAS, in the past there has not been an aggressive business and industry
recruitment effort for the Southport Oak Island area;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, City of Southport supports the Southport-Oak
Island Area Chamber of Commerce in its creation of the Southport Oak Island
Area Economic Development Committee and further resolves to recognize them as
the lead support agency in promoting industry and business recruitment in our
local community and agrees to appoint a representative to the committee.
This the 10th day of September, 2015
                     /s/ Robert D. Howard,
Mayor

8.   Waterfront Steering Committee Presentation
   Mr. Tommy Harrelson, Chair, Waterfront Steering Committee, thanked the Board
for the trust they placed in the committee. He stated the committee worked hard
and well with each other, the consultants and the public. He thanked the
members of the Beautification Committee that participated and he praised the
assistance of city staffers John Allen, Gayle Jones and the city manager. Mr.
Harrelson expressed appreciation for the use of the former visitor center and
the valuable news coverage provided by Jason Tyson of the State Port Pilot. Mr.
Harrelson stated there were many ideas shared at the public meetings and the
consultants were careful capturing them. He indicated the committee endorsed
living shorelines and placing erosion control as the top priority of the
project. He added that the committee recommends Plan D which they feel offers
the least change and protects the view. He stated that the committee recommends
improvements in green areas, a limited number of trees, a maritime memorial
funded with donations and adoption of the erosion control measures.
   Mr. Mark Arcuri, P.E., Criser Troutman Tanner, gave a PowerPoint
presentation detailing the Southport Waterfront Project. He described the
recommendations for shoreline stabilization at six (6) identified segments, and
park improvements to the area bordered by S. Lord Street and S. Atlantic Avenue
and between Bay Street and the water. He explained the cost breakdown of the
project and apprised the Board of funding options through grant agencies.

process continues.

13.   Discussion on Merging the Fire Department and Rescue Squad
   Mayor Howard reported that the bids are out for the renovation of the Rescue
Squad facility and is estimated to be $330,000. He pointed out that the
Emergency Services Committee, comprised of Alderman Poole, Alderman Coring,
Chief Drew, Chief Johnson and Chief Smith, have worked diligently over the last
several years to bring all departments together. Mayor Howard stated his
opinion that it is sensible to consider the feasibility and advisability of
merging fire and rescue. Mayor Howard asked Alderman Coring to comment on the
issue.
Alderman Coring suggested that the Emergency Services Committee meet to
evaluate the issue further. He stated that the chiefs of both fire and rescue
have been working with the Committee. He indicated he believes a merger would
be a good partnership, cost effective, would upgrade overall response time and
improve customer service. He pointed out that many of the rescue squad
personnel hold firefighter certifications.
Alderman Poole concurred with Alderman Coring, and as Chair of the Emergency
Services Committee, she will schedule and post a meeting.
Alderman Adams urged caution funding a renovation to the Rescue Squad
Headquarters on E. Nash Street. He shared his opinion that money could be
better spent constructing a new building at a more central location.
Alderman Powell endorsed the recommendation for the Emergency Services
Committee to discuss the feasibility of merging the two departments and scaling
back the renovation to the current Rescue Squad facility.
Chief Drew thanked the Board for the opportunity to explore merging the Fire
Department and Rescue Squad. He expressed his belief that if an organization is
not changing and evolving, it is not growing. He stated he looks forward to
holding discussions with the Rescue Squad and coming up with solutions and
ideas.
Chief Johnson agreed with Chief Drew and stated his belief that the merger
would be a benefit to the citizens and departments.
Alderman Barnes motioned, second by Alderman Powell to direct the Emergency
Services Committee to meet and report back to the Board of Aldermen at their
October regular meeting on merging the Fire and Rescue Department. Unanimous
vote; motion carried.
14.   Consideration of a Proposal from Brunswick Community College
Mayor Howard announced that the City has been asked to join with Brunswick
Community College and the University of North Carolina School of Government to
consider effective community uses for the 9,000 square feet of unused space in
the Brunswick Community College Lord Street Annex.
Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Coring to join with Brunswick
Community College in meeting with the School of Government on Thursday,
September 17, 3:30 p.m. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
Board Comments
Mayor Howard remarked about the Brunswick County Commissioners announcement to
take over maintenance and operation of Southport’s water and sewer systems. He
stated his surprise at the announcement noting that the cost suggested by the
County appears more expensive than what the city can do in house. He also
pointed out that if the Board considered a contractual arrangement, the city
employees could not be displaced from their jobs. He expressed appreciation for
the Commissioners taking a look at a possible partnership and he looked forward
to reviewing the proposal.
Mayor Howard addressed comments made concerning the recent reorganization of
city staff. He stated the city manager is charged with the responsibility of
carrying out the city’s work and he chose to divide his departments into five
(5) groups: Public Safety, Finance, Public Works, Parks & Recreation,
Administration and to appoint group leaders. Mayor Howard pointed out that no
departments had been eliminated, no department head positions were eliminated,
and there were no demotions and no salary adjustments. He stated his support
for the city manager and he praised the job city staff performs.
Alderman Coring stated his concerns about the reorganization, specifically the
Human Resources/Payroll Department answering to the City Clerk and the
additional responsibilities of a Public Safety Director. He emphasized caution
about how the reorganization is presented and the need to assure the public has
a clear understanding of it.
Mayor Howard contested the letter Ms. Bray presented regarding the financial
condition of the City. He stated the City is in a solid financial position and
carries a fund balance. He noted that the audit is underway and he expressed
confidence that the audit will show that Ms. Bray’s accusations and assertions
are unfounded.
The Clerk was directed to provide dates to the Board for a workshop to discuss
the waterfront plans.

SEPTEMBER 17, 2015
SPECIAL SESSION MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN           SPECIAL SESSION MINUTES
BRUNSWICK COMMUNITY COLLEGE SEPTEMBER 17, 2015
BOLIVIA, N.C.               3:30 P.M
PRESENT:         Mayor Robert D. Howard
            Aldermen Nelson Adams, Emily Humphreys, Jim Powell,
            Todd Coring, Buddy Barnes
STAFF PRESENT:      City Manager Kerry McDuffie
         City Clerk Michele Windham
   Mayor Howard and Aldermen met with members of the Brunswick Community
College Board of Trustees to hear a presentation from Mr. Rory Dowling, a
project manager with the University of North Carolina School of Government’s
Development Finance Initiative (DFI). Mr. Dowling explained that the mission of
DFI is to partner with North Carolina municipalities to attract private
investors for transformation projects.
   Mr. Dowling gave a detailed presentation of the process for redevelopment of
the unrenovated portion of the Brunswick Community College satellite campus on
N. Lord Street and on the former site of the Brunswick County Training School,
and the adjoining gymnasium that the college deeded to Southport. He explained
the 4-prongs of the pre-development methodology: site analysis, market
analysis, public proposal and financial feasibility. Mr. Dowling stated the
goal is to attract a private developer, maximize public interest but minimize
public investment.
   Responding to a question from Dr. Suzanne Adams, Brunswick Community College
President, Mayor Howard stated the city’s current plans for the gym is to make
it available to the community as a multi-use facility. He pointed out that the
gym has historical value for the citizens of Southport.
   Mr. Dowling noted the area is zoned residential and he indicated the
potential to rezone the area to mixed use to accommodate other options, such as
a neighborhood grocery, would need to be considered by the Southport Planning
Board and Board of Aldermen.
   Concerns about the condition of the building were raised and it’s potential
for development.
   Mr. Dowling advised that the pre-development process would take an estimated
nine months and the fee for the study would be $27,000.
   Alderman Adams concurred with Mayor Howard’s statements and he thanked the
college for imparting the city with the opportunity to bring the gym back for
recreational uses by the community.
                        /s/ Robert D. Howard, Mayor
Attest: /s/ Michele Windham, City Clerk

BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL SESSION MINUTES
COMMUNITY BUILDING SEPTEMBER 29, 2015
223 E. BAY STREET  4:00 P.M
 
PRESENT:         Mayor Robert D. Howard
            Aldermen Mary Ellen Poole, Nelson Adams, Emily Humphreys,
            Jim Powell, Todd Coring, Buddy Barnes

   Frank Marchetti, Paul Swenson, Bill Duke, Harley Lemons
A)   Call to Order – 4:00 p.m.
   Mayor Howard called the meeting to order at 4:00 p.m. and stated the purpose
of the meeting was to discuss the riverfront restoration.
B)   Invocation
   Alderman Barnes welcomed everyone and led the gathering in the Lord’s
Prayer.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
   Alderman Barnes led the assemblage in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)   Announcements
   Mayor Howard discussed the significant tidal flooding experienced September
26-27, 2015 in the Yacht Basin area. He pointed out that the Board had engaged
Norris & Tunstall Consulting Engineers to submit proposals for drainage
improvements at Davis Street, Yacht Basin Drive, Bay Street and Moore Street.
He discussed the planned widening of the 300 block of W. Moore Street and
expressed his hope the widening and drainage improvements could be completed
simultaneously. He advised that the City Manager and staff would provide
information for the October 8 regular Board meeting.
   Mayor Howard announced that the Board met with Brunswick Community College
officials to hear a presentation from the School of Government regarding the
City joining the College in development of the Lord Street facility. He pointed
out that the School of Government only works through municipalities and the
College would like Southport to support the endeavor. He stated that
consideration of the request would be placed on the October 8 regular meeting
agenda.
   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Barnes to table consideration
of the operating and maintenance (O&M) proposal of the City’s water and sewer
systems from Brunswick County until such time the City can resolve the sewer
availability issue and transfer to the City the water service for the Rivermist
Subdivision.
   Discussion
   Alderman Adams stated his perception that the issue of an O&M proposal was
previously addressed by a consensus of the Board that the City was not
entertaining a proposal.
   Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   City Manager McDuffie announced that two (2) poles at the Atlantic Avenue
and Bay Street intersection had been knocked down and would be replaced with
one of the new style poles which would better direct light.
   Southport Waterfront Project
   Mayor Howard thanked the Waterfront Steering Committee for an outstanding
job. He guided the Board towards selection of a specific plan and establishing
priorities. He noted that the Committee recommended Plan D.
   Committee member Paul Swenson stated his personal recommendation that
erosion should be the highest priority and bulkheads with wide walkways
implemented. He cited successful bulkheads in New Bern, Beaufort, Charleston,
South Carolina and Savannah, Georgia. He also recommended preservation of the
beach from Old American Fish Company to the Bay Street pump station.
Additionally, he endorsed the living shoreline that has been successful along
Kingsley Park.
   Alderman Barnes commented that bulkheads are known to last 100 years+.
   Alderman Humphreys suggested the Board focus on erosion control.
   Alderman Barnes motioned, second by Alderman Poole to adopt Plan D as the
official city recommendation. Unanimous vote by an uplift of hands; motion
carried. 
   Mayor Howard noted that Plan D encompasses the area from American Fish to S.
Atlantic Avenue. Responding to a query from Alderman Barnes, Mayor Howard
stated that funding of shoreline erosion control on private property would have
to be considered.
   Mr. Frank Marchetti pointed out that the erosion control recommendation of
the Plan extends past Atlantic Avenue to Bonnets Creek.
   Alderman Poole agreed with Alderman Humphreys that the first priority of the
Plan should be erosion control.
    Alderman Powell agreed with Aldermen Humphreys and Poole. He stated his
opinion that North Carolina had, in recent years, built rip rap walls that have
been successful building beaches back out.
   Alderman Coring echoed the comments of fellow board members. He stated he
would like to look into the positives and negatives of additional types of
erosion control.
   City Manager McDuffie pointed out that Criser, Troutman & Tanner (CTT) is
contracted to identify funding sources. He indicated proposals to write grants
would be solicited from engineers and he would prefer to work with an
engineering group that had written similar grants.
   Mayor Howard stated his personal opinion that using an engineering firm to
write grants may not be the best approach. Alderman Powell agreed and cited the
Bay Street pump station preservation project with the Corps of Engineers. He
stated there are good grant writers that reside in Southport.
   Alderman Humphreys noted that the Plan is divided into segments and she
recommended focusing on one segment at a time for funding purposes.
   Alderman Barnes agreed, pointing out that the park cannot be built until the
erosion problem is solved. He stated support for a bulkhead with walkway.
   Alderman Barnes motioned, second by Alderman Coring for completion of the
erosion control and stabilization to be the #1 priority of the project.
Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   Mayor Howard suggested consideration of partnering with someone that could
open doors in Washington, D.C. He further encouraged scrutiny of the city’s
budget and making prudent decisions for setting aside funding for the project.
He recommended contacting Mike McIntrye, former Congressman, to ascertain the
feasibility of him assisting the city in the endeavor. Mayor Howard emphasized
the valuable relationship Mr. McIntrye has with the Corps of Engineers.
Aldermen Powell and Poole concurred with Mayor Howard.
   Alderman Poole motioned, second by Alderman Barnes to ask Mike McIntrye to
come in and make a proposal. Unanimous vote; motion carried. 
   Waterfront Steering Committee member Frank Marchetti suggested involving
Senator Bill Rabon on the State level. He pointed out that the wake created by
the Bald Head Island Ferry contributes to the shoreline erosion and he
recommended opening dialogue with Bald Head Island officials to address the
issue.
Announcement
   Alderman Poole announced that the Board would be hosting a public reception
for Mayor Howard who will be leaving office in December. The reception will
take place Thursday, October 8, 4:30 p.m. in the Community Building with the
regular Board meeting following at 6:00 p.m.
Adjournment – 4:55 p.m.
   Alderman Powell motioned to adjourn the meeting, second by Alderman Barnes.
Unanimous vote; motion carried.
                        /s/ Robert D. Howard, Mayor

Alderman Poole motioned, second by Alderman Barnes to approve the Resolution of
Recognition for the 60 th Anniversary of MOTSU. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
Resolution of Recognition
Military Ocean Terminal Sunny Point
Whereas, in 1950, the Department of Defense selected the remote region of
Southeastern North Carolina, known to locals as “Sunny Point”, on which to
build the largest munitions terminal in the free world, and
Whereas, On October 25, 1955 the terminal became operational, and
Whereas, the terminal was constructed as Wilmington Ammunition Loading
Terminal, then Sunny Point Army Ammunition Loading Terminal; further, Sunny
Point Army Terminal and now Military Ocean Terminal Sunny Point (MOTSU), and
Whereas, MOTSU is the home of the surface deployment and distribution command’s
596th Transportation Brigade, and
Whereas, Sunny Point fulfills the essential task of supplying munitions to the
United States Military, and
Whereas, Sunny Point is an integral part of Southport and the surrounding
communities, providing well-paying jobs for 250 people, and
Whereas, Sunny Point extends mutual aid to Southport’s Fire and Rescue
Departments, and
Whereas, Sunny Point was instrumental in re-building Southport after Hurricane
Hazel.
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that Mayor Robert D. Howard and the Southport
Board of Aldermen extend abiding appreciation for outstanding contributions,
and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that we urge all citizens to join with the Southport
Board of Aldermen in honoring the 60th anniversary of Sunny Point.
Adopted this the 8th day of October 2015.
                     /s/ Robert D. Howard, Mayor
Attest: /s/ Michele Windham, City Clerk

Bay Street & Yacht Basin Drive
   The Board heard a conceptual plan from Phil Norris of Norris and Tunstall
Consulting Engineers for a project to improve drainage and reduce tidal
flooding in the Yacht Basin. Mr. Norris cited a previous report that identified
tide levels. He noted the normal high tide is 2.5 ft. and historical high tide
is 4.1 ft. He explained the recommended improvements would raise the street
elevation to 3.5 ft. which would improve stormwater drainage and be more
manageable than putting in culverts and catch basins. He emphasized that
private property owners would have to participate in the project. Mr. Norris
estimated the cost of the project would be $125,000.
   Mayor Howard pointed out that the Yacht Basin area is included in the
overall Waterfront Project. He stated his support for moving forward to the
design stage of the plan.
   Alderman Adams emphasized taking time to obtain a formal design that would
be presented to affected property owners and to Southport citizens.
   Alderman Barnes expressed support for the concept and pursuing more details
and costs of the different types of materials to be used.
   Asked by Mayor Howard to comment, Building Inspector, Wayne Strickland
stated the project would likely require a Coastal Area Management Act (CAMA)
major permit.
   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Aldermen Coring to authorize Norris &
Tunstall to prepare the design drawings, bring same back to the Board and to
contact CAMA and staff to concurrently have conversations with property owners.
Ayes:   Aldermen Powell, Coring, Poole, Barnes, Humphreys
Nay:   Alderman Adams
Motion Carried 5-1
Response to a Citizen’s Letter
   Mayor Howard reported that legal and auditing services were engaged to
address assertions and accusations of improper activities made by a former
employee.
   City Attorney Isenberg stated he had met with Menton Padgett, auditor, who
thoroughly reviewed all city budget amendments. Attorney Isenberg presented
responses to each specific allegation:
By statute the city manager has no authority to spend more money than is
approved in public hearings before the board – Generally true but only one
“public hearing” is required and that is for the Budget Ordinance. It appears
that all money spent in 2014/15 was approved by board of aldermen.
Inter-departmental transfers are limited to $ 5,000 – G.S. 159-15 provides that
“The governing board by appropriate resolution or ordinance may authorize the
budget officer to transfer moneys from one appropriation to another within the
same fund subject to such limitations and procedures as it may prescribe. Any
such transfers shall be reported to the governing board at its next regular
meeting and shall be entered in the minutes.” Our board has authorized the
manager to transfer up to $5,000 within the same fund pursuant to this
provision. If more than that is transferred there needs to be a budget
amendment first. If money is expended before the budget is amended, it is a
violation of state statutes, until the budget is amended. The pre-audit
requirement mandates review of the current budget to determine that budgeted
funds are available before an expenditure is made.
In 2015 McDuffie obligated the city to more than $ 150,000.00 outside of this
process, without hearings or budget amendments—There were budget amendments for
the expenditures approved by the board. No hearing is required for budget
amendments.
  Expenditures approved in April 2015 included $ 143,000.00 in costs incurred
many months prior –This amendment did not appropriate fund balances. It
decreased 3 line items within the water fund and appropriated these amounts
within the water fund. It did not increase the expenses of the water fund. .
There were some improvements that were budgeted in the prior year that did not
get completed. The April budget amendment re-budgeted them because there was no
budget for them in the current budget.
A June 2015 amendment added $ 170,000.00 for spending actions taken throughout
the previous year – No fund balance was used. There was an increase of 170,000
in revenues and this additional revenue was appropriated within the fund for
expenditures.
McDuffie unilaterally gutted the budget in a series of actions take away from
the public eye. He shrunk 8 departments and added a full time position and
eliminated a tourism department funded by occupancy tax. He also did not do
this in an open session and the board did not authorize the amendments – Again,
money was transferred within the fund but no additional money was appropriated.
Both the city charter and GS 160A-148 empower the city manager to supervise the
administration of all departments. Those personnel actions do not have to be
approved in a public meeting. The board did approve the additional full time
position at its’ special meeting and did in fact approve the necessary budget
amendments at its next regular meeting.
Aldermen Barnes, Poole, Humphreys and Mayor Howard expressed their confidence
in the job performance of the City Manager.
City Manager McDuffie thanked the Board for their continued support.
2.   Emergency Services Committee Report; Fire & Rescue Merger
Alderman Poole reported that the Emergency Services Committee consisting of
herself, Alderman Coring, Fire Chief Drew, Rescue Chief Johnson, Public Safety
Director/Police Chief Smith and the City Manager, had met and reached a
recommendation for the merger of the Fire Department and Rescue Squad.
Alderman Coring outlined the proposal:
∙   Rescue Squad would dissolve and their Emergency Medical Services function
would become a division of the Southport Fire Department.
∙   One department would be established with a fire division and an EMS
division.
∙   Current members of Rescue would transfer over to Fire Department.
∙   Headquarters at 1011 N. Howe Street would be the main station of operation.
∙   A full-time Deputy Chief position would be established to supervise the EMS
division.
∙   The current Rescue Squad building would become a Southport Fire Department
downtown substation.
∙   Renovations to the current Rescue Squad building would be modified.
   Alderman Coring noted that the two departments worked hard through
challenges and compromises to reach the consolidation.
   Public Safety Director Smith stated his support for the merger noting that
it will enhance the services.
   Chief Drew stated the merger would be cost-effective for the citizens of
Southport and he received 100% cooperation among the members of the Fire
Department.
   Chief Johnson said the Rescue Squad membership fully supported the merger
and it would improve all aspects of rescue services.
Alderman Barnes motioned, second by Alderman Powell to accept the committee
recommendation with a November 1, 2015 effective date. Unanimous vote; motion
carried.
The Mayor directed the committee and City Manager to work with the City
Attorney to assure the ordinances and by-laws are in compliance with State
statutes.
Alderman Poole stated the committee also discussed the potential for the animal
control function to be assumed by Brunswick County. Chief Smith was charged
with communicating with the County on the issue and reporting back.
3.   Consideration of Bids for Renovation of EMS Building
   City Manager McDuffie reported that the low bid of $430,000 for renovation

   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Poole to reject all bids.

7.   Board Setting Powell Bill Fund Priorities
Mr. Allen provided the Board with a listing of projects eligible for Powell
Bill funding and options for completing the projects:
Project:   Resurfacing of city streets         $ 125,000
   Davis Street drainage improvements   $ 40,000
   Yacht Basin Drive improvements      $ 125,000
   Moore Street widening         $ 6,500
   ADA improvements to sidewalks at
    Moore Street & Caswell Avenue      $ 11,000                              
Total $ 307,500
Mr. Allen reported that the city currently has approximately $100,000 in
unallocated Powell Bill funds and receipt of another $100,000 is expected
during the fiscal year.
Option 1
Eliminate the Davis Street project, the Moore Street widening and the sidewalk
improvements at Caswell and Moore to save $57,500. We would cancel the purchase
of a new dump truck, saving $41,500 in the general fund (one-half the cost of
the truck) and would appropriate $9,000 in extra funds that have been realized
from the sale of surplus property. When added to Powell Bill Funds, sufficient
funding would be available for the resurfacing work and the Yacht Basin Drive
project.
Option 2
Complete all the projects through an assessment on the adjoining property
owners. The assessment would bring in $62,500 for the Yacht Basin project, and
$10,000 for Davis Street. Combined with the additional funds described in
Option 1, funding would be available to complete all projects.
Option 3
Eliminate the work on Yacht Basin Drive, saving $125,000, and funding the rest
of the work entirely with Powell Bill funds.
Option 4
Complete all projects using Powell Bill Funds ($200,000) and finance the
$107,500 gap, paid back with future Powell Bill Funding. This option may not be
desirable due to the cost of borrowing and the need to obtain LGC approval.
Option 5
Complete all the projects using funding as described in Option 1, and use
approximately $65,000 in fund balance to make up the difference. The city’s
current unallocated fund balance above the required 8% of revenues is $650,000.
Alderman Adams questioned the potential change in priorities, the rush to pave
the Yacht Basin and spending money before it is received.
Mayor Howard pointed out that the Board had previously made commitments to pave
the streets and make drainage improvements to Davis Street.
Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Barnes to authorize funding of the
street paving, Davis Street drainage improvements and to defer consideration of
the Yacht Basin Drive improvements until sufficient information is received and
affected property owners are contacted. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
