AGENDA
   1.   Wastewater Treatment Plant 
   City Manager McDuffie reported to the Board that since Oak Island had not
made a decision about selling sewer capacity, Brunswick County could not
guarantee that they would be able to sell sewer capacity to Southport. He added
that the County did say that they could sell Southport capacity if the county
treatment plant was expanded at a cost of $34M.
   City Manager McDuffie stated that the State has said that Southport could
use the $19.8M loan approved earlier in the year and apply for an additional
$14.3M by application deadline of April 28.
   City Manager McDuffie directed the Board to a spreadsheet provided in the
agenda packet. He pointed out that costs for customers would increase
regardless of which option the city pursued. He stated that the Rate Review
Committee had met, will meet again and will continue their due diligence and
make a recommendation to the Board.
   City Manager McDuffie noted that the City’s wastewater capacity lease with
the County expires in January 2019 which requires a decision be made by the
Board. He outlined the options:
Apply for an additional State loan in order to invest in the County plant
expansion
If unable to obtain loan from the State, borrow $14.3M on the open market at an
estimated 4% interest rate
Southport build its own treatment plant
   County advantage:      The County would manage and the City’s sewer district
would be                guaranteed
   City plant advantage:      Southport would own and operate its own plant.
Construction               estimated at $19.8M
   City plant disadvantage:   Southport sewer district would not be guaranteed
   Responding to Mayor Dove, Attorney Isenberg stated that as long as the City
purchases capacity from the County, city and county sewer districts would
remain in effect. If the City builds its own plant, that agreement would stop.
   Alderman Powell & Pukenas disagreed with the estimated cost per month per
customer as provided in the agenda packet information. Alderman Powell stated
his belief that the cost would be in the range of $60 per month per customer.
   Alderman Adams stated his opinion that it would be better for the city to be
independent instead of dependent on the County.
   Responding to a query by Mayor Dove, City Manager McDuffie stated that he
and Public Works Director Fox, were licensed to operate a wastewater treatment
plant. He added that personnel would have to be hired as he and Director Fox
would not have time to operate a plant and do their current jobs.
   Alderman Powell noted that in the past the city had contracted operation of
the wastewater treatment plant.
   Alderman Adams stated his support for hiring an operator or sending a
current employee to school to become licensed.
   Pointing out that the city had land already paid for and filtration basins
in place, Alderman Pukenas stated his support for constructing the city’s own
plant.
   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to proceed with
development of the city’s own wastewater treatment plant.
   Discussion
   Alderman Mosteller asked how the sewer territory could affect the city.
   City Manager McDuffie explained that if both the County and City could serve
a new property, there would be no reason for the property to annex into the
city limits.
   Responding to a query by Alderman Mosteller, City Manager McDuffie talked
about the fixed costs to operate a million gallon wastewater treatment plant,
potential growth from the current 2,800 customers, and the State requirement to
build in extra capacity. He added that the lines will be built big enough for
1.5M capacity.
   Vote: Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   City Manager McDuffie proposed contracting with Phil Norris, Norris &
Tunstall Engineering, to manage the project on behalf of the city. Alderman
Powell agreed.
   Alderman Adams endorsed using Phil Norris to manage the project for the city
with a stipulation that Alderman Powell serve as the liaison for the city.
   City Manager McDuffie also proposed contracting with Emily Miller,
President, McAdams & Associates, LLC, who wrote and obtained the grant for the
city, to administer the grant, do all paperwork and submit documentation to the
State as required. City Manager McDuffie pointed out that her fee for the two
year project would be covered in the $19.8M.
   City Manager McDuffie estimated approximately $350,000 for the services of
Phil Norris and his staff for two years, 20 hours a week at $175 per hour.
   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to proceed with hiring
Phil Norris and Emily Miller for administration of the project and grant
documentation. Unanimous vote; motion carried.

   4. a.   Budgeting
   Citing a map in the Board agenda packet depicting where electric can be run,
City Manager McDuffie reported that Booth & Associates, LLC had walked the
property, determined the amount of electricity needed and provided a cost
estimate to extend Southport electric service to the 88 acre tract at NC211 &
Long Beach Road Extension. He advised the Board that it was their decision to
provide electric service to the newly annexed area or let Brunswick Electric
Membership Corp. (BEMC) serve it.
   Alderman Powell maintained that if the city provided electric, the
development would have only one line of service to it versus multiple
connections available with BEMC.
   City Manager McDuffie stated that Southport electric service currently runs
to a building behind the Verizon Store on NC 211.
   Alderman Mosteller read into the record the following:
   “Part of being a resident of Southport is not only paying property taxes to
support our city services but also participating in our city owned water/sewer
and electric services as well. As Southport grows, our ability to deliver
services, more cost effectively, expands.
   In the case of our right to serve the electric service to the 88 acres
project…the right to serve exists for a reason. As new members of the
community, commercial and residential property owners should expect to have
access to the same services that the rest of Southport enjoys. Whether it’s
parks and rec, water/sewer, electric, fire, police.
   And revenue generated by their participation helps to share the cost of
these city services. As we increase the economy of scale, we have a larger base
to share expenses.
   If we restrict the growth of our utility services by giving away our right
to service a portion of our city, then we are placing the responsibility and
benefits of owning and operating our electrical services on only a portion of
our citizens… what’s the criteria for making this judgment call? How do we say
to some citizens, you are responsible for Southport’s electrical utility
services …How do we say to other Southport citizens, we are not going to
provide the same services for you that we provide for other citizens of
Southport?
   For those who qualify, Southport’s load management rate is the lowest priced
electricity in Brunswick County. How do we provide the opportunity to
participate in load management for some citizens and not all our citizens?
The details in the engineering report, done by Booth and Associates, a well
respected electrical engineering firm, is in line with the first estimate we
received. It seems to me looking at the numbers, we can afford to provide the
part of Southport that we refer to as the 88 acres electrical service.
   Just as an example, our Rivermist neighborhood is serviced by Brunswick
Electric. That’s 350 homes in Southport that do not participate in our utility
program.
   Currently, Southport services approximately 2800 customers. We would have
12% more customers if we had exercised our right to serve in Rivermist. Adding
over $100,000 in revenue annually to our electric utility budget.
   I would say, we can’t afford not to provide the electrical service. The
engineer’s total cost analysis including a 10% contingency fund, is $650,000.
The anticipated annual revenue once the project is built out is $100,000. Once
it’s up and running, that’s a 15% annual return on our investment. And
Southport’s electrical utility grows, our economy of scale increases and if in
the future we decide to get out of the electric business, we will have more
assets to offer a potential buyer.
   Since our electric fund is an enterprise fund…and we can only spend the
revenue within this fund on electric…it does not impact our general fund.
The electric fund budget for this year is $7,953, 000
In addition, as of February 2017…We have $ 3, 821,000 in reserves (for
emergencies)
We have $800,000 in this year’s budget that has not been spent…$350,000 of this
money has been budgeted for the replacement of the electrical line on the old
ferry road.
So we have $450,000 immediately available. And due to a rate decrease, we are
anticipating a savings of approximately $130,000. This is annual savings for
the next three years.
Even if we borrowed the whole amount from a bank …$650,000 at 4.5% amortized
over a 20 year period without a pre-payment penalty, our return on investment
would be 7.5% annually once it’s built out. Debt service would be $50,000 a
year and revenue would be $50,000.
   Our decision tonight may also determine who provides future electrical
service to any additional development adjacent to the 88 acres and Rivermist.
   Expanding our infrastructure is investing in our future. For long term
benefits … to help keep rates lower and still provide adequate revenues to meet
the needs of operating our electrical service.
   If this board chooses to give our right to serve to BEMC and the estimated
value once it’s up and running the expected revenue is approximately $100,000
annually. It’s valuable…..would it be reasonable to expect some kind of
compensation. We are just giving it away?
   Booth and Associates has been in business since 1960 as a leading
engineering consulting firm. They are who ElectriCities uses for their
projects. Booth and Associates specializes in all aspects of overhead and
underground distribution design for over fifty years.
   Over the long term, our utility services must expand to all our residents if
we are going to continue to provide the best, most cost effective utility
services.
   I called the engineer that did the analysis, Raymond Collins, Manager of
Distributing Engineering for Booth and Associates and asked typically how long
should it take to do this work? He stated “an average would be about two
months.” I asked him how long he had worked for Booth and Associates and he
said 31 years.
   Regarding duplicity – our whole city operates on one system so that having
duplicity really shouldn’t be a factor.
   Walmart’s peak load generator can power the entire store so I Would expect
Lowes Foods to have a generator for back up as well.
   Booth & Associates, LLC provided the following Construction Cost Estimate to
extend underground electric service to the 88 acre development at a total cost
of $649,230.00:
As part of this estimate, we reviewed the anticipated additional load to be
connected to the existing overhead feeder. Based on the information provided,
the overhead circuit should be adequate. The estimated 1MW development would
need three-phase, 1/0 Al, 15 kV underground conductor. 1MW is about 64 amps and
the 1/0 cable is rated for +or-155 amps. This would give you some excess
capacity.
We decided to use 4-4” conduits. The quantity of 4 based our discussions last
week – pulling the conductors in individual conduits, as well as a spare
conduit, offers an increase in reliability in the event someone digs into the
conduit & ease of conductor replacement in case of a fault. The 4” diameter
conduit would allow space to increase the size of the conductor in the future,
if necessary, to accommodate additional load.
In review of the area the proposed underground is to be installed, we
determined that the best location for the new facilities would be on the north
side of the road. The north side of Southport – Supply Road offers more options
in terms of equipment locations than the south side. Overall the cost would not
change a great deal regardless of which side is ultimately chosen. We also
elected to price the construction of this project on the basis that the
installation method for the conduit would be entirely by directional boring.
This method was chosen due to the existing number of underground utilities
already in place in the area. Boring will eliminate the necessity to hand dig
over or under the other utilities. The bore could be made below the existing
facilities as much as possible to reduce the potential conflicts.
If you have any questions or comments, please let me know. It was nice meeting
you, Kerry and seeing you again, Ellie. Thanks for allowing Booth and
Associates to provide our services to the City of Southport. We look forward to
working with you in the future.
Thank you,
Ray
Raymond J. Collins
Manager of Distribution Engineering
Booth & Associates, LLC
5811 Glenwood Avenue
Raleigh, NC 27612
919-851-8770 x 186 office
919-810-6343 cell
919-859-5918 fax
   Alderman Pukenas stated his opinion that undertaking the project to serve

   Alderman Poole pointed out that servicing the 88 acres gives the city the

   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to not proceed with

   Discussion

   4. c.   Police Department Budget
   City Manager McDuffie reported that the Police Department is in need of a

recently wrecked. He stated that a $61,000 budget amendment is needed and could

   Alderman Powell stated his concerns that the separation allowance for a

   Alderman Adams agreed and asked if officers could share a car. He motioned,
second by Alderman Powell to not do a budget amendment and to not hire a

which would be required during the development of the commercial portion of the
88 acres.

CITY OF SOUTHPORT
PROCLAMATION
Recognizing
Quinton Antoine McCracken
WHEREAS, Quinton Antoine McCracken, one of Southport’s favorite sons, is being
recognized for his sporting achievements; and
WHEREAS, Quinton began his sporting career at South Brunswick High School
playing football, basketball, track and baseball; and
WHEREAS, in his senior year he led his baseball team to a 29-0 record and the
state Championship; and
WHEREAS, after graduating from Duke University, Quinton was selected by the
Colorado Rockies in their inaugural draft in 1992; and
WHEREAS, Quinton went on to play for the Tampa Bay Devil Rays, Minnesota Twins,
Arizona Diamondbacks, Seattle Mariners and Cincinnati Reds; and
WHEREAS, Quinton has been inducted into the Greater Wilmington Sports Hall of
Fame for his distinguished career; and
WHEREAS, it is an honor to extend this expression of esteem and congratulations
on this auspicious occasion.
NOW, THEREFORE by virtue of authority vested in me as Mayor, I, J.V. Dove
proclaim Sunday, April 30, 2017, as “Quinton Antoine McCracken DAY IN THE CITY
OF SOUTHPORT, NORTH CAROLINA.”
BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED that “Welcome to the Home of Quinton Antoine
McCracken” be displayed on a Southport entry way sign in his honor.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I do hereby set my hand and the official seal of the City
on this 23rd day of March 2017.

RESOLUTION TO ESTABLISH WRITTEN CRITERIA TO DETERMINE WHETHER DESIGN-BUILD IS
APPROPRIATE FOR THE PROJECT TO CONSTRUCT A NEW WASTEWATER TREATMENT PLANT AND
APPROVAL OF DESIGN-BUILD METHOD FOR SAID PROJECT
   WHEREAS, G. S. 143-128.1A authorizes Design-Build Contracts when authorized
in accordance with the terms of said statute; and
   WHEREAS, the Board of Aldermen wishes to proceed in accordance with said
statute to set criteria to use the Design-Build method and to apply said
criteria to the construction of a new wastewater treatment plant;
   NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen that the following
criteria is hereby established pursuant to G. S. 143-128.1A to determine the
circumstances under which the Design-Build method is appropriate:
Criteria 1: The extent to which the City can adequately and thoroughly define
the project requirements prior to the issuance of the request for
qualifications (RFQ) for a design-builder.
The design-build delivery method may be used if it is determined that, for the
project, the City has professional personnel that are both qualified and
experienced to thoroughly define project requirements prior to the issuance of
a request for qualifications for a design-builder. Consideration will be given
to the qualifications and experience of the personnel in the Public Works
Department and the availability of professional personnel in the areas of
engineering, purchasing, finance and legal to assist in the development of an
RFQ.
Criteria 2: The time constraints for the delivery of the project  .
The design-build delivery method may be used if a project has a firm date by
which a facility must be operational and the normal delivery method is likely
not to be timely (typically RFQ, study, design, bid and construct). The size
and cost of a project will dictate complexity and schedule.
Criteria 3: The ability to ensure that a quality project can be delivered .
The design-build delivery method may be used if it is determined that, for the
project, the City has professional and experienced personnel to ensure that the
design-build firm will provide a quality project within a budget constraints
established by the Board of Aldermen. Consideration will be given to the
qualifications and experience of the personnel in the Public Works Department
and the availability of experienced, qualified professional engineers.
Criteria 4: The capability of the City to manage and oversee the project,
including the availability of experienced staff or outside consultants who are
experienced with the design-build method of project delivery.
The design-build delivery method may be used if it is determined that, for the
project, the City has professional and experienced personnel that are
knowledgeable regarding design-build projects or, in the alternative,
experienced consultants local to Southport who are available to be retained to
perform the construction management of a design-build contract.
Criteria 5:
A good faith effort to comply with G.S. 143-128.2, G.S. 143-128.4, and to
recruit and select small business entities .
The design-build delivery method may be used if it is determined that, for the
project, requirements will be imposed to ensure that contractors will comply
with the M/WBE goals set by Board.
Criteria 6: The criteria utilized by the City, including a comparison of the
costs and benefits of using the design-build delivery method for a given
project in lieu of other delivery methods identified .
The criteria utilized by the City when considering a design-build delivery
method for a project will be as follows:
Is the project well-defined and does it include qualitative and quantitative
characteristics that make a design-build contract more appropriate than other
methods of delivery?
Is the project timeline overly constrained and will it be necessary to have the
facility complete and operational within a short time frame?
Will it be necessary to have the beneficial use of a portion of the facility
while it is under construction?
Given the scope of the project, is there a maximum budget that must be adhered
to in order to allow negotiations and flexibility to make appropriate decisions
on scope as the project progresses?
Does the design-build delivery method meet the ultimate operational goals
established for a given facility and the quality of product achieved as a
result of a more fluid and flexible delivery method?
In general terms, if it is determined that the expected expense of a design-
build project will be no more than ten (10%) percent greater than the expected
expense of a traditional RFQ, study, design, bid and construct project, the
design-build delivery method may be utilized.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen as follows:
   In applying the criteria set forth above to the new wastewater treatment
plant project, it is determined that the design-build delivery method be used
for this project, said determination being based upon the review of the above
criteria as it relates to the project as follows:
Criteria 1:   Through the Public Works Department and local professional
engineers, the City has professional personnel available that are both
qualified and experienced to thoroughly define project requirements prior to
the issuance of a request for qualifications for a design-builder.
Additionally, qualified personnel are available in the areas of purchasing,
finance and legal to assist in the development of an RFQ.
Criteria 2:   It is necessary for the City to build and have operational a
wastewater treatment plant no later than January 1, 2019, in order to comply
with an agreement with Brunswick County which has been providing wastewater
treatment to the City. This is a period of approximately 20 months. Typical
procedure would be to procure a design consultant, complete design and
undertake construction. This process would take approximately 24-30 months thus
preventing the treatment plant from being operational by January 1, 2019. The
Design-Build process provides the best option for the City to meet this time
frame.
Criteria 3:   Within the Public Works Department and with local professional
engineers, the City has professional and experienced personnel to ensure that
the design-build firm will provide a quality project within the budget
constraints established by Board.
Criteria 4:   Within the Public Works Department and with local professional
engineers, the City has professional and experienced personnel available that
are knowledgeable of design-build projects. Should it become necessary to
contract construction management of a design-build contract, there are
experienced consultants local to Southport that are available.
Criteria 5:   The City complies with G.S. 143-128.2, G.S. 143-128.4. The City
has an established and successful M/WBE program which requires contractors to
comply with the M/WBE goals set by Council.
Criteria 6:   As stated under Criteria #2 above, one of the benefits of the
Design-Build process is that it may reduce the overall project schedule by 6 to
12 months. This has a direct benefit on the project budget. The design-build
delivery method is not expected to involve any additional expense than the
expected expense of a traditional RFQ, study, design, bid and construct
project. The budget for the building of the new wastewater treatment plant is
$19.8 million. By reducing the time frame by 6-12 months, we are eliminating
the price escalation that would occur within that year. Additionally, the scope
of the design efforts will be reduced. It is expected that the design-build
process will save 2% of construction cost over what are typical design-bid-
build process. These benefits to both the project schedule and cost make the
design-build option more appealing than the more conventional design-bid-build
in this instance.
   This the 13th day of April, 2017.         City of Southport
                     /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor            
ATTEST: /s/ Michele Windham, Clerk

ARBOR DAY RESOLUTION
 
[https://export.amlegal.com/media/199f40a54a06f19a9324bf64df539e216304d812/
IMAGES/0-0-0-1860_1366x1395.jpg]
WHEREAS, in 1872, J. Sterling Morton proposed to the Nebraska Board of
Agriculture that a special day be set aside for the planting of trees, and
WHEREAS, this holiday called Arbor Day, was first observed with the planting of
more than a million trees in Nebraska, and
WHEREAS, Arbor Day is now observed throughout the nation and the world, and
WHEREAS, trees can reduce the erosion of our precious topsoil by wind and
water, cut heating and cooling costs, moderate the temperature, clean the air,
produce life-giving oxygen, and provide habitat for wildlife, and
WHEREAS, trees are a renewable resource giving us paper, wood for our homes,
fuel for our fires, and
WHEREAS, trees in our city increase property values, enhance the economic
vitality of business areas, and beautify our community, and
WHEREAS, trees in our city are a great source of joy and spiritual renewal.
NOW, THEREFORE , The City of Southport Board of Aldermen, do hereby proclaim
April 28, 2017 as ARBOR DAY in the City and urge all citizens to celebrate and
support efforts to protect our trees and woodlands, and
FURTHER, The City of Southport Board of Aldermen urges all citizens to plant
trees to gladden the heart and promote the well-being of this and future
generations.
DATED, this 13th day of April, 2017.
                  /s/ J.V. Dove, Mayor
Attest: /s/ Michele Windham, Clerk

   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to approve the
Proclamation
Unanimous vote; motion carried.
ProclamationA Sample Proclamation
Recreational boating is fun and enjoyable, and we are fortunate that we have
sufficient resources to accommodate the wide variety of pleasure boating
demands. However, our waterways can become crowded at times and be a place of
chaos and confusion. While being a marvelous source of recreation, boating, to
the unprepared, can be a risky sport. Not knowing or obeying the Navigation
Rules or the nautical “Rules of the Road,” drinking alcohol or taking drugs
while operating a boat, or choosing not to wear your life jacket when doing so
is clearly NOT the smart thing to do, are all examples of human error or a lack
of proper judgment. One particular behavior that can reduce the number of
boaters who lose their lives by drowning each year by is the wearing of a life
jacket. It is a simple task that has the potential to reduce terrible loss in
lives.
Knowledge and skills are important in reducing human error and improving
judgment. If people are aware of the risk, they are likely to take the
precautionary measures to protect themselves and their friends and family. That
is why we must continue to spread the messages of boating safety not only
during National Safe Boating Week but also throughout the entire year.
Whereas, on average, 700 people die each year in boating-related accidents in
the U.S.; approximately 71% of these are fatalities caused by drowning; and
Whereas, the vast majority of these accidents are caused by human error or poor
judgment and not by the boat, equipment, or environmental factors; and
Whereas, a significant number of boaters who lose their lives by drowning each
year would be alive today had they worn their life jackets; and
Whereas, today’s life jackets are more comfortable, more attractive, and more
wearable than styles of years past and deserve a fresh look by today’s boating
public.
Therefore, I, JV Dove, do hereby support the goals of the North American Safe
Boating Campaign, the United States Coast Guard and the Coast Guard Auxiliary
and proclaim May 20–26, 2017, as National Safe Boating Week and the start of
the year-round effort to promote safe boating.
In Witness Thereof, I urge all those who boat to Wear It! and practice safe
boating habits.
Given under my signature and the seal of
/s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor, Southport, North Carolina
/s/ Erich White, Officer-in-Charge USCG Station Oak Island
at the city of Southport
this 11th day of May, 2017

CITY OF SOUTHPORT
RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF CREATION OF A
FERRY TRANSPORTATION AUTHORITY
   WHEREAS, the City of Southport is located on the banks of the Cape Fear
River and Intracoastal Waterway and has a rich maritime heritage; and
   WHEREAS, the City of Southport is home to the mainland ferry terminal
facilities and vehicle parking for access to Bald Head Island; and
   WHEREAS, many Southport residents are employed on and/or regularly visit
Bald Head Island and depend upon the ferry services and parking facilities, and
many residents living on and visitors to Bald Head Island regularly transact
business in Southport; and
   WHEREAS, ferry services and facilities for access to Bald Head Island are
presently operated and owned by several privately held corporations, and
therefore the City of Southport currently has no formal role in the ownership,
management, or operations of the ferry services or parking facilities; and
   WHEREAS, Senate Bill 391 entitled “An Act to Authorize the Creation of a
Ferry Transportation Authority” would provide the potential for the facilities
and operations serving Bald Head Island to be consolidated into a single ferry
transportation authority that would be a public body with public
accountability; and
   WHEREAS, the creation of a ferry transportation authority appears to be in
the best long-term interest of the City of Southport, its residents and
businesses,
   NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of
Southport:
   1.   Southport supports and calls upon the General Assembly of North
Carolina to enact Senate Bill 391or similar legislation creating a ferry
transportation authority with the capability of owning and operating the water
transportation and parking facilities and services presently provided to Bald
Head Island;
   2.   Upon the effectiveness of legislation authorizing the creation of a
ferry transportation authority, it is the intention of the City of Southport to
promptly conduct, upon due notice, a public hearing on a Resolution to form an
Authority under such legislation, including, if necessary, the City of
Southport serving as an incorporator of the Authority.
   3.   The City Attorney and Staff are directed to draft said Resolution and
to coordinate, as necessary, with the Village of Bald Head Island and Brunswick
County in the drafting of Articles of Incorporation that set forth all of the
following:
      a.   the name of the Authority;
      b.   a statement that the Authority is organized under the legislation;
      c.   the name of each organizing entity;
      d.   and such other information as may be required by the legislation.
   This is 11th day of May, 2017
                     /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor
ATTEST: /s/ Michele Windham, City Clerk

with increases in the property and liability insurance costs, bonds and fuel.

Resolution
Lions Club International 100th Anniversary
WHEREAS, the Lions Club International was established 100 years ago (June 7,
1917) with the mission of empowering volunteers to serve their communities,
meet humanitarian needs, encourage peace and promote international
understanding through Lions Clubs; and
WHEREAS, the Lions Club International is the largest service club organization
in the world with approximately 1.35 million members in more than 46,000 clubs
around the world; and
WHEREAS, since 1925, Lions have served as “knights of the blind in the crusade
against darkness”, in addition to serving in Community and Environmental
programs, Disaster Relief, to include Sight, Hearing, Diabetes Awareness
programs, International Relations, and Children and Youth programs, and
WHEREAS, since 1990, through their SightFirst Program, Lions are restoring
sight and preventing blindness on a global scale by targeting the major causes
of blindness: cataract, trachoma, river blindness, childhood blindness,
diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma; and
WHEREAS, our own Southport Lions Chapter, established in 1945, continues to
serve the noted mission of the Lions Club International by providing assistance
with eye examinations and glasses, cataract surgery, vision screening,
recycling glasses; and
WHEREAS, the Southport Lions provide scholarships, support the NC Boys & Girls
Home, the ICCF Food Pantry, and many other worthy causes;
NOW THEREFORE, I, J.V. Dove, Mayor of the City of Southport, NC and the Board
of Aldermen, hereby congratulate the Lions Club International on 100 years of
community and global service.
ADOPTED, this 8th day of June 2017 by the Southport Board of Aldermen.
                        /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor
ATTEST: /s/ Michele Windham, Clerk

Offer of Donations of Property or Services to City of Southport
The City of Southport has a review process in place, for liability reasons,
when an offer for a service or property is extended. Please allow us 1-2 weeks
for a response. We will get back to you by _________________. At that point we
will advise you of the next steps in securing the donation if we believe we can
responsibly accept the donation.

Email of donor:

Donors projected value of donation: $ _____________
1. How would you like the item or service to be used by the City of Southport?

2. Where would you like the item placed and how will it get there? Will you
need help from the City? Is there a cost involved? If so, what is the estimated
cost? Explain.

3. Does the item require maintenance? If so, what needs to be done and who will
provide that service? If you want the City to take on the maintenance, what is
the expectation and projected annual cost?

4. What is the projected life span of the item? At the end of usable service,
what do you want the City to do with the item? Do you want to be notified? How?

5. Does the item require electricity or a water supply or other service?

QUESTIONS TO ASK YOURSELF AND OTHER DEPARTMENTS EFFECTED BY PROSPECTIVE
DONATION:
1. Is this something that the City/your department really needs and wants? Does
it support/fit a quaint, seaside village image?
2. Where will the item be placed and how will it get there? Will donor need
help from the City? If so, explain.
3. Who will maintain the item and at what cost?
   a. If your department is going to be responsible for maintenance, what are
the maintenance requirements?
   b. Will your department/the City be able to fund that cost over the life
span of the item?
4. What is the life span of the item? (for example a wood bench will last 3-
5 years)
   a. How will the property be disposed of at the end of the life span?
   b. Will the donor be notified? If yes, how?
5. If required, does your department have space to store it?
6. Does the item require insurance?
   a) If yes, does your department have a budget to pay for the insurance?
   (Note: Please contact the City Manager to be sure the gift does not require
insurance)
7. Does the item require electricity or any other utility to work?
   a) If yes, does your department have the appropriate utility connections?
   (Note: If you are not sure, please contact the Facilities Department to make
sure)
8. How will the donor be thanked?
9. Do you recommend that the City accept this gift? Please note any
reservations or conditions.

ORDINANCE APPROVING A ZONING MAP AMENDMENT REZONING ONE PARCEL FROM PUD TO LI
   THAT WHEREAS, the City has enacted a Unified Development Ordinance, other
land use ordinances, and a zoning map that control land development within both
the City’s incorporated areas and within its extraterritorial area; and
   WHEREAS, in order to promote the public health, safety and general welfare
and to promote the best interest of the city and community, it is necessary for
the City Board of Aldermen from time to time to consider appropriate revisions,
modifications and additions to the city’s zoning map; and
   WHEREAS, the City Planner has prepared and submitted to the Planning Board a
favorable staff recommendation to rezone parcel 2220000613 from PUD to LI; and
   WHEREAS, the Planning Board has considered this matter and has recommended
that this proposed zoning be approved; and
   WHEREAS, pursuant to the NC General Statutes and city ordinances, a public
hearing, properly noticed, was held on June 8, 2017, before the Board of
Aldermen regarding this issue; and
   WHEREAS, the Board of Aldermen hereby finds that the proposed zoning map
amendment is consistent with the Southport CAMA Land Use Plan; and
   WHEREAS, the Board of Aldermen further finds that this zoning map amendment
is reasonable and in the public interest in that (i) the proposed rezoning of
the above property is compatible to adjacent uses, (ii) the proposed rezoning
will not have a noticeable impact on traffic circulation due to its location on
Rob Gandy Boulevard, (iii) and that the proposed property is an appropriate
location for the uses permitted under Light Industrial (LI);
   NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED by the City of Southport Board of Aldermen
that
The Official Zoning Map of the City of Southport, an element of the Unified
Development Ordinance of the City, is amended by changing the zoning
classification of the below-described property from PUD to LI:
Tax Parcel ID Numbers of property to be rezoned: Parcel ID # 2220000613
This ordinance shall be effective upon its adoption, and the Official Zoning
Map of the City of Southport shall be revised accordingly.
This, the 8th day of June, 2017            City of Southport
                     BY: /s/ J.V. Dove, Mayor

9.   Consideration of Purchasing Capacity on County Sewer Plant
   City Manager McDuffie presented a renewed offer from Brunswick County to
sell 750,000 gallons of sewer capacity at the West Brunswick Regional
Wastewater Reclamation System, to the city. He explained that the allocation
purchase was an option because other municipalities that own capacity in the
county’s 6.5 million-gallon-per-day (GPD) use only a fraction of that flow. He
cited Oak Island as an example, pointing out that Oak Island owns 3 million GPD
but averages 800,000 gallons.
   Referring to the price comparison provided in the agenda packet, City
Manager McDuffie advised that Norris & Tunstall Consulting Engineers calculated
the city’s cost to build its own wastewater treatment plant and calculated the
city’s cost to purchase capacity from the county.

1. 1.53 is a not to exceed rate.
2. County O&M is $2.2 per 1,000 gallons times 500,000 gallons per day
3. Neither number includes collection system O&M
   City Manager McDuffie pointed out that for the city to build and operate its
own one-million GPD plant, the cost would increase from $34 to $79 per customer
per month. The cost to purchase 750,000 gallons of capacity from the county
would be $57 per customer per month.
   City Manager McDuffie stated that staff recommends that the Board accept the
county’s offer to purchase 750,000 GPD capacity, as the most cost-effective
option. He explained that no matter what the city does, the cost to provide
sewer in the future is going to be more. He noted that currently the city
leases capacity and that lease will expire in 2019.
   Alderman Poole motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to purchase wastewater
capacity in the Brunswick County Sewer Plant.
DISCUSSION
   Alderman Powell asked for clarification of the cost. City Manager McDuffie
responded that the city’s cost to purchase the capacity was estimated to be
$25.7 million, along with an operation and maintenance cost of $400,000 per
year.
   Alderman Powell disagreed with the estimated cost per customer, stating that
in his 50 years’ experience dealing with sewer and wastewater treatment, the
cost would be in the $60 range. He stated that he could not support paying the
county $27 million for 750,000 GPD when the city could build its own one-
million-GPD plant for $20 million. He referenced a presentation that showed an
increase in flow for Southport in October attributed to Hurricane Matthew
impacts.
   Alderman Powell pointed out that the state requires a wastewater treatment
operation to begin expansion plans when the capacity reaches 80 percent of the
total capacity. He said that the decision on sewer was the most important
decision that the city will make or has made in 100 years. He stated his
opinion that he wants to control his own destiny – not give it to someone else
to control.
   Acknowledging that Brunswick County officials fielded questions from the
aldermen about the proposed agreement, Alderman Coring asked how rainfall
affected the flow and how that could impact the allocation.
   Ms. Ann Hardy, Manager, Brunswick County, stated that the county looked at
the plant as a whole when calculating the flow ratio. She added that plant
participants would need to exceed 80 percent of 6.5 million GPD total
capacities before the County would need to begin planning an expansion. She
emphasized that the county would do everything possible to control costs during
the construction and design process. She stated appreciation for the
partnership with the city as a lease participant in the last seven years and
she stated her hope that the county can continue to provide good service to the
city.
   Ms. Hardy assured the Board that the city’s sewer district would stay intact
and that the current county customers in Rivermist would become full city
customers in exchange for county servicing the planned 88 acre development at
NC 211/133, Southport Crossing .
   City Attorney Isenberg stated that a map of the city’s sewer district would
be included in the 30 year contract. He added that the contract would have
automatic 10-year renewals, with a 3-year termination by either party.
   Aye:   Aldermen Poole, Mosteller, Pukenas, Adams, Coring
   Nay:   Alderman Powell
   Motion carried 5-1
   (contract on file in the Clerk’s office)

11.   Consideration of Street Lighting Policy
   Expressing appreciation for all the hard work the committee and staff put
into developing a street lighting policy, Alderman Coring motioned, second by
Alderman Poole to adopt the Street Lighting Policy. Unanimous vote; motion
carried.
STREET LIGHTING POLICY
Adopted by Board: (June 8, 2017) Effective: (June 8, 2017)
POLICY PURPOSE
The purpose of this policy statement is to adopt an official policy for the
City of Southport pertaining to the installation of street lights for the
purposes of traffic safety and crime control.
COVERAGE
This policy, upon adoption, shall apply to all public rights of way within the
municipal limits of the City of Southport and any public rights of way annexed
in the future until such time that the Policy Statement is altered, modified,
or rescinded by the Board of Aldermen.
DEFINITIONS
Streets in the City of Southport will be defined as the following:
HOA/POA Subdivision Streets : Areas where street lights will be provided by
Homeowners Associations and Property Owners Associations.
Waterfront and Downtown Area Streets : Streets in the Waterfront Area, Yacht
Basin and Downtown Central Business District as designated on the Southport
Street Lighting map.
Residential Streets : Streets in primarily residential areas as designated on
the Southport Street Lighting map.
Main Roadway Corridor Streets : Main roadway corridor streets as designated on
the Southport Street Lighting map.
Walkway Lights on Public Right-Of-Way
POLICY FOR LIGHTING ON ALL STREETS
The City of Southport Board of Aldermen hereby establishes the following policy
applicable to all streets:
Relocation
Residents along a street may petition to request the relocation of a street
light provided that the proposed street light location meets City standards and
the relocation is approved by the City, and is not opposed by any persons
within the area of influence. The City shall determine the area of influence on
a case by case basis. Relocation cost and all facilities abandonment costs must
be paid in full to the City, in advance, by the resident(s) requesting the
relocation.
Requests for Additional Lighting
Residents along a street may petition to request additional street lighting
beyond that already installed, provided current street lighting does not meet
City standards, and the requested additional street lighting is approved by the
City and is not opposed by any persons within the area of influence. The City
shall determine the area of influence on a case by case basis. After approval,
the City will process the request and pay all costs associated with street
light installation.
STREET SPECIFIC POLICIES
The Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport hereby establishes the following
policy applicable to specific types of streets:
Streets in a HOA /POA in a Subdivision: Street lights will be provided by
Homeowners Associations and Property Owners Associations and will be paid for
by these entities.
The City will not pay for any costs associated with the lighting of private
streets or drives.
Street light fixture types and locations in HOA/POA Subdivision areas must be
approved by the City of    Southport.
Will be minimum 70 Watt LED and a maximum of 300 feet apart.
B. Street Lights on Waterfront and Downtown Area Streets: Street lights on
these streets shall conform to the following standards:
Street lights will be on concrete poles with bell-shaped lights and a 50W LED
bulb.
Street lights will be lit at all intersections and an average of 150 feet
intervals.
Street lights shall be as close to lateral property lines as possible, or where
the vertical or horizontal street alignment or natural features necessitate
shorter or longer spacing intervals.
C. Street Lights on Residential Area Streets : Street lights on residential
area streets as shall conform to the following standards:
Street lights will be lit at all intersections and an average of 300 feet
intervals.
Street lights shall be as close to lateral property lines as possible, or where
the vertical or horizontal street alignment or natural features necessitate
shorter or longer spacing intervals.
All fixtures on residential streets shall be at least 70 watts and no more than
80 Watt LEDs
Fixtures shall be on aluminum poles twenty-five (25) feet in height on a 6 foot
arm.
D. Street Lights on Main Roadway Corridors : Main roadway corridor street
lights shall conform to the following standards:
Street lights will be lit at all intersections and at 140 feet intervals.
Street lights shall be as close to lateral property lines as possible, or where
the vertical or horizontal street alignment or natural features necessitate
shorter or longer spacing intervals.
All fixtures along thoroughfares shall be at least 100 and no more than 110
watt LEDs.
Fixtures shall be on aluminum poles twenty-five (25) feet in height on a 6 foot
arm.
E. Walkway Lights on Public Right-Of-Way : Walkway Lights shall conform to the
following standards:
Walkway lights will be lit at 90 feet intervals.
Walkway lights shall be as close to lateral property lines as possible, or
where the vertical or horizontal street alignment or natural features
necessitate shorter or longer spacing intervals.
All fixtures along walkways shall be at least 75 watts and no more than 85 watt
LEDs and will be dark sky fixtures.
Fixtures shall be on aluminum poles twelve (12) feet in height with a
decorative design.

15.   Budget Amendment #6; Waterfront and Atlantic Street Park Bulkhead Repairs
   City Manager McDuffie reported that FEMA had written and agreed to reimburse
the City for repairs of Waterfront Park and Atlantic Avenue CAMA Beach Access
for damages sustained during Hurricane Matthew. Noting that the tourist season
was not the ideal time to be making repairs at the waterfront, City Manager
McDuffie pointed out that there was a one-year time frame after the event for
repairs to be made with an exemption for a Major CAMA permit. He noted that the
one-year extension period would expire in early October. He stated that a Major
CAMA Permit could be pursued and would require a significant amount of
engineering, notification to multiple State agencies and a 90-day waiting
period. He stated that there was no guarantee that all State agencies would
approve the project. He stated that staff recommended doing the repairs now.
   Alderman Coring motioned, second by Alderman Poole to move the project ahead
and adopt Budget Amendment #6. Unanimous vote; motion carried.

BOARD OF ALDERMEN   SPECIAL SESSION MINUTES
                   JUNE 12, 2017
1029 N. HOWE STREET SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:         Mayor J.V. Dove
            Aldermen Mary Ellen Poole, Karen Mosteller, Rick Pukenas

            Tanya Shannon, Deputy City Clerk      
A)   Call to Order
Mayor Dove called the meeting to order at 4:00 p.m.
   Mr. Chris May, Cape Fear Council of Governments (COG), provided an agenda
for the meeting, noting that the desired outcome of the meeting is to develop
an attribute list for a permanent city manager and to discuss the status of the
selection process. He noted that Alderman Poole had prepared a tool for the
process and time table. Mr. May stated he would prepare and provide an
attribute list outlined by the Board’s recommendations and give the list to the
Deputy City Clerk for distribution to the Board. He advised the Board to also
take into consideration those attributes they did not want in a manager.
   Quality traits were discussed:
Ethics/Integrity; a small town manager must have a moral compass and say what
they mean, mean what they say and do what they say
Good Social/People Skills
Maintain good written and verbal communications with staff and Board
Ability to create good team concept; be a leader and lead by example
Seven (7) years’ experience in city/county government
Five (5) years’ management experience
Who and how to access resources; grants, etc.
Experience with ElectriCities and water and sewer systems
Knowledge of budget process and financial reporting
Quality interaction with private, civic and volunteer organizations
Current in information technology
Versed in emergency operations relative to a coastal community; CAMA, FEMA
Ability to work well with the Board
   Mr. May indicated that the above would be used to craft interview questions
along with examples he received from the N.C. School of Government.
   Noting that the position posting stated applications would be received until
the position is filled, Mr. May noted there were 19 candidates to date. Mayor
Dove indicated the position had been advertised with the NC League of
Municipalities, in the State Port Pilot and on the city’s web page. Mr. May
stated that once a month the COG sends out a newsletter that lists open
positions. All applications were copied and provided to Board members for
review. Mayor Dove stated that a special meeting would be held on Wednesday,
June 21, 6:00 p.m. to select specific candidates to interview.
   Mr. May asked if applicants would be compensated for travel expenses to and
from an interview. Alderman Poole explained that the Board had not compensated
applicants in the past. She added that the Board had provided for phone
interviews if an applicant was unable to appear for an interview and during one
city manager search, when a large number of applications were received, the
Board provided three (3) questions to be answered via a video.
   It was pointed out that moving expenses would be paid up to a specific
amount (provided by the Human Resources Department) to the chosen applicant and
the employment contract spelled out salary and benefits. It was noted that an
employment contract is open for negotiations.
   Interview techniques and format were discussed along with restricted
questions that cannot be asked. Mr. May provided and reviewed a listing of
sample questions. He emphasized sticking to the facts. He stated he would be
happy to assist with the interview process.
   Alderman Poole reported that Board members were in the process of rating the
applicants in order to determine who to interview and would meet June 21 to
narrow the search and schedule interviews. She discussed past city manager
search processes utilized by the Board, including videos. 
   Mr. May suggested scheduling interviews for an hour, possibly requesting
hand written responses to questions. He speculated getting through the process
and having a manager on board by Labor Day.
Adjourn

2018 budget.
   Mayor Dove introduced Mr. Chris May, Executive Director, Cape Fear Council
of Government, prior municipal and county manager and professional facilitator

June 8, 2017
Mayor Dove and Board of Aldermen
1029 N. Howe Street
Southport, NC 28461
Re: Budget Message Update 2017-2018
Dear Mayor Dove and Board,
After the May 30th Budget Workshop, with the Board of Aldermen, the staff has
revised the budget to reflect the Board’s wishes. The updated budget reflects
the following:
The proposed 2017-2018 Budget is a balanced budget for the City of Southport.
The budget proposes a 28 cents per $100 of evaluation tax rate. There was a
slight increase in the tax base from new construction and the Southport Marina
being purchased by a private entity versus being owned by the state of North
Carolina which does not pay property taxes. There is no change in fees for
recycling or yard waste. The Planning and Zoning Department is working on the
fee schedule to make improvements to the planning, zoning and inspection fees.
The budget is balanced without appropriating funds from fund balance. Also,
there is no proceeds budgeted from loans for capital projects other than the
Fire Department equipment.
The Water and Sewer fund is balanced with enough funds to cover the
depreciation as indicated by the most recent audit. The revenue does include
the increase in rates as adopted by the Board at the May 11, 2017 Board
meeting. The Water and Sewer Budget is a solid responsible budget that proposes
reasonable capital replacement.
The Electrical Budget is also a solid responsible budget. It continues to
support the effort to underground the electrical system with no change in
rates.
The budget has a COLA (cost of living adjustment) for employees of 2.1%. This
is based on the change in the Consumer Price Index for the calendar year 2016.
Also, there is a 1% total salaries for merit raises. The cost for health care
will increase 10%. Considering under the old health insurance plan Southport
has a 15% rate increase for 12 consecutive years, this is a good thing.
The Budget has no new employee positions other than the 2 in the Fire
Department. With the loss of revenue from Wells Fargo leasing the upstairs at
the 1029 building and their share of the common area maintenance negatively
impacts the General Fund by $150,000. Also, the city lost the revenue from the
City Boat Docks. The capital expenditure added to the General Fund are:
Caviness Park improvements         $ 12,000
Franklin Sq. Gallery building improvements      $ 42,000
Brunswick Family Assistance         $ 2,000
Greenway to Walmart            $ 30,000
2 Police Ford Explorers $38,000 each      $ 76,000
Key fob entry for Police Department      $ 3,800
Parking Atlantic Street Park         $ 7,000           
Walkway at Garrison            $ 2,500
Community Building HVAC         $ 15,000
UDO Update by COG            $ 10,000
TOTAL                  $ 200,300
This budget continues the great services for the citizens at a reasonable cost.
Respectfully submitted,
Kerry McDuffie
City Manager

C)   Approval of Agenda
   Alderman Coring motioned, second by Alderman Mosteller to approve the

AGENDA
Discussion of Proposed FY 2017-2018 Budget
   Mayor Dove opened the floor for comments.
   Alderman Pukenas proposed a 5-cent increase on the property tax rate noting
that the previously discussed $.344 cents increase would only cover the basic
needs. He pointed out that the state is requiring improvement in the city’s
general fund balance. He stated he felt the additional money could be used for
that purpose.
   Alderman Poole stated she felt the issue of raising taxes needed more
consideration. She said that she had reviewed the budget multiple times and did
not want to be that girl that increases taxes. She suggested going through the
budget to determine if it could be tightened and what the city has to have.
   Alderman Adams stated he would not vote in favor of an increase in taxes. He
pointed out that property owners pay a hospital tax, the County may be raising
the fire fees, and Southport is considering going up on water and sewer rates.
He stated his opinion that some budget cutting can be done and he suggested an
in depth study on the amount of money the city needs and do more than a
temporary “band aid fix.” He stated the tax rate may need to go up 10 – 15
cents. He emphasized that there is a faction in town that cannot bear the
financial burden. He stated the city’s only obligation was to make repairs to
Franklin Square Art Gallery and funding for that project could be found by
making cuts in the budget.
   Alderman Powell agreed with comments made by Aldermen Poole & Adams. He
shared his opinion that past generations had made Southport a place that
everyone (outsiders) wanted to come to. He stated that the city needs to look
after its long-time residents. He said he felt the city’s needs could be met if
the Board went through the budget and made cuts. He likened the budget to a
wish list and the only obligation of the city was to do repairs to Franklin
Square Art Gallery.
   Alderman Coring stated he was “riding the fence” on increasing property
taxes. He noted that the idea of raising taxes had just come up in the past
couple weeks and he recalled during his first term that the Board said no
raising taxes. He commented that it had been quite some time since the city had
raised taxes. He said he looked at the needs and wants of the budget and he
struggled with how the city was going to meet its needs and continue to provide
services. Noting Ms. Mosteller’s previous remarks, he emphasized that the city
needs to take steps to establish a capital/maintenance plan for all of its
buildings and facilities. He discussed the public perception that the Board is
to blame for the shortfall, the desire for more accountability and that there
are loopholes and overtures in the budget that he has concerns about. He
acknowledged the urgency of the situation but was not ready to say yes to
raising taxes.
   Alderman Mosteller stated her appreciation for citizens that attended the
June 12 public forum. She spoke about the suggestion to tier taxes and her
research results that such an approach would not be permitted under state law.
She did say that the state has a Homestead Tax Exemption of 50% off county and
city taxes with no required pay back for long-time residents age 65 and older
or 100% disabled and the city could assist people in applying for the
exemption. She suggested providing the Homestead Tax Exemption information and
the city’s offer to assist in the process on the monthly electric bills. She
explained that $ .5 cents on the $100 valuation would amount to $4.17 a month
per $100,000 valuation. She pointed out that the capital improvement items in
the budget, she sees not as wants but needs. She suggested looking again at
overtime and making sure the policy is enforced, i.e., prior written approval.
She noted that there had been no tax increase since 2009, and the sewer rate
increase is a break even from years of being undercharged. She expressed her
concerns about receiving a budget with no monies for capital improvement which
is problematic for running the city.
   Alderman Adams reiterated his comments about an in-depth budget review to
decide if a tax increase should be 5 cents or 10 cents, prepare the citizens
for it and leave it there for some time. He pointed out that $12,000 in Police
Overtime is expended during the 4th of July and he cautioned “beating up”
overtime unless the city withdraws itself from public activities.
   Mayor Dove talked about the change in the character of Southport and the
affluent people coming to the area, displacement of long time Southport
citizens and loss of jobs that supported them, the crab industry, fishing,
poggy boats. He stated that Southport now supports the tourism industry. He
encouraged the Board to think about it and the people the 5 cents could affect.
   Alderman Pukenas motioned, second by Alderman Mosteller to raise the city’s
tax rate by 5 cents on the $100 valuation.
   Aye:   Aldermen Pukenas, Mosteller
   Nay:   Aldermen Adams, Powell, Coring, Poole
   Motion failed 4-2
Interim City Manager
   Mayor Dove reported that an interim city manager candidate recommended by
the Cape Fear Council of Government (COG) was unable to accept the position due
to family obligations.
   Mayor Dove stated that the Board also considered contracting with the Raben
Group but decided not to pursue that option.
   Mayor Dove stated that another recommendation from COG, Mr. John Bauer, a
retired county and city manager, met the city’s qualifications and could work
for the city on a part-time basis.
   Mayor Dove pointed out that Chris May, Executive Director of COG, had agreed
to serve as acting city manager per state law, from the minute City Manager
McDuffie left, until an interim manager comes on board. Mr. May indicated that
there was no charge to the city for the COG service.
   Alderman Poole motioned, second by Alderman Coring, to hire Mr. John Bauer
as the interim city manager, at $1,113.60 a week which includes travel,
starting Monday, June 19 and for Mr. May to serve as acting city manager until
Mr. Bauer arrives. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   City Attorney Isenberg stated that there is a legal requirement to have a
balanced budget in place by June 30. He recommended scheduling a workshop and a
budget meeting.
   Mayor Dove instructed department heads to review their budgets and make any
cuts possible.

Budget Discussion
   Mayor Dove opened the floor for discussion of the proposed FY 2017-2018
budget.
   Noting the Police Department requested two new vehicles, Alderman Adams
suggested looking at budget cuts in the department. He recommended replacing
only the vehicle that was wrecked and using the $17,000 insurance proceeds to
offset the cost. Finance Director Trexler indicated that a budget amendment
would be required to properly appropriate the insurance funds toward purchase
of a new police vehicle.
   Alderman Poole stated her opinion that the budget did not have many items to
cut. She commented to staff that they be judicious about overtime. She
suggested going through the capital expenditures in the budget memo and
discussing each one.
   Alderman Pukenas stated that public safety should be the number one concern.
He shared comments he received about the Dodge Chargers being inexpensive up
front but more costly in the long run. He stated his opinion that vehicles have
a shelf life and he emphasized giving the officers the best equipment possible.
He indicated he did not support making cuts to the Police Department. He
pointed out that cuts he felt could be made throughout the budget amounted to a
half cent in the tax rate. He stated he felt a tax increase was the best option
for the city.
   Alderman Powell stated his opinion had remained unchanged from the previous
meeting and that raising taxes would run people out of town whose relatives
from 175 years ago made the city what it is today. He said he could not vote
for raising taxes, he agreed to go through the proposed capital expenses
individually and agreed with Alderman Adams that the Police Department could
get by with just one car.
   Responding to a question from Alderman Powell, Police Chief Smith stated
that there is a special certification required for officers to ride a bicycle
for community policing. He noted that the department has one officer at this
time with the certification. Chief Smith added that officers are “walking the
beat” every day, downtown, weather permitting.
   Alderman Powell discussed needed water line upsizing on Owens and Brown
Streets funded in the water and sewer budgets. He suggested doing the work in-
house to save money.
   Alderman Coring talked about budget issues that are beyond the city’s
control, i.e. state budget cuts and increased health care benefits for
employees. He noted that many of the city’s buildings need maintenance and
several capital projects need to be done. He stated his opinion that the Board
not consider cutting services. He added that he did not see where significant
cuts could be made in the budget and he did not think it would be fair to keep
going back to employees and asking them to cut when it could become a danger
for them to perform their jobs. He reviewed the 10 capital projects, noting
four (4) of which he considered a “need” and six (6) “wants.” He discussed the
Police Department need for two (2) vehicles and he suggested outfitting the
current administration car for police service with the insurance proceeds and
then purchasing one new vehicle for police. He stated his opinion that he is
leaning towards a tax increase and adoption of a capital improvement long range
plan.
   Alderman Mosteller addressed Alderman Powell’s comments about putting
additional stress on the city’s long-time residents. She pointed out that the
State has a Homestead Exemption Act to provide relief for residents 65 & older
or 100% disabled. She noted that 41 households in Southport had taken advantage
of the Act which applies to county and hospital tax as well. She stated her
belief that there were things the community could do to help citizens. She
talked about analyzing prior years’ property valuations and the ultimate
impacts on the city’s budgets. She noted that the budget is based on
anticipated revenue based on previous year-end data and there are factors that
affect the revenue that the city has no control over. She referenced Senate
Bill 126 that could change the way local option sales taxes are calculated and
it could result in over $100,000 loss of revenue projected in the proposed
budget.
   Alderman Mosteller acknowledged that the Board can only make decisions on
what they know today and the Board knows it has to grow the general fund as
notified by the North Carolina Local Government Commission, knows it has future
projects; i.e. 201 E. Moore Street renovation and waterfront improvements,
along with funds to cover emergencies. She stated her support for the 5 cent
tax increase. Responding to a query by Mayor Dove, Alderman Mosteller stated a
5 cent increase equals $4.17 a month on $100,000 valuation.
   Alderman Poole asked what the average home valuation in Southport was. Staff
responded that $214,600 is the median home value in Southport.
   Mayor Dove agreed with all board members’ observations. He stated that the
city is in for challenges. He said the city needs to continue to provide and
improve its services. He acknowledged that a tax increase may be the best
option to improve the general fund balance up to 30% over the next three years,
proceed with capital projects and provide a high level of services to the
citizens.

BUDGET ORDINANCE - FISCAL YEAR 2017-2018
CITY OF SOUTHPORT
BE IT ORDAINED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport, North
Carolina, that, following a duly advertised public hearing, the following
annual budget ordinance is adopted to estimate revenues and make appropriations
for the financial operations of the City of Southport for the fiscal year
beginning July 1, 2017, and ending June 30, 2018.

the General Fund for the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2017, and ending June
30, 2018:

Fund for the expenses of the city government and its activities for the fiscal
year beginning July 1, 2017, and ending June 30, 2018:
Governing Body                        $   284,205   
Administration                           295,498
Finance                              234,500
Solid Waste                                         240,000

SECTION II. ELECTRIC FUND

Expenditures. The following amounts are hereby appropriated in the Water and
Sewer Fund for expenses for the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2017, and ending
June 30, 2018:
Total Expenditures                     $ 3,447,000
SECTION IV. TAX RATE
There is hereby levied, for fiscal year 2017-2018, a tax at the rate of $0.2956
on each one hundred dollars ($100) of assessed valuation of property located
within the City of Southport for the purpose of raising revenue in the General
Fund. The assessed value of property is 741,875,518.
SECTION V. BUDGET OFFICER AUTHORITY
The city manager (budget officer) is hereby authorized to transfer
appropriations within a fund and between funds under the following terms:
He may transfer amounts between appropriations within the same fund, provided
that a report of such transfers shall be made no later than the next regular
financial report to the Board of Aldermen.
He may authorize temporary transfers of cash among funds as necessary to meet
cash flow needs.
All other transfers of funds between appropriations or budget funds shall be
accomplished by Board amendment of this ordinance.
SECTION VIII. CONTINUING AUTHORIZATION
Prior year Capital Reserve Fund is no longer a restriction of Fund Balance.
Previously-adopted capital project budgets, grant project budgets, and special
reserve funds are hereby un-authorized as all such projects have been completed
and all monies shall be returned to the associated funds upon adoption of the
Budget ordinance.
SECTION IX. BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION
This ordinance and the supporting budget document shall be the basis of the
financial plan for the City of Southport municipal government for the 2017-2018
fiscal year. The budget officer shall administer the budget and shall insure
the finance officer and department heads of the city are provided with
sufficient guidance to properly implement this plan. Copies of the budget
ordinance shall be furnished to the city manager and the finance officer for
their use and direction in the disbursement of funds and to the city clerk for
the official records of the city.
SECTION X. ADOPTION
This ordinance has been adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in special
session on June 21, 2017, upon the motion of Alderman Coring and the second of
Alderman Pukenas, with a vote of 4 ayes and 3 noes, and shall be effective July
1, 2017.
                     /s/ Jerry V. Dove, Mayor

RESOLUTION REQUESTING THE CHEMOURS COMPANY TO HALT PROCESSES WHICH RESULT IN
THE DISCHARGE OF THE GenX CHEMICAL INTO THE CAPE FEAR RIVER
WHEREAS, the majority of Brunswick County’s drinking water supply comes from
the Cape Fear River; and
WHEREAS, Chemours is a company that operates a facility on approximately 2200
acres of land in Bladen County along the Cape Fear River and which withdraws up
to 26 million gallons per day from the Cape Fear River and discharges treated
wastewater back into the river; and
WHEREAS, Chemours manufactures GenX, a chemical used to make Teflon and other
products; and
WHEREAS, Chemours operates under a permit or agreement with the EPA that
requires the company to reclaim 99% of the GenX chemical it manufactures prior
to discharge; and
WHEREAS, Chemours contends that it complies with the 99% recapture rule for its
facility for production of GenX, but believes that GenX may be entering the
river as a byproduct of a vinyl ether process used at its Fayetteville Works
Plant; and
WHEREAS, GenX has been shown in some studies to cause cancer and other health
issues in lab animals, and is an emerging chemical for which the EPA has yet to
establish a safe regulatory level; and
WHEREAS, The City of Southport recognizes that the availability of safe
drinking water is of paramount importance to the health and well-being of its
citizens;
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the City of Southport Board of Aldermen
does hereby request the Chemours maintains a zero discharge policy permanently,
or at a minimum until such time as the North Carolina Department of
Environmental Quality and the Environmental Protection Agency concludes any
investigation into the effects of discharge of this chemical in the water
supply and create specific regulations or guidelines pertaining to acceptable
levels, if any, for the presence of this chemical in the water supply.
   This the 13th day of July, 2017                        
                        /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor
ATTEST:
/s/ Michele Windham, Clerk
RESOLUTION OF ACCEPTANCE FOR WASTEWATER ASSET INVENTORY & ASSESSMENT PLAN GRANT
WHEREAS,   the North Carolina Clean Water Revolving Loan and Grant Act of 1987
has authorized the making of loans and grants to aid eligible units of
government in financing the cost of construction of wastewater treatment works,
wastewater collection systems, and water supply systems, water conservation
projects; and
WHEREAS,   The North Carolina Department of Environment and Natural Resources
has offered a Grant in the amount of $45,000 to the City of Southport in order
to complete an Asset Inventory and Assessment Plan for its Wastewater
Collection System; and
WHEREAS,   the City of Southport intends to complete said project in accordance
with the approved plans and specifications;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE BOARD OF ALDERMEN OF THE CITY OF
SOUTHPORT:
   That the City of Southport does hereby accept the Grant offer of $45,000.
That the City of Southport does hereby give assurance to the North Carolina
Department of Environmental Quality that all items specified in the grant
offer, Section II Assurances will be adhered to.
That Interim City Manager John Bauer, and successors so titled, is hereby
authorized and directed to furnish such information as the appropriate State
agency may request in connection with such application or the project; to make
the assurances as contained above; and to execute such other documents as may
be required in connection with the application.
That the City of Southport has substantially compiled or will substantially
comply with all Federal, State, and local laws, rules, regulations, and
ordinances applicable to the project and to Federal and State grants and loans
pertaining thereto.
This, the 11th day of July, 2017            City of Southport
                     BY: /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor

Southport Firefighter’s Supplemental Retirement Plan
Under Chief Greg Cumbee’s administration, a supplemental Retirement Plan was
put in place to help retain firefighters from leaving the department after 20
years of service. This retirement plan was through the Fire Department’s city
budget, and was in addition to the NC Fire Fighter’s Pension Plan. The plan was
set up that when a Firefighter put in 20 years with the Southport Fire
Department, and turned 55 years of age, they would receive $100.00 a month. If
they stayed active in the department, beyond the 20 years, the supplement would
increase $5.00 per month for each year. For instance, if a fire fighter had 20
years, he would receive $100.00 per month, if a firefighter had 25 years, he
would receive $125.00, a firefighter that had 35 years would receive $175.00
per month. The calculation was $60.00 X (Years of Service) divided by 12.
The plan was only eligible for fire fighters that put in 20 years at Southport
Fire Department, not any other department, and was not payable until the
firefighter reached 55 years of age. Currently, the following retirees listed
below are being paid the supplemental retirement:
Firefighter Monthly Supplement Yearly Supplement

13.   Yard Waste Amendments
   Interim City Manager Bauer presented amendments to the contract with Waste
Industries for solid waste collection. He advised the Board that some residents
had been mixing garbage with their yard waste and others had been putting yard
waste in their trash or recycling containers which are a violation of city
code. Referencing the information provided in the agenda packet, he stated that
the yard waste issues would be resolved with placement of a sticker on all yard
waste containers.
   Alderman Powell contended that the containers were the property of Waste
Industries, not the City, and that the contract specified Waste Industries
would be responsible for maintaining them. He added that issues with Waste
Industries arose last year when some containers fell into disrepair and Waste
Industries would not repair them. He stated his opinion that Waste Industries
needed to be held to the original agreement.
   City Attorney Isenberg pointed out that the contract amendments provided
more benefits.
   Will pick up:   2 - 95 gallon carts + 2 bundles or
         1 - 95 gallon cart + 5 biodegradable bags + 2 bundles or
         10 biodegradable bags + 2 bundles
   Alderman Pukenas motioned, second by Alderman Mosteller to adopt the
amendments to the Solid Waste Collection & Disposal Agreement with Waste
Industries. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
AMENDMENT TO SOLID WASTE COLLETCION, TRANSPORTATION AND DISPOSAL AGREEMENT
   THIS AMENDMENT TO SOLID WASTE COLLECTION AGREEMENT (this “Amendment”) is
made and entered into this 13th day of July 2017, by and between WASTE
INDUSTRIES, LLC, a North Carolina limited liability company (herein referred to
as “Company”) and the TOWN OF SOUTHPORT, a municipal corporation duly
incorporated under the laws of the State of North Carolina (herein referred to
as “Town”).
RECITALS
   A.   Company and Town are parties to a Solid Waste Collection Agreement
dated June 13, 2013, as previously amended and extended (the “Agreement”).
   B.   The parties desire to extend the term of the Agreement and make certain
other changes as set forth herein.
AGREEMENTS
   NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the Recitals, the mutual covenants and
agreements set forth herein, and for other good and valuable consideration, the
receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, the parties agree as
follows:
   1.   2B. Delete the work “BULK”.
   2.   Delete 3B
   3.   Replace 3C with the following:
         Yard Waste “will be” serviced only if:
   ∙    In approved resident owned 95 gallon rollout cart with Waste Industries
designated Yard Waste decal.
   ∙    In Biodegradable paper bags (no plastic bags of any type accepted).
   ∙    Bundles must be securely tied in 5’ lengths and a maximum of 50 lbs. in
weight.
   Yard will “will not” be serviced if:
   ∙    Trash or recycle carts are used.
   ∙    Trash or recycle is mixed in with yard waste in approved yard waste
cart.
   ∙    No vacant lots will be serviced.
   ∙    All yard waste 95 gallon rollout carts are considered the property of
the resident/homeowner and are to be maintained/repaired by same.
   Yard Waste “limits” per residence/per pickup (choice of 1):
   ∙    2 approved 95 gallon Yard Waste rollout carts with Waste Industries
decal, plus 2 bundles.
   ∙    1 approved 95 gallon Yard Waste rollout cart with Waste Industries
decal, plus 5 biodegradable paper bags, plus 2 bundles
   ∙    10 biodegradable paper bags plus 2 bundles.
   Except as specifically modified herein, the Agreement shall remain in full
force and effect as written. Capitalized terms used and not otherwise defined
herein will have the meanings set forth in the Agreement.

BOARD COMMENTS
   Alderman Adams raised concerns about the $5 fee for paying a utility bill on
line with a credit card. He stated it was his impression the service was being
provided as a convenience. He contended that the $5 fee is a financial burden
to some city residents. He recommended re-addressing the fee.
   Finance Director Trexler pointed out that utility bills can be paid in
person at City Hall, by check or via an automatic draft.
   Alderman Poole, chair of the Rate Committee, stated that the fee was
implemented to cover the credit card charges the city pays to the issuing bank.
She stated that the Committee could look at the fees again.
   Alderman Pukenas recommended putting the bill payment options on the utility
bills and on the city’s web page.
   Alderman Poole welcomed Interim City Manager John Bauer.
   Alderman Coring suggested that the Board look at tabling construction of the
proposed greenway to Tidewater Plaza. He stated that he had heard from
citizens, had walked the woods, looked at the area at night and was having
doubts that it was a good project to pursue. He expressed concerns that it
would not be used when the North Carolina Department of Transportation (NCDOT)
put in sidewalks during the NC 211 widening project and the money budgeted for
the project could be better spent elsewhere.
   Alderman Adams agreed with Alderman Coring, as did Alderman Powell.
