Coring.
   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to accept the
resignation of Alderman Coring. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   City Manager Oakley announced that Todd Coring had been chosen to be the
next Chief of Police for the city of Southport. Manager Oakley’s comments
included in their entirety:
October 23, 2018 – Todd Coring has agreed to become the next Police Chief for
the City of Southport. Todd brings over twenty years of law enforcement
experience with the Brunswick County Sheriff’s Office, where he currently
serves as a Lieutenant. He is also a lifetime resident of Southport who has
served the City since he was a teenager. He has not only worked for the City
but also currently serves as the Assistant Chief of the Southport Fire
Department and has served on the Board of Aldermen since his first election in
2011. Through all these endeavors, he has consistently demonstrated the
leadership qualities needed to be a great Police Chief.
Todd’s vast experience in law enforcement along with his dedication to public
service made the decision to hire Todd an easy one. He not only knows a lot
about law enforcement in general, but is very familiar with City’s Police
Department having worked there as a dispatcher before becoming an Officer with
Brunswick County Sheriff’s Office. His experience as an Alderman has also given
him a great understanding of how the City operates and has helped him develop a
strong trust with the community.
Another strong advantage he brings is the relationship he has developed with
Sheriff Ingram while working for him. This experience will only strengthen our
relationship with the Sheriff’s Office and will hopefully lead to partnerships
that help the Southport Police Department carry on the example the Sheriff’s
Office has set over the past few months.
After gauging his interest in the position and evaluating his credentials, it
was clear that we should pursue him for the job. Although the position vacancy
was not officially announced, we received dozens of resumes from some highly
trained and capable people, but no matter how hard we looked, I don’t believe
we could find one with the combination of Todd’s experience and his long
dedication to the service of Southport. Therefore, I decided not to formally
announce the vacancy or conduct a candidate search before making this decision.
Hiring him now, before the Internal Audit of the Police Department that the
U.S.I.S.S. Agency is working on is completed, gives him the opportunity to work
with them as they finish the report and he can see firsthand where improvements
and changes are needed. It will also give him additional insight and the chance
to ask them questions as he develops new policies, procedures, and establishes
a new direction for the department. It will also allow us to re-activate the
department sooner.
   Noting that Southport native Todd Coring has been involved in community
relations while serving in the Sheriff’s Office, and has a history of law
enforcement in his family, Mayor Dove commended the City Manager for choosing
Todd for the next Southport Police Chief. Mayor Dove stated that he has had the
privilege of working with Todd for 20 years.
ADJOURN
   Alderman Pukenas motioned, second by Alderman Powell to adjourn the meeting.
Unanimous vote; motion carried.
                        /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor
                              
Attest: /s/ Michele Windham, Clerk

The Military Ocean Terminal Sunny Point (MOTSU) as it exists today was
established in 1955 by the Department of The Army and is the largest military
terminal anywhere in the world. It serves as a transfer point between rail,
trucks, and ships for the import and export of weapons, ammunition, explosives
and military equipment for United States Army. In event armed conflict since
its creation the Military Ocean Terminal Sunny Point has played a role in
supporting deployed units.
August 15, 2018 was an important day in history for Military Ocean Terminal
Sunny Point. It's the first time a woman has reported for duty to serve as
commander of the 596th Transportation Brigade. Colonel Carlisle credits her
father, a veteran of the U.S. Air Force and her family for being her
inspiration to join the U.S. Army. Throughout her 23 year career she has been
deployed to Korea, Iraq, Afghanistan and has been stationed in Hawaii and
Alaska. This is her first time living in North Carolina.
Please join myself and the Board of Aldermen in welcoming Colonel Heather J.
Carlisle to Military Ocean Terminal Sunny Point and out community.

   6.   Consideration: 11th Street right-of-way and alley abandonment
   City Planner Lloyd explained that RHH Land Investors has a project going
through the Planned Building Group site plan process. He stated the developer
is requesting the Board of Aldermen abandon a portion of the 11 th Street
right-of-way as well as a 10 ft. wide alley in between the project and
properties fronting on Caswell A venue in order to make use of the property to
enhance the landscape plan. Mr. Lloyd emphasized that closure of the 10 ft.
alley would result with half of the alley going to the developer and half going
to the adjacent property owners.
   Planner Lloyd explained the process outlined in GS 16A-299 that must be
followed if the Board decides to close the right-of-way and alley.
      •   Publication of the resolution once a week for four successive weeks
prior to the public hearing.
      •   Registered or certified mail notice to owners of property adjoining
the public way.
      •   Posted notice of the proposed closing in at least two places along
the public way.
   Alderman Mosteller expressed her opinion that abandonment of the alley would
allow for better maintenance of the property and she stated her support. She
shared her hesitation to support abandonment of the right-of-way.
   Alderman Powell stated he would not support the requested abandonment.
   Responding to a query from Alderman Sharkey, City Attorney Isenberg advised
that if the Board decides to abandon the alley, a utility easement can be
reserved.
   Alderman Spencer motioned, second by Alderman Mosteller to proceed to call
for a public hearing and for staff to prepare a resolution.
AYE: Aldermen Spencer, Mosteller, Sharkey, Pukenas
NAY: Alderman Powell
Motion carried 4-1

A RESOLUTION HONORING THE 103rd BIRTHDAY OF
ROBERT C. RUARK, JR.
WHEREAS, Robert C. Ruark,, Jr. was born in Wilmington on December 29, 1915; and
WHEREAS, Ruark achieved international success as a newspaper and magazine
columnist and author; and
WHEREAS, Ruark spent a great deal of his childhood visiting his maternal
grandparents, Capt. Ned and Lottie Adkins at their home in Southport; and
WHEREAS, Among Ruark's works were the beloved book, The Old Man and the Boy; a
semi-autographical work defined by the philosophical musings of his
grandfather; and
WHEREAS, Ruark's success brought much attention to Southport which continues to
this day.
BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport, North
Carolina, that the City of Southport hereby designates December 29, 2018 as
"Robert C. Ruark, Jr." day in his honor.
Adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in regular session, December 13,
2018.

   3.   Ordinance Amending Chapter 10, Article VII of the Southport City Code,
For-Hire Tours – approved
AN ORDINANCE AMENDING CHAPTER 10, ARTICLE VII, OF THE SOUTHPORT CITY CODE
BE IT ORDAINED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport that Chapter
10, Article VII, of the Southport City Code is hereby amended to read as
follows:
ARTICLE VII. FOR-HIRE TOURS
DIVISION 1. GENERALLY
Sec. 10-156. Purpose and authority.
It is the purpose of this division to require that all walking and vehicle
tours operated within the City of Southport for profit be licensed and
regulated as set forth in this article. This article is not intended to
regulate walking and vehicle tours conducted by nonprofit organizations such as
the Southport Historical Society, the North Carolina Maritime Museum at
Southport or schools. Furthermore, the provisions of this article shall not
apply to tours conducted entirely off the public streets, sidewalks, rights-of-
way or municipal property.
Sec. 10-157. Definitions.
The following words, terms, and phrases when used in this article shall have
the meaning described to them in this section, except where the context clearly
indicates a different meaning:
Amplifying device shall mean any equipment or apparatus that broadens or
magnifies the human voice, music or any sound.
Charter routes shall mean the approved route of travel for any tour.
Person shall mean a natural person, corporation, company, partnership, limited
liability company, or other organization operating for profit.
Public right-of-way shall mean any street, highway, sidewalk, parking lot or
alley that is owned, controlled, maintained or operated by the "city" or State
of North Carolina.
Tour or touring shall mean the conducting of or the participation in
sightseeing on foot or in a vehicle in the "city" for hire or in combination
with a request for donations.
Tour guide shall mean any person who acts or offers to act as a guide for hire
or compensation through any part of the "city" to pedestrians or vehicle
passengers.
Tour guide permit shall mean the written authority granted by the tourism
commission for an individual to conduct a sightseeing tour on foot or by
vehicle within the "city".
Vehicle shall mean bicycles, pedicabs, animal drawn or motorized vehicles used
to transport members of a sightseeing tour.
LICENSES AND BUSINESS REGULATIONS
DIVISION 2. TOUR GUIDE PERMIT
Sec. 10-158. Required Permit; Number of Permits.
No person shall offer a for-hire tour within the corporate limits of the City
of Southport unless such person shall have first applied for and obtained from
the City a tour guide permit. It shall be unlawful for any person to operate a
tour in any manner contrary to the provisions of this article or without first
having obtained said permit. No more than three (3) walking tour permits, four
(4) low-speed vehicle tour permits and one (1) animal-drawn vehicle permit may
be issued and in effect at any time. Issuance of permits is determined by the
date in which it is received.
Sec. 10-159. Application.
Each applicant for a tour guide permit shall submit in writing an application
to the City of Southport Code Enforcement Officer containing the following
information and documentation: (Application forms available at Southport City
Hall)
   The name, address and telephone number of the owner and operator of the
business. If the applicant is a partnership, the names and addresses of the
general partners; if a corporation the names and addresses of the    directors
and officers; if a limited liability company, the names and addresses of the
members and managers.
   A copy of a valid North Carolina driver's license.
   A criminal record check of the previous 5 years which includes criminal and
driving record.
   The address and phone number from which the applicant will conduct business
operations.
   A description of the charter route to be used by the applicant including
starting point and stopping points along the route.
   A description of the hours of operation of the proposed business and the
proposed hours during which the tours will be conducted.
   A detailed description (script) of the information to be given to the
members of the tour related to those sights    to be viewed within the "city",
including a copy of any published literature proposed to be provided by the
tour guide to any members of the tour.
   A schedule of the rates and charges proposed by the applicant in the
operation of the business.
   A certificate of general liability insurance in a minimum amount of one
hundred thousand dollars ($100,000.00) which specifically provides that the
same may not be cancelled without thirty (30) days written notice to the
"city".
(10)   Application fee of fifty dollars ($50.00) payable at the time of
application and annually, on the first of January of each calendar year,
thereafter as a renewal fee.
Sec. 10-160. Handicap accessibility.
All proposed charter routes must follow handicap accessible public rights-of-
way appropriate to tours where walking is utilized by a walking tour or exiting
a tour vehicle.
Sec. 10-161. Permit Approval
Upon receipt of the complete application, the applicant will receive their
permit if they meet the following conditions:
The applicant has not within five (5) years of the date of the application been
convicted of a felony, driving while impaired or any crime of moral turpitude.
The application is complete and sufficient with all necessary documentation.
The applicant meets all of the minimum qualifications for the tour guide
permit.
The applicant is solvent and financially able to furnish adequate service on a
continuing basis and have the necessary insurance required.
The proposed service will be carried out in a reasonably safe manner so as not
to interfere with the health, safety and welfare of pedestrians, motor vehicles
and the general public and the proposed tour will not unreasonably interfere
with the use of the streets, sidewalks, parking lots, alleys, parks and other
   public properties within the "city".
The maximum number of permits have not already been issued and in effect.
The tour, including any vehicle or conveyance, will be compatible with the
history and area of the City where the tour is conducted.
Each tour guide permit granted by the City of Southport shall be valid for a
period of one (1) calendar year and must be renewed annually, by the first day
of January of each calendar year thereafter. Any changes in an application for
renewal will be considered a new application and need to follow Sec. 10-159
guidelines. The City of Southport shall have the authority to set other
conditions to the tour guide permit as deemed necessary in the interest of the
health, welfare and safety of the public.
Sec. 10-162. Prohibited acts.
It shall be unlawful and a violation of this article and a violation of a tour
guide permit for any tour guide or any tour guide permit holder to:
Fail to follow the approved charter route or move in a manner blocking
entrances to stores, homes, public parks, cemeteries or other places of
business or interfere with street traffic.
Fail to follow the lawful commands of a law enforcement officer.
Move on a sidewalk in excess of a column of two (2) persons abreast.
Solicit members of the public verbally while such member of the public is on
any public street, public sidewalk or public property.
   Operate an amplifying device during the course of the tour without specific
written tourism commission approval.
Violate the terms and conditions of the tour guide permit.
Place a sign in a public space to promote the business except as allowed below.
To enter onto private property without the express permission of the owner of
said property.
Conduct a tour within the confines of a cemetery after dark pursuant to Sec. 5-
13 guidelines.
A temporary A-Frame sign may be placed four (4) hours before the operating
hours of the tour, within one (1) block of the starting location of the tour
and must be removed at the end of the business day of the permit holder.
Sec. 10-163. Revocation.
The City of Southport Code Enforcement Officer may revoke a tour guide permit
after notice to the permit holder thereof upon finding any of the following:
A violation of the terms and conditions of this ordinance or the conditions of
the tour guide permit.
Upon determining that false information was given on the application for a tour
guide permit.
The cancellation or revocations of the tour guide permit holder's liability
insurance coverage.
The business closing of the holder of a tour guide permit.
Conviction of a felony, driving while impaired or crimes involving the moral
turpitude by a tour guide or permit holder.
Three (3) violations in one year will result in the loss of a permit for the
remainder of the year, as well as, the following calendar year.
Any tour guide permit holder who has received a revocation order under Sec. 10-
163 may appeal the order to the Board of Aldermen by giving notice of appeal in
writing to the Code Enforcement Officer and to the City Clerk within ten (10)
days following issuance of the order. In the absence of an appeal, the order of
the Code Enforcement Officer shall be final. The Board shall hear an appeal
within a reasonable time and may affirm, modify and affirm, or revoke the
order.
Sec. 10-164. Transfer.
The tour guide permit issued pursuant to this article shall not be transferred
by the permit holder to any other persons.
Sec. 10-165. Violations.
In addition to revocation of a tour guide permit, the violation of the
provisions of any City of Southport Ordinance shall subject the offender to a
civil penalty to be collected by the City of Southport in the nature of a debt.
Each day a continuing violation occurs, shall be deemed a separate violation.
Sec. 10-166. Exemptions.
Exempt from this article are walking and vehicle tours conducted by non-profit
organizations such as the Southport Historical Society, The North Carolina
Maritime Museum at Southport and schools. The City of Southport shall have the
authority to determine such groups. Exempt, non-profit organizations are
subject, however, to the provisions of this article in all matters related to
health and safety, right-of-way and public access concerns.
This the 13th day of December 2018.         City of Southport

STATE OF NORTH CAROLINA
ORDER
BRUNSWICK COUNTY
   THAT WHEREAS, G. S. 160A-299 requires that when a city proposes to
permanently close any street or public alley that the Board of Aldermen first
adopt a resolution declaring its intent to close said street or alley and
calling for a public hearing on the question; and
   WHEREAS, G. S. 160A-299 further requires that the resolution to close the
street or alley be published once a week for four successive weeks prior to the
date of said hearing, that a copy thereof be sent by registered or certified
mail to all owners of property adjoining the portion of the street or alley to
be closed as shown on the county tax records, and that notice of the closing
and public hearing be prominently posted in at least two places along the
street or alley to be closed; and
   WHEREAS, on December 13, 2018, the Board of Aldermen of the City of
Southport passed a resolution proposing to close the following described public
alley, and also calling for a public hearing on said question:
   Being that 10 foot wide alley running from the northern line of W. Eleventh
Street
   in a northerly direction to its terminus in Block 15 of the Smith & Weeks
Addition
   as shown on a plat of the Smith & Weeks Addition to the City of Southport
recorded
   in Book II at Page 35 of the Brunswick County Registry; and
   WHEREAS, the City of Southport has complied with all requirements of G. S.
160A-299, including the holding of the public hearing and the giving of all
required notice; and
   WHEREAS, no portion of the street or alley to be closed is under the
authority or control of the Board of Transportation; and
   WHEREAS, adjoining property owners and other persons were heard on the
question of whether or not the closing would be detrimental to the public
interest or the property rights of any individual; and
   WHEREAS, it appears to the satisfaction of the Board of Aldermen after the
hearing that the closing of the northernmost 93 foot portion of the public
alley described above is not contrary to the public interest and that no
individual owning property in the vicinity of this portion of said alley or in
the subdivision in which it is located would be deprived of reasonable means of
ingress and egress to their property and that said portion of said alley
described above should be closed;
   NOW, THEREFORE, IT IS HEREBY ORDERED pursuant to G. S. 160A-299 as follows:
   1. That the following described public alley in the City of Southport is
hereby closed:
   Being the northernmost 93 foot portion of that 10 foot wide alley running
from the northern line of W. Eleventh Street in a northerly direction to its
terminus in Block 15 of the Smith & Weeks Addition as shown on a plat of the
Smith & Weeks Addition to the City of Southport recorded in Book II at Page 35
of the Brunswick County Registry.
   2. That the City of Southport hereby reserves and retains all right, title
and interest in all utility improvements and easements, if any, located within
said alley as described above.

5. Major Subdivision Preliminary Plat; 11th Street Subdivision
Planner Lloyd explained that the proposed subdivision would be the first
development using the Residential Cluster Development standards found in
Article 15 of the UDO which provides an alternative development option that
promotes more efficient use of land, better preserves the natural character of
the site, provides desirable and useable open space and tree cover, preserves
environmentally sensitive areas and provides design flexibility relating to
location of units to unique site conditions. He pointed out that Cluster
Subdivisions are a Conditional Use. He indicated that the Board of Adjustment
had approved the Conditional Use at a January 7th meeting. Planner Lloyd added
that the Planning Board reviewed the preliminary plat and found that the
subdivision met the standards of preliminary plat. He noted that an additional
access point on 9th Street is being pursued and an additional access onto 11th
Street is a second option if the 9th Street access does not materialize.
Alderman Sharkey acknowledged the hard work performed by the Planning Board and
staff addressing how open space would be oriented, storm water and the review
process. She stated concerns regarding another project proposed in the area by
the same developer and the impact the developments would have on 11th Street
traffic and road condition. She suggested requiring the developer to improve
11th Street from the point where it intersects with Caswell Avenue.
City Attorney Isenberg pointed out that the UDO does not require two entrances
for the size of the proposed subdivision. Alderman Powell noted that there has
been a policy requiring two access points since the early 2000’s.
Planner Lloyd pointed out that the threshold requiring a traffic impact study
is 800 trips per day determined by an estimated 10 per day per household which
results in 490 trips per day for the proposed subdivision.
Noting that a 9th Street connection would be beneficial for all residents of
the area, Mr. Perry Davis, Cape Fear Engineering, expressed confidence that the
access would materialize.
Alderman Sharkey asked if 11th Street conditions were adequate for the
development. Public Works Director, David Fox stated that the street was in
good condition to the edge of the woods, the culvert had been replaced, and the
street will be paved in the near future.
Alderman Pukenas motioned, second by Alderman Powell to approve the Preliminary
Plat.
Vote: Ayes: Aldermen Pukenas, Powell, Mosteller, Spencer
Nay: Alderman Sharkey
Motion carried 4-1

   City Manager Oakley displayed an aerial picture of the W. West Street site
and explained particulars of the site and the offer:

   ∙   Offer includes:

      2.   .11 acres of upland for picnic area for public

      4.   Stormwater will be caught on site

   ∙   Property currently used by City for storage of materials and drying of

   ∙   130ft. frontage on Cottage Creek; no frontage on Intracoastal Waterway
   ∙   Appraised at $440,000; 1.3 acres useable land
   ∙   Cost of demolition, $365,000
   ∙   If developed as proposed, $20,000 tax revenue not including fire

    Alderman Mosteller contended that the appraisal comparisons were 3 – 5
years old, the property was undervalued and the offer was negligible in
relation to the city’s entire budget. She stated her belief that the structures
could be repurposed. Referencing the 2015 – 2020 Parks and Recreation and Open
Space Master Plan, Alderman Mosteller emphasized the goals and objectives:
   1.   Enhancement and Appropriate Operational Maintenance of Existing Parks
Areas and Facilities
   2.   Provision of New and Expanded Active Recreation Opportunities and
Experiences
   3.   Enhancement and Safety of Movement for Pedestrians and Non-Motorized
Vehicles
   4.   Protection, Preservation and Conservation of Open Space and Green Space
   5.   Free, Easy and Open Access to the Waters and Shoreline in and Around
the City of Southport
   Alderman Mosteller pointed out that the Master Plan recommends aggressive
purchase of property for open space, parks and public access to waters and the
CAMA Core Future Land Use Plan depicts the site as Open Space.
   Alderman Powell asked the City Manager to report on the City’s financial
standing. City Manager Oakley stated that the Local Government Commission (LGC)
would like municipalities to maintain a 30% fund balance, the City’s is
currently 12%. He reported that he had met with Representative Iler and Senator
Rabon regarding funding for hurricane repairs and he pointed out that at best
FEMA will reimburse 75%, it could take up to 4 years for reimbursement and
there is no guarantee the City will receive any money. He added that there is
some hurricane relief funding from the State in the form of grants and the City
is pursuing those. City Manager Oakley stressed that it is imperative to
bolster the General Fund before another disaster and he pointed out that
Electric system funds can only be used for electrical projects.
   Alderman Sharkey commented that her job is to look at the big picture and
she stated her opinion that a return on any monies invested by the City on the
site would not be lucrative. She noted that there are other properties in the
city that could be pursued for parks. She stated that acceptance of the offer
provides a recreational opportunity.
   Noting that the City is not in a position to borrow money and that there is
a need for financial stability, Alderman Spencer expressed his views about the
offer. He stated that he does not take the decision to sell lightly and he
remarked that beyond the initial sale proceeds, the buyer will be boosting the
local economy by providing jobs and boat owners will be spending money on
services throughout the community. He agreed with Alderman Sharkey that there
are other properties in the city for potential parks.
   Alderman Sharkey motioned, second by Alderman Powell to adopt the Resolution
Authorizing Negotiated Offer and Upset Bid Process.
Discussion
   Alderman Mosteller commented that the Planning Board and Parks & Recreation
Advisory Board have recommended keeping the site, the property will continue to
appreciate in value and the $650,000 offered for the property is negligible
when considering the entire city budget.
   Vote
   Aye:   Aldermen Sharkey, Powell, Tucker
   Nay:   Aldermen Mosteller, Pukenas, Spencer
   Aye:   Mayor Dove
   Motion carried 4-3
RESOLUTION AUTHORIZING NEGOTIATED OFFER AND UPSET BID PROCESS
   WHEREAS, the City of Southport owns certain real property adjacent to West
West Street in the City of Southport described as follows:
      Parcel of approximately 2.5 acres bounded by Cottage Creek on the West,
property of Admiral Holdings, LLC, and W. West Street on the North, and
property of Southport Marina, Inc. on the South and East. The property was
formerly used as the City of Southport’s Wastewater Treatment Plant and is
identified at Tax Parcel 237LF021;
   and
   WHEREAS, N. C. G. S. 160A-269 permits the City to sell real property by
upset bid, after receipt of an offer for the property; and
   WHEREAS, the City has received an offer to purchase the above-described
property at the price of $ $650,000 from Southport Marina, Inc.; and
   WHEREAS, Southport Marina, Inc. has paid the required five percent (5%)
deposit on its offer;
   NOW, THEREFORE, the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport resolves
that:
   1. The Board of Aldermen authorizes the sale of the property described above
through the upset bid procedure of N. C. G. S. 160A-269.
   2. The City Clerk shall cause a notice of the proposed sale to be published.
The notice shall describe the property and the amount of the offer, and shall
state the terms under which the offer may be upset.
   3. Persons wishing to upset the offer that has been received shall submit a
sealed bid with their offer to the office of the City Clerk within 10 days
after the notice of sale is published. At the conclusion of the 10-day period,
the City Clerk shall open the bids, if any, and the highest such bid will
become the new offer. If there is more than one bid in the highest amount, the
first such bid received will become the new offer.
   4. If a qualifying higher bid is received, the City clerk shall cause a new
notice of upset bid to be published, and shall continue to do so until a 10-day
period has passed without any qualifying upset bid having been received. At
that time, the amount of the final high bid shall be reported to the Board of
Aldermen.
   5. A qualifying higher bid is one that raises the existing offer by not less
than ten percent 10% of the first $ 1000.00 of that offer and five (5%) of the
remainder of that offer.
   6. A qualifying higher bid must also be accompanied by a deposit in the
amount of five percent (5%) of the bid; the deposit may be made in cash,
cashier’s check or certified check. The City will return the deposit on any bid
not accepted, and will return the deposit on an offer subject to upset if a
qualifying higher bid is received. The City will return or credit the deposit
of the final high bidder at closing.
   7. The terms of the final sale are that the Board of Aldermen must approve
the final high offer before the sale is closed, which it will do within 30 days
after the final upset bid period has passed, and the buyer must pay cash at the
time of closing.
   8. The City reserves the right to withdraw the property from sale at any
time before the final high bid is accepted and the right to reject at any time
all bids.
    Adopted February 2, 2019            City of Southport
                        
                        J. V. Dove, Mayor

4.   Maritime Museum Update; Lori Sanderlin
   Ms. Lori Sanderlin, Manager of the North Carolina Maritime Museum at
Southport addressed the Board. She spoke about her first year as manager, 7
years as an educator, the Friends of the Museum successful fund raisers, and
facility renovations. She emphasized that the museum’s mission is to collect,
preserve, and interpret the material and culture pertinent to the maritime
history of the lower Cape Fear region. Ms. Sanderlin spoke about how the museum
impacts Southport:
   ∙   Tourism – Money spent in the community
   ∙   Higher Quality of Life
   ∙   Enhance Education – provide programming to school systems at no cost
   ∙   Community Collaboration – festival participation; Springfest, 4th of
July, coordinate with Southport Tourism Department
   Ms. Sanderlin talked about the free monthly 3rd Tuesday program, fundraiser
events held by the Friends of the Museum to supplement operating costs not paid
by the State; i.e., electric service fees. She spoke about a ribbon cutting for
the newest exhibit, a 5K run, and Maritime Day expanding into a public program
with hands on coordinated activities with the Yacht Club and Coast Guard
Auxiliary.
   Ms. Sanderlin invited everyone to attend events in October commemorating the
56th anniversary of Hurricane Hazel. She stated that there would be multiple
different programs and interactive exhibits on how to prepare for a hurricane.
   Pointing out that the Cape Fear region was one of the first 10 areas in the
country to receive station of a Coast Guard cutter, Ms. Sanderlin announced
that the museum will be getting a 30 foot model of the Diligence Cutter.

D)   Public Comment
   Ms. Musette Steck, 4635 Willow Moss Way, speaking on behalf of Mr. Donnie
Joyner, thanked the City for supporting and publicizing Black History Month
events. She emphasized that the community building was filled multiple times
during the events.
   Ms. Joanne Clair-Mayer, 710 N. Atlantic Avenue, spoke in support of the sale
of the former wastewater treatment plant. She discussed three (3) topics: 1.
the site has been unused for eight (8) years, is a potential biohazard, and
poses legal liability if someone were to be hurt on the site; 2. Clean up of
the site is estimated at $440,000, there is a greater need for infrastructure
repairs; 3. Citizens elect the Board to make decisions best for the city and
all of its 3,600 citizens.
   Dr. Kim Jones, 1001 Pete’s Camp Drive, spoke in opposition to the sale of
the former wastewater treatment plant. She stated that Coastal Water Watch has
set precedent for transforming a wastewater treatment facility into a park. She
added that many years ago she had proposed a renewable energy park for the
site. She stated that the University of North Carolina at Wilmington (UNCW)
could develop an oyster hatchery at the site.
   Mr. Sandy Mitchell, 513 N. Atlantic Avenue, spoke in opposition to the
property sale, stating his assumption that a public hearing would be held on
the matter.
   Mr. Dale McPherson, 108 S. Rhett Street, and former Planning Board member
spoke in opposition to the property sale. He cited the Unified Development
Ordinance (UDO) Article 3- 10 which referenced the Planning Board’s role in the
acquisition and disposal of public property.
   Mr. Jim Newman, 301 East West Street, stated his opinion that the proposed
sale of the former wastewater treatment plant requires more discussion and
consideration of uses such as a park with a boardwalk through the marsh.
   Mr. Fred Fiss, 216 N. Atlantic Avenue, stated his opinion that the property
proposed to be sold belongs to the public and the existing structures could be
reused. He expressed his disappointment in the Mayor and Aldermen that in his
opinion, by-passed public input.
   Ms. Lowe Davis, 504 W. Brunswick Street, spoke in opposition to the property
sale. She emphasized full transparency of all information along with
explanation of how the sale is consistent with the CAMA Core Land Use Plan and
Parks & Recreation Master Plan. She stressed getting a more recent appraisal,
pursue a request for proposals of possible uses, and conduct a public hearing.
   Referencing a January 16 State Port Pilot newspaper article, Mr. Joe Pat
Hatem, 610A W. Brown Street, stressed that the voices of citizens, in
opposition to the sale of the former wastewater treatment plant, must be heard.
He asked the Board of Aldermen to not circumvent the review process by the
Planning Board.
   Mr. Brian Stevens, 503 Cades Trail, expressed his disappointment that the
City is not pursuing a waterfront park at the former wastewater treatment plant
site.
   Ms. Bonnie Bray, 515 Quartermaster Drive, commended the Aldermen for their
leadership following Hurricane Florence. Ms. Bray stated that nearly 50 people
had wanted to speak to the issue of the sale of the former wastewater treatment
plant at the February 2nd Board meeting, and were not permitted to do so. She
urged the Board to address the matter with leadership and to engage in public
discussion.

Presentation – Load Management Program
   Ellie Pittenger, Load Management Coordinator, explained the Load Management
Program which rewards residential and small commercial electric customers with
incremental discounts when they participate. Mr. Pittenger described the “peak”
hour; normally 7:00 – 8:00 a.m.in the winter and 4:00 – 5:00 p.m. in the summer
and he emphasized that the one peak hour can make up over half of the City’s
entire monthly electric bill. Mr. Pittenger explained the load management
discount tiers and stated that Southport is the only municipality in the state
that offers a discount rate on each level of Load Management:
   - Tier 1:   11.5¢ per kilowatt hour
   - Tier 2:   10.5¢ per kilowatt hour
   - Tier 3:    9.5¢ per kilowatt hour
   - Tier 4:    8.5¢ per kilowatt hour
Mr. Pittenger shared statistical information demonstrating the increase in the
number of customers utilizing the program. He announced that informational
pamphlets were available during the meeting, he had Wi-Fi thermostats with him
for anyone who wanted to sign up and he is available for questions and
assistance    at the Public Works Department, 1010 N. Howe Street, 910-457-
7938, epittenger@cityofsouthport.com
   Alderman Mosteller praised the program stating that she participates, has
never noticed a difference in the service and the savings can be upwards to
30%.
   Mayor Dove encouraged everyone to pick up a pamphlet.

   Mr. Scott Jones, Chairman of the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board, reported
on the February 5 meeting of the Advisory Board. He stated that there were
discussions about ongoing classes and programs of the Southport Parks &
Recreation Department, and moving forward with plans for Taylor Field. He noted
that much of the meeting was taken up with discussion of the proposed sale of
the former wastewater treatment plant site. He pointed out that the Advisory
Board submitted a letter January 2016 requesting the City to keep the property
for green space. He cited the Parks & Recreation Master Plan that placed a
priority on protecting and preserving open/green space and providing three (3)
water access points. Mr. Jones asked the Mayor and Aldermen to consider the
opinion of the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board when deciding the fate of the
property.
   Alderman Mosteller gave an update on Taylor Field. She stated that through
the generous gift of the property, the city is in the planning stages of
development for the site. She reported that proposals were received from
multiple groups and it is anticipated the preliminary designs will be ready by
the end of the month with subsequent review by the Planning Board followed by
submittal to the Board of Aldermen at their April 11 regular meeting. Alderman
Mosteller reported that the PART(F) grant is due April 30 and the City is able
to take advantage of the appraised property value towards its matching grant.
Alderman Mosteller stated that citizen input is crucial towards the development
of the site.

Core Land Use Plan and UDO has been completed. She stated that the next UDO
review meeting would be held Thursday, February 28, 4:00 p.m. in the City Hall
2nd floor conference room. She added that a final draft of the Ordinance is
anticipated to be complete the first quarter of 2020. She recognized the
dedication and commitment by staff’s service and investment in the project.

2.   Resolution Opposing ABC Board Proposed Legislation
   City Manager Oakley explained that there are proposed legislative bills to
change how the sale of liquor is conducted. One bill wishes to privatize ABC
sales and another recommends placing the control under the jurisdiction of
County governments. City Manager Oakley pointed out that the current system of
control provides revenue to the City. He pointed out it is in the financial
interest of the City to oppose the proposed legislation.
   Alderman Mosteller motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to adopt the
Resolution in Support of the Current ABC Control System for the Sale of Liquor.
Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF THE CURRENT ABC CONTROL SYSTEM FOR THE SALE OF
LIQUOR
   WHEREAS, the citizens of the City of Southport voted to permit the sale of
liquor through the establishment of an ABC Board, which is a part of the North
Carolina’s control system for the sale of spirituous liquors;
   WHEREAS, North Carolina is a “control” state and private retail liquor
stores are prohibited;
   WHEREAS, the General Assembly’s nonpartisan Program Evaluation Division
(PED) was directed to examine whether other systems for alcohol beverage
control, including privatized systems, are appropriate for North Carolina,
specially to include the State of Washington, which recently changed its
beverage control system from state government control of wholesale and retail
control of spirituous liquor to a licensure model;
   WHEREAS, The PED Report, “Changing How North Carolina Controls Liquor Sales
Has Operational, Regulatory, and Financial Ramifications”, released on February
11, 2019, (1) did not recommend privatization, (2) found that among the
southeastern states, NC collects the most revenue per gallon, has the lowest
outlet density and has the second lowest per capita consumption; and (3) the
PED expects retail liquor consumption to increase by 20% with privatization.
   WHEREAS, for fiscal year ending 20187, local ABC boards distributed
$430,635,861: County-City Distributions $80 million; State General Fund $323
million; Local Alcohol Education/Treatment $13 million; Local Law Enforcement
$8.8 million; Rehabilitation Services $5 million; Operation of ABC Commission/
Warehouse $17.7 million.
   WHEREAS, North Carolina is unique as it allows communities to vote to
establish local ABC boards for the sale of liquor in their communities, with
liquor profits distributed back to those communities, thereby reducing the need
to increase local property taxes.
   WHEREAS, the citizens of the City of Southport, in voting to permit the
operation of ABC stores, did not vote to allow spirits to be sold in private
retail liquor stores and did not vote to allow spirits to be sold retail
outlets where beer and wine are sold;
   WHEREAS, No State funds are spent to distribute or sell liquor as the state
and local operation of the ABC system is receipt supported;
   WHEREAS, Of the 50 states, North Carolina ranks 44th lowest in consumption
per capita and 7th highest in revenue per capita and NC’s ABC system
accomplishes both revenue and public health, welfare and safety objectives;
   WHEREAS, when Washington State privatized its liquor system the number of
retail outlets increased from 328 to over 1400, hours of sale/week increased
from 73 to 140 hours, and Washington State received only $30.75 million from
auctioning off the rights to apply for retail spirits permits at 167 stores;
   WHEREAS, privatization will result in a marked increase in the number of
outlets, longer hours of sale, greater advertising and more promotion and
significantly more consumption; and the 9,000 outlets in NC that sell beer/wine
off-premises could be permitted to sell liquor in a privatized system;
   WHEREAS, local revenue from ABC stores operations is important to the City;
   WHEREAS, local control over the sale of liquor is an important function.
   NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED:
   That the City of Southport desires to retain North Carolina’s current
control system for the sale of liquor and believes that privatization of liquor
will lead to many adverse effects.
                        By: /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor      
Attest: /a/ Michele Windham, City Clerk         Date: February 26, 2019
3.   Consider Resolution Approving Sale of Property
   City Manager Oakley stated that Southport Marina has offered the City
$650,000 for the former wastewater treatment plant site. He added that the
clean-up is estimated to be $365,000. He emphasized that the Marina will
dedicate a 10’ access easement, retained in perpetuity, along the northern
property line and .11 acres of upland area for public access and other public
uses. City Manager Oakley pointed out that the Marina has 150 days of due
diligence once the contract is executed before finalizing the deal.
   Responding to a query from Alderman Pukenas, City Manager Oakley stated that
the $365,000 estimate did not include environmental clean-up; it was for just
the demolition.
   Per Alderman Mosteller’s request, verbatim comments provided in their
entirety:
“Before we consider the resolution approving the sale of the West West
property…
I want to recognize that last week, at the February Planning Board meeting…The
Planning Board discussed the importance of following the UDO and unanimously
voted to support a motion to let the Board of Aldermen know, the Planning Board
stands ready to complete their responsibilities regarding the disposal of
public property.
I am asking for the Board to follow the ordinances of the City of Southport …I
am making the following motion…
In accordance with Article 3-10 in the Southport Unified Development Ordinance…
table the Board of Aldermen’s consideration of the resolution on this agenda to
approve the disposal sale of the publicly owned West West property and for this
Board to ask the Planning Board to review and report recommendations to the
Board of Aldermen regarding the potential disposal sale of the publicly owned
West West property.
And as outlined in Article 3-10 of the UDO, for this Board to submit in
writing, the following questions to the Planning Board for review at the next
regularly scheduled Planning Board meeting and report recommendations, if any,
to the Board of Aldermen within 30 days subsequent to the Planning Board
meeting.
The questions for the Planning Board…
   ∙   Is the proposed disposal sale of the publicly owned West West property
consistent with the Southport Core Land Use Plan and other city long term
strategic plans?
   ∙   Do the two proposed city easement accesses, named in the current West
West property purchase offer under consideration by the Board of Aldermen,
provide the opportunity to design and build adequate public structures and
facilities for public water access to Cottage Creek and the Indigo Plantation
March Reserve?
   ∙   After the Planning Board has completed the review of the proposed
disposal sale of the publicly owned West West property, are there other factors
recommended by the Planning Board for the consideration of Board of Aldermen
regarding the future disposal sale of the West West property?
There are clear processes that should be followed before decisions regarding
the sale of public properties are acted on.
The members of the Planning Board are sworn in and take their responsibilities
to the Board of Aldermen and the future of Southport very seriously. The Board
of Aldermen have entrusted the Planning Board with powers and duties that are
vital to promoting the orderly development of our city. The Board of Aldermen
relies on the review and recommendations of the Planning Board to help make
development decisions that will shape the future of our city. This should be no
different… the Board of Aldermen must follow the ordinances of the City of
Southport.”
Motion died for lack of a second.
   Responding to a question from Alderman Mosteller, City Attorney Isenberg
stated that Article 3- 10 of the UDO is an unusual local provision and has
nothing to do with due process as the Board is free to disregard the
recommendation of the Planning Board. He pointed out that state statutes set
out seven (7) basic duties for the Planning Board related to land development
and the sale of property is not one of them. In fact, the sale and disposition
of property is in a separate article in 160A from the article dealing with
planning boards and land development. He added that state statutes give the
governing Board complete discretion in the decision to sell or dispose of
property. He recommended that the Board repeal the UDO article and make the
repeal effective retroactively if it did not intend to follow section 3-10.
   City Manager Oakley noted that Section 3-10 is recommended to be removed
from the UDO per the current review and update.
   Alderman Sharkey stated her opinion that inserting the Planning Board into
the sale process at this time was not practical. She pointed out that the buyer
will be submitting development plans that will be thoroughly reviewed by the
Planning Board for compliance with the UDO. Additionally, Alderman Sharkey
emphasized that the Planning Board has no history of reviewing acquisitions or
sales made by the City.
   Alderman Sharkey motioned, second by Alderman Tucker to direct staff to
submit a text amendment to repeal UDO Article 3-10, Public Facilities,
effective February 26, 2019 to the Planning Board for review.
   Vote:   Aye:   Aldermen Sharkey, Tucker, Powell, Spencer, Pukenas
      Nay:   Alderman Mosteller
   Motion carried 5-1

   6.   Fire Department Budget Review
   Chief Drew provided clarity regarding a situation that was recently brought
up in the State Port Pilot regarding city employees being volunteers for the
department and responding to calls. Emphasizing that Southport is a community
of volunteers, Chief Drew named some of the past/present fire volunteers who
were/are city employees
      ∙    Mr. Otto Hickman      Police Chief & Fire Chief
      ∙    Jack Hickman      Police Chief & Fire Captain
      ∙    Walker Aldridge      Finance Director & Fire Captain
      ∙    Harold Aldridge      Alderman & Fire Chief
      ∙    Robert Howard      Alderman & 19 years on Fire Dept.
      ∙    Joe Medlin         P & R Director & Fire Lieutenant
      ∙    Mark Southerland      Grounds Maintenance Crew Leader (30 years)
                     & 34 years with the Fire Department
      ∙    Todd Coring         Police Chief & Assistant Fire Chief
   Chief Drew pointed out that in 1995 Mayor Bill Crow and the Board of
Aldermen adopted a resolution permitting city employees that were fire
department volunteers to respond to calls. Chief Drew emphasized that city
employees are not paid a stipend for responding to a fire call while working.
He added that extra credit has been given to the Southport Fire Department by
Insurance Services Office (ISO) for permitting city employees to respond to
fire calls, which ultimately lowers citizens' insurance costs.
   Chief Drew presented the proposed Fire Department 2019/2020 Budget. He
stated that the budget is due to Brunswick County by March 10 in order to begin
the Fire Fee Rate Setting process. Chief Drew pointed out that the budget is
balanced on the projected revenues for the upcoming fiscal year and there is no
fire fee increase requested. He stated that the County requires the Southport
Board of Aldermen review the budget prior to submittal to the County.
   Chief Drew reported that he would be requesting some full-time members, to
provide for better coverage, without the need for any additional funding. He
added that some volunteer shift pay would be eliminated.
   Responding to a question by Alderman Spencer, Chief Drew stated that there
are currently three (3) city employees who are also fire department volunteers.
   Alderman Sharkey asked about job descriptions for the proposed positions,
the City Manager's opinion on the additional employees, added work load created
for supportive city employees, and she asked to be included with the Emergency
Services Committee and the hiring process.
   Stating that he serves on the Emergency Services Committee, Alderman Spencer
stated appreciation for the Chief's efforts and for bringing the proposed
budget to the Board.
   Mayor Dove appointed Alderman Sharkey to the Emergency Services Committee.
   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Tucker to approve the Fire
Department 2019/2020 Budget as presented. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   7.   Animal Welfare Ordinance
   Alderman Mosteller explained that the Animal Welfare Committee held six
public meetings while revising the 22-year-old Animal Ordinance. She stated

County Ordinance. She added that a draft of the Ordinance was thoroughly
reviewed by the Committee, County animal welfare services, Southport's newly
hired Animal Protective Services/Code Enforcement Officer, the School of

written, addressed rabies laws and requirements, bites, impoundment, tethering,

custodians of animals. Responding to a query by Alderman Spencer, Officer

clipped ear would identify a cat that had been through the TNR process.
   Alderman Sharkey asked about the proposed new licensing program. Officer
Marshall stated the launch date for the licensing program is expected in May.

Ordinance. City Attorney Isenberg suggested the fee be included in the City's

BOARD OF ALDERMEN       SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES

1011 N. HOWE STREET     SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:         Mayor J.V. Dove
            Aldermen Karen Mosteller, Lora Sharkey, Jim Powell,
            Marc Spencer, Rick Pukenas, Robert Tucker
STAFF PRESENT:      Bruce Oakley, City Manager
   Michele Windham, City Clerk
   Todd Coring, Police Chief
   Charles Drew, Fire Chief
   Tyler Johnson, Deputy Fire Chief
   David Fox, Public Works Director
   B. Wayne Strickland, Building Inspector
A)   Call to Order – 5:00 p.m.
Mayor Dove called the special meeting to order at 5:00 p.m. He stated the
purpose of the meeting was to discuss the agreement for funding of the
Wastewater Expansion Agreement and Sewer Service Agreement with Brunswick
County and to adopt a resolution Designating an Applicant’s Agent for FEMA
Disaster Relief.
B)   Invocation
Chief Drew gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
   Mayor Dove led the assemblage in the Pledge of Allegiance.
AGENDA
   1.   Discussion of Agreement for Funding of Wastewater Expansion Agreement
and Sewer Service Agreement
   City Manager Oakley explained that the City currently has a sewer service
agreement with Brunswick County for 750,000 gallons per day of sewer flow
capacity. He added that the City also has an agreement to fund expansion of one
of the County’s treatment facilities and to upgrade the transmission lines. He
stated that the City is proceeding with a loan from the North Carolina Clean
Water State Revolving Fund for $26M to pay for the expansion and upgrades.
   City Manager Oakley reported that the project was reevaluated, a third-party
engineer was hired to review the City’s options and based on their findings,
the City could likely build its own plant with a capacity of 1M gallons per day
with the ability to expand for the same cost. He pointed out that long term
operations and maintenance costs of operating a city owned plant would be
higher, but the City would not be responsible for funding the expansion of the
County’s plant. He emphasized that the City would likely exceed the 750,000
gallons of capacity before the funding agreement term was over.
   City Manager Oakley noted that the City would need to work with the County
to ensure a smooth transition if the Board decided to construct a plant. He
pointed out that the City owns 400 acres of land near Military Ocean Terminal
Sunny Point where the plant could be located.
   Pointing out that Southport would sooner rather than later reach the
750,000-gallon wastewater capacity guaranteed by the County, Alderman Powell
commented on upcoming developments in the Southport sewer service area.
Alderman Tucker agreed and stated that in 20 years’ time, an additional County
plant expansion would be needed. He added that the Southport wastewater
treatment plant site would be capable of sustaining 2M gallons of capacity.
   Aldermen Pukenas and Spencer stated their support for Southport building its
own wastewater treatment plant and having 100% ownership.
   Aldermen Powell and Tucker remarked on the benefits of using purple pipe in
new developments.
   Alderman Sharkey stated she was pleased that the city decided to review the
proposal. She pointed out that there are Aldermen on the Board with the
industry experience who were able to ask the right kind of questions and
confirm that the City had done an in-depth evaluation. She shared her opinion
that the best course of action for the City is to construct its own wastewater
treatment plant.
   Noting that a thorough review had been made of all options, Alderman
Mosteller agreed with fellow Board members and supported building a wastewater
treatment plant.
   Mayor Dove commented that during discussions with County representatives,
Alderman Tucker inquired about membership for Southport in a regional
wastewater treatment area and was told a membership would not be an option for
Southport.
   Alderman Tucker motioned, second by Alderman Powell that the Board of
Aldermen take the necessary steps to terminate the Sewer Service Agreement
dated June 8, 2017, and the Interlocal Agreement for Funding of Wastewater
Plant Expansion dated July 12, 2018, between the City and Brunswick County;
that the City Manager notify the County of the City’s intent to terminate said
agreements; and that the City Manager be authorized to negotiate the terms of
an exit agreement with the County and report to the Board the terms of said
agreement for consideration by the Board.
Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   2.   Designation of Applicant’s Agent for FEMA Disaster Relief
City Manager Oakley explained that a resolution needs to be adopted that
designates an applicant’s agent for release of FEMA disaster relief payments.
He stated that he and the Finance Director, Melanie Trexler would be the
Primary and Secondary Agents respectively. He added that a reimbursement in the
amount of $365,129 will be forthcoming after submittal of the resolution and
additional reimbursements are being pursued.
Alderman Mosteller motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to adopt the Resolution
Designation of Applicant’s Agent. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
ADJOURN
   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to adjourn the special
meeting. Meeting adjourned at 5:16 p.m.
                        /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor
Attest: /s/ Michele Windham, Clerk

ARBOR DAY RESOLUTION
[https://export.amlegal.com/media/199f40a54a06f19a9324bf64df539e216304d812/
IMAGES/0-0-0-2038.jpg]
WHEREAS, in 1972, J. Sterling Morton proposed to the Nebraska Board of
Agriculture that a special day be set aside for the planting of trees, and
WHEREAS, this holiday called Arbor Day, was first observed with the planting of
more than a million trees in Nebraska, and
WHEREAS, Arbor Day is now observed throughout the nation and the world, and
WHEREAS, trees can reduce the erosion of our precious topsoil by wind and
water, cut heating and cooling costs, moderate the temperature, clean the air,
produce life-giving oxygen, and provide habitat for wildlife, and
WHEREAS, trees are a renewable resource giving us paper, wood for our homes,
fuel for our fires, and beautify our community, and
WHEREAS, trees in our city increase property values, enhance the economic
vitality of business areas, and beautify our community, and
WHEREAS, trees wherever they are planted are a source of joy and spiritual
renewal.
NOW, THEREFORE, I J.V. Dove, Mayor of the City of Southport, NC, and the Board
of Aldermen, do hereby proclaim April 26, 2019 as ARBOR DAY in the City and
urge all citizens to celebrate and support efforts to protect our trees and
woodlands, and
FURTHER, I urge all citizens to plant trees to gladden the heart and promote
the well-being of this and future generations.
DATED, this 11th day of April, 2019
                        /s/ J.V. Dove, Mayor
Attest: /s/ Michele Windham, Clerk

   7.   Creation of Deputy Finance Director/Financial Specialist Position
Pointing out that the City's annual audit has been late for numerous years,
City Manager Oakley explained that the Finance Department is overwhelmed, and
he would like to add a Financial Specialist position that could also be
appointed Deputy Finance Director.
FINANCIAL SPECIALIST
General Statement of Duties
Performs difficult professional work in the accounting and fiscal services and
activities for the City.
Distinguishing Features of the Class
An employee in this class leads and participates in the accounting of revenues
and expenditures for the City. Work involves leading and participating in
accounts payable, accounts receivable, general ledger preparation and
maintenance, payroll functions, bank reconciliation, fixed assets and general
financial reporting. The role serves as lead worker, acts in the absence of the
Finance Director, and provides technical guidance to other finance staff. The
employee must exercise judgment and initiative in identifying and resolving the
daily problems and activities of the fiscal control system. Work is performed
in accordance with established finance procedures, local ordinances and North
Carolina General Statutes governing the responsibilities of local government
fiscal operations under the North Carolina Fiscal Control Act. The employee
functions with decision-making authority and performs responsibilities with a
degree of independence, receiving instruction and advice only on matters
involving significant departure from established policy, assisting the Finance
Director in any phase of the fiscal operations. Work is performed under the
supervision of the Finance Director and is evaluated through conferences,
performance appraisals, reports, and an independent audit of financial records.
Duties and Responsibilities
Essential Duties and Tasks
Leads and participates in the preparation of accounts payable and payroll,
general ledger, budgetary accounting, financial reporting, bank reconciliation,
fixed assets, miscellaneous invoicing and related tasks; provides guidance as
needed to staff engaged in accounting activities ensuring adherence to
established policies, procedures, and standards; assists and advises
subordinates, as necessary, resolving problems as non-routine situations arise;
performs fixed assets accounting.
Leads and assists with daily priorities for the operation of the accounting
functions and activities for the office; guides workflow and adjustment of work
among the staff as needed.
Provides back up for the payroll function including review and input of time
sheets; generation of checks and payroll reports and records; ensures proper
remittance of federal and state taxes; ensures payment of payroll vendors.
Provides back up for accounts payable and utility billing; may be designated as
lead for delinquent collection of utility bills, taxes, and other revenues;
administers Debt Setoff program.
Updates daily cash collections to general ledger; posts occupancy taxes;
ensures updates to utility accounts for returned checks or bank drafts; may
process bank drafts for utility accounts.
   Analyzes, tabulates and completes a wide variety of state, federal and other
records and reports; monitors capital and grant projects to insure timely
reimbursement requests are submitted and projects are closed out in a timely
manner; performs grant accounting and administration.
   Assists the Manager and Finance Director with budget development including
revenue calculation from ad valorem tax valuations; prepares sample tax rate
collections, projected payroll expenses, and provides other assistance as
needed.
   Assists other municipal departments with accounting related questions and
procedures.
       Interprets and enforces current fiscal policies and practices for the
department.
   Assembles statistical, tax, and accounting data on request.
   Assists the auditors during the annual audit of the financial records.
   Generates special reports and statements for management as requested.
Additional Job Duties
   Maybe appointed Deputy Finance Officer by the Board of Alderman.
   Check signer at the bank in absence of Finance Director.
   Performs related duties as required.
Recruitment and Selection Guidelines
Knowledges, Skills, and Abilities
   Considerable knowledge of professional accounting concepts, principles, and
practices as applied to local government.   
   Considerable knowledge of North Carolina General Statutes, laws, rules,
regulations and of local ordinances governing Town financial practices and
procedures.
   Considerable knowledge of the principles and practices of public finance
administration and budgetary processes in the public sector.
   Considerable knowledge of the principles and practices of statistics with
particular reference to their application to financial and operational
activities.
   Knowledge of the application of information technology especially as it
related to financial packages, spreadsheets and related technology.
   General knowledge of the current literature, trends, and developments in the
fields of governmental accounting and public finance administration.
   Skill in collaborative conflict resolution and performance coaching and
feedback.
       Ability to plan, organize, assign and assist with the work of employees
in the specialized field of accounting in an automated environment.
   Ability to analyze and interpret financial and accounting records and
complete financial statements from such records.
   Ability to establish and maintain effective working relationships with the
public, department heads, governmental officials, and with other employees as
necessitated by work assignments.
   Ability to operate office technology.
   Ability to express ideas effectively both orally and written.
   Ability to prepare and submit accurate, clear, complete, and concise
reports.
Physical Requirements
   Must be able to perform the basic life operational skills of stooping,
kneeling, crouching, reaching, walking, lifting, fingering, talking, hearing,
sitting, and repetitive motions.
   Must be able to perform sedentary work, exerting up to 10 pounds of force
occasionally and/or a negligible amount of force to lift, carry, push, pull or
otherwise move objects.
   Must possess the visual acuity to prepare and analyze data and statistics,
perform accounting tasks, do extensive reading, and operate a computer
terminal.
Desirable Education and Experience
   Graduation from a four-year college or university with a degree in
accounting including progressively responsible professional experience in
public sector accounting and experience with spreadsheet software; or an
equivalent combination of education and experience.

   10.   City Dock Discussion
City Manager Oakley provided design options for the City Dock.
Alderman Pukenas emphasized the need to get the permit process moving forward.
Alderman Sharkey pointed out that after discussions with the Department of
Marine Fisheries, it was clear that they were not favorable towards any kind of
slips towards the marsh area. She discussed the challenges of getting boat
slips, dredging, spoil disposal, who would get the slips, and for how long. She
stated her mindset was to provide recreation for as many people as possible and
she suggested a floating dock within the City's property for the Crab Derby,
programs through the Maritime Museum, casting nets, enjoying nature and other
low-key activities.
Alderman Mosteller suggested the consultant submit a permit for the most that
could be done on the site. She also suggested scheduling a public meeting for
citizens to review the three concepts. She pointed out that approximately
$9,000 had been donated towards the project.
   Responding to a query by Alderman Pukenas, City Manager Oakley stated that a
dredge application runs concurrently with a CAMA permit. He added that a dredge
application must be submitted nine to 12 months prior to dredging and a
designated spoil site is required.
   Alderman Pukenas favored the idea of changing from boat slips to a multi-
purpose floating dock. He stated his opinion that a concept is irrelevant until
a spoil site can be identified for the dredging material.
   City Manager Oakley was requested to pursue scheduling another meeting with
NCDOT regarding dredging.
   Alderman Tucker motioned, second by Alderman Sharkey to table the discussion
until the next regularly scheduled meeting and to receive an update and
recommendation from staff.
Discussion
   Alderman Mosteller repeated that she would like to hold a public meeting
Tuesday, April 30, 6:00 p.m. for the public to review the three concepts.
   Alderman Sharkey stated that she would be willing to attend a public
information session with Alderman Mosteller.
Unanimous vote; motion carried.

NATIONAL SAFE BOATING WEEK PROCLAMATION
   For nearly 100 million Americans, boating continues to be a popular
recreational activity. From coast to coast, and everywhere in between, people
are taking to the water and enjoying time together boating, sailing, paddling
and fishing. During National Safe Boating Week, the U.S. Coast Guard and its
federal, state, and local safe boating partners encourage all boaters to
explore and enjoy America’s beautiful waters responsibly.
   Safe boating begins with preparation. The Coast Guard estimates that human
error accounts for 70 percent of all boating accidents and that life jackets
could prevent more than 85 percent of boating fatalities. Through basic boating
safety procedures – carrying lifesaving emergency distress and communications
equipment, wearing life jackets, attending safe boating courses, participating
in free boat safety checks, and staying sober when navigating – we can help
ensure boaters on America’s coastal, inland, and offshore waters stay safe
throughout the season.
   National Safe Boating Week is observed to bring attention to important life-
saving tips for recreational boaters so that they can have a safer, more fun
experience out on the water throughout the year.
   •Whereas, on average, 650 people die each year in boating-related accidents
in the U.S.; approximately 76 percent of these are fatalities caused by
drowning; and
   •Whereas, the vast majority of these accidents are caused by human error or
poor judgment and not by the boat, equipment or environmental factors; and
   •Whereas, a significant number of boaters who lose their lives by drowning
each year would be alive today had they worn their life jackets.
   Therefore, I, J. V. Dove, Mayor, City of Southport, do hereby support the
goals of the Safe Boating Campaign and proclaim May 18-24, 2019 as National
Safe Boating Week and the start of the year-round effort to promote safe
boating
Given under my signature and the seal of:
               /s/ J.V. Dove, Mayor, Southport, North Carolina
               /s/ Tyler Ford, Petty Officer, USCG Station Oak Island at the
City of: Southport, North Carolina
this day of: May 9, 2019
   Alderman Sharkey read into the record the Proclamation Recognizing May 2019
as Water Safety and Drowning Prevention Month in Southport.
Proclamation Recognizing MAY 2019 as WATER SAFETY
and DROWNING PREVENTION MONTH in SOUTHPORT, NC
WHEREAS According to the U.S. Center for Disease Control, the leading cause of
injury death among 1-4 year olds and the second leading cause of injury death
among children aged 5-9 years is drowning.
WHEREAS By our geographical location we are surrounded by natural and manmade
water sources that are beautiful but provide risks. Drowning can happen quickly
and quietly anywhere there is water. Drowning happens in bathtubs, swimming
pools, lakes, and at the ocean, even in the presence of lifeguards.  Air-filled
or foam toys, such as "water wings", "noodles", or inner tubes should not be
used in place of life jackets. These items are toys, not life jackets and are
not designed to keep swimmers safe.
WHEREAS According to the Centers for Disease Control, the following factors
influence the risk of fatal drowning: Lack of swimming ability, lack of
barriers or supervision to prevent unsupervised water access, lack of
lifeguards, swimming location, failure to wear life vests, alcohol use, and
seizure disorders.
WHEREAS Drowning can be prevented by learning to swim. Many adults and children
report that they cannot swim.  Research has shown that participation in formal
swimming lessons can reduce the risk of drowning among children aged 1 to 4
years.   However, even when children have had formal swimming lessons, constant
supervision when children are in the water and barriers, such as pool fencing
to prevent unsupervised access, are still important.
WHEREAS Seconds count—learn CPR. CPR performed by bystanders has been shown to
save lives and improve outcomes in drowning victims. The more quickly CPR is
started, the better the chance of improved outcomes.
Be It Resolved, that the Mayor and Southport Board of Aldermen on this the 9th
day of May 2019 proclaim May 2019 as Water Safety Month in the City of
Southport and urge all citizens to be diligent and safety minded when caring
for children near water.
            /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor
Attest: /s/ Michele Windham, Clerk
