2.   Public Hearing Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 160A-364; Unified Development
Ordinance (UDO) Text Amendment Article 3,    Administrative Mechanisms, Section
3-10 Public Facilities
   City Planner Lloyd explained that staff was directed by the Board of
Aldermen to initiate a text amendment to repeal UDO Section 3-10. He stated
that the Planning Board had reviewed the amendment and voted to not recommend
approval of the proposed text amendment repealing Section 3-10. Corresponding
information was provided in the agenda packet.
   Alderman Powell stated that during the original adoption of the UDO, many of
the sections were standard boiler plate language, including Section 3-10.
   Recalling his time on the Planning Board and experience in local government,
Alderman Tucker stated that a previous consultant had recommended the section
be removed as it was not applicable to a UDO.
   City Planner Lloyd indicated that the current consultant guiding the UDO
Phase I update recommended removing the section.
   Alderman Mosteller provided her verbatim comments for inclusion in the
minutes:
      “In 2010, the Board of Aldermen initiated changes in the UDO regarding
the Planning Board’s duties and Article 3-10 was one of the items in that
discussion. After careful consideration over several months, with
recommendations from the Planning Board, in 2011, the Board of Aldermen agreed
3-10 should remain in t he UDO and only made changes to Article 3-1.”
   Alderman Tucker motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to open Public Hearing.
Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   Mr. Ed Glenn, 202 N. Atlantic Avenue, spoke in opposition to the proposed
text amendment.
   Mr. Dale McPherson, 103 S. Rhett Street, expressed his opposition to the
proposed text amendment and his opinion that the Board of Aldermen are giving
away Southport’s heritage.
   Ms. Tish Hatem, 610-A West St. George, and Chairman of the Planning Board,
described the Planning Board’s role is to review, report, repeat and ensure
consistency with Southport’s long-range plans. She asked that the Board of
Aldermen re-consider repealing Section 3-10.
   Ms. Lowe Davis, 504 Brunswick Street, spoke in opposition to the proposed
text amendment and implored the Board of Aldermen to be a government for the
people.
   Referencing previous Planning Board and Board of Aldermen actions, Mr. Rich
Bandera, 309 Clarendon Avenue, asked the Board to table action on the proposed
text amendment.
   Pointing out that the Planning Board is the checks and balance system, Mr.
Fred Fiss, 216 Atlantic Avenue, stated disappointment in the sequence of events
pertaining to the proposed text amendment and he urged the Board to think twice
before removing Section 3-10. He noted that there is an opportunity for a new
Board in November.
   Stating she had called each Board member, Ms. Bonnie Bray, 515 Quartermaster
Drive, made an impassioned plea for the Board to table the proposed text
amendment.
   Alderman Powell motioned, second by Alderman Sharkey to close Public
Hearing. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
3.   Consideration of UDO Text Amendment Article 3, Section 3-10
   City Attorney Isenberg stated that the Aldermen had four (4) options;
      Table or defer consideration;
      Do nothing and leave Section 3-10 in place;
      Repeal in its entirety Section 3-10;
      Amend Section 3-10 by repealing only the part dealing with acquisition
and disposal of property
   Alderman Mosteller provided the following comments for inclusion in the
minutes:
      “I appreciate the time that the Planning Board members have spent to
consider the text amendment to remove Article 3-10 from the UDO. For land use
decisions, our Board looks to the Planning Board to review and make
recommendations in context of the Comprehensive Plan and Southport’s long-range
planning documents. A retroactive change to Article 3-10 in the UDO, to
facilitate one decision, will eliminate the procedure put in place to help
provide guidance for Board of Aldermen when considering the acquisition and
disposal of public properties. As a municipality, our stewardship of the
limited amount of publicly owned land, must first take into account, the
strategic planning documents and the future land use plans named within these
documents. Southport’s Comprehensive Plan and the Parks and Recreation and Open
Space Master Plan, both, contain long term planning goals that include the
city’s future needs for specific public land acquisitions. Southport has made a
large investment and commitment to our future by creating long-range plans.
      The discussion in our agenda packet endorsing the removal of Article 3-10
mentions that the consultant currently assisting the Planning Board’s work to
update the UDO, identified 3-10 as something that needed to be removed because
the Planning Board should not be examining and advising on the city’s financial
decisions…that alone should be the responsibility of the Board of Aldermen.
      Clearly…the Board of Aldermen does not seek financial advice from the
Planning Board.
      Article 3-10 is meant to be the first step when the Board of Aldermen
considers selling a publicly owned property. The first question to the Planning
Board is simply …
      Is the sale of this publicly owned property consistent with Southport’s
established long-range plans?
      The process of selling any public land should always include the city’s
long-range planning goals as part of the discussion.
      At the heart of Article 3-10…is not seeking recommendations from the
Planning Board regarding the city’s financial decisions, it’s to ensure that
the decisions we make about citizen owned land are consistent with the
Comprehensive Plan and the city’s strategic long-range planning documents. And
if the decision is to sell the land for solely for financial reasons, forsaking
other goals, the Board of Aldermen can make that decision.
      And to say, 3-10 should be removed because the state does not require it
as part of state statue regarding Planning Boards …We have many examples of
language in our UDO that exceed state requirements. The language in Article 3-
10 is found in the UDO documents of many small communities across North
Carolina. Many times, I have heard our city planning staff say they think the
Planning Board review process is important to provide another set of eyes.
      Updating the UDO is currently a work in progress, and is not due to be
brought to the Board of Aldermen for consideration until next year, 2020.
      At this point, to identify a change to the UDO, from the ongoing UDO
update discussions, undermines the process and the participation of the members
of the Planning Board.
      Before we throw the baby out with the bathwater, I would ask that instead
of voting tonight to eliminate or modify Article 3-10 in the UDO, we ask the
Planning Board and staff to propose updated language to clarify that the
Planning Board is not making recommendations to the Board of Aldermen regarding
financial decisions related to the acquisition and disposal of citizen owned
property.
      The real value of Article 3-10 and why the Planning Board voted
unanimously to recommend keeping 3-10 in the UDO, is to help us consider
decisions about publicly owned property in context of the Southport
Comprehensive Plan and our strategic long-range planning documents. “
   After reading aloud the proposed amendment for Section 3-10 to repeal the
part dealing with acquisition and disposal of property as recommended by staff
to the Board, Alderman Tucker motioned, second by Alderman Sharkey to adopt the
Ordinance Amending Section 3-10 of the UDO as prepared by staff to repeal the
part dealing with acquisition and disposal of property and to approve and adopt
the Statement of Consistency related thereto attached to the Ordinance.
AYE:   Aldermen Tucker, Sharkey, Powell, Spencer, Pukenas
NAY:   Alderman Mosteller
Motion passed 5-1
AN ORDINANCE AMENDING ARTICLE 3 OF THE CITY OF SOUTHPORT UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT
ORDINANCE
THAT WHEREAS, the City has enacted a Unified Development Ordinance and other
land use ordinances that control land development within both the City’s
incorporated areas and within its extraterritorial area; and
   WHEREAS, in order to promote the public health, safety and general welfare
and to promote the best interest of the city and community, it is necessary for
the City Board of Aldermen from time to time to consider appropriate revisions,
modifications and additions to the city’s land use ordinances; and
   WHEREAS, City Staff has prepared the proposed amendment at the instruction
of the Board of Aldermen to repeal Section 3-10 Public Facilities of Article 3
in the Unified Development Ordinance; and
   WHEREAS, the Planning Board has reviewed this matter and found that the
proposed repeal of Section 3-10 of the Unified Development Ordinance to be
inconsistent with the City of Southport CAMA Core Land Use Plan and does not
recommend its approval; and
   WHEREAS, pursuant to N. C. General Statutes and city ordinances, a public
hearing, properly noticed, was held on May 9, 2019 before the Board of Aldermen
regarding this issue; and
   WHEREAS, the Board of Aldermen, after considering the public hearing
response and the recommendation of the Planning Board, and the recommendation
of staff, hereby finds that Section 3-10 of the Unified Development Ordinance
should not be repealed in its entirety but should be amended as hereinafter
stated and that this text amendment is consistent with the 2015 CAMA Land Use
Plan for the reasons stated in its Statement of Plan Consistency attached
hereto and incorporated herein; and
WHEREAS, the Board of Aldermen further finds that this amendment is reasonable
and in the public interest because this text amendment will remove language
that has no place in a development ordinance, language that is outdated and
having not been adhered to in the past, and clearing up issues that could arise
in the financial decisions of the city when it comes to the acquisition and
disposal of property.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED by the Southport Board of Aldermen that Section
3-10 of the Unified Development Ordinance is hereby amended to read as follows:
Upon request by the Board of Aldermen, the Planning Board shall review with the
city manager, planning director and other appropriate city officials, and then
make recommendations to the Board of Aldermen regarding (i) the extent,
location and design of public structures and facilities, and (ii) the
establishment of building lines, mapped street lines and proposals to change
existing street lines.
This amended shall be effective as of May 9th, 2019.
This, the 9th day of May, 2019.
City of Southport
                     s/s J. V. Dove, Mayor

City of Southport Board of Aldermen Statement of Plan Consistency (As per NC
General Statute 160A-383)
   Zoning regulations shall be made in accordance with a comprehensive plan.
Prior to adopting or rejecting any zoning amendment, the governing board shall
adopt one of the following statements which shall not be subject to judicial
review; 1) A statement approving the zoning amendment and describing its
consistency with an adopted comprehensive plan and explaining why the action
taken is reasonable and in the public interest. 2) A statement rejecting the
zoning amendment and describing its inconsistency with an adopted comprehensive
plan and explaining why the action taken is reasonable and in the public
interest. 3) A statement approving the zoning amendment and containing at least
all of the following: 1) A declaration that the approval is also deemed an
amendment to the comprehensive plan. 2) An explanation of the change in
conditions the governing board took into account in amending the zoning
ordinance to meet the development needs of the community. 3) why the action was
reasonable and in the public interest.                                (NCGS
160A-383)
ZONING AMENDMENT:   ZA-19-0226-01
STATEMENT OF CONSISTENCY:
The City of Southport Board of Aldermen hereby finds that the zoning text
amendment amending and revising Article 3-10 of the Unified Development
Ordinance by repealing a portion thereof is consistent with the 2015 CAMA Land
Use Plan adopted November 13, 2014. The Board of Aldermen feels that the
proposed amendment to Section 3-10 is consistent with the 2015 CAMA Land Use
Plan because the powers designated to the Planning Board in Section 3-10 are
not addressed in the policies of the CAMA Land Use Plan. In order to promote
the best interest of the city, it is necessary for the Board of Aldermen to
consider appropriate revisions, modifications, and additions to the City’s Land
Development Ordinance. This is an appropriate and needed revision. The Board of
Aldermen supports and appreciates the Planning Board’s advisory status on land
use decisions that are not financial in nature. With this amendment, there will
still be public forums for important land use decisions such as annexations,
zoning map amendments, text amendments, and land use plan amendments. It is
reasonable and in the public interest because the Board of Aldermen finds that
the language restricting the Board of Aldermen’s statutory right and authority
to acquire and dispose of public property has no place in a development
ordinance. The Governing Board’s require autonomy and flexibility when making
financial decisions. Further, the provision in the ordinance was outdated, not
used, and was recommended to be taken out by staff and the consultant in the
UDO Update process. At their meeting on May 9, 2019, the Board of Aldermen
found that the text amendment is CONSISTENT with the overall goals, objectives,
and policies, of the 2015 CAMA Land Use Plan.
The statement and motion was seconded and passed May 9, 2019.
                        /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor

6.   City Dock Discussion
   City Manager Oakley pointed out that a public information session was held
April 30 to review the options for replacement of the city dock destroyed
during Hurricane Matthew in 2018. He reported that the most popular option was
a fixed pier and platform with no boat slips. He noted that in order to have a
floating pier and any boat slips, dredging would be required.
   Alderman Mosteller stated that she was leaning towards the fixed pier and
platform because dredging would be required for a floating structure and
dredging slows the permitting process. She added that if the City would decide
at a later date to do boat slips or something else, permit requests could be
submitted at that time.
   Alderman Pukenas endorsed the fixed pier and platform option and stated it
would provide the best public access.
   Alderman Spencer supported the fixed pier and platform option and stated he
would like to see consideration of transient slip(s) in the future.
   Alderman Tucker motioned, second by Alderman Powell to approve Option C3.3
and proceed with using a fixed dock.
Discussion
   Alderman Sharkey expressed her opinion that an opportunity is missed for
providing a floating dock for the end for tie ups.
   Alderman Tucker amended his motion to include a kayak launch at the end of
the pier. Alderman Powell seconded the motion.
   At the suggestion of Alderman Pukenas, Alderman Tucker amended his motion to
include an expediated 30-day CAMA process. Alderman Powell seconded the motion.
Unanimous vote; motion carried.

SOUTHPORT
RESOLUTION OF COMMENDATION AND SUPPORT OF ESTABLISHMENTS PARTICIPATING IN THE
SKIP THE STRAW PROGRAM TO PROMOTE THE REDUCTION OF PLASTIC WASTE IN OUR CITY
WHEREAS, the City of Southport is committed to being a good steward of the
coastal environment, recognizing the value of well-maintained waterfront and
unsullied water in Southport and in neighboring communities; and
WHEREAS, the economic value of clean public spaces and water is recognized as
important to residents and business owners; and
WHEREAS, the presence of plastics in the marine environment is commonly
regarded as unsightly and is known by the marine science community as dangerous
to the health and safety of marine life, including fish and shellfish enjoyed
by many locally; and
WHEREAS, plastic straws constitute an enormous number of plastic fragments that
are not recyclable and often escape into the environment; and
WHEREAS, Coastal Water Watch and Keep Brunswick County Beautiful have
implemented the nationally recognized Skip the Straw Program in Brunswick
County, and continue to promote additional methods to reduce the harm that
single-use plastic poses to our environment, fish, and birds.
BE IT RESOLVED that the Aldermen and Mayor of the City of Southport recognize
the importance of reducing the use of plastic straws and other single-use
plastics and commend the dining venues currently participating in the Skip the
Straw program and identified as Ocean Friendly Establishments.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Aldermen and Mayor of the City of Southport
encourage other businesses, as well as individuals, to participate in the Skip
the Straw program and to reduce or eliminate the use of plastic straws and
other single-use plastics.
Adopted this 13th day of June, 2019               /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor

PROJECT REPORT
   City Manager Oakley presented the job description for additional Public
Information Officer (PIO) duties to the Tourism Director position.
Essential Duties and Tasks
   The PIO manages, plans, and executes information dissemination
   Coordinates public relations activities
   Manages the city website
   Promotes and maintains positive media relations
   Responds to request for public information
   Distributes general communication regarding events, operations, and programs
for the City.
Knowledge, Skills and Abilities
   The PIO will be able to establish good working relationships with the media
and the public and to maintain those relationship by answering queries
promptly, arranging interviews or speakers when requested and being a familiar
and involved presence at community events.
   Develops marketing and public relations materials for the City.
   Writes, edits, reviews, and approves public relations materials including
news releases, articles, speeches, on-line information services.
   As a key member of the City team, the PIO collaborates with City Department
Heads to ensure the development of communication strategies.
   Is responsible for developing guidelines for disseminating information and
outlining procedures to follow in a crisis.
   The PIO administers crisis/emergency communications during critical
incidents by collaborating with key personnel and disseminating vital
information to the media and the public both quickly and effectively.
   Serves at the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) when activated. Position
will report directly to the City Manager.

SECTION V. TAX RATE
   There is hereby levied, for fiscal year 2019-2020, a tax at the rate of
$0.2956 on each one hundred dollars ($100) of assessed valuation of property
located within the City of Southport for the purpose of raising revenue in the
General Fund. The assessed value of property is $938,025,702. Revenue neutral
tax rate adjusted for growth is $.2654 on each one hundred dollars ($100) of
assessed valuation.
SECTION VI. BUDGET OFFICER AUTHORITY
   The city manager (budget officer) is hereby authorized to transfer
appropriations within a fund and between funds under the following terms:
   He may transfer amounts between appropriations within the same fund,
provided that a report of such transfers shall be made no later than the next
regular financial report to the Board of Aldermen.
   He may authorize temporary transfers of cash among funds as necessary to
meet cash flow needs.
   All other transfers of funds between appropriations or budget funds shall be
accomplished by Board amendment of this ordinance.
SECTION IX. CONTINUING AUTHORIZATION
   Prior year Capital Reserve Fund is no longer a restriction of Fund Balance.
Previously adopted capital project budgets, grant project budgets, and special
reserve funds are hereby un-authorized as all such projects have been completed
and all monies shall be returned to the associated funds upon adoption of the
Budget ordinance.
SECTION X. BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION
   This ordinance and the supporting budget document shall be the basis of the
financial plan for the City of Southport municipal government for the 2019-2020
fiscal year. The budget officer shall administer the budget and shall insure
the finance officer and department heads of the city are provided with
sufficient guidance to properly implement this plan. Copies of the budget
ordinance shall be furnished to the city manager and the finance officer for
their use and direction in the disbursement of funds and to the city clerk for
the official records of the city.
SECTION XI. ADOPTION
   This ordinance has been adopted by the Southport Board of Aldermen in
special session on June 17, 2020, upon the motion of Alderman Powell and the
second of Alderman Tucker, with a vote of five (5) ayes and zero (0) noes and
shall be effective July 1, 2019.

AGENDA
2.   Public Hearing Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 160A-364; Unified Development
Ordinance (UDO) Text Amendment Article 11, Table of Area, Yard, Density, and
Height
   Alderman Pukenas motioned, second by Alderman Sharkey to open Public
Hearing. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   City Planner Lloyd explained that an application for a zoning text amendment
to the Unified Development Ordinance Article 11, Table of Area, Yard, Density,
and Height Requirements had been submitted by Preston Development and Southport
Marina. He stated that the request is to allow a maximum height of 50 feet for
a marina dry storage structure. He reported that the Planning Board reviewed
the proposed text amendment and voted to not recommend approval. He stated that
a public hearing was advertised to receive public comments and for the Board of
Aldermen to consider the text amendment. He noted that an existing 50-foot dry
storage structure was approved in 2008.
   Mr. Ed Glenn, 202 N. Atlantic Avenue, voiced his opinion that the proposed
text amendment would potentially change the character of the city and that the
Board of Aldermen are out of touch with the electorate.
   Noting that a number of Southport residents moved to Southport from
somewhere else, Ms. Lowe Davis, 504 W. Brunswick Street, implored the Board to
be wise, careful stewards and not let Southport become unrecognizable like
Myrtle Beach, South Carolina.
   Mr. John Allen, 110 W. Nash Street, member of the Planning Board and former
City Planner, stated his opinion that the proposed text amendment allows a
specific exception and is not good planning or good policy.
   Mr. Jody Wilmoth, 315 Clarendon Avenue, native of Southport, expressed his
opinion that the height limit should remain at 40 feet.
   Alderman Sharkey motioned, second by Alderman Spencer to close Public
Hearing. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
   Responding to a query by Alderman Tucker, Building Inspector Strickland
stated that the original marina dry storage building was constructed in the
1980’s, was over 40 ft. tall, and could have been rebuilt but the developer
failed to do so within the 180 day allotted time requirement.
   Per Alderman Mosteller’s request, verbatim comments provided in their
entirety:
“I appreciate the work of the Planning Board, staff and the citizens that have
shared their concerns.
We would not be here considering this text amendment if the City was not trying
to sell land to the Preston Group. In order to execute a one-time sale of a
city property, we are now considering the Cary based Preston Group’s demand for
an exemption from the Business District height restriction for dry storage
buildings.
This is not about the sale of a piece of property. This discussion is about a
text amendment change that will affect the Business District zone, not just one
parcel of land. If we approve this text amendment, we will be the ones setting
the precedent.
The idea that the questions used by the Board of Adjustment to determine a
conditional use permit should guide the decision about this text amendment is
an error. The only thing that the Preston Group’s special interest 50’ height
text amendment has in common with a conditional use permit is that it is for
the benefit of one individual. There is nothing else like this text amendment
in Article 11. The table of area, yard, density and height requirements does
not contain special exemptions for the benefit of one property owner.
Lamenting that there isn’t a conditional use permit process for height cannot
be the basis for approving this text amendment. Trying to apply conditional use
standards to this conversation is talking about a process that doesn’t even
exist. We CAN NOT make good zoning decisions by doing an end run around our own
zoning policy to give an individual business a special exemption benefit at the
expense of the citizens of Southport and our future.
The city is currently working to update the UDO and these updates are due for
consideration in April of next year. And tonight, we are again considering
reaching into the UDO for the Cary based Preston Group and giving them a height
exemption that we will not give to other Business owners.
It’s important to note that unlike the last text amendment that this Board
voted to approve, our city planning staff, and the UDO consultant did not make
a recommendation for the Board to approve this special interest text amendment.
In 2007, the Board of Aldermen changed the process so that height could not be
determined in a zoning district based on the desires of one business. In 2007,
the Board of Aldermen assured that the 50’ height for the Dry Storage Building
could never be considered a precedent, by eliminating the ability to get a
height variance through the conditional use permit process. At that time, the
Board recognized the importance of height and the need for height to be
uniformly administered within each zoning designation.
I sat down with one of the most committed and respected members of the
Southport community, former Alderman Paul Fisher, to ask him why, in 2007, the
Board voted unanimously to deny height exemptions. Colonel Fisher said, “In our
small waterfront community, height restrictions cannot be for the benefit of
one, they must be equal for all.” And that’s why he and all the Board members
voted in 2007 to do away with conditional use height variances.
The past did not set a precedent. But to make an arbitrary change and allow one
use, one business, marinas on the waterfront, to have an exemption to the
required height restriction is setting a precedent.
Consider the statements in our packet that advocate for the Preston Group’s
text amendment; the statements extracted from the CAMA Land Use Plan to attempt
to justify this special interest height text amendment need a closer look.
The first statement: P.1 Southport strongly supports all efforts to maintain
the Southport Marina as a public access facility in perpetuity.
The words “public access facility in perpetuity” are important.
If you read through the CAMA Land Use Plan, very quickly you realize that all
the statements, and there are many throughout the document, regarding the
Southport Marina as a public access facility, in context, are referring to the
Marina as owned by the state or owned by the city.
For example:
Page 103
“The City of Southport will continue to request the state to sell the Southport
Marina parcel to the City for use by citizens.”
Page 98
“Southport will annually review the status of the standing lease” …” to ensure
that the property remains open to public access.”
Page 162
Public Access: “These policies are intended to improve existing access
facilities and provide for acquisition of additional public access sites in
accordance with NC CAMA standards.”
Policy 82: “The Southport Marina is important to residents in and visitors to
the area. If developed by a private developer, the public access component
could be lost.”
I have read the Preston Group’s deed for the marina. The only part of the
Southport Marina that must be maintained as public access in perpetuity is the
boat ramp. When the state of NC chose to not honor the original agreement to
return the Southport Marina to the City of Southport and decided to sell the
city marina to the Cary based Preston Group, there was no binding agreement to
ensure that the marina will remain a public access facility.
So, the words in the CAMA Land use Plan, “public access facility in
perpetuity”, are now relegated to a hope and should not be used to defend the
Preston Group’s desire to exceed the maximum business district height
requirement.
The next statement: “Southport recognizes that tourism is important and will
support activities that promote tourism.” I am not quite sure how warehousing
150 private boats is effectively an ongoing promotion for tourism? If we are
going to approve a height exemption for the benefit of one business, we would
better promote tourism if we allowed the waterfront restaurants to all build to
50 feet. That would promote more tourism.
The consistency statement that favors the Preston Group says giving them a
height exemption is reasonable because it will not adversely affect the use of
adjoining properties. Tonight, we have heard from property owners that
disagree. These citizens own residential property adjacent to the properties
that would qualify for this special interest text amendment. It’s one thing if
our community decides to allow the entire business district to build to 50 feet
but, it is not right to give one business a zoning exemption so they can make
more money at the expense of other citizens.
It is the right of the citizens of Southport with residential property adjacent
to properties zoned business to expect that the Business District height
requirements are consistent. It is the right of other business owners in the
Business District to expect a level playing field. The conditional use process
has nothing to do with our decision tonight but, even the conditional use
permit process gives adjacent property owners the right to weigh in with their
objections as a key factor in conditional use permit approval process.
We have a plan, the Unified Development Ordinance provides for consistent,
ordered growth. If this Board approves the Preston Group’s request for a
special height exemption in the Business District zone, it is not a thoughtful
update to the UDO; it can only be seen as a hack to cut the deal.
I appreciate that the Preston Group wants to make more money, they are in the
business to make money. But we cannot facilitate their continued expansion in
Southport, in defiance of the city’s zoning plan. If this text amendment is
approved, besides giving this exemption to the Preston Group there are at least
two other properties that could immediately qualify for this height exemption
to allow future construction of 50’ tall marina dry storage buildings.
Approval tonight will set a precedent. In the future, what do we say to other
business owners? What are we going to say to waterfront restaurants, that are
required to build on pilings? When they say, you gave a 50-foot height
exemption for Marina Dry Storage buildings. We can make more money if we can
build our restaurant 50 feet tall. Make no mistake, currently no precedent
exists but if we approve this text amendment tonight, we will be setting the
precedent for future 50-foot structures.
We are a small town, here at the mouth of the Cape Fear. When do we give away
what makes us this special place? Drop by drop the stone is washed away. What
is the tipping point? When do we lose that unique balance that makes us so very
special? This year, five years, ten years. I would ask that we stay the course
and trust the zoning principles that will protect our future. Please do not
approve this text amendment.
It is the right of the citizens in this room to believe we serve them too. It’s
been said that this proposal should be considered rationally and objectively.
There is nothing wrong with having an emotional connection to our community.
There is no rational or objective reasoning that can be applied to selling our
city to serve the needs of one owner.
Approving this special interest text amendment will set more than a building
height precedent; it will send a signal to others that the City of Southport
sells land and includes a special interest zoning change to cut the deal. I
hope the next time we sell our zoning principles; we get more than $650,000
dollars.”
 
Alderman Sharkey expressed her views regarding the proposed text amendment
(comments included verbatim in their entirety):
   “I think it is important to consider any kind of text amendment, ordinance,
etc. with facts, being rational, looking at the pros and cons, and looking at
what is trying to be accomplish for the City. We need to have a mix of
commercial and residential properties. We need to foster good relationships so
that we have commercial entities that want to be here. We need to evaluate our
ordinances so that they are reflected of the needs of a community at a current
time and not live in the past or be outdated; everything from storm water
management to building heights or zoning. It’s all together, it’s not just one
thing.
   To answer some of the remarks that were made earlier about if this amendment
is adopted and the dry storage building is built, it would impact residential
property, the residential property might be zoned but not built there, that
would be the choice of somebody to decide if they wanted to live across the
street from the marina or not.
   Concerning the marina property, it is open to the public, it’s not private,
it is not a club, it is there and provides a service that we (City) can’t
provide. We can not provide, as a City, those boat slips, we can’t provide the
amenities to people at that scale, we can’t manage that. There is nothing that
requires the City to not have it owned by a private corporation, but it is open
to use. You have to pay for it, everything can’t be free.
   The proposed building is not going to impact the enjoyment of our
waterfront. This text amendment would be in compliance with some of the goals
of the CAMA Core Land Use Plan, despite what others may think. This text
amendment would provide the means to clean up a property that is a hazardous
waste site right now. This would allow for, in many cases, to be viewed as a
win/win. We are working with a commercial entity that has a proven track record
of being a good property owner that has worked with the City in many ways,
provides money to the Maritime Museum, hosts the King Mackerel Tournament, and
is probably open to other partnerships if we extend the hand to work with them.
   I understand the concerns that a 50 ft. building request could expand. That
I absolutely understand and where we should address that is with other
conditions that we can adopt through the UDO (Unified Development Ordinance).
We could adopt a different comprehensive marina definition to better define it,
so it is limited to truly one or two locations in the city. We could limit
where marinas are placed, we could designate a marina district on our zoning
map. That is a note in the current UDO but because its written for either State
property or city owned property, it’s not enforced, but why don’t we modify
that and use that to our advantage. Change the CUP process, we use conditional
use in very beneficial ways, it allows you to evaluate whether a use in a place
that is not generally zoned for that is appropriate or not. It may allow a
bakery to be operated in a residential area. That is going to be up before the
Board of Adjustment, that is a reasonable thing to entertain if there is not
impacts on other property owners. So, I appreciate the expansion of things
beyond the dry storage building. So, we should work to limit that, so it is
limited to this site. That is fine, I am not suggesting that we have dry
storage building everywhere that are 50 ft. tall. That’s why I feel a
conditional use process does apply to this or should apply to this because we
are talking about an exact location in a specific time and place, not a general
opening up of everything in the Business District.
   But we must move forward now, we do have an offer to buy the land and we
know what the intent is, the intent is to build a dry storage building. There
is no secret, they are not trying to be devious, it has all been very open and
if you ask questions and you ask to get information, I am sure they will share
it with you, but instead we are being ugly about it. We need to work forward to
be the best city we can and that means providing a mix of residential/
commercial.
   Marinas are part of a waterfront community. We are not bringing in an
industry that is not cohesive with what our identity is. We can’t just base
judgment or our ordinances on esthetics. We need to evaluate functionality,
purpose, location, and what it is going to provide. The land that is going to
be sold is an asset. This is the best use of that asset right now and I believe
we should facilitate this. I have taken in information from people that have
been for and against it but overall, this is best for our future because I have
evaluated it from both sides. We could leave it as it is or we can get it
cleaned up, we can have positive influx to our commercial tax base, we can work
with a good commercial business owner, and we can also say this is where the
marina lives, this is it. If we work within this document (UDO), that’s a
living, breathing document, that is supposed to be revised and updated every so
many years, so that it changes with the needs and the times that are before us.
It is a reasonable request.”
   Alderman Pukenas expressed concerns about the definition of a Marina;
“Any waterfront structure or development commercially providing permanent or
temporary harboring or storing for two (2) or more boats (pleasure and/or
commercial) and providing marina sales including but not limited to retail
sales for fuel, repairs, convenient foodstuffs, boats, engines, and
accessories.”
   Noting he had over 40 years’ experience, Alderman Tucker talked about the
Conditional Use Permit (CUP) process and he stated his opinion that
consideration of a 50 ft. marina dry storage structure should be assessed
through the CUP process that allows for negotiation with the builder/developer
resulting in benefits for both the City and the developer. Alderman Tucker
pointed out that the existing definition of a marina could open up other areas
in the Business District zoning to a marina development. He noted that there is
already a 50 ft. boat storage building at the marina and another structure of
that height would be on the outside periphery of town and would be a good use
for that site.
   Alderman Mosteller noted that a 40 ft. marina dry storage structure could
currently be permitted, and she stated her opinion that the request for an
additional 10 feet of height is strictly about making more money.
   City Attorney Isenberg pointed out that the applicant submitted a text
amendment application, did not apply for a Conditional Use Permit and the Board
can only consider this application for a text amendment. He added that when
considering the text amendment, the Board must consider that a marina dry
storage building anywhere in the Business District could have a height of 50
ft.
   City Manager Oakley verified with the City Planner and Building Inspector
that the way the Ordinance is written as this time would not allow an option
for the applicant to pursue a CUP for a 50 ft. marina dry storage building.
   Alderman Mosteller motioned, second by Alderman Pukenas to adopt the
Planning Board consistency statement and not approve the proposed text
amendment.
   Aye:   Aldermen Mosteller & Pukenas
   Nay:   Alderman Sharkey, Tucker, Spencer
   Motion failed 3-2
   Alderman Sharkey motioned, second by Alderman Spencer to approve the
proposed zoning text amendment with superscript to the Table of Area, Yard,
Density and Height, Article 11 to allow maximum height of 50 ft. for Marina Dry
Storage structure in Business District in compliance with the CAMA Core Land
Use Plan objectives.
   Discussion
   Alderman Mosteller pointed out that the CAMA Core Land Use Plan, Policy 85
states; “The City supports building heights that are consistent with the
surrounding areas.”  She added that the Plan further identifies a maximum
height of 40 ft. in the Business District and allows construction of marinas
and associated dry stack storage facilities in compliance with the zoning
ordinance. She stated her understanding of Alderman Tucker’s concerns and she
stated her opinion the text amendment was ad-hoc without consideration of the
unintended consequences.
   Alderman Tucker suggested including language that would limit where a marina
could be established; “must have at least 40 wet boat slips.”
   Alderman Sharkey was amenable to including in the motion the language
suggested by Aldermen Tucker; “marinas containing at least 40 wet boat slips
within the district may have a maximum height of 50 feet for the dry storage
buildings.”
   Attorney Isenberg stated that the original motion had to be withdrawn.
Alderman Sharkey withdrew her original motion with acquiescence of Alderman
Spencer.
   Pointing out that an Alderman was absent, Alderman Pukenas motioned, second
by Alderman Tucker to defer consideration of the text amendment to the next
Board meeting, August 8, 2019.
   Aye:   Alderman Pukenas, Mosteller, Tucker
   Nay:   Alderman Spencer and Sharkey
   Motion carried 3-2
   Alderman Mosteller asked if the text amendment had to go back to the
Planning Board and if the proposed amendment is contract zoning. City Attorney
Isenberg advised that another Public Hearing would not be necessary as long as
any proposed modification to the proposal was not substantial and would draw
the same basic comments and speakers. He added that the text amendment is not
contract zoning as it could apply to more than one property owner within the
district who could meet the standards.

   City Manager Oakley acknowledged the concerns about the sewer rate increase.
He read a prepared statement:
The City of Southport Sewer rates increased on July 1, 2019. The base rate for
3,000 gallons increased by 35% and the rate for usage above 3,000 gallons went
up 5%. This was the last year in a three-year plan of rate increases needed to
pay for future debt service on infrastructure improvements and wastewater
treatment capacity. Starting next year, rates will only go up incrementally
based on the Consumer Price Index. The rates were calculated using a rate
calculator model developed by the UNC School of Government Environmental
Finance Center that allowed the City to look at several scenarios and choose
the one it felt was the most equitable for its citizens. The Environmental
Finance Center’s model took in consideration our current cost to operate our
system and the significant cost the City must incur to provide wastewater
treatment capabilities in the future.
The City is currently leasing sewer capacity from Brunswick County and this
agreement is temporary and is set to expire soon. Therefore, the City had to
develop plans for its future wastewater treatment. In 2017, the City decided to
enter into an agreement with Brunswick County to expand their treatment
capabilities. This expansion would provide the City 750,000 gallons of capacity
per day for the next twenty years and would cost approximately $26,000,000.
Fortunately, the City was able to secure a low-interest loan from the State’s
Clean Water Revolving fund to pay for the expansion. Without this loan, sewer
rate would have to be set at much higher rates.
Before construction of the expansion of the Brunswick County started, the City
decided to review the agreement with the County and look at its long-term
wastewater treatment needs. During this review, the City realized it would need
more than 750,000 gallon per day of sewer capacity well before the twenty-year
agreement with the County ended. This means the City would need to pay for
another expansion which would cost the City millions more and require even more
rate increases. Therefore, the City reviewed its options and realized it could
build its own wastewater treatment plant at approximately the same costs of the
County expansion, but with enough capacity to last well beyond twenty years.
Before a decision was made to leave the agreement with the County and build its
own plant, the City verified that the loan from the State’s Clean Water
Revolving Fund would pay for the new plant. In fact, the loan was originally
awarded based on the idea of the City building its own plant. Based on all this
information, the City notified the County this past spring that it was
terminating the agreement and was going to build its own plant.
The City is currently in the process of designing the new wastewater treatment
plant on property that the City already owns and is working closely with the NC
Clean Water Revolving Fund and expects to start drawing proceeds from the loan
next spring. The plant is scheduled to be operational in 2022. Once the plant
is operational, the City will be able to hold rates steady or even reduce them.
The City has also applied for over $8,000,000 in grants to replace old sewer
lines and lift stations. The replacement of these lines will vastly improve the
efficiency of our sewer system and make even further reductions in sewer rates
possible.
   Mayor Dove directed the City Manager to schedule a Rate Committee meeting to
address the concerns raised about the sewer rates.

A RESOLUTION ACCEPTING AND ADOPTING THE RESULTS OF THE ASSET MANAGEMENT PLAN
FOR THE CITY’S WASTEWATER COLLECTION SYSTEM
E-AIA-W-17-0090 & E-AIA-W-18-0125
WHEREAS, the City of Southport was awarded grants from the State Reserve Fund
for the purpose of developing an Asset Inventory and Assessment of the City’s
Wastewater Collection System; and
WHEREAS, the City has conducted the investigative inspections of the system;
and
WHEREAS, the purpose of these investigations was to develop an inventory of the
assets and to assess these assets for condition and function, and to document
the degree of criticality of each asset to the safe and efficient functioning
of the City’s Wastewater Collection System; and
WHEREAS, the results of this effort include a list of priority projects for the
City that establish a roadmap for future investments in the system;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE BOARD OF ALDERMEN:
That the City appreciates the investment of State Funds for this purpose.
That the City has completed the work and accepts this Asset Management Plan as
a tool to guide future investments in the collection system.
That the City will update and maintain the database system developed for the
assets.
That the City hereby adopts this Resolution to close the project.
Adopted this, the 8th of August 2019 Southport, North Carolina.

AGENDA
   4.   Consideration; Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) Text Amendment
Article 11, Table of Area, Yard, Density, and Height
Mayor Dove pointed out that the Public Hearing on the proposed UDO text
amendment had been held on July 11.
Noting that the UDO currently permits a marina to build dry storage structures
40 foot tall without restrictions, Alderman Tucker motioned, second by Alderman
Powell to adopt the UDO Article 11, Table of Area, Yard, Density, and Height
Requirements text amendment with findings, Note to the Table, Marinas with 40
or more wet boat slips in this district may have dry storage buildings with a
maximum height of no more than 50 feet.
 
Discussion
Per Alderman Mosteller’s request, verbatim comments provided in their entirety:
I appreciate the work of the Planning Board, staff and the citizens that have
shared their concerns.
I am still struggling to understand why our Board would consider approving this
special interest height exemption.
We would not be here considering this text amendment if the City was not trying
to sell land to the Preston Group. In order to execute a one-time sale of a
city property, we are now considering the Cary based Preston Group’s demand for
an exemption from the Business District height restriction for dry storage
buildings.
In my struggle to understand, I called the School of Government. This is where
professionals go to get advice on all things government. I was able to speak
with David Owens.
Mr. Owens is considered one of the foremost experts on zoning in North
Carolina. He wrote the book, “Land Use Law in North Carolina”.
Again, trying to understand how we got here, I started at the beginning. We
know that in order to approve the sale of the West West property, our Board
voted to repeal UDO Article 3-10 effective retroactively. And then immediately
made a second motion to take an action to sell the West West property based on
the repeal to amend that text. The repeal of Article 3-10 eliminated the
Planning Board’s required participation in the process of selling public
property.
I confirmed with Mr. Owens, there are three steps required by law in order to
make any text amendment to the UDO:
   1) the Planning Board must review it and make a recommendation to the Board
of Aldermen for our consideration
   2) A public hearing must be held
   3) then the Board of Aldermen can vote to approve the text amendment.
And this is the part I have struggled to wrap around. If these steps are
legally required to amend the UDO, then how can the Board of Aldermen
circumvent this process by moving to retroactively change text in the UDO and
then immediately moving to take an action based on that amendment? According to
my conversation with the representative from the School of Government, the
actions taken by our Board back in February of this year disregarded this
process.
Mr. Owens said that once you do the Planning Board review, notice and hearing,
then and only then can you do the amendment to take that provision out and
then, once it’s out, it’s out. When it is effective, and that process is
amended, then you follow the amended process after the date that it’s amended,
not before that.
In other words, it makes sense that you must complete the process before you
take an action.
Mr. Owens also indicated that he did not know if you could make the change in
process retroactively effective. Going back and applying the amended process to
something that was done prior to the amendment at least raises some questions.
Mr. Owens said it was a murky area of the law and he was not sure taking action
before the process was complete, was clearly illegal but, it does raise a
question mark.
The second question I asked him about was about the Preston Group’s special
interest height exemption text amendment, that the Board is considering this
evening - a 50’ height exemption for the benefit of one business, contractually
motivated by the sale of city property. I asked Mr. Owens, is it a typical
zoning practice to create a height exception for the benefit of one property
owner?
Mr. Owens said he had not seen it done this way, usually the text for a
particular district would typically have the height limit as a standard for
that zoning district. Mr. Owens went on to say, normally, if you want to get
into site specific standards, you do it through a conditional zoning process
rather than a text amendment or superscript. This text amendment in Mr. Owen’s
words would be “unusual.”
The third question I asked was, would this special interest text amendment set
a precedent for future property owners in the business district to build to 50
feet?
Mr. Owens answered, in a legal sense no, but in a political sense yes.
Politically meaning …setting public policy. Property owners could say if 50
feet was ok for this use, why can’t I have 50’ also? If it’s good for the
goose, it’s good for the gander.
Mr. Owens said, and I quote, “Once you create an exception for one thing, that
just creates the demand for more exceptions.”
The Planning Board is in agreement with Mr. Owens and unanimously voted to not
recommend this text amendment. John Allen is our former City Planner and
currently serves as a member of the Planning Board. Mr. Allen spoke on behalf
of the Planning Board at the public hearing last month stating that “the
proposed text amendment has the potential to create a patchwork of specific
rules that serve to slowly undercut the existing height limit. And he said he
believed this was neither good planning nor good public policy.”
In 2007, the Board of Aldermen assured that the 50’ height exception for
rebuilding the Dry Storage Building could never be considered a precedent, by
eliminating the ability to get a height variance through the conditional use
permit process. At that time, the Board recognized the importance of height and
the need for height to be uniformly administered within each zoning
designation.
Let’s be clear, our current business district zoning allows the Preston Group
to build a Marina Dry Storage Building to 40 feet. Tonight, we are considering
giving the Preston Group a height exemption to build to 50 feet. In the future,
how do we say no to our waterfront restaurants, when they say we are maxed out,
we can’t expand, we would like to add another story and we need to build to 50
feet to do that?
I ended my conversation with Mr. Owens by reading him the section in the
original offer to purchase document accepted by the Board in February of this
year…. it states that, “Preston Group’s purchase contingencies are based on
receiving all necessary City, State and Federal approvals and permits to
construct a 50’ tall dry storage building” and also says “Seller will cooperate
with Buyers pursuit of approvals, easements, and rights of way as required for
Buyer’s Intended Use.”
When I talked about this document with Mr. Owens, he referred to the word
“cooperate” as the weasel word and he said this seemed uncomfortably close to
the line of the city promising to take regulatory action in return for the
sale. And, the city should avoid even the appearance of doing that.
Earlier today, I had the opportunity to speak with Mike, our city attorney and
because the final contract did not have the stipulation that the city would
cooperate with the buyer regarding the zoning change, Mike said, the city is
not obligated to give the Preston Group this text amendment. But the Preston
Group’s intention was clear.
The city staff and Planning Board are currently working to update the UDO and
these updates are due for consideration in April of next year. And tonight, we
are again considering reaching into the UDO for the benefit of one property
owner, the Cary based Preston Group and giving them a height exemption that we
do not want to give to other Business owners.
Please understand I appreciate the Southport Marina and I do not hold the
Preston Group accountable for the actions of the Board. The Preston Group is
just being entrepreneurial. There is no question, our community recognizes that
the Southport Marina is successful and a good corporate citizen. Fortunately,
Southport has some amazing business owners that bring value to our community.
With that said, being a good corporate citizen is not the criteria for giving
UDO text amendments and height exemptions.
It is the Board of Aldermen, that is accountable for disregarding the
recommendations of the Planning Board to help facilitate the sale of a piece of
city property, in defiance of the city’s zoning plan.
Whether they are given a 50-foot exemption, or this Board maintains the maximum
height of 40 feet in the Business District, do we really think the Preston
Group will not purchase 2 ½ acres of contiguous water access property for the
bargain price of $650,000 dollars?
Back in February, $650,000 may have seemed like a lot of money to some of the
members of the Board, who were concerned with the impact of Florence on the
city’s budget. But we just completed the $8,000,000 annual general fund budget
for 2019 - 2020 and know that we are on track with projected FEMA
reimbursements to meet the 30% surplus that the state prefers; without the sale
of this property.
And if the Preston Group decides to not purchase the land because the city did
not give them the special height exemption to allow them to build to 50 feet,
the Board would then have the opportunity to offer the property up for sale on
the open market and frame the terms of the sale to maximize the benefits for
the citizens of Southport.
Ms. Sweeney could not be here tonight but as the adjacent property owner with
acres of property zoned R-10, she attended the Planning Board meeting and has
twice attended our Board meetings to ask us not to allow the 50-foot exemption
on the business zoned property next to her residentially zoned property. It is
the right of the citizens of Southport with residential property adjacent to
properties zoned business, to expect that the Business District height
requirements are consistent. It is the right of other business owners in the
Business District to expect a level playing field.
When a representative of the School of Government uses words like raises a
question, precedent and murky when discussing potential actions that we as a
Board have considered or are considering - we should pause.
Mr. Owens words bear repeating “Once you create an exception for one thing,
that just creates the demand for more exceptions.”
We cannot make good zoning decisions by doing an end run around our own zoning
policy to give an individual business a special exemption benefit at the
expense of the citizens of Southport and our city’s future.
Approval tonight will set a precedent. In the future, what do we say to other
business owners? Currently, no precedent exists but if we approve this text
amendment, we will be setting the precedent for future 50-foot structures.
It is the right of the citizens that live next to properties zoned business and
the citizens in this room to believe we serve them too.
I would ask that we stay the course and trust the zoning principles that will
protect our future. We are a small town, here at the mouth of the Cape Fear.
We need to be thoughtful and intentional about the decisions we make so we do
not look back and realize we have given away that which makes Southport so
special.
Please do not approve this text amendment.
Stating that he had also spoken with Mr. Owens of the School of Government,
City Attorney Isenberg declared that the City did not accept any proposal or
contract with the word “cooperate” in it, and that the signed contract did not
require the City to take any action in regard to the Purchaser’s applications.
He stated that Mr. Owens said the proposed text amendment was not contract
zoning as contract zoning would be when the City contracts itself to take some
legislative action in return for a property owner building something or taking
some action. Attorney Isenberg emphasized that the Board was not obligated to
do anything, it did not have to pass the text amendment, and would not be in
breach of the purchase contract if the text amendment was not passed. Attorney
Isenberg added that Mr. Owens stated that the way the Board is considering the
text amendment, as a footnote to the Table of Area, Yard, Density & Height
Requirements, is unusual, but he had no doubt it was legal as long as a Public
Hearing was held and the process was followed. Attorney Isenberg reiterated
that the purchase contract did not require the Board to do anything.
VOTE
Aye:   Aldermen Tucker, Powell, Pukenas, Sharkey, Spencer
Nay:   Alderman Mosteller
Motion Passed 5-1
AN ORDINANCE AMENDING ARTICLE 11 TABLE OF AREA YARD & DENSITY OF THE
CITY OF SOUTHPORT UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE
   THAT WHEREAS, the City has enacted a Unified Development Ordinance and other
land use ordinances that control land development within both the City’s
incorporated areas and within its extraterritorial area; and
   WHEREAS, in order to promote the public health, safety and general welfare
and to promote the best interest of the city and community, it is necessary for
the City Board of Aldermen from time to time to consider appropriate revisions,
modifications and additions to the city’s land use ordinances; and
   WHEREAS, Southport Marina has filed an application for an UDO text amendment
to amend Article 11 of the Unified Development Ordinance to add a footnote to
the Article 11 Table of Yard, Area, Density and Height Requirements to allow
Marina dry storage buildings to have a height of 50 feet in the BD District;
and
   WHEREAS, the Planning Board has reviewed this matter and found that the
proposed amendment to Article 11 of the Unified Development Ordinance to be
inconsistent with the City of Southport CAMA Core Land Use Plan and does not
recommend its approval; and
   WHEREAS, pursuant to N. C. General Statutes and city ordinances, a public
hearing, properly noticed, was held on July 11, 2019 before the Board of
Aldermen regarding this issue; and
   WHEREAS, after considering the public hearing response, the concerns of the
public, the recommendation of the Planning Board, together with the comments of
staff, and after full discussion, the Board of Aldermen finds that the footnote
to Article 11 as requested by the applicant should be limited to marinas in the
BD District with 40 or more wet boat slips; and
   WHEREAS, the Board of Aldermen, after considering the public hearing
response and the recommendation of the Planning Board, together with the
comments of staff, hereby finds that this text amendment is consistent with the
2015 CAMA Land Use Plan for the reasons stated in its Statement of Plan
Consistency attached hereto and incorporated herein; and
   WHEREAS, the Board of Aldermen further finds that this amendment is
reasonable and in the public interest because there is a precedent for 50 foot
marina dry storage buildings in the BD District, 50 ft high marina dry storage
buildings will accommodate the need for more boat storage in the city, which
will encourage tourism and related recreational activities contributing to the
local economy, and they will provide safer and more direct access to the water
for recreation.
   NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED by the Southport Board of Aldermen that
Article 11 the Southport Unified Development Ordinance is hereby amended as
follows on Exhibit A attached.
This, the 8th day of August 2019.             City of Southport
                        /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor

City of Southport Board of Aldermen
Statement of Plan Consistency
(As per NC General Statute 160A-383)
Zoning regulations shall be made in accordance with a comprehensive plan. Prior
to adopting or rejecting any zoning amendment, the governing board shall adopt
one of the following statements which shall not be subject to judicial review;
1) A statement approving the zoning amendment and describing its consistency
with an adopted comprehensive plan and explaining why the action taken is
reasonable and in the public interest. 2) A statement rejecting the zoning
amendment and describing its inconsistency with an adopted comprehensive plan
and explaining why the action taken is reasonable and in the public interest.
3) A statement approving the zoning amendment and containing at least all of
the following: 1) A declaration that the approval is also deemed an amendment
to the comprehensive plan. 2) An explanation of the change in conditions the
governing board took into account in amending the zoning ordinance to meet the
development needs of the community. 3) why the action was reasonable and in the
public interest.
      (NCGS 160A-383)
ZONING AMENDMENT:         ZA-19-0408-01
STATEMENT OF CONSISTENCY AND RECCOMENDATION:
The City of Southport Board of Aldermen hereby finds that the proposed zoning
text amendment amending Article 11 of the Unified Development Ordinance is
consistent with the 2015 CAMA Land Use Plan adopted November 13, 2014. The
Board of Aldermen finds that the proposed amendment is consistent with goals
and policies in the 2015 CAMA Land Use. More specifically, the text amendment
allowing 50 foot marina dry storage buildings is consistent with the following
policies: the city supports all efforts to maintain the Southport Marina as a
public access facility in perpetuity (p.5), the city supports tourism and
recreational related developments that protect and preserve the natural
environment while promoting the City as a tourist destination (p. 1), Southport
recognizes that tourism is important and will support activities that promote
tourism (p. 89). In order to promote the best interest of the city, it is
necessary for the Board of Aldermen to consider appropriate revisions,
modifications, and additions to the City’s Land Development Ordinance. The
amendment is reasonable and in the public interest because it will not
adversely affect the use of adjoining properties, there is a precedent for 50
foot marina dry storage buildings, 50 ft high marina dry storage buildings will
accommodate the need for more boat storage in the city, and they will provide
safer and more direct access to the water for recreation. At their meeting on
August 8th, 2019, the Board of Aldermen found that the proposed amendment is
CONSISTENT with the overall goals, objectives, and policies, of the 2015 CAMA
Land Use Plan.
         The statement and motion was seconded and passed 5-1.
                              /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor

                                       CONTRACT AMENDMENT
BRUNSWICK COUNTY
   THIS AMENDMENT to the Agreement for Sale and Purchase of Real Property is
made and entered into this the 8th day of August, 2019, by and between the City
of Southport, a body politic and corporate of the State of North Carolina,
(hereinafter referred to as “City”), and Southport Marina, Inc., (hereinafter
referred to as “Buyer”);
                     WITNESSETH:
   THAT WHEREAS, the parties entered into an Agreement for Sale and Purchase of
Real Property (Southport former wastewater treatment plant site) effective
March 18, 2019; and
   WHEREAS, said Agreement provided for Buyer an examination period beginning
on the date of the Agreement and extending through August 15, 2019, at 5:00 pm;
and
   Whereas, Buyer, in order to complete the examination of the Property, needs
more time and has requested City to extend the examination period; and
   Whereas, City has agreed to extend said period upon the terms and conditions
hereinafter set out;
   Now, therefore, for valuable consideration, the parties do hereby agree and
covenant as follows:
   1.   Within 5 days of the execution of this contract amendment, Buyer shall
pay to City a fee of $ 2,000 as consideration for the agreement of City to
extend the examination period set forth in Section 1(e) of the Agreement. In
the event of closing, this fee shall be applied towards the purchase price of
the Property and credited to Buyer. In the event that Buyer elects not purchase
the Property for any reason, this fee shall be retained by City as
consideration for the extension granted herein.
   2.   Upon payment of the above-referenced fee, the examination period
provided for in Section 1(e) of the Agreement is hereby extended through 5:00
pm on November 15, 2019.
   3.   Upon payment of an additional fee of $ $2,000 on or before November 15,
2019, Buyer shall be entitled to one further extension of the examination
period through February 15, 2020. In the event of closing, this fee shall also
be applied towards the purchase price of the Property and credited to Buyer. In
the event that Buyer elects not purchase the Property for any reason, this fee
shall also be retained by City as consideration for the extension granted
herein.
   4.   Except as specifically set forth herein, all other terms and conditions
of the original Agreement shall remain unchanged and in full force and effect.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have executed this instrument effective the day
and year first above written.

(BEMC) and Duke Energy;
   He contacted Senator Rabon who was in contact with the CEO of Duke Energy;

subsequent issues getting the substation back online;
   Meetings will be scheduled with BEMC, North Carolina Eastern Municipal Power
Agency (NCEMPA) and Duke Energy to discuss outages, in an effort to improve
communications and response during an emergency event.
   Noting that Southport sustained minimal damage from Hurricane Dorian, City
Manager Oakley commended city staff for their work prior, during and after the
storm. He pointed out that a lot of work occurs during storms that is not
visible to the general public, i.e. employees leave their families to make sure
calls were answered and public safety was ensured; fire, rescue and law
enforcement officers slept on cots, and Public Services employees were out near
the peak of the storm to make sure the sewer lift stations were operating
properly. He noted that many employees went beyond the call of duty, such as
the Public Services employees, who during their lunch period, and after hours,
assisted senior citizens preparing their homes for the storm. Additionally,
long hours have been spent documenting every penny spent for reimbursement
purposes.
   City Manager Oakley reported that the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) ran
efficiently at all times with staff rotating in and out, there were designated
scribes who documented every incident and action during the event, and the City
was able to get out clear, concise information thanks to the Public Information
Officer.
   City Manager Oakley thanked citizens for their patience during the event and
he touched on the need for a curfew during the storm. He noted that the storm
was predicted to be worse than it was, it was expected to make landfall at high
tide, and situations were occurring with sightseers putting themselves in
harm’s way.

staff and the normal schedule for yard debris pick up by Brush Bandit would

SOUTHPORT RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF INTERNATIONAL DAY OF PEACE
WHEREAS, The United Nations in 1981 established a yearly International Day of
Peace, a day devoted to strengthening the ideals of peace both within and among
all nations and people; and
WHEREAS, The International Day of Peace is now observed around the world each
year on September 20 to put aside all that separates us and to experience
peace; and
WHERE, in 1984, the General Assembly adopted the Declaration on the Right of
Peoples to Peace; and
WHEREAS, Southport residents are coordinating a celebration of the
International Day of Peace on a local level; and
WHEREAS, Peace Day Southport promotes world peace, local peace and inner peace
through art, education and celebration; and
WHEREAS, the Celebration of Peace will be held and will include songs, dances,
art, informational booths, exhibits, children’s crafts, and a Peace Pilgrim
film; and
NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Mayor and Southport Board of Aldermen
on this the 12th day of September 2019, hereby proclaim Saturday, September 21,
2019 as “Peace Day” in the City of Southport and urge all citizens to join in
the festivities of this day and promote peace among all peoples.
                        /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor
Attest: /s/ Michele Windham, Clerk

Exhibit A

Deletions in Strikethrough
Sec. 17-80. - Golf carts.
REGISTRATION AND PERMIT REQUIREMENTS
Registration and Permit required. In order to operate a golf cart in the
corporate limits of the City of Southport under this section, the golf cart
must be registered annually with the City of Southport using an application
furnished by the city. A twenty-five dollar ($25.00) per year registration fee,
from July 1 through June 30, must be paid to the City before a registration
sticker is issued. The registration sticker must be displayed on the left rear
fender of the golf cart. Low speed vehicles subject to state regulation and
licenses will be exempt from a permit and inspection., but the City of
Southport requests low speed vehicle owners to register with the City and
obtain a sticker free of charge so the City can maintain an accurate count of
low speed vehicles in Southport.

Resolution Regarding Location of Southport Wastewater Treatment Plant.
Unanimous vote; motion carried. Mayor Dove read the resolution into the record.
RESOLUTION
REGARDING LOCATION OF SOUTHPORT WASTEWATER TREATMENT PLANT
   THAT WHEREAS, in order to better serve its’ citizens, residents and property
owners, the City of Southport finds it necessary and in the public interest to
construct a new wastewater treatment plant; and
   WHEREAS, the City currently owns a large tract of land containing over 400
acres located east of Hwy 87 and north of Bethel Church Road in Brunswick
County; and
   WHEREAS, said tract of land is suitable for the location of a wastewater
treatment plant; and
   WHEREAS, the portion of said tract located adjacent to Bethel Church Road is
located near property which is currently developed for residential use with
many persons living nearby; and
   WHEREAS, the Board of Aldermen feels that it is preferable and desirable
that the wastewater treatment plant be located in the northwestern portion of
the City’s property or in another area which would not affect the homeowners
living along or near Bethel Church Road;
   NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen that it direct the
City’s engineers, Hazen & Sawyer, to focus on and find a suitable location for
the new Southport wastewater treatment plant in the northwest portion of the
City’s property or other area located further away from Bethel Church Road.
   This the 10th day of October, 2019.      City of Southport
                     /s/ J. V. Dove, Mayor
Attest: /s/ Michele Windham, City Clerk

City of Southport
Fire Department
   WHEREAS, cancer affects millions of people all over the world, and the fact
that there is a proven correlation between firefighting and cancer, confirm
both the need to eradicate the terrible disease and, until a cure is found,
promote prevention, and help alleviate the suffering of its victims; and
   WHEREAS, in 2019 the American Cancer Society expected about 2 million new
cancers to be diagnosed in the United States. This year nearly 600,000
Americans are expected to die of cancer, more than 1,500 people a day; and
   WHEREAS, cancer is one of the deadliest diseases of all. We need to come
together to fight it. Those of us who haven’t been affected, need to step up
and promote prevention, early detection, and urge women to have routine
checkups and mammograms.
   WHEREAS, Southport Fire Fighters normally wear blue shirts 365 days a year.
For the month of October, they will don pink shirts to show their support of
breast cancer awareness, early detection, and prevention of the horrible
disease.
   THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the SOUTHPORT FIRE DEPARTMENT gives an image
of hope and encouragement to those battling breast cancer. The department
stands united with them, you are not alone in your fight. The City of Southport
encourages, recognizes, and supports the Southport Fire Department in their
efforts of promoting early detection and prevention of breast cancer.
   BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Aldermen and Mayor of the City of Southport
implore all citizens to support efforts promoting early detection and
prevention of breast cancer.

INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL USE POLICY
STATEMENT OF PURPOSE
The Indian Trail Meeting Hall is maintained and operated exclusively to
facilitate municipal government in Southport and to enable the governmental and
proprietary functions of the City of Southport. It is the policy of the City of
Southport that every use of the Indian Trail Meeting Hall shall be for the
purpose of providing services to the citizens of Southport, by the City itself
through its officers, employees, agents, contractors, official town boards or
official ad hoc bodies, or through organizations which conform to the criteria
for “community use” as set forth below.
COMMUNITY USE OF INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL
Any use of the Indian Trail Meeting Hall other than by the City itself acting
through its officers, employees, agents, contractors, official town boards or
official ad hoc bodies, shall constitute a “community use.” A community use for
a purpose which the City of Southport itself is authorized to undertake and
which shall have the primary intent of enhancing generally the health, safety
and welfare of all the citizens of Southport, shall be allowed, subject too the
terms and conditions of this police. No other community use or other use of the
Indian Trail Meeting Hall shall be allowed.
INDIAN TRIAL MEETING HALL FACILITY AVAILABLE FOR COMMUNITY USE
Subject to availability, the facility shall be available for community use, on
a first-come, first-services basis. The official business of t he City of
Southport shall at all times have priority of use, and any scheduled community
use may be cancelled without notice in the event the official business of
Southport requires the use of the facility.
TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF COMMUNITY USE
Nonprofit organizations servicing the City of Southport and providing a non-
profit identification number, shall constitute a “local community user” under
this policy and may use the Indian Trail Meeting Hall facilities for purposes
herein authorized at no charge and without security deposit.
Political Activity
Political Campaigning or Political Organizing shall not be permitted as a
community use in the Indian Trail Meeting Hall.
Business Use
Use of the Indian Trail Meeting Hall by for-profit businesses, including but
not limited to sales events of other types of solicitation, shall not be
permitted as a community use.
Qualified Use
A community use otherwise permitted under this policy may be denied as to a
previous user responsible for damage to the facilities. In such case, the City
Manager in his/her sole discretion may deny the application.
MINIMUM REGULATIONS FOR COMMUNITY USE OF INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL:
Any community use of the Indian Trail Meeting Hall shall comply strictly with
the following regulations as a condition of use:
1.   Lock all exterior doors before leaving.
2.   Close and lock all windows.
3.   Turn off all indoor and outside lights before leaving.
4.   If the kitchen is used, assure that the kitchen sink is completely
drained, the refrigerator door is completely closed, and all appliances are
turned off, before leaving.
5.   Clear the facility of all refuse, using the trash receptacle for refuse
and the recycling receptacle for recyclables located at the side of the
building.
6.   Attach nothing to walls or furnishings using tacks or nails, or using
adhesives leaving residual adhesive traces.
7.   Return the facility to its original order as found.
8.   Remove all equipment or supplies brought by the user into the facilities.
9.   Do not use or display any advertisement, banner or sign on the exterior of
the building.
10.   Remove any perishable food items or other supplies brought by the user
into the facilities.
11.   Observe all applicable fire code regulations and ensure that all
attendees are aware of fire extinguishers and escape routes out of the Indian
Trail Meeting Hall.
12.   Do not permit the use of alcohol, tobacco, firearms or illegally
possessed controlled substances.
13.   Comply with all ordinances of the City of Southport and all laws of the
State of North Carolina.
