Letter read by City Clerk; Tanya Shannon submitted by Kathy Cabral; 308 W. West
St. as followed:
To Our Elected Officials:
The UDO is the overarching document that dictates development in Southport and
will drive the character of the town in the future. From what I can see, the
UDO was last updated 10+ years ago and will not likely see another update for
another 10+ years.
Because of those 2 points, it is imperative that nothing in the approved UDO
creates “unintended consequences” as future development is considered for
Southport. I do not believe people will object to development, but it should be
responsible development. It should reflect the wishes of the citizens of
Southport and should be emblematic of the vision for the future of our city. It
should also reflect our size, our infrastructure limitations and the city’s
financial condition.
I refer you to Section 2.11 B 2 of the August 10, 2020 draft UDO which deals
with conditional zoning. How is “nonresidential zoning district” defined? Does
it include open space? Does it include PUDs? I think it is important that the
term be very clearly defined in the document. I believe both Open Space and
PUDs should be excluded from the definition of a non-residential zoning
district. I believe this would completely eliminate the prospect of a
conditional zoning change to be allowed for a PUD and allow the citizens of
Southport to have more input on future development in the town. In a
circumstance like Project Indigo, the strict definition of a non-residential
zoning district would limit the developers from getting the property rezoned
without public comment. Given the recent press in the Wilmington Business News,
it is important that the language in the UDO is amended.
It is no secret that the 211 corridor is facing development on a dramatic scale
with those residents looking. To Southport as their “urban center”. This will
put additional strain on our infrastructure and community. I am seeking a
commitment from the Alderman to seriously consider including a clear-cut
definition to “non-residential zoning district” to further protect our city and
maintain responsible development in Southport. This is our last best chance to
preserve the heart and soul of the city that we care for so deeply.
Thank you.
Mayor Hatem introduced Senior Planner from the Cape Fear Council of Government,
Mr. Wes MacLeod and City Planner, Mr. Thomas Lloyd .
Discussion on off-street parking regulations page 3-89 . Mr. MacLeod gave an
overview of the off-street parking ratios. He said if there is new construction
or change of use of the business there are certain parking requirements that
need to be met. He said depending on the location in the City there are
constraints with the off-street parking. He said in all zoning districts except
BD and CBD all the parking is unchanged. He said the proposed standard is if
there is a change of use no additional parking will be required. But if an
applicant wants to expand the usage area of the building by 25% then additional
parking will be required. He also said that if a residential use is being
obtained in the CBD or BD the applicant will need to provide parking, as well
as new construction on a vacant lot.
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller stated that she understands the conflict with off-
street parking in the CBD. She stated the City has buildings that need to be
protected and that it why the 25 % increase of usage requires additional
parking. She recommended to extend the parking overlay
district further down Howe St; and leave
the BD as is. She felt like this was more of zoning issue.
Alderman Allen asked if there would be an issue with extending Parking
Overlay District.
Mr. Lloyd said it could be done thru a separate process of a Zoning Map
Amendment. He said potentially it could be unfavorable to certain properties.
Mr. MacLeod said that in the current UDO there are many business that operating
without following the off-street parking guidelines. However, it has not been
enforced in certain parcels since there some small lots that would be unable to
follow the current guidelines. He said the goal is to update the UDO for off-
street parking to help allow businesses to continue to operate.
Alderman Allen stated that in the current UDO there zero setbacks, and he said
the Planning Board agreed that there was a need and value for setting setbacks
between BD and adjoining residential properties. Mr. Llyod said rezoning would
also affect the buffer yard standards and the uses of the properties.
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller wanted to clarify that in BD which includes the Yacht
Basin area, no additional parking is required unless expanding 25% or more. She
stated the proposed draft offers expansion up to 100 sf versus the current
measurement of parking is for a four-top table in a restaurant. She said the
proposed revision is essentially more forgiving in the Yacht Basin BD for
required parking.
Alderman Allen asked what the definition of redevelopment is: Redevelopment
definition was read by Mr. MacLeod as : “ Any combination of repairs,
reconstruction, rehabilitation, addition, or other improvement of a structure
or lot, including demolition and replacement of a structure, taking place
during any one-year period. Redevelopment may also be associated with a change
of use.”
Alderman asked where does the 25 % increase of space come from. Mr. MacLeod
said it was a calculation that was proposed bit it could be more or less.
Alderman Davis asked Alderman Allen if he would like to see the 25% increased
or decreased. Alderman Allen stated possibly less. He stated the majority of
the businesses currently do not have the ability to expand currently.
Alderman Spencer clarified that this included 25% of the gross area, including
outdoor and expanding up would trigger additional parking requirements. Mr.
MacLeod confirmed.
Mayor Hatem stated he would like to see City remain vibrant and safe by keeping
the parking requirements as proposed in the revised UDO. He said he understands
the challenges that some businesses have with parking but would like to
encourage the community to continue to find a safe and legal parking space and
walk around the CBD and BD area.
Alderman Allen proposed modifying the requirements that trigger additional
parking in CBD and BD reduced to 10% increase of usage.
Mayor Pro Tem stated that the purpose of the percentage of expansion that
requires more parking was to keep the existing structures on scale. She said it
would be unfortunate to see a lot of the old buildings torn down and rebuilt
out of proportion to the area.
Planning Board member Mr. Rich Bandera made comment that part of the reasoning
of the Planning Boards decision to make the trigger 25 % was because currently
restaurants are taking advantage of the outdoor space, especially during the
COVID-19 pandemic. He felt that reducing the percentage to 10% would be too low
because of the business utilizing more space outdoors. He also said that the
Building Occupancy requirements from a safety point and how many occupants can
be allowed into the building should also be considered when deciding on the
parking ratio in the CBD and BD.
Alderman Sharkey stated she felt keeping the percentage at 25% was reasonable
for now without having any data to prove otherwise. She said the goal is to
have an occupied CBD and BD.
Mayor Pro Tem wanted to clarify that if the space was available a business
could expand by 25 % or less every year without having to provide additional
parking. Mr. MacLeod confirmed and stated that this formula is close to what is
currently being utilized for parking in the CBD and BD area.
Mayor Hatem asked how parking is proposed in the revised UDO where the Yacht
Basin Eatery used to be, that is now being redeveloped. Mr. Llyod said the
parking will remain as it was before redevelopment and the building permit has
already been issued. Mr. Lloyd said the owner of this parcel also owns Fishy
Fishy restaurant and has the allocated parking requirements for both businesses
including the boat slips.
Motion was made by Alderman Sharkey to revise the proposed draft table 3.4
Minimum Off- Street Parking Spaces Required: Change of Use of Redevelopment in
the CBD and BD. “ A change of use or redevelopment whereby the floor area of
the building is not expanded by greater than 15%.” Second by Alderman Davis.
Mayor Pro Tem asked if this also included the second part of the table for
Residential Uses.
Mr. Macleod stated that 15% would include the entire table for Minimum Off-
Street Parking Spaces Required including Residential Uses.
Motion by Alderman Sharkey to amend her motion to state the revision of Table
3.4 to include the entire table that includes Residential Uses “ by greater
than 15%”. Second by Alderman Davis.
Alderman Spencer commented that as a realtor he is worried about putting too
many restrictions on the growth of future redevelopment for some businesses. He
said for some businesses the only way to expand is up. He said this revision
will burden some owners who would be unable to comply with the requirements in
order to have future growth.
Alderman Sharkey stated after hearing the conversation and what the Planners
and the Planning Board recommended for parking requirements in the CBD and BD,
she stated she may now disagree with her motion.
Mr. Bandera commented that he sees no problem with 15 % expansion for indoor
space, but for outdoor space thinks it should be 25 % to allow for more
flexibility. He said enforcement will be a challenge because of the amount of
businesses that are trying to sustain.
Mayor Hatem commented that it will take businesses currently operating years to
recover from the loss due to COVID-19. He feels that outdoor space is important
to help businesses to continue to recover and strive during this
time especially.
Mr. Macleod said this would include the outdoor usable area.
Alderman Allen stated that this parking provision of 15 % would only be for
redevelopment or change of use or expansion of greater than 15%. He reiterated
that the City is still allowing the same provisions to utilize outdoor space
for businesses unless the business is expanding more than 15% indoors
or outdoors.
Mayor Hatem asked for a vote for a motion on the table. Aye: Mayor Pro Tem
Mosteller, Alderman Allen, Alderman Lombardi, Alderman Davis. Nay: Alderman
Spencer and Alderman Sharkey. 4-2. Motion carried.
Alderman Lombardi stated that the City should be researching ways to provide
parking especially in downtown ( CBD) Southport to help support the businesses
and the community to thrive and Alderman Spencer concurred.
Alderman Spencer wanted to address the question and concerns raised in Public
Comment by Mr. Greg Mitchell. Mr. MacLeod stated that his understanding is the
footprint of the accessory structure cannot be over 530 sf. Mr. Lloyd said the
footprint originates from the setback requirements.
Alderman Allen clarified for accessory uses the discussion is two separate
issues. One is total sf of the total accessory structure and the other is the
footprint existing structure (or garage). He states you can not have an
existing footprint over 800 sf for an accessory structure. He stated he
believed the intent is that a property owner cannot have a two (2 )story
accessory storage “Lording” over the neighbor’s property.
Planning Board Member Mr. Bandera commented that reason for putting a cap on
the accessory structure size for setback limitations is if there is a primary
structure over 5,000 sf than a cap should be maintained for
allocation services.
Jennifer Fontaine; 5223 Shipmast Way; made a public comment that appreciated
the attention made to open and green space and making the small community very
natural and livable. However, she is concerned about the density requirements
for new development requirements. She would like the setbacks to remain the
same or increased slightly. She understands that prohibits development, but the
City should consider preserving the trees and wetlands.
Mayor Hatem asked Mr. Mitchell if his concern was answered. Mr. Mitchell stated
that he is now clear on the situation.
Mr. Lloyd said the next comment was submitted by Alderman Sharkey regarding
Light Source 3.16 ( C) on page 3-94. Alderman Sharkey proposing change in item
1. (C) to allow for LED lighting in addition to as stated and allow for energy
conservation as stated:
Incandescent, florescent, metal halide, light emitting diodes (LED), fiber
optics, or color corrected high-pressure sodium are permitted. The UDO
Administrator shall have the authority to deny use of particular lamps based on
the color spectrum emitted or the lamp brightness. Non color corrected high
pressure sodium lamps are prohibited.
The same light source type must be used for the same or similar types
of lighting on any one site throughout any development.
The light source color temperature for outdoor lighting shall not exceed 3,000
degrees Kelvin.
Motion to approve revised language submitted by Alderman Sharkey, second by
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous vote; motion carried.

appointment. He said to change to three-year terms instead of two-year terms to

Motion to approve to 3-year term for Board of Adjustments by Alderman Allen,

Mr. Lloyd wanted to clarify that a new term/ definition for Transitional
Housing Facility was added and is stated:
“Transitional Housing Facility. A facility configured as a multifamily
development but operated and funded by a nonprofit, charitable, religious, or
governmental organization to provide temporary housing and appropriate
supportive services to families or individuals to facilitate movement to
independent living over a 3 to 24-month period. A transitional housing facility
may provide social services, counseling, and other programs to assist residents
in the transition to permanent housing This classification shall not be
construed to include uses licensed or supervised by any federal, state, or
county health/welfare agency, such as group homes, halfway houses, boarding
homes for children, and convalescent nursing homes.” Mr. Lloyd said that it
would be added as use the table of uses and adding as special use in the OI
district with supplemental standards.
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller recommended to add on page 2-36 (B) PUD and open space
because it is not residential. Shall read as follows: Applications and
proposals for conditional zoning approval shall only be considered within a
nonresidential zoning district. All proposals for a conditional zoning
application must abide by the uses and the dimensional standards required by
the underlying base zoning district for which the proposal is located. No
conditional zoning proposals shall be considered within the Open Space or PUD
zoning district. The Board agreed.

   3.   Recognition of Constitution Week, September 17-23rd . (Proclamation by
Mayor Joseph P. Hatem).
Proclamation
WHEREAS, September 17, 2020 marks the two hundred thirty anniversary of the
drafting of the Constitutional of the United Stated of America by the
Constitutional Convention; and
WHEREAS; It is fitting and proper to accord official recognition to this
magnificent document and its memorable anniversary; and to the patriotic
celebrations which will commemorate the occasion; and
WHEREAS; Public 915 guarantees the issuing of a proclamation each year by the
President of the United States of America designating September 17t h through
September 23rd as Constitution Week,
NOW, THEREFORE, I, Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, by virtue of the authority in me as
Mayor of the City of Southport do hereby proclaim the week of September 17t h
through 23rd as:
CONSTITUTION WEEK
AND, ask our citizens to reaffirm the ideals of the Framers of the constitution
had in 1787 by vigilantly protecting the freedom guaranteed to us through this
guardian of our liberties, remember that lost rights may never be regained.
IN WITNESSS WHEREOF, I hereunto set my hand and caused the Seal of the
City of Southport to be affixed this 10th day of September of the year of our
Lord two thousand twenty.
                  Signed:   Mayor, Joseph P. Hatem
   4.   Special recognition of interim City Manager Chris May by the Board of
Aldermen and presentation of the key to the City by Mayor Joseph P. Hatem.
   5.   Salary Study presentation by Mr. Chris May. Mr. May stated the City
needed to review and compare salaries from other counties and communities to
get a comprehensive idea of what other salaries are relative to Southport. He
stated that in 2015 the City did a survey on job descriptions and a personnel
policy submitted by the NCLM and MAPS Group. Mr. May presented the Board with
the Salary Study and said it was important to keep competitive salaries to
ensure hiring and keeping quality employees. His recommendation was to take the
regional national average starting salary and align it with the pay scale that
shows each of the steps (how the employee progresses) and the grade (the
employees job placement and responsibilities). He explained it will be
difficult during budget time and he suggested that the City simply take what
the employee is making at that time and compare the grade on the Salary Study
and merge it up. He said the City would not be able to fully comprehend what
the Budget will be like in the Spring, but that the Board should highly
consider the goal of achieving comparable salaries and pay increases with
adjacent counties and cities that is predictable and fair.
   Mr. May thanked finance Director Melanie Trexler for her hard work with
assisting him with the Pay Salary Study.
   Alderman Allen clarified that the 2.5% merit increases are based on the
employees performance review. Mr. May said that is correct and the 2.5 % merit
raise would be the minimum pay increase for an employee. Alderman Allen asked
if the City also needed a regional maximum salary and does that mean that once
the employee has reached the maximum, they can no longer achieve a higher pay/
salary. Mr. May stated the employee must stay in service for at least 30 years,
but this study only goes to 20 years for comparison. He said the wage shift
must be coordinated with the experience and the time the person has been in
service. He stated 20 years would become the maximum pay/salary, but he
suggested to continue at least a 2.5 % merit increase for good service.
   Alderman Davis asked Mr. May to state why the salary study was needed. Mr.
May said there were a couple of positions that he felt needed a pay increase
and he felt it best to compare other wages from other counties. Alderman Davis
applauded Mr. May for the study and how this will help employees understand
their position wages and the potential increases they could achieve. Mr. May
also said merit raises are assumed but not guaranteed. The study is available
for the Public on the City’s website.

Manager’s Report:
City Manager Hargrove said that the last day to bring the storm debris to side
of the road will be September 18th and he anticipated having an entire
community cleaned up by the second week in October. He also gave an update on
the Howe Street sidewalk project and said the City is waiting for a traffic
study to be completed. He said once that study is completed the project will
move forward. Manager Hargrove announced that Short Street will reverse
directions for in and out traffic flow that he hopes will help alleviate a lot
of the concerns by September 25th. He said the pedestrian corridor in the Yacht
Basin area should also be completed by the end of September.
Alderman Allen asked if Taylor Field was being used as temporary place to bring
storm debris and if so, will there be another location in the future for storm
debris once the new park is developed.
Manager Hargrove said that Taylor Field was currently being used as a stage for
yard debris and that Construction and other debris will be hauled directly to
Sampson County. He said the contractor is aware that the debris must be
completely removed by mid-October. Manager Hargrove also said that he is
looking into options for other storm debris staging sites like the 400 acres
outside of the City near Sunny Point.
Alderman Spencer asked the City Manager to clarify the process of the storm
debris pick up.
City Manager said the strategy is to pick up leaf and limb debris first which
will be a quicker process versus the CND ( construction and demolition) debris.
He explained the county is not accepting the CND debris and this will have to
be directly hauled to Sampson County which will take a little longer, but he
still anticipated having both jobs completed by mid-October. Alderman Spencer
questioned why the City could not participate in “ free week” by the county.
City Manager Hargrove said that it was for residents only and not for
municipalities.
Alderman Allen asked why Brunswick County is not accepting CND from their own
municipalities. City Manager Hargrove said that he has had many discussions
with the County Manager, and this is the decision that he could discuss with
him in more detail at a later time. Alderman Allen stated that he thought it
was ridiculous and unfair.

   CZ: Conditional Zoning District. A special district where uses and densities
are established through public input for a development that has a high level of
certainty of being constructed and the most commonly expected application will
contain a specified use or uses, permitted by right or conditional use, on
small- and large-scale projects.

items with conditions. Mr. Macleod said that this is most likely for small
nonresidential parcels with minimal constraints but need flexibility.

   K. Outdoor Vending Machine page 3-34
   Where permitted, the following shall apply: Within the CBD zoning district,
only attached automatic bank teller machines which are associated with the
principal financial institution shall be permitted. No other outdoor vending
machines or outdoor independently owned teller machines shall be permitted
within the CBD zoning district.
   Outdoor vending machines shall not obstruct pedestrian pathways, driving
aisles, parking spaces, or any areas necessary for proper vehicular circulation
or loading activities. A clear path of travel at least four feet wide must be
provided around outdoor vending machines.
   Outdoor vending machines shall not be located within four feet of the public
right-of- way or located in such a manner as to encourage or require customers
to stand or park in the right-of-way in order to use the machine.
   The back of an outdoor vending machine may not be located more than 18
inches from an exterior wall of the primary structure on the lot.
   If exposed conduits or pipes are required (e.g., to supply the outdoor
vending machine with power, coolant for refrigeration, or the product being
dispensed), they shall be secured to the building and painted or otherwise
screened to match the building exterior. Exposed conduits, pipes, and utility
connections shall not bridge a span or gap greater than 18 inches.
   All outdoor vending machines shall be maintained in a clean and attractive
condition. Any graffiti on an outdoor vending machine shall be removed within
24 hours. If the outdoor vending machine is removed, the area shall be cleaned
and restored to its previous condition, including the removal of any abandoned
pipes, conduits or other connecting hardware.
   In addition to the above, the following criteria shall apply to outdoor
vending machines:
   Outdoor vending machines shall not block or visually obstruct the sales
counter as viewed from outside the establishment.
Alderman Mosteller clarified that vending machines are not allowed in CBD.
Alderman Allen reiterated that this would help create a more aesthetically
pleasing area in BD.

Proclamation for Emergency Nurses Week October 11-17 was read by Mayor Hatem.
 
[https://export.amlegal.com/media/199f40a54a06f19a9324bf64df539e216304d812/
IMAGES/0-0-0-2228_1439x1074.jpg]
PROCLAMATION
EMERGENCY NURSES WEEK
OCTOBER 11-17, 2020
WHEREAS,    There are approximately 167,0000 emergency nurses in the United
States who have expertise in caring for all emergency patients across the
spectrum of the lifespan; ushering life in at birth and allowing for dignified
death, and
WHEREAS,   Emergency nurses are highly trained to recognize life-threatening
problems and solve them on the spot, playing a vital role in treating patients
in emergency situations, caring for those most in need, and saving lives daily,
and
WHEREAS,   These characteristics provide a broad scope of practice for the
delivery and complex care within a limited timeframe to healthcare consumers of
all ages and backgrounds, and
WHEREAS,   Through research, education, and emergency nursing advocacy , the
Emergency Nurses Association supports and honors the advancement of
professionalism of emergency nurses everywhere, and
WHEREAS,   Let us join together to honor extraordinary acts of service,
compassion, and commitment that emergency nurses provide to patients every day,
and especially to honor the Emergency Nurses at J. Arthur Dosher Memorial
Hospital.
NOW THEREFORE, I , Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor, do herby proclaim October 11-17,
2020 as:
“EMERGENCY NURSES WEEK”
In Testimony Whereof, I hereto Set my hand to be affixed the great seal of The
City of Southport on this 8th day of October in the year of our Lord 2020.
                  Mayor, Joseph P. Hatem
Attest: Clerk, Tanya Shannon
Proclamation for Breast Cancer Awareness Month read by Mayor Hatem. Mayor Hatem
also wanted to remind everyone to get scanned for early detection and to wear
pink to show support for Breast Cancer Awareness.
[https://export.amlegal.com/media/199f40a54a06f19a9324bf64df539e216304d812/
IMAGES/0-0-0-2231_541x957.jpg] Proclamation
Breast Cancer Awareness Month October 2020
Whereas, October is National Breast Cancer Awareness Month, which is an annual
campaign to increase awareness of this disease,
Whereas, National Breast Cancer Awareness Month remains dedicated to increasing
public knowledge about the importance of early detection and treatment,
Whereas, it is estimated by the National Cancer Institute that there will be
276,480 new cases of Breast Cancer in 2020 and 42,120 will die from the
disease,
Whereas, due to improved early detection with advanced technology such as 3-
D Mammography, which is available at Dosher Memorial Hospital, and through
medical research with more innovative therapeutics and surgical intervention
available, there is a 90 percent 5-year survival rate as compared to 80% in
1990,
Whereas, with the utilization of annual screening, early detection, and
advanced therapies, Breast Cancer patients are living longer, we honor and
celebrate their resolve, their resilience and hope for the day when medicine
and its institutions including the National Cancer Institute, major cancer
centers such as Sloan Kettering and MD Anderson, as well as university medical
schools such as UNC School of Medicine at Chapel Hill, find a cure,
Whereas, this October, we recognize Breast Cancer Survivors, those battling the
disease, and also their family members and friends who are also affected by
this disease and are a tireless source of support and comfort,
Whereas, We the Citizens of Southport, the Board of Aldermen, the City Manager,
the City Attorney and all City Employees, will wear pink ribbons, pink
clothing, including pink Chuck Taylor All Stars, to honor and celebrate our
neighbors, family, and friends who are Breast Cancer Survivors, and quietly
mourn and remember those whom we have lost,
Therefore, I, Dr. Joe Pat Hatem, Mayor of the City of Southport, do herby
recognize all of the above and encourage all citizens, government agencies,
private businesses, nonprofit organizations, and all other interested groups to
join in activities that will increase awareness and support all entities that
promote prevention, early detection, treatment, and research concerning Breast
Cancer and do so hereby proclaim October 2020 Breast Cancer Awareness Month.
                     Mayor Joseph P. Hatem

Resolution for Fire Prevention Week read by Chief Drew.
[Image]
Resolution
Proclaiming October 4 - 10, 2020 Fire Prevention Week
WHEREAS, the Southport Fire Department is committed to ensuring the safety and
security of all those living in and visiting our Fire District; and
WHEREAS, fire is a serious public safety concern both locally and nationally,
and kitchens are the locations where people are at the greatest risk of fire;
and
WHEREAS, the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) has documented through
its research a significant increase in kitchen fires, and due to this fact, it
is important that everyone “Cook with Care” and “Watch what you Heat” while
cooking in your home in case of a fire; and
WHEREAS, the Firefighters of the Southport Fire Department are dedicated to
reducing the occurrence of residential and commercial structural fires and fire
related injuries through prevention and protection education; and
WHEREAS, the residents of the Southport Fire District are responsive to public
education measures and are able to take personal steps to increase their safety
from fire; and
WHEREAS, being prepared in the event of a kitchen fire will have a positive
effect on the home fire problem; and
WHEREAS, each home fire that is prevented in the Southport Fire District is an
opportunity to prevent painful injury and costly property damage; and
WHEREAS, the 2020 Fire Prevention Week theme, “Serving up Fire Safety in the
Kitchen” effectively serves to remind us all of the simple actions we can take
to stay safer from fire every day.
THEREFORE, I Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor of the City of Southport do hereby proclaim
October 4-10, 2020 as Fire Prevention Week throughout this City, and I urge all
the citizens of Southport to heed the important safety messages from the
Southport Fire Prevention Team, and the Office of the Fire Chief and to support
the many public safety activities and efforts of the Southport Fire Department.
                     Mayor Joseph P. Hatem
Attest: Clerk, Tanya Shannon

Major Subdivision Preliminary Plat, The Oaks at Highland Park Phase 3.
City Planner, Mr. Lloyd gave an overview of the Plat. He said  Southport
Development Associates had filed for a Preliminary Plat approval for Phase 3 of
the Oaks at Highland Park. He said this project has been in the works for some
time and they are now ready to continue with phase 3. The subdivision is
located off Stuart on Highland Park avenue. The Final Plat for phase 1 was
approved in May of 2015 consisting of 6 lots and the final plat for phase 2
consisting of 6 lots was approved in December of 2018. They are proposing to
extend the existing Raven Glen Dr to Atlantic and are looking to construct the
infrastructure for 19 additional lots on a 7.31-acre property located inside
the City limits. The zoning of the property is R-10 so each lot must be 10,000
sf and must conform with the criteria in Article 25 Major Subdivisions. The
average lot size is 10,897 sf. The setbacks will be 25 front, 8-foot side, and
20 rear. The width must be 75 feet frontage, except on a cul-de sac where there
can be a minimum frontage of 40 feet per lot provided that fifty feet from the
property line has a width of 75 feet. All of the lots meet this requirement.
The open space provision for R-10 Major Subdivisions is 1/57 acre for every
residential lot. Based on that that ratio, 23,690.51 sf of open space must be
provided. 38,417 sf of open space is provided. It’s also important to note that
this subdivision plat is being judged based on what the standards are in the
previous ordinance, not the recently adopted one. He said as far as
infrastructure goes, they are proposing 60 foot right of ways with 5-foot
sidewalks on both sides. The city consulting engineer will need to review and
approve the stormwater, erosion control, and utility plans prior to the start
of any site work in consultation with the Public Works Department. Mr. Lloyd
said the Planning Board reviewed this preliminary plat at its August 13th and
September 17th meeting. The Planning Board found that it meets the standards of
a preliminary plat and recommended that the Board of Aldermen approve it. Mr.
Lloyd continued that staff found that all preliminary plat requirements are
met. If the preliminary plat is approved, the developer and their engineer will
then submit the erosion control, stormwater, and utility plan to the City’s
consulting engineer and to the State.
Alderman Sharkey asked if the development was entirely in the City Limits. Mr.
Lloyd is said that Highland Park Avenue itself is not in the City Limits. He
said there was discussion regarding on incorporation Highland Park Avenue Road
maintenance and who will be responsible for the maintenance.
Alderman Sharkey questioned if the HOA for the development will be responsible
for the streets and the stormwater and recommended waiting for the
determination of who will take responsibility for road repairs and stormwater
regulations.
Motion to approve The Oaks at Highland Park Phase 3 plat by Alderman Allen,
second by Alderman Davis. Aye: Aldermen Lombardi, Spencer, Davis, Allen, and
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Nay: Alderman Sharkey . 5-1 Motion carried.

Pedestrian Corridor in the Yacht Basin by City Manager Hargrove.
Mr. Hargrove gave an overview of the Pedestrian Corridor. He stated that during
the Memorial Day Holiday city staff installed a temporary pedestrian corridor
that extended from Caswell Ave onBay Street to Yacht Basin Drive and W. Moore
St. to increase pedestrian safety. The Board of Aldermen voted to keep the
Pedestrian Corridor; however, he explained that the markings painted on the
road to identify the pedestrian walkway are not always visible because of the
extreme high tides that the area has had recently. Mr. Hargrove said local
businesses are concerned about the one-way traffic flow when the tides are high
because vehicles will turn around and go in the wrong direction to avoid the
high water. He said this becomes a safety issue to pedestrians and other
vehicles. Mr. Hargrove said that the City can continue with the one-way traffic
pattern or pause the project and get more input from the local businesses and
residents.
Alderman Allen stated that he likes the plan. He said what should happen is to
block off Bay St. at Caswell Avenue on the days that we anticipate high tides.
Alderman Lombardi agrees that he doesn’t see changing it at this time either.
Alderman Davis asked who would be responsible for blocking off the streets
during the high tides. City Manager Hargrove stated that it should be public
works who does the barricades since they have better equipped vehicles.
Alderman Sharkey stated this was the first she has heard of people not liking
the traffic flow. The City needs to do better with signage and investigate the
cost of flashing high water signs to divert traffic before getting down to the
end of Moore Street.
Chief Coring wanted to note that the high tides and the flooding in the yacht
basin area have inspired curiosity and some vehicles have chosen to drive thru
and disobey procedures regarding safety established by the City. He stated they
will continue to monitor and discourage the disobedience of procedures.
Motion to use barricades at high tide by Public Services Department by Alderman
Allen and second by Alderman Lombardi. Unanimous vote ; motion carried.
Alderman Spencer suggested using flashing lights instead of using the manpower
and barricades. Chief Coring spoke about his experience with the high tides and
how he thought of the tides in his decision for the cross walk and in his
experience with people will not always be compliant.
City Manager Hargrove spoke on behalf of the Southport City Dock. He asked for
the Board to consider either the approval of the CAMA Major Permit with the
Divisions of Coastal management or repairing the dock or demolishing it. Mr.
Hargrove asked the Board of Aldermen on the direction on how to proceed. If it
is not acceptable to the adjacent property owners, then they will have to get a
variance.
Motion to authorize the City Manager to proceed with 50% repair at this time
while still seeking the Major Permit Approval from CAMA by Alderman Sharkey and
second by Alderman Spencer. Unanimous vote; motion carried.

Ethics Statement by Mayor Hatem: ”If any members know of any conflict of
interest or the appearance of a conflict of interest with respect to matters on
the agenda please so state at this time.”
Mayor Hatem gave a brief history from the State Port Pilot “ Time and Tide”
from the September 2, 2020 edition.
The article dated September 1, 1965 reported “bids for the construction of a
new sewer treatment plan for Southport had been opened.” Mayor Hatem said as
you can see this has been a very long process.
Agenda
Discussion and consideration of sewer agreement with Brunswick County.
Mayor Hatem stated that at the February 13, 2020 Board of Aldermen Meeting
there was a discussion regarding the wastewater treatment service agreement
with Brunswick County. He explained that this is an important issue for our
City. He said it was a complex discussion that involved growth projections,
existing flows, storms and hurricanes. He said there was an intuitive aspect
and a capacity issue. Consulting engineers Hazen and Sawyer estimated usage of
approximately 750,000 gallons per day. Mayor Hatem said that in September 2019
there was much discussion during the time of the election on how to proceed
with the sewer service.
He explained initially the City had decided to contract with Brunswick County
and then decided to build a Wastewater Treatment Plant. He said there has been
many issues with the location of the proposed Sewer Plant. Mayor Hatem
continued to explain that the campaign was based on the “regionalization of
services.” He stated now is the time to make a permanent solution of the City
of Southport’s sewer needs.
City Manager Hargrove provided the Board with a Memorandum from Attorney Mr.
Gray Styers. He said the City has studied the average flows from the past 12-14
months. He said the City has a built-in capacity of .75 million gallons that
the County is going to allocate to the City in the proposed agreement.
City attorney Mike Isenberg, city representative attorney Gray Styers, and City
Manager Gordon Hargrove have been in negotiation with Brunswick County to
complete an agreement.
Mr. Isenberg said that in the agreement the City of Southport has the absolute
right to serve any property in the city limits, including any potential
annexations. Mr. Isenberg said the agreement will also allow Southport to keep
all existing customers even if they are not currently in the city limits. Mr.
Isenberg said that the county will not agree to a sewer service district.
Alderman Allen make a recommendation to hire an independent engineering
consultant to oversee the process to ensure the best interest of the City.
Alderman Lombardi agreed that the City is should hire an engineer to oversee
the process. Mr. Isenberg said the DEQ is overseeing the project in some degree
to protect the investment and cost. Mr. Isenberg said that Mr. Styers also
recommended that the City hire an engineer that would oversee the plans, bids,
and coordination with the county.
Motion to approve entering into the West Brunswick Regional Wastewater System
sewer regional participant agreement with Brunswick County; and
To authorize the City manager and the City Attorneys to negotiate any minor
revisions to the agreement that improve and clarify the rights of the city so
long as the substantive terms of the agreement are not altered; and
To authorize the Mayor to execute said agreement upon advice of the City
Manager and City Attorneys by Alderman Allen, second by Alderman Davis.
Unanimous vote; motion carried
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller provided comments as stated:
“The deliberation about the future of Southport's sewer system has been a long
and protracted conversation with stops and starts.
Relying on experts to guide our decisions regarding a 25,000,000-dollar
project.
First, to go with the County, then build our own, and now resuming the
negotiations with the County.
The citizens of Southport have overwhelmingly voiced their support for the city
to buy sewer capacity from the county instead of building our own treatment
plant.
In January of this year, our newly elected Mayor and the Board reached out to
the County for what we believed would be a simple process of resuming the
previously negotiated contract with the terms the County had previously offered
the City.
Unfortunately, over the months that have followed, we learned that the
Brunswick County Commissioners were not offering the previous terms of the
contract to the citizens of Southport.
The previous contract written by the County had advantages for the County and
advantages for the City.
Among them, Southport gave the County a portion of our service area within our
city limits and for Southport ...Southport was supposed to retain Southport's
Sewer District designation.
It is important for Southport to retain our sewer district...first... economy
of scale.
As our city grows, and we expand our sewer infrastructure, just like with the
County, long term, the maintenance and service becomes more affordable.
Secondly ... the only carrot Southport has to offer development for voluntary
annexation, is sewer and without a designated sewer district ....as development
continues outside of our city limits, but in the ETJ communities that do not
annex into the city will not be contributing city taxes
to maintain our city's resources. For example, future development on Robert
Ruark, which is at the edge of our city limits, in the Extra Territorial
Jurisdiction or ETJ as it's called, with a planned 200 homes will be using our
city's infrastructure, sidewalks, roads, our city's parks and facilities. If
the developers do not annex into the city, those 200 properties will be using
resources but not contributing taxes necessary to help maintain them.
Southport's future zoning decisions and what type of future development happens
within the ETJ is a separate issue from retaining a sewer district designation.
The Southport Sewer district was originally approved by Brunswick County
Commissioners to give Southport the opportunity to grow. It appears that
according to the proposed terms of the contract now being offered by the
county; Southport will be competing with Brunswick County for sewer customers,
even in the Extra Territorial Jurisdiction, the onemile area immediately
outside our city limits that is under the jurisdiction of Southport's Unified
Development Ordinance. It's worth noting that in the past, if Southport thought
the County could better serve a community, Southport allowed the County to
provide service.
Without growing our tax base, the limited number of actual Southport tax payers
within the existing city limits, approximately less than four square miles,
will continue to have the sole responsibility to maintain the city now and into
the future. A future that most certainly will result in higher and higher taxes
for the small base of Southport's tax payers to meet the ever-growing demands
of development outside the city limits utilizing the city's infrastructure and
facilities. Most Southport citizens are surprised to learn that Robert Ruark
and Jabbertown Road are not within Southport’s City limits and do not pay city
taxes.
The Southport waste water project is going to cost Southport tax payers roughly
25 million dollars. It has been a long process...and I certainly appreciate
that the Brunswick County Commissioners are fatigued with the process and our
due diligence. And quite honestly, I can understand their frustration. With
that said, it is in the long term best interest of the citizens of Southport
and ultimately Brunswick County to allow Southport to retain the ETJ as the
designated sewer district.”
I would ask the city manager that before you sign the contract, please reach
out to the County Manager to ask the Brunswick County Commissioners just once
more to please reconsider their refusal and allow the citizens of Southport to
retain the Extra Territorial Jurisdiction, the ETJ as the city's sewer
district.
I support the motion to pursue an agreement with the County to join the
county's regional sewer treatment system for the benefits that come with
economy of scale and also with the knowledge that the City of Southport would
be better served if Brunswick County would allow Southport to have a smaller
designated sewer district that included the ETJ, the area within a mile of our
city limits that is under the jurisdiction of Southport's Unified Development
Ordinance.”
There being no further business Alderman Allen made a motion to adjourn, second
by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
Adjournment at approximately 2:51 P.M.
Mayor, Joseph P. Hatem
               Attest:   Clerk, Tanya Shannon   
***** See exhibit (A) for comments by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller.
Exhibit A
The deliberation about the future of Southport’s sewer system has been a long
and protracted conversation with stops and starts. Relying on experts to guide
our decisions regarding a 25,000,000 dollar project.
First, to go with the County, then build our own, and now resuming the
negotiations with the County.
The citizens of Southport have overwhelmingly voiced their support for the city
to buy sewer capacity from the county instead of building our own treatment
plant.
In January of this year, our newly elected Mayor and the Board reached out to
the County for what we believed would be a simple process of resuming the
previously negotiated contract with the terms the County had previously offered
the City.
Unfortunately, over the months that have followed, we learned that the
Brunswick County Commissioners were not offering the previous terms of the
contract to the citizens of Southport.
The previous contract written by the County had advantages for the County and
advantages for the City. Among them, Southport gave the County a portion of our
service area within our city limits and for Southport…Southport was supposed to
retain Southport’s Sewer District designation.
It is important for Southport to retain our sewer district…first… economy of
scale. As our city grows, and we expand our sewer infrastructure, just like
with the County, long term, the maintenance and service becomes more
affordable.
Secondly… the only carrot Southport has to offer development for voluntary
annexation, is sewer and without a designated sewer district ….as development
continues outside of our city limits, but in the ETJ communities that do not
annex into the city will not be contributing city taxes to maintain our city’s
resources. For example, future development on Robert Ruark which is at the edge
of our city limits, in the Extra Territorial Jurisdiction or ETJ as it’s
called, with a planned 200 homes will be using our city’s infrastructure,
sidewalks, roads, our city’s parks and facilities. If the developers do not
annex into the city, those 200 properties will be using resources but not
contributing taxes necessary to help maintain them. Southport’s future zoning
decisions and what type of future development happens within the ETJ is a
separate issue from retaining a sewer district designation.
The Southport Sewer district was originally approved by Brunswick County
Commissioners to give Southport the opportunity to grow. It appears that
according to the proposed terms of the contract now being offered by the
county, Southport will be competing with Brunswick County for sewer customers,
even in the Extra Territorial Jurisdiction, the one-mile area immediately
outside our city limits that is under the jurisdiction of Southport’s Unified
Development Ordinance. It’s worth noting that in the past, if Southport thought
the County could better serve a community, Southport allowed the County to
provide service.
Without growing our tax base, the limited number of actual Southport tax payers
within the existing city limits, approximately less than four square miles,
will continue to have the sole responsibility to maintain the city now and into
the future. A future that most certainly will result in higher and higher taxes
for the small base of Southport’s tax payers to meet the ever growing demands
of development outside the city limits utilizing the city’s infrastructure and
facilities. Most Southport citizens are surprised to learn that Robert Ruark
and Jabbertown Road are not within Southport’s City limits and do not pay city
taxes.
The Southport waste water project is going to cost Southport tax payers roughly
25 million dollars. It has been a long process…and I certainly appreciate that
the Brunswick County Commissioners are fatigued with the process and our due
diligence. And quite honestly, I can understand their frustration. With that
said, it is in the long term best interest of the citizens of Southport and
ultimately Brunswick County to allow Southport to retain the ETJ as the
designated sewer district.
I would ask the city manager that before you sign the contract, please reach
out to the County Manager to ask the Brunswick County Commissioners just once
more to please reconsider their refusal and allow the citizens of Southport to
retain the Extra Territorial Jurisdiction, the ETJ as the city’s sewer
district.
I support the motion to pursue an agreement with the County to join the
county’s regional sewer treatment system for the benefits that come with
economy of scale and also with the knowledge that the City of Southport would
be better served if Brunswick County would allow Southport to have a smaller
designated sewer district that included the ETJ, the area within a mile of our
city limits that is under the jurisdiction of Southport’s Unified Development
Ordinance.

PROCLAMATION
VETERANS DAY November 11, 2020
WHEREAS, the freedoms we enjoy as Americans have been purchased and maintained
at a high price throughout our history; and
WHEREAS, since the establishment of the original 13 states, Americans have been
willing to fight and die to preserve their individual rights as guaranteed in
the United States Constitution and the Bill of Rights; and
WHEREAS, we owe a great debt to those who have served in defense of this
nation; and
WHEREAS, throughout the generations, their sacrifices have preserved our unique
form of government dedicated to human rights and respect for the individual;
and
WHEREAS, for many, that sacrifice ended in permanent injury or death, yet their
spirit remains in continued preservation of our freedoms and the promise of
liberty established as an example for all oppressed persons of the world; and
WHEREAS, in honor of these dedicated men and women, we pledge continued defense
of our nation so that their sacrifice will stand before the entire world as a
tribute to the spirit and determination of people dedicated to the principals
of freedom and democracy.
NOW, THEREFORE, I, Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor of the City of Southport do hereby
call upon the citizenry of the City of Southport to participate in services and
to observe the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month with
expressions of gratitude to all veterans known to them and the further extend
this gratitude to the families of deceased veterans and to solemnly remember
the sacrifices of all those who fought so valiantly, on the seas, in the air,
and on foreign shores, to preserve our heritage of freedom. Let us re-
consecrate ourselves to the task of promoting an enduring peace so that their
efforts shall not have been in vain.
Dated this 12th day of November 2020.
Mayor, Joseph P. Hatem   Attest: Clerk, Tanya Shannon

of the property is .14 acres (6,121.86 sf) and it is currently vacant and is

interested in annexation in order to have access to City Water & Sewer service.

meeting.

hearing.

1151 N. Caswell Avenue, second by Alderman Spencer. Unanimous vote; motion
carried.
3.   Public Hearing and Consideration for 116 E. 13th Street Zoning Map
Amendment.
Mayor Hatem opened the public hearing and called on the City Planner.
Mr. Lloyd gave the background of the proposed zoning map amendment. He said the
zoning map amendment application is for a .46 acre (20,212.25 sf) tract in the
ETJ owned by Christopher Eckert and Katherine Narron at 116 E. 13th St. Mr.
Lloyd said It is currently zoned BD and the applicant would like to rezone the
property to R-10. He said that the property is noncontiguous to the City Limits
and is currently undergoing consideration for annexation. Mr. Lloyd explained
that the Planning Board reviewed the zoning map amendment application at their
September 17th and October 15th meetings. He said the Planning Board voted to
recommend approval of the proposed zoning map amendment and stated that the
proposed amendment is consistent with the overall goals, objectives, and
policies of the Land Use Plan.
No questions or comments. Mayor Hatem closed the hearing for the public
hearing.
A motion was made by Alderman Allen to adopt the ordinance approving the zoning
map amendment for 116 E. 13th Street, second by Alderman Sharkey. Unanimous
vote; motion carried.

for 116 E. 13th Street.

vacant and is currently zoned business district.

6.   Up Your Arts Agreement Phase 2:
Mr. John Keiffer, on behalf of Chairman Mr. Robert Carroll and the Board of
Directors with Up Your Arts presented a draft memorandum of understanding (MOU)
to re-purpose Southport’s former city hall building on Moore Street into a
community based creative and preforming arts center. He explained the phase one
agreement was entered into with the City of Southport last year to allow UYA to
conduct feasibility studies. Mr. Keiffer said the membership of the board will
be selected from various stakeholders throughout the greater Southport
community , including representatives from civic organizations such as Downtown
Southport, Inc., the Southport-Oak Island Chamber of Commerce, the Brunswick
Arts Council, and the Southport Historical Society.
Mayor Hatem asked how the hazardous materials from the old building will be
disposed of. Mr. Keiffer said that a remediation team will be implemented to
ensure that all hazardous materials are disposed of properly.
Alderman Spencer inquired about all past police records, evidence and other
personal information. Manager Hargrove said that the building was covered in
toxic mold and he was unsure if there was anything left inside that was
salvageable.
Mr. Hargrove asked the Board if they were ready to vote on continuing the
agreement with Up Your Arts for repurposing the Old City Hall.
A motion was made by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller to have the City attorney review
the memorandum of agreement and report to the Board before a decision was made,
second by Alderman Lombardi. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
7.   Discussion on the advantages/disadvantages of the Short Street reversal.
City Manager Mr. Hargrove stated that the reversal of Short Street’s one way
traffic pattern has improved the safety for pedestrians, bicyclists and other
non-motorist. However, he said that some people are confused and do not realize
that the traffic flow has been reversed.
Alderman Sharkey asked if there were any complaints, accidents or factual data
that has negatively impacted the reversed flow.
Alderman Allen said that pedestrian safety has improved with the reversal of
Short Street, but more awareness needs to be brought to motorists of the
change. He is in favor of the permanent change.
Police Chief Todd Coring stated that he feels the safety aspect has been met
but complaints with the confusion on the change have been noted. He said more
public awareness needs to be brought to the direction change, such as flashing
warning signs, patrol officers, and other signage.
Alderman Sharkey said there is a positive accomplishment with the traffic
change other than the fact that some people are not aware of the change. Mayor
Pro Tem Mosteller thanked Staff and agreed with Alderman Sharkey. She supports
the permanent change.
A motion was made by Alderman Allen to permanently keep Short Street in the
reversed direction, second by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous vote; motion
carried.
8.   Police Bike Patrol Feedback.
Police Chief Mr. Todd Coring gave an update on the bike patrol. He said that
the police department has received a lot of positive feedback from the
community and they will continue to utilize this method of patrol.
9.   Budget Summary.
Mr. Scott Rogers, Finance Specialist gave an update on the budget. He stated
that the City overall is in good shape. He said the general fund revenues are
currently at roughly 22% and 25 % total for the quarterly update.

provide service.
Without growing our tax base, the limited number of actual Southport tax payers
within the existing city limits, approximately less than four square miles,
will continue to have the sole responsibility to maintain the city now and into
the future. A future that most certainly will result in higher and higher taxes
for the small base of Southport’s tax payers to meet the ever growing demands
of development outside the city limits utilizing the city’s infrastructure and
facilities. Most Southport citizens are surprised to learn that Robert Ruark
and Jabbertown Road are not within Southport’s City limits and do not pay city
taxes.
The Southport waste water project is going to cost Southport tax payers roughly
25 million dollars. It has been a long process, and I certainly appreciate that
the Brunswick County Commissioners are fatigued with the process and our due
diligence. And quite honestly, I can understand their frustration. With that
said, it is in the long term best interest of the citizens of Southport and
ultimately Brunswick County to allow Southport to retain the ETJ as the
designated sewer district. I supported the motion to pursue an agreement with
the County to join the county’s regional sewer treatment system for the
benefits that come with economy of scale and also with the knowledge that the
City of Southport would be better served if Brunswick County would allow
Southport to have a smaller designated sewer district that included the ETJ,
the area within a mile of our city limits that is under the jurisdiction of
Southport’s Unified Development Ordinance. “
There being no further business, questions or concerns, motion to adjourn by
Alderman Lombardi, second by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous vote; motion
carried.
Adjournment at approximately 8:48 P.M.
Mayor, Joseph P. Hatem
Attest; Clerk, Tanya Shannon

closed the public hearing.

   Mr. MacLeod, Senior Planner with the Cape Fear Council of Governments replied that because the Marina is in the Light Industrial Zoning District in its entirety, it would not necessarily preclude the City from having Open
Space in this area. He said that if it was the pleasure of the Board for that

   Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller asked if this would inhibit the Marina from use of
the property in the
Business District. Mr. MacLeod said it would not. Mr. Macleod reiterated that conflict comes in when a major Cama Permit application is submitted. He said that if the area is designated in the Open Space district the Coastal Division Management would deny the permit.
   Alderman Davis asked for clarification of the specific area in discussion.
Alderman Sharkey stated the vision for this area located near the creek off W.

Southport Marina. Alderman Sharkey explained that although the Marina had
offered to put in up to $50,000.00 to help with the construction, the City must
provide the rest to complete the plans. She said if the area remains as
open space, and never becomes an area for the public to use then it would be
inhibiting the Marina’s use of the property.
   Mayor Hatem said the City Attorney Mr. Mike Isenberg said that a way to
reconcile the situation could be to adopt a resolution approving the City of
Southport’s Land Use Plan update with an amendment that tax parcel id
# 237LF021 be designated as light commercial instead of open space. Mayor Hatem

   Alderman Spencer said that he would like to prevent future problems with the
overlay on the
easement area. He would like to preserve the City’s right on that location.

Alderman Sharkey said if the plan is implemented than the City could rezone

   4)   Rate Committee recommendation to change the billing policy for solar customers:
      Alderman Sharkey gave an overview of the proposed policy revision. In
2014 the Board of Aldermen approved a solar policy. She said currently the City
has only a Buy All Sale All Metering policy
for residential solar customers. Customers have
asked for another option called Net Metering.
      The City’s Electrical Superintendent, Mr. Ellie Pittenger stated: The
adoption should have the term 'Rooftop' in the verbiage. The intent of the
adoption does not include 'solar farming'. Self-contained solar lighting would
not be considered 'solar farming'. BEMC is capable and ready to bill our solar
customers at the rates the City dictates, including any base rate increase (+$5
is typical for residential).
      The Net Metered buyback rate should reflect any discounted retail rate
the solar customer may be on through participation in Load Management.
Applications and related documentation should be similar to BEMC's solar net
metering program, such as (but not limited to): A) 'Proof of Insurance'
document from the customer should be required and updated annually. This is
typically updated at the end of each
Fiscal Year during the June 'True Up' with the solar customer, which is part of
the billing process.
      Alderman Sharkey made a motion on behalf of the Rate Committee to adopt
the policy to have net metering for rooftop solar customers, this includes the
base rate to BEMC, second by Mayor Pro
Tem Mosteller. Unanimous vote; motion carried.

D) Public Comment:
   1.   Mr. Jim Powell, City of Southport Bald Head Island Transportation
Authority (BHITA) Board Appointee gave an update on the progress of the
Authority. He said the Authority was created by the Legislature and went into
effect in 2017. He said that after three years from its inception, the Bald
Head Island Transportation Authority has taken its largest step yet, achieving
the goal it was created to accomplish, which is to transition the island’s
ferry system from a private to public system.
   He said the authority’s 11-member board settled on a $47 million price that
is needed to acquire the ferry system.
   Mr. Powell said that after the post-closing transition period, the public
authority will own and operate a wide network of assets, including on the
mainland and on Bald Head Island.
   He said there will not be any cost to the City for the operation. However,
he said the City’s Planning Board will have to review the zoning requirements
for the 56 acres formerly known as Deep Point Marina.
   Alderman Davis asked Mr. Powell if he had specifics on what would be coming
to the City’s Planning Board. He said that he does not know the exact
specifications.
   Alderman Spencer wanted clarification that the 47 million dollars would
include the entire package for the Authority including the services on Bald
Head Island. Mr. Powell confirmed that the Authority would own everything
needed to operate in Southport and Bald Head Island.
   Alderman Allen asked if there was any financial responsibility from the
City. Mr. Powell said there is no fees, costs, or responsibility to the City.
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller stated that the Transportation Authority will be paying
a franchise fee to replace the lost property tax revenue.
   2.   Mr. Matt Thorne, the owner of the Saucy Southerner, located at 503 N
Howe Street, did not agree with the revised sign ordinance. He said that he
would like the Board to reconsider the Ordinance for signs, and that a
committee be established that included staff and local businesses to come to
agreement that would help promote and save businesses. He said signs are vital
to promote business and are unique to each business.

Agenda:
1.   Mayor Hatem opened the Public Hearing for the Zoning Map Amendment for the
Parking Overlay District. (RZ 20-1112-01)
   City Planner Mr. Thomas Lloyd gave an overview of the proposed amendment. He
said that City staff is requesting that the Board of Aldermen take the
following action: Approve a zoning map amendment that would remove the Parking
Overlay District from the City of Southport’s Official Zoning Map. Mr. Lloyd
explained that as part of the City’s recent update and rewrite of the Unified
Development Ordinance (UDO), parking regulations and provisions were revised
for the Central Business (CBD) and Business District (BD) zoning designations.
Within the CBD, there are no parking requirements and within the BD zoning
district, significantly reduced standards have been provided. As a result of
this change, the current Parking Overlay District is no longer necessary. He
said that removing the Parking Overlay District from the zoning map is the
first step. He said as part of the proposal, only the overlay district is
proposed
for deletion.
   There were no questions or comments.
   Mayor Hatem closed the Public Hearing.
A motion was made by Alderman Allen to approve the Consistency Statement and to
adopt the Ordinance removing the Parking Overlay District, second by Alderman
Spencer.
Unanimous vote; motion carried.
2.   Mayor Hatem opened the Public Hearing for the Zoning Map Amendment, BD to
MF, at 1208 N. Caswell Ave, submitted by David & Brenda Baker, Parcel ID
221MAO00104 (RZ 20-1020-01)
   City Planner, Mr. Lloyd, said the applicants are requesting a zoning map
amendment that is for a .141 acre (6,138.5 sf) tract in the ETJ owned by David
& Brenda Baker at 1208 N Caswell St. It is currently zoned BD and the applicant
would like to rezone the property to MF. He said the property is concurrently
going through the annexation process.
   Mr. David Baker, the property owner, stated that the parcel is very small
and there are not many things that he can do with the property zoned BD to MF.
He said he would like direction on how to proceed without adjacent properties
having to also rezone. He said there are other parcels in the vicinity that
have the same situation.
   Alderman Davis asked if he was open to the suggestion made by the Planning
Board. Mr. Baker said that he was open to any suggestion. Mr. Lloyd said that
there are about two blocks in the area that have small lots and he is
recommends reaching to reach out to the owners of the small lots to see if they
would be interested in rezoning.
   City Attorney Mr. Mike Isenberg said that Mr. Lloyd is trying to help the
applicants by encouraging other property owners to rezone to R-10 rather than
MF which would be more beneficial.
   Alderman Davis asked if the applicants would have to get surveys and
applications. Mr. Lloyd replied that the City would take the initiative to
create a solution that would first be reviewed by the Planning Board.
   Alderman Allen asked if the property was rezoned to R-10 would this create
“spot zoning”. Mr. Isenberg said not if other property owners in this area
would also rezone.
   Mr. Baker asked approximately how long this process would take. Mayor Hatem
said that the Planning Board would review the applications first and make a
recommendation before the final decision was approved by the Board of Aldermen.
Mayor Hatem said this may take a few months.
   No further questions or comments.
   Mayor Hatem closed the Public Hearing.
A motion was made by Alderman Allen to adopt the Consistency Statement prepared
by Staff and the Resolution denying the zoning map amendment on the application
submitted by David & Brenda Baker, second by Alderman Spencer. Unanimous vote;
motion carried.

RESOLUTION EXTENDING PROVISIONS OF FAMILIES FIRST CORONAVIRUS RESPONSE ACT
   THAT WHEREAS, pursuant to the requirements of the Families First Coronavirus
Response Act, the City of Southport previously adopted a policy granting
employees 80 hours of paid sick leave for Covid-19 related reasons (emergency
paid sick leave or EPSL) and up to 12 weeks of paid FMLA leave (Emergency
Family and Medical Leave Act or EFMLA) to care for a child whose place of care
or school is closed for Covid-19 related issues; and
   WHEREAS, the requirements of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act
have now expired; and
   WHEREAS, the City is allowed to choose to continue to be bound by the
Families First Coronavirus Response Act leave requirements through March 31,
2021; and
   WHEREAS, the City has determined that it is in the best interests of the
City that it continue to be bound by the requirements of the Families First
Coronavirus Response Act through March 31, 2021, as authorized by The
Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021;
   NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of
Southport that:
   (1)   EPSL is hereby extended through March 31, 2021, for employees who have
not yet exhausted their 80 hours of emergency paid sick leave; and
   (2)   EFMLA is hereby extended through March 31, 2021, for those employees
who have not yet exhausted their 12 weeks of EFMLA (or their 12 weeks of EFMLA
and regular FMLA combined).
This the 14th day of January 2021.
City of Southport

Mayor Hatem welcomed everyone to the Board of Aldermen 2021 Retreat/Workshop.
He quoted Mark Twain: “The secret of getting ahead is getting started.” He
explained that the workshop will be analytical and focused on the goals the
city would like to accomplish.
 
Agenda
 
   Finance Director, Melanie Trexler gave an introduction on the requirements
of establishing a balanced budget that begins on July 1, 2021. Planning a
balanced budget allows the City to avoid excessive spending and allows the body
to focus funds on areas and services that require them the most. The process
requires each department to provide a list of reasonable needs and incorporate
that into a balanced budget. She went over the revenue manual and the audit
report that is available at the Clerk’s office.
 
Workshop Facilitated by City Manager Hargrove:
 
Manager Hargrove provided an overview of the workshop and thanked everyone for
attending. He gave a presentation on the following topics:
 
 City of Southport's Core values
 
Preserve the city's historic character.
Protect the city's shoreline vista.
Continue to support a vibrant Central Business District.
Preserve the city's residential areas.
Protect the city's Areas of Environmental Concern consistent with 15ANCAC 7H.
 
2019/2020 Highlights in Review.
 
Continued Community response to Covid – 19.
Formalized a sewer agreement with Brunswick County.
Completed the update for the Unified Development Ordinance.
Completed the CAMA land use plan (waiting on DCM approval).
Started the Howe St . sewer line replacement project.
Received CAMA exemption to repair city dock Started development of the Taylor
Field park project.
Recovery from Hurricane Isaias.
Continued work on the Weather Tower replacement.
 
Thinking Strategically
 
Focus on prioritizing the most pressing needs the community faces that be
FUNDED and COMPLETED within a strategic time frame from t to 5 years.
Strategic thinking is simply an intentional and rational thought process that
focuses on the analysis of critical factors and variables that will influence
the long-term success of a municipality, a team, or an individual.
 
This types of thinking must account for economic realities, market forces, and
available resources.
Strategic planning is an ongoing process that continuously reappropriates
resources to initiatives that must be prioritized.
 
Long Term Planning
 
Long term planning is about setting the process by which the strategic plan
will be achieved.
Long term planning is often a timeframe that exceed 5 years and normally
depends on the strategic objective it is trying to accomplish.
Long term planning is about aligning city project to fit in with city strategic
goal and coordinating departments so that everyone is in sync and ready to
accomplish city goals.
 
Capital Projects
 
Capital project is a project that helps maintain or improve a city asset, often
called infrastructure.
It can be new construction, expansion, renovation, or replacement project for
an existing facility or infrastructure.
Usually, the project must have a total cost of $5,000.00.
 
Authorized Capital Financing Mechanisms.
Current Revenues:
General Fund: property taxes, sales and use tax.
Enterprise funds: user fees, other specialty charges.
 
Authorized Capital Financing Mechanisms
 
Savings
Fund balance
Capital Reserve Fund
 
A municipalities governing board may establish a capital reserve fund and
periodically appropriate money to it . A local government may establish and
maintain a capital reserve fund for any purpose for which the unit may issue
bonds.
To establish a capital reserve fund, a units governing board must adopt an
ordinance or resolution.
 
Authorized Capital Financing Mechanisms in North Carolina
 
   Special levies
 
Targeted revenue generation mechanisms, (user charges), that are paid only by
the citizens or property owners who most directly benefit from the specific
services or projects.
 
Special assessment is a charge levied against a property to pay for public
improvements that benefit the property.
 
Authorized Capital Financing Mechanisms in North Carolina
 
   Special Taxing districts
 
State Constitution requires that property tax rates be uniform throughout the
jurisdiction with the EXCEPTION that the Constitution authorizes the General
Assembly to allow a local government to carve out one or more areas within the
unit as service districts.
Examples of a service district: beach erosion and flood and hurricane
protection, downtown revitalization projects, urban area revitalization
projects, transit oriented development projects, drainage projects, off-street
parking facilities, sewage collection and disposal, watershed improvements,
drainage, and water resources development.
A service district is simply a geographic designation---a defined area in which
the government levies an extra property tax and provides extra services or
undertakes capital projects that more directly benefit the properties in the
district.
 
Types of Bonds
 
General Obligation
Revenue
Special Obligation
Project Development financing bonds
Installment Financing

Project Ordinance:
 
A governing board may adopt a project ordinance at any regular or special
meeting by a simple majority of board members if a quorum is present.
It can be done any time of the year.
The ordinance must (1) clearly identify the project and authorize its
undertaking, (2) identify the revenues that will finance the project and , (3)
make the appropriates necessary to complete the project.
 
Capital Improvements Fund:
 
Allow for better short and long term planning.
Individual departmental budgets would not be distorted in any given year by
capital projects assigned to them.
Allows for better identification and public visibility projects.
Unspent funds can be rolled over from one year to the next.
Allow for better prioritization and scheduling of projects among limited
resources.
Revenues and appropriations for designated capital projects would be placed in
this CIP fund, which could be used for improvements which repair or increase
the long-term capital asset base of the City.
 
Manager Hargrove announced that the next Workshop/Retreat will be on February
15, 2021 at the Community Building at 9:00 AM.
 
Comments:
Mayor Hatem and the Board thanked Mr. Hargrove for the informative
presentation.
 
Adjourn:
 
There being no further business Alderman Lombardi made a motion to adjourn, and
second by Alderman Allen. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
Adjournment at approximately 11:51 A.M.

Agenda
1. Public Hearing: The Parking Overlay Zoning Text Amendment.
   Mayor Hatem opened the Public Hearing.
   Developmental Services Director, Mr. Thomas Lloyd, gave an overview of the
proposed text amendment. He said as part of the City’s recent update and
rewrite of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), that parking regulations
and provisions were revised for the Central Business (CBD) and Business
District (BD) zoning designations. He said that within the CBD there are no
parking requirements and within the BD zoning district, significantly reduced
standards have been provided. Mr. Lloyd said that because of this change the
current Parking Overlay District is no longer necessary. He said at the
Aldermen’s regular meeting in January the Board of Aldermen voted to remove the
parking overlay district from the zoning map. Mr. Lloyd said at this meeting in
February, the Board should remove the language in the UDO. He explained as part
of removing the overlay district from the official zoning map, the text
referencing the district should be stricken. Article 3 of the City’s recently
adopted UDO includes a section on overlay districts. He said given the
potential for future overlay districts, it is recommended that this section
remain in the UDO, but the language regarding the parking overlay district be
removed.
   There were no questions or comments.
   Mayor Hatem closed the Public Hearing.
A motion was made by Alderman Davis to adopt the proposed Consistency Statement
as recommended by the Planning Board and to approve the ordinance removing the
Parking Overlay District text from the Unified Development Ordinance, second by
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous vote; motion carried.
2. Resolution to Adopt the Southeastern NC Regional Hazard Mitigation Plan.
   Mr. Lloyd gave an overview of The Southeastern NC Hazard Mitigation Plan. He
explained that it is a collaboration between the Municipal and County
governments of Brunswick, New Hanover, Onslow, and Pender counties. He said
that the purpose of the plan is to develop, adopt, and update as needed a local
hazard mitigation plan. Mr. Lloyd said the hazard mitigation plan establishes
the broad community vision and guiding principles for reducing hazard risk, and
further proposes specific mitigation actions to eliminate or reduce identified
vulnerabilities. He said the purpose of the 2021 Southeastern NC Regional
Hazard Mitigation Plan update is to: 1) Completely update the existing
Southeastern NC Regional Hazard Mitigation Plan to demonstrate progress and
reflect current conditions. He said the existing plan will need to be updated
since it was completed in 2015. 2) Integrate Onslow County and all its
municipalities into the Southeastern NC Regional Hazard Mitigation Plan. 3)
Increase public awareness and education. 4) Maintain grant eligibility for FEMA
Public Assistance in participating jurisdictions. 5) Update the plan in
accordance with Community Rating System (CRS) requirements. 6) Maintain
compliance with state and federal legislative requirements for local hazard
mitigation plans. Mr. Lloyd stated the plan has been reviewed and approved by
the NC Emergency Management and is currently being reviewed by FEMA. He said
that the State and FEMA require the participating jurisdictions to adopt the
plan to receive public assistance funding for disasters.
A motion was made to adopt the Resolution for the Southeastern N.C. Regional
Hazard Mitigation Plan by Alderman Spencer, and second by Alderman Allen.
Unanimous vote; motion carried.
