Agenda
Brunswick County Comprehensive Transportation Plan.
Development Services Director, Thomas Lloyd, gave an overview of the 20-30-year
multi-modal plan that will assist with identifying deficiencies in the County’s
transportation systems. The proposed plan will also help in setting short and
long-term priorities. He said that most people in the area are aware of the
growth, but Brunswick County is experiencing a growth rate of 2.93%. The County
and municipal staff involved with the project are asking for community input by
completing an online survey. The link to the survey will be shared on all of
Southport’s social media websites and has already been distributed to the Board
of Aldermen. Mr. Lloyd suspects that it will be completed within the next year.
Annexation Resolution.
Mr. Thomas Lloyd explained that the City has received a petition for annexation
by the property owner, Jere McMillan for 1136 Delaware Street. The property is
located off 11th Street and is requesting annexation to have access to City
water and sewer. Alderman Lowe Davis asked if there were water and sewer
connections close to the property, or if would be a great expense to connect
utilities to that address. Mr. Lloyd stated that there should be connections
close by, but it would be verified for the next meeting. The first step in the
annexation process is for the Board to direct the Clerk to investigate the
petition and verify the sufficiency of the request. Then the public hearing
could be scheduled. After a motion made by Alderman Sharkey, and seconded by
Alderman Spencer, the Board approved the Resolution directing the clerk to
investigate the petition for the voluntary non-contiguous annexation for 1136
Delaware Street, as presented. All ayes. Motion carried.
NCDEQ Groundwater Standards.
Alderman Lora Sharkey addressed the Board of Aldermen regarding groundwater
standards. Southport has a history of promoting environmental protection.
Brunswick County is constructing a reverse osmosis system to deal with
contamination in the water supply and the cost will be borne by the residents.
NCDEQ will be hosting a public hearing and Alderman Sharkey would like the
Board to endorse a statement that will be sent for consideration during the
hearing. PFAS are common contaminants in groundwater that have been linked to
cancer and thyroid issues. NCDEQ has established an interim standard allowed
for the time being until further research can be done to establish the most
accurate limits of PFAS that are allowed. The City of Southport supports a new
groundwater standard that is at least as strong as the Chemours Consent Order,
which is no more than 10ppt for a single PFA and no more than 70 ppt for the
sum of all PFAS. Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller stated that in the CAMA Land Use Plan,
water quality is mentioned 124 times. Alderman Sharkey made a motion for Board
to approve the statement and that the Clerk will submit it to NCDEQ before the
March 16th deadline, so that it can be included in the public hearing. Alderman
Lowe Davis seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
Utility Delinquent Fees.
Finance Director, Melanie Trexler addressed the Board regarding charging
customers delinquent fees for accounts that are not paid by the 25th of each
month. The City has been disconnecting customers already, but as a courtesy, no
delinquent fees of $35.00 have been applied. Currently, all accounts but one,
have fulfilled their payment agreements that was allowed during Executive Order
124. Ms. Trexler feels that if delinquent fees are not charged, some customers
would start to accumulate a hefty balance again. Alderman Sharkey agreed that
the timing is right to start charging the fee again. After a motion made by
Alderman Sharkey and seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller, the Board agreed to
resume charging utility customers the $35.00 delinquent fee for payments made

BUSINESS
1.   Change order for Howe Street Sewer Project
a. Resolution Authorizing the Contract with ECS Southeast. Tom Stanley
addressed the Board with regards to the compaction contract that is needed with
a company who can complete the backfilling, paving, inspection services, lifts,
ten hours a day and travel for the next eighteen weeks. All of these
requirements just recently came to light when NCDOT gave us a stop work order
because we did not have the permits that were required. Alderman Lowe Davis
asked how the City just became aware or the requirement. Tom Stanley stated
that the City began the planning for this project back in 2018-2019 with the
engineer and other staff members. At that time, we were told by an NCDOT
engineer that the work was covered as repairs. But recently, they discovered
that it wasn’t the case. Alderman Davis asked if the work that was done, has to
be pulled out and done again. Mr. Stanley said that he hoped not, but NCDOT
hasn’t given their final determination. Alderman Allen asked that the City do
whatever we can do push back on NCDOT so that we do not have to re-do all that
has been completed so far. It is fine to put back what was there, but to do
more is absurd. Alderman Davis asked why this company was going to be used? Tom
Stanley said that the company comes very highly recommended, and they seem to
have a good relationship with NCDOT. Mayor Hatem read through a sample motion.
After a motion was made by Aldermen John Allen and seconded by Alderman
Lombardi, the Board approved the Resolution Authorizing the Contract with ECS
Southeast, LLP, as presented and authorizing the City Manager and Mayor to
execute the contract and all related documents, as presented. All ayes. Motion
carried.
 
CITY OF SOUTHPORT BOARD OF ALDERMAN

b. Resolution Authorizing the Change Order for the Howe Street sewer project.
The Mayor explained that the cost of asphalt for the Howe Street project is
changing from $65.00 per square yard, up to $125 per square yard. This is
because of a change in what NCDOT is requiring. Alderman Allen asked if the
City could put gravel back down and use the road that way until we get the
issues with NCDOT hashed out. Tom Stanley said that it was possible, but it
might cause some unnecessary work at an expense. There was some discussion
about who would be held responsible for the drastic change in cost and design.
Alderman Mark Spencer asked whether the inspector from ECS Southeast would be
present on the job site soon and work could commence? Alderman John Allen
reiterated that he wants the City to exhaust every avenue to change NCDOT’s
edict for paving. Mayor Hatem read a sample motion. After a motion made by
Alderman John Allen and seconded by Alderman Tom Lombardi, the Board approved
the Resolution in Support of the change order increasing the cost of asphalt
paving to $ 862,500.00and authorizing the City Manager and/or Mayor to execute
any necessary contracts and required documents, as presented.
 
CITY OF SOUTHPORT BOARD OF ALDERMAN
RESOLUTION AUTHORIZING CHANGE ORDER
FOR THE HOWE STREET SEWER PROJECT
 
WHEREAS, the City of Southport has entered into a contract with 274
Construction Group for a project known    as the Howe Street Sewer Replacement
Project; and
WHEREAS, regarding the asphalt replacement on Howe Street, the original
contract specifications in said contract required 2 inches of asphalt and 16
inches of ABC stone; and
WHEREAS, the North Carolina Department of Transportation is now requiring 3
inches of fine heavy- duty    paving, 3 inches of intermediate paving and 4
inches of rough black base; and
WHEREAS, said NCDOT requirements will dictate that the cost of the asphalt
pavement repair will increase from $ 65.00 per square yard to $ 125.00 per
square yard; and
WHEREAS, this change will result in an increase for the cost of asphalt
replacement under said contract from $ 448,500.00 to $ 862,500.00.
 
NOW, THEREFORE, THE BOARD OF ALDERMEN OF THE CITY OF SOUTHPORT RESOLVES
THAT the City Manager and/or Mayor are each hereby authorized and directed to
execute any necessary change orders to the above-referenced contract in order
to comply with the NCDOT requirement regarding the asphalt replacement.

statement.
"As Southport grows, the stewardship of our trees continues to be critical to
our community's quality of life and our economic success. With inevitable
growth come the pressures of change.
We all sit in the shade of trees we did not plant. And as members of the
community, it's our turn to help maintain the health and future of Southport's
Urban Maritime Forest.
While Arbor Day is the official celebration of our trees, we celebrate our
trees every day in Southport. With gratitude, as the former liaison to the
Forestry Committee, I would like to take a moment to recognize all the members

I want to make sure everyone knows that Clay first joined the Forestry
Committee in 2004. Clay continued to serve on the Forestry Committee for 16
years. Clay Fairley advocated for our Live Oaks and helped maintain the quality
of life we are afforded by the trees surrounding us. Clay Fairley, because of
you and your commitment and dedication and advocacy for Southport's trees, our
community is a better place to live. That is large to say, and it is true.
Thank you.
The second individual joined the Forestry Committee in 2015 and agreed to co-

   2.   Mayor Hatem said that the following proclamation was very dear to him
because it was for National Public Health Week. The proclamation mentioned the
local history of Southport and the Quarantine Station that was in operations
between 1895-1937. In addition, Dr. J. Arthur Dosher, Acting Assistant Surgeon
in the U.S. Public Health Service, was the Brunswick Hospital founder. The
proclamation recognized that there are inequities with respect to minorities
and economic status, and public health. Mayor Hatem reiterated that Southport
has stayed strong during the pandemic and will continue to hold the course to
come out on the other side.
CITY OF SOUTHPORT
PROCLAMATION FOR NATIONAL PUBLIC HEALTH WEEK
WHEREAS, the week of April 5-11, 2021, is National Public Health Week, and the
theme is "Building Bridges to Better Health"; and
WHEREAS, since 1995, the American Public Health Association, through its
sponsorship of National Public Health Week, has educated the public,
policymakers, and public health professionals about issues important to
improving public health; and
WHEREAS, there is a significant difference in health status, such as obesity,
poor mental health and drug use, among people living in rural areas compared
with people living in urban areas, and this variance increases because rural
residents are often more likely to face social determinants that negatively
impact health, such as poverty, transportation barriers, and lack of economic
opportunity; and
WHEREAS, public health professionals help communities prevent, prepare for,
withstand and recover from the impact of a full range of health threats,
including disease outbreaks such as the COVID-19 pandemic, measles, natural
disasters, and disasters caused by human activity; and
WHEREAS, public health action, together with scientific and technological
advances, has played a major role in reducing and, in some cases, eliminating
the spread of infectious disease, and in establishing today's disease
surveillance and control systems; and
WHEREAS, the COVID-19 pandemic has illuminated and exacerbated inequities with
respect to minority and economic status and that public health and government
leaders have declared these barriers to health care a public health crisis; and
WHEREAS, Southport has held a historic place in public health-the U.S.
Quarantine Station-active from 1895 to 1937, located on the Cape Fear River,
east of the City, where ships and their crews were inspected, decontaminated,
those sick, placed in the Quarantine Hospital, all to prevent the spread of
contagious diseases; and
WHEREAS, in 1919, Dr. J. Arthur Dosher, Southport native and founder of
Brunswick County Hospital, now Dosher Memorial Hospital, was appointed Acting
Assistant Surgeon in the U.S. Public Health Service and served as the
Quarantine Officer at the Southport Quarantine Station until 1937;
NOW, THEREFORE, I, Joseph P. Hatem, MD, M.P.H., Mayor of the City of Southport,
on behalf of the Board of Aldermen do hereby recognize April 5-11th, 2021, as
National Public Health Week.
Dutifully executed this date, April 8, 2021.
                      ___________________________________
                     Joseph P. Hatem, MD, MPH
                     Mayor, City of Southport, NC

   2.   Melanie Trexler addressed the Board to explain that the Families First
Coronavirus Response Act is scheduled to expire, but the state is offering tax
credits to those organizations who extend providing benefits to their
employees. The state recommends extending the benefits through September. The
employee benefits would be a fresh (80) hours of paid leave if needed because
of the Coronavirus pandemic. As Ms. Trexler explained, most City employees have
either already had Covid-19 or a complete vaccination for the virus. Therefore,
it appears that the cost of participation in the extension would be minimal.
After a motion made by Alderman John Allen and seconded by both Alderman
Sharkey and Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller, the Board approved the extension of the
Families First Coronavirus Response Act, as presented. 
CITY OF SOUTHPORT BOARD OF ALDERMEN
RESOLUTION EXTENDING PROVISIONS OF FAMILIES FIRST CORONAVIRUS RESPONSE ACT
   THAT WHEREAS, pursuant to the requirements of the Families First Coronavirus
Response Act, the City of Southport previously adopted a policy granting
employees 80 hours of paid sick leave for Covid-19 related reasons (emergency
paid sick leave or E.P.S.L.) and up to 12 weeks of paid FMLA leave (Emergency
Family and Medical Leave Act or E.F.M.L.A.) to care for a child whose place of
care or school is closed for Covid-19 related issues; and
   WHEREAS, the requirements of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act
expired on December 31, 2020; and
   WHEREAS, the City elected to continue to be bound by the Families First
Coronavirus Response Act leave requirements through March 31, 2021, as

   3.   Alderman Tom Lombardi introduced the next speaker, Brayton Willis. Mr.
Willis is a lifetime member of the N.A.A.C.P. and has been involved with many
organizations, including the Army Corp of Engineers. Mr. Willis thanked the
Board for allowing him to speak at their Board meeting. He asked the audience
and Board to imagine being taken from your home and transported by boat while
in chains to a new land where no one speaks your native language. Through the
enslavement and blending of many African peoples, the Gullah Geechee people
developed. They created a new language and a food chain where groups of Gullah
Geechee people could share and distribute food to assist each other. There are
already some existing trails to recognize and celebrate the Gullah Geechee
people, but the focus is now on the coast of N.C., from Navassa to Southport.
The proposed trail would be a shared-use path for pedestrians and cyclists.
There are six overarching goals: educational outreach, economic development,
documentation, and preservation, promoting healthy living, protecting the
environment, and connecting this trail to the 3,000-mile East Coast Greenway.
Alderman Sharkey asked Mr. Willis what the next steps were or what was he
asking the Board of Aldermen for? Mr. Willis stated that he would love for the
Board to adopt a resolution in support of the trail and prepare a letter of
support for the project. Alderman Lowe Davis asked if he had any samples that
he could share with the City and Mr. Willis agreed to send some examples to the
Clerk. All of the Board members agreed to bring a Resolution to the next
meeting in May.

RESOLUTION OF THE CITY OF SOUTHPORT IN SUPPORT OF THE BALD HEAD ISLAND
TRANSPORTATION AUTHORITY
   WHEREAS, on July 18, 2017, the Governor of the State of North Carolina
signed the Ferry Transportation Authority Act, as ratified by the North General
Assembly, 2017 Session Law 120, codified at North Carolina General Statutes,
Chapter 160A, Article 29 (the "Act");
   WHEREAS, the Village of Bald Head Island (the "Village") is a municipal
corporation that is only accessible by watercraft vessel;
   WHEREAS, the Village is dependent upon a reliable, safe, and affordable
ferry system (including passenger and barge transportation services, terminal
facilities, and vehicle parking) that operates on the Cape Fear River between
Deep Point Marina in the City of Southport and Bald Head Island Marina in the
Village;
   WHEREAS, the City of Southport ("Southport") is a municipal corporation
where the mainland ferry terminal, the mainland barge terminal, and vehicle
parking for access to Bald Head Island are located;
   WHEREAS, Southport and the Village are both located in Brunswick County (the
"County");
   WHEREAS, many Southport and other Brunswick County residents are employed on
and/or regularly visit Bald Head Island and depend upon the ferry services and
parking facilities, and many residents living on, and visitors to Bald Head
Island regularly transact business in Southport and Brunswick County;
   WHEREAS, the ferry system, barge system, on-island tram system, terminals,
and parking facilities are presently owned and operated by two privately held
entities (collectively, the "Seller");
   WHEREAS, pursuant to the Act, the Village, Southport, and the County each
passed a resolution in 2017 creating a single ferry transportation authority
known as the Bald Head Island Transportation Authority (the "Authority") for
the purpose of purchasing the assets used in the operations of the ferry
system, barge system, on-island tram system, terminals, and parking facilities
(collectively, the "Ferry System"), and consolidating those operations into a
single, publicly owned entity;
   WHEREAS, in creating the Authority, the Village, Southport, and Brunswick
County engaged with each other in order to coordinate and plan for the
Authority that will operate a reliable and safe ferry and barge transportation
system to transport passengers and freight between Southport and the Village,
to provide parking facilities for those passengers on the mainland, and to
provide tram service on the island; to enhance the quality of life, mobility,
and circumstances of residents of the Village, Southport, and Brunswick County;
and to promote economic development and tourism throughout the Cape Fear
region, while protecting and preserving the environment;
   WHEREAS, the Board of Aldermen has previously determined that the creation
of the Authority pursuant to the Act, was to be in the best long-term interest
of the Village, Southport, and Brunswick County, and their residents and
businesses;
   WHEREAS, the Authority was formed in August, 2017 by concurrent resolutions
adopted by the Village Council of the Village, the Board of Aldermen of
Southport and the County Commissioners of the County after public hearings as
required by the Act;
   WHEREAS, the Authority performed extensive due diligence regarding the
status, operation, and value of the Ferry System in order to complete its
statutory mandate under the Act to purchase the Ferry System at or below its
appraised value;
   WHEREAS, after completion of such diligence and extensive negotiations with
the Seller, the Authority has authorized the execution of an Asset Purchase
Agreement with the Seller to purchase the Ferry System at a purchase price that
is below its appraised value;
   WHEREAS, pursuant to the Act, the Authority intends to issue its revenue
bonds (the "Bonds') to finance the purchase of the Ferry System, and in
connection therewith has engaged an underwriter and has obtained an investment
grade rating for the Bonds;
   WHEREAS, the issuance of the Bonds must be approved by the North Carolina
Local Government Commission (the "L.G.C.");
   WHEREAS, the Authority has made application to the L.G.C. for such approval,
and has provided to the L.G.C. staff and members the information required in
connection with the issuance of the Bonds;
   WHEREAS, the L.G.C., at the request of the Village, deferred action on the
Authority's application in order for the Authority to provide additional
information to the public about the pending purchase and related bond issue,
and the Authority has held a public information session (which was attended by
more than 230 people) and provided much information to the public;
   WHEREAS, on March 22, 2021, the Village Council submitted a letter to the
L.G.C. indicating that it now wishes to purchase the Ferry System itself and
asking the L.G.C. to work with it to acquire the Ferry System instead of the
Authority, on the basis that the Ferry System exists to serve the property
owners, visitors, non-profits, and businesses that compose the unique community
of Bald Head Island;
   WHEREAS, the Village Council is elected by the permanent residents of the
Village, who constitute less than 10% of the annual ridership of the Ferry
System;
   WHEREAS, Southport continues to believe that the Authority is the best
entity to own and operate the ferry system for the benefit of the citizens of
the entire region, including the employees and contractors who work on Bald
Head Island, most of whom live in Southport, and the assets of the Ferry System
that are located in Southport;
   NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, by the Board of Aldermen of the City of
Southport, as follows:
   1.   The City of Southport supports the acqms1t10n of the Ferry System by
the Authority, which Southport believes is in the best interest of Southport,
the County, and the Village, and will best support the quality of life,
mobility, and circumstances of residents of the Village, Southport, and the
County and promote economic development and tourism throughout the Cape Fear
region, while protecting and preserving the environment, in accordance with the
provisions of the Act.
   2.   The City of Southport objects to any attempted purchase or operation of
the Ferry System by the Village.
   3.   In the event the Village pursues the purchase of the Ferry System,
Southport intends to explore the possibility of acquiring and owning that
portion of the Ferry System located within the city limits of Southport.
   4.   The City Manager is instructed to provide a copy of this Resolution to
the members and staff of the L.G.C., to the County Commissioners of Brunswick
County, and to the Village Council of the Village.
   5.   This Resolution shall become effective upon its adoption.
ADOPTED by the Board of Aldermen of the City of Southport, this the 8th day of
April, 2021.

   6.   Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller reviewed the Yacht Basin project options and
all that the Yacht Basin Committee considered. There are two main options: A
and B. Option A consists of a pedestrian/bicycle path on the waterside of Bay
Street with a crosswalk over to Yacht Basin Drive. The path continues down
Yacht Basin Drive on the land side. Traffic would remain one-direction, but
additional signage, flashing lights, and road stripping would be installed.
Option B allows the pedestrian/bicycle path to stay on the waterside on both
Bay Street and Yacht Basin Drive. In this option, a portion of the right of way
on Yacht Basin Drive would have to be shifted because the businesses are closer
to the road. Directional signage, flashing lights, and road stripping would
also be installed. Option B does require more thermoplastic stripping.
   7.   Alderman Lombardi commented that most people walk on the waterside and
that a twelve-foot-wide lane for one-way traffic is plenty. Alderman Lombardi

D.)    Approval of Agenda
After a motion made by Alderman Allen and seconded by Alderman Lombardi, the
Board approved the agenda as presented. All ayes. Motion carried. The Mayor
took a moment to announce that it was Earth Day and how important it was. Then
he handed over the meeting to Gordon Hargrove. He welcomed the Board and Staff
to the meeting and then asked Melanie Trexler to introduce the first department
head presenter.
E.)    Department Presentations
   1. Development Services (Thomas Lloyd). 
   Mr. Lloyd said he would run through the line items in his department's
budget. He requested (1) additional position, which was already approved in the
Fall. The position is for a full-time Code Enforcement Officer. A part-time
building inspector might also be required for Level 2 & 3 inspectors. Other
requests include funding for supplies, software upgrades, forestry funds,
travel/training. The proposed department budget also included a portion of the
utilities and vehicles. Mr. Lloyd is also requesting that the City begin work
on a new CAMA Land Use Plan. The whole plan might take two years and should
cost between $30,000- 40,000. The budget includes funding for the first year of
the plan. In addition, Mr. Lloyd requested $15,000 in the budget for training
and continuing education. Mr. Lloyd explained that he did not allocate or
request any funding for digitizing existing records, like Laserfiche. Alderman
Davis asked about funding in the budget for any tree work or studies that would
be needed. Mr. Lloyd stated that he would look into that type of funding more,
but it usually gets covered through the Streets budget. Gordon Hargrove added
that the following Special Meeting would be to discuss capital improvement
projects. Mayor Hatem thanked Thomas Lloyd for his presentation and asked when
the CAMA land use plan would begin? Mr. Lloyd stated that if it were an
approved expense, a request for qualifications would be submitted, and then it
would be based on the group selected to update the plan.
   2. Public Services (Tom Stanley).
   Mr. Stanley started with the water and sewer department. He is requesting
one new employee because they need help on the crew. With David Fox retiring,
Mr. Stanley has been working in the office more. The water/sewer crew helps out
a lot in other departments, too. Mr. Stanley stated that every year, this
department has money allocated for manhole repairs, inflow and infiltration
studies, and backup pumps. This year, he is asking for two backup pumps for
aging stations. An engineer will also need to assess the best placement for 2"
lines to be installed. Last year there were 2200 feet of line scoped using a
camera. In those areas, two whole notebooks of issues were identified. Mr.
Stanley is asking for $300 000 to work on these repairs. He is also proposing a
new department fund that would serve as a preventative maintenance program
fund. The state requires that at least 10% of the lines get cleaned out and
scoped each year. Three new generators are needed: a new Ford Ranger (smaller)
truck and two administration computers. Alderman Sharkey wanted to clarify that
the position he was asking for is not new; it was a position that was not
filled previously but was already established.
   Mr. Stanley then shifted to the Buildings and Grounds Division budget.
Because of the pandemic last year, they were not able to hire any part-time
help. He is requesting one new full- time position for year-round work and two
part-time positions. The Buildings and Grounds Division also helps with the
Forestry Committee and Beautification Committee. A cargo van, (2) zero-turn
lawnmowers, and a new F150 is requested to replace aging equipment. The
gymnasium floor vacuum needs to be replaced, and it would be nice to make the
City Hall more presentable by painting or installing vinyl siding. The falling
gutters need to be repaired, and all of the ac units have maintenance twice a
year. Alderman Davis asked what the cost is of painting the City Hall. She
mentioned that there were discussions about this project last year. Tom Stanley
said that the vinyl siding installation was scheduled for $63,000. The hardy
boards were almost double that figure. Alderman Davis said that even though
painting might not be the best long-term option, it would be okay since many
other projects need funding. Tom Stanley said that this year is the first year
that all repair projects for buildings are being covered under the Buildings
and Grounds division; there are bound to be omissions and errors until we all
get used to it. Alderman Sharkey suggested that more funding goes into the
buildings that the public uses, not just the City Hall. She suggested that
maybe we shift the focus to the best of the buildings we have now and move the
activities to those facilities. The Senior building is aging out, but the
Jaycees Building is in better condition. There was some discussion about
installing audio-visual equipment in the Community Building. Alderman Davis
said that she thinks that it is so essential to allow the public to look at the
same materials that the Board is using. Gordon Hargrove commented that it was
important to get all of the maintenance under one department's umbrella, and
now a preventative maintenance program can be created. Mr. Hargrove said that a
Civil Engineering position will be added to the budget and split between water/
sewer and administration. Adding this position will reduce the contracted
services line item.
   Tom Stanley switched discussion to the Streets Department. He is requesting
a new message board sign so that both sides of the City will see updates on
road closures and projects. It will be a mobile sign and is estimated at
$17,000. Tree trimming is expensive, as well as sidewalks. He is requesting
funding for these items as well as $30,000 for new street name signs. Melanie
Trexler, the Finance Director, said they hoped to group several projects into
one Capital Project Fund and Ordinance. Mr. Stanley said that the vehicle
maintenance garage needed a tire machine for bigger tires, a new ac machine, a
new welder, and a diagnostic machine for diesel trucks. He is also requesting a
steam cleaner to degrease and a new oil receptacle. There are opportunities for
cost- sharing some of the equipment since the Fire Department uses diesel
equipment.
   3. Parks and Recreation (Heather Hemphill).
   Ms. Hemphill said that she was not requesting any staffing changes. Last
year all of the budget figures were skewed because of the pandemic. Several
projects got put on hold because government funding was cut or postponed. Ms.
Hemphill explained that part-time Staff includes summer camp counselors, rec
assistants, basketball referees, basketball coordinators, scorekeepers, and
before/after school assistants. Alderman Sharkey asked if she knew the life
expectancy is on the gymnasium? Ms. Hemphill replied that she would predict ten
to fifteen years remaining. There is a massive crack in the cement floor. She
would love for the City to develop a new community center with outdoor fields
and an indoor gym facility. We are currently the only indoor basketball
facility in the County. The bathrooms are new, and the roof probably has
fifteen years left. Alderman Spencer asked if there was an estimate for
replacing the floor. Ms. Hemphill said that she would not recommend using the
same floor. Instead, she would recommend something that would absorb the shocks
better. Laminate would be a good option once the crack was repaired. Alderman
Spencer mentioned the earlier request to purchase a new vacuum for the gym
floor and wondered if it was a better option to replace the floor instead of
buying the vacuum and replacing the floor in a few more years. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller mentioned that a new Parks & Recreation Plan is needed before
Southport can apply for grants. Ms. Hemphill said that the work for the Parks
and Recreation plan is included in contract services. Ms. Hemphill stated that
Staff agrees that participating in a lease for two lightning strikes equipment
towers would be helpful. There can be up to ten users. While it does not
replace the National Weather Service, it would be great to help identify
lightning patterns to make the community safer. There is a loudspeaker at each
tower that alarms the public. In addition, information would be distributed to
registered Staff members. Then information could be shared via Code Red or
social media platforms. Alderman Spencer asked whether the City contributes or
would contribute to some of the summer camps that are scheduled, in particular,
a summer camp for robotics. He said that he would love for the students who
participate in summer camps to go home with a computer at the end of summer.
Gordon Hargrove suggested adding a new line item in the budget to help support
this cause. It would start with $2500 for now.
   Ms. Hemphill shifted over to speak about the Community Building. Staff costs
haven't changed, but there was a considerable decrease in utilities because we
haven't rented the building out in a year. Routine and staffing costs are the
primary use. There are some marketing expenses, but no repairs to the building
are proposed. She suggested the need for a full-time staff member to coordinate
all facility rentals and coordinate clean-up and setups within a six-hour
window. At this point, it is hard to estimate revenues from rentals.
   4. Electrical Facilities (Ellie Pittenger).
   Mr. Pittenger addressed the Board with his budget information and requests.
He is requesting $4000 in software for power management. He is also requesting
more funding towards travel and training if things open back up and he can
attend the electrical summit. He would also like to start training some other
personnel on some of the duties that he performs. He asks for more load
management devices, backup materials for streetlight installs, Wi-Fi
thermostats, extra repeaters for the AMI system, and aluminum poles. The
connection of the public service department to a generator with an automatic
transfer switch has become more of a necessity. And he is requesting funding
for any maintenance on the department's electric (Hybrid) Ford Escape. Alderman
Allen asked if the City was giving away the Wi-Fi thermostats and load
management switches. Mr. Pittenger said that they were free to customers, but
the City did not install them. Typically, a customer has two weeks to have the
equipment installed. Once it is installed, a discount is applied. Alderman
Allen asked if an analysis had been done to compare leasing vehicles versus
purchasing them. Finance Director Melanie Trexler stated that there had been an
analysis done. The company helps the City sell vehicles and helps keep the City
from being upside-down on a vehicle payment. Alderman Davis asked what company
we were working with. Ms. Trexler said that the City has been working with
Enterprise and have been happy with the level of service. Mr. Pittenger thanked
the Board.
   5. Tourism and Communications (Randy Jones).
   Mr. Jones reminded the Board that this was the first time listing Tourism
and Communications together, and the budget reflects that. He is proposing a
full-time marketing specialist. Over the last year, Sharon Venis switched to
part-time, and Lisa Anderson moved into a full-time position. Mr. Jones said
that he was very proud of everything that Ms. Anderson has accomplished this
year. The visitor's center will be opening in June. Beautification is the only
group that there is currently a line item. Mr. Jones is requesting funds for
travel and training, IT security, special programs, including Code Red.
Alderman Davis mentioned installing a screen at the Community Building so that
the public can see the same things that the Board is seeing. Mr. Jones said
that he was under the impression that Facilities would cover it. He mentioned
that logistically it would be a challenge because of the lighting and size of
the building and social distancing issues. Mr. Hargrove stated that he would
like for the project to fall under the Communications budget. Mr. Jones said
that he is trying to balance communicating with the citizens and attracting
tourists. Mayor Hatem said that Mr. Jones does a great job, and Alderman
Lombardi said that the Beautification Committee wouldn't get half as much done
without him.
   6. Animal Protective Services (Kate Marshall).
   Ms. Marshall explained that her budget is primarily operational, with a
slight increase in supplies. She is hoping to form a partnership with
Pawsability to help support trap and release. The storing kennel is operational
and is being used. There are approximately 500 dogs who are microchipped, and
half are registered. She uses the chip reader often.
   7. Fire Department (Chief Charles Drew). 
   Chief Drew thanked the Board for allowing him to serve as Fire Chief. When
he joined the department thirty years ago, most of their funding was made
selling hotdogs or through donations. He mentioned that now people pay fire
tax. This is the third year where no increase in fees was requested. Over the
last year, the Fire Department has answered over 700 calls. They have also
transferred over 600 calls to medical facilities. The main budget item that is
requested is for a full-time EMS captain. This person would serve as a
firefighter and EMS. The City's ambulances can respond to local emergencies
within four minutes, but there has been a lack of volunteers in the last year.
They have more Fire volunteers than EMS volunteers. There was some discussion
about the fire station space that was donated by Lowe's. Once that facility is
open, they will not use the Long Beach Drive station. The Fire fees are based
on square footage.
   8. Police Department (Chief Todd Coring & Major Burke). 
   Chief Coring thanked the Board for taking the time to listen to their
requests. This past year was challenging because of the pandemic, hurricanes,
and national attention on police officers nationwide. In order to make
retention a priority, he recommends increasing everyone’s salary by $4,000. If
they compare themselves with other departments of a similar size, their
salaries are less. The Police Department is requesting funding for training and
travel, contract services, and technology upgrades to the vehicles. Outfitting
a new officer costs between $3500-$4500. Since he became Chief, two officers
have left their positions because of salaries. They are working on moving
evidence over into the City hall evidence room because there is mold in the old
building. Chief Coring said that he does not want Southport to become a
training department where new officers get training, get a good start, and then
transfer to a different department somewhere because there is more money. He
would like to raise the starting salaries to $40,000. Mayor Hatem agreed that
retention is necessary and creates a sense of familiarity and investment in the
community. He thanked the department for their responsiveness to the hospital.
Chief Coring said that community policing is so important. Now the Police
Department participates in delivering gift bags to a nursing facility, helps
deliver meals, and works with local businesses to help develop an
individualized security plan. Alderman Spencer asked how many police officers
live in Southport. Chief Coring answered that two officers did. Alderman
Spencer said that he would encourage the officers to buy a home in Southport.
Perhaps the City could help incentivize living in Southport by paying closing
costs, etc. Alderman Davis mentioned that there are always calls out to Walmart
and asked if there was an officer there all the time? Chief Coring said that
they have a good relationship with Walmart now since they met with corporate
leadership. They have worked with the security staff at Walmart to create
better security patterns.
   9. Finance Department (Melanie Trexler).
   Ms. Trexler began by stating that she is very proud of the ladies and
gentlemen in the administrative and finance departments. They are all doing a
great job, and customers appreciate the information that they have. She said
that when everyone uses open communications, it helps things go smoothly. We
have all learned lessons because of Covid. The City is on track to have a
timely audit this year. The Board's budget is spread between three funds:
general fund, water fund, and the sewer fund. The Board pays a portion of the
attorney's fees. Travel and training line item has increased. Some trainings
are opening back up, and there is no substitute for interacting with people in
person for trainings. The City Clerk is proposing CivicClerk software and
tablets for the Board of Aldermen for the agendas. For the software and
tablets, Ms. Trexler has allocated $11,000. Alderman Spencer said that he was
in full support and was glad that it was considered and budgeted. The
transition from paper agendas to electronic agendas should take place by July
1, 2021.
   Alderman Davis asked if the City needed to allocate election funding this
year for municipal elections? Ms. Trexler said that was correct, and the
funding was listed. She wasn't sure what happened to the spreadsheet but would
make sure to fix it. Administration salaries have a built-in bump up of 4% for
the following year. The three departments also fund the City Manager, City
Clerk, and Deputy Clerk positions. Travel, training, and supplies increased.
Alderman Davis asked about how many years are left paying the debt service
payment for the Fire Department building? Ms. Trexler said that she wasn't
exactly sure, but it was still a long time. Lastly, Ms. Trexler said that FEMA
has allocated a little over a million in reimbursements. She said that if any
Board members have questions, they are welcome to call her anytime.
   Ms. Trexler said that it would be excellent to hire a company to handle
payroll. There is a company that would handle all of the payroll processing,
taxes, and reporting for $6700. Over the last five years, the payroll position
has evolved to something more complicated. Now it takes up a lot more time than
it used to. If we contract with the payroll company, we don't have to pay
benefits, and employees will be able to use an online platform to make changes
to their information. Staff is currently reviewing health care options because
our contract with Medcost ends June 30, 2021. The weather tower funds will be
added to the spreadsheet for the next meeting. Alderman Allen asked if the City
could do something about the area's appearance where the tower was? City
Manager Hargrove said that it is coned off because we were worried about people
using metal detectors on the site. Ms. Trexler also mentioned that three
capital projects were omitted from the spreadsheet by accident. They will be
added to the spreadsheet by the next meeting. Ms. Trexler asked if the Board
had any other questions?
   Gordon Hargrove summarized by saying that there had been a lot of good
information presented today. The revenue-building ideas selected will determine
what capital projects that the City can complete. We also need more water in
our reserve. The following Special Budget meeting on April 28, 2021, will
include time to discuss water allocation. Mr. Hargrove is very proud of Staff
for developing this budget. Thanks to Ms. Trexler and Department heads.
F.)    Adjournment
After a motion made by Alderman Marc Spencer and seconded by Mayor Pro-tem
Karen Mosteller, the Mayor adjourned the Special Meeting at 1:27 p.m. All ayes.
Motion carried.
                     ____________________________________
                     Joseph P. Hatem, MD, MPH
                     Mayor, City of Southport

APRIL 28, 2021
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
223 E. BAY STREET  APRIL 28, 2021
COMMUNITY BUILDING SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:      Mayor Joseph P. Hatem
         Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Lora Sharkey, Lowe Davis,
         Marc Spencer,   John Allen, Tom Lombardi
STAFF PRESENT:
Gordon Hargrove, City Manager         Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
Melanie Trexler, Finance Director         Thomas Lloyd, Development Services
Director
Randy Jones, Communication/Tourism Director   Lisa Anderson, Communications,
Asst. Director
Ralph Treadway, Battalion Fire Chief          Adam Montgomery, Water
Distribution ORC
OTHERS PRESENT: Richard Alt
          Gary Pethe, State Port Pilot
A)   Call to Order – 9:08 am.
   Mayor Hatem called the special meeting to order at 9:08 am.
B)   Invocation
   Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
   Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D.)   Approval of Agenda
   After a motion made by Alderman Allen and seconded by Alderman Sharkey, the
Board approved the agenda as presented. All ayes. Motion carried. The Mayor
expressed his thanks to everyone in attendance. He said that working on the
budget is like painting a canvas. We want future generations to look back and
say that the Board and Staff made the best decisions. A strong budget takes not
only the financial allocations but a lot of ideas and hard work.
Summary from Previous Meetings
   Gordon Hargrove approached the podium. He wanted to remind everyone that
this was not the final version of the budget. Staff will go back and add
capital projects and revenue-generating ideas. The budget will be presented
again, hopefully at the end of the following week. He said that a few items
that were discussed last week have been added. These include the diesel
diagnostic machine, $10,000 for consulting fees, $2500 for robotic camps,
$25,000 for an audio-visual system in the Community Building, election
expenses, 1.5 positions for public services, and a full-time position for
marketing and Community building management. There was some discussion about
the Community Building moving under the Tourism department. Randy Jones said
that he wanted to make sure that he would maintain the quality of the position.
Mr. Hargrove stated that all of the other buildings (Jaycees, Senior Center)
would remain under Parks and Recreation. Tourism and Communications would have
a total of three and a half employees.
E.)   Water Allocation
   Mr. Hargrove started discussions about water allocation by referencing the
memo that he provided to the Board. The State of NC requires us to have a
reserve capacity of water for emergencies equal to at least 50% of daily usage.
Right now, we are bumping up against that figure. Adam Montgomery approached
Mr. Hargrove about the concerns, and they began exploring options. The existing
water tower is not in good condition, so it cannot be used. A new water tower
would cost approximately 4 million dollars to construct. We have six wells at
Sunny Point providing good quality and plentiful water, but the problem is
connecting it to the main City area. Staff agrees that the best option would be
to increase the reserve purchase from the County. After trying to calculate the
proposed growth in the next five to ten years, Southport might have as many as
3,000 new residences. City staff anticipates needing 230,000 gallons of water
capacity for the next five to ten years. The County is offering to finance it
for nine years, making our yearly payment around $140,000. Now, we need to
figure out how to pay for it.
   Last year, approximately $68,000 was paid in water development fees. We are
also going to be receiving funding from the American Rescue Plan. We will be
receiving two payments of $600,000, one year apart. The ARP funding can improve
infrastructure, and Mr. Hargrove believes that the City will be collecting even
more Water Development Fees in the next few years. Mr. Hargrove and Staff need
authorization from the Board to begin negotiations with Brunswick County.
   Alderman Lombardi asked for more information about the water tower on Howe
Street that is inoperable. Mr. Montgomery explained that the existing water
tower has areas where the metal is so thin that it is leaking. A contractor
made repairs to the tank because it is unstable without water inside. Alderman
Allen asked if anything besides water could fill the tank, but Mr. Montgomery
stated that an engineer would have to approve that. There were discussions
about purchasing half of the proposed capacity. Mr. Hargrove mentioned that the
capacity fee now is more reasonable, at approximately $4.00 a gallon, and the
interest rate is between 2-3%. Because of the price of the contract, the Local
Government Commission will have to approve the financing. Melanie Trexler added
that with 2.25% interest, the yearly payment would be around $147.400 a year
for nine years. Alderman Allen recommends entering into a contract for 115,000
gallons of capacity now and maybe 115,000 gallons of capacity in five years.
Alderman Allen made a motion authorizing the City Manager to negotiate with
Brunswick County to purchase water reserve capacity in the amount of 115,000
gallons with the option to purchase an additional 115,000 gallons in five years
with the same rate, allowing for inflation. Mr. Montgomery explained that the
City has a lot of construction going on already, and we are close to exceeding
our current allocation. Alderman Allen stated that he would think that the
County would be willing to sell some capacity each year if needed. Mr. Hargrove
stated the County has already said that they do not want to negotiate every two
years, that the City should purchase as much as they will need for the future.
After more discussion, the motion was revised. A motion was made by Alderman
Allen and seconded by Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller to authorize the City
Manager to negotiate with Brunswick County to purchase water reserve capacity
with the provision that he should request 115,000 gallons initially with the
option to purchase an additional 115,000 gallons, as needed. Mr. Hargrove is
authorized to negotiate the purchase of up to 230,000 gallons if needed. All
ayes. Motion carried.
   Mr. Hargrove suggested a quick break, and Mayor Hatem dismissed everyone at
10:11 am for a ten-minute break.
F.)   Capital Projects and Revenue Generation Discussion
   The meeting was called to order at 10:28 am by Mayor Hatem. Mr. Hargrove
asked the Board to look over a spreadsheet that was provided. There is no way
to predict the cost of some of the projects listed, including items like open
space conservation and public safety. The items are color-coded by level of
priority. Yellow is the least important, orange is moderately important, and
red is the highest priority. There are some other funding mechanisms, including
loans. The Local Government Commission will only allow the City to leverage
themselves to a certain point. A tax increase is one option. For every penny
that taxes are raised, it generates $100,000. At the last Board meeting, Mr.
Hargrove mentioned the reimbursements from FEMA. The Kingsley Park project is
the last one to go into the portal. The City just received reimbursement from
Hurricane Dorian. The City will likely be about 99% reimbursed from FEMA by the
end of the year. The City has to front the money for projects, and then FEMA
will reimburse us. The reimbursement funds are proposed to be allocated such
that $300,000 will return to the Electric fund. $700,000 can be used as seed
money for other capital projects. Some funding usually stays in reserve for
storms. Mr. Hargrove recommends considering a three-cent tax increase and a
combination of taxes collected and FEMA refunds for projects. Then the balance
can remain in the storm fund.
   City roads are in terrible condition. Mr. Hargrove recommends allocating
$400,000 in road projects. We need to address a stormwater plan community-wide.
Some grants are available, but there are obstacles when applying for grants.
Southport has a high median income, which often reduces our chances of being
awarded grants. The American Rescue Plan has to be directly applied to the
response to the Covid-19 impacts. Mr. Hargrove doesn't think that we can repair
roads with the funds, but we can possibly use the funds to improve the sewer
system. Mr. Hargrove stated that of all the complaints he receives, the three
most prevalent complaints are street, stormwater, and pedestrian safety.
Another option for funding is to monetize tourist visits by installing a pay
for parking program.
   Alderman Allen stated that he needs more visual aids to help delineate the
amounts coming in, the cost of the proposed projects, and funding ideas. The
state government requires a 30% fund balance. Alderman Sharkey suggested making
the projects that are shovel-ready a priority. These projects are the
pedestrian safety plan at the Yacht Basin, Howe Street sidewalk project, the
kayak launch, Bay Street and sidewalk repair, and managing erosion on Brunswick
Street. Mayor Hatem stated that road improvements are essential. The citizens
of Southport do not deserve to ride through all the craters. Powell bill
funding provides $108,000 a year towards road improvements. Assistant Public
Works Director, Tom Stanley, estimates that it would cost approximately 4.7
million dollars to improve all the roads in the City. Alderman Lombardi
recommends that inspections will be done of the roads and then proceed with
improvements as needed. Alderman Sharkey said that she also speaks to citizens
and tourists about the condition of the roads. She also asked about the
feasibility of a pay-for-parking system. Mr. Hargrove stated that he has
already started that process. He is looking into other coastal communities, and
Major Burke from the Southport PD is gathering information. A committee of
Staff was asked to identify the number of parking spaces available near the
intersection of N. Howe Street and Moore Street. The group identified 850
parking spaces. He has not brought the item to the Board yet because he wants
to weed through the information first.
   Mr. Hargrove reminded the Board that a 30% fund balance is recommended, but
it doesn't have to be upwards of 50%, either. That is the citizens' money, and
the City doesn't need to sit on it; they need to invest back into the
community. Alderman Sharkey said that she would suggest dropping the kayak
launch project to focus on the erosion on Brunswick Street if needed. Alderman
Allen said that the marina was willing to contribute 50% to the kayak launch,
so we should move on that while we have that offer. There was a brief
discussion about the Kingsley Pier repairs and parking area. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller said that the erosion on Brunswick Street should be prioritized
because we are one storm away from nonexistent. Mr. Hargrove said that we are
waiting on CAMA approval, but they will find the funding.
   Mr. Hargrove asked the Board if a tax increase could be included as an
option in the proposed budget. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said that she would like
to see all the scenarios with the current revenues first before making that
decision. Mayor Hatem agreed that the Board needs to see where the existing
funding will be spent and see where there are deficits before a decision is
made about taxes. Mr. Hargrove stated that any tax increase would be used for
capital projects. Overall, the Board was willing to entertain a tax increase as
long as it was justified. Alderman Spencer asked if we could hold out a couple
of years until the next County tax valuation was completed. Then the City would
potentially already get more tax revenue. Alderman Sharkey stated that the City
should fund the most visible projects to the public, not more studies. The
public is more receptive to tax increases if there is a more tangible benefit.
Alderman Lombardi believes a tax increase should be at least considered.
Alderman Davis stated that she understands that a tax increase is a
possibility. The median income is higher, but many people do not have a high
income. Mr. Hargrove said that they would present different scenarios with
varying tax increases.
   Mr. Hargrove introduced the idea of implementing a stormwater fee. Short of
having a stormwater engineer on Staff, it will be difficult to assess the
correct fee. Mr. Hargrove suggests a possible blanket fee for all households,
even $5.00 a month. That is not a lot, and the money can be allocated for city-
wide stormwater improvements. Stormwater issues are City-wide. Alderman Davis
asked if there are other models that we can use to compare and find a way to
make it work for us? Mr. Hargrove said that every municipality is different
geographically, and we need to make sure that our plan suits us. Alderman
Lombardi suggested that maybe it be called something else to prevent everyone
getting upset if the City is making improvements in other areas, away from
where they reside. Alderman Sharkey suggested that $5.00 a month is too much
for people to pay right now because people that don't have a stormwater issue
won't think it is justified. There was more discussion about the need for
better stormwater management. Alderman Allen said that we all pay County taxes,
even though we don't use all the provided services. He thinks it is good to
have a study done before fees are implemented, but he favors working on a
stormwater solution. Mr. Hargrove explained that much of the City's stormwater
comes from Cottage Creek and Bonnett's Creek.
   Mr. Hargrove said that the discussions have come full circle and have been
very thorough. Lunch had arrived, so he suggested taking a break and then
coming back together to go through the departmental requests. He said that at
least one additional meeting is needed after he and Ms. Trexler reorganize the
requests and priorities. He suggested Friday, May 7, 2021, from 9:00 am until
around noon. And then, if it looked like one more meeting was needed, they
could meet on Friday, May 14, 2021, from 9:00 am to around noon. The Board all
agreed. Once everything was pinned down, the budget is submitted to the Local
Government Commission for approval, and the FY 21-22 Budget can be approved at
the June Board meeting. Mayor Hatem excused everyone for lunch.
   Mayor Hatem called the Board to order at 12:32 pm after a brief lunch break.
Mr. Hargrove stated that the Board needed to consider all of the requests from
the different departments. Development Services requested an increase in
contract services, up to $30,000. At least a portion of this would be spent
updating the CAMA Land Use Plan, but the expense might be shared over two
fiscal years.
   Mr. Hargrove said that they could not develop the funding for all of the
positions that Public Services requested, but they have budgeted for (1) full-
time and (1) part-time person. Everyone has a specific job title, but they all
tend to work together to complete tasks. Alderman Sharkey asked about what will
happen after David retires, and Tom Stanley is promoted to Director of the
department. It was determined that the extra position would be added back into
the budget if the budget allowed. There are no new positions proposed at the
garage. The diesel diagnostic machine and some other equipment will be split
between the garage and the Fire Department. In the streets budget, road
improvements are to be funded by the capital improvement fund. There are no
changes to the water/sewer fund. Alderman Sharkey asked which department would
host the proposed civil engineer, and Mr. Hargrove said it would be grouped
with the Public Services department.
   The only proposed change for the Parks and Recreation department is the
$2600 added to departmental supplies to donate to the robotics and other summer
camps. The Community Building could remain under Parks and Recreation, but Mr.
Hargrove is proposing adding a new position under Tourism and Communications.
The position would serve 50% in marketing and 50% Community Building. Mayor
Pro- tem Mosteller and Alderman Allen both agreed that dividing the time is
wise. Mr. Randy Jones said that he would figure out how to make it work for
them. In addition, they are budgeting $25,000 for audio-visual improvements at
the Community Building. No are no proposed changes to the Electric funding.
Animal Protective Services department did not propose any significant changes,
but Code Enforcement is being split from the department and will fall under
Development Services. Mr. Hargrove stated the cat storage area at the Indian
Trail Meeting Hall would have to be relocated.
   The Fire and Police departments make up half of the budget. The Fire
Department asked for an EMS Captain. The department has trouble finding
volunteers, so hiring a captain would eliminate the need for so many volunteer
hours. The Board agreed on the position. The Police Department requested an
increase in wages to make their salaries in line with other departments in the
area. Hiring officers is an expensive investment between training and
equipment. We want to try to retain officers once they are here. The Mayor
reminded everyone that the Police department has the same number of officers
all year long, but when it is summertime and all the tourists are here, they
have a lot more work to do to ensure that everyone stays safe. The entire Board
was in support of the salary increases.
   Mr. Hargrove said there were just a couple of general government budget
changes. Ms. Dutton reminded the Board that tablets and agenda software were
included in the budget. The Deputy Clerk, Tanya Shannon, and Ms. Dutton had
narrowed the possible tablets down to either the 8th generation iPad or the
Samsung Galaxy S7. The Board stated that they were ready to move forward. A
couple of months ago, the Board approved a 2.5% raise for all employees that
would be backdated to February. This proposed budget includes a 1.5% cost of
living raise. Performance appraisals will begin in the departments soon. Ms.
Melanie Trexler stated that she recently spoke to Enterprise, from whom we
lease vehicles. The Police Department is requesting (4) new vehicles, but they
can sell many others to be almost fiscally neutral. She expects the projections
about health insurance soon, and she has been informed there will likely be a
decrease in rates. Mr. Hargrove said that they have gone through everything
that they had planned for the Board. There has been a lot of progress in
narrowing things down. He wanted to thank Melanie Trexler for all of her effort
and time. He also wants to thank the department heads for working on their
parts of the budget. And lastly, thanks to the Mayor and Board of Aldermen. He
predicts a balanced budget in June.
   All of the Aldermen took turns thanking the City Manager, Finance Director,
and Department Heads for their hard work on the proposed budget. Mayor Hatem
provided some closing comments, expressed gratitude to the Board and Staff for
their hard work, and thanked Randy Jones and Lisa Anderson for their efforts to
broadcast the meeting information to the public. After a motion made by Mayor
Pro-tem Karen Mosteller and seconded by Aldermen Thomas Lombardi, the Mayor
adjourned the meeting at 1:26 pm. All ayes. Motion carried.

                  Joseph P. Hatem, M.D., M. P.H.
                  Mayor, City of Southport

MAY 7, 2021
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
COMMUNITY BUILDING MAY 7, 2021
223 E. BAY STREET  SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:      Mayor Joseph P. Hatem
         Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Lora Sharkey, Lowe Davis,
         Marc Spencer,   John Allen, Tom Lombardi
STAFF PRESENT:
Gordon Hargrove, City Manager         Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
Melanie Trexler, Finance Director         Ralph Treadway, Battalion Fire Chief
Randy Jones, Communication/Tourism Director   Lisa Anderson, Communications,
Asst. Director
OTHERS PRESENT: Richard Alt
       Gary Pethe, State Port Pilot
A)   Call to Order – 9:04 a.m.
Mayor Hatem called the special meeting to order at 9:04 a.m.
B)   Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D.)    Approval of Agenda
After a motion made by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and seconded by Alderman Allen,
the Board approved the agenda as presented. All ayes. Motion carried. The Mayor
informed everyone of a fire that occurred at the Christian school the night
before the meeting. Thankfully, no one was injured. He expressed his gratitude
that no one was hurt and for all of the work by the Southport Fire Department.
   Mayor Hatem reminded everyone that at the hospital, the emergency staff has
to make quick decisions. With the budget, the Board has some time to think
about each issue and ensure that they make the right decisions. He said that
the City Hall is a reflection of the City, Staff, and all citizens. We should
not let it get in too bad of shape because it will be harder to repair. He
asked the Board to think about the maintenance at the cemeteries and whether
the City should contract with a lawn care company to help maintain its
appearance.
E.)    Capital Projects and Funding Mechanisms
City Manager Gordon Hargrove approached the podium at 9:14 a.m. to address the
Board. He explained to the Board that the version of the budget that was
distributed was a good representation of the final budget, that only minor
changes might need to be made.
As an update from the last budget meeting, Mr. Hargrove stated that Brunswick
County was amenable to participating in the water allocation contract with the
City. They are also happy to accommodate the request to sell half (115,000
gallons) of the expected allocation now and then the other half in
approximately (36) months. They will start working on getting a contract in
place and finalizing the details.
   Mr. Hargrove stated that the City has a healthy fund balance of 60%, and he
is not proposing a tax increase this year. Capital projects can be funded with
fund balance. Previously, Staff was proposing $700,000 for capital projects,
but now they are proposing $1.2 million. The Bay Street collapse is a top
priority. There will be an erosion control project from the high-water mark to
the pavement, including sandbags, backfilling, and rip wrap. Alderman Lowe
Davis suggested that the area of Brunswick Street in front of her home needs
some erosion control measures. Mr. Hargrove said that it might be too late to
add it to the current proposed budget, but it is always good to identify
projects that need work. Alderman Allen asked if the money proposed in the
budget for paving was inclusive of Powell Bill funding, but Ms. Melanie Trexler
said that it was not included.
   Mr. Hargrove stated that it seems that NCDOT was willing to work with the
City on the repaving of Howe Street so that the City won’t have such a great
expense. The Kingsley Park repairs are only going to include the portions that
were damaged. FEMA should be obligating funds within the next week or two.
Staff is proposing $100,000 “seed” money to start addressing the City’s
stormwater issues. While a complete stormwater plan would probably cost about
$5 million, it is just a start. The improvements of the pedestrian corridor at
the Yacht Basin might have to be postponed until the fall since tourists are
already here. The improvements at the Yacht Basin will be expensive because of
the amount of thermoplastic striping and paving. Alderman Mosteller suggested
allocating $150,000 for the kayak launch. This amount does not include the
promised contribution by the Marina. She suggested the City look into possible
grants through CAMA.
   The City Hall improvements would consist of either vinyl siding or
Hardiplank siding. There is a significant difference in cost. All of the
capital projects included in the upcoming fiscal year budget total
approximately 1.7 million dollars. The City is expecting FEMA reimbursements of
about $575,000. The total amount that Staff suggests reallocating from the
general fund towards capital projects is around 1.2 million dollars.
   Melanie Trexler, the Finance Director, explained that even after the
allocation from the general fund, the fund balance would be approximately 41%.

MAY 26, 2021
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
223 E. BAY STREET  MAY 26, 2021
COMMUNITY BUILDING SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:      Mayor Joseph P. Hatem
         Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Lora Sharkey, Lowe Davis,
         John Allen, Tom Lombardi, Marc Spencer
STAFF PRESENT:      
Gordon Hargrove, City Manager         Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director   Randy Jones, Communication/
Tourism Director Lisa Anderson, Communications, Asst. Director   Ralph
Treadway, Battalion Fire Chief    
Adam Montgomery, Water Distribution ORC      Tom Stanley, Public Services
Director
OTHERS PRESENT: Allen Serkin, Executive Director, Cape Fear Council of
Governments
       Jean Klein, CES Administrator, Lumber River Council of Government
       Gary Pethe, State Port Pilot
A)   Call to Order – 10:10 a.m.
Mayor Hatem called the special meeting to order at 10:10 a.m.
B)   Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
Presentation
   Mayor Hatem asked Development Services Director, Thomas Lloyd, to introduce
the Council of Government's presenters. Mr. Lloyd introduced Allen Serkin,
Executive Director with the Cape Fear Council of Governments.
   In 2018, the City applied for and was awarded a $65,000 grant to complete an
Asset Inventory and Assessment grant through the Division of Water
Infrastructure and the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality. The
Council of Governments was the project manager for the asset inventory and
mapping.
   Asset Management is the practice of managing infrastructure capital assets
to minimize the total cost of owning and operating the assets and prolong the
useful life of the assets while delivering the desired level of service. All of
the identified hydrants, mains, valves, interconnections, and specific meter
information are documented. A complete inventory is established, and all of the
assets are mapped. Each asset is assigned a unique identifier. Along with help
from City Staff, the condition of the assets is documented. A risk assessment
was completed to see what the impact would be if a component fails. As part of
the process, an application was created for the City Staff to use on their
tablets. The application allows information to be sent to the Council of
Governments more easily.
   The Council created a digital map that identifies the size and location of
water pipes and color-coded them for easy identification. In addition, a paper
atlas was created that shows the material, location, and sizes of the lines
along with street names and address points. Mr. Serkin introduced Ms. Jean
Klein with the Lumber River Council of Governments.
   Ms. Klein stated that there are two sources of water-ground or surface. A
“purchase water only” system is what the City of Southport uses. This means
that the water supply, including storage capacity, is secured from Brunswick
County. Drinking water assets are actively managed through careful maintenance,
repair, and replacement. Brunswick County is adding a filtration system on NC
211 Hwy. The City’s original water system that was installed in approximately
1915 was made of cast iron. Between 1920-1969, many small projects were made
off of the original system. Between 1970-1979, several large projects were
initiated by the City to extend water along the major corridors. Since 1980,
most water infrastructure work has been done for subdivisions.
   The most problematic line is small diameter cast iron lines that are close
to the surface. They are now corroded and subject to breaking. Southport has a
significant inventory of undersized lines. The current recommendation is not to
use pipes that are smaller than 6 inches in diameter. Of the 257 valves that
were inventoried, the poorest valves are due to age. Some of them were
installed before the 1940s; the current life expectancy is usually thirty-five
years. There are 224 hydrants inventoried, and 54% are in average condition.
Hydrants generally last between 45-60 years. Ms. Klein commended the City for
the investment in water meters. 88% of the City’s meters are residential, 11%
are commercial, and 1% are City-owned. The City's system is more accurate and
helps to reduce non-revenue water in the system through leak detection sensors.
   Risk analysis is comparing the likelihood of failure versus the consequence
of failure. There are 55,847 linear feet of line that is the weakest point of
vulnerability. Line breaks in this area would result in significant reportable
violations. Out of 82 assets, 39 are identified as high risk because of age.
   A Water System Capital Improvement Plan includes scheduling, financing, and
implementing future capital projects. It allows City decision-makers to think
over a large, multi-year period and can assist in developing an asset
improvement strategy where costs can spread over ten years.
   When water and sewer rates are not adjusted annually, the system absorbs all
of the costs to purchase and distribute water. It is best to increase rates
gently, about 2% a year. It is responsible to raise rates a little each year to
pay for improvements and infrastructure. Currently, the water fund appears to
be operating at a break-even level or slightly better. Once capital projects
are planned, there will be loans and debt service that the City will have to
assume.
Ms. Klein made the following recommendations:
The City should plan to replace the cast iron lines in the system, including
valve changeouts.
While water loss is not a significant problem, the City has numerous failing
lines that would cause water loss.
Continue the valve exercise program to ensure that valves are inspected and
assessed for function regularly.
Continue paying attention to water use because the City is a purchase-water-
only system and track water allocation.
An annual assessment of water rates should be monitored to ensure the revenues
are sufficient to cover operation, maintenance, existing and future debt
service.
Ms. Klein then expressed her gratitude to Tom Stanley and Adam Montgomery for
their help in this process. She reiterated that it is important to keep moving
forward with repairs and improvements.
Alderman Davis asked about whether the streets would have to be dug up again
and how long it would take to do the work to replace those weak lines. Tom
Stanley stated that it would depend on the project, but the first projects he
would recommend are Howe Street and East/West Moore Street. Alderman Spencer
said that most of the lines are located on the sides of the roads, and Tom
Stanley said that was mostly accurate. But some lines cross or zigzag under
roads. He also said that although the water repairs/improvements project seems
scary, the City still has a very good system. Ms. Klein remarked that this City
is old and historical, and we also have an old, historical utility system. She
said that the City has a lot of space to increase our rates because we are
towards the bottom of the range compared to other municipalities our size. Our
rates should be based solely on what the City’s needs are. The rate structure
should be based on our base rate that includes operating costs and a volumetric
rate. The volumetric rate funds that are collected are funding that can go into
a capital reserve fund.
One recommendation by Ms. Klein is to change the number of gallons included in
the base rate but leave the same rate. There would be more steps in the rate
structure. She suggested that the City look at consumption groupings and
averages. That is one way to protect vulnerable populations, too. Alderman
Davis asked if contaminants were anywhere else in the system, and Alderman
Spencer asked about contamination from asbestos concrete lines. Adam Montgomery
stated that he had just tested some asbestos lines, and there was no
contamination in the water sample. PVC piping has a 100-year life expectancy.
Mayor Hatem said that anytime he learns something new, he considers it a good
meeting. He summarized what was learned by saying that Tom Stanley is a good
man; cast-iron belongs on the stove, water rates should not be reduced, the
roads might be disheveled again at some point, but now the City has some ideas
about the future. Mayor Hatem thanked the Board, Thomas Lloyd, Adam Montgomery,
Tom Stanley, Gordon Hargrove, Allen Serkin, and Jean Klein for their hard work.
A Resolution to adopt the plan will be ready for consideration at the June
meeting.
After a motion made by Alderman John Allen and seconded by Mayor Pro-tem Karen
Mosteller, the Mayor adjourned the meeting at 11:40 a.m. All ayes. Motion
carried.

                     Joseph P. Hatem, M.D., M.P.H.

ayes. Motion carried.
At the Special Called Meeting on May 26th, 2021, the Board of Aldermen listened
to a Cape Fear Council of Government presentation. Thomas Lloyd explained that
the presentation was part of a grant that the City received in 2018. Mr. Lloyd
went over the main recommendations, as provided by Allen Serkin and Jean Klein.
Their recommendations are: 1.) The City should plan to replace the cast iron
lines in the system, including valve changeouts and undersized lines beyond
their useful life period; 2.) While water loss is not a significant problem,
the City has numerous lines that could cause water loss in the future. The City
should continue to monitor these through its metering system; 3.) Continue the
valve exercise program to ensure that valves are inspected and assessed for
function regularly; 4.) Continue paying attention to water use because the City
is a purchase-water-only system and track water allocation; 5.) An annual
assessment of water rates should be monitored to ensure the revenues are
sufficient to cover operation, maintenance, existing and future debt service.
At this point, all the Board is required to do is accept and adopt the
assessment results. After a motion made by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and seconded
by Aldermen Tom Lombardi, the Board approved the Resolution, which adopted the
Water Asset Inventory and Asset project results as presented. All ayes. Motion
carried.  
Gordon Hargrove explained that the water allocation agreement with Brunswick
County has two parts: the wholesale bulk water service agreement and additional
capacity. The City is currently seeking 115,000 gallons of capacity now, and in
approximately 18-24 months, the City will have the option to purchase another
115,000 gallons. These arrangements were approved at an earlier Board of
Aldermen meeting. Mr. Hargrove would like the Board to approve the agreement
and authorize the Mayor to sign the agreement. Alderman Sharkey asked if
interest was being applied, and Mr. Hargrove stated that there was interest,
but he was unaware of the percentage. After a motion made by Alderman Lombardi
and seconded by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller, the Board approved the contract with
Brunswick County and authorized Mayor Hatem to sign the agreement. All ayes.
Motion carried. Alderman Allen suggested that the rate committee meet to
recommend how much is included in the base rate and the rate steps. Other
municipalities' rates are increasing to help finance the osmosis filtration
system that the County is building.
The Mayor asked Thomas Lloyd to explain the request for annexation at 1147 S.
Caswell Avenue. The request was made by Terry and Sue Finch, the new owners of
the property. The annexation is contiguous, and the property does not need to
be rezoned. Annexation is a requirement for tapping onto City utilities. After

accepted the petition for annexation, requested that the Clerk investigate the
sufficiency of the request, accepted the Certificate of Sufficiency, and

8th, 2021. All ayes. Motion carried.
Mayor Hatem asked Ms. Trexler to approach the podium. She explained that Scott
Rogers left his position with the City, and he will be missed. But he spent the
