BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
223 E. BAY STREET  JUNE 28, 2021 at 4:30 p.m.
COMMUNITY BUILDING SOUTHPORT, N.C.

         Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Lora Sharkey, Lowe Davis,

Director      
Tom Stanley, Public Services Director

A)   Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special meeting to order at 4:35 p.m.
B)   Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
.D)   Approval of Agenda-
After a motion made by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and seconded by Alderman
Lombardi, the agenda was approved as it was presented.
Business
Mayor Hatem stated that the first budget amendment (#11) was to pay Brunswick
Electric for the work that was done installing the electrical underground on NC
211 Hwy. Melanie Trexler explained that this amendment was essentially a
formality because NCDOT has already agreed to pay the difference between the
estimate and the actual cost. The difference in cost was mainly due to a larger
bore that was unexpected. After a motion made by Alderman Allen and seconded by
Alderman Sharkey, the Board approved Budget #11.  All ayes. Motion carried.
Mayor Hatem announced that Budget Amendment #12 was for the Howe Street sewer
project. He asked Tom Stanley to explain the need for additional funding. Tom
Stanley, the Public Services Director, said that basically, there was an
underestimation of materials that would be needed to pave the road. Often, the
ditches were wider than anticipated, and there had been a couple of
interference manholes that required more work. The engineer for the project was
very short in his estimation. The new estimate is approximately 150% of the
original estimate. Tom Stanley said they are asking the Board for an additional
$250,000 to cover the difference in paving costs and the interference manholes.
Alderman Allen asked and it was confirmed that the additional funds would come
from the water/sewer fund balance. Alderman Allen also asked if Tom Stanley
thought that this would be the last unforeseen issue that would arise. Tom
Stanley said that he thought it would be the last issue with the project
planning, but that the underground is unknown. There might be other
interference manholes. He is particularly concerned about the area where the
hospital is located. He also knows that there is a manhole that was filled with
dirt. Alderman Davis asked if there was any updates on the date of completion
for the project. Tom Stanley said that he would love to say that it would be
finished July 2021, but it would more than likely be August 2021. After a
motion made by Alderman Allen and seconded by Alderman Sharkey, the Board
approved Budget Amendment #12, for the Howe Street Sewer project. All ayes.
Motion carried.  
Mayor Hatem applauded Tom Stanley, his department and the City Manager, Gordon
Hargrove, for being so resilient during this project and moving forward.
E.)     After a motion made by Alderman Lombardi and seconded by Alderman
Allen, the Mayor adjourned the meeting at 4:51 p.m. All ayes. Motion carried.

H.)   Agenda
   1.
   Mayor Hatem opened the public hearing at 6:28 p.m. to discuss the proposed
Short-Term Rental Ordinance. Mayor Hatem thanked the Planning Board and City
staff for their diligence. He said that it is crucial to protect our
neighborhoods and quaintness. The Mayor called on Thomas Lloyd to start the
dialogue. Mr. Lloyd stated that STR’s would be allowed, but only in certain
zoning districts. Existing short-term rentals in residential zoning districts
would be allowed to continue as lawful non-conforming uses, as long as they
obtained a permit within (60) days. If the use ceases for at least (180)
consecutive days, then it will not be allowed to resume its short-term rental
status. Several use standards are being applied: an emergency contact or
responsible party on-site or within (20) miles; the property owner must carry
at least $1 million in liability insurance; three violations of the ordinance
within one year will prevent the conforming short-term rental for operating for
a year; no storage of goods, no excessive outdoor lighting, signage, no
additional parking requirements, and no large gatherings or events can take
place at the dwelling. In addition, the dwellings are subject to the City’s
noise and other nuisance standards. An annual zoning permit shall be issued for
homestays and short-term rentals. The permits are valid from January-December.
 Alderman Lombardi asked how much the zoning permit fee would be and who would
be responsible for enforcing the ordinance? Thomas Lloyd said that the permit
would be the typical $100 zoning permit fee. He is already working on creating
a process using the existing permitting software. The Mayor opened the meeting
up to the public.
With the Business Alliance for a Sound Economy, Tyler Newman expressed concerns
about adopting a short-term rental ordinance. He asked the Board to consider a
few points: 1. There is no silver-bullet, once-size-fits-all ordinance, and
there are often staffing issues regarding enforcement; 2. Other ordinances
address the concerns that are raised-parking, trash, noise, and other
nuisances; 3. There is a financial need for short-term rentals in this day and
age. He urged the Board not to approve the amendment. 
Becky Felton, a citizen that resides at 230 N. Caswell Avenue, said that she
and her husband looked into buying the former Catholic church years ago. Other
dwellings surrounded it, and she never considered short-term rentals would
surround them. Neighbors have already moved out of the area because of the
number of short-term rentals in the area. She said that we do not need to
encourage more short-term rentals into the area.
John Beroset, a citizen who resides at 118 N. Atlantic Avenue, lives on a
portion of one of the original platted lots from 1792. He and his wife
originally moved to Brunswick County in 1994. They sold their home in St. James
and found a long-term rental house on Atlantic Avenue two years ago. Now they
love their neighborhood and home. They would not consider moving to an area
where there are so many short-term rentals. They did not want to live in a
beach community. He is concerned that the nature of Southport will be lost. He
said that he is not opposed to change, but it should be balanced with the
consideration of long-term effects and regulated accordingly.
Ginger Harper, who resides at 105 E. Bay Street, addressed the Board next. She
said that she has seen people come together more than ever before over the last
few years, especially through hurricanes, emotional upheaval, and the pandemic.
She commended the Board for their willingness to approach challenging issues.
She stated that unless you live in Southport, most people are unaware of the
general concerns in the community. These concerns include rambunctious
visitors, fighting, smoking marijuana, loud noises, and partying. She fully
supports the proposed ordinance. The citizens/residents will not be able to
keep their property values up if short-term rentals are allowed into the
community. The neighborhoods should continue to be filled with neighbors.
Melissa Hinnant, who resides at 303 E. 8 th Street, said she has lived here for
eight years. She said that there is more technology now. She used her home as
an Air BnB when she and her family were in a financial bind. She said that as
far as she could research, the crime increases have not been verified. She
feels like Southport can benefit from having short-term rentals because it
helps people financially take care of their families. She was concerned that
the City would be sued because of the amendment.
Casey Silar, who resides at 116 Stewart Avenue, stated that she used an
accessory dwelling in her backyard as a short-term rental when she lost her
job. She and her associates support their being standards and an ordinance, but
it needs to be reasonable. She feels that the sixty-day permit requirement and
the nonconforming-use clause are not reasonable. She asked the Board to
consider several factors: 1. COVID_19 prevented the ability of the public to
participate in the process of developing the ordinance; 2. Short-term rentals
were made into a scapegoat for other issues that are going on in Southport; 3.
Residents spoke in the public comment, but many people don’t realize there are
short-term rentals around them; 4. How does the City plan on enforcing the
standards?; and 5. Even the Planning Board did not vote unanimously for the
amendment. She would ultimately like for the Board of Aldermen to take more
time to discuss the issues.
Melaney Marshall Robbins read a statement to the Board that requested the Board
to discuss with companies like hers so the Board could understand both sides of
the issue truly. She requested that the Board take it back to the committee for
more discussion and include others in the decision and development.
Hugh Fosbury resides at 120 W. Moore Street and has lived in Southport for
eight years. He and his wife own a Bed and Breakfast, reside in town, and
manage a short-term rental company. He would like for the Board to consider
some questions before deciding. He wants to know how many short-term rentals
are being operated in town. Which zoning districts are the current short-term
rentals located? How will complaints be handled? And how many total homes do we
have in the City compared with the number of short-term rentals-what is the
percentage? Mr. Fosbury said that he does understand the need to prevent big
problems.
Rebecca Kelly, who resides at 5971 Dutchman Creek, stated that she grew up in
Southport and now lives here and is a business owner. She is the broker for a
realty office and operates the River Oaks Inn. Ms. Kelly had several questions/
comments that she asked the Board to consider. She said that a realtor cannot
guarantee that the zoning of a property will remain the same as when it was
purchased. So many people who are in favor of the amendment are complaining
that crime levels are increasing. Has this been verified? Have there been more
calls to the police department? All sorts of people in the City leave trash and
park illegally. How can you tell if it is a renter of a short-term rental
property, a resident, or a day visitor? The River Oaks Inn is not always fully
occupied, depending on the season. If it is vacant for (180) days, does it lose
the ability to be used as a rental property? Ms. Kelly said that the motion had
to be put before the Planning Board four times before someone moved on the
motion. She closed by saying that we are all a part of Southport. We need to
guide and support Southport towards appropriate growth. Several derelict
properties have been purchased and renovated and used as short-term rentals.
They have now become contributing properties with a higher property value.
Beth Hammonds resides at 506 W. Owens Drive. She said that there need to be
some standards for short-term rentals. She and her husband purchased a property
and renovated it. It is now a long-term rental. They are trying to save
cottages instead of tearing them down. The owners should have the right to
decide how to use their properties. The ordinance could be returned to the
committee and made fairer for everyone. She and her husband are not from here,
but they appreciate the history and charm of the area. They coexist well with
short-term rental properties and have not had any issues with short-term
renters. She asked the Board again to send it back to the committee to make it
less restrictive.
Rich Alt, who resides at 6165 Cottage Creek Road, had two questions for Mr.
Lloyd. He asked Mr. Lloyd to explain and identify what areas were zoned PUD.
And he also wanted to know if this document would supersede any Homeowner
Association policies. Mr. Lloyd said that an example of a PUD was Indigo or
Harper Lakes. And he stated that HOA restrictions were the prevailing rules for
any property.
Tracy Beaulieu was the final speaker. She resides at 206 W. Nash Street. She
stated that her neighborhood has a real problem with short-term rentals. People
are walking around using drugs, rummaging in people’s vehicles, and carrying
weapons. She said that she is hesitant to call the police because the people
might retaliate. She stated that the economy is thriving in Southport already.
If the area becomes unsavory because of all the transients using short-term
rentals, tourists will stop visiting. Mr. Beaulieu believes that the proposed
ordinance is fair.
Ms. Dutton, the City Clerk, read several letters and statements sent ahead of
the meeting from people who could not attend. Mayor Hatem closed the public
hearing at 7:57 p.m. He said that he appreciates everyone’s patience.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller thanked everyone for attending. She gave the following
statement in support of the proposed ordinance:
“There are cautionary tales from communities across the country that have been
affected by the relatively new internet-based Airbnb business model that began
in 2008. This business model has grown into a multi-billion dollar lodging
industry. Business changes at a much faster pace than a municipality.
To respond to the question that some have asked…Why does Southport need these
regulations and what are the policy objectives?
Our community’s core values can be found in the Southport CAMA Core Land Use
Plan. The CAMA Land Use Plan is the city’s strategic long range planning
document. Every land use decision and zoning change we make, must be supported
by this comprehensive plan.
Within the plan, on page 9, the city’s vision and core values are identified.
The City Planner, Mr. Lloyd included this in the statement of consistency to
support the proposed regulations. And it reads, “Southport desires to have an
affordable quality of life while maintaining its quiet residential atmosphere
and protecting the city’s historic assets…” and goes on to say, specifically,
Southport will endeavor to accomplish the following: 2 of the 5 core values
speak directly to the reasons for the proposed Short Term Rental regulations. •
Preserve the city’s historic character. • Preserve the city’s residential
areas.
On page 14, the plan recognizes that “Southport appears more like inland
Brunswick communities such as Shallotte or Calabash than a beach community like
Oak Island or Ocean Isle Beach…”. Again this speaks to our historic and
residential character as a small town not a beach rental community. And goes on
to acknowledge that Southport’s economy benefits from region-wide tourist
populations, and day-trippers from the surrounding communities.
Finally, summarized on page 149 are the nine general principles used to develop
the Land Use Plan. Four of the nine principles support the short term rental
regulations recommended by the Planning Board.
“The City of Southport Land Use Plan was drafted with consideration given to
the following:”
• “Southport’s Vision and Core Values”
• “Preservation of existing urban form” (And the character of Southport’s
historic residential neighborhoods is an important part of our urban form)
• “Limiting potential land use conflicts” (conflicts that could change our
character) and
• “Preservation of existing residential neighborhoods”
Clearly, Southport’s long range comprehensive plan directs us to preserve that
which makes Southport this unique small town community here at the mouth of the
Cape Fear.
Because of our location, here at the water’s edge, we are particularly
vulnerable to the changes that would make us become a resort town rather than a
community of neighbors.
I have an MLS sheet for a home in our old town area that Zillow shows as
recently sold. The first line in the realtor’s write up about the house. And I
quote, “TURN KEY Airbnb opportunity in the heart of Southport!”
Southport’s old town is an extremely small, densely populated residential area,
and the impact of land uses like whole house transient lodging dilutes the
residential character of the neighborhood.
The proposed Homestay accessory use allows permanent residents to generate
income by renting rooms while remaining a member of the neighborhood. Like the
Bed and Breakfast rules that require a full-time resident to be present.
The ordinance provides regulations that allow established legally operating
non-conforming Short Term Vacation Rentals in residentially zoned area to
continue to operate.
Southport’s successful tourism industry is not dependent on having Short Term
Vacation Rentals within the city’s residential neighborhoods. Southport is
surrounded by beach rental communities that provide Short Term Vacation
Rentals.
The quality of life in Southport in large measure depends on the residents who
live here. We have said over and over again, we are a city of volunteers. We
live much larger than most communities our size, because neighbors participate
and volunteer their time and talents to help make their community better. The
future of Southport, the community we love and our quality of life depends on
keeping the neighbor in the neighborhood.”
Alderman Lombardi stated that he had received a lot of calls and must support
the proposed ordinance.
Alderman Lowe Davis thanked everyone for speaking. She said that this was one
of the most complex decisions she has had to face, but she supports the
ordinance.
Alderman Lora Sharkey said that she reviewed the documents and has listened a
lot. She has looked at the Nags Head ordinance and the ordinance from Chapel
Hill. Those ordinances are not as stringent and allow more time to respond. She
questioned whether the Planning Board had worked with any experts from the UNC
School of Government. Alderman Sharkey had specific questions about property
owners who want to live in their dwelling part-time and use it as a short-term
rental the other portion of the year. Overall, she wonders if Southport is
overstepping our abilities. Alderman Sharkey stated that the Planning Board and
staff missed a valuable opportunity to collaborate with realtors and rental
property owners in the area. She said that she does think that registration and
limiting it to certain zoning districts are reasonable, but the proposed
ordinance is too stringent. Southport needs a reasonable and legal ordinance.
Alderman Marc Spencer thanked everyone for living in Southport and for
attending the meeting. He said that as everyone was talking about the character
of Southport, it was making his stomach turn. His grandmother had a tenant that
rented a room from her for a long time. Other people rented rooms in their
homes if they needed the income. In addition, his mother had a rental on VRBO
(Vacation Rentals By Owner) to hold on to their life-long home because of the
additional income it generated. He said he feels like it is an elitist view
that if you cannot afford a house in Southport, you don’t deserve to live in
Southport. If we all had jobs where people could afford to live here, they
would. He said that the people driving the ordinance are the same people who
spend half a year in Southport and live in France for the rest of the year.
Alderman Allen asked if City Attorney Mike Isenberg had reviewed the proposed
ordinance. Mr. Isenberg said that he had reviewed it and conferred with Rebecca
Badgett from the School of Government and a few other attorneys from towns with
similar ordinances. Mr. Isenberg stated that if there is a provision for
“grandfathering” the short-term vacation rentals that have been in operation
within the residential districts, that the term “have been in operation” should
be defined and he suggested that the short-term rentals will have to provide
verifiable proof of bookings before the date of the adoption of the ordinance.
He also questioned whether it was the intention of the ordinance to punish
people who may want to rent their property during portions of the year for
longer than (30) days. He suggested adding some language that occupancy of the
dwelling for longer than thirty (30) days by a renter, does not count as
discontinuation for the purpose of this ordinance. Alderman Allen made a motion
to adopt the Statement of Land Use Consistency and the Short-term Rentals
Ordinance, with the two changes recommended by the City Attorney. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller seconded the motion. Those in favor were Mayor Pro tem Mosteller,
Alderman Allen, Alderman Davis, and Alderman Lombardi. Alderman Sharkey and
Alderman Spencer voted against the Land Use Consistency Statement and Short-
term Rental Ordinance. Majority ruled. Motion carried.  
The Mayor dismissed everyone for a ten-minute recess at 8:26 p.m.
   2.
   The meeting was reopened at 8:42 p.m. The next item on the agenda was the
System Development Fees (SDF) for the marina’s new dry storage building. They
are ready for their building permit, but the SDF must be paid before issuing
the permit. The Mayor read the definition of System Development Fees. Gordon
Hargrove explained that there have been discussions about how to calculate the
SDF since the use is less than recommended. The owner of the marina claims that
at no point will all the boat slips be used. Mr. Hargrove said that are a few
options to consider: 1. Base the SDF on the number of parking spaces (54) for a
total of $15930.00; 2. Leave the rates/SDF as they are calculated using the
prescribed/studied rates; and 3. Adjust the entire rate schedule for peak daily
usage. But the study would be paid for by the requester. The marina owner, Mr.
Rose, explained to the Board his request for a lower SDF rate. He said that the
peak usage on all of his existing buildings/use is 4800 gallons per day. Mr.
Rose suggested the methodology used includes other amenities like swimming
pools. He proposed that because there is no water/sewer in his proposed dry
storage building, he shouldn’t have to pay any SDF. Mr. Rose thanked Mr.
Hargrove and Mr. Lloyd for explaining SDF to him. Mr. Hargrove asked about the
process when boats return to the storage area and whether the boats get rinsed
off before they are put back in storage. Alderman Sharkey said that the marina
is an excellent business. They have great employees and are great to the
community. But she said that all businesses need to be treated fairly. It
wouldn’t be fair to base the SDF on the parking spaces because all businesses
would expect that consideration. Alderman Allen said that a sprinkler system
still has to be serviced there at the marina and that the City just finished
working out a water allocation with Brunswick County. He suggested the fees
stand as calculated because there is no correlation between parking spaces and
boat slips. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller agreed that the City already had to
purchase more water allocation for the marina to get a permit. She is hesitant
to try to rewrite the SDF ordinance for one customer. Alderman Spencer said
that the marina is doubling its capacity. More information is needed about the
regular water use for the dry storage building and bathhouse. He said he
appreciates the marina and all they do for the community and hopes that a
compromise can be made.
Alderman Allen made a motion to charge the older SDF rate applicable when the
application was made. Alderman Sharkey seconded. Mr. Hargrove restated that the
City is not asking him to shut down his existing bathhouse, but the new renters
would not be able to use the amenity, or more SDF would be charged. Mr. Rose
said that he would have porta-johns placed on the property if needed. After the
motion and the second, the Board voted unanimously to use the old SDF rates.
Motion carried .

JULY 30, 2021
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
COMMUNITY BUILDING JULY 30, 2021 3:30 P.M.
223 E. BAY STREET  SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:      Mayor Joseph P. Hatem
         Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Lora Sharkey, Lowe Davis,
         John Allen, Marc Spencer, and Tom Lombardi
STAFF PRESENT:
Gordon Hargrove, City Manager         Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
Melanie Trexler, Finance Director         Tom Stanley, Public Services Director
OTHERS PRESENT: Carolina MacGregor, from the State Port Pilot, Richard Alt,
Robert Carroll, Tish Hatem
A)   Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special meeting to order at 3:31 p.m.
B)   Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)   Approval of Agenda-
After a motion made by Alderman Allen and seconded by Alderman Lombardi, the
agenda was approved as it was presented.
Business
   1.
   The Mayor summarized the purpose of the Special Meeting was to discuss a
change order to the Bay Street erosion repair project. Public Services
Director, Tom Stanley approached the podium to address the Board. He said that
once the stones were being dropped, he noticed the rocks were being placed at a
thirty-degree angle. The contractor came up with a different design that would
minimize the possible damage to the Bay Street and Waterfront Park area. The
new design would be more of a tabletop design. The rocks would be built 15-18
feet off the sidewalk and then would drop down to the shoreline. This design
gives the water a place to crash that would not be in the road. The water can
hit the rocks and dissipate down through the rocks. Under the new design, we
are 500 tons of rock short to complete the project. The difference in cost is
$75,000. The labor cost won’t increase.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked if the new design was recommended by the
installer, has been used other places? Tom Stanley, said that he is sure that
it has been used other places and that given the current status of the area, it
is the best design to protect us in the future.
Alderman Davis asked where the additional $75,000 would come from and Gordon
Hargrove explained that the money was already in the Capital Improvement Fund.
Alderman Spencer asked if there would still be a low-tide area and Mr. Stanley
said that there would. Alderman Spencer also asked about how urgently the
repairs are needed. Mr. Stanley said that it does not make sense to wait
because there were several sections that had collapsed. Hurricane season is
approaching, and we don’t know what will happen next time. Alderman Sharkey
asked is the new design would provide better protection for the area under the
pier than the original design. Tom Stanley said the new design was definitely
better for that area and the contractor is saving the smaller rocks to place
under the pier. Alderman Davis asked what the estimated completion date would
be, and Mr. Stanley said that it should be completed in two to three weeks.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked about additional FEMA financing. If FEMA
originally offered $330,000 to the project and with the prior design, were only
spending $314,000, maybe the City can request the difference. Tom Stanley said
that were already looking into that possibility.
Mayor Hatem asked if there were any questions from the audience. Robert Carroll
said he had one question. “
Mayor Hatem thanked Tom Stanley, Gordon Hargrove, and other staff for coming up
with this plan and getting projects done. After a motion made by Alderman
Sharkey and seconded by Alderman Lombardi, the Board approved the transfer of
$75,000 from the Capital Project fund to pay for the change order on the Bay
Street Erosion Improvement project, as presented. All ayes. Motion carried.  
E.)
After a motion made by Alderman Allen and seconded by Alderman Lombardi, the
Mayor adjourned the meeting at 3:57 p.m. All ayes. Motion carried.

   2.
   Mayor Hatem said the Street Light Committee has been working hard to get a
draft policy together. He asked Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller to begin her
presentation. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller provided the following comments:
“This update grew out of the recognition by the City Manager that the current
street light policy needed additional clarification.
For several month’s we have been working on updating the city streetlight
policy. Streetlights can be part of the health and safety of a community and an
important design element that contributes to the overall look and feel of a
community.
This is an important policy update that affects existing lights as well as new
subdivisions. … Article 4 in the UDO requires the subdivider of a major
subdivision creating new streets to install street lighting in accordance with
the city’s street light policy.
The Street Light policy update committee has been working for several months to
produce this draft. This is the first public meeting to review the proposed
draft, and we are looking forward to input.
Some general overall comments about the document…
The draft is consistent with Article 3.16 Lighting section in the UDO …
•   Identifying the maximum color temperature to be 3000 degrees Kelvin which
is a warm white. Also
•   Recognizing overhead light fixtures shall be designed to prevent light from
emitting upwards towards the sky.
The stated purpose of the draft is to reduce negative impacts on wildlife,
human eye sensitivity, and the natural beauty of the night sky while providing
light to enhance safety and the City's appearance.
We live in an environmentally sensitive coastal area, and while all artificial
light impacts wildlife, we refer to recommendations from the International Dark
Skies Association, a non-profit recognized as leader providing support and
technical assistance for policymakers.
International Dark Skies recommendations help mitigate the effects of exterior
lighting.
The draft includes a list of approved fixtures and a map identifying the
locations for the types of fixtures. Fixtures that are consistent with Dark
Skies certification.
The draft also clarifies the responsibilities of the city regarding maintenance
and operation of streetlights on city-maintained roads.
And clarifies the city responsibility regarding streetlights in communities
like Rivermist. When Rivermist was developed, the city decided to allow
Brunswick Electric to be their provider of electricity.
While Rivermist has city-maintained roads, they are unique because the city
does not provide their electric service, and the HOA pays for all the
streetlights starting with J. Swain Blvd.”
Alderman Sharkey stated that the policy intended to address who is responsible
for maintaining the streetlights. The style used downtown will not change, but
the color of the light is proposed to change. Intensity can be addressed
differently. People don’t want yellow lights in their neighborhoods. All
neighborhoods should have access to having the City maintain their lights as
long as it is a City Road.
Alderman Davis said that she has surveyed all of the lights in the City, and
there is a wide variety. The blue-white lights are very harsh on the eyes. The
“yellow” lights are not really yellow, they are just a warmer light. We will
not overhaul all of the lights in the City at one time, but we want to have a
guide in place moving forward, as things need to be replaced. At the Hammocks
subdivision, there are several different intensities and kelvins installed for
comparison. Alderman Davis encouraged the public to use the map and drive
through the Hammocks to see the different kinds of lighting.
Mayor Hatem asked the Clerk to call the first name on the list to speak, and
Harley Lemons was called and approached the podium. Mr. Lemons, who resides at
6228 Navigator Way, stated that he served on the homeowner’s association for
the Landing, and he has also served on many City committees. It was recently
discovered that the Landing was getting billed $200 a month for lighting. The
HOA is waiting for reimbursement from the City. He said that nonconforming
lights are still confusing, and he isn’t sure who is responsible for the
lighting in those areas. He said that it seems that areas zoned PUD (Planned
Unit Development) are treated differently and not like a residential area.
Glen Price, who resides at 6142 River Sound Circle, thanked the Board, Mayor,
and Manager. He stated that he lives at the Landing. He was at a Board meeting
a few months ago addressing the stadium-style lighting in front of his home. He
hopes to go through the Hammocks to see the lighting tests that were set up. In
2013, when his family moved here, the coastal community feel was most
appealing. They toured the City during the day and in the evening. He said that
the natural beauty was preserved at the Landing.
Wayne Deutscher, who resides at 1015 Softwind Way, said that he lives where
light “Example B” is located, and he said it was the brightest light ever. The
Hammocks subdivision is in transition between the Developer passing control
onto the homeowner’s association. After speaking to others in the subdivision,
there was a consensus that light “Example D” was the best. Mr. Deutscher said
that he was on the Board when he lived in St. James. They were spending close
to $300,000 on streetlights a year in St. James. He said that he was confused
because the Hammocks subdivision will have to apply to the City to take over
the streetlights.
Adam Steadman asked if he could speak, even though he had not signed in for
comments. He had addressed the Board a few months ago about streetlights. He
has read through the proposed policy and recommends changing the policy to
state that replacements must be 3000 kelvins or less. He recommends using 2700
kelvin bulbs if they are available. He stated that he agrees with some of
Alderman Sharkey’s comments and some of the information that Alderman Davis and
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller presented. Mr. Steadman suggested that the language be
changed so that HOA neighborhoods are treated the same as non-HOA
neighborhoods. Any property owner close to a streetlight should have input on
what type of light is used, not just in HOA neighborhoods.
Alderman Lombardi stated that in Rivermist, where he resides, a streetlight is
so bright that the house closest to the streetlights doesn’t have to use its
inside lights in certain rooms.
Alderman Sharkey thanked Mr. Deutscher for attending the meeting and providing
a more substantial community opinion. She agrees with Mr. Steadman that the
opinion of a homeowner should be considered as much as an HOA. She hopes that
the Streetlight Committee can make appropriate changes and get it back to the
Board for adoption.
Mayor Hatem said that it would be taken back to the committee and revised as
quickly as possible. He encouraged the public to continue sending comments.
Alderman Allen said that street lighting is such a complex topic, he would like
to schedule a Board workshop to understand everything more thoroughly.
Rebecca Kelly, from the audience, stood and suggested that a survey be created
through Survey Monkey so that the whole town can participate. Alderman Davis
agreed that the City needs to get as much information out to the public as
possible.
   3.
   The Mayor opened the public hearing at 7:09 p.m. to discuss the annexation
request for 1304 N. Howe Street. The parcel is a 0.38-acre tract owned by
Oceanside Holdings LLC. The owners would like access to City utilities and do
not have to be rezoned since it is currently in the ETJ. At the last Board
meeting, the Board accepted the Clerk’s Certificate of Sufficiency and set the
public hearing for August 12, 2021. Appropriate notice was given. Alderman
Spencer stated that he works with one of the applicants, and there is no
conflict of interest, but he wanted to make sure that he was allowed to vote.
City Attorney, Mike Isenberg, said that he was allowed to vote. The Mayor
closed the Public Hearing at 7:12 p.m. After a motion made by Alderman Allen
and seconded by Alderman Spencer, the Board approved the annexation of the
property at 1304 N. Howe Street (Par ID# 221MB018) and the annexation
ordinance, as presented. All ayes. Motion carried.  
   4.
   Alderman Sharkey was asked to introduce the next agenda item, the Alderman
of the Month program. The program would allow each Board member the opportunity
to open the meeting twice a year. The Alderman can invite a guest to do the
invocation, act as the greeter for the meeting, or take more of a leadership
role during the meeting. It provides a sense of purpose and allows the public
to get to know the Board better.
Alderman Allen stated that the meetings are fine without the program and
doesn’t see the need to reinstate that program. Alderman Spencer said that the
program was beneficial because it “forced” him to give the invocation. He
thought it would be nice to be able to bring people into the meeting. Alderman
Davis stated that she didn’t see how it would increase attendance at the
meetings. She said that she has never had any problem adding things to the
agenda as long as they are brought up ahead of time. Alderman Davis said that
she is opposed to it because it adds a whole other level of bureaucracy for
City staff. She sees no real benefit. Alderman Lombardi commented that he was
not aware of the program until recently. He feels like he has enough
opportunity to speak already between the reports and comments. He doesn’t feel
the need to reinstate the program.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller stated that she thinks “it is more inclusive if the
Mayor keeps a list of all the Churches in Southport and the ETJ and invites one
each month rather than us individually asking someone. Seems a more effective
way to be inclusive. That is all that occurs to me. The Board Comments agenda
item gives us the opportunity to speak directly to the Board and citizens about
experiences or issues in the community.” She does not see the need to use the
program.
Alderman Spencer commented that right now, the Board has the opportunity to
speak at the end of the meeting with their comments. This program would allow
the Board members to greet the public, recite the Pledge of Allegiance and act
as a leader. A motion was made by Alderman Spencer and seconded by Alderman
Sharkey to approve using the Alderman of the Month program. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller and Aldermen Allen, Davis, and Lombardi all voted opposed to the
motion. The motion did not carry, and the Alderman of the Month program will
not be reinstated.
   5.
   Mayor Hatem read a portion of a letter from the NC Governor, Roy Cooper,
regarding the American Rescue Plan funds. Then he called Melanie Trexler to the
podium to explain the proposed ordinance. The state requires that a separate
fund be created to track how the ARP funding is used appropriately, with the
state guidelines. The Board has not yet determined what to spend the funding
on, but Alderman Sharkey pointed out a deadline to confirm how the funding will
be spent. City Manager Hargrove explained that the first part of the program
funding would be spent on the sewer expansion project. The second part of the
funding will likely go towards sewer processing. After a motion made by Mayor
Pro-tem Mosteller and seconded by Alderman Spencer, the Board approved the
Capital Project Ordinance for the American Rescue Plan funding. All ayes.
Motion carried.

AUGUST 31, 2021
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
COMMUNITY BUILDING AUGUST 31, 2021 5:00 P.M.
223 E. BAY STREET  SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:      Mayor Joseph P. Hatem
         Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Lora Sharkey, Lowe Davis,
         John Allen, Marc Spencer, and Tom Lombardi
STAFF PRESENT:
Gordon Hargrove, City Manager               Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director         Tom Stanley, Public
Services Director
Todd Coring, Police Chief                  Ralph Treadway, EMS Battalion Chief
Randy Jones, Tourism & Comm. Director         Lisa Anderson, Asst. Director
Tourism & Comm.
Kate Marshall, Animal Protective Services         Tony Burke, Major, Police
Department
Sgt. Wigmore, Police Department               Sgt. Moore, Police Department
OTHERS PRESENT: Carolina MacGregor, from the State Port Pilot, Richard Alt,
Robert Carroll, Tish Hatem, Rebecca Kelly, Jennifer, and Arthur Fontaine, Larry
Ashley, Lois Gandy, Judy Tharp, Will Hewitt, Katie, William, and Andrew Boyd,
Cailtin Marks and Keith Eason with the NCDOT and several other concerned
citizens.
A)   Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special meeting to order at 5:02 p.m.
B)   Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance. Mayor Hatem asked
everyone to remember the people in Louisiana with the effects from Hurricane
Ida, as well as the people in Afghanistan.
D)   Approval of Agenda
After a motion made by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and seconded by Alderman
Lombardi, the agenda was approved as it was presented.
E)    Town Hall/Workshop Agenda
   1.
   Mayor Hatem welcomed Caitlin Marks and Keith Eason with the NCDOT. He
explained that the first portion of the meeting was for the public and Board
members to mingle and ask the NCDOT representatives and the Police Department.
There are two tables set up in the lobby with officers, and they can review
some of the data gathered regarding speeding in the City.
   2.
   Mayor Hatem encouraged everyone to find their seats. He asked Police Chief
Coring to begin his presentation. Chief Coring said that the Police Department
had received many phone calls and emails regarding speeding, stop signs, too
many stop signs, reckless driving, etc. They have City-wide complaints, not
just specific areas. Once a complaint is lodged, the officers go out and
observe the area and often use the radar to observe speeds. The Department uses
two different pieces of equipment to obtain information. The speed trailer is
older, but it reads the speed and counts traffic. The information is logged and
can be extracted to look at the overall picture. The other equipment is a
message board that clocks speed. This device also counts traffic, keeps track
of the day and time, and helps create percentage charts. Chief Coring has
spoken to the Highway Patrol, and they similarly do their speed observations.
The speed limits in the City range from 15-35 miles per hour. The Southport
Police Department is comprised of thirteen officers. Southport is essentially a
small town with big town problems. The Department reviews the data and tries to
figure out where they can best place resources. Bay Street is one of the
biggest attractions in the City. Out of 11,000 vehicles that were logged, only
0.03 were going at least ten miles over the speed limit. On Park Avenue, which
is between Leonard and Moore Streets, 12,000 vehicles were logged, and 6% of
those vehicles were driving at excessive speeds.
The Police Department tries to focus on safety. They also are proactive through
education programs like “Schools In, Speed’s Out.” During the Howe Street
construction project, it was necessary to create four-way stops in some areas,
which seemed to decrease excessive speeds. Mayor Hatem asked what the threshold
was for speeding before traffic control devices would be installed. Chief
Coring said that he is unaware of a threshold or recommended limit, but he
would reach out to the NCDOT for suggestions. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller stated
that Park Avenue and Stuart Avenue had been problems for a long time. She would
like to see some traffic control devices installed as a test and for the Police
Chief to bring the results back for them to review.
Alderman Davis said that the speed limit in many residential areas is 25 miles
per hour. She thinks that is too fast for a residential area. Park Avenue
residents are concerned. The chart provided indicates that over 50% of vehicles
were speeding between May 21-May 24th. She suggests the City install some
devices since we don’t have the personnel to manage all the streets all of the
time. Alderman Lombardi recommended installing more stop signs to slow people
down. Alderman Sharkey suggested that because of the stop signs, some people
might be speeding to get through the intersection since they have to stop. She
suggests waiting until Howe Street opens up and collecting at least a weeks’
worth of data to see if that helps reduce the speeding problems. Chief Coring
thanked the Board for their time.
   3.
   Mayor Hatem introduced Tom Stanley, and he approached the podium. Mr.
Stanley stated that the topcoat on Howe Street should be done on Wednesday, and
then hopefully, it will be opened to the public by the weekend. Mr. Stanley
said that the Board members all have a street ranking sheet. The list is not
engineered; staff road around and ranked the streets from 1-10. Once Howe
Street is opened up, they will be able to better look at the secondary streets
and any damage that has occurred. He recommends that the secondary streets that
were used during the detours should be repaired next. His staff is not equipped
to fix potholes. Most of the roads in the City have no base under the asphalt.
Road edges are being taken over by grass. Funding is needed to overhaul the
streets and bring them up to where they need to be. Alderman Lombardi said that
he wishes the City could have a small crew of 3-4 people to do nothing but work
on roads. The money would be saved in the long run. Alderman Spencer asked
Alderman Lombardi how long he thought it would take to repair all the roads?
Alderman Lombardi suspects that it would take years because they need to be re-
formed and paved correctly. Based on the Powell Bill information provided,
there are 28.34 miles of roads that the City is responsible for. Mayor Hatem
and Tom Stanley mentioned that there are several orphaned roads in the City,
too. Mayor Hatem asked if there was a mechanism in place or guidelines for
starting to fix the roads? Alderman Lombardi said that there was an alternative
to paving, called chip-seal. But to use that method, the road has to be in
decent condition to start. It would extend the road for 7-8 years, which is a
third of the cost. Chip-seal uses a thin layer of heated liquid asphalt first,
followed by a layer of chips or stones. Tom Stanley recommended using chip-seal
on E. Nash Street to start since there is a lot of traffic on that road.
Alderman Lombardi offered to help get someone to speak with Mr. Stanley about
the process.
   4.
   Mayor Hatem asked Chief Coring to come back to the podium to discuss
pedestrian safety. Chief Coring said that more pedestrian crosswalks are
needed, for sure. He primarily sees a need around the downtown area and as far
out as St. George Street. The water tower area needs more crosswalks, and the
yacht basin area is an area of concern. Alderman Allen stated that in 2014, the
City had a comprehensive pedestrian plan that lays out a plan for adding
crosswalks and new sidewalks and prioritizes each project. There was a lot of
work done in that plan, and the City should start working on it. Alderman Davis
asked if the plan was available to the public, and Alderman Allen said that the
plan was on the website. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked if using a street as a
“through-street” was ticketable and if it can be enforced? Chief Coring said it
could be addressed, but the City would have to adopt an ordinance.
F)    Public Comment
City Clerk Dorothy Dutton read a letter submitted by D. Scott Crook, who
resides at 118 Park Avenue. He stated that the disparities in street
maintenance are unacceptable. Stuart Avenue, W. West Street, Park Avenue,
Turtlewood, and Jabbertown Road are all “cut-through routes.” The people that
live on those streets are not able to enjoy their neighborhoods. They are
afraid to “walk for exercise, take their dogs for a walk, or ride a bicycle.”
In addition, only one of those streets has a sidewalk. Mr. Crook proposes speed
tables be installed because increased law enforcement isn’t feasible. In the
past, Mr. Crook has provided engineering studies to the Board and City Manager.
As proven in Decatur, GA, Clintonville, OH, and many European cities, speed
tables are effective. Several years ago, the former City Manager quoted $1250
for each speed table. Some of the residents of Park Avenue have offered to
contribute financially to the installation of speed tables. Mr. Crook
encouraged the Board to tackle this issue before anyone gets hurt.
Ms. Dutton called Ms. Jennifer Fontaine up to address the Board. Ms. Fontaine,
who resides at 5223 Shipmast Way, said that this meeting has been great because
she was unaware of all of the small steps the City has taken to improve
transportation. Mrs. Fontaine wants to emphasize walkability and safety. She
encouraged the Board to chip away at it. While she appreciates that the Board
has not raised the taxes, she quoted the old adage, “A penny wise and a pound
foolish.” Not too long ago, she went into a pothole, and it ruined her tire.
She said that the sides of the roads and the structure of speed bumps are
critical to making this a lovely community.
Ms. Dutton called Katie and William Boyd, residents at 828 N. Caswell Avenue,
to speak. Mrs. Boyd stated that she doesn’t think that all transportation
problems are because of the Howe Street project. She said that the City has
enforcement issues and construction woes. She came into the office and spoke to
Tori Deviney and Dorrie Dutton to get information about all of the new
developments planned for the area around Caswell Avenue. She said that it is
hard to ride a bike because the sidewalks and the roads are not good. Her cat
was hit by a car by a speeder that didn’t even stop. Her son, William, cannot
ride his bicycle to school because there is too much traffic. She closed by
saying that action is needed, not just more talking. William Boyd expressed
similar frustration about the conditions of the roads and sidewalks. He said
that he doesn’t feel safe riding his bike to school, even though he was looking
forward to going into his 5th grade school year. Mayor Hatem said that he was
very proud of William for speaking to the Board at such a young age.
Next, Ms. Dutton called Andrew Boyd, who resides at 828 N. Caswell Avenue, to
speak to the Board. He said he understands that large trucks must drive down N.
Caswell, but the large trucks are not covered, and all sorts of debris fly out
all the time. He has called the non-emergency line and complained many times.
He read a portion of a state regulation that requires that dump trucks must be
covered or that the height of the load is at least six inches below the top of
the truck walls. The drivers of the trucks should be held accountable.
Larry Ashley, a resident at 637 Wild Rose Way, addressed the Board and stated
that crosswalks were most important. He said that they connect across streets
and that sidewalks should line up when possible. He also suggested that the
City invest in a striping machine so that parking spaces, handicapped spaces,
and crosswalks can be clearly marked.
Ms. Dutton called Lois Gandy to speak. She resides at 5961 Spikerush Trail. Her
main concern is safety, especially for kids. She has lived here for sixteen
years and would have never thought it would grow as it has. The side streets
seemed dangerous before, but more so now with the construction. Southport is a
wonderful community, but we must keep it safe. She thinks that the speed limits
should be lowered to twenty miles per hour. She likened the yacht basin area to
a festival. Her suggested slogan was, “Slow down; it’s Southport.”
Lastly, Judy Tharp, resident of 230 River Drive, was asked to speak to the
Board. Her husband handed out a PowerPoint to the Board members. Her focus was
primarily on the Yacht Basin area. She explained that she and her husband fell
in love with the yacht basin area years ago. There are 4-5 iconic venues in
that area. Many people complain about the tourists and pedestrians in the area,
but that road looks more like a walking path than a road. She remembers
occasions before the Covid pandemic when tour buses would drop people off at
the yacht basin area. Adequate parking is an issue, too. People often park
along Brunswick Street. But then they are in danger of slipping off into the
marsh. When Bay Street and Yacht Basin Drive were made into a one-way road,
traffic increased onto Brunswick Street.
Mrs. Tharp has several suggestions that she and her husband feel would benefit
that area. First, she thinks Moore Street should be made into a one-way street.
That would make a loop and would probably reduce the number of one-way
violators. Ms. Tharp also stated that “No Thru Traffic” signs should be
installed on Brunswick Avenue. And finally, she suggests marketing the yacht
basin area as an official scenic old yacht basin that encourages pedestrian
traffic primarily. She said that the area’s natural beauty should be showcased.
Ms. Tharp thanked the Board for the opportunity to speak.
There was no one else who requested to speak.
G)    Adjourn
Mayor Hatem thanked everyone for attending and participating in the meeting. He
said that the City would be working on compiling all of the presented
information and would start implementing the plans as soon as possible.
After a motion by Alderman Lombardi and seconded by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller,
the Mayor adjourned the meeting at 7:06 p.m. All ayes.

                     Joseph P. Hatem, M.D., M.P.H.
                     Mayor, City of Southport

   1.   Lora Sharkey read through the Proclamation in Recognition of the Adopt-

H.) Agenda
   1.
   Mayor Hatem invited Chad Kimes from the NCDOT to address the Board with
project updates and information about the CASSI program. Caitlin Marks
distributed a packet of materials. Alderman Davis asked if the materials were
available to the public, and Mr. Kimes said they would be made available soon.
Mr. Kimes explained the process for project selection. He reviewed several
ongoing and funded projects that will take place soon. NCDOT is currently
working to improve the flow of traffic moving away from Oak Island. Portions of
NC-211 will be made into a 4-lane road. US-16 Highway will have a lot of
improvements throughout Brunswick County to South Carolina. Two bridges on NC-
133 will be replaced to help alleviate flooding.
   CASSI is a fully electric trolley that can be programmed for specific
routes. It has been tested out at Kill Devil Hills, and Southport is another
possible testing site. The trolley will host 5-6 people comfortably. Alderman
Davis asked if the route could be changed once it had been programmed. Mr.
Kimes stated that it could be changed. He said that there were a few things to
figure out first. A 20% match would be required from the City. Currently, CASSI
is restrictive. The trolley can only make right turns and has a low maximum
speed. There is a two-foot sensor buffer around the trolley, so branches and
limbs must be cleared along the route. Alderman Lombardi asked if there were
any plans to install electric car charging stations. Mr. Kimes stated that he
was not able to answer that question. If Southport participates in the trolley
test, it would likely run from November through January.
   Mr. Kimes stated that two areas were identified as needing crosswalks-Davis
and Moore Streets. There are two possibilities moving forward. Concrete bump-
outs are better for pedestrians but cost around $124,000. The other option is
to paint the crosswalks without the bump-outs. That option is around $15,000.
If the City wants to move forward with the concrete bump-outs, the project will
have to wait for funding. Page 32 of the handout is the contact information for
NCDOT. Mr. Kimes said that Board members are welcome to contact Caitlin or
himself any time. Mr. Kimes also provided his cell number. He said that
Brunswick County is one of the fastest-growing counties in the state. Ms.
Rebecca Kelly asked if it was safe to have both of our major thoroughfares be
closed at the same time? Mr. Kimes said that the NCDOT would plan and plan for
any possible evacuations. Mr. Kimes said that they would meet with the City to
discuss any plans regarding the subdivisions that have been discussed. Mr.
Kimes also explained that “letting” means to go out for bids.
   Mayor Hatem thanked Mr. Kimes and Ms. Marks for attending the meeting and
providing updates.
   2.
   Mr. Hargrove stated that the City staff would like to finance the entire
cost of the two fire trucks with Truist. Truist is offering 1.42% interest for
five years. The total being financed is $824,210.00. After a motion made by
Alderman Allen and seconded by Alderman Spencer, the Board adopted the
Resolution in Support of the Financing terms with Truist, as presented. All
ayes. Motion carried .
   3.
   Mayor Hatem stated that next on the agenda was the Development Agreement
with Osprey Landing. The site plan and rezoning have already been approved.
This development agreement addressed utility connections and annexation
periods. Mayor Hatem opened the public hearing at 7:13 p.m. Mr. Thomas Lloyd
explained that this type of agreement is expected in projects this size.
Agreements can be a good tool for all parties involved. The development
agreement lists the uses that are entitlements on the property, establishes an
expiration date. Voluntary annexation is required within (30) days from when
the final plat is approved and recorded. The deadline for all of Phase 1 to be
recorded is June 2022.
   Attorney Mike Isenberg reiterated that the agreement has nothing to do with
density, layouts, etc. The developer has (12) years for complete build-out. The
County will provide water and sewer, but the City will get the tax base.
Alderman Allen asked what options the City has if they fail to file for
annexation? Mr. Isenberg stated that they would breach the contract, and we
could force the annexation by asking for an injunction. The agreement is a
legal contract. The only actual cost to the developer is if a lot isn’t sold,
they will be responsible for the taxes. Alderman Allen stated that the
developer has (15) years for build-out. And Mr. Isenberg stated that the
developer could also break the phases into smaller phases if needed. Mr.
Isenberg also stated that the development would be connected to the sewer line
on Howe Street. The Mayor closed the public hearing at 7:24 p.m. The agreement
was arranged between the developers and their attorney and the City staff and
attorneys. Alderman Sharkey commented that this agreement provides more
oversight than they usually get. Alderman Davis stated that she had not been a
fan of this project or the impacts on the adjacent neighborhoods from the
beginning. The developer made it clear that they were unwilling to work with
the City on traffic impacts, alternate ingress/egress, setbacks, and buffers.
She is voting in favor of the agreement now only because she thinks that it is
the only way to make the best of a bad situation, and it will lessen the cost
for the City and increase tax revenue. After a motion made by Alderman Sharkey
and seconded by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller, the Board approved the Development
Agreement with Vanguard Farms/Osprey Landing. All ayes. Motion carried.
   4.
   Gordon Hargrove explained that at the last Board meeting, staff was asked to
review the penalty applied to 6099 Turtlewood Drive and make a recommendation
to the Board. The Crumplers were assessed a penalty of $4000 based on removing
trees and vegetation without obtaining a permit in advance. Mr. Hargrove
explained three options: eliminate the fine, reduce the fine or leave the fine
as it stands. The permit process was delayed for a few days because the
permitting software was not working. But the Crumplers didn’t try to obtain a
permit until City staff issued a violation. The Crumpler’s have already paid
the fine, but the check was not deposited because they appealed the penalty.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller offered the following comments:
“In the UDO, article 2.6 B 2 regarding the zoning permit process clearly
states, it shall be unlawful to commence site preparation or excavation for the
construction of any building, including site disturbance and tree removal until
a zoning permit has been issued.
Under the Tree Protection and Landscape Preservation section, Article 3.18 B
states that part of the purpose of tree protection is to prevent the
indiscriminate removal of trees.
Clearly, a violation was committed, and there must be consequences for clearing
a lot and removing trees without a permit.
The UDO was updated last year to provide safeguards and consequences because
the originally adopted tree ordinance language fell short. Under the old
language, when a vacant lot was cleared and trees were removed without a
permit, the fine was only $100. Not much of a consequence. One developer
cleared three lots right after Hurricane Florence and was fined $300.
I certainly appreciate the frustrations that can be associated with building a
new house however, work must not be done without the required approvals and
permits.
I thank staff for the detailed summary of the events, and I support staff’s
decision to enforce the ordinance.”
   Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller thanked the Manager for the detailed summary and
made a motion to support the decision to uphold the ordinance. Alderman Davis
and Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. Alderman Allen suggested reducing
the fee to $3,000. Ms. Mosteller said that issues arise all the time, but the
ordinance should be upheld. Alderman Davis commented that Southport has an
excellent tree protection ordinance. There might have been only two or three
trees removed in this instance, but they still should’ve waited for the permit
first. During the last meeting, the owner “asked for forgiveness.” Alderman
Davis suggested that was an admission of guilt. Alderman Spencer made a motion
to waive the fee entirely. There was no second made. Alderman Spencer stated
that it is interesting that people can buy a property but don’t own it. He said
that property rights get stepped on every day. Alderman Davis said, “That did
not make any sense to her because that would mean we would not have any
zoning.” Alderman Spencer did not reply. The Mayor asked for a vote for who was
in favor of leaving the penalty in place, as it was issued. All ayes except for
Alderman Spencer. Motion carried 5-1.
   5.
   City Manager Gordon Hargrove reminded the Board about the request to reduce
System Development Fees for the dry storage building proposed at the marina.
The original calculation was $63,000, but that was calculated as a wet slip
area. City staff met with McGill and Associates, who recalculated the fee based
on a transportation hub with two people per unit. The proposed fees are now
$15,930.00. Alderman Allen asked if their sprinkler system was included in the
calculation. Mr. Hargrove stated that there was no way to include it because we
don’t include it for other users. Mike Isenberg stated that the original amount
was not correct and that the engineer and staff that were involved all
recommended using the $15,900. After a motion made by Alderman Sharkey and
seconded by Alderman Allen, the Board approved the revised System Development
Fee of $15,900.00 for the marina’s proposed dry storage building. All ayes
except for Alderman Davis. Motion carried 5-1.
   6.
   Alderman Davis stated that the Forestry Committee had received two
applications for appointment. Interviews were conducted. Both candidates were
impressive, but the Committee would like to recommend that the Board appoint
Jerry Donaldson. He expressed more depth of knowledge and policies. The
Committee would also like to reappoint Peg Ingalls for a new term . After a
motion made by Alderman Davis and seconded by Alderman Lombardi, the Board
appointed Jerry Donaldson to the Forestry Committee and Peg Ingalls to a new
term with the Forestry Committee. All ayes. Motion carried.  
   7.
   Mayor Hatem explained that the next item for consideration is a resolution
exploring a merger between County and City utilities. Mayor Hatem said that he
favored regionalization instead of the City building a new wastewater facility.
Gordon Hargrove added that the resolution would support our application for
grants to further study a merger's feasibility. The City needs to improve our
system to the point that the County will take over and possibly assume the debt
associated with improvements that the City has tied up in the system. Alderman
Allen asked how likely it would be that Southport would be awarded a grant. Mr.
Hargrove said that he is under the impression that as long as we get everything
turned in on time, it is a slam dunk. After a motion by Alderman Allen and
seconded by Alderman Lombardi, the Board adopted the Resolution in Support of
Exploring a Merger of City and County Utilities, as presented. All ayes. Motion
carried.

Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller reported:
“During the public discussion about streetlights at the last meeting, it was
decided that we would plan a street light policy workshop for a more in-depth
look at the proposed draft policy.
Some may know that Brunswick Electric had previously set up a demonstration in
the Hammocks neighborhood before the last meeting; however, Brunswick Electric
re-located the P-30 3000 kelvin light in the line up to a different
neighborhood.
We can all agree that street lighting is a design element that is very
important to the look and feel. And to make the future street light workshop
more productive, before the workshop, the city will create a new demonstration
that includes three light fixtures; all P-20 model fixtures in different color
temperatures 4000, 3000k, and 2700 kelvin.
The demonstration will be an opportunity for citizens to evaluate the same
fixtures with varying color temperatures for input to help finalize the policy
selection. The city had to order two of the lights as they are not stocked by
Brunswick Electric, and the delivery will be about six weeks.
As soon as the demo lights are installed, the city will notify the website to
let us know the location. Once the demonstration is active, we can then
schedule the workshop.
In the meantime, citizens may reach out to Alderman Davis, Alderman Sharkey, or
myself with any questions or concerns regarding streetlight policy.”

OCTOBER 12, 2021
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
COMMUNITY BUILDING OCTOBER 12, 2021
223 E. BAY STREET  SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:   Mayor Joseph P. Hatem
   Mayor Pro-
tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Lora Sharkey, Lowe Davis, John Allen,
Marc Spencer, and Tom Lombardi
STAFF PRESENT:
   Gordon Hargrove, City Manager
   Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
   Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director
   Tom Stanley, Public Services Director Todd Coring, Police Chief
   Ralph Treadway, EMS Battalion Chief Randy Jones, Tourism & Comm. Director
   Kate Marshall, Animal Protective Services
OTHERS PRESENT: Robert Carroll, Tish Hatem, Rebecca Kelly, Vickie Potter,
Rhonda Davis, Paul, Marie Swenson, and many family
members and other concerned citizens.
A.)   Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special meeting to order at 6:02 p.m. He explained that
this special meeting was scheduled to discuss and receive citizen input on the
pedestrian corridor in the Yacht Basin area.
B.)   Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C.)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D.)   Approval of Agenda
Mayor Hatem said there was no need to discuss the additional
committee recommendations at this meeting, but otherwise, the agenda would
remain the same. After a motion made by Alderman Allen and seconded by Alderman
Lombardi, the agenda was approved with the change as presented.
E.)   Town Hall/Workshop Agenda
   1.
   Mayor Hatem summarized that there are two options for a pedestrian
walkway. Option A places the walkway on the land side, and Option B is on the
waterside. Alderman Allen was asked to lead the discussions. He said that the
committee was a mix of property owners, citizens, himself, and Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller. The committee identified problems and current conditions at the
Yacht Basin. While they realized that the plan would never be perfect for
everyone, they developed reasonable solutions. Their focus was on
traffic patterns and safety.
   The committee was in consensus with some elements. They agreed that Yacht
Basin Drive and Bay Street should remain one-way streets. The pedestrian
walkway is essential, and the City should take full advantage of its existing
20-foot right of way. The committee also agreed to use thermoplastic markings,
build a raised planting area on Moore Street, add lighting, and reduce the
speed limit. Alderman Allen explained that Option A utilizes the current one-
way traffic pattern, but Bay Street would have to shift a bit to meet
Yacht Basin Drive. At the intersection of Bay St. and Yacht Basin Dr., the
pedestrian walkway would shift from waterside to landside. Option B would be
the same expect the pedestrian walkway would continue on the waterside through
the Yacht Basin area.
Option B would require more improvements at that intersection.
   Alderman Allen stated that both plans are approximately the same cost. At
some point in the past, the right of way was paved about 4-feet from where it
should be. That will have to be addressed when improvements are made.
   Mayor Hatem asked Police Chief Coring to talk about when and why the traffic
pattern was changed about a year ago. Chief Coring stated that a restaurant
owner suggested the one-way traffic pattern at the Yacht Basin. Bay Street was
made a one-way road for a while. When the traffic went back to normal, the
public contacted the Police Department and preferred the one-way traffic
pattern. The majority of people enter Bay Street and ride the length of the
street towards the Yacht Basin. Mayor Hatem commented that in May 2020,
City officials were concerned about crowding and waiting for restaurants. They
even considered closing a portion of Bay Street. Chief Coring said that it is a
complex area to navigate. He is grateful that there have not been any injuries
at the Yacht Basin, only some fender benders. Some people have requested to
completely close Yacht Basin drive to vehicle traffic, but that would make it
too difficult for people who are disabled to access the area. Chief Coring said
that as a reminder, anytime there is standing water on the road, drivers have
the legal authority to stop and turn around regardless of the
traffic pattern. Safety is first.
   Alderman Sharkey asked if the committee considered having the pedestrian
walkway on the landside beginning at the intersection of Caswell, so the road
would be open for vehicles towards the restaurants. Alderman Allen stated that
the committee considered every option. The biggest challenge is that the
sidewalk on Bay Street is on the waterside. Alderman Sharkey asked about the
status of the parking overlay district. Alderman Allen said that the committee
is still working to develop a plan. A resident who is a landscape architect is
currently working on a plan; and the concept continues to evolve.
   Alderman Davis said that she was glad to see that the City was seeking input
from the community. She suggested that the City reach out to a transportation
expert at a state university for assistance. Sometimes these situations seem
like unsolvable problems. She said that it is incredible that we have gotten
this far without any pedestrian accidents.
   She is very interested to hear what the public has to say. Alderman Allen
said that he hoped that one benefit of
having the parking overlay district would be to pull traffic off of Yacht
Basin Drive.
   Alderman Lombardi said that he thinks the pedestrian walkway should be
placed on the waterside. He suggested changing traffic so that people on Moore
Street have to turn right instead of continuing towards Fishy Fishy Café. That
would reduce traffic from people who are just driving through. The pedestrian
walkway would be striped but level with the road. Alderman Allen stated that
the City would not have to acquire any new right-of-way. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller said that Alderman Allen had done a great job presenting the
information. She wants to emphasize that the City will take full
advantage of our existing rights-of-way.
   Mayor Hatem asked Gordon Hargrove to speak about the funding for this
project.
Mr. Hargrove stated that during the last budget meeting, the Board created
a Capital Projects Ordinance. This year there was approximately $125,000
allocated for this project. Mr. Hargrove said that the options range in price,
but staff is just waiting for the Board to decide.
   Alderman Allen said that he wanted to point out that the first two projects
listed in the Capital Project Ordinance were already completed.
F.)   Public Comment
   1.   Paul Swenson, 
   who resides at 107 N. Atlantic Avenue, approached the podium to comment. He
is also the owner of Provision Company, a restaurant at the Yacht Basin. He
said that the current situation is the price of success. During the high
season, there are probably
3000 people that visit a day. There is no simple solution. He and his family have been there for thirty
years. He doesn’t know of any pedestrians that have been hit or even any
accidents.
The blessing is that there are so many pedestrians that the vehicles cannot move very quickly. Mr. Swenson
suggested that the City have the Yacht Basin area surveyed to identify the
right-of- way correctly. He has seen the clay sewer pipes, and they are not
going to last forever. He said that the sewer line could be replaced at the
same time as the pedestrian walkway was installed. He would like to see the Bay
St. 10-feet wide, but people will walk in the road regardless. Mr. Swenson
suggested that the City add 2-3” of paving to help prevent the road from
flooding. And he would also like to see the walkway concrete or more than just
using striping. He also suggested the City install some solar lights. Mr. Swenson said that he doesn’t think
the City has enough money to do this project the best way; these improvements
will be a band-aid.
   2.   Maria Swenson,
   who also resides at 107 N. Atlantic Avenue, approached the podium. She said
that she thinks the City treats the Yacht Basin businesses like a “red-headed
stepchild.” The Yacht Basin is a huge moneymaker for the City. She said
that even more problems would develop with the landside walkway. There are
stormwater issues. Mrs. Swenson said that she
does appreciate what the community has done and that the Aldermen are considering improvements. The City is
growing, and we need to grow forward with positive changes.
   Mayor Hatem agreed that the infrastructure has to be in
place to support the businesses in the Yacht Basin.
   3.   Debbie Barnes,
   who resides at 425 W. West Street, prefers the walkway on the waterside. She
said that putting in a walkway doesn’t mean that people are going to use it.
She
would like to see some painted crosswalks in the area. Mrs. Barnes suggested changing the direction of
traffic in the Yacht Basin. She said that people can’t turn left to go back
towards
the restaurants when people travel down Moore Street. When drivers have to turn right and go all the back around, they tend to get frustrated. There are a lot of pedestrians on Brunswick Street. Between
Short Street and the marina, there is a 20-foot-wide roadway and there aren’t
places for people to step off the road to make room for vehicular traffic.
She suggests sending the one-
way traffic pattern in the other direction. Then vehicles from Moore Street could take a left and drive past all
of the restaurants. There is more visibility at Bay Street for traffic signs
indicating one- way traffic. There is also flooding at the Yacht
Basin. It is safer for the drivers and pedestrians if traffic shifts to the
other direction.
Mayor Hatem said that he now sees that there are more options. The one thing
they want to do is to preserve the existing heritage and businesses in the
Yacht Basin. Alderman
Lombardi asked if there was an accurate survey of the area? Gordon Hargrove stated that Tidewater
Surveying will put markers out for now, and we could get a complete
survey done. Alderman Davis remarked about how expensive surveys are. Alderman Allen
said that the Board needs to figure out what they want to do first and then the
survey. He added that there are probably areas in the Yacht Basin that have eroded and muddied along the way,
making it impossible to figure out ownership.
Alderman Sharkey suggested that once a consensus is made, at least the striping
should be done in time for spring, even if the City can’t afford the whole
project at one time. Mr. Hargrove asked Tom Stanley to speak on that topic.
Public Services Director Tom Stanley said that thermoplastic striping is
expensive. He suggests that the Board should definitely decide which plan they
want first, so the money isn’t wasted.
In terms of a timeline, Mayor Hatem said the project wouldn’t start until after
the
wooden boat show. We will come back together during a Board meeting with another public comment period before making a decision. But we would like to have it open before the springtime and tourist season.
G.)   Adjourn
Mayor Hatem thanked everyone for attending and participating in the meeting. He
said that the City would decide what is best for the community and get it
