H.)   Agenda:
Mayor Hatem stated that the news reporter at the State Port Pilot and welcomed
Elliot Duke to the meeting.
   1.
   The first item of business was a presentation by the Brunswick County
Homeless Coalition. Joe Staton, a representative of the organization, provided
a brief history of the group. The coalition began in 2011 after a group of
people attended a social justice meeting. Their vision is that instances of
homelessness in Brunswick County will be brief and rare. During the first half
of 2021, they helped 158 clients. There is no permanent shelter in Brunswick
County, so they often have to use hotels and shelters in other counties. That
makes it more difficult when there are school-aged children. The coalition
maintains a hotline for people to call when they are in need. They need
volunteers of all sorts-answering phones, fundraising, administration, or
personal service. If anyone is interested in volunteering, they can contact a
current volunteer or look online at brunswickhomeless.com.
   2.
   Mayor Hatem introduced the next agenda item. Each year, one way the City
shows its appreciation to staff is by providing a holiday bonus. This year, it
is proposed that full-time employees net $500 and part-time employees net $250
after taxes. After a motion made by Alderman Spencer and seconded by Alderman
Sharkey, the Board approved the holiday bonus pay as presented. All ayes.
Motion carried.
   3.
   Mayor Hatem opened the first public hearing at 6:26 p.m. This hearing was to
consider the rezoning of Parcel ID 221MD01011 from R-20 to R-10. Thomas Lloyd
explained that the parcel was undersized for the R-20 zoning district, but it
was an existing lot. Mr. Lloyd went on to describe that the property is
adjacent to both R-10 and R-20 zoning districts. Even though they are both
residential districts, the dimensional standards are different. The Planning
Board considered the rezoning at their meeting in October and were concerned
that the rezoning would negatively affect neighbors because of the change of
required setbacks. In addition, they felt that the rezoning was beneficial to
only one party, not the community's greater good. The Planning Board found that
the request was not consistent with the Land Use Plan and recommended that the
Board of Aldermen deny the request.
   The applicant, Cindy Waseleski, explained that she and her family, including
her and her husband, sister’s family, and their mother, reside in Weaverville,
NC. When visiting, they found the property at 110 Highland Park Avenue and
thought it was the perfect place to build a house. They planned to start
building the home in spring 2022 and had the property surveyed. The surveyor
mistakenly indicated that the parcel was zoned R-10 but found out from Thomas
Lloyd that it is zoned R-20. They hope to build a single-family dwelling and
also an accessory dwelling to reside. They found a floorplan that has just the
right amount of space, but the structure would be a bit too close to the
property line to meet the setback standards. Ms. Waseleski has signatures from
the neighbors on both sides, indicating they do not have any problems with the
rezoning. Close by to the property in question is the subdivision the Oaks at
Highland Park. That subdivision was assigned R-10 zoning when it was approved.
Since much of that area is already zoned R-10, Ms. Waseleski didn’t think there
would be much contention. Her family needs a one-story home with a separate
accessory dwelling. Mayor Hatem closed the public hearing at 6:39 p.m. Alderman
Sharkey asked about the existing homes in that area and how far the homes are
set off the road. She also suggested that other parcels in the area get rezoned
at the same time. Mr. Lloyd said that was feasible if the Board wanted to
pursue that. Alderman Spencer asked what might have caused the two zoning
districts in that area? Mr. Lloyd suggested that the original zoning map was
initially correct, but over time, the lines got shifted because of GIS
shapefiles, and it is possible that these parcels were annexed at some point.
After a motion made by Alderman Davis and seconded by Alderman Allen, the Board
adopted the resolution stating the rezoning request was not consistent with the
Land Use Plan. Alderman Allen said he certainly sympathizes with the request
but doesn’t think rezoning is the best solution. He would be open to pursuing a
rezoning of all of the adjacent properties at the same time. There was some
discussion about the ordinance standards and whether there was a way she could
get a waiver of some sort. Mr. Lloyd said that this circumstance wouldn’t
qualify for a variance. She asked what her next options were if the request
gets denied. Attorney Mike Isenberg said that she could build a house there but
follow the required setbacks. She also has the option to try to get the other
adjacent properties to rezone to R-10. Alderman Sharkey recommended that Mr.
Lloyd contact the other property owners in the area to see if they are
interested in rezoning. She said that it seemed to be a mix-up if all of the
lots were the same size. Mayor Hatem thanked everyone for participating. He
reviewed the motion made by Alderman Davis and seconded by Alderman Allen to
approve the resolution denying the rezoning request. Ayes given by Alderman
Allen, Alderman Lowe Davis, Alderman Tom Lombardi, and Mayor Pro-tem Karen
Mosteller. Aldermen Sharkey and Spenser did not vote in favor of approving the
resolution. Motion carried 4-2.
   4.
   Mayor Hatem opened the public hearing at 7:01 p.m. to discuss the rezoning
of a ten-acre tract at Southport Crossing from PUD to Highway Commercial.
Thomas Lloyd explained that the Planning Board reviewed the rest at their
September and October meetings. The Planning Board discussed infrastructure,
and the future land use plan specifies that commercial development should be
located at intersections of major thoroughfares. The current developer wants to
add another anchor store to the shopping center. Site plans would have to be
approved separately. The public hearing was closed at 7:10 p.m. Alderman
Sharkey made a motion to adopt the Land Use Consistency statement and the map
amendment, as presented. Alderman Lombardi made the second. All ayes. Motion
carried.
   5.
   Mayor Hatem opened the public hearing at 7:13 a.m. to consider the revised
tree preservation tex amendment. The Planning Board reviewed the tree
preservation ordinance over the last few months and has made some changes. The
name of the permit will be changed to Tree Impact Permit. Under the new
amendment, a tree removal permit will be required for each lot, not as a whole
subdivision. 80% of lots are to be left untouched before development.
Mitigation requirements have also been replaced. Understory cannot exceed 50%.
A minimum of 25% live oaks and canopy trees is required for replanting. Rebecca
Kelly approached the podium and asked for clarification about what trees must
be used if a live oak is removed. Ms. Dutton read the letter submitted by Scott
Len, who serves as Chair for the Forestry Committee. The civil penalty for
removing trees without a permit is $1.00 for every square foot of the parcel.
Commercial violations are $2.00 per square foot of the parcel. During the last
Planning Board meeting, they decided to approve the resolution in support of
the statement of land use consistency and recommend approving the text
amendment regarding tree preservation. Alderman Davis said that the UDO is a
living document and suggested that the Board adopt this amendment, for now,
understanding that changes and additions can be brought back to the Planning
Board in the future. Mayor Hatem closed the public hearing at 7:33 p.m. After a
motion made by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and seconded by Alderman Davis, the
Board adopted the Resolution in Support of the Land Use Consistency Statement
and the proposed text amendment with the following changes:
      D.   TREE IMPACT PERMIT
2.   For previously platted residential lots or one or two-family residential
uses, a tree impact permit shall be required to remove or conduct any
development within the critical root zone of any protected, regulated tree
located within any setback and for a protected specimen tree located anywhere
on said property.
      E.   EXCEPTIONS
1. The UDO Administrator may waive the requirements of this section during a
city-declared state of emergency in accordance with NCGS 166A-19.322.
      F.   TREE PLAN
3.   For residentially zoned vacant lots or one and two-family residential
uses, the tree plan to be submitted as part of the permitting process shall
include a hand-drawn sketch, rendering, or copy of an existing plat or survey
of the property indicating the location of those regulated or specimen trees
proposed to be removed, as well as any trees proposed to be planted as
mitigation (if applicable).
         (a).   TREE RETENTION REQUIREMENTS PER LOT SIZE UNDER IN THE R10, R20,
MF, AND PUD ZONING DISTRICTS
            1.   3,000 sq ft - 1 broadleaf canopy tree
            2.   6,500 sq ft - 2 broadleaf canopy trees
            3.   11,000 sq ft - 3 broadleaf canopy trees
            4.   14,000 sq ft - 4 broadleaf canopy trees
            5.   20,000+ sq ft - 5 broadleaf canopy trees
   All in favor were Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and Aldermen Davis, Lombardi, and
Allen. Aldermen Sharkey and Spencer voted against the amendment. Motion carried
4-2.
   6.
   Mayor Hatem opened the public hearing at 7:46 p.m. to discuss a text
amendment that would allow outdoor storage and displays overnight in the
highway commercial zoning district. Paramount Engineering sponsored this text
amendment. Paramount Engineering is representing their client, a large agri-
supply store chain. Mayor Hatem closed the public hearing at 7:51 p.m. Alderman
Sharkey said he has no problem passing this amendment, and Mayor Pro-tem
agreed. After a motion made by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and seconded by Alderman
Lombardi, the Resolution in support of the land use consistency statement    
and text amendment, as presented. All ayes. Motion carried.

E)   Town Hall/Workshop Agenda
Mayor Hatem thanked the City Manager and staff for providing the important
content. Technology was a priority of the previous Board, and additional media
plans are underway. Mayor Hatem encouraged the Board to think about serving the

everyone for attending. He said that the Board has a lot of decisions to make
to set Southport in the right direction. The City must set some goals and look
out onto the horizon and current conditions. We all want to preserve
Southport's heritage by carrying forth its culture and history. These Board

   1.   Ms. Dutton began her presentation by speaking about the council-manager
form of government. Based on GS 160A-148(2), the city manager shall direct and
supervise the administration of all departments, offices, and agencies of the
City, subject to the general direction and control of the council.
   2.   Ms. Dutton reviewed the duties, responsibilities, and best practices of
the Mayor, Mayor Pro-tem, and Aldermen. These include ensuring that resources
are adequate to serve the public, regularly reviewing the government's
finances, programs, and services, respecting local government employees, and
following the appropriate protocols for interacting with staff.
   3.   Ms. Dutton reviewed some background on the City Manager and Department
Heads, including their roles and responsibilities.
   4.   Finally, the City Clerk reviewed the City charter, financials, and
planned projects. She discussed the importance of maintaining a strong fund
balance and the current budget.

G.)
   Mayor Hatem called the meeting back to order at 11:32 a.m. Ms. Dutton
addressed the Board     with information about how to amend the City charter.
There have been some discussions about changing the Mayoral term to four years
instead of the two-year terms that are in effect now. There was some discussion
between Board members about the benefits of a longer-term, including
continuity. Ms. Dutton explained that there are essentially two methods to
change the charter. The easiest method would be to adopt a resolution
requesting the General Assembly to consider changing the charter. If he agreed
to proceed, the staff at the state level would write the local bill for the
City. Staff has already been told by our State Representative,     Charlie
Miller, that he wouldn't take it straight to the General Assembly. He prefers
the City place the topic on the ballot at an election first and let the people
decide. If the public votes     in favor of the change, the General Assembly
would likely amend the charter. The other method to change the charter is for
the Board to adopt a resolution describing the proposed amendment. A public
hearing must take place no more than (45) days after the resolution is adopted.
Then, not more than (60) days after the hearing, the Board may adopt an
ordinance amending the charter. The ordinance should state whether the public's
vote is required or not. If a public vote is not required, and the Board adopts
the ordinance, there is a petition     that the public can file opposing the
amendment. For the amendment to pass, 10% of registered voters, or 5,000
people, must vote in favor.
    Ms. Dutton explained that this process would be valid for any charter
change that the Board    wanted to make, such as ending the two different wards
for voting purposes.
    There was more discussion about which method would be best and whether the
public would have any concerns about extending the mayoral term.
H.)

for essential workers; revenue loss; and infrastructure improvements. Alderman
Davis asked Mr. Hargrove if he had any suggestions. He stated that the

Alderman Allen said that it would be nice if the Board came to a consensus

Alderman Allen said we should replace the water lines on Howe Street when NCDOT

And the sooner that Southport upgrades the utilities, the sooner we can hand

would be eligible to receive the funding. Alderman Allen said he would like to
see each employee receive $2000 and the balance spent on infrastructure. There
was a discussion about when the City will find out about     possible grant
funding. Mr. Hargrove stated that it is his understanding that when the County

I.)
     Mayor Hatem called the meeting back to order at 12:55 p.m. and called City
Manager     Gordon Hargrove to the podium. Mr. Hargrove stated that the
pandemic has changed the world we live in. The labor market is one area of a
significant amount of change. There is a shortage in the labor market, and
salaries have become more competitive. The City Clerk gathered a lot of
information from the NC League of Municipalities and other similar communities.
Southport is unusual because we have such a large tourist population at times.
Southport hosts about 4000 residents and closer to 20,000 during any given
summer day. Based on the information collected, Southport is more competitive
than expected. There are still a few deficient positions. Not to mention that
inflation is driving up the cost of everyday goods and services. Southport
needs to be able to attract and retain top-shelf talent. Local     government
is never going to be competitive with private industry. But there can be
adjustments made that would help defer the rise of inflation. Alderman Lombardi
added that if Southport is going to attract people to come to the City, we will
have to pay people. Alderman Alt said he would like to see what the increase
would look like and where the money would come from. Mr. Hargrove said that it
would depend on the salary of each staff member. Mayor Hatem added that we have
to find a way to meet the market so our employees are not losing 6-7% from
inflation. We want our staff to be happy working here. Alderman Allen asked if
Mr. Hargrove had any recommendations for the positions that were already below
average. Mr. Hargrove said that he suggests doing a salary study internally
with the amount of information we already have. The City can go ahead and make
some adjustments on those few deficient positions now and then look at the
extra percentage that     would bring Southport to a more competitive level and
cover the inflation rate. He suggests somewhere between 6-10% across the board.
Alderman Allen said that the salary increase would be covered in the next
budget cycle. Mr. Hargrove added that we want to be good stewards of citizens'
money, but we also need to maintain a certain level of service.
    Mayor Hatem mentioned that the Board and Manager discussed Merit pay last
year. He is interested in moving forward with merit pay and cost of living
increases due to inflation. Mr. Hargrove stated that merit pay would be awarded
to those who score highest during     performance appraisals. Training goals
and progress will be reviewed, and increases will be based on staff scores
overall. These performance appraisals are also a way to identify and
potentially remove less valuable employees. Mr. Hargrove said that the scoring
mechanism places people in categories. If a staff member continuously falls
into the bottom third quadrant, they would potentially be let go from their
position with the City.
    Mr. Hargrove stated that the administration had hoped that State
Representative Charlie Miller would be available at the beginning of the
meeting, but his schedule did not match up. Mr. Miller is now present and would
like to answer any questions the Board might have.

K.)
     Revenue Generating Ideas: City Manager Hargrove asked the Board to think
about how much revenue a one-cent tax increase would generate. He said he was
surprised that it wasn't more, but the increase would only generate an
additional $108,829. He said that the residents expect a certain level of
services, but it is getting more expensive to provide those services. It might
be time to consider other alternatives for generating revenue.
      1.   City Manager Gordon Hargrove said that he wanted to provide a
30,000-foot view of paid parking for the Board. He passed out a packet of
information that Major Burke provided. It will be a complicated topic because
many of the City's parking is on state roads. The NCDOT has been challenging it
in some areas. Specifically, we have a lot of parking in encroachment areas.
Paid parking will generate some revenue, but would the cost of operating the
equipment outweigh the revenue? Alderman Carroll said we would focus on
encroachments regardless of paid parking. Mr. Hargrove thanked Alderman Carroll
for bringing that topic up. Mr. Hargrove explained that addressing
encroachments will be a Board decision that will be political and financial.
Alderman Davis suggested that the topic of paid parking be turned over to an ad
hoc committee that would make a recommendation. Alderman Carroll said that the
parking issue is bigger than just whether the City should use paid parking. He
would like to find ways to educate people about where parking is located. And
he would like for City residents to have a parking decal. Alderman Alt asked if
the Southport Police Department has the authority to write parking tickets? Mr.
Hargrove stated that the Police Department did not write parking tickets.
Writing tickets fall under Code Enforcement. Mr. Hargrove said that paid
parking is the ideal way to monetize visitors that come to Southport. Alderman
Carroll said he would like to see a committee do more research and make sure
that City staff isn't taking parking away from residents or tourists. Alderman
Allen said that it takes a lot of staff time and money to dive into the topic
and develop solutions fully. The City has a lot going on right now, and he
thinks that we need to prioritize.
      2.   Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director, approached the podium
to speak about accommodations taxes. Mr. Lloyd said that the City Manager asked
him to    overview the occupancy tax and the history here in Southport. Mr.
Lloyd said that there is no general authorization to collect occupancy tax.
Local acts give authorization. If a local government wants to use additional
taxes, we have to get permission or authority. In 1989 House Bill 615
authorized a 3% occupancy tax. In 2001 House Bill 668 authorized the City to
levy an additional 2%. If the City levied more than 3%, the state would require
the City to create a tourism authority that would dictate how the funds could
be spent. And the funds can only be spent on    marketing, commercials, market
research, or increasing the use of lodging facilities or convention centers.
Alderman Lombardi said that it looks like the 1% meals tax might be the best
path for generating revenue.
      3.   Mr. Thomas Lloyd defined motor vehicle tax. The tax can be assessed
on any self-propelled motor vehicles registered in the City limits. Any City or
Town can collect between $5.00 to $30.00 per vehicle and be used for specific
purposes, including paving. $5.00 of the tax levied can be used for general
public purposes. Anything more than $5.00 must be spent on public, City-
maintained streets. Mr. Lloyd said that currently, Leland charges a $30.00
motor vehicle tax. Boiling Springs Lakes charges $25.00 per vehicle, and the
funds are used for paving projects. Boiling Springs Lakes makes about $135,000
annually for street projects, and they have approximately 5400 vehicles.
      4.   The City Manager asked the Board if we needed money to repair
streets and correct the stormwater issues, how much money would the City need?
The Board guessed between $25-50 million dollars. Mr. Hargrove said that we
need a holistic fix. If we acquired a general obligation bond, we would have
the money upfront to fix things upfront and pay for it afterward. The roads in
Southport are not getting any better, and    the process will only cost more in
the future. We can bond about $50 million based on the recent audit.
Installment financing is the most common type of borrowing. This method of
financing includes purchasing vehicles or equipment.
L.)
      Mayor Hatem thanked everyone for attending and participating in the
meeting. He said that there was a lot of information provided today. Thanks to
the City Manager and staff for organizing everything. Today was the first of
several workshops. After a motion by Alderman Allen and seconded by several
other Board members, the Mayor adjourned the meeting at 3:13 p.m. All ayes.
Motion carried.

   1.
   Thomas Lloyd approached the podium to review the Lookout Point Major
Subdivision. There was a copy of the plat shown on the Vibe Board. Although it
was hard to see from far away, it gave a general idea of the subdivision
request. Mr. Lloyd stated that the property is at the end of Lookout Point and
is owned by the Harper family. The applicants are asking to subdivide the
parcel into two lots of varying sizes. Water and sewer are already serving the
property. Mr. Lloyd stated that typically this would be a minor subdivision,
but because the applicants want to extend the road, it triggered a major
subdivision. With the addition of the cul de sac, the road frontage requirement
is met. There are special flood hazard areas and coastal wetlands on the
parcel. The applicants' project manager explained that the construction would
be outside those areas. And the applicants are working with all of the
associated agencies, including CAMA. The Planning Board recommended approving
the subdivision at their December meeting.
Alderman Lowe Davis asked the neighboring or adjoining property owners had been
notified. She said that she is reluctant to approve the subdivision without
their input. Alderman Allen clarified that it is an existing right of way.
Alderman Lombardi asked Mr. Lloyd if the neighboring properties have a say on
the matter? Mr. Lloyd said that they do not. And there is no requirement for
the neighboring properties to be notified. Attorney Mike Isenberg states that
except for the addition of the cul-de-sac, it is like an administrative
decision. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked if emergency services had approved the
turning radius.
Alderman Allen made a motion to approve the Lookout Point subdivision as
presented. Alderman Lombardi seconded. All ayes except for Alderman Davis.
Alderman Davis stated again that even though it is not required by law, she
thinks it would have been wise to notify the neighbors. Motion passes 5-1.

   6.
   City Manager Gordon Hargrove reviewed the status of water rates with
Brunswick County. The new rates were effective January 1st. As a wholesale
customer, our rates have increased by 80%. The increase is because of the
reverse osmosis plant and the expansion of the sewer plant. Without a rate
increase in Southport, the City would not have enough revenue to cover the
increases. The focus of the new rate schedule is on tiered use and
conservation. Mr. Hargrove asked Finance Director Melanie Trexler to explain
the possible rates. Ms. Trexler said that the conversation to increase rates
first came up about four years ago. Now the City has to cover the expansion of
the sewer project, the reverse osmosis plant, and the increase in our cost. Our
projections have to be revamped. We have to cover our operating expenses and
our debt service payments. Several months ago, the rate committee started
analyzing the gallons included in the base rate. Now, instead of including 3000
gallons in the base tier, there are only 1000 gallons included. The less water
used, the less financial impact on the customer. Many projects need funding,
such as the closing costs of the sewer plant expansion, the reverse osmosis
plant, hurricane infiltration, a new truck needed in public utilities, and
investing in infrastructure. There has to be capital to cover those projects.
Ms. Trexler explained that she used the rate calculators at the UNC
Environmental Finance Center. If we don't raise our rates, the City will be in
the negative for the next several years.
Alderman Alt asked why irrigation rates were increasing when the wastewater
doesn't have to be processed? Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller explained that irrigation
is more of a luxury. It was 61% of the regular water usage. We have to have
drinking water. Increasing the irrigation rates helps to encourage
conservation. Alderman Alt said that he finds it confusing that the City is
trying to plant trees and encourage beautification projects, but we are
increasing our irrigation rates. Ms. Mosteller explained that the increase has
got to be somewhere. We need money for all of the capital projects and reserves
to work on other projects. Alderman Alt said that he understood better now;
these proposed rates keep rates for drinking water from increasing so much. He
asked why the City never joined in the lawsuit with Brunswick County for the
GenX contamination. Attorney Isenberg replied that any financial payments for
damages would not funnel down to the City. Alderman Allen reiterated that the
City doesn't have standing.
Attorney Isenberg asked Ms. Trexler to clarify the chart included in the Budget
Amendment. The first category was mislabeled; it should've had the heading
'FY22.' He said that was just a clerical error and doesn't change the substance
of the ordinance, so it was okay to proceed.
Alderman Allen said there are a few points to reiterate because all of this
information can get convoluted quickly. The City has to increase our rates
because the County has raised their rates because of their projects. There is a
cost with it. The sewer rates are increasing because the wastewater plant cost
has increased to $30 million. The rate committee did its best to balance out
the increases among the residents' usage. It is projected that water usage will
decline because of more efficient appliances and conservation. Alderman Davis
thanked the rate committee for all of their hard work. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller
said that this process was a combination of science and art. There was no real
formula. Staff and the rate committee will have to monitor the changes
quarterly to ensure that everything stays balanced and the tiered system works
well.
Mayor Hatem said it seems simple, but it is actually very complicated. Every
municipality has increased its rates because of the County's projects. All
customers-residential, commercial, nursing facilities, are being affected.
Alderman Allen made a motion to adopt the budget amendment and new utility rate
fee schedule as presented with the clerical change to the heading in the chart.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. All ayes.
Motion carried.

   Withers-Ravenel and the Development Planning & Financing Group (DPFG) have

the second phase of Indigo will have on the City. Withers-Ravenel will focus
more on the impacts on the City's infrastructure, and they will create a cost-

Withers-Ravenel has estimated their cost would be $42,750.00.
DPFG will focus more on fiscal, economic, feasibility, and benefit-cost

Alderman Allen said that he is grateful that staff is moving forward on these
analyses. He is aware of both companies, and they are top-notch. After

Then she read the following statement:
   "Starting February first, the new rate structure will represent significant
increases in water and sewer bills for homes and businesses that have higher
levels of utilization.
A few years ago, we started funding the Neighbors-4-Neighbors program to help
neighbors with financial challenges and reduce the monthly impact of the
increased water and sewer rates.
This fund is administered through the Brunswick Family Services non-profit. I
would like us to review the number of citizens participating to make sure this
resource is being utilized. We should also see if we can raise the amount
offered to our citizens and to see if the qualifying income can be raised.
For example, the guidelines for the CARES ACT funding to determine income
eligibility is higher than other data I've seen.
It is important that the available funds are utilized to the extent possible,
and I would like to ask the City Manager to facilitate a review with Brunswick
Family Services of Southport's Neighbors-4-Neighbors program and make
recommendations if, within the budget, eligibility can be broadened, or the
amount of aid could be increased."
Adjourn
Mayor Hatem said that it had been a good meeting. These meetings are the only
time when you typically see the full Board. Thanks for all of the hard work
that goes into the Board packets. He stated that the article in the State Port
Pilot was shocking, but we move forward. After a motion made by Alderman Davis
and seconded by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller, Mayor Hatem adjourned the meeting at
8:20 p.m. All ayes. Motion carried.

Mayor Hatem asked Development Services Director Thomas Lloyd to review the next
agenda item. Mr. Lloyd said that he was providing an update on the Brunswick
County Comprehensive Transportation Plan status. The plan addresses the
potential transportation needs of the County and the municipalities in the
County, based on expected growth and development. The plan provides multi-modal
maps identifies deficiencies and proposed improvements. It also considers the
local needs for the various areas, but it is not fiscally constrained. The 20-
30 plan addresses long-term goals that will help us apply for grants and ask
for funding from the NCDOT. Once the study is in draft format, the Board will
be asked to review the plan and adopt the plan for the City of Southport. The
last time information was provided to the Board was before the survey to the
public. There were over 7000 surveys submitted, which was the most public input
that NCDOT has ever seen from a CTP plan. Once the draft plan is complete, it
will be available online for the public, and notice will be sent to the public.

Mayor Pro-tem made the following comments: The Rate Committee will be meeting
on March 2nd, 2022, at the Indian Trail Meeting Hall at 11:00 a.m. “The process
to update the Parks and Recreation and Open Space Master Plan has begun. The
staff has contracted with Dr. Jim Herstine to lead this effort. Dr. Herstine
served as a professor in Parks and Recreation and has recently retired from UNC
Wilmington. Dr. Herstine was the subject matter expert for our previous master
plan.
Besides the obvious need for planning, one of the important reasons we need to
update the Parks and Recreation and Open Space Master Plan every five years is
grant applications. There’s a lot of competition for grant money, and grants
are typically awarded on a point system. For example, North Carolina’s Parks
and Recreation Trust Fund, known as PART-F, awards 20 points to a grant
applicant for having a current Master Plan. In part, Southport was able to
compete and was awarded a PART-F grant for over $400,000 to do the Phase One
Taylor Field project because PART-F credited our submittal with 20 points for
having a Master Plan.
Citizen participation is critical for the success of the master plan update
process. Surveys will be sent by mail to the residents of Southport, and you
will be able to return your completed survey by mail or complete it online. Our
Parks and Rec Director, Heather Hemphill, asked me to emphasize the importance
of completing the survey. There will also be public workshops with discussion.
Again, citizen input will drive the success and outcome of this process and the
planning goals in Southport’s 2023 to 2028 Parks and Recreation and Open Space
Master Plan.
With regard to the streetlight committee, the city has received the
demonstration streetlight fixtures, and the installation is scheduled for
tomorrow. The demonstration will include P-20 model fixtures in different color
temperatures 4000, 3000, and 2700 kelvin.
Once the installation is complete, we will put a notice on the City website to
direct citizens to the demonstration location, so everyone will have an
opportunity to see the differences in the color temperatures and consider
preferences. The demo lights will be labeled A, B, C, and D and will be the
first four streetlights on Southwind Way off of Stuart Ave. in the Hammocks
neighborhood.
During the previous public discussion about streetlight policy, we decided that
we would plan a workshop for a more in-depth look at the draft language in the
streetlight policy update.
There will be one more streetlight committee meeting to re-address comments
from the last public discussion, and then we will schedule the workshop. Both
meetings will be noticed on the City website, and the public is invited to
participate.
In the meantime, citizens may reach out to Alderman Davis, Alderman Carroll, or
myself with any questions or concerns regarding streetlight policy.”

BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL WORKSHOP MINUTES
COMMUNITY BUILDING FEBRUARY 17, 2022
223 E. BAY STREET  SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT: Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Tom
Lombardi, Lowe Davis,  John Allen, Robert Carroll, and Rich Alt
STAFF PRESENT:

Mayor Hatem called the special workshop to order at 9:03 a.m. He welcomed
everyone in attendance and those watching virtually.

Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.

Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
Mayor’s Opening Comments
Mayor Hatem said many topics would be discussed today, including electric
services with BEMC, Bee City USA, pesticides, strategic planning, and capital
improvements. He thanked Randy Jones, Lisa Anderson, and Allayna Dail for
setting the meeting space up and for technology advancements during the
meetings.
Mayor Hatem compared painting a canvas and how the Board plans and decides
which projects should move forward. Southport is the waterfront for Brunswick
County and a destination in the state, and we want to preserve the natural
resources. Mayor Hatem said he wonders if the leaders of Southport in 1792
could envision where we are today? The Board’s job is to set the vision and
plan for the future.
Approval of Agenda
There were no changes to the agenda, as presented. After a motion  was made by
Alderman Allen and seconded by Alderman Lombardi, the agenda was approved as
presented.
BEMC Presentation
Mayor Hatem asked Mr. Ellie Pettinger to introduce the guests from BEMC. Mr.
Pettinger said that his goal is to be as descriptive as possible to see
everything that he is requesting. There is a need for upgrades and additional
infrastructure to prepare for all the proposed growth and development. He
introduced the representatives from BEMC.
Tim Tippet spoke to the Board first. He introduced Deborah Fish, a private
engineer who has been working with Southport since 2005. She does a lot of
communicating with the City and others involved in projects. Mike Blue was just
promoted to Regional Manager. Tim Tippet is the Systems Operations Manager of
BEMC. The City asked BEMC for proposals in 2001-2002. The first time TIM came
to help the City was in 1988. BEMC has been in business for over 80 years. They
have 200 miles of transmission line, 30 substations, and over two hundred
employees on the payroll. They have a GIS and a Finance department willing to
help Southport. Mike Blue went on to speak about upcoming projects. Mr. Blue
said he has worked closely with Ellie Pettinger and Randy Jones to put the
Christmas decorations up. The Lord Street project is almost completed. The Cape
Fear-River Road project had a rotten pole and other issues. They are putting
together a plan to put the service underground. They estimate the project will
cost $332,000.
The service conversion to underground on River Drive will cost approximately
$580,000. Trenching costs are 50% less than boring the service. We would have
to get permission from homeowners to trench. Alderman Allen asked if there was
money already in the budget to cover those two projects? Mr. Pettinger said
that there is $118,000 on a line item to order the materials. The project would
start in this budget year and conclude during the next budget year.
Focus shifted to the FY22/23 work plan. The conversion of side streets from W.
Bay to W. Brown Street, including Brunswick and N. Caswell, will cost about
$1.2 million. Next would be E. Moore Street from S. Atlantic Avenue to Cape
Fear, at the cost of $600,000. The FY2025/2026 work plan consists of converting
E. Moore Street from S. Atlantic to Cape Fear at $1.5 million.
And finally, during the FY2027/2028, the conversion to underground from Howe
Street from Moore to W. Brown and moving the primary feeder would cost
approximately $1.5 million.
The BEMC representatives discussed all of the potential growth expected in
Southport. Deborah Fish said that sometimes the City installs the primary
infrastructure, and the developers install the secondary. If there is no
current electrical service in the area, the developers sometimes pay the
expense of service at their developments. There are (48) townhome units
proposed for Rob Gandy Blvd. A new feeder must be built to provide service to
Osprey Landing. It will cost $100,000 to build the feeder, and it will be a
three-phase line. Ms. Fish explained that there are also expenses included in
the budget that are not for any particular project, just supplies needed. For
example, for unsafe poles, because they are rotten, or limb trimming.
For new development, they were asked to identify the rough cost. It is up to
the City and the developers to determine who will pay for the work. There is
one feeder that Duke Energy owns that needs upgrading at $325,000. BEMC has a
total of (5) feeders in the City.
The Indigo Project has two viable options to provide electrical service. The
first option includes a new substation or delivery point, the upgrade to the
Duke Energy feeder, 3-phase feeders to back up the existing substation and
would cost approximately $3 million. The second option is to upgrade the
existing Duke transformers to 30MVA, upgrade the Duke feeder, and add (2)
feeders from spare bays. The cost would be approximately the same. Ms. Fish
explained that the developer would pay for any required upgrades. But if we
want to use the substation as a backup to the City, the cost could be shared.
It would be up to the City to determine how much the developer would be
responsible for. Mr. Hargrove said that there is a zoom meeting scheduled with
the legal team that would be helping us write the development agreement.
Hopefully, we will have more information after that meeting. Ms. Fish said that
their job was to find out HOW to serve them.
Ellie Pettinger explained that he would be asking for a few things on the
budget this upcoming year. He requires funding for switches, maintenance
contracts, software, extra electrical poles, load management switches,
infrastructure, leasing his work vehicle, and possibly replacing his computer.
Mr. Pettinger is also working with Ms. Trexler about hiring new personnel. He
is looking at May 16, 2024, as a retirement date, and he would like to get
someone hired to start training in preparation.
Mayor Hatem called for a fifteen-minute break at 9:59 a.m.
G.)      Pesticides
   Mayor Hatem called the meeting back to order at 10:21 a.m. He summarized
some of the infections that have been caused by insect bites, including yellow
fever in 1852. He introduced Mr. Jeffrey Brown, the Brunswick County Vector
Control Supervisor. Mr. Brown said that he has worked with pesticides for over
(40) years. He works a lot with David Kelly and has a great working
relationship with all of the municipalities in Brunswick County. Mr. Brown gave
a brief history of the conflict between man and mosquito. 1996 was the first
time an aerial plan to end mosquitoes was used. The West Nile Virus was
prominent in 1999, and the Zika virus in 2015. In 2017, Hurricane Florence
dumped excessive amounts of water in North Carolina, and the standing water
created an abundance of mosquitoes.
The Environmental Protection Agency authorizes the use of pesticides, and the
Center for Disease Control also works with post-disaster response. The NC
Department of Agriculture oversees pesticide licensing, annual training, annual
equipment calibration certification. Brunswick County has taught a workshop
every spring, and participants received continuing education credits and have
their equipment calibrated. FEMA also provides information.
Integrated Pest Management consists of several concepts: surveillance,
biological control, physical control, public education, larviciding, and
adulticiding. There are over 3000 species of mosquitoes in the world.
Mosquitoes have four stages of life: egg, larvae, pupae, and adult. When a
mosquito lays eggs, about half of them are female. Mr. Brown’s organization
speaks to HOA’s as requested and tries to do much public education. Some areas
are listed as “Do not spray areas.” Some people that have allergies to
petroleum can request not to spray. Pesticides must be labeled according to
federal law. The spray drift of pesticides is approximately 4.2 minutes.
Several parts of a label are required, including the active ingredients,
directions for use, storage and disposal instructions, and any dangers or
warnings.
Mr. Brown’s department collects data about rainfall, mosquito data, citizen
requests, larvicide, and adulticide applications. They can run that data to
help identify where the largest populations of mosquitoes are located. Woodland
pools present a problem in Southport, and they are treated with larvicide.
Ditches filled with water have not presented a huge problem in this area. They
use GIS to predict where mosquitoes might be located, but they physically walk
to confirm the locations.
He added that developing an Integrated Pest Control Plan is a very
individualized process.
Alderman Davis asked how long the pesticides stay in the air. Mr. Brown said
that the spray usually stays in the air for about 4.2 minutes. Sometimes one
spray is enough in any particular area, but sometimes, you would have to spray
every other day. A mosquito lives about three weeks, and the last week of the
life cycle, the potential to spread disease is the highest. Spraying only
affects adult mosquitos. More rain causes more mosquitoes, which causes a need
for more spraying.
There are (100) active beehives in Brunswick County and (5) active hives here
in Southport. We work with beekeepers. At the owner's request, spraying will
not take place near the hives. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller stated that butterflies
and pollinator bees are affected, too. Mr. Brown said that other aspects affect
the mosquitoes, including the phase of the moon, temperature, and time of day.
There are ways to moderate the mosquitoes by encouraging certain fish in the
bodies of water or specific plants. Mr. Brown said that humans had been around
for 30 million years, and humans have been around for about 3 million years.
Mosquitoes have a lot more experience in surviving. There was more discussion
about the drainage issues in Indigo.
Mr. Brown said that if residents are more sensitive to spraying, they will
avoid that home. The Board asked if the County could start mapping Southport to
identify those areas that could be treated. Alderman Alt said they are trying
to find a happy line between wholesale spraying and public health concerns.
Mayor Hatem said that a message would go out on Southport Connected before any
spraying occurred to notify the residents and what areas would be included.
There were no other questions. Mr. Brown thanked the Board for having him.
   David Kelly said that he has been doing this job for three years but worked
with others before obtaining his license. Because there is only him in that
position, it is hard for him to complete the surveillance and spraying required
to manage the program best. Last year, Mr. Kelly didn’t spray until the end of
the season. He noticed a problem at Indigo. Spraying does help, but Southport
also tries to be environmentally friendly. If he goes out to properties and at
least (7) mosquitoes land on his arm at once time, that constitutes a real
problem. At that point, he lets Randy Jones know to put a message out to the
public. There are (5) zones in the City. Usually, one or two zones are sprayed
at a time. Mosquito dunks can be purchased from Lowe’s, but the chemicals go
out with the water. Mayor Hatem suggested that the City might need more
personnel to help with the responsibilities. City Manager Gordon Hargrove said
that we have to use all the tools available to us, and we need to identify the
resources to help David Kelly do the best job possible. It is hard to find help
right now.
   City Clerk Dorothy Dutton presented information about the Bee City USA
program. She was contacted by a member of the Beautification Committee about
participating in the Bee City USA program. The program has a few requirements,
including signage, at least one educational presentation a year, progress
reports, and the use of an Integrated Pest Control Plan that prevents bee-
sensitive areas from being sprayed with pesticides. Currently, there are two
gardens that the City cannot spray- the pollinator garden and the community
garden. The Committee will purchase the required signage, maintain the gardens,
and host the community education program. The benefits of participation include
improving local food production, supporting small businesses, building
community, helping to ensure the survival of vital species and increasing
awareness of biological diversity. The resolution was included in the Board
agenda packets but will be included at the March meeting for consideration.
Alderman Lombardi stated that he had spoken with Sharon Salvaggio of the Xerces
Society about Bee City not interfering with the Cities spay program and will
not dictate any rules. They are willing to speak to us about mosquito
population prevention if the Board would like.
Mayor Hatem dismissed the Board for lunch at 11:54 a.m. The meeting was called
to order by Mayor Hatem at 12:51 p.m. Allayna Dail reminded the Board to speak
into their microphones directly.

Strategic Planning/Capital Improvements
   Gordon Hargrove went to the podium to begin his presentation about strategic
planning. He mentioned that we are all lucky to live in such a beautiful area
and showed pictures of scenery from the City. After several pleasant pictures,
he switched to pictures of cracked sewer pipes and worn-out components to the
sewer system. He said that things are not so beautiful if we look below the
surface. All of the horizontal assets are strained. Many of the underground
pipes are deteriorated and have weeds and roots growing through them. All of
the pictures he just showed the Board is from a 100-foot section of the pipe.
How does the City find a path forward? We want a plan that works for everyone.
A capital improvements plan usually spans 5-10 years. It is a living document.
The City received $7.95 million from the NC General Assembly. Our water and
sewer rates just increased, generating money for capital improvement projects,
too. Mr. Hargrove said that the City should not get used to receiving grants
and funding from the General Assembly because it doesn’t happen very often.
Portions of the City are eligible for American Rescue Plan funding, mainly
because we are considered a distressed utility. We will go after funding
aggressively.
We have also discussed other revenue-generating ideas, including the prepared
meals tax and the motor vehicle tax. Staff is also looking into a stormwater
tax based on residential, commercial, or industrial parcels. If property taxes
increased by 1%, revenue generated would be an additional $108,000 a year.
Several projects need to be funded. Public Works needs a backhoe, street
sweeper, stormwater mitigation, two dump trucks, and water/sewer upgrades. The
Police need a City-wide camera system. The Fire Department needs a new heavy
rescue truck, HVAC upgrades, and possibly a satellite office. The Tourism-
Communications department needs to upgrade its A/V and streaming capabilities.
Animal Protective Services would like to consolidate the dog/cat enclosure to
the City. Parks and Recreation needs a new rec center and a stage at Franklin
Square Park. Development Services needs more personnel and updated software.
And finally, the Finance Department will need software upgrades.
There was some discussion about all of the elected officials’ priorities:
water/sewer infrastructure, road repairs, stormwater mitigation, sidewalks and
crosswalks, historic preservation, preserving the yacht basin, dredging the
yacht basin, new rec center, and technology upgrades. Mr. Hargrove said that he
thinks, based on the Board comments, the “big five” would be: infrastructure,
roadway repair, shoreline stabilization, stormwater mitigation, and electrical
upgrades. The other projects would be the sidewalks/crosswalks on Howe Street,
the kayak launch, speed calming devices, yacht basin dredging, and other
sidewalk improvements concerning the pedestrian plan. The current year Capital
Improvement Plan funding includes shoreline stabilization, repaving Howe
Street, Taylor Field, and electrical underground. There is some money left over
from the previous Capital Project Ordinance. Mr. Hargrove reported that the
City pays $317,000 per year to treat wastewater because of I & I (inflow &
infiltration). It will not get any cheaper as we move forward.
Alderman Allen asked if once we get some of the infrastructure replaced and
repaired, there is a chance that water and sewer rates could be reduced. Mayor
Hatem said that he learned that it is never wise to decrease rates. We have
applied for the USDA loan and also some grants. There is some benefit to
accepting the loan and grant. We can use the grants in some areas and use the
loan for other areas. We are about to close the loan for the new sewer
treatment plant for the County. We have to use the first tranche of ARP funding
to keep the loan cost down. Mr. Hargrove recommended concentrating on the 3-
5 year time frame for planning. We will not be able to develop a strategic plan
in two hours. We will schedule another planning meeting, but it will soon be
budget season. City staff needs to shift focus onto preparing the budget
documents. A general obligation bond is the most secure form of borrowing
because if the City cannot pay the bond payments, the taxes are raised to
secure the loan payments. We have funding to upgrade (3) pump stations. We can
use $5 million to focus on shoreline stabilization. That leaves $1,059,772 from
the ARF tranche. Alderman Allen said it is hard to make decisions when the cost
is unknown of specific projects. Mayor Pro-tem said that we would likely need
an engineer to help design the kayak launch. Alderman Carroll stated that he
did not want to miss out on the funding that the Marina offered. There was a
discussion about the kayak launch, the expected building, and the timing.
Mr. Hargrove stated that it is the Board’s decision how to prioritize projects.
But it is easier to come up with $125,000 than $5 million. The focus of the
conversation shifted to wastewater pump stations. Public Services Director Tom
Stanley went to the podium to answer questions. Mr. Stanley said that BEMC
works closely with the Electrical Superintendent and provides engineering
services. He said that he doesn’t understand why there is no engineer for water
and sewer. Alderman Alt asked if the project needed to go to an engineer first?
Gordon Hargrove stated that the City has already begun the RFQ process for the
wastewater pump stations. The project has to be designed by an engineer. There
were questions about when the utility merger feasibility study would be done.
Mr. Hargrove said there was no guaranteed time, but he has seen it take a
couple of years. There is a chance that the County would accept the debt
service payment for improvements when they take over the utilities. Mr.
Hargrove recommends improving (5) stations and building the sidewalk down Howe
Street that was put off last year. Alderman Allen said that we could focus on
the water and sewer infrastructure, but not to the exclusion of everything
else. He suggested wrapping the meeting up for today. Mr. Hargrove said that he
needed to make a few more comments. The funding provided by the General
Assembly and the ARF does not happen often. We need to use the money for the
greatest good, the biggest impact. All experts, like the School of Government
and the NC League of Municipalities, suggest using the money for
infrastructure. The Board decides on policies and directives, and Gordon is the
conduit for staff to get projects done. Mr. Hargrove asked all staff to enter
the room and stand.
We all have a duty to protect Southport. In the 21 months he has been in
Southport, he has learned that staff is all very good at what they do. This is
the team that will be leading Southport in turning the curve. He added that he
is blown away by the staff’s professionalism every day. Alderman Allen made a
motion to authorize the City Manager to begin the process of rehabbing the (2)
additional pump stations and the sidewalk on Howe Street. Instead of making the
motion and voting today, Alderman Allen and Mayor Hatem suggested moving it to
the agenda at the regular March meeting. Mr. Hargrove reiterated that it takes
a while to develop a strategic plan, and it will take months to pull the
engineer’s reports together.

H.)   Agenda
   1.   Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director, introduced Mr. Patrick
Flanagan, a regional planner with the Café Fear Council of Governments. He is
here to review the plans for the East Coast Greenway Study. Mr. Flanagan
thanked the Board for having him. The East Coast Greenway Trail is a 3000-mile
multi-use trail from Maine to Florida. So far, 1000-miles have been
constructed. The trail enters near the ferry and runs to US 17 Hwy. A
feasibility study is needed to identify the best path in Brunswick County. The
Rural Planning Organization and the Council of Governments are sponsoring the
study. They want to make sure what they build here serves the people who live
here and other people who want to use the routes. They also wanted to make sure
that there are loops and features that local residents can use for travel and
enjoyment. Aldermen Allen asked who was paying for the plan and the
infrastructure. Mr. Flanagan explained that this is a planning document. Once
the plan is adopted, organizations can apply for funding through NCDOT or other
agencies. The City does not have to pay for anything in particular, but it
helps the City comply with the Complete Streets Policies. The Greenway goes
through both central NC and the coast of NC. A resident asked if the plan
provides access to natural areas. Mr. Flanagan said that the plans do not
specifically go to certain areas, but they tried to incorporate natural beauty.
He explained that he and the other planners decided to use NC 211 to allow as
many people to use the trail as possible. A motion to approve the plan was made
by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and seconded by Alderman Lombardi. All ayes, Motion
carried.

Alderman Lombardi expressed a special thanks to Jennifer Fontaine for over ten

A)   Call to Order
   Mayor Hatem called the special joint meeting to order at 6:00 p.m.
B)   Invocation
   Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
   Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)   Approval of Agenda
   After a motion was made by Alderman Allen and seconded by Alderman Lombardi,
the Board of Alderman approved the joint meeting agenda as presented. All ayes.
Motion carried.
   After a motion made by Will Hewitt and seconded by Gustavo Mibelli, the
Planning Board approved the joint meeting agenda as presented. All ayes. Motion
carried.
E)   Mayor's Opening Comments and Agenda
   Mayor Hatem welcomed the Aldermen, Planning Board members, the developers,
and the public to the meeting. He thanked the City Manager Gordon Hargrove,
Thomas Lloyd, the City Clerks, Communications staff, and Eileen Hennessy. He
explained that if approved and built out, the Indigo Plantation Phase 2 project
will be the most significant planned development since Southport was first
developed. Mayor Hatem said that many studies are being conducted to consider
the impacts of the development, including infrastructure, traffic, personnel,
and finances. He said that part of his responsibility is to ensure that the
Boards and the public have enough information to make a good decision. He also
reminded the public that there is a Town Hall meeting scheduled for April 4,
2022, at 6:00 p.m., which is the best opportunity for the public to ask
questions. Mayor Hatem asked Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director, to
introduce the project.
   Mr. Lloyd explained that the developers have submitted an application for a
PUD Master plan rezoning. The property is adjacent to Smithville Woods, Cades
Cove, and the existing Indigo Plantation. The property is already in the City’s
extraterritorial jurisdiction. The Planning Board has (90) days to review the
proposed PUD, and then they must make a recommendation to the Board of
Aldermen. The Master development bubble diagram identifies different densities
and what uses are allowed in those areas. The maximum number of units is
included in the master plan approval. This property is 346.7 acres with 1500
residential units and some commercial areas reserved. City staff is currently
working with two consulting groups to complete an infrastructure and fiscal
analysis. Mr. Lloyd announced Chad Paul, the CEO of Bald Head Island Limited,
and Roger Perry and McKay Siegel from East West Partners. Mr. Chad Paul said
that he was involved with the original Indigo Plantation project; he dug the
footers for the original fence. After so much time has passed, now is the right
time to focus on phase 2. The property owner, Mr. Mitchell, passed away seven
years ago, but the estate is still being settled. The Mitchell family wants to
do a great job because they want to leave a good legacy. Mr. Paul said that
they wanted to work with East West Partners because they have an excellent
record of stewardship. The inspiration for the homes is the historical homes
along Bay and Lord Streets. The County will provide water and sewer utilities.
   Mr. Roger Perry, the President of East West Partners, thanked both Boards
and said they are here to try to come together with the public to figure out
the best possible use of the property. They want to help the social wealth and
health of the communities. All of the existing communities that East West
Partners developed have a high level of satisfaction. The best example is
Meadowmont in Chapel Hill. They worked very well with Chapel Hill, and now it
is one of the most imminent developments. The development added $1 billion to
tax value and includes single-family detached, condos, townhomes, apartments,
and retail/office space.
   McKay Siegel introduced the project from a holistic approach. He said that
there is a beautiful marina, open space, and the unique character of Southport.
The bubble diagram is color-coded based on density. The purple and red areas
are the densest with apartments or townhomes. The number proposed is their best
guess right now, but it will likely change. There are many areas identified for
open space. The planned open space areas, trails, and parks will be open to the
whole City of Southport. Mr. Siegel and another representative walked through
Southport and compared housing styles, prices, and sidewalks. They want to use
styles and materials similar to what is already used in Southport. The
developers will install the water and sewer infrastructure and give it to the
County. The City will provide electrical service and stormwater management.
There will be sidewalks on both sides of the roads, and they will use good
caliber, native street trees. The traffic engineer was unavailable to attend
this meeting, but he will be attending the April 4 th meeting.
   The project's residential portion should add a value of approximately $750
million to our tax base, and the commercial portion should add $26 million.
   Mr. Chad Paul said that some developments outside the City limits still use
City resources. By annexing into the City, they will at least provide ad
valorem taxes to help pay for infrastructure upgrades. There is a dirt road
from 11th Street to the hydrant beside the VFW on 9th Street. The City owns a
piece of property at the end of 11th Street and where the pump station is
located. Mr. Roger Perry explained that the traffic projections were made
through 2040. The recommended improvements were derived from the traffic impact
analysis. Signalization and additional exits will be added. All of the roads
will be built to NCDOT standards. The intersection of Robert Ruark and NC211
(Howe St) is a unique opportunity because it serves as the front door to the
City.
   Alderman Lombardi thanked the developers for the presentation. He asked for
more information about the types of retail that would be included. Mr. Paul
said that it depends on how much traffic we want on the streets. There would
probably not be anything like a full grocery store, but they want to consider
the hospital's needs. They have also considered an assisted living facility.
   Alderman Alt stated that he is concerned about the impact on school traffic
and asked if the traffic impact analysis considered that. Mr. Perry said that
the TIA did take that into account because it looked at the trip generation
during peak rush hour. Mr. Perry also added that there would be deed
restrictions against short-term rentals. He noted that they waited until the
new Unified Development Ordinance was adopted so that they would fall under the
new standards. He said they do not want to be a closed community; they want to
encourage non-vehicular traffic and the public to use the amenities.
   Planning Board member Christopher Jones expressed concern that they did not
have the entire TIA, so Mr. Lloyd emailed it to everyone. Mr. Jones also asked
how adjacent neighborhoods affected the necessary resources for their other
developments, such as medical care and restaurants. Chad Paul stated that the
planned commercial space would include some of the resources that the residents
would need. He also agreed that demographics are changing, and some younger
folks are moving in. They have to be accommodating to all people. Mr. Perry
added that the build-out time is likely ten years, and they will have to be
flexible to allow for market changes. Planning Board member Scott Jones asked
if they were open to reducing the density at all or would they walk away from
the entire project. Mr. Perry and Mr. Paul agreed that it is not all or
nothing. They are open to discussion, but historically speaking, this type of
development is successful.
   Mr. Will Hewitt asked if the traffic engineer would be available at the
April 4th meeting, and Mr. Perry assured him that he would be present. Mr.
Gustavo Mibelli asked for more information about the proposed density compared
to the existing density. They discussed creating a map/picture that would
overlay the proposed sketch drawing on top of the aerial picture. That would
better show connectivity. Also, it would be helpful to see comparisons of
different streetscapes; with the number of houses on existing streets versus
what is proposed. Planning Board Chair Sue Hodgin asked if they planned to
build in phases and, if so, what are the phases? Mr. Perry replied that the
soonest the first house would likely not be ready to move in for 2.5 years. He
also stated that they intend to pay for all offsite utility connections and
traffic mitigations. Sue Hodgin stated that she hopes that younger folks, Bald
Head Island employees and service workers will also be able to live there. Chad
Paul said they don’t know precisely what the demographics will be, which is one
benefit of having a PUD. It allows for some changes in housing types, as
needed.
   Planning Board member Fred Fiss was concerned about construction traffic
having a major impact. Chad Paul said construction traffic would be mitigated
by using a central laydown yard and coordinating with law enforcement for the
concrete trucks. Alderman Carroll is concerned that a second commercial core
would be created. Mr. Perry said there might be a restaurant and a store, but
he believes that the project will encourage more development on the edge of the
City limits.

APRIL 4, 2022
SPECIAL MAYOR'S MEETING
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL MAYOR’S TOWN HALL MEETING
COMMUNITY BUILDING APRIL 4, 2022
223 E. BAY STREET  SOUTHPORT, NC
 
6:00 p.m.
PRESENT: Mayor Joseph P. Hatem
BOARD MEMBERS IN ATTENDANCE: Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Alderman John
Allen, Alderman Robert Carroll, Alderman Rich Alt, and Alderman Tom Lombardi
STAFF PRESENT:
Gordon Hargrove, City Manager   Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
Randy Jones, Tourism & Comm.    Lisa Anderson, Assistant Comm. Director
Allayna Dail, Tourism & Comm Administrator   Thomas Lloyd, Dvlpmnt Services
Director
Todd Coring, Police Chief   Ralph Treadway, EMS Battalion Chief
A)   Open Forum
Attendees were given the opportunity to walk through the lobby, ask the
developers questions, and review the plans. There were so many people in
attendance that most everyone took a seat to reserve it for the meeting instead
of walking through.
B)   Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the meeting to order and welcomed everyone in attendance and
watching from home. He said that he was proud to provide a public forum where
the public could come and ask questions and review the proposed Indigo
Plantation Phase 2 project.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)    Invocation
Mayor Hatem read a prayer.
E)   Presentation
Mayor Hatem introduced the most involved individuals with the project. Chad
Paul is the CEO of Bald Head Island Limited; he thanked everyone for attending.
He stated that he became CEO of Bald Head Island Limited in 2010. He explained
that there are 386 acres involved in the proposed project. Thirty-seven of
those acres are already within the City limits, and 358 acres are in the ETJ of
the City. Mr. Paul stated that they are aware that the City will decide how the
358 acres are zoned. He added that he realizes that most of the development
occurring in Brunswick County will still affect the City of Southport. Those
people will still come to Southport to use the waterfront and drive on our
roads. He hates the idea that Southport wouldn’t be able to receive any of the
additional tax revenue for the proposed developments. He also added that Bald
Head Island was developed with the fewest environmental impacts possible. There
was no clear-cutting or mass grading.
Roger Perry is the Founder and President of East-West Partners. He said that
they are sincerely appreciative to be there tonight. They are asking for 1500
dwelling units, but they are “allowed” to build approximately 900 based on the
current zoning of R-20. He said that building relationships is more important
than making money at his age. He invited the public to drive out to Chapel Hill
and visit the Meadowmont Community. That is a project developed by East West
Partners and is similar to what they hope to do here in Southport.
Eric Pohlman is a Principal with Land Design who focuses on site plans and
programming. He said this property is really special, and they want to design
an intentional plan. He considers facets like open space and wellness. He asks
what will attract people here. They have included a central park area in their
design. It is planned for front and center and will be the heart of the
community. The linear greens go through the neighborhoods and lots. They would
like every home to be within two blocks of a trailhead or park. The proposed
plan also focuses on tree preservation and the diversity of open space. There
will be active recreation, waterfront- marina redevelopment, nature trails, and
greenways. Great streets breed great communities. Sidewalks and walkability
build communities. Not everything is front-loaded or alley-loaded. Mr. Pohlman
explained the bubble diagram that was available for the proposed development.
He suggested that the public think of it as a heat map. The closer to the
marina you get, the more density. Historic districts typically use multiple lot
widths. Narrower lots have small cottages or taller homes. Wider lots have
larger one-story homes. They hope to create a grid network that connects to the
existing City.
Jonathan Guy, a transportation engineer with Kimley-Horne and Associates,
explained his role in the project. He was hired to complete the traffic impact
analysis. He said that NCDOT manages and sets guidelines for how the study
should be completed. All of the growth for the widening of NC211 was taken into
account. SYNCRO software is used to enter all the data, and the model has to be
approved by NCDOT before the analysis can be done. It takes between 2-3 months
to prepare the analysis because there are so many active studies in Brunswick
County. Once the analysis is ready, they send it to NCDOT for the preliminary
review. It is either accepted for a complete review, or they ask for revisions.
It can take up to four months to get NCDOT approval. The engineers look at the
number of homes and use the number to determine how many trips would be
generated. They also consider trip distribution, the development volume,
operational analysis, land uses, phasing of development, and the year at total
build-out. The NCDOT and the City of Southport determine when a Traffic Impact
Analysis is required. They consider various traffic scenarios, different times
of day for traffic counts, and the different trip generations. A Traffic Impact
Analysis tells us the existing conditions, impacts on any NCDOT TIP project,
and how operations might be affected after the development. NCDOT rates each
intersection with a level of service ranging from A through F. When a new road
opens up, it is usually rated a C or D. Usually, a turn lane is warranted when
they compare the expected volume to the threshold. Mr. Guy reiterated that
NCDOT controls every aspect of the Traffic Impact Analysis. He said that there
are a lot of resources on the NCDOT website that help explain the process.
The development group mentioned that they hoped to include affordable housing,
apartments, and an assisted living facility on the property. There is also
80,000 square feet of commercial space planned, and a lot of that will be
medical offices.
F)   Public Comment
Mayor Hatem thanked the developers for their presentation. He said that because
this was a Town Hall Meeting, he wanted to be able to give the public plenty of
time to ask questions and make comments. In-City residents would be given
preference to speak first, and then we would go back around and call on the ETJ
or non-City speakers. He asked City Clerk Dorothy Dutton to call the names of
those who signed up to speak. Ms. Dutton called on the first person, Shirley
Sullivan. Ms. Sullivan stated her name and said she resides at 5002 Seaward
Court. She stated that she did a lot of reading about the area before she moved
here. She read about how charming the area was. Now, she is worried about
traffic and parking. She asked the developers if the development would become
part of Bald Head Island or become incorporated with Southport. Mr. Chad Paul
answered that it would not become part of Bald Head Island Limited.
Jim Lightbourne stated that he resides at 316 W. West Street. He said that he
had not formed an opinion at this stage. He would like to go through some of
the assumptions being made. He asked if the annexation of the property would be
a financial benefit to the City? He added that the benefits might not apply to
Southport. The infrastructure might suffer to the point that there would be no
actual benefit.
He said that he had read through portions of the traffic impact analysis, and
he believes the study was only done for a few streets. He asked if the
assumption could be made that everyone would follow 9th Street straight to Howe
Street. He said he would cut through on Burrington down to the waterfront area.
Karen Rife, a resident at 5980 Dutchman Creek, was called to speak. She said
that when she and her family purchased their property, they knew that that area
would be developed. But she asked for clarification on how many units could be
built. Mr. Chad Paul stated that they are requesting to build 1500 units. Ms.
Rife asked what the complete environmental impacts of the project were? She
added that stormwater is already an issue. She noticed all the green areas on
the bubble diagram and asked if they would be bringing in any dirt? And she
also asked who would be paying for the roads that get torn up? Mr. Chad Paul
said they do not plan to bring any aggregate into the development. If the roads
get torn up, they will fix them. But to prevent that, they do not plan on
having the construction trucks driving in and out with supplies. They will have
a central laydown yard. The site is currently very flat and sandy. But all of
the stormwater improvements have to be approved at a state level. Their plan
probably includes more stormwater provisions than would be required.
Rebecca Kelley, a resident at 5971 Dutchman Creek, stated that she had grown up
in the Indigo Plantation area. According to the Traffic Impact Analysis, the
traffic counts were done in the morning and the afternoon. School lets out
between 3-4:00 p.m. She suggested they revisit the traffic count during that
time. Ms. Kelley asked what they planned to do with all of the coal ash dumped
on the site? And she added that Bald Head Island Limited owning the property at
the corner of Howe and 9th Street doesn’t help the general population of
Southport unless they plan to make it into a turning lane. Mr. Chad Paul said
that was the idea, to take the parking area and make it into a turning area.
The old Stevens Park area is landlocked. Coal ash was used to seed the old
fields. There is no plan to build homes on that area now. Ms. Kelley reiterated
her comment by asking if they intended to build a park on the coal ash? Mr.
Paul said that the state wants to cap it and make it a park. Mr. Jonathan Guy
said that they would revisit the traffic at the school because there have been
so many comments about the school traffic.
Frank Popelars, a resident at 1023 Captain Adkins Drive, stated that the 2021
City budget was around $8 million. If Indigo Plantation Phase 2 is approved, it
could generate $2.2 million more. That is a shortfall of almost $9 million. The
tax rate would have to be increased by 0.22 cents. Economically, the proposed
development might not be beneficial at all. Mr. Roger Perry said that Mr.
Popelars calculations were absolutely unfounded. The ad valorem taxes would
total approximately $3 million for the City. The amount of traffic has been
grossly overrated. A traffic study is science, not art. He said that City staff
would review all the documentation submitted for the project. Mr. Perry asked
Mr. Popelars to submit his calculations for review; everyone is here to work
through the process.
David McHattie, a resident of 205 E. West Street, said that he is concerned
about the traffic impacts. Their sales presentation was great for people who
