residents of Southport. We need to grow Southport’s core. He wants the City to
do more to grow the existing parts. He also commented that in the 1990s, the
second phase was considered for development, and even then, they determined it
wasn’t a good idea.
Opal Grey Boehmer, a resident at 5983 Spikerush Trail, asked about the animals
already living in the forest. “Have you checked with the EPA to look for
endangered animals?” Mr. Chad Paul answered that all the lighting would be
faced down. The mass of the development is clustered, and there is plenty of
green space. The tree study has already been done. Bald Head Island Limited and
East-West Partners are great stewards of the land. They will monitor the roads
and areas like they do on Bald Head Island. Mr. Perry added that they are
pretty good at what they do. No one will move to Brunswick County to live in
the subdivision. Where do you put people who are already moving to the area? It
is better ecologically to concentrate the people and leave larger and more open
spaces. This type of development is better for the animals. McKay Siegel, with
East West Partners, said that he also has a soft spot for animals. There will
be 140 acres left on the property that will be undisturbed to save more
habitat. There was a request for City staff to speak about the two studies
being conducted.
Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director, explained that the City works in
concert with the developer and shares the cost 50/50 to complete two studies.
One of the studies is a fiscal impact analysis. With Development, Planning &
Financing Group, Lucy Gallo will look at the proposed development and how it
would impact the general fund, fire district, etc. She will consider the
increase of services to that development and any revenue assumptions that can
be made.
Withers-Ravenel is conducting the second study. They are studying the street
conditions, sidewalk conditions, and water & sewer collaboratively with the
developer to complete the model. They are studying this particular development
and assessing the City’s infrastructure in its entirety.
Jim McKee, a resident at 114 S. Davis Street, thanked the developers for their
time. He asked how long the developers have lived in Southport? He remembers
when Bald Head Island was developed. Mr. McKee said that we have talked about
the animals and the people of Southport, but what about the dead? Mr. Perry

state laws. Mr. McKee asked who was going to be conducting the cultural
resource study? He is aware of a cemetery on the Indigo Plantation project site
and added that Southport could not handle another 900 people. Mr. Perry stated
that the City is under no obligation to rezone the property.
Donna Parisi, a resident at 5992 Gray Squirrel Path, asked if anyone had

signs. Are they planning to make any changes regarding the ferry traffic? Mr.

still go out and review that area. Mr. Guy added that stop signs are one of the
things that just have to be dealt with; sometimes, they aren’t visible or are
put in the wrong place.
Jim Gandy from 5961 Spikerush Trail asked if the City has the infrastructure to
support the subdivision? He is more concerned with roads than utilities. There
might be as many as 3000 additional vehicles coming into Southport. Emergency
Services would potentially be impacted. His wife was involved in a car accident
because of the traffic near the school.
Kathy Cabral, a resident at 308 W. West Street, questioned that the annexation
was a binary choice; they will only annex if the rezoning is approved. Mr. Paul
said that it was about balance. If the City doesn’t want the things included in
the proposed project, that is okay. Mr. Perry added that this request is up to
the City, and the City should do what is best for the City. But is there a
balance or solution that suits the City and developers? He said that there is
no benefit to the developers if they only are permitted to build 900 units.
Whoever develops the property will be in it for a profit.
Mayor Hatem said that this is a learning process, and he is grateful to have
everyone in the same room. He would be happy to host another town hall meeting.
Chap Haddon, resident at 6105 Turtlewood Drive, thanked the Mayor and
developers for the opportunity to speak. He said the City needs a vision for
the next twenty years. Will the City be able to provide water? Road
maintenance? The TIA is lacking in its ability to mitigate traffic. There have
been some points of egress and ingress considered, but not all of them. Also,
the housing being built should benefit those in the service industry, too the
housing should be affordable. The current stressors on the community should be
handled before we allow more. 
Donna Mibelli, a resident at 5995 Gray Squirrel Path, questioned whether there
are enough entrances/exits in Southport to accommodate all of the current and
proposed population, especially if there is an emergency. Mr. Guy responded

concerns.
David Rose, a resident of Burrington Avenue, approached the podium and said

G).   Adjourn

APRIL 6, 2022
SPECIAL WORKSHOP MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL WORKSHOP MINUTES
                   STREET LIGHT POLICY
COMMUNITY BUILDING APRIL 6, 2022
223 E. BAY STREET  SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT: Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Tom
Lombardi, John Allen, Robert Carroll, and Rich Alt
ABSENT: Alderman Lowe Davis
STAFF PRESENT:
Gordon Hargrove, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
Lisa Anderson, Assistant Comm. Director
Allayna Dail, Tourism & Comm Admin.
A)   Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special workshop to order at 6:01 p.m.
B)   Invocation
Mayor Hatem said that in the absence of Alderman Reverend Davis, we would have
a moment of silence for Ukraine.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)   Approval of Agenda
Alderman Lombardi made a motion to approve the agenda, which Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller seconded. All ayes. Motion carried.
E)   Draft Street Light Policy Review
Mayor Hatem quoted Emily Dickenson, Alfred Lord Tennyson, Conrad Richter, and
the book of Genesis with sentiments and thoughts about the importance of light.
He added, “without light, where would we be?” Mayor Hatem thanked the street
light committee and City staff. The Mayor asked Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller to
begin her draft policy review. She said that street lights are important for
the City-for staying in character and maintaining health and safety. The light
policy applies to existing and new subdivisions. Preserving the natural beauty
of the night sky is of the utmost importance, but we also want to maintain a
safe environment and preserve the historic character. The Dark Skies program
recommends facing street lights down and using lightbulbs that are no brighter
than 3000 kelvins. This draft policy includes the City limits and the ETJ
areas.
There are three choices for use in subdivisions if the subdivision wants the
City to take over the light maintenance. The “standard City street lights” use
a wooden pole to camouflage into the background. Alderman Mosteller explained a
flowchart to help people understand the policy. The “Southport special dome”
lighting is preferable in the designated historic district. When an electrical
service goes underground or something breaks, it will be replaced with the new
policy selections.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller began walking through the draft policy. Typically,
artificial lights are mounted at thirty-feet high. The draft policy specifies
that they cannot be mounted more than forty feet high. Different areas of the
City have different electrical providers. For example, Rivermist is in the City
limits but gets electricity from Brunswick Electric Membership Cooperative. The
City will reimburse Rivermist for the amount we would pay for our light
fixtures, $11.75 each. Alderman Alt asked if we would do the same for Price’s
Creek subdivision if we take over their roads and street lights? Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller agreed that we would.
One of the biggest conversations to have is the color of the lights. A
demonstration was set up on Softwind in the Hammocks subdivision, with (4)
different color temperatures. We appreciate any feedback. LED lights have
become the standard. Years ago, the LED lights had temperature colors over 4000
kelvins. But now LED lights with 2700 kelvins are available. 2700 is a typical
incandescent light color/temperature. Currently, we still have some sodium-
vapor fixtures. They are about 2000 kelvins, so they look so amber-hued.
Alderman Alt mentioned that the Dark Skies program states that 3000 kelvin is
the maximum. That means that we can choose between 2700 and 3000 kelvin. He
mentioned that most everyone supports the 2700 kelvin light temperature.
Alderman Lombardi asked if amber lighting was better in the fog? Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller said that was true. She had recently learned that the wave of light
doesn’t scatter as much with amber lighting. Alderman Alt asked if an HOA could
pay for the updated fixtures so that they could upgrade them all at the same
time? Ms. Mosteller said that was absolutely a possibility.
F.) Public Questions and Comments
Jenny Prunty, a resident at Indigo Plantation, wanted to confirm that it would
be replaced with one of the newer fixtures when a light goes out. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller agreed.
Glen Price applauded the move to the 2700 kelvin lights. He said that he still
feels like the intensity of the light fixtures needs to be addressed. It is not
good if it is still beaming into someone’s home. While doing research, he has
found a device that allows the intensity to be dialed back. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller said that they are recommending 20 as the peak intensity. And she
added that now if a resident wants to change a light or the location of a light
in your neighborhood, there must be approvals from the adjacent properties.
Adam Steadman, a resident at Indigo Plantation, thanked the committee,
especially Ms. Mosteller, Mr. Alt, and the City Manager. He fully supports the
2700 kelvin light fixtures. He also supports the intensity reduction device. He
added that if his HOA wanted to change all of the fixtures simultaneously, he
would be willing to help. Mr. Steadman said that he has one more suggestion for
the residential areas. He thinks it would be fantastic if there were one more
type of fixture that would block the light all around, except for the point or
tip of the lightbulb, and that it would be faced down, more like a spotlight.
Yvonne Moody resides on Marshgrass Court. She asked if the regulations apply to
the marina area. The lights from the marina are visible from her porch. She
added that it is not shielded and seemed particularly bright. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller said that the marina light fixtures would be considered
grandfathered. But any future lighting or replacement lighting would have to be
compliant.
City Manager Gordon Hargrove asked Ms. Mosteller to explain the process when a
resident asks for additional lights. The adjacent properties would have to
agree to the extra lighting. The City would have to approve the request, and
the City would bear the financial expense. If a resident wants a light fixture
relocated, they would have to pay for the total cost.
G.) Board Comments-there were no other comments from the Board. 
H.) Adjourn
Mayor Hatem thanked everyone again for attending and participating. Mayor Pro-
tem said that she looks forward to having this on the agenda at the April Board
of Aldermen meeting. After a motion to adjourn by Alderman Lombardi and
seconded by Alderman Allen, the meeting was adjourned at 6:40 p.m. All ayes.
Motion carried.

                     Joseph P. Hatem, M.D., M.P.H.
                     Mayor, City of Southport

   7.
   Public Services Director, Tom Stanley addresses the Board about some
misconceptions about the 9th Street pump station. There was a page in the
agenda that lists all of the sewer spills over the last few years. There
haven’t been many. Sewer spills are never good news, but we know that our sewer
system is in bad shape. The pump stations overflow because of the amount of
inflow and infiltration. They have already changed all of the mechanical
aspects of the station that they could manage. The pump station rehabs will
help the situation, but it will not fix everything. Typically, they send about
400, 000 gallons of wastewater a day for processing. During Hurricane Florence,
1 million gallons was sent for processing. That means that 600,000 gallons of
that was rain or ground water. Alderman Lombardi asked how much that is costing
us? Tom Stanley said he believed it to be around $317,000 that we paid the
County. Alderman Alt asked if the pump stations were rebuilt, would the 300,000

   11.
   Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller reviewed the proposed Street Light Policy.
   “ Street lights can be part of the health and safety of a community and an
important design element that contributes to the overall look and feel of a
community.
   Part of the stated purpose of the policy is to reduce negative impacts on
wildlife, human eye sensitivity and the natural beauty of the night sky while
providing light to enhance safety and the City appearance.
   This policy has been available for review, we created a test light situation
so citizens could evaluate different color temperatures. The overwhelming
feedback we received favored the warmest color which was 2700 Kelvin.
   We had a special public workshop last week to review this policy and provide
for additional public comment…briefly just a few comments…
   The policy includes a list of approved fixtures that are consistent with
Dark Skies certification and a map identifying the locations for the types of
fixtures.
   We live in an environmentally sensitive coastal area and while all
artificial light impacts wildlife, we refer to recommendations from the
International Dark Skies Association, a non-profit recognized as a leader in
providing support and technical assistance for policy makers.
   We have some unique situations with regard to our electric utilities. The
policy also clarifies the responsibilities of the city regarding maintenance
and operation of street lights on city maintained roads. And clarifies the
city’s responsibility regarding street lights in communities like Rivermist.
When Rivermist was developed, the city decided to allow Brunswick Electric to
be their provider of electricity.
   While Rivermist has city maintained roads, they are unique because their
electric service is not provided by the city and the HOA pays for all the
street lights starting with J. Swain Blvd.
   This year’s City Budget includes about $99,000 dollars designated for street
light operation and maintenance. This is not part of the Electric enterprise
fund; this is a line item in the general fund.    The $99,000 breaks down to a
monthly charge of $11.75 for operation and maintenance of each of the City’s
street lights.
   Because the Rivermist Community and Townhomes electric service is provided
by Brunswick Electric, they have lease agreements and pay Brunswick Electric
for their street lights. Since Rivermist has city maintained streets, which
would typically include the city maintaining the street lights, the committee
thought it appropriate for the city to reimburse the Rivermist HOA’s, $11.75, a
month, per street light. This would result in an additional $10,575 dollars
annually reflecting a 10% increase to the Street light budget.”
   Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion to adopt the proposed Street Light
Policy and plan for    the inclusion of the Rivermist Community and Townhomes
for a total of 75 street lights in the     Street Light budget in the General
Fund starting with the adoption of the 22-23 city budget    beginning July 1,
2022. Alderman Alt wanted to clarify that any Home Owners Association can
   spend their own money to replace all of their street lights at one time.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller    agreed that was correct. The motion to approve the
proposed street light policy was seconded by    Alderman Carroll. All ayes.
Motion carried.

consultant, Dr. Jim Herstine, to finalize the citizen survey that will, along
with focus groups, be the basis for much of the updates to the Parks and
Recreation and Open Space Master Plan. The survey will be available beginning
in May.
In addition to being able to access the survey online on the City website,
citizens will be able to pick up a hard copy of the survey at City Hall or the
Parks and Recreation Dept. Office beside the gym.
Our Parks and Rec Director Heather Hemphill asked me to emphasize the
importance of completing the survey. There will also be three public workshops
to provide opportunities for citizens to be actively involved.
Please be on the lookout…the survey and public workshops are going to be
scheduled in May and June of this year. Citizen input will drive the success
and outcome of this process and the planning goals in  Southport’s updated 2023
to 2028 Parks and Recreation and Open Space Master Plan.
Also, on April 22, the Parks and Rec. Department will be submitting the pre-
application for the NC Public Beach and Waterfront Access Grant, otherwise
known as a CAMA Access Grant . This is the first step in the CAMA grant process
to determine if a future kayak launch at the end of West West is eligible for
grant funding.
As a reminder, the Parks and Rec Advisory Board regular meeting is scheduled
each month on the second Tuesday at 6:30 pm at the Indian Trail Meeting Hall.
The public is invited to attend.”

MAY 9, 2022
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
223 E. BAY STREET  MAY 9, 2022 10:00 A.M.
COMMUNITY BUILDING SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:      Mayor Joseph P. Hatem
         Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Lowe Davis, Rich Alt,
         John Allen, Tom Lombardi, and Robert Carroll
STAFF PRESENT:
Gordon Hargrove, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director
Randy Jones, Tourism & Comm. Director
Melanie Trexler, Finance Director
Allayna Dail, Tourism & Comm Administrator
Kate Marshall, Animal Protective Services
Heather Hemphill, Parks & Recreation Director
Charles Drew, Chief Southport Fire Department
OTHERS PRESENT: Eliot Duke, from the State Port Pilot and one concerned
citizen.
A)   Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the budget workshop to order at 10:05 a.m.
B)   Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)   Mayor Remarks
   Mayor Hatem welcomed everyone to the meeting. He said it is impossible to
move  forward without knowing where you came from. He mentioned that last year,
the Board had established some goals focusing more on preserving the natural
beauty of the City. He also added that the County does their revaluation, but
what are some other sources of revenue? The City wants to retain the talent by
providing competitive wages. Mayor Hatem said that he was happy to be at the
workshop and part of the discussion.
E)    Approval of Agenda
Alderman Allen made a motion to approve the agenda as presented. Alderman
Lombardi seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
F)   Opening Comments
   City Manager Gordon Hargrove thanked the Mayor and Board of Aldermen for
their time. He said that there was a lot of work in front of the Board. The
Board will be considering a COLA increase. It is important to retain talent and
attract good talent to the City. Staff is asking for a few new positions to
help increase the efficiency and handle the upcoming workloads. The EMS budget
has been separated from the Fire Department budget this year. A tax increase is
necessary this year. The revenue needed to complete some of the City’s projects
can be derived from a combination of a tax increase and general fund balance.
Mr. Hargrove then welcomed Ms. Heather Hemphill to the podium to review the
Park and Recreation proposed budget for FY 22-23.
G) Department Presentations
   a.)
   Ms. Hemphill gave a status update for several ongoing projects. She said
that the PART-F grant project Taylor Field will be starting soon. The proposed
salaries are dependent on    Board decisions. Everything in their budget has
gone up because general costs for goods and    services have increased,
including t-shirts, fuel, and supplies. They are requesting to lease an
additional 15-passenger van to rotate the big bus out of line. She recommends
keeping the bus because it is a huge help in emergency evacuation situations.
The Kingsley Park and Taylor Field projects have separate budgets. She is
asking for funding for cross braces under the capital building fund. The City
must be ready to provide a 25% match    towards the kayak launch. They applied
for a grant through CAMA, but the 25% match    combines the $25,000 donation
from the marina and $13,000 from the City. The proposed cost of the kayak
launch is $150,000, including the walkway to the launch and two launches. If
CAMA thinks the project is worthy based on the pre-application, they will ask
the City to officially apply at the end of June. Alderman Davis asked for
clarification about how    much the marina was donating. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller said that during the meetings with the marina, they didn’t agree to
donate a percentage, but a total of $25,000. Alderman Davis also asked whether
Parks and Recreation have considered leasing electric vehicles or hybrids?
Alderman Lombardi said that the price for hybrid vehicles is too high right
now. Alderman Davis suggested they consider all the aspects of vehicles,
including maintenance and fuel expenses. She said that it might be worth
considering. Mr. Hargrove agreed that it    was a    good idea, but there is
not enough time to work it in for this budget cycle. If the Board would like
staff to research it, they certainly can.
   Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked about the Parks and Recreation utility budget.
Ms. Hemphill    said that the line item covers all her facilities, but the
Garrison building. Mayor Pro-   tem Mosteller suggested that Ms. Hemphill bring
her rates to the Rate Committee for review, the rates have not changed since
2018. Ms. Hemphill said there are (2) full-time employees and (5) part-time
employees in the department. They are a small department, but they offer a lot
to the citizens. Mayor Hatem mentioned the friendships that come from using the
services with Parks and Recreation and how much impact they have on the
   children. Ms. Hemphill encouraged the Board, City staff, and the public to
attend the basketball games. They are very good games, and they are free. The
gym is where a lot of    players get their start and end up playing for their
college or even with the NBA.
   Aldermen Davis asked if there was enough in the budget to cover all the
necessities like dog-waste bags, signage, and other necessities for the dog
park. Ms. Hemphill said that the Animal Protective Services Director, Kate
Marshall, had applied for a grant that would help cover some of these expenses.
Alderman Davis asked about placing benches at the proposed    dog park at
Taylor Field. Ms. Hemphill said that the funding for the benches would have to
be approved by the committee, but she knows many people who have asked about
donating    a bench to the facility. She believes that they will have enough
donations to offset the cost.
   There was some discussion between Mr. Hargrove, Aldermen Lombardi, Alderman
Alt, and Alderman Carroll about electric charging stations for vehicles. Mr.
Hargrove said City staff would have to research the topic and report back to
the Board later.
   b.)
   Mayor Hatem welcomed Fire Chief Charles Drew. Chief Drew thanked the Mayor
and    Board for allowing him to speak to the Board and for all of their
continued support. Chief Drew gave a brief history of the Southport Fire
Department and the staffing throughout the years. He said that the current
scheduling needs had been a    challenge because of the size of    the fire
district and the increased population during the tourist season. They must
answer fire calls with a flow rate of 3000 gallons per minute, so they
typically have to take more than one truck. The required fire flow is based on
the number of homes and businesses in the district. The fire department
includes the main headquarters on Howe Street and three substations. The fire
department is a City department, but they also have other funding mechanisms,
including fire fees and grants. There are currently (5) full-time firefighters.
   Chief Drew said that he truly appreciates their volunteers for everything
they do. Because volunteers are not employed with the City, City staff doesn’t
have as much control over    what the volunteers say and do. In addition, there
have been some occasions when volunteers make more than full-time staff because
they do receive some pay per shift. Chief Drew would like to shift some of the
funding in his budget that covers the volunteers over to cover an additional
(5) full-time staff members. Alderman Davis asked if this type of staffing was
common for other municipalities? Chief Drew said that it was becoming more
common and that some stations have up to thirty full-time staff members.
   Alderman Davis asked if anyone had made a cost comparison or considered
whether EMS should become a regional service instead of falling under the City?
Chief Drew said that it had been discussed in the past. He recommends keeping
it in Southport. Recently there was a cardiac arrest event. Our EMS personnel
reached the man within the necessary four-minute window. The County cannot get
anywhere in four minutes. There is a unit at Caswell    Beach, Boiling Springs
Lakes, and across from St. James. There is always a shortage within the County.
   Mayor Hatem added that he also feels strongly that the EMS service should
remain in the City. Not all calls require transport, and the emergency
personnel can treat some patients or transport them to the appropriate
facility.
Alderman Alt added that the fire fee rate was set to the maximum after the most
recent fire commission meeting. To further increase the fees, the state
Legislation has to approve a request made by the County. The City can
supplement the Fire/EMS budget after the County has established its funding
levels. Alderman Alt would like the City to prepare a legislative package for
next year because we will likely need more funding. Chief Drew stated that a
committee was created to study funding mechanisms for future use. Alderman
Allen asked if the fees were set up like ad valorem taxes? Chief Drew said that
was true, except they do not increase based on population. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller asked if the firefighters were trained as EMS, too? Chief Drew said
they were all trained for both except for one staff member awaiting training.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked if each staff member was expected to respond to a
certain number of calls or other metrics used for measuring performance? Chief
Drew said that staff is expected to respond to 20% of the calls hat are
received in a month. If they cannot reach that obligation, they have to spend
ten hours at the fire station doing chores. He added that there is more
volunteerism on the fire side than in the EMS department.
   Gordon Hargrove said that he reached out to the Board members separately
about splitting the EMS department out of the Fire department in this budget.
Now, they can see where the funding is going. As a result, the budget is
increasing to $250,000 a year. That is one reason to consider a tax increase.
   Mayor Hatem announced that there would be a quick break at 11:17 a.m. The
meeting     reconvened at 11:37 a.m. He thanked Gordon Hargrove and City staff
for putting everything together for the workshop.
   c.)
   Mayor Hatem asked Development Services Director, Thomas Lloyd up to the
front for    his department presentation. Mr. Lloyd said that he had been very
busy lately. He has had    some conversations with the City Manager, and
because of the expected growth, he is asking    for an additional person. The
position is still to be determined, but it could be a Planning Technician,
Planner I, or Planner II. Mr. Lloyd read through a list of all the proposed
developments and how many residential units are expected. All of these
approvals take staff resources, especially time. There are more application
reviews and committee meetings. If all of the proposed developments get
approved, there will be a need for an additional building inspector. Building
Inspector Kiley Barefoot is doing a great job getting his certifications, but
so much work will be generated. The other item that Mr. Lloyd is requesting in
this year’s budget is funding for travel and training. Mr. Barefoot will likely
   have to travel farther away for his Level 2 certifications. In addition,
Code Enforcement staff and the Permitting Technician will need to maintain
their Certified Zoning Official certification. Mr. Lloyd said that he would
like to start updating the CAMA    Land Use Plan, and there have been mentions
of creating a Historic Preservation Commission.
   Mr. Hargrove added that without his help and the help of City Clerk Dorothy
Dutton, both of whom are Certified Zoning Officials, the level of service would
be impossible to maintain. Alderman Alt asked for the total of all of the
residential units he listed previously. Alderman Lombardi stated that it was
approximately 600 units. Mr. Lloyd added that this growth would not be
immediate, but it is coming. Alderman Davis asked if for the definitions of the
three possible positions. Thomas Lloyd said that he didn’t have specific job
descriptions, but typically the permitting technician has less education and
experience. They would handle the more routine reviews. Planner I positions are
entry-level positions, typically with a bachelor’s or master’s degree. The
Planner II position would be for 3-5 years’ experience and higher education.
Mr. Lloyd said that having a Planner I or II would be most valuable. If he had
more time freed up, he would write more updates to the Unified Development
Ordinance. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller suggested hiring a Senior Planner. Mr.
Hargrove said that the budgeted salary would have to be increased for a
   Senior Planner position. Alderman Allen said that a Planner II might better
fit the City’s needs.
   Since there is some extra time, Mr. Hargrove said he would like to move the
Administration and Finance department presentations to today.
   d.)
   Kate Marshall, Director of Animal Protective Services, presented her
department budget next. She began by stating that her first week in this
position was the week of Hurricane Florence. This is the first time she has
contemplated hiring a part-time on-call staff    member. She is asking for a
stipend to hire some help. She said that she is also asking for    $2,000 for
tracking software. The software will help her keep track of all the calls she
   receives and if any of the areas are repeat-offenders. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller asked if she is compensated for her time on the weekends? Ms.

anyone in mind. Ms. Marshall does have someone in mind for the position, and
they are usually in town on the weekends already. But she has not approached

   Mayor Hatem added that Kate Marshall is always willing to help other
departments or citizens. Naturefest and APS’s other programs are always so
great for the community.
   Mayor Hatem announced the lunch break at 12:08 p.m. Mayor Hatem reconvened
the workshop at 12:54 p.m. He stated that the City Manager asked to revise the

to approve the revised    agenda as requested. All ayes. Motion carried.
   e.)
   Finance Director Melanie Trexler addressed the Board. She stated that she
had been with the City for eight years. She presented the Board’s budget first.
Not much would be changing. The salaries are still split between three funds.
The same is true for the City Attorney’s fees and the audit contract. Also

    Ms. Trexler said that the City Manager’s, City Clerk, and Deputy Clerk’s

preparedness funds have been used for Covid for the last few years. The debt
service payment is the annual payment for the fire station.
   Ms. Trexler moved to the Finance Department budget. She said that the Human
Resources department used to be included with Administration, but a former
Manager moved it under Finance. Ms. Trexler said that it takes quite a bit of
her time to help Teresa Parker with payroll and human resources work. She would
like the Board to fund a Human Resources Director position. The HR Director
could do more programming and training. We also need a revised Personnel
Policy. Ms. Trexler added that the City now has 62 full-time staff    members.
It is too much for her to serve in both capacities. Ms. Trexler said that it is
a goal for the finance department to have all employees trained in Government

That way, new hires wouldn’t have to wait so long to use the benefits.
   There was some discussion about shifting offices around at City Hall. There

Hargrove added that we are    at a premium for office space.

G)   Department Presentations
   a.)
   Tom Stanley said that the Electric department would be speaking first.
      i.)   Ellie Pettinger said that the City presently has 3500 electrical
customers. In two and a half years, the City could easily be serving 5000
customers, based on projected growth and proposed projects. The substation is
in fairly good shape now, but we could overload it. Higher continuous peaks are
more stressful for the system. We need to move quickly to upgrade the
substation. Alderman Davis asked if there would still be urgency if Indigo
Plantation Phase 2 weren't a factor? Mr. Pettinger said that it would still be
a more urgent need. He said that he had never seen so many vacant lots be
purchased and built on. The central substation needs to be upgraded. Alderman
Alt mentioned that he was trying to figure out the magic number that triggers
the upgrade. Mr. Pettinger said that he would say between 900-1000 customers.
Alderman Davis asked about how the City would pay for the upgrades, and Mr.
Hargrove said that the electric fund is an enterprise fund and is in good
shape. The City has to provide the power that we have available. Regardless of
the Indigo project, some upgrades were needed. There are 128 wooden poles that
need to be replaced because of their condition. Alderman Carroll asked if the
City could be more aggressive in converting electrical services to the
underground? Mayor Hatem suggested that the budget for underground should be
doubled. Gordon Hargrove announced that he had forwarded the BEMC proposed work
plan to the Board.
      ii.) Public Services Director Tom Stanley stated he feels like it has
been a successful year. He thanked his staff, Gordon Hargrove, Melanie Trexler,
Dorothy Dutton, and Jackie Smith, for all of their help.    
      There used to be three mechanics in the City garage. There is currently
just one.    There was one applicant that he wanted to hire, but they couldn't
accept the amount of money that the City could offer. Mr. Stanley is asking the
Board to fully fund a mechanic position so that another mechanic can be hired.
There is a need because of all the vehicles and generators. Previously, half of
the mechanic position was paid for by the Fire department, but there was a
stipulation that the mechanic had to be a firefighter. If the Board fully funds
the position, the mechanic does not have to be a firefighter. The expected
salary is around $18 an hour, but Ms. Trexler said she had budgeted up to $25.
There was some discussion about not charging departments for labor, only for
parts. Ms. Trexler stated that charging each department for services makes
things too complicated.
      Mr. Stanley said that the Buildings and Grounds department includes (10)
   full-time employees. There is an additional position that has remained
unfilled. City Clerk Dorothy Dutton has been placing the ads for the positions.
The department needs more help to maintain the cemeteries. After more
discussion, it was suggested that a request for proposal be submitted for a
crew to maintain the cemeteries. Mr. Stanley said that some equipment purchases
were included in the budget for routine equipment that needs to be replaced.
      This year, the 4th of July streamers were included in the Streets
department budget. Alderman Davis asked about the street sweeper listed in the
proposed budget. Mr. Stanley said that it was TYMCO 600 that was approved at
the last meeting. Since there had been more discussion about alternatives, the
street sweeper would be placed back on the Regular May Board of Aldermen
meeting agenda.
      There are (7) employees in the Water and Sewer department currently. When
he was \pulled from his regular position on a crew, his position was never
filled. Currently, there is only (1) person in charge of water. Mr. Stanley
would like to hire a person to help the water distribution operator. Alderman
Alt asked if the staff was cross trained? Mr. Stanley said that they were
cross-training. The water distribution    operator works solely with water; he
takes samples and handles meter infrastructure. He does have some staff working
with the water distribution operator, but it is hard to manage because there is
so much work for them to do. As Southport grows, so do the needs.
      Alderman Carroll said that he could tell that Tom Stanley was frustrated
by the compensation situation. The City Manager is proposing an 8% COLA.
Alderman Carroll asked Tom Stanley if that was enough? The City Manager
interjected that a few positions would need to be adjusted in addition to the
COLA increase. Alderman Alt suggested that an analysis should be done to better
account for the time spent on each type of project. Mayor Hatem explained that

that was never filled when Tom Stanley was promoted. Gordon Hargrove added that

Aldermen Carroll, and Lombardi agreed that the City needs a full-time engineer.
Mayor Hatem thanked Tom Stanley, Gordon Hargrove, and Melanie Trexler for the
good discussion.
   b.)
   Police Chief Todd Coring addressed the Board next. He thanked everyone for
their time. He said that the Southport Police Department is (13) member staff
and (2) civilian positions. Chief Coring said that there are currently (25)
festivals on the police calendar. He needs more personnel to help fill some

   Randy Jones presented his departments' budgets next. He overseas tourism,

said it needs to be replaced. Mr. Jones said that he wanted to commend Allayna
Dail for her work marketing the community building. The proposed revenue from
the community building was $77,000. But already, the building has made $118,000
in revenue. There was some discussion about replacing some railings outside of
the building, but Mr. Jones said that falls under Public Services, and they
have been looking at it already.
H.)   REVENUE PROJECTIONS AND BUDGET SHORTFALLS
   City Manager Hargrove said that the capital improvement plan and asset
management plan were discussed at the meetings in January. He asked the Board
to hold off on discussions because of the ARPA funding. The plans would include
water and sewer, buildings, facilities, and streets. The City is still moving
forward with the pump station rehab project. The Capital Project Ordinance
approved last year still has a balance of $480,000. The cost to pave Howe
Street is $1.8 million but is covered already. Mr. Hargrove handed out
information about how much various tax rates would increase the City revenues.
The City is approximately $1 million or $1.2 million short in the budget,
including every department's request. Mr. Hargrove explained a few options,
including a transfer of fund balance to cover the difference, increasing the
tax rate by a dime, or a combination of increasing the tax rate using fund
balance. The other option is to make no changes to salaries, personnel, or
equipment and no tax increase.
Alderman Carroll said that a ten-cent increase is just the base. He suggested
the dime tax increase and using fund balance to help with other projects. He
stated that the increase was a no-brainer for him if we continued offering the
same services. Alderman Alt suggested that fund balance remain untouched to
have the funding to cover any possible storm damage. Alderman Lombardi stated
that it seems a tax increase is inevitable this year. Mayor Hatem said the
Board could sit back and wait until the County revaluations are complete to see
how much difference it makes. In summary, the Board supported the ten cent ad
valorem tax increase to fund salary increases, create positions, and
underground electric.
Gordon Hargrove reiterated the dime increase and reserving $800,000 to relocate
electric service underground. Alderman Allen asked if BEMC even could complete
the underground electrical workload?
Gordon Hargrove said that he believed they would be able to complete the tasks.
He summarized again that the Board wanted to move forward with the ten-cent tax
increase. They want to double the efforts in converting electrical to
underground, fund the requested positions, bring the lacking positions up to
par, the 8% COLA, and the 5% merit raises. He said that Melanie Trexler would
move forward with the proposed changes and distribute it to the Board for
review.
The City Clerk was instructed to publish the notice of public hearing for the
budget for the regular Board meeting in June. Mayor Hatem thanked the Board and
City staff for attending the meeting and working hard to get through the
material.
I)    Adjourn
After a motion by Alderman Allen and seconded by Alderman Carroll, the Mayor
adjourned the meeting at 2:49 p.m. All ayes. Motion carried.

                     Joseph P. Hatem, M.D., M.P.H.

   1.
   Mayor Hatem said the first item on the agenda was to renew our contract with

   2.
   David Kelly addressed the Board next regarding the draft Integrated Pest
Management Plan. Mayor Hatem added that mosquitoes pose a public health issue.
Cities need to be proactive and preventative, provide education, and manage
mosquitoes at different phases of development. David Kelly explained that the
main focus of pest management is surveillance. The threshold for treatment is
(7) mosquitoes landing on the personnel within one minute. He and other City
staff look for standing water in ditches, urban flower pots, old tires, etc.
The county will help City staff map the areas in Southport that are more likely
breeding grounds for mosquitoes. They look for larvae in standing water and,
because there is no threshold, can apply a larvicide if any larvae are
identified. The treatment for pupae is oil-based, such as neem oil. And
treating adult mosquitoes is using spray trucks. By being proactive and
unclogging culverts and other openings, they can reduce the number of
mosquitoes in a given area. Mr. Kelly added that some biological controls like
mosquito fish could be used. But arrangements would have to be made with the
homeowners' associations. Over time, patterns of "hot spots" will develop,
allowing preventative treatment. Mr. Kelly added that it is impossible to
eliminate all of the mosquitoes.
Mayor Hatem asked David Kelly if he had all the resources he needed to get
started? Mr. Kelly said that he is typically the only staff that works in pest
management, and he would like to train another staff member or hire someone to
help him with the program next year.
Alderman Alt thanked David Kelly for his hard work. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller
asked if there was a way that a resident could go online and make a complaint
if they needed mosquito treatment? Mr. Kelly said that if someone calls a
complaint into the office, a work order gets issued. Then he can keep track of
areas that might need more aggressive treatment. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said
that she rode around most subdivisions looking at stormwater ponds. It seemed
that an area in Indigo Plantation is like a bog and would be a prime spot for
early treatment. David Kelly stated that was the area he had already started
surveilling. The Clarke T-30 tablets work great for treating wet areas. The
tablets stop working when the water dries up but resume when water collects.
There was some discussion about residents calling to request their homes not be
sprayed, but Mr. Kelly said that would mean the entire block would not get
sprayed. Mayor Pro-tem suggested that the residents could sign a waiver stating
they would take care of their property. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion
to adopt the Integrated Pest Management Plan, as presented. Alderman Allen
seconded the motion. Alderman Davis commented that she had a lot to say about
this in the past. She applauds Public Services for developing the most
effective and least harmful program but still recognizes there are health
concerns. While she understands that residents can call private companies to
spray for pests, she is still concerned about the potential damage to the bees.
And spray pesticides are not 100% effective. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller urged the
City Manager to find the funds to purchase the supplies to start treating
mosquitoes at all stages and ensure that Mr. Kelly has all the tools he needs.
Public Services Director approached the podium to inform the Board that pellets
were included in last year's budget and are available for use. He added that
the Environmental Protection Agency approves everything that is used. Mayor
Hatem called for a vote on the motion to approve the policy. Five ayes and
Alderman Davis was opposed. Motion carried 5 to 1.

tem Mosteller motioned to reappoint Mr. Davis to the ABC Board. Alderman

   4.
   Mayor Hatem called Public Services Director Tom Stanley to discuss the
street sweeper purchase. Mr. Stanley stated that the Board approved the
purchase of the TYMCO 600 Regenerative street sweeper at April's regular Board
meeting. But the Board was interested in revisiting the options. He explained
that regenerative air technology has many benefits, including improving
stormwater run-off, air quality improvements, and reducing road hazards.
Alderman Davis asked Mr. Stanley to obtain information about different street
sweepers, including electric or hybrid street sweepers and more manual
equipment. The diesel TYMCO 600 street sweeper will cost approximately
$275,000. The hybrid street sweeper is estimated at $700,000, and the electric
street sweeper is approximately $500,000. Mr. Stanley said that he didn't
understand the apprehension with ordering the diesel sweeper; was it the money?
Was it the noise? There are expected pros and cons with each type of sweeper.
But the technology is very new, so the long-lasting expectations and reviews
are unknown. We don't know the maintenance costs associated with the electric
or hybrid sweepers. The last year that the City used its old sweeper, the
maintenance cost was $1700.
Alderman Davis thanked Mr. Stanley for investigating other options. She asked
if it would be feasible to share a street sweeper with another municipality?
Mr. Gordon Hargrove said that he had contacted some other municipalities, but
they were not interested. Alderman Davis said that she thought it was a bad
investment to purchase an expensive piece of equipment that will be used for
twenty years that uses diesel fuel. Alderman Allen made a motion to approve the
purchase of the TYMCO 600 street sweeper as presented. He added that he is not
in love with spending so much, but it is part of best management practices.
Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. Everyone voted in favor of the motion
except Alderman Davis. Motion carried 5 to 1.
   5.
   Mayor Hatem asked Mr. Thomas Lloyd to explain the tree preservation
ordinance amendment . Mr. Lloyd said that the proposed amendment states that
trees in stormwater pond areas do not have to be mitigated. There will still be
protection for live oaks. If a live oak is removed, it will have to be
replaced. This amendment allows some flexibility in road design. Mitigation
will no longer be required for dead or damaged trees. Mr. Lloyd added that the
Planning Board found the amendment consistent with the Land Use Plan and
recommended approving the amendment. Alderman Davis stated that the Forestry
Committee had worked with the Planning Board on this amendment. Mr. Lloyd
agreed and stated that one concern of the Forestry Committee was overplanting.
The urban forest would not be healthy because there were too many trees.
Alderman Carroll motioned to adopt the Land Use Consistency Statement and the
amendment as presented. Alderman Davis seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion
carried.

However, Up Your Arts is so much more! They promote the arts with festivals

JUNE 3, 2022
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN  SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
                   BUDGET WORKSHOP
223 E. BAY STREET  JUNE 3, 2022 2:00 p.m.
COMMUNITY BUILDING SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
PRESENT:   Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Lowe
Davis, Rich Alt, John Allen, Tom Lombardi, and Robert Carroll
STAFF PRESENT:
   Gordon Hargrove, City Manager
   Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
   Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director
   Randy Jones, Tourism & Comm. Director
   Melanie Trexler, Finance Director
   Allayna Dail, Tourism & Comm Administrator
   Kate Marshall, Animal Protective Services
   Heather Hemphill, Parks & Recreation Director
   Charles Drew, Chief Southport Fire Dept.
   Todd Coring, Chief Southport Police Dept.
   Tom Stanley, Public Services Director
A)   Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the budget workshop to order at 2:05 p.m.
B)   Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)   Mayor Remarks
   Mayor Hatem thanked city staff for all their hard work. He said that this
budget process has
   felt a bit rushed, and next year, the process will start earlier. He also
said that more money is involved this year, and the population is larger. Mayor
Hatem said there is no public comment at this meeting, but comments can be made
at the regular Board of Aldermen meeting on Thursday evening.
E)    Approval of Agenda
Alderman Lombardi made a motion to approve the agenda as presented. Mayor Pro-
tem Mosteller seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
F)   Opening Comments
Mayor Hatem explained that the street sweeper had been voted on and approved.
There has been a significant amount of research on the subject, but the
intended street sweeper is to replace the one that the City has had for twenty
years.
The Mayor said that safety, health, prevention, and preparedness is important
for the public and the police officers that respond to emergencies. They have a
lot of property to cover, from the Yacht Basin to the Lowe's Foods. Historic
preservation and the maintenance of the cemeteries are so important. There is
money in the budget for cemetery maintenance. Thirty years ago, the City
created a Buildings and Grounds department that would cover the upkeep and
maintenance of the cemeteries. He added that the proposed ten-cent tax increase
is to help maintain the level of services the citizens expect. We want to
retain and recruit talent. The tax increase will help with maintenance and
preventative measures. He mentioned a few new positions: a City Engineer,
Planner, and Human Resources Director. Infrastructure is very costly but
greatly affects the quality of life for our citizens. Also, when tax rates
increase, it shows our Legislators that we are working towards accomplishing
our goals. The budget process is grueling, but it is the roadmap for the City
and the prioritized projects. Mayor Hatem turned the meeting over to City
Manager Gordon Hargrove.
G)   Department Presentations
Mr. Gordon Hargrove explained that the presented budget includes the changes as
directed by the Board. It reflects a general fund increase of 1.5%. Mr.
Hargrove read through the budget message and listed some infrastructure
projects. He said that he was open to questions from the Board.
Alderman Allen and Alderman Carroll had no questions. Alderman Alt asked if
there has been a study about the proposed Indigo Plantation Phase 2 and its
impacts on personnel. Mr. Hargrove explained the impact studies being done will
consider the proposed population. Alderman Alt said that he has a long history
of law enforcement. He said he is proud of the Southport Police Department but
has questions about whether the positions are really needed.
Alderman Allen interjected that he would reclaim some of the time he was
allotted and stated that he was not in favor of going over the street sweeper
again. The Board has voted twice to purchase the sweeper, and it is a waste of
time to review it again. Alderman Davis asked if Chief Coring could lay out the
positions and provide justification.
Police Chief Todd Coring stated that he had the justification forms ready but
was told not to provide them to the Board yet. He explained that the Police
department was running out of room at the City hall. They have to use (2)
evidence vaults at two different locations. The department has had a 70%
increase in calls received. Each call typically takes forty minutes. On
average, it takes about 6.2 minutes for an officer to respond. They aim to have
two officers on each shift, but that is not always possible.
There is an increase in police officers being more present around town,
including in the City parks. There are 13 officers altogether. We don't have
officers to fill in when someone is sick or on vacation. The citizens and the
tourists like to see the officers on bike patrol or foot. Chief Coring said
they would like to do more of that, but they have to be ready to respond to
calls. He said he realizes it is a big ask, but the positions are justified if
the Board wants more of a presence in the City. Alderman Alt asked if the
department had enough resources to cover all the events? Chief Coring said he
tries to keep some stress off the full-time officers, but sometimes the
officers are on shift alone. Chief Coring said the county has fifteen officers
per shift to cover eight districts. The officer that would respond to Southport
is coming from Bolivia. There is only one state trooper for the whole county.
Alderman Davis asked if the police records specialist would be a full-time
position, and Chief Coring confirmed it would. Alderman Lombardi asked how many
hours the officers work each week. Chief Coring said they work twelve-hour
shifts, with two days on and two days off.
   Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said that she is practical in her approach. In her
interaction with citizens, most everyone wants officers walking around
downtown. There is also Rivermist and Southport Crossing to consider. She
understands that at current staffing levels, it would be difficult to have
coverage here in town and at Lowe's Foods, especially if the officer is on
bicycle patrol. She asked Chief Coring if three new officers would provide
enough coverage. Chief Coring said that he thinks the three additional officers
will allow a blanket to provide the safety and security we need.
Mr. Hargrove disclosed some information that was provided at an exit interview.
He learned that officer safety was the biggest concern. Two officers should
respond to domestic calls. He said there is not as much respect for law
enforcement officers as there once was. It has become a very dangerous job.
Chief Coring added that a simple interaction could turn dangerous in the blink
of an eye. He doesn't consider any calls to be routine. Mayor Hatem said that
there had been both qualitative and quantitative input. More officers provide a
higher level of comfort and stability.
Alderman Davis said that she wanted to discuss the street sweeper again. She
said it was difficult to justify the purchase of a $270,000 street sweeper
while asking for the ten-cent tax increase. She said it wasn't a good use of
money. Alderman Carroll asked Tom Stanley to explain which streets would be
swept. Mr. Stanley listed Moore Street, Rhett Street, Howe Street, Atlantic
Avenue, Nash Street, and Bay Street. He added that the proposed street sweeper
is regenerative. That means it blows air down and vacuums up, and essentially
every street in the City can be swept. Alderman Carroll mentioned that he saw
the street crew working manually to sweep the roads. He said it looked great
when they were done, but so many other tasks needed to be completed. Mayor Pro-
tem Mosteller said that the street sweeper is not only used to help manage
stormwater, it also collects pollutants from the streets, contributes to air
quality, and provides dust control. She also added that $270,000 is a lot of
money, but if you divide it by twenty years, it is more manageable. The last
street sweeper lasted twenty years. Alderman Alt said that now that he knows
the whole town can be swept using the street sweeper, he feels better about the
purchase. Alderman Davis commented that the new street sweeper might be more
efficient so that less time will be spent in operation. Alderman Carroll said
that tourists and residents benefit from the downtown streets being swept. Mr.
Hargrove mentioned all the debris discovered in the storm drains when the old
utility lines were being replaced. He added that recently he was at the dog
park with his dogs when a street sweeper drove by. He noticed how great the
streets looked afterward.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller mentioned the rate changes for public utilities. Mr.
Stanley said that the tap fees had not increased in eight years. The collected
fee barely covers the tap's cost, not to mention the labor for installation.
The City has been losing money. He would like to stop cutting roads and
contract out for the more intensive work. He also stated that he would like to
set a tampering fee for people who turn their water back on once it has been
turned off. We need to hold people accountable for tampering. Alderman Alt
asked if the City has the capability of boring under the roads. If not, can the
City enter into a contract with a company for on-call service? City Clerk
Dorothy Dutton stated that the City has a contract with Hickman Utilities
already. The average taxpayer shouldn't have to pay for new development.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked Animal Protective Services Director Kate Marshall
if her fees were changing? Ms. Marshall said that they were increasing. General
penalties across the board are $100.00, and the dangerous dog permit is
increasing to $500.00. Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director, explained
that the System Development Fees are increasing. These fees cover the capacity
of water and sewer based on the estimated use. It is due when an application is
approved or submitted. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller added that this increase was the
last planned increase based on the adoption of the System Development Fee
program. Alderman Davis asked about tree removal permit fees. Dr. Lloyd
explained that tree removal permits are treated like zoning permits now.
Improved lots are not charged a permit fee. Alderman Alt asked if removing a
tree leaning onto another lot would warrant the $100 permit fee? Mr. Lloyd
explained that the current ordinance would require the fee and permit, which
can be amended. There is no fee required when the tree is dead or damaged.
Parks and Recreation Director Heather Hemphill reviewed proposed changes to her
fee schedule. Most of the proposed increases result from inflation and the
increase in fuel costs. Summer camp rates are increasing, gym rental fees are
increasing, and the gym is only available to movie companies.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked Mr. Hargrove to explain the new system for merit
raises. Mr. Hargrove said that the performance appraisals had gone very well.
City staff is buying into the program. He will provide a list of all the staff
accomplishments at the July Board meeting. The cycle will include the 2.5%
general salary funding amount and will be distributed to staff based on
performance.
Alderman John Allen had nothing further to add. Alderman Carroll thanked City
staff. He said that this was the first time he had participated in adopting a
budget, and he enjoyed it. He believes in the City Manager and City staff.
Alderman Alt thanked the City staff and asked to start the budget process
earlier in the year next year. Alderman Davis thanked the staff and asked about
receiving a final paper copy. Alderman Lombardi thanked everyone. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller thanked staff for their patience and attention to the budget.
Mayor Hatem said that the budget workshop was a success. He thanked the City
staff and Mr. Hargrove. Alderman Lombardi motioned to adjourn the meeting,
which Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller seconded. All ayes. Motion carried. Mayor Hatem
adjourned the meeting at 3:43 p.m.

                     Joseph P. Hatem, M.D., M.P.H.
                     Mayor, City of Southport

Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk

BOARD OF ALDERMEN  REGULAR MEETING MINUTES
COMMUNITY BUILDING JUNE 9, 2022
223 E. BAY STREET  SOUTHPORT, N.C.
 
6:00 p.m.
Present:    Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro Tem Karen Mosteller, Aldermen
Thomas Lombardi, Rich Alt, Lowe Davis, Robert Carroll, and John Allen.
Staff Present:   Gordon Hargrove, City Manager
   Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
   Norwood Blanchard, III, City Attorney
   Thomas Lloyd, Developmental Services Director
   Randy Jones, Communications/Tourism Director

   Teresa Parker, Payroll & Benefits Specialist
Others Present: Tish Hatem, Will Hewett, Pat Kirkman, Eric Maynes, Bonnie Bray,
John Keiffer, Adam Steadman, Fred Fiss, Rebecca Kelly, Renee, and Marc Spencer,
Eliot Duke with the State Port Pilot, and many other interested citizens
attended.
Meetings are now open to the public. Complete audio/video is available on the
City's website or can be requested from the City Clerk's office.
A.)
   Mayor Joseph P. Hatem called the meeting to order at 6:01 p.m. and welcomed
everyone to the meeting. He thanked everyone for attending the meeting and
watching online.
B.)
   Mayor Hatem announced Mr. Gene Tomlinson, Senior Pastor at the Point at
Southport, would provide the invocation. Mr. Tomlinson grew up in Southport and
shared some anecdotes from his youth.
C.)
   Mayor Hatem led the pledge of allegiance.
D.)   Public Comment: 
Mayor Hatem asked the City Clerk to call the individuals who signed up for
public comment. John Morrison, a resident at 513 Majesty's Court, wanted to
speak about the proposed Indigo Plantation Phase 2 project. He said that East
West Partners are reputable developers. Mr. Morrison mentioned the wetlands on
the property and the proposed open space. He can't imagine what 1500 dwellings
will look like on the property. He asked why Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and
Alderman Allen are the only Board members that voice their opinions at the
Planning Board meeting? If the build-out is ten years, won't the roads get torn
up with that much construction traffic going back and forth?
Eric Maynes, a resident at 83 Cherry Road, spoke next. Mr. Maynes worked for
the City as a police officer. He has worked in very small rural areas, the
airport authority, and other agencies. He recently wrote an article that was
published in the State Port Pilot. He continues to have a great interest in the
community of Southport. Police Chief Coring used to be his boss. He thinks that
Chief Coring did a good job of explaining why more officers are needed. He has
been one of the officers responding to calls alone before. He explained that
the officers and their families deserve better than that.
Next to speak was Jim Gandy, a resident at 5961 Spikerush Trail at Indigo
Plantation. He said three or four entrances into the Indigo Plantation Phase 2
area had not been considered. The two entrances will cause significantly more
traffic. 11th Street has less residential development. If the proposed Indigo
Plantation Phase 2 subdivision is approved, it should be mandatory to use 11th
Street as an entrance. The UDO allows six units per acre for Planned Unit
Developments. The requested density is more than three times the allowed
density. The developers should be required to follow the UDO standards. Three
or four-story condos do not conform with the character of Southport.
Restaurants and shops should not be allowed in the marina area. It seems like
development in a larger metro area. Mr. Gandy said it is obvious that the
developer knows nothing about Southport. Mr. Gandy summarized five main points
for denying the proposed project: there is too much traffic at the two proposed
entrances, the number of proposed units fails to comply with the UDO standards,
the multifamily dwellings do not comply with the character, commercial
development does not comply with the residential area, and vehicle traffic from
580 units is too much for the City's infrastructure.
Lora Sharkey, a resident at 432 Cades Trail, spoke next. Ms. Sharkey said that
the Up Your Arts organization is wonderful. They have done so much to support
the arts. The City already has a list of buildings that it must maintain. Ms.
Sharkey encouraged the Board to examine their priorities and reevaluate them.
The City Clerk read the comments that Ms. Shirley Sullivan submitted. Ms.
Rebecca Kelly, a resident at 5971 Dutchman Creek Road, commented that the Bald
Head Island ferry system was operating in that area when she was a child. The
area was highly signaled, and there was not as much traffic.
E.)   Approval of Agenda
Alderman Allen motioned to approve the agenda as presented. Alderman Lombardi
seconded the motion.
Mayor Hatem read the Ethics Statement aloud. Alderman Carroll asked to recuse
himself from the Up Your Arts Memorandum of Understanding item.

   -Mayor Hatem explained that the Noise Ordinance Amendment and the Resolution
to Surplus Personal Property had been removed from the Consent Agenda.
   1.   Minutes of the Special Budget Workshop May 9, 2022

   3.   Minutes Regular Board of Aldermen Meeting May 12, 2022

   7.   Resolution for Closing Capital Project Budget Ordinance-Howe Street

   8.   Transfer Budget Amendment
