Mayor Hatem said that a Hurricane Expo had been scheduled for Tuesday, June 21,
2022. It will be wonderful to provide so much information to the public. June
is also Alzheimer's and Brain Awareness Month.
   1.   Mayor Hatem read the Proclamation in Celebration of Juneteenth
   2.   Mayor Hatem explained that recently a kayaker got caught in the Cape
Fear River and was drifting away from the Yacht Basin area. Without hesitation,
Captain Mike Villano rushed to save the man and was the first on the scene,
although the Coast Guard and Southport Water Rescue arrived. Mr. Villano
navigates former Mayor Peterson's boat back and forth from Bald Head Island and
Southport. Captain Villano is an example of how we should all respond. Mayor
Hatem read the Proclamation of Heroism.
H.)   Agenda
   1.   
   Mayor Hatem provided a brief summary of the proposed budget. The City hopes
to maintain providing excellent services to the residents of Southport. He also
added that we need competitive salaries and insurance for the employees, to
provide the right equipment to complete their work, maintain the City's
facilities, and hire an engineer to help the City complete all the proposed
projects. Mr. Gordon Hargrove reviewed the main points of the budget message.
The net operating budget is $30.5 million. The general fund is $10.6 million.
Mayor Hatem opened the public hearing at 7:00 p.m. Ms. Dutton called those who
signed up to speak. Ms. Pat Kirkman, who resides at 119 Park Avenue, addressed
the Board. She said that she likes all the Board members, and her comments are
not directed at them personally but as a reflection of their positions. She
wants to speak about the preservation and maintenance of the cemeteries. Almost
1000 bodies, the leaders and providers of the things and places we have today,
are buried there. We must not let their burial place be neglected. Many
visitors stop to see the cemeteries, which increases the amount of money spent
in the City. For the last few years, there was zero funding on a line item for
the cemeteries. This year, the line item was completely erased originally.
Mayor Hatem emailed her, explaining that the new building inspector was
enthusiastic about maintaining the cemeteries. The Board has made several
comments that historical preservation is important. She has emailed all six
Board members and only received two replies. Mayor Hatem stated at a budget
workshop that there would be a line item in the budget for the cemeteries. The
current proposed budget shows $1200 for cemetery maintenance. She said she does
not favor purchasing the street sweeper because of the cost. She provided her
email address (patkirkman@gmail.com) and welcomed others to contact her if they
wanted to discuss the cemeteries. She thanked the Board for their time and
attention.
Adam Steadman, a resident of Indigo Plantation, thanked the Board for the
opportunity to speak. He has met with the City Manager and three Aldermen
directly and appreciated the time. He is generally opposed to a ten-cent tax
increase, but most of the expenditures are worthy. He expressed some concern
about purchasing the street sweeper because the cost of everything is going up.
The initial proposal was for using the sweeper on Howe and Moore Streets. Now
that we know the sweeper can be used throughout the City, it seems to be a
better use of money. Mr. Steadman proposed waiting a year to purchase the
sweeper to see if the cost or technology changes. He also commented on the
three proposed police positions. Mr. Steadman asked if a civil patrol could be
considered to cover some of the community policing. He also recommends
beginning the budget process earlier in the year moving forward.
Marc Spencer, a resident at 701 E. Moore Street, asked if there would be an
allocation from the ABC Board for Southport Elementary? He said that there are
a lot of projects that are needed, and he appreciates everyone's hard work.
City Clerk Dorothy Dutton read public comments submitted before the meeting by
Jerry Day and Kathy Cabral. Mayor Hatem closed the public hearing at 7:25 p.m.
Mayor Hatem reiterated that money is in the budget to maintain the cemeteries.
The Buildings and Grounds department was created in part to maintain the
cemeteries. The proposed street sweeper is to replace the one that the City has
had for twenty years.
Alderman Allen said that no board member is happy about the tax increase. We
have some very real concerns in the City. A street sweeper is standard
equipment in most municipalities, and he thinks it has gotten more attention
than needed. City employees are leaving because they have so much work on them.
Alderman Carroll said he appreciates Alderman Allen's comments. He supports the
budget, the Mayor, and department heads. He was also surprised by how much
traction the street sweeper attracted.
Alderman Alt said he wants to address the comments about the police department.
He applauded Mr. Eric Maynes for coming forward during public comment. Alderman
Alt said that he looks at things differently; he considers processes and how to
make them better. The EMS department was draining the fire department fund, so
this is the first year the EMS has been a separate department. He said that the
City had spent money to look at what the City will need to do because of the
proposed Indigo Plantation Phase 2. He was questioning whether there was a
standard number of police officers based on population. The tax valuation will
be about a 30% increase, and the tax rate can be adjusted later. The City needs
money, but he doesn't think enough has been done to determine the most critical
needs.
Alderman Davis said she trusts that we will be taking care of the cemeteries.
She said she appreciates fellow Board members listening to her talk about the
street sweeper. She still doesn't agree with the purchase and cannot support
the budget for that reason.
Alderman Lombardi stated that the tax increase also affects everyone on the
Board. He has witnessed previous Boards kicking the can down the road and never
thought he would be on the Board. He said the tax increase is the right
decision, even though it is tough.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller reiterated that the street sweeper could be used on
every road. If the community wants community policing, we need more workforce.
The Board wants to be good stewards of the environment. We need to repair our
roads and sidewalks. Erosion has crept up to the sidewalks on Bay Street. We
need a new parks and recreation facility; the existing facilities are 70 years
old. Staff has demonstrated an ongoing commitment to seeking grants and is
focused on working with the state and federal organizations to secure funding.
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller said she supports the budget as presented for all of
these reasons.
Mayor Hatem thanked the Board for their comments. He commended the department
heads and City staff for managing the budget preparation in addition to the
ARPA grant applications and the Indigo project reviews. Mayor Hatem added that
the City hadn't raised taxes for five years, but it is necessary.
There was some discussion about paying for the street sweeper from different
funds, but ultimately, they would be coming from the same fund. Mayor Hatem
said he would entertain a motion. Alderman Allen motioned to adopt the FY 2022-
2023 budget as presented. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller seconded the motion. The
final vote was four ayes. Aldermen Alt and Alderman Davis made the two noes.
Motion carried 4 to 2. The FY 22-23 Budget was adopted.
   2.   
   Mayor Hatem asked Development Services Director Thomas Lloyd to explain the
next few items on the agenda. Mr. Lloyd said the first request is to rezone
(27) lots between W. 14th Street and W. 12th Street. They are drawn as one
parcel on the tax map, but they were never recombined legally. The lots are
part of the Southport Heights subdivision established in 1910. The applicant is
requesting a down-zoning from BD/MF to R-10 zoning. The Planning Board
recommended approval of the rezoning request. Mayor Hatem opened the public
hearing at 8:03 p.m. No comments were made, and the public hearing was closed
at 8:03 p.m. Alderman Alt asked if the rezoning would generate less density
than its current zoning designation? Mr. Lloyd stated that was correct. Someone
in the audience asked what kind of housing was being considered, and Mr. Lloyd
said there were no applications for housing yet, but he imagined it would be
cottage-style single-family dwellings. City Attorney Norwood Blanchard stepped
in to clarify that the City cannot lock the applicant into a specific use. A
rezoning is comparing one table of uses to another. Mayor Hatem reminded the
Board that the Land Use Consistency Statement must be approved along with the
map amendment. Alderman John Allen motioned to approve the statement of land
use consistency and the zoning map amendment from BD/MF to R-10 for parcel#
221MA00110. Alderman Carroll seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
Mayor Hatem announced there would be a ten-minute break.
   3.
   The meeting resumed at 8:27 p.m. Mr. Thomas Lloyd explained the next
rezoning request was for a 0.84- acre parcel at the corner of W. 14th Street
and N. Caswell Street. There are six lots included in this parcel. The lots are
also part of the Southport Heights subdivision, and they are requesting a down-
zoning from Multifamily to R-10. The Planning Board recommends approval of the
map amendment. Mayor Hatem opened the public hearing at 8:29 p.m. There were no
public comments. The public hearing was closed at 8:29 p.m. Alderman Lombardi
motioned to approve the Statement of Land Use Consistency and the map amendment
for parcel# 221MA00101. Alderman Carroll seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion
carried. 
   4.
   Thomas Lloyd explained the next request was a little bit different. Four
lots are included in parcel# 237DC006, which is a total of 0.403 acres. This
parcel is currently zoned BD, but they are requesting to rezone it to R-10. The
R-10 designation is consistent with the surrounding area. Mayor Hatem opened
the public hearing at 8:32 p.m. There were no comments, and the hearing was
closed at 8:32 p.m. Alderman Carroll stated that he would recuse himself
because the property is listed with his real estate firm. Alderman Allen
motioned to approve the Land Use Consistency statement and the map amendment
for parcel# 237DC006. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller seconded the motion. All ayes.
Motion carried. 
   5.
   Alderman Lombardi stated that he had interviewed five candidates for the
Beautification Committee. Several of them were existing members who sought
reappointment. Alderman Lombardi motioned to reappoint Karen Pasquale, Kenneth
Geiman, Lynne Geiman, and Rob Thatcher to the Beautification Committee and
appoint Scott Bushman to the Beautification Committee. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller
seconded the motions. All ayes. Motion carried. Ms. Mosteller also said she
wants to recognize how awesome the beautification committee is. Alderman Davis
added that Southport is fortunate to have many who want to volunteer.
   6.
   The Memorandum of Understanding with Up Your Arts was next on the agenda.
Mayor Hatem asked Mr. Norwood Blanchard if he had any comments on the document.
Mr. Blanchard stated that he didn't see any issue, practically speaking. He
said he is not giving a policy opinion, but the document is open-ended and can
be terminated with (60) days' notice. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said there had
been some questions about the genesis of this project. In February 2016, the
old City hall building was put on a list of buildings that need to be protected
and preserved. Near the same time, Up Your Arts was formed. She said this
memorandum of understanding was the next step, and she motioned to approve.
Alderman Allen seconded the motion. Alderman Alt stated that it ties to a
bigger scope of things that must be addressed. He said that as the building
sits now, it continues to rot away and collect mold. He asked that the
agreement be set for six months and then revisited. There should be clear
expectations and guidelines. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller disagreed by saying he was
describing a contract more than a memorandum of understanding. Mr. John Keiffer
with Up Your Arts addressed the Board. He said they hoped things would progress
faster than they have, but everything started when the Covid-19 pandemic was
ramping up. It was hard for them to find an engineer to do the design work. Up
Your Arts is serious about being partners with the City. They have already
invested about $20,000 on the project thus far. Mr. Keiffer said that a public
meeting would be scheduled soon and discussions about establishing a Board of
Directors. Alderman Alt asked about the investment in the City's building and
who would own the equity if the agreement fell through. Mr. Keiffer explained
that this project is at no cost to the City. He is happy to provide monthly
reports to the Board to help them stay updated on the progress. The Mayor
called for a vote to approve the memorandum of understanding with Up Your Arts.
Alderman Carroll was recused from voting. All ayes. Motion carried.
I.)  Committee Reports
Alderman Allen, Alderman Carroll, and Alderman Alt did not have anything to
report. Alderman Davis said the Forestry Committee and the Parks and Recreation
Committee had not met yet. Alderman Lombardi thanked everyone who helped with
installing the memorial bricks. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said that the Parks and
Recreation Committee had finalized the survey for the master plan. The survey
is available on the website, at City Hall, and the Parks and Recreation office.
Community meetings are scheduled for June 14, June 15, and June 20. The
Planning Board meeting is scheduled for the following Thursday at 6:00 p.m. at

Mayor Hatem reminded the Board that the Planning Board minutes, Board of
Adjustment minutes, and Forestry Committee minutes are included in their agenda

Mr. Hargrove thanked the City staff and the Board of Aldermen for the budget

Mayor Hatem thanked the City Manager, Finance Director, City Clerks, and

   Mayor Hatem added that staff reports are in the packet for review.
M.)   Board Comments
Mayor Hatem suggested that the Board Comments be moved ahead of the Closed

N.)   Closed Session
Mayor Hatem accepted a motion by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller to go into closed
session. Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. The

a closed session pursuant to N.C.G.S.143-318.11 (6). The closed session
adjourned at 11:00 p.m., and the Board relocated to their regular seats.
Alderman Carroll motioned to increase the City Clerk's base salary by $5,000.
Ms. Dutton will still receive the 8% COLA, and the City Manager will assign the

carried.
Alderman Carroll motioned to increase the City Manager's salary a total of 13%,
including the 8% COLA and a 5% merit raise. Mr. Hargrove's contract is extended
for three years, and the City-residency requirement is removed. Alderman Allen
seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
Mayor Hatem said that all City employees are valued, but the Board hires these
two positions. He thanked the Board and staff for their time during the long
meeting.

6:00 p.m.

was one of the most successful festivals in years. Freedom was proclaimed in

   1.   Thomas Lloyd, Development Services Director, explained the first

After a motion by Alderman Carroll and seconded by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller, the
Board accepted the petition for annexation, accepted the Clerk's Certification,
and adopted the Resolution to set the public hearing for August 11, 2022. All
ayes. Motion carried.
   2.   Thomas Lloyd described the second request for non-contiguous
annexation. This request is for the first phase of Osprey Landing. The parcel
is a 25.59-acre tract, and the annexation is required as part of the
development agreement that the City and the Developer approved. The City Clerk
has investigated the sufficiency of the request and found it to be sufficient.
Alderman Lombardi motioned to accept the petition, accept the Clerk's
certification, and adopt a Resolution setting the public hearing for August 11,
2022. Alderman Davis seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. 
   3.   Mr. Lloyd explained the final annexation was for 8.35 acres identified
as Osprey Landing Phase 2. This request is for contiguous annexation and is
also required as part of the development agreement. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller
motioned to accept the petition, accept the Clerk's Certificate of Sufficiency,
and adopt the Resolution setting the public hearing for August 11, 2022.
Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. Alderman Davis
wanted to state that annexations have to be voluntary for the public's benefit.
The City cannot force annexations.
   4.   Mayor Hatem asked Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller to explain the next item
regarding an ordinance amendment for exterior lighting. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller
explained that the Street Light Policy was updated, but the Code of Ordinances
should be amended to coincide with that. Typically, code of ordinance
amendments are not sent to the Planning Board for review but since lighting is
an important part of the design elements in a community, she recommends the
draft ordinance be sent to the Planning Board for review. The proposed changes
include recommended light fixtures that would shield the light to protect the
night sky. The amendment does not allow flashing lights or fixtures that cause
light trespass onto adjacent properties. Holiday lights are exempt. Lighting
installed after the adoption of the ordinance would have to be in compliance.
Alderman Alt said a huge part of the population has existing lights that are
non-compliant. The non-compliant lights would be allowed until they needed to
be replaced, and then compliant replacement fixtures would be required.
Alderman Alt encourages having a public meeting.Alderman Allen clarified that
the ordinance should go to the Planning Board first and then host the public
meetings. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller motioned to move the proposed amendment to
the Planning Board. Alderman Carroll seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion
carried.
   5.   Thomas Lloyd explained the proposed text amendment. Approximately (10)
parcels in the Central Business District are smaller than the district
requires. These lots will have trouble meeting the parking requirement. This
text amendment proposes to exempt lots under 4000 square feet from the parking
requirement, but only lots that were platted before 1973. Mr. Ron Thompson
requested the text amendment. Mayor Hatem opened the public hearing at 7:54
p.m. Mr. Ron Thompson addressed the Board. He said he initially wanted to build
on the property, but his wife convinced him to sell the parcel. In its current
state, the parking requirement could not be met. He met with the Planning Board
and worked out some of their concerns. He added that several other properties
in the area do not meet the parking requirement. Mr. Thompson said there are no
parking issues in his property area. He just wants to be treated fairly, like
others in the area. Alderman Davis asked Thomas Lloyd how many parcels would be
affected by the text amendment. Thomas Lloyd said that when first starting, the
text amendment included about ten parcels, but the Planning Board whittled it
down so that only two parcels qualify for the exemption. Mayor Hatem closed the
public hearing at 8:01 p.m. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller stated the table of
permitted uses included 40 to 50 uses that could be built on these properties,
all with potentially differing impacts. The conditional rezoning process
requires more specificity. She feels that a text amendment wasn't the right
process for this request. The two affected lots are both on the same block.
Theoretically, the proposed text amendment would allow the two parcels to build
40-foot buildings, property line to property line with only a 10-foot rear
setback. The conditional rezoning process is intended to provide applicants a
public process to address things like parking relief with design and use
details. The conditional rezoning application would include the identification
of potential uses and elevation drawings. Alderman Alt stated that the proposed
process would require more paperwork than the Indigo Plantation Phase 2
project. Mr. Lloyd said that it is the same process as Indigo. Mr. Thompson
thinks the project is very simple; he has a 33-foot lot. Alderman Allen said
that he reluctantly agrees with Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller. He apologized to Mr.
Thompson. There are proposed projects that are having damaging effects on the
City. Alderman Davis made a motion to approve the text amendment as proposed.
Alderman Alt seconded the motion. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said she is concerned
that people will request changes incrementally for relief. Alderman Allen said
that it would likely be a slippery slope. Alderman Davis said that only one
additional lot would qualify for the exemption. Alderman Alt said that the
Planning Board had already directed Thomas Lloyd to move forward with the
amendment and reduce the requirement. Mr. Thompson said that he had exhausted
every avenue with the City. He believes the next step would be to take the
request to the Board of Adjustment. He just wants to utilize the property. Mr.
Lloyd reiterated that the process is legislative, not quasi-judicial. Mayor
Hatem called the request to a vote. Alderman Davis motioned to approve the text
amendment, and Alderman Alt seconded the request. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller,
Alderman Allen, and Alderman Lombardi voted no. The motion was denied. Mayor
Pro-tem Mosteller asked staff to inform Mr. Thompson with the options fully.
   6.   Mr. Ellie Pettinger, Electrical Superintendent, introduced Ms. Debra

only minor changes to the contract. They update the service fees yearly based

number of new customers. There was some discussion about solar meters. Alderman

Mosteller; Aldermen Lowe Davis, Tom Lombardi, Robert Carroll, and Rich Alt.

A)   Call to Order
   Mayor Hatem called the special joint meeting to order at 6:08 p.m. He
welcomed the Board of Aldermen, Planning Board, the Developers, and the Public.
B)   Invocation
   Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
    Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)   Approval of Agenda
Alderman Davis made a motion to allow the public to ask questions. Mayor Hatem
stated that Alderman Davis should’ve made the request sooner. He said that
there was a motion to add item G. to the meeting for Public Questions. Mayor
Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion to add an item for public question and move
adjourn down to item H. Alderman Lombardi seconded. Motion carried.
   Planning Board member Will Hewett made a motion to approve the amended
agenda, which was seconded by Maureen Meehan. All ayes. Motion carried.
E)   Agenda
   1.   Lucy Gallo, a Principal with Development, Planning, Financial Group,
LLC presented the findings from the fiscal impact analysis. She said the key
fiscal assumptions are based on a snapshot in time, and consider the net impact
to the general fund, excluding the enterprise fund. She explained that the
expected needs for each department vary. The Fire District already covers this
project area, so it is not expected to need more equipment or substations. But
other departments will be affected differently. Ms. Gallo studied the fiscal
impacts based on two scenarios. The first scenario considered the Indigo
Plantation Phase 2 property annexed into the City limits. Based on
calculations, there seemed to be a $1.4 million net fiscal benefit, which will
help offset the City’s fixed capital.
Scenario 2 was based on the property not being annexed. This would create a
negative fiscal effect because approximately 550 homes would be added to the
fire district without the benefit of tax revenue to offset the expense. In
addition, those individuals would still be using the City’s infrastructure.
   2.   Eddie Staley, Shannon Moore, and another staff member from Withers-
Ravenel presented the findings of their impact analysis. Mr. Staley said the
project objectives was to review the developer’s schedule for new
infrastructure, review the most influential revenues and expenditures, and to
provide a 10-year financial analysis of infrastructure needs. Ms. Moore
explained that they did not increase the tax rate or revaluations in the
analysis. They did consider sales tax increases, ABC Revenues, Fire District
fees, and the utility franchise. The total additional expense base was
estimated at $1,796,000, including $200,000 for paving inside the proposed
project area. The 10-year cumulative revenue surplus is estimated at $15.5
million, but it starts to level off after the seventh year. Mr. Staley
explained that the location of this project make it more favorable to the City.
The project is already inside the fire district. There would be no water and
sewer, or stormwater expense to the City.
Mayor Hatem said that the City’s Police Department already needs more room. The
revenue from the project, if approved, could help fund that building. Mayor
Pro-tem Mosteller asked if there were any markers for understanding the long-
term benefits of annexation? Mr. Staley said that generally speaking, annexing
property, and gaining the tax revenue is one of the biggest benefits. But it
also depends on the level of services provided, revaluations, and tax rates.
F.)
    Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked if the density was cut in half, could an
assumption be made that the revenue would also be cut in half. Ms. Moore said
there were too many factors to make that assumption. Alderman Davis asked if
the City has to maintain the roads if they do not annex. Thomas Lloyd said
there is no obligation to maintain the roads if they do not annex.
Fred Fiss, Planning Board member, asked about the electrical infrastructure,
and Mr. Staley said that they never include electrical components because they
do not have expertise in that area. Planning Board member Chris Jones asked
Withers-Ravenel about how many reports like this they do each year, and if they
ever look at projects after build-out to see how accurate the reports are. Mr.
Staley said there is a certain amount of sensitivity that comes into play with
these analyses. There are so many variables. This particular analysis allowed
70% sensitivity, so there is a lot that could happen, but it would still be of
benefit to the City. There is no guarantee that this project would be
financially beneficial to the City, but there is confidence in the model.
Planning Board member Gustavo Mibelli said that the consultants were asked to
compare apples to oranges. He suggested comparing the same number of units with
annexation and without. He thinks there will be a short-term benefit to the
City, but after several years, the benefit will diminish. The reality of the
project is that it is not consistent with the Land Use Plan.
Sue Hodgin, Planning Board Chair, said that the Board’s should look past the
money. The tax base should not push them into approving the project.
Alderman Lombardi asked if the developers are only approved for 550 units,
would they still annex into the City. Lucy Gallo said that it wasn’t
financially feasible for the developers to annex at that density.
G.) Public Comment
Rebecca Kelly, resident of Indigo Plantation, asked for clarification about the
$200,000 for paving roads. That amount ifs just for the roads inside the Indigo
Plantation Phase 2. She also added that a portion of the land area included is
already in the City limits. Regardless of whether the developers annex, we
would still get tax revenue on that portion.
David Roach said he wondered what the impacts would be on the quality of life
in the City. He also asked if the developers had actually placed the proposed
number of homes on the property to see if they would fit.
Shirley Sullivan asked when the analyses would be available to the public and
when the Planning Board would be making their recommendation.
There were questions about the electrical grid impacts and who would be paying
for those improvements. Gordon Hargrove stated that there have been discussions
with the City Attorney and an electrical systems expert. The developer will
likely have to help pay for the improvements, but we don’t know the cost at
this time.
Jim Lightbourne, a resident at 116 W. West Street, said that these studies
didn’t show as much as an annexation study would have shown. Mr. Staley said
that wasn’t what they were tasked to do. If they go through the scenarios and
there were all red flags, everyone could stop talking about the project today.
But when there are some green and some red, they have to keep looking. He added
that the consultants were not asked to review Land Use Consistency, only fiscal
and infrastructure impacts.
Another citizen asked where NCDOT was during the review. He was particularly
concerned about what would happen considering that traffic already gets backed
up on 9th Street and Robert Ruark.
Shirley Sullivan said that a growth rate of 2% was included in these studies,
but Brunswick County is growing at 4%. There are a lot more trips generated
with that percentage.
Mr. Chad Paul said that he believes Bald Head Island Ltd is the largest tax
payer in the City. The proposed 1542 dwelling units will fit on the property.
He concluded by saying that they are paying more than there share of the
project reviews.
H.)   Adjourn

cares about Southport. He appreciates everyone in attendance and all of the
consultant’s work. Alderman Lombardi made a motion to adjourn, which was

Gustavo Mibelli made a motion to adjourn the Planning Board meeting. Will

acres of undeveloped land currently zoned R-20. The applicants have requested a
map amendment to PUD and approval of a master development plan. The developers
propose 4.1 dwellings per acre, 80,000 square feet of non-residential use. The
City and the developers partnered in having two analyses done; one was fiscal
impacts on the general fund, and the other was impacts on the City's
infrastructure.
   6.   Mr. McLeod continued with the Planning Board recommendation for the
Indigo Plantation Phase 2 project. He said that the Planning Board had
thoroughly reviewed all of the aspects of the proposed project. At the Planning
Board's July meeting, they unanimously recommended denying the proposed master
plan and rezoning request. The Planning Board submitted a statement of
consistency with the recommendation.

parcels on W. 11th Street. The request is to rezone the three lots from MF to

Alderman Davis motioned to approve the zoning map amendment for 300,302 and 304
W. 11th Street. Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion

Caswell Avenue. The parcel is currently zoned Business District, and the
applicant requests R-10 zoning. The property is currently in the City's ETJ and
is part of the old Southport Heights subdivision. The Planning Board heard this

approve the map amendment for 1208 N. Caswell, rezoning it to R-10. Alderman
Lombardi seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
   9.   Mr. McLeod explained the proposed text amendment that was citizen-
initiated. The proposed amendment would change Section 3.5 Table of Uses to
allow outdoor recreation in the Business District. Outdoor recreation includes
mini golf and water parks. The Planning Board reviewed the request, found it
inconsistent with the Land Use Plan, and recommended denying the text
amendment. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller motioned to deny the text amendment for
outdoor recreation. Alderman Davis seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion
carried. Alderman Davis asked if Conditional Rezoning would be useful in this
case. Mr. McLeod agreed it would be the appropriate process because a site plan
would be required. Alderman Davis asked Wes McLeod to explain the difference
between a text amendment and a conditional rezoning. He explained that a text
amendment wherein a use is amended in the Table of Uses. The proposed use would
be allowed anywhere in the specific district. Conditional zoning requires a
site-specific site plan, and the proposed use would only be valid on that
parcel, not the entire district. Also, the Board can establish conditions
regarding the use of the property by using Conditional Rezoning.

SEPTEMBER 6, 2022
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN         SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL EXTERIOR LIGHTING WORKSHOP
SEPTEMBER 6, 2022          
 
PRESENT: Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller, Aldermen Tom
Lombardi, Lowe Davis, John Allen, Rich Alt, and Robert Carroll.
STAFF PRESENT: Gordon Hargrove, City Manager, and City Clerk Dorothy Dutton
Mayor Hatem called the workshop to order at 10:02 a.m. Alderman Lowe Davis
provided the invocation, and Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of
Allegiance.
Mayor Hatem stated that the City was not applying to be a dark skies community,
but the lighting policies are still very important to the City. Lighting should
face away from the sky, other dwellings, and the night birds and insects. Mayor
Hatem asked Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller to expound on the proposed Ordinance
amendment.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller explained that the amendment was proposed to provide
consistency between the UDO standards and the Code of Ordinance. She reviewed
the amendment. In summary, exterior lighting must be of a certain color
temperature (3000 kelvins or less). Exterior lighting must be installed and
oriented so as to not create a direct glare or illumination onto streets,
adjacent properties, or the night sky. Blinking or flashing lights are
prohibited. Private security lights may not exceed (25) feet in height, and all
accent or landscaping lights must be aimed and shielded. Existing exterior
lighting fixtures do not need to be replaced until they are not longer
functional. But existing lights should be adjusted or shielded so they do not
shine away from their intended focus. Any fixtures that are in need of
replacement, must be replaced with a conforming light fixture (as shown on
provision P.). Holiday lighting and decorative string lighting is exempt from
the provisions except the height and direction of the light. Temporary lighting
installed by an official government agency to address public safety is also
exempt.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller described the conforming light fixtures.
Alderman Davis said that there are many different options in Lowe’s Home
Improvement that are in compliance with the ordinance. Alderman Alt expressed
concern because most of the churches in the area have lights that shine up.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said that if they are shining up onto the church
itself, it is fine. Any lights facing up onto the sky or out, would need to be
shielded.
There was some discussion about which department is responsible for enforcing
this ordinance. City Manager Gordon Hargrove stated that it would fall under
the umbrella of Code Enforcement. Some of the Aldermen suggested that a copy of
the light policy and the tree protection ordinance be distributed to new
residents of Southport.
Adam Steadman, a resident of Indigo Plantation, stated that he was in support
of the proposed ordinance, but wanted to make sure the information was
available to the public.
Ms. Brown-Busch, a resident on Burrington Avenue, explained how important the
exterior lighting policy is. She realized that she had a non-compliant fixture
at her home, and she added gorilla tape to shield it away from the neighbor’s
property.
Mayor Hatem explained that this was a workshop to educate the Board and allow
discussion before voting on the amendment at the September 8, 2022 Regular
Board Meeting.
Alderman John Allen made a motion to adjourn the meeting, which was seconded by
Alderman Carroll. Mayor Hatem adjourned the meeting at 11:09 a.m. All ayes.
Motion carried.

                     Joseph P. Hatem, M.D., M.P.H.

Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk

Regular Meeting Minutes
 
Board of Aldermen  Regular Meeting Minutes
SEPTEMBER 8, 2022  223 E. Bay Street
Community Building 6:00 p.m.
 
Present: 
Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro Tem Karen Mosteller, Aldermen Thomas Lombardi,
Rich Alt, Lowe Davis, Robert Carroll, and John Allen.
Staff Present:   Gordon Hargrove, City Manager
   Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
   Norwood Blanchard, III, City Attorney
   Randy Jones, Communications/Tourism Director
   Allayna Dail, Assistant Director of Tourism and Community Building Manager
   ChyAnn Ketchum, Communications and Public Information Officer
   Heather Hemphill, Parks and Recreation Director
   Kate Marshall, Animal Control
   Todd Coring, Police Chief
   Charles Drew, Fire Chief
   Melanie Trexler, Finance Director
   Tom Stanley, Public Services Director   
   Wes McLeod, Cape Fear Council of Governments
Others Present: There were many concerned citizens who attended, as well as
Eliot Duke with the State Port Pilot, and Renee Spencer with the Star News
Online.
Meetings are now open to the public. Complete audio/video is available on the
City's website or can be requested from the City Clerk's office.
Mayor Joseph P. Hatem called the meeting to order at 6:01 p.m. and welcomed
everyone to the meeting. He thanked everyone for attending the meeting and
watching online.
Fire Chief Charles Drew provided the invocation, as he does every September.
The invocation included prayers for the families who lost someone on September
11, 2001.
Mayor Hatem led the pledge of allegiance.
Public Comment: 
Mayor Hatem announced that the proposed Indigo Plantation Phase 2 project has
been removed from the agenda. He asked Mr. Chad Paul, with Bald Head Island
Limited, to read a letter concerning the project. Mr. Paul read a letter
stating that East-West Partners Management Co., and Bald Head Island Limited,
elected to voluntarily withdraw all of the pending applications with the City
associated with Phase 2 of Indigo Plantation. They withdrew the application in
order to allow the time necessary to work with the City and negotiate and
appropriate changes.
Mr. Paul added that they have heard from everyone-the public, and the Board.
Their goal is to have a good and healthy conversation and negotiation with the
City. They will not submit an application for exactly the same thing again. He
is confident there is a happy place for both the City and the developers.
Mayor Hatem thanked Mr. Paul and other developers for their willingness to work
with the public and the Board. Alderman Carroll asked City Manager Gordon
Hargrove to explain the difference between an application withdrawal, and a
denial. Mr. Hargrove said that with the voluntary withdrawal of the
application, there is no time requirement before resubmitting an application.
If the project is denied officially by the Board, the applicant must wait at
least six months to reapply unless the Board waives the requirement. Mayor
Hatem added that the Board will do what is right for the citizens and City of
Southport.
City Clerk Dorothy Dutton started calling names from the Public Comment sign-in
sheet. Mr. Karl Bliss, a resident at 1011 Softwind Way, spoke to the Board
about the proposed project at 115 N. Howe Street. He said that the proposed
building will take away the charm of the City. He has lived in Southport for
four years. He said if the building was allowed, there would be overflow. He
suggested limiting the height of buildings to two stories. He added that if
more bars open downtown, there will be beer cans and drunks in the downtown
area.
Another resident from Robert Ruark, discussed traffic concerns, especially with
hurricane preparedness. He asked when the Board was going to do something to
preserve animal habitats.
El Lambert, resident at 109 W. Nash Street, stated she was opposed to the
proposed building at 115 N. Howe Street. She is submitting a petition on behalf
of those opposed to the project.
Tracy Beaulieu, resident of 206 W. Nash Street stated that the current
proposals for 115 N. Howe Street, includes the grease storage and dumpsters are
next to a residential home. This is the only project in the Central Business
District that buts up exactly to a residential home. She said there will be no
privacy for the people who live on W. Nash Street, and where are all the people
going to park?
Ms. Pat Kirkman addressed the Board next. She said that she has been a resident
of Southport for 26-years and resides at 119 Park Avenue. She was speaking
about the cemeteries. She thanked Public Services Director Tom Stanley and his
staff for their work on the cemetery. She started to name a City employee that
she considers partly to blame for the cemetery conditions, but Mayor Hatem
gaveled and told her that, naming a specific employee to accuse them of
something is prohibited. The purpose of public comment is to address the Board.
She apologized and redirected her questions to the Board. She stated that the
cemetery superintendent position has no job description, and the records are
lacking. There are no records of who is buried in each location, and the
financial records have still not been provided. She suggested to the Board that
an ad hoc committee be created to seriously consider a cemetery committee. She
also added that the (4) part time positions that were advertised over the
summer could be combined into one full-time position. She thanked the Board for
their time.
Francesca Slaughter, resident at 6243 Cottage Creek Road, asked the Board to
consider a referendum regarding the proposed Indigo Plantation Phase 2 project.
City Attorney Norwood Blanchard explained that legislative actions allow for
more Board discretion. When a zoning amendment is sought, it is not uncommon to
hear the opinions of the Board members. The public can also speak, but they
have power in voting. If people don’t like the way a Board member is voting on
zoning matters, they can vote for a different candidate next election. But
developers cannot be tied down to one particular use in a zoning map amendment.
Ana Scott, resident at 6272 Cattail Court, stated she has been in Southport for
37 years. She said the Board members were chosen and elected because they
seemed to be the best stewards of Southport. The Board has the power to change
the course of Southport forever. She believes they should decline the Indigo
Planation proposed project and added that development should not be at the
expense of the residents.
Jack Gordon, resident at 5921 Dutchman Creek, explained that he moved to
Southport in 2005, and there was already a lot of traffic. At that time, it
took three hours to get from the yacht basin to his home on Robert Ruark during
the 4 th of July festivities. There are simply not enough roads, and the
condition is poor.
Bob Brogan, resident at 4011 Robert Ruark Drive, said that the proposed Indigo
project would back up to his property. He is a license home inspector in the
region. He expects homes to be built, but the intersection of Howe and Robert
Ruark are not able to handle the amount of traffic that would be added. There
are housing developments going up all along NC 211 Hwy and US 17, all the way
to Myrtle Beach. Southport doesn’t have the schools or stores to support a huge
increase in population. Bigger populations bring drugs, violence, and gangs to
the area. He added that Southport doesn’t want to become another Wilmington.
Lois Gandy, resident at 5961 Spikerush Trail, said she is concerned about 9 th
Street. She urged the developers to reconsider the location of the proposed
Indigo Phase 2 project, for the safety of the children at Southport Elementary
School. She said that safety in classrooms is already a concern, and now, the
parents and teachers would have to worry about the children dealing with
traffic.
Pearline Messer, a resident at the senior apartments on Dosher Cut-off, said
that there is not enough senior housing in the area. The rent where she resides
keeps increasing and now most of the elderly people there will have to find
somewhere else to live. She said that she has lived in the apartment for five
years, and her rent went up to $1084 a month. People have to make the decision
to pay rent or buy the prescriptions they need. There is no where for people to
go in the area.
Mayor Hatem read the Ethics Statement.
E.) Approval of Agenda.
Alderman Lombardi made a motion to approve the agenda to include the omission
of the Indigo Project. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller seconded the motion. All ayes.
Motion carried.

H.) Agenda
Mayor Hatem invited Mr. Eric King from Morningstar Marina to speak to the
Board. Mayor Hatem added that the marina will be great partners with the City.
The company is out of Monroe, North Carolina. Mr. King said that they are in
the business of storage. They are in the process of installing a living
shoreline by the gazebo open space area. The shoreline is decreasing every day,
so they are using oyster shells and sea oats where they can and will evaluate
what each section needs. Morningstar Marina will provide $25,000 towards the
kayak launch. They are happy to help the City and the public however they can.
Mr. King said that he would like to see Military Appreciation Day return to the
marina. He also said that there are a lot of questions about a restroom at the
kayak launch. Morningstar Marina is open to building a unisex restroom for use
at the kayak launch. Mr. King thanked all of the City staff that has helped-
permitting, and the fire marshal, and everyone else. Mr. King invited the
public to visit the marina anytime.
Mayor Hatem asked City Attorney Norwood Blanchard to provide some insight about
the court case in Wilmington, NC, regarding short-term vacation rentals. Mr.
Blanchard explained that in April 2022, the courts agreed with the Plaintiffs,
and declared that using a registration program to monitor short-term vacation
rentals was unconstitutional. As a result, short-term rentals can only be
managed through zoning. The City of Southport’s ordinance was modeled after
Asheville, NC, but it was similar to the City of Wilmington’s, too. The Court
did not strike down all the provisions, just the registration program. For
example, a municipality can still require an off-street parking space, and can
require the owners to post important emergency numbers in a prominent area. Mr.
Blanchard advised the City to suspend the permit requirement and direct the
staff to prepare a list of those who paid for their permits, and issue refunds.
He also recommended that the ordinance go back to the Planning Board for review
and amendments . Alderman Allen made a motion to suspend the registration and
fees for the short-term rentals and homestays, refund the fees, and send the
ordinance back to the Planning Board. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller seconded the
motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
Mayor Hatem stated the next item was a public hearing to consider adopting an
ordinance that would create a Historic Preservation Commission in Southport. He
mentioned J. Arthur Dosher, Art Newton, history of the river pilots, historic
homes, churches, and cemeteries. Mayor Hatem asked Mayor Pro-tem to elaborate
on the proposed ordinance. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller explained that the
conversation about a Commission started about 40 years ago. This evening, we
are considering the first step in protecting the City’s heritage. The purpose
of this ordinance is to establish a local Commission. This ordinance is based
on the state model ordinance, and describes the power, duties, and rules of
procedure. If adopted, it will become part of our Code of Ordinances. Once the
members are appointed, they will present the appropriate districts, inventory,
and guidelines. That portion would be adopted as part of the Unified
Development Ordinance, after review and recommendation by the Planning Board.
Mayor Hatem opened the Public Hearing at 7:30 p.m. There were no comments from
the public or the Board. Mayor Hatem closed the hearing at 7:31 p.m. Mayor Pro-
tem Mosteller made a motion to adopt the ordinance to create a Historic
Preservation Commission. Aldermen Carroll, Allen, and Davis all seconded. All
ayes. Motion carried.
Mayor Hatem called on Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller to explain the proposed Exterior
Lighting Ordinance. She stated that the proposed ordinance is a result of the
work of the Street Light Committee. While working on the street light policy,
the committee recognized the need for additional ordinance regarding exterior
lighting. One of the important issues the ordinance addresses is light
trespass. The purpose is to shield the lights from adjacent properties and the
night sky. This ordinance will help protect nighttime insects and birds.
Seasonal and string lights are exempt unless they cause problems for neighbors.
Alderman Davis added that lights should shine down, not up. There is a page of
examples for light fixtures. Light fixtures are not exclusive to those shown on
the page, but merely examples of conforming light fixtures. Existing lights are
grandfathered. However, when fixtures fail and are being replaced, the new
fixtures should comply with the proposed ordinance standards. Alderman Alt
stated that the purpose of the ordinance is not to consider churches with up-
lighting in violation. If the light shines up, but shines on the structure,
that is not a violation of the ordinance. Mayor Pro-tem summarized that there
should be no light trespassing and lighting should comply with dark skies.
Mayor Hatem opened the Public Hearing at 7:42 p.m. Jeanne Brown-Busch walked to
the podium. She said that she chose to live in Southport over a decade ago. She
loves the sheer beauty of Southport and loves to sit at the waterfront. She
commended the Board for the previous adoption of the new UDO standards, and now
considering the Code of Ordinance update. She added that we will all be held
accountable to protect the night sky. She urged the public to take a walk at
night and let the beauty seep into our souls. Tracy Beaulieu thanked the Board
for the lights on Howe Street. The Public Hearing was closed at 7:47 p.m.
Mayor  Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion to adopt the proposed amendment to the
Code of Ordinances regarding exterior lighting. Alderman Davis seconded the
motion. All ayes, Motion carried.
Mayor Hatem asked Wes McLeod with the Cape Fear Council of Governments to
explain the next few items. Mr. McLeod stated the next item was a proposed
amendment to Section 3.18 of the Unified Development Ordinance, regarding Tree
Preservation. He reviewed the proposed amendment including the new mitigation
language, regulated trees, and tree impact permits. This amendment was a
coordination of the Planning Board and the Forestry Committee. The Planning
Board made a favorable recommendation to the Board of Aldermen. Mayor Hatem
opened the Public Hearing at 7:49 p.m. There were no questions from the public
or the Board. Mayor Hatem closed the Public Hearing at 7:50 p.m. A motion was
made by Alderman Davis to approve the Statement of Land Use Consistency, and
the amendment to 3.18 Tree Preservation, as presented. Alderman Lombardi
seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.  
Wes McLeod reviewed the proposed UDO amendment to several sections of the
ordinance regarding the standards in the Central Business District and Business
District. The proposed amendment would reduce the maximum height in those
districts to (30) feet and places a maximum of two stories for buildings in
those districts. The proposed amendment also increases buffer requirements
between those districts and residential districts, redefines the allowed uses
on each level in a mixed use building, and establishes minimum off-street
parking spaces. Mayor Hatem opened the Public Hearing at 7:52 p.m. Alderman
Davis asked Mr. McLeod to expound on the specific standards and how much they
were changing. Mr. Swenson, owner of Provisions and Company, and resident of
Southport, said that he was trying to picture everything in his head. He said
that the proposed ordinance amendment would place restrictions on design
because of the maximum height. That would be a problem in flood zone areas. Mr.
McLeod stated that there is an exemption for property in the floodplain.
Rebecca Kelly, resident of Indigo Planation and local business owner, thanked
the Board. She expressed concern about the existing businesses in older
buildings. If they decline to a point where renovations or reconstruction
should be needed, would they not be allowed to rebuild in the exact manner?
These new standards would make some of the existing lots somewhat unbuildable.
She asked the Board to look at the buffer requirements particularly because
that would cause the biggest problem.
Andrew Laing, owner of a local business and resident approached the podium
next. He stated that he has a lot at stake in the downtown. Reduction of
height, potential loss of tax revenue, etc. He believes that these proposed
changes are a response to some of the proposed projects in the central downtown
area. His proposed project to the existing Bullfrog Corner building and the
application to build a three-story mixed use building at 115 N. Howe Street,
have sent people into a panic. He guarantees that after a few years, the new
building will blend in with the character that is currently present. He also
questioned why commercial districts maximum height lower than in residential
zoning districts. In closing, he added that investments that are made to a
downtown area, will create a prosperous downtown.
Tracy Beaulieu asked if there was any language in the proposed amendment that
would limit the number of short-term vacation rentals or boutique hotels in the
Central Business District. Mr. McLeod answered that there was no language
concerning short-term rentals.
Alderman Alt asked for an explanation and purpose of extending buffers in
between residential and commercial districts. Mr. McLeod explained the purpose
and added that the buffer requirements would be increasing to twenty (20) feet
in the CBD and BD, and to ten (10) feet in MF and PUD.
Attorney Norwood Blanchard added that there would be instances where a variance
could still be obtained for certain projects. If all of the value is removed
from a property because the zoning standards are so strict, that is considered
a taking. A taking is illegal. Alderman Alt suggested the amendment be tabled
until there is more information. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller suggested that
property owners should use the variance process. Mr. McLeod said that the Board
is welcome to change the standards, adopt them tonight, and tweak later.
Rebecca Kelly stated again that she would ask the Board to add a statement that
existing buildings can be rebuilt in the same footprint. Mayor Hatem said that
the standards can always be changed later.
Mr. Swenson approached the podium again to say that it seemed this was a knee-
jerk reaction, and he doesn’t think the proposed language was thought through.
There is no preservation of the town commercially. He suggested that
architectural drawings should be required for commercial buildings. He added
that at the moment, he could build an igloo with an ice cream cone and there is
nothing that could prevent it.
Glen Patterson, resident of 102 W. Nash Street, stated that there are no
limitations to what people can do right now. He doesn’t think that setting a
maximum height is a bad thing. Additionally, there is no noise limitation in
the City. The rooftop bar will have people out all hours making noise. He is
not against development of the property, but there has to be a ceiling to what
people can do.
Rich Gephardt, a local resident,  suggested the ordinance be looked at more
closely. The City is opening themselves up for a lawsuit. Even a partial taking
can result in a lawsuit.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said that the first sentence in Item 2 should be
removed, so that it is consistent with the table. And she also said the mixed
use parking standards should be updated to (2) parking spaces per residence.
Mayor Hatem closed the Public Hearing at 8:30 p.m. Alderman Allen made a motion
to approve the Statement of Land Use Consistency and proposed amendments, as
presented and revised. The motion was seconded by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and
Alderman Carroll. All ayes. Motion carried.

SEPTEMBER 16, 2022
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN        SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL KAYAK LAUNCH-CAMA GRANT
SEPTEMBER 16, 2022         
 
PRESENT:
Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Tom Lombardi,
John Allen, Lowe Davis, Robert Carroll, and Rich Alt
STAFF PRESENT:
Gordon Hargrove, City Manager   Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
Heather Hemphill, Parks and Recreation Director
OTHERS PRESENT: Pat Kirkman, Roberta Dosher, Emma Thomas, Brian Stevens, Tish
Hatem, Eliot Duke (State Port Pilot)
Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special workshop to order at 10:06 a.m.
Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
CAMA Grant Application and Process for Kayak Launch
Mayor Hatem explained that part of the grant application requirement was to
hold a public meeting/hearing to explain the funds matching requirement and the
plans for the project. Mayor Hatem asked Parks and Recreation Director to
explain the process to the Board and public. Ms. Hemphill thanked the Board for
attending the meeting. She explained that the City was granted an easement by
the marina years ago and has never had their own kayak launch. Ms. Hemphill
said that the City had to submit a pre-application to CAMA first, and then the
City was asked to complete the full application, provide engineered drawings, a
cost estimate, a scope of work, and a proposed schedule. After submitting the
pre-application in April, 2022, the City was asked to complete the next step,
and the full application is due by September 19, 2022. The closest ADA
compliant kayak launch is at Oak Island. Ms. Hemphill spoke to a local
contractor about the project to get a cost estimate. Because Brunswick County
is a Tier 3 county, the City must provide a 25% cost match. The marina has
generously donated $25,000 towards the project, and the City has already
budgeted $13,000. We are asking for $150,000 as a grant. The application will
be submitted, and hopefully the City will know the outcome in October 2022.
Ms. Hemphill described the process and explained that obtaining a CAMA permit
will take the majority of the time. Construction will be fairly quick once
things get started. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked for clarification on a
permeable access path that was shown on the plans. Ms. Hemphill said that
traditional boardwalk areas are expensive, so this will allow a workable
boardwalk until the Boardwalk can be extended out further. Alderman Carroll
expressed concern about not having enough parking available. Ms. Hemphill
explained that more parking, a bathroom, and a picnic area is planned for the
future.
E)    Public Comment
1. Emma Thomas, who owns the Adventure Company in Southport, said that this
project is a great opportunity. At the planned entrance location, there is
incredible wildlife and birds. The water is tidal, but it doesn’t take you out
too far into the Cape Fear. And it is navigable water.
2. Roberta Dosher asked if the City had funding to complete the additional
phases of the project already, or if the City will apply for additional grants?
Ms. Hemphill said that she will always try to get grant funding if it is
available. She added that the City can apply again with CAMA, or the City can
apply for PART-F funding. After Ms. Dosher asked when the kayak launch would be
open, Ms. Hemphill said that it will take approximately (18) months because the
plans get reviewed by every regulatory organization. State Port Pilot reporter,
Eliot Dukes, told the Board that the parking area is already finished and
suggested the Board members go to the site.
3. Brian Stevens saluted the City for getting this project done. He asked if
there was a special name selected for the launch. He suggested the City place a
storage apparatus at the launch. People could pay monthly rent to the City for
use of the storage option. The money coming in could be used to maintain the
launch area. He added that five spaces for parking is probably not enough, but
it was a great start.
F.)     Board Questions and Comments
The Board had no other questions or comments.
Alderman Allen made a motion to adopt the Resolution in support of the CAMA
grant application and fund matching for the proposed kayak launch. Alderman
Carroll seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
G. ) Adjourn
After a motion by Alderman Lombardi, and seconded by Alderman Allen, Mayor
Hatem adjourned the Special Public Meeting at 10:35 a.m. All ayes. Motion
carried.

PRESENT:

A)   Call to Order

   Mayor Hatem welcomed everyone to the special meeting. He explained that the
meeting
Was noticed appropriately, but somehow it was not on the website. Regardless,
the Public Hearing was noticed at the Regular Board meeting, and now the
deadline is close. The meeting would qualify as an Emergency meeting, too. He

D)    Asset Management Plan
Mr. Hargrove said that a couple of years ago, the Cape Fear Council of
Governments completed an Asset Management Plan for the City, but it was not
complete. Because it was not complete, the City was not awarded as much money
as possible. He said that the City has been working with Carter Hubard, an
engineer with W.K. Dickson, to complete the plan. Mr. Hargrove introduced Mr.
Hubard. Carter Hubard said that they are trying to secure as much money as
possible for the City. W.K. Dickson had to supplement the information that was
provided by the CFCOG. They have also created a capital improvement plan. There
is some targeted funding that they are pursuing. Mr. Hubard explained the
projects that the City is applying for funding for: Mulberry Wastewater
Treatment Plant Expansion, Sewer Replacement, Stormwater, and an Inflow &
Infiltration Study.
Alderman Davis asked for more information about smoking the lines. He
summarized that a “smoke bomb” goes off and then gaps or leaks in the system
can be identified because the smoke is coming out. In addition, videoing the
lines helps identify cracks and other leaks.
Alderman Alt asked if we had enough money to camera or smoke all of the lines
that have not been done yet. Mr. Hubard said that they will focus on the older
lines first. Alderman Alt also mentioned the presence of bacteria in some water
testing that was done by a private group. Public Services Director said that
the water that was tested is surface water. He was skeptical that the
contaminants are leaking from a sewer line that is 8-9 feet deep. Mr. Hubard
said they would definitely look into those areas.
    Ms. Emily Miller added that the approval and adoption of the Asset
Management Plan would give the City more points when applying for funding. The
City already has a loan to cover the debt service payment for the USDA Loan for
the Wastewater Treatment Plant expansion, but if we were awarded ARPA funding,
it would reduce our debt service. Because that is such a large ask. We are
submitting the other applications, too. The sewer rehab and I & I study work
together.
E)   Ms. Miller asked the Board to make a formal motion to approve, adopt, and
implement the Asset Management Plan.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion to adopt, approve, and implement the
Asset Management Plan to include the operations and management portions.
Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
   Alderman Allen made a motion to approve the Resolution in Support of
Applying for ARPA funding for the sewer rehab project. Alderman Davis seconded
the motion. All ayes. Motion carried 6-0.
   Alderman Alt made a motion to approve the Resolution in Support of Applying
for ARPA funding for the Inflow and Infiltration Study. Alderman Carroll
seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried 6-0.
   Mayor Hatem said that the Wastewater Treatment Plant Expansion is in pursuit
of the regionalization of the water and sewer systems. Alderman Lombardi made a
motion to approve the Resolution in Support of Applying for ARPA funding for
the expansion of the Mulberry Wastewater Treatment Plant. Alderman Davis
seconded. All ayes. Motion carried 6-0.
   Alderman Allen made a motion to approve the Resolution in Support of

to speak to the Board and review the City’s wastewater assets and plans for
moving forward. Gordon Hargrove clarified that the previous presentation from
W.K. Dickson was not sufficient, and he had reached out to Wooten. It was a
quick turnaround, but Wooten was able to make the deadline for the City.
   Walter Gross stated they had focused on the wastewater treatment plant,
inflow and infiltration, and pump station rehab. The City needs $100,00o a year
to maintain the current system. Currently, 38% of flow into the system is I &
I, which is considered excessive. The City has 891 manholes, and 203 are in
poor condition. Five of the City’s pump stations are in poor condition. There
was discussion about the amount of money the City is paying the County for I &
I to be processed. The City would need $54.3 million dollars to bring
everything up to good condition. The City is hoping to receive $15 million
through the fall round of ARPA funding.
   Gordon Hargrove added that the Wastewater Treatment Plant was currently
going out for bid. Mr. Hargrove thanked Emily Miller, Melanie Trexler, Tom
Stanley, and Dorrie Dutton for all their hard work in getting everything ready
so quickly. The Board had no further questions. Walter Gross thanked the City
for the opportunity.

H)   Agenda
 
1.    Yacht Basin Plan-Options Presentation by Patrick Flanagan & Wes Macleod,
CFCOG.
   Mr. Flanagan presented a power point on the Yacht Basin Mobility Study and
said that he recommended creating a 5 year Capital Improvement program to begin
the process. He explained that the elements of the study include purpose,
process, existing conditions S.W.O.T analysis, and recommendations. Mr.
Flanagan said that the S.W.O.T analysis is a strategic planning and strategic
management technique used to help a person or organization identify strengths,
weaknesses, opportunities for project planning. It is sometimes called
situational assessment or situational analysis. He shared an illustration of an
example of a similar concept called Woonerf/Living Street: Madison, WI.
 
   The S.W.O.T analysis: Opportunities:
Create defined space through visual & physical improvements
Embrace waterfront asset through boardwalk connection
Increase availability of bicycle & golf cart parking
Accentuate the unique setting through a formalized and designed Woonerf/Living
Street concept
Establish branding for the “Yacht Basin District”
 
   Generalized Recommendations:
West Bay Street: Repaint existing striping to separate non-motorized traffic;
install armadillo dividers; formalize parking.
Yacht Basin Drive: Create “Yield Roadway”; formal Woonerf/living street and
shared roadway; waterfront Boardwalk.
West Moore/South Caswell: Repaint parking spaces to match CBD dimensions;
install bulb outs and high visibility cross walks; additional sidewalks and
stormwater features Brunswick Street: Paint striping to separate non-motorized
traffic; install armadillo dividers; construct boardwalk to connect to Yacht
Basin.
 
Next Steps
Consider adoption of this study.
Designate staff to oversee the implementation of this study.
Designate the Yacht Basin Overlay District Committee (YBODC) as the potential
responsible board for implementation of this study.
Create a five to six-year Pedestrian and Bicycle Capital Improvement Program
(CIP) to assist with prioritization of projects outlined by the YBODC.

4.   Historic Preservation Commission Appointment (Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller,
Alderman Davis,    Alderman Carroll):
   Mayor Hatem reflected on the History of Southport and how it is important to
him and so many    others. He has a great appreciation for the establishment of
the Southport Historic Preservation    Commission and all the great things that
will be achieved by protecting and preserving the history of our City.
   Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller stated “I want to start by thanking everyone that
volunteered to share their time and talents for historic preservation in our
community.
   The Historic Preservation Commission ordinance that was adopted last month
is only the first step towards creating processes that support the City’s
comprehensive plan’s first core value to, ‘Preserve our historic character’.
   Over the next year, it will be the responsibility of the Commission to hold
public meetings to establish the rules of procedure, identify historic district
boundaries, catalog inventory within the district and create guidelines.
   Once the Commission completes these tasks, the Commission’s recommendations
will be forwarded to the Planning Board and then to the Board of Aldermen for
consideration, recommendations, and adoption.
   Additionally, Commission members will participate in training sessions with
the State Historic Preservation Office, learn about grants and hold public
workshops.
   Commission members will serve as ambassadors in our community, helping to
educate us about the history of Southport and why historic preservation is
important to who we are today and for our future.
   During the past two weeks the ad hoc committee, Alderman Davis, Alderman
Carroll, and I interviewed over 20 volunteers. Everyone we interviewed
demonstrated a passion for Southport and a willingness to serve.
   With a finite number of members on the Commission, we asked every volunteer;
in the event they were not appointed to commission this time around… to please
stay engaged, attend the public meetings and workshops, and participate. There
is a lot of work to be done and for the Historic Preservation Commission to be
successful, this must be a community wide effort.”
   Alderman Carroll

of the first    appointments to be staggered as 1-year, 2-year and 3-year
terms. Going forward, after the initial terms are complete, all terms will be
