       5.    Proposal for Land Purchase or Licensing Rights-Polote Corporation
(Lloyd Ludlow, Polote Corporation and Raymond DiGuiseppe, Attorney)
    Mr. DiGuiseppe presented the proposal for the City. He said the Polote
Corporation has    supported small to mid-sized construction projects
throughout the east coast, with a specific focus on the southeastern region,
for the last 40 years, providing essential program and construction management
services that include supplying the necessary materials and labor for
successful and cost-effective projects. This includes supplying projects with
soils, dirt, gravel, and other raw materials, through excavation, transport,
and delivery of those materials to the construction site.
   Polote’s history in this industry has involved previous projects involving
the excavation, transport, and sale of raw materials from the City of
Southport’s 441-acre tract parcel located near the Military Ocean Terminal
Sunny Point (parcel ID number 1900002). Through this current proposal, Polote
seeks to engage in additional such projects using the same property— this time
by either purchasing the tract (or as much of the tract as the City is willing
to sell) or obtaining exclusive rights and privileges to excavate, transport,
and sell soils, dirt, rock, and other surface materials from the tract.
   As with the previous projects involving this tract, Polote’s ownership and/
or access to it for these additional projects would enable the company to
provide essential materials supply services for major construction projects in
the local area. Over at least the next five years, the projects supported by
Polote’s access to this tract would benefit the community by improving the
local real estate and infrastructure, creating numerous jobs in the
construction industry, and supporting the many local businesses whose products
and services Polote will need in connection with carrying out the projects.
   For a purchase of this tract, or as much of it as the City is willing to
sell, Polote would pay at a price    of $4,000 per acre. For any portion of the
tract that City may not wish to sell, Polote would alternatively propose that
the City license to Polote for a fixed period of time exclusive rights and
privileges to excavate, transport, and sell for soils, dirt, rock, and other
surface materials from    those acres of the tract for which the City grants
such rights and privileges. The parties would    establish a mutually agreed
upon price per cubic yard for any such licensing agreement that they may
establish.
   Mr. DiGuiseppe said that he understands the public comment from the
concerned citizen on Bethel Rd. He said they are aware of the regulations and
said this type of use in permissible in this area. He said the Military
Terminal is looking for a supplier of soils and materials in order to renew the
berms that they use to protect against explosions and operations. He said the
Polote Corporation built those berms 15 years ago and he said the base would
like them to use the same materials that’s close by to renew those berms. He
said 15 years ago the same materials were used from this same parcel with an
agreement with Army Corps of Engineers. Mr. DiGuiseppe said    a benefit of
being near the location of where the project is would mean that materials would
not have to be transported on heavy trucks on public roads because it will be
contained in this location. He explained that Sunny Point Military Terminal
will need the supplying of these materials regardless. He said that it could go
out for bid, but they are hoping to keep the supply of the materials in close
proximity to maintain the safest and most cost efficient manner. He said the
necessary permissions and consents from the US Government would be in place
because the military base is the source of the solicitation for this type of
activity to occur.
   Mr. Lloyd Ludlow Senior Vice-President for the civil operations division for
the Polote Corporation, said he has been in this business for over 35 years
specializing in dam building, construction of heavy berms, and levee building.
He said they are proposing to use the same pit or area located    on the
outskirts of the site. He said the reason for this location is because of the
transportation of the material and the material quality itself is excellent and
perfect for this job. He said this would be a 5 phase project organized by the
Corps of Engineers to enhance and repair the existing berms around the rail
road tracks on the site. He said first phase is bidding process which starts on
   October 19 th . Each bid is around 10-15 million dollars’ worth of material
and the funds have been    passed for these projects over the next five years.
Mr. Ludlow explained that the Polote Corporation has been involved with
material for the berm building area and the nearest suitable materials is
approximately 42 miles away. He said over the life of project approximately 5
years, this would mean over 100,000 trucks of dirt. Thus, will cause dust and
road potential road damage. Mr. Ludlow said the dirt is not only perfect for
this berm building project it is also the    right material for the Boiling
Spring Lakes dam rebuilding project.
   Alderman Carroll asked if the Polote Corporation had the funding available
to offer more than    $4,000 per acre if the City so chose to sell instead of
leasing. Mr. Ludlow said that if the City did    decide to sell the price of
the acreage offered could be negotiated. Alderman Carroll questioned if Bethel
Road or any other public roads would be accessed for this project or the BSL
dam rebuilding project. Mr. Ludlow said that no public roads including Bethel
Rd. would be accessed for the current proposed berm rebuilding project. Mr.
Ludlow said the only time that public roads    would be accessed would be for
the BSL project. Alderman Carroll asked if there was a proposal for this
project and where access points would be. Mr. Ludlow said that he did not know
those accesses yet, but he could find out. Mr. Ludlow pointed out that the BSL
dam rebuilding project is a secondary project that would have to get separate
approval for where and when this project would take place.    
   Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller asked if this was like “strip mining” and what would
the landscape look like after the completion of the project. Mr. Ludlow
explained that the term is called “burrow pit mining”, where they would bench
down 10-15 ft. , take of the top soil, and utilize that mix of sand and clay
type soil that is ideal for a compaction to build the berm. He said they would
be using the    same technique that they used 15 yrs. ago at this same
location. He said after proper engineering, grading, sloping, and reseeding the
excavated area would become a large lake.   
   Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller clarified that the proposal would be deferred to the
Planning Board for full review before any decision is made by the Board of
Aldermen.
   Alderman Davis asked if the proposal was an “all” or “nothing” deal for the
entire tract. She said the City will need to keep at least 20 acres for various
needs of the City. Mr. Ludlow said that are open to any offers, but ideally,
they would need approximately 50 acres for lease or purchase for the Sunny
Point berm building project.   
   Alderman Alt asked how this project would delineate from the Hwy 211 mining
project that was shut done due to the infringement on the Castle Hayne aquifer.
Mr. Ludlow said he was not familiar with that project, but he said that they
would not be going that deep and would be away from the aquifer.
   Alderman Alt stated that looking at the area where the mining is proposed
there are marked trees around the acreage that are protected for the endangered
woodpeckers. Mr. Ludlow said that they are aware of the protected trees and the
endangered species and would follow all    regulations and environmental
protections. Alderman Alt confirmed that the soil will have to be    mined from
somewhere whether it be at this location or from a remote area. Mr. Ludlow said
that    was correct, and the Corporation would like to utilize this familiar
location 15 years prior. Alderman Alt asked if they were aware that the City
could request an environmental impact study be performed and submitted prior to
approval. Mr. Ludlow said that they would submit a professional engineering and
environmental plan.
   Alderman Carroll asked if there was a time frame on a decision from the
City. Mr. Ludlow said that is was a 5 year project with 5 phases, and they were
just beginning the process, and were not in a restricted time frame. Alderman
Carroll asked if the City decided to do a licensing agreement for lease would
that be per year or for the total 5 year agreement. Mr. DiGuiseppe said that
there was not a leasing agreement fee amount offered. If the leasing
alternative was the option for the City, there would be a licensing agreement
and fee per acre negotiated.
   City Attorney Blanchard explained the 2 options. That the land could either
be purchased or leased. If the licensing agreement was opted, then it would
just be for the extraction of the soil and nothing else. The City could decide
how much of the land would be negotiable for purchase or lease. Mr. Blanchard
said that the project site would look like a lake. Mr. Ludlow said that was
correct and there could be multiple locations on the site that would be used
for the soil excavation. He said that they are hoping that it would look
exactly like the dirt mining preformed 15 years ago. He said that this is an
assumption that nothing has changed since that time period, the project
engineers will have to observe and test the site for the exact details.
   Alderman Davis asked if the property is sold and the project has been
completed, and there is a large lake left what else could be done on that
property. Mr. Ludlow said that the land would be restricted for recreational
use and the land would never be developed. He said there are very strict rules
from the US Army. Alderman Davis asked if there would be any blasting involved.
Mr. Ludlow said there would not be any.
   Alderman Allen questioned if it is anticipated to have the burrow pit mining
on approximately 50 acres does that have to be contiguous or is it possible
that would be multiple different sites. Mr. Ludlow said that it could be
multiple site over the 50 acre tract. He said the City could decide if they
want it to be contiguous or over multiple sites, that it would not interfere
with the project. Alderman Allen asked what type of machinery would be used for
the project. Mr. Ludlow said that nothing bigger than a track hoe and
bulldozers to push the soil and compact it on the berms. Also, excavator road
worthy trucks and not off-road trucks. Alderman Allen asked how much dust or
sand is expected for the wind to carry offsite. Mr. Ludlow said that they would
have to adhere    to the dust control policy set by the Corp of Engineers , and
therefore the dust will be controlled and contained.
   With no other questions from the Board at this time, Mr. Ludlow concluded
that he is looking forward to working with the City and the Community to ensure
that the project will be successful without any complications to the City or
adjacent property owners.
   Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller made a motion to forward the written request for
the Proposal for Land Purchase or Licensing Rights of the City’s 441 acres land
near Sunny Point Military Terminal submitted by the Polote Corporation to the
Planning Board and ask that the Planning Board    provide a written
recommendations to the Board of Aldermen regarding this proposal and was
   seconded by Alderman Lombardi. Unanimous vote; motion carried.

Comments:
Indigo Phase 2: They are zoned R-20 currently. They submitted a plan for a PUD.
August 17, 2022-headline “Mayor 1,542 units is not acceptable.” We heard the
voice of the people. We look at multiple things-HP, PHS, wildlife, cultural
heritage and neighborhoods. We are looking for least impact but best result for
the City. There is no application currently. We instituted an agreement with
BRUNSCO that doesn’t allow parallel lines. Any development has to be annexed in
order to have sewer. The City hired a development agreement attorney to help
the Board navigate the project and help us negotiate for the best outcome. They
have given some direction to the attorney as to what is best for the City. We
will have a town hall meeting with the new planners. There is no vote or
anything expected any time soon. There are no applications right now.
There is no action on the yacht basin right now. We will have a meeting in 2023
to discuss possibilities.

Item E. Sunny Point Property-Presentation Only
Chesley Ward-thank you for having them here tonight. Land acquisition is a very
important tool for conservation. Rare wildlife and habitats-White Springs
Natural Habitat Area-the Southport tract has the highest significance because
of more natural habitats. Discussions back in 2020. Investigations Report. Dec
2021-partial funding of the tract. That is where they are in the process. What
comes next?
Order an appraisal-couple of months.
State Property Office makes an offer.
IF accepted, the Wildlife will pursue remaining funds. Phase 2 conducted.
Letter of Intent between the City and Wildlife. No contractual agreement.
Once we have a funding plan-project goes before the NC Council of State. Open
agreement. Title search. NCWRC receives all funds and then close on the
property. Usually a year and a half. Turn over to Kacy Cook.
Kacy Cook-Conservation Importance: 1000 vertebrate wildlife-significant decline
of populations. We have 8 of 21 most endangered ECO systems. Pine leaf is one
of the most endangered.
Only 5% of longleaf pine forest remains. Numerous ponds on the property that
support these endangered species. As these habitats disappear, the species go
with them.
Animals hide underground most of the time to escape the extreme temperatures.
Gopher frog is one of the species. Fire is an extremely important component of
conservation. Gopher frogs can travel up to 2 miles to the same stumphole each
year. The breed in the winter. 32 known sites, now only 7 populations known.
The most important pond at MOTSU-largest natural pond. This is the pond where
most of the breeding has happened in the last 6 years. If something happens to
that pond, the entire population/species could disappear. We want to confirm
their interest in pursuing the tract from the City. We they need that type of
confirmation for them to move forward.
Rich Alt-is they had this property, what would they do with it?
Chesley-open to hunting/trapping to archery only. Not exclusive to hunting.
Public allowed to use the property for outdoor recreation. Periodic fire to
mimic the natural processes. Have you seen the easement? He suggests they look
into it.
Polote: Raymond DeGuiseppe : Thanks for having them for a third time. He
created a slide with more information about the process. The proposal intents
to work with the Wildlife Conservation however the City is willing. The soils
have to come from somewhere. This is the closest contiguous property where soil
can be taken from. They are happy to use only 25 acres, and leave the rest for
wildlife. The City could lease the property for ten years. Collaborative or
cooperative effort. They would only use the soil for the berms at MOTSU now,
not other projects. Vice President-Lloyd Ludlow. They are very interested in
working with Wildlife. Once they had access to the property and do the testing.
They continue to say they are willing to work with the City, Wildlife, MOTSU.
Ray is happy to answer questions, as needed.
Ludlow needs 25-50 acres. They need to do bore sampling. Terra-Core. The Polote
Corp is the company that built the berms originally.
Karen-said that she spoke to Mr. Martin at the herpetology organization. The
Wildlife organization has already invested money and time on the track.
Speaking for herself, she couldn’t support mining and drilling on the property.
Rich-because he is a rep of MOTSU-he got a call from MOTSU, he had asked for
the easement. Malcolm Charles is not present. The Board would have to visit
MOTSU and sign a non-disclosure agreement before they could find out what MOTSU
would use it for.
Karen-asked if Wildlife was considered one of the correct public/nonprofits?
Norwood-said that there were separate statutes that would allow us to work with
Wildlife.
Karen-Since the City is not building a sewer plant, is selling the property in
the best interest of the City.
She and Alderman Carroll visited the property with Tom St. Retaining 20 acres-
topography on the Bethel side isn’t conducive. It seems like a better idea to
sell this property and buy
Sewer enterprise fund. Therefore, the property has to be used for that purpose.

Bonnie-we paid back the grant money. Any money that we get for the property
would have to go back to the enterprise fund.
Mayor-let the land stay there. We have time to make a decision. Do our
research. No rush. Good presentations.
Agnes: Why is the City entertaining another deal if we have been working with

Meetings are open to the public. Complete audio/video is available on the
City's website or can be requested from the City Clerk's office.
Call to Order
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. She explained
that Mayor Hatem could not attend, and she was asked to preside over the
meeting.
Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller led the pledge of allegiance.
 
Public Comment: 
The City Clerk called Pat Kirkman, who resides at 119 Park Avenue, forward for
public comment. Ms. Kirkman stated that the City's cemetery ordinances need
review and alteration. The last time they were amended was December 1991. She
asked the Board of Aldermen to appoint a Cemetery Commission to maintain the
records and coordinate the upkeep of the cemeteries with the Public Services
Department. She added that she would keep asking the Board to place more
attention on the cemeteries unless the Board tells her they are not interested
in pursuing any action.
Francesca Slaughter, a resident at 6243 Cottage Creek Road, stated that she is
a member of the "No High-Density Southport" group. They would like to ask the
Board why the City is interested in negotiating with the developers for Indigo
Phase 2. She added that if the City is in a position of power, the City doesn't
have to negotiate. Rezoning to a higher density might attract a better project,
but the City should focus on getting grants to fix our existing infrastructure.
She asked the Board to please share what the City is negotiating.
Aldermen John Allen said that he would like to speak. He wanted to clarify that
PUD does not equate to high density. Preservation of open space is done much
better in the PUD district. The Board is not negotiating; they offer opinions
on the proposed plan. R-20 will still cause traffic problems, and they are only
required to have two points of ingress and egress. He said he would rather have
slightly more dwelling units and three entrances/exits. He said he wished
everyone would understand the decision on not binary; there are many different
ways to work with the developers.
 
   Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller read the ethics statement.  
Alderman Lombardi stated that he wished to recuse himself from item H. 1., the
dedication of the road in Rivermist, because he is the president of the
Rivermist HOA. Alderman Alt motioned to recuse Alderman Lombardi. Alderman
Allen seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
Approval of Agenda
Alderman Lombardi made a motion to approve the agenda as presented. Alderman
Carroll seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
 
Approval of Consent Agenda- Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller summarized the items on the
Consent Agenda.
Minutes of the Closed Session Board of Aldermen Meeting November 8, 2022
Minutes of the Board of Aldermen Regular Meeting November 10, 2022
Capital Projects Ordinance-Shoreline Stabilization
 
Special Recognition-None
 
Agenda
Alderman Lombardi recused himself from considering and voting on this matter.
Attorney Raymond DiGuiseppe represented the Rivermist Property Owner's
Association. He explained that the portion of the road on the side of the
clubhouse was never dedicated to the City. The street is identified as Flank
Court and extends straight to a cul-de-sac. The 60-foot cul-de-sac is not
included in the dedication nor the parking areas for the clubhouse. Ms. Dutton
reported that the Public Services Director, Tom Stanley, had inspected the road
and was comfortable assuming responsibility for its maintenance. Attorney
Norwood Blanchard stated he was comfortable with the language in the deed of
dedication. Alderman Allen motioned to approve the Resolution in Support of
Accepting the Flank Court and agreed to the Deed of Dedication. Alderman Davis
seconded the motion. All ayes, except for Alderman Lombardi, who was recused.
Motion carried.
Interim City Manager Bonnie Therrien introduced the request from two residents
to abandon an alleyway. She said that nothing final was to be decided; other
steps must be taken, including publishing the Intent to Abandon the Alleyway
and contacting adjacent property owners. So far, no department heads were
opposed to abandoning the alley. Mr. Gaines Brown approached the podium to
speak on behalf of the proposal. He explained that after the last storm, there
were trees and branches all over the ground and leaning onto other trees in the
alley. He would like permission to maintain it but not use it actively. It will
remain a natural/green area. There was some discussion about the types of
easements on the property. Currently, the alley is a vacant wooded area.
Typically, the abandoned property would get divided down the center, and those
properties on either side would absorb each side. Ms. Therrien said this
sometimes happens when property owners don't pay their taxes, and the City gets
the property. Alderman Allen motioned to send the item to the Planning Board
for further review before making any decisions. Aldermen Carroll and Davis
seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.  
The Development Services Director reviewed the request for the final plat
approval for a Southport Crossings outparcel. The Southport Crossings project
is vested under the previous ordinance. Staff requested the Board of Aldermen
approve the final plat with three conditions. Alderman Allen approved the final
plat for Southport Crossings with the following conditions:
a. The Plat should not be signed for recordation until a performance guarantee,
and a bond is received and accepted by the City of Southport staff for all
roadways;
b. The Plat will not be signed for recordation until Brunswick County Utilities
has inspected and certified the water and wastewater infrastructure and signed
the plat;
c. The Plat shall not be signed for recordation until all required certificates
are in conformance with the applicable standards of the Unified Development
Ordinance and have been signed by the appropriate parties.
Alderman Carroll seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.

Mayor's Report
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller commented, "the Mayor and "First Lady" send their very
best wishes to everyone for a Merry Christmas and a safe and Happy New Year. We
are so very blessed to live in Southport. Feeling gratitude and not expressing
it is like wrapping a present and not giving it to anyone. So, I would like to
take a moment to say thank you. As citizens of Southport, we are indebted to
the talented individuals that work for the City. With humility, we recognize
that we can never repay you for all the countless, unseen things you do for the
good of the City and its citizens. Whether it's Public Services that keep our
City running or our Police and Fire Departments that keep us safe, or Community
Relations and Parks and Recreation that help to maintain our culture.
Our City is blessed with committed individuals that work here. Also, when I
look around this room, I see neighbors that share their time and talents, day
to day, for the benefit of the City they love. The spirit of volunteerism
within our community appears boundless, whether it's the Beautification
Committee planting bulbs or helping to spread Christmas cheer or the Forestry
Committee helping to watch over our beloved trees, or the kindness of neighbors
checking in on neighbors. I am so very proud to be a part of the community that
you all live in. For all these reasons, Southport is an awesome place to call
home. And please don't forget to take a moment and visit the Southport Garden
Club's Candy Cane Garden at Keziah Park; it's guaranteed to make you smile!"

Meetings are open to the public. Complete audio/video is available on the
City's website or can
be requested from the City Clerk's office.
Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the meeting to order at 6:03 p.m. He welcomed everyone to
the meeting and thanked the Fire/EMS Department for hosting the meeting.
Invocation
Fire Chief Charles Drew provided the invocation.
Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led the pledge of allegiance.
 
Presentation:
Parks and Recreation Master Plan. Parks and Recreation Director Heather
Hemphill introduced Dr. Herstine. Dr. Herstine has been a professor at NC State
University and UNC Wilmington. He was the Parks and Recreation Director in
Chapel Hill and the District Manager for DCM/CAMA in Wilmington. Dr. Herstine
completed the most recent Master Plan and will review the study's most
important findings. The master plan is a vital, living document that guides and
directs what the Parks and Recreation department does for the upcoming years
and is created using public input. Dr. Herstine reported the five most
important facilities the public asked for were sidewalks, bike lanes, an indoor
swimming pool, an outdoor pool, and hiking paths. These projects could be
funded through grants, private sources, bond referendums, or tax increases. Dr.
Herstine recommends that the City add a Parks and Recreation maintenance
division and reclassify the program specialist to Senior Citizen Program
Specialist. A full-time supervisor position should also be added, as a youth
programs specialist. The Parks and Recreation Master Plan is not a financial
document, it is a planning tool, and no funding is committed upon adoption of
the plan.
Mayor Hatem thanked Dr. Herstine for the presentation and asked the public to
come forward to ask questions. Brian Stevens, a resident of Cades Cove, asked
why the kayak launch wasn't listed in the master plan. And he also asked if the

provide.

18-hole disc golf courses in Brunswick County. It takes between half an acre
and an acre per hole. NC is 4 th in the County with registered disc golfers.
Usually, a disc golf trail includes a nature trail.

6. Dredging has not been completed in the Yacht Basin area since the 1990s.
There is a need to have the area dredged to allow for safe passage along the
navigable waters and the City dock area. The first step is to have the area
surveyed. There is an option to coordinate the actual dredging with the marina.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller motioned to authorize the use of Parks and Recreation
funding and City funding to complete surveying the Yacht Basin area. Alderman
Davis and Alderman Allen seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
7. City Manager Bonnie Therrien explained that she had been asked to
investigate a meal tax. The General Assembly must approve the additional tax.
If approved, the Resolution will be sent to the representatives. It is not
required to hold a referendum, but usually, the General Assembly requests a
referendum before they will approve it. Alderman  Lombardi made a motion to
approve the Resolution in support of requesting a one percent meal tax.
Alderman Carroll and Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller. All ayes, motion carried.
8. Ms. Therrien stated that scheduling several Board workshops is necessary.
The Board hears from all the departments and discusses the City issues and
priorities. There is a list of dates included in the packet. January 17 are the
interviews for the new City Attorney. January 19 is a team-building workshop in
the morning, followed by strategic planning in the afternoon.
There will also be a workshop to discuss rights-of-way. In addition, Alderman
Allen has made the recommendation before to schedule an additional regular
board workshop to review the agenda before the meetings. City staff has
reserved the Fridays before the Regular Board meetings, but the Board should
give some direction about what time to schedule. Alderman Carroll suggested
starting the meetings at 9:00 a.m. Alderman Alt explained that at least six
ongoing projects involving the sewer system. All the projects are tied
together, so he proposes hosting a public meeting to educate the public about
all the projects and how they are connected.

attorney. The City received four proposals from interested firms. City staff
can interview the four attorneys and narrow it down to two before the Board
interviews. Or the Board can interview all four. Alderman Davis proposed to let
Staff interview the attorneys first. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller and Alderman Allen
said they would rather ask questions of all four, and Mayor Hatem agreed. Most
of the Board agreed and asked the City Clerk to publish the notice.
10. Next on the agenda was a discussion about the electrical service for the
Osprey Landing subdivision. Ellie Pittenger, the electrical superintendent, was
asked to come forward with questions. Ms. Therrien explained that historically
it seems the City has paid for the system upgrades. No ordinance dictates who
is responsible. Mr. Pittenger added that there are between 180-296 homes in
total. Those properties will be the City's customers, so eventually, the City
will get its money back. Interim Manager asked the Board for a motion to
approve investing $189,000 now because the cost of the materials will increase.
Ms. Therrien asked Ellie Pittenger if that was all that was needed or if a
cushion should be added. Mr. Pittenger explained that the $189,000 was his
calculation, and he always adds extra room for unexpected costs. Alderman
Carroll motioned to invest $189,000 in the  electrical upgrades for Osprey
Landing. Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. Alderman Davis was the only one
opposed. Motion carried.
11. There has been a lot of discussion about relocating the Southport Police
Department to a new location because there is not enough space at City Hall.
Interim City Manager Bonnie Therrien explained that the visibility of the
Police Department is not good. In addition, the other Staff located in City
Hall are also in need of more space. Before anything is done, a feasibility
study should be completed to plan out the City's space needs over the next
twenty years. One company was referred to us. They are proposing $48,000 to
conduct the study plus expenses. That is a very good price. Because it is a
contract, the City does not have to go out for bids. Alderman Alt remarked that
building a police department is a lot different than building a City Hall
because of the extra security features that are required. Alderman Alt motioned
to move  forward with the RFP for a feasibility study with an amount not to
exceed $50,000 using funding from the Police department and City Hall. Alderman
Carroll seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. Ms. Therrien thanked the
Police Department for all their help.
12. Development Services Director Travis Henley explained the Historic
Preservation Commission Rules of Procedure that the commission drafted. They
were able to use some other regional rules as a guideline. Mr. Henley asked the
Board if they would consider adopting them. After a motion made by Aldermen
Carroll and seconded by Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller, the  Board approved the Rules
of Procedure for the Historic Preservation Commission. All ayes. Motion
carried.
13. Interim Manager Bonnie Therrien stated that Olsen Associates were already
awarded the contract for the shoreline stabilization project. The City already
has $5 million in funding. Alderman Allen motioned to authorize the Mayor and
City Manager to sign the contract.  Alderman Carroll and Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.

Presentation: Parks and Recreation Master Plan. Parks and Recreation Director
Heather Hemphill introduced Dr. Herstine. Dr. Herstine has been a professor at
NC State University and UNC Wilmington. He was the Parks and Recreation
Director in Chapel Hill and the District Manager for DCM/CAMA in Wilmington.
Dr. Herstine completed the most recent Master Plan and will review the study's
most important findings. The master plan is a vital, living document that
guides and directs what the Parks and Recreation department does for the
upcoming years and is created using public input. Dr. Herstine reported the
five most important facilities the public asked for were sidewalks, bike lanes,
an indoor swimming pool, an outdoor pool, and hiking paths. These projects
could be funded through grants, private sources, bond referendums, or tax
increases. Dr. Herstine recommends that the City add a Parks and Recreation
maintenance division and reclassify the program specialist to Senior Citizen
Program Specialist. A full-time supervisor position should also be added, as a
youth programs specialist. The Parks and Recreation Master Plan is not a
financial document, it is a planning tool, and no funding is committed upon
adoption of the plan.
Mayor Hatem thanked Dr. Herstine for the presentation and asked the public to
come forward to ask questions. Brian Stevens, a resident of Cades Cove, asked
why the kayak launch wasn't listed in the master plan. And he also asked if the
plan harmonized well with other potential trails that will be built in the
area, including the Gullah Geechee trail. Heather Hemphill explained the kayak
launch wasn't specifically listed as a priority from the public, but also,
because it has already been planned and funded, there was no need to include it
in the master plan. The master plan focused on possible facilities inside the
City limits but welcomed the connectivity that other trail systems would
provide.
A resident who did not provide her name, asked when the survey was available to
the public. She said she has lived in Southport for four years and hasn't heard

facility.

18-hole disc golf courses in Brunswick County. It takes between half an acre
and an acre per hole. NC is 4 th in the County with registered disc golfers.
Usually, a disc golf trail includes a nature trail.

C)    Attorney Interviews
   The first attorney arrived just before 9:00 a.m. Grady Richardson has been
working with Sunset Beach and St. James for years. He discussed some of his
experiences working with the elected boards, planning boards, and boards of
adjustment in different municipalities. He answered the questions from the

Mr. Richardson's normal rate is $525 an hour, but he uses a municipal rate of

   Matt Nichols, a practicing attorney in Wilmington, arrived next. Most of his
experience is in land use law, for which he has over twenty years of
experience. He answered the Board of Aldermen questions and explained that he
is the only attorney in his law firm. He has a very experienced paralegal. Mr.
Nichols said that he does not like to offer legal advice in areas that he is
not an expert, so topics like social media and contracts would probably be
referred to a different attorney. Mr. Nichols charges $220 an hour for his
services, and the paralegal's fees are $90 an hour.
He thanked the Board of Aldermen and staff for their time.
   Raymond DiGuiseppe was the next attorney scheduled for an interview. Mr.
DiGuiseppe explained that he was local to Southport. He has experience in land
use, HOAs, POAs, subdivisions, and local ordinances. In addition, he serves
individual/private clients with stormwater issues, CAMA permits, and floodplain
issues. The Board asked Mr. DiGuiseppe the questions. Attorney DiGuiseppe said
that he tries to be prompt when responding. If he cannot help at that moment,
he will estimate when he can get back to us with the information. He also has a
lot of experience reviewing contracts. Because he lives in Southport, his
availability is more flexible. He could attend the Regular Board meeting and
the newly established Board Agenda Review meeting. After reading through the
resume, Mayor Hatem asked Mr. DiGuiseppe about his background in music and
psychology. Raymond DiGuiseppe compared law and music because they are both
interpretive. Psychology is a part of the law because you must understand the
individuals involved and communicate with them. Mr. DiGuiseppe explained his
rate is $200 an hour but negotiable. He could attend meetings for a flat rate
instead of hourly. The Board of Aldermen thanked Mr. DiGuiseppe for meeting
with them, and he thanked City Staff and the Board for their consideration.
   The last scheduled interview was with the Brough Law Firm. They are based
primarily in the Chapel Hill area. In attendance were T.C. Morphis and Brady
Herman. Seven attorneys in the office practice mainly local government and land
use, and they are currently contracted with twenty-three municipalities. They
cover land use, board governance, personnel, contracts, and writing ordinances.
One of the attorneys, Bob Hornik, currently works with Boiling Springs Lakes,
so distance has not presented any issues. The Brough Law Firm takes a team
representation approach, which assigns two attorneys for each municipality.
Their philosophy is to be legal advisors, not dictators, and they serve to
guide and advise the Board through the parameters of the law. By the time Brady
Herman gave his presentation, most of the Board's questions had been answered.

JANUARY 19, 2023
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
BOARD OF ALDERMEN
BOARD TRNG AND STRATEGIC PLANNING INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL
JANUARY 19, 2023
 
PRESENT:
Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Tom Lombardi,
John Allen, Robert Carroll, and Rich Alt
ABSENT: Alderman Lowe Davis was not able to attend due to illness.
STAFF PRESENT:
Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, Assistant City Manager/City Clerk
OTHERS PRESENT FOR THE MORNING:
Vickie Miller, Director of Learning and Development, NCLM
Ann White, Municipal Operations Manager, NCLM
   
Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special workshop to order at 8:49 a.m.
Invocation
Mayor Hatem suggested a moment of silence instead of an invocation.
Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in reciting the Pledge of Allegiance.
Approval of Agenda
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion to approve the agenda as presented.
Alderman
Lombardi seconded. All ayes. Motion carried.
Communication and Team Building
City Manager Bonnie Therrien welcomed the Board and said the first part of the
meeting would be spent training and team building to have better communication
and revisit the Board's responsibilities. Ms. Therrien introduced Vickie
Miller. Ms. Miller is the Director of Learning and Development with the NC
League of Municipalities and has many years of leadership training and
municipal leadership positions.
Ms. Miller explained that they would begin the morning with a question. She
asked the Board to think about why they ran for office. She gave them a few
minutes and also asked them to work in groups of two. The purpose was to
explain to your partner why you ran for office. Then, each Board member would
take turns explaining why their partner ran for office. This icebreaker allowed
the Board to get to know more about each other.
Ms. Miller reviewed what topics she would speak about, including best
practices, data research for Board success, and characteristics of thriving
communities. Ms. Miller explained the five stages of team development: forming,
storming, norming, performing, and adjourning. Most teams follow through the
stages but also can move back during times of conflict. She asked the Board to
think about which stage they are operating from. Most of the Board members
agreed it was between norming and performing, with brief periods back in
storming. Ms. Miller said that all Board members should be able to speak to
each other, but some Board members communicate with the members with similar
thoughts and opinions.
Ms. Miller explained the difference between dialogue and debate. Listening to
argue is not listening fully. Cognitive dissonance is defined as holding two
contradictory beliefs that cause mental discomfort. Cognitive dissonance can be
eliminated by denying one set of information, gaining additional information,
or enacting a change or acceptance.
There are four core components of highly functioning teams. These teams
prioritize communication, manage complexity, identify a vision for the future,
set clear goals, and are persistent in achieving them.
Vickie Miller reviewed the City of Southport Charter and described the roles
and responsibilities of each Board member and the full Board of Aldermen. The
full Board sets policies. Each Board member has an obligation to attend
official meetings and to vote. The General Statutes, City Charter, and
Ordinances give authority to the Board. Ms. Miller divided the Board into
smaller groups and asked each person to list two things they consider
themselves an expert about and two things they know the least about. After
reviewing in small groups, each Board member stated their perceived strengths
and weaknesses. There was some discussion about whether the Board of Aldermen
trusts the department heads to do a good job because the Board often hires
consultants instead of listening to them.
In closing, Ms. Miller described the characteristics of thriving communities.
These include committing to uniting for the common good, accepting
responsibility, action-oriented and proactive behavior, and developing strong
plans with benchmarks. Characteristics of dying communities include avoiding
controversy, choosing sides based on relationships and people instead of facts,
deferring investments, and having a small group of long-term residents
controlling everything.
Ms. Miller thanked the Board for hosting her and offered her contact
information if they had any questions.
Lunch break
Mayor Hatem called for a lunch break at 12: 15 p.m.
Afternoon session
The following department heads and others arrived for the afternoon: Travis
Henley, Kate Marshall, Ellie Pittenger, Tom Stanley, Patti Fortuna, Battalion
Chief Ralph Treadway, Melanie Trexler, Heather Hemphill, Randy Jones, ChyAnn
Ketchum, Police Chief Todd Coring, Tish Hatem, and Eliot Duke with the State
Port Pilot. Vickie Miller and Ann White departed.
Mayor Hatem resumed the meeting at 1:02 p.m. He called on Ms. Bonnie Therrien
to explain the purpose of the afternoon workshop. She explained that strategic
planning helps the Board and Staff decide where our energy, resources,
staffing, and money goes for the upcoming years. It is the vision that directs
us. It is a guide and a communication device for the public and can be used for
evaluation purposes. Ms. Therrien asked Finance Director Melanie Trexler to
review the status of the FY22-23 budget. Ms. Trexler explained how to interpret
the budget sheets for each department. Then she summarized how much of the
budget is remaining for the second half of the budget year. Sometimes, if the
percentage remaining is lower than 50%, it is because there have already been
purchase orders opened for that department.
Ms. Therrien asked the Board to list some strengths and weaknesses of the City,
and Ms. Dutton wrote the answers on a large pad so the public could read. Some
of the strengths included the natural beauty of the area, the staff, the rich
history, and a large volunteer base. Some weaknesses included aging
infrastructure, the construction on NC211, and the lack of City policies. At
that point, Ms. Therrien asked each Board member to state any goals or
priorities for each department, and Ms. Dutton listed each response on the
large pad. Each department head stood at the podium, available for responses
and suggestions. Some goals and projects included City branding, signage,
competitive wages, more space for personnel, stormwater management, relocating
electrical underground, a new comprehensive plan, updating the development
ordinances, more proactive code enforcement, and the yacht basin pedestrian
corridor.
Ms. Therrien thanked the Board and Staff for their input. She will bring all
the information back to the Board for adoption. All items listed will be
considered as the FY23-34 budget preparation progresses. Mayor Hatem thanked
everyone for attending and said the meeting was a big help as we move forward.

FEBRUARY 7, 2023

OTHERS PRESENT FOR THE MORNING:
John Nichols, Brunswick County Utilities Director

Emily Miller, McAdams and Associates

Call to Order
Mayor Pro tem Mosteller called the special workshop to order at 9:00 a.m.
Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Pro-tem led everyone in reciting the Pledge of Allegiance.
Approval of Agenda
Alderman Lombardi made a motion to approve the agenda as presented. Alderman
Allen seconded. All ayes. Motion carried.
 
Agenda
1. City Manager Bonnie Therrien welcomed the Board, Brunswick County staff, and
Mr. Hartog from Wooten Engineering. Ms. Therrien said she was glad to have the
meeting to review the agenda for the Regular meeting and to discuss the big
issue of funding the expansion of the County's wastewater treatment facility.
The City Manager reviewed the secured funding, but a gap of approximately $27
million remains. At the Regular February Board meeting, the staff is asking the
Board to accept the second ARPA payment and transfer a total of $1.2 million
toward the treatment plant. The question for the Board is how much debt they
are willing to assume to make this project happen. Depending on how much debt
the City has, the utility rates could be extraordinarily high. Ms. Therrien
said she has been contacting financial advisors to see if they can help analyze
the City's finances.
Alderman Alt asked how much capacity the County has today and how much capacity
the expansion will create. It appears to him that this expansion is very small.
Mr. John Nichols answered that the capacity needed is calculated by the actual
flow and differs from the permitted capacity. It takes a significant period of
time to reach the permitted capacity. The entire County is growing, and there
are many facility expansions in the County's capital improvement projects plan.
Alderman Alt mentioned that the City sends approximately 59 million gallons of
rainwater to the County to be processed due to inflow and infiltration (I & I).
As the City's wastewater system gets repaired and replaced, will that amount
decrease?
County Manager Steven Stone added that Southport had not contributed any
capital costs towards the wastewater processing or infrastructure. The capacity
that Southport leases from the County is no longer available. Once the WWTP
expansion is complete, the City will still have 750,000 gallons of wastewater
capacity, but the City will own that capacity, not lease it. A facility is
designed for peak flows. Southport has gone over its leased capacity during
peak flows.
John Nichols explained what an infiltration basin is and said it is the most
cost-effective method for processing wastewater. Mr. Nichols added that
Southport is not expected to pay toward the land costs. Right now, the City's
flow is going into an equalization (EQ) basin at one facility. The City is
expected to pay for the EQ basin at the Mulberry Branch, so it is an equivalent
facility.
Alderman Allen said the timing was poor because of all the increased costs. The
project has been kicked down the road for as long as possible.
City Manager Bonnie Therrien said that no decisions have to be made at this
meeting. The topic will return to the Board after staff meets with the
financial advisors. She thanked Mr. Stone for including the City in this
process.
Alderman Carroll expressed frustration and said they don't have any
alternatives. Ms. Therrien said that the County has offered to help finance the
project, but the utility rates would still increase because the City would pay
the County back. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller reminded the public about the meeting
on February 27 at the Community Building. The meeting will allow the public to
ask questions of the engineers involved with the wastewater projects.
2. Travis Henley, the Director of Development Services, presented information
about rights-of-way to the Board. He said within Southport's core, many carve-
outs have been given to residents. There are many nonconforming lots, and many
property owners are building out to the maximum of their lots. He read a
reference to right-of-way, and it mentioned the horizontal plane. But there is
no definition of horizontal plane in the ordinance. In the past, City staff was
asked to stand down instead of enforcing the rights-of-way. Now City staff is
asking for direction from the Board of Aldermen. Should it be enforced as
written? Mr. Henley also suggested creating a "clear zone" where nothing could
be placed.
Alderman Alt commented that because there is not enough parking downtown, some
people will park in the residential areas. Alderman Davis mentioned that the
Forestry Committee occasionally plants trees in the right-of-way. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller thanked City staff for working on this process. She explained that
historically, the rights-of-way were created to allow the breeze to move into
the City from the Cape Fear River. She urged the importance of preserving what
makes Southport, Southport. Many things must be considered, including public
safety, parks and recreation activities, runners, pedestrians, bicycles, church
parking, and fire and rescue vehicles. Alderman Lombardi asked if the clear
zone would include where vehicles park horizontally on the roads. Mr. Henley
said it would be from the edge of the pavement. Alderman Allen stated that
individual property owners do not own those parking areas adjacent to the
roads. Alderman Davis said there must be a huge education effort before
enforcement begins. Alderman Carroll said having a smaller clear zone area
might be beneficial. Travis Henley suggested that vegetation would still be
allowed outside the clear zone, and trees could remain.
Mr. Henley said that rights-of-way could be enforced in Southport, similarly to
NCDOT. Development Services, Public Services, and the Fire Marshal would review
applications for right-of-way encroachment. If the City starts enforcing the
ordinance, there would likely be a grace period to allow homeowners to comply.
After the grace period, City staff would aggressively enforce the ordinance.
Travis Henley added that staff also need direction about whether to be
proactive or reactive in code enforcement. Alderman Lombardi said that too many
people are trying to make these decisions and changing their minds. Ms.
Therrien said that once staff received direction, the ordinances would be
enforced the same for everyone. Mr. Henley said that proactive enforcement
would likely require another staff member.
There was further discussion about restaurants in town that have outdoor
seating. At the onset of the Coronavirus pandemic, the City allowed restaurants
to put tables and chairs outside to help their business. Now the pandemic is
over. Some restaurants still have all the outdoor seating, and some even
expanded those areas without paying system development fees. City staff needs
unified direction about these instances.
3. The Board reviewed the agenda for the next regular meeting of the Board of
Aldermen scheduled for Thursday, February 9, 2023. Alderman Alt asked for
clarification about "at large" dogs and how the Animal Protective Services
staff can enter a property to search for a dog.
Alderman Davis mentioned that if the Mayor and Aldermen want to change the
charter regarding the mayoral term, the ward election system should also be
addressed. And the changes should be approved by voters via a referendum.
Alderman Allen suggested the Mayoral term be addressed first. Alderman Davis
explained that the County is getting close to adopting its new master plan. She
asked the City Clerk to write a resolution supporting the adoption of the Plan
and encourage the County to consider building a new regional pool facility
closer to Southport. There were no more questions or discussions needed about
the agenda.
Mayor Comments

Additional Comments

Special Presentations:
Mr. John Mosely, Director of the Maritime Museum, addressed the Board. He said
he started at the museum in October 2022. His previous professional experiences
include Fort Fisher and over thirty years of service. He stated he loves
working in this area because of the history, particularly within the African
American community. During wartime, turpentine harvesting relocated enslaved
people from the fields, and many local shrimp boats became militarized and used
to defend against U-boats. Women joined the service, too, as shipbuilders,
welders, librarians, and caring for the children of the women who wanted to
volunteer. Some women joined the military and formed the Women's Air Force. Mr.
Mosely explained the museum is changing its collections. There are new
educational programs with hands-on activities. Next month is Women's History
Month. He said that a woman created the flares used on boats in emergencies. He
has enjoyed working with the Southport Historical Society. The museum staff and
programming aim to help bring people to Southport, which will also help build
the economy.
Mr. Alan Thompson, a Certified Public Accountant, presented the City's audit
report to the Board. He ran through the report, highlighting areas that need
improvement, including the timely processing of capital project transfers. The
fund balance has increased since last year. The tax collection rate is
excellent. Aldermen Alt confirmed with Mr. Thompson that an audit doesn't
consider the efficiency of the policies and procedures.

FEBRUARY 27, 2023
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
SPECIAL PUBLIC MEETING MINUTES
BOARD OF ALDERMEN
FEBRUARY 27, 2023
SOUTHPORT COMMUNITY BUILDING
PRESENT:
Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller; Aldermen Tom Lombardi,
John Allen, Lowe Davis, and Rich Alt
STAFF PRESENT:
Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, Assistant City Manager/City Clerk
Heather Hemphill, Parks, and Recreation Director
Tom Stanley, Public Services Director
   
Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special public meeting to order at 3:06 p.m.
 
Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis gave the invocation.
Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
 
D)    Approval of Agenda
Alderman Allen made a motion to approve the agenda. Alderman Davis seconded the
motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
E)    Agenda
   1. City Manager Bonnie Therrien stated the purpose of this meeting was to
provide the public with an update on some of the projects ongoing in Southport,
particularly the shoreline stabilization and wastewater projects. She added
that the legislators awarded the City $5 million for the shoreline
stabilization project and introduced Chris Creed, the engineer with Olsen
Associates, who was selected for the project.
Chris Creed thanked the Board of Aldermen for having him attend the meeting. He
explained that he has worked with the City of Southport since 2018. At the
time, there was no funding source identified. He described the waterfront of
Southport and how storm surge, wind waves, and ship-generated waves cause high
erosional stress. In addition, a channel deepening is planned for the Cape Fear
River to allow larger ships through. Mr. Creed added that sea level rise is
estimated at a foot per century. The shoreline in Southport has been divided
into six sections for consideration. Ideally, the coastline could be walkable
all along the water from the yacht basin to the eastern portion near Bonnet’s
Creek. There is cultural and historical significance in parts of the shoreline.
The cultural assessment is ongoing. Some of the rocks and features could be
parts of historic structures. Section 5 has more evidence of structures, old
piers, etc. There is a small rock structure in front of the marsh. It allows
the marsh area to survive because it reduces the wave action in that area.
Ship waves likely are the most impactful on our shoreline. He described the
options available for stabilizing the waterfront. Option One uses T groins, a
sand beach, and a living shoreline. Option Two includes breakwaters, a sand
beach, and a living shoreline; Option Three would involve revetment and a
living shoreline. He added that the sand would likely not stay in place for
very long because of the boats that go by. The sand would have to be imported
and need to be stabilized.
Mr. Creed explained that Olsen Associates is currently updating the topographic
and hydrographic surveys and the cultural resource survey and investigation.
The Board of Aldermen must decide which option to choose before moving forward.
Permitting this project will likely take two years. Some considerations are
water depths seaward of the project, available funding, riparian ownership, and
cultural resources. An environmental survey will have to be completed to
include fish and other wildlife. Aldermen Alt asked about whether funding could
be requested back by the state if the project includes some of the privately
owned areas. Chris Creed said they would ensure they follow the grant
guidelines. Alderman Alt questioned whether taking action in Sections 5 and 6
would be considered for the public betterment. Mr. Creed might not let us work
in those areas, but the sections can be included to inform the property owners.
The City could always partner with private owners to repair all the sections.
Alderman Davis asked if there were any negative impacts if the City only does
work in Sections 1-4. Mr. Creed said he doesn’t foresee any negative impacts.
There are many issues in the yacht basin because the shoreline is not a
straight line. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller informed the public and Mr. Creed that
the City is working on a dredging project. Mr. Creed said the shoreline project
should not interfere with the dredging area. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller also asked
if building up the shoreline would help the City be more resilient to sea level
rise. Mr. Creed said the yacht basin and lower areas are in the most danger. He
added that building up the shore doesn’t mean the water won’t find another way
in.
Mayor Hatem explained that no decisions were being made today, but they would
happily take public comments or questions.
2. Brian Stevens, a resident of Cades Cove, said he remembers considering this
type of project in 2014 or 2015. Based on public input, a study was done, and
it was determined that ships were shown not to harm the shore. Chris Creed said
most of the damage is done by storms. Mr. Stevens also asked about the
stabilization project and its impact on the proposed kayak launch. Mr. Creed
explained that kayaks would still be launched between gaps in the
reinforcements.
Jesse McPherson, who owns McPherson Marine, stepped up to the podium to speak.
He stated that he had previously worked for the City but also lives in the
area. He explained in the past, the private property owners from Atlantic
Street to Kingsley Park were told they had to give up their riparian rights if
the City did work. He urged the Board to allow the private owners to contribute
to the project.
Mayor Hatem reiterated that wave energy is so powerful he suggested the Board
consider the entire 4000 feet of waterfront.
   3. Carter Hubard with W K Dickson Engineering reviewed the Mulberry Branch
Wastewater Treatment Plant expansion project with Brunswick County. Bids were
received in November 2022, but all the bids were too high, and they were all
rejected. The cost of labor was significantly higher than anticipated. The
County is ready to request bids but is waiting for the City of Southport to
decide how much debt can be assumed and the best path forward to completing the
project.
   4. Mayor Hatem introduced Mr. Walter Gross with Wooten Engineering to review
the ongoing Water and Wastewater Merger Feasibility Study. Mr. Gross explained
the City received grant funding from the NC Division of Water Infrastructure to
investigate a regional utility system. Wooten Engineering has received much
information from Brunswick County and will start working through it. They will
complete the wastewater portion first. Wooten Engineering will assess the age
and condition of the existing inventory. The study usually takes a year to
complete.
   5. Mr. Gross reviewed the USDA sewer repair and replacement project. This
project will identify weaknesses in the infrastructure and make suggestions
about either repairing components or replacing them. For example, a line might
be the correct size, but different material is recommended. Wooten is currently
surveying the infrastructure. Next, they will make a preliminary design with
estimated costs. Construction for this project should start around June 2024.
   6. Carter Hubard explained that the City was awarded $400,000 towards a
“find it, fix it” project. This study will allow the engineers to take a
broader look to see where the water gets into the system. The City sends a lot
of extra water to the County to be processed because of storm and groundwater.
   7. Carter Hubard said that W K Dickson has been working on the lift station
rehab project. They are looking to the future to determine where repairs can
make the most impact on the system overall. W K Dickson has been doing the
field testing with the help of City staff. The lift station on Moore Street was
worse than expected. They will continue to study the stations and also consider
any potential developments. The lift station project considers existing
conditions, peak capacity, pump improvements, and force main improvements. Mr.
Hubard added that construction for this project is tentatively scheduled for
2024.
Alderman Alt asked Mr. Hubard if he had been provided the information about the
contamination in the creek. Alderman Alt said that the sewer pipes around the
creek areas need to be inspected, and those areas should be prioritized.
Alderman Allen stated that there are other possible sources of contamination,
including septic systems and boats. There are a lot of septic systems in
Smithville Woods.
     8. Ms. Morrison said they are grateful to have the Cape Fear River
Watchers working with them to test the water scientifically. She would like the
engineers to review their historical data.
F)    Board Comments
Mayor Hatem said the presentations were great, and the information was very
helpful. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller thanked the engineers for coming today to
present the different projects. Alderman Alt thanked City Manager Bonnie
Therrien for putting the meeting together and simultaneously getting all the
pieces together. There were no other Board comments.
G.) Adjourn
   Mayor Hatem adjourned the meeting at 4:54 p.m. after a motion from Alderman
Lombardi. Alderman Alt seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.

SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
BOARD OF ALDERMEN         SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL      MARCH 1, 2023
PRESENT:
Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller, Aldermen John Allen, Lowe
Davis, and Rich Alt
ABSENT: Alderman Lombardi and Alderman Carroll were absent from the meeting.
STAFF PRESENT:
Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, Assistant City Manager/City Clerk
Melanie Trexler, Finance Director
Tom Stanley, Public Services Director
Tom Zilinek, City Engineer
OTHERS PRESENT:
David Cheatwood, First Tryon Advisors
Steve Stone, Brunswick County Manager
Walter Goldsmith, First Tryon Advisors
A) Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special workshop to order at 9:01 a.m.
B)
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
C)
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance. Mayor Hatem read the
ethics statement.
D)
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion to approve the agenda. Alderman Davis
seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. 
E) Agenda
   1.   Mayor Hatem thanked the consultants and City staff for arranging the
workshop. He explained that the Board would discuss funding options for
expanding wastewater treatment plants with Brunswick County. Mayor Hatem read
the mission statement for First Tryon Advisors. City Manager Bonnie Therrien
welcomed everyone to the second of three meetings scheduled for the week. She
thanked the County manager for attending. Brunswick County needs direction from
the City about how the project can be funded. First Tryon Advisors has been a
blessing. City staff met with Mr. Cheatwood and Mr. Goldsmith on February 14,
2023, for the first time. First Tryon Advisors has been working quickly to
create a model showing the options. They have included many of the ongoing
projects. Ms. Therrien added that the model shows a conservative estimate, but
the advisors would love more time to work through the options. Unfortunately,
the County needs an answer as soon as possible.
   2.   Mr. David Cheatwood provided some background on the advisory firm. They
are not lenders or underwriters; they have a fiduciary duty to advise the City.
First Tryon Advisors know the Local Government Commission well and are familiar
with their practices. First Tryon Advisors sit on the City’s side of the table
to review dept capacity, financial impacts, and available options for funding.
Mr. Cheatwood explained that they enjoy using models because they are
interactive.
   3.   For the City’s project, they have considered existing revenues,
operating expenses, and any potential impacts on the utility rates. Mr.
Cheatwood said they had loaded the City’s existing debt, revenues, and expenses
into the model, but it is a preliminary model only. Mr. Cheatwood provided the
facts of the project. The total estimated cost is $55 million. The City has $30
million secured as a State Revolving Fund loan to repay over twenty (20) years
at 1.3% interest. A revenue bond is typical because it pledges the City’s
taxing power. The Local Government Commission prefers revenue bonds to be (25)
years, but (30) is possible. They assumed a 5% interest rate and $3.5 million
must be generated for debt service at that rate. The City wouldn’t have to
start paying it back until the project is complete. Key assumptions were
customer growth, average consumption, rate growth, and collected fees. Mr.
Cheatwood and Mr. Goldsmith used the model to provide different scenarios,
including various rate increases, account growth, and consumption decreases.
They included an elasticity factor that states as rates increase, users may use
less to balance the rate increase. Mr. Cheatwood added that some communities
are anti- growth, so they choose to limit the growth factor. Alderman Alt
mentioned that there are currently between 500-600 lots in various forms of
development. Alderman Alt asked if the loan/bond could be paid off early. Mr.
Cheatwood said that after ten years, they could be paid off early.
   Basic operating expenses increase by 2.5% annually for all line items. The
advisors have included $670,000 this year for general repairs. Theoretically,
the Contract Services line item would decrease if the utilities merged. Mr.
Cheatwood explained some financial terms, such as debt service coverage, days
cash on hand, and senior lien coverage. The advisors loaded up all the projects
into the model, and the model indicated the City would need to generate revenue
of up to $9.2 million in the next five years to cover all debt and operating
expenses. The Board and advisors used the model to review different options,
including rate increases and extending loan repayment dates.
   Alderman Alt asked about how the regionalization of utilities and how the
wastewater treatment project debt would be assumed. County Manager Steve Stone
explained that all customers would contribute to the debt if the City and
County truly merged our systems. Alderman Davis reviewed the poverty levels and
asked if the Board would consider creating a different rate for the customers
that fall in that category. The Utility Commission does not allow a lower rate
for special customers. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller mentioned the extra annual
assessment charged for Oak Island customers for ten years. She suggested that
might be a path to generate revenues. Alderman Allen suggested using 1000
gallons a month to see how much revenue that creates. He asked Ms. Trexler to
bring it to the next meeting.
   Ms. Therrien asked Mr. Stone what the absolute deadline was for the City to
decide. Mr. Stone said that the state would likely put the whole County in a
moratorium if a plan were not made soon. The County needs to have an answer
soon, to rebid the project in the next (60) days. Mr. Stone said the County
Finance Director would conduct a cost analysis to see the City’s special rates
if the County assumed the debt and reimbursed them. It is important to remember
that the Board can change its course if additional funding becomes available.
Ms. Therrien said she would put together a tentative schedule to show the Board
how the timing works.
   Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked if the County would get a better rate for a
bond, could they obtain a bond for the remaining cost, and let the City pay the
debt service. Mr. Cheatwood explained the difference in rates would be the
equivalent of $175-200,000 a year. Mr. Cheatwood stated he would ask bond
counsel if system development fees could be used for repayment. Mr. Stone
reiterated that the project is already two years behind, and the County is
waiting for the City’s decision, and then the bid request has to be posted for
(45) days.
F) Board Comments and Questions:
   There were no further questions or comments from the Board.
G) 
Mayor Hatem said that it was an excellent meeting. He thanked Ms. Therrien for
arranging it and for making it straightforward. He also thanked City staff.
H) Adjourn
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion to adjourn the meeting, which was
seconded by Alderman Allen. All ayes. Motion carried. Mayor Hatem adjourned the
meeting at 10:44 a.m.
