SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
BOARD OF ALDERMEN
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL
MARCH 3, 2023
PRESENT: Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller, Aldermen John
Allen, Robert Carroll, Lowe Davis, Tom Lombardi, and Rich Alt
STAFF PRESENT:
Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, Assistant City Manager/City Clerk
Kate Marshall, Animal Protective Services
Tom Stanley, Public Services Director
Tom Zilinek, City Engineer
Travis Henley, Development Services Director
Todd Coring, Police Chief
Heather Hemphill, Parks, and Recreation Director
Ellie Pittenger, Electrical Superintendent
OTHERS PRESENT:
Wes McLeod, Cape Fear Council of Government      Brady Herman, City Attorney
A) Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special workshop to order at 9:12 a.m.
B) Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
C) Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance. Mayor Hatem read the
ethics statement. Mayor Hatem reviewed the agenda by listing the items.
D) 
Alderman Allen made a motion to approve the agenda. Alderman Lombardi seconded
the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. 
E) Agenda
   1.   Wes McLeod, Director of Government Services with the Cape Fear Council
of Governments, addressed the Board and said that the COG had been hired to do
a basic study to provide conceptual recommendations for moving forward with the
Yacht Basin Corridor. They did onsite visits, inventoried impediments,
strengths, and weaknesses. They focused on the area from Brunswick Street to
Caswell Avenue to the Marina. There is an existing pedestrian path on W. Bay
Street. Yacht Basin Drive has the greatest number of traffic conflicts; the
width is typically twelve feet. The behavior and traffic has become somewhat
normalized over the years. There have been no serious incidents in recent
history. There are a lot of pedestrians, and golf carts. The SWOT (strengths,
weaknesses, opportunities, threats) analysis derived the following
recommendations: 1. Create a more defined space through visual and physical
improvements; 2. Embrace the waterfront asset through a boardwalk connection;
3. Increase the availability of bicycle and golf cart parking; 4. Accentuate
the unique setting through formalized and designed Living Street concept; 5.
Establish branding for the yacht basin district.
Mr. McLeod said a riverwalk is the most logical solution if the City wants to
embrace the waterfront area. He further recommended the creation of a Yacht
Basin Overlay District and Committee. Mr. McLeod stated that he does not like
doing studies like this because it just skims the surface. It would probably
cost $100,000 to really figure out what would be the best plan for the Yacht
Basin area. There was some discussion about the difference between a
prescriptive easement and right-of-way. Mayor Hatem asked Police Chief Coring
to give the Board his opinion. Chief Coring explained that the traffic in the
Yacht Basin was set up with on-way traffic at the beginning of the pandemic. It
was to allow the businesses to serve people with less congestion and less risk.
But now, the pedestrian striping is fading. The faded line encourages folks to
walk into the street. He recommended repainting the pedestrian lane and adding
armadillo paddles to help slow down traffic. Chief Coring reminded everyone of
the slogan, “turn around, don’t drown,” that is used when there is standing
water, because the Yacht Basin often floods. There are several business owners
in the Yacht Basin who are requesting the traffic return to two-way, and add
more signage to reflect the change. Alderman Lombardi stated that he has
considered traffic remaining one way but change the direction. He added that
the City should not wait until there is a major incident before anything gets
done.
Mr. McLeod added that there are some short-term recommendations including
repainting the pedestrian area, and Alderman Allen suggested those
recommendations should be implemented as soon as possible. There was some
discussion about prescriptive easements, deeded easements, and encroachments in
the Yacht Basin area. Mr. McLeod suggested the City have a survey done of the
area to clean up and formalize the correct property lines. Alderman Alt stated
that the Yacht Basin is one of the City’s best assets; the City needs to move
now and not be paralyzed because it is such a big project.
Mrs. Maria Swenson, owner of Provision Company, said she would like to see the
traffic return to two-way traffic. In the past there were no issues with the
two-way traffic and having it as one way hinders business. The boardwalk idea
would take away the boat slips that they use in the Yacht Basin area. Mayor
Pro-tem Mosteller asked Chief Coring and his staff to go back and look for some
quick and easy solutions for the interim, because it might take a while to get
things right. Alderman Allen stated that there has been plenty of consideration
already and Memorial Day is coming soon. City Manager Bonnie Therrien said that
staff needs a decision one way or the other, and the item will be added to the
agenda the following week.
Alderman Davis asked for an estimate of the costs for different options, too.
Mr. Paul Swenson addressed the Board and said that they were never in favor of
one-way traffic. He expressed concern about the condition of water and
wastewater lines in the Yacht Basin because a lot of the older areas have clay
pipes. Because water is critical in the Yacht Basin, he recommended replacing
the lines before making any other changes.
   2.   Animal Protective Services Director, Kate Marshall, addressed the Board
and recommended approval of the definition of leash and add it back to Chapter
3 Animal Welfare in the City’s Code of Ordinances. Ms. Debbie Barnes, who had
expressed concerns about the ordinance previously, said that adding the
definition of leash is the right thing to do for Southport. The definition
states that electronic leashes are not in conformance with the leash laws.
Alderman Allen said that he is sympathetic to her situation. Ms. Dutton added
that even the ADA requires service pets to be on a leash. She also recommends
not adding a provision for exceptions in the ordinance, but that exceptions be
given on an as-needed basis.
Mayor Hatem announced that there would be a brief recess. After the break, the
meeting resumed at 10:38 a.m.
   3.   Mr. Travis Henley, the Development Services Director, approached the
Board to discuss the City’s rights-of way areas. He stated that he had taken
into account the discussion from a previous meeting with regard to clear zones,
clarifying parking areas, and the term horizontal plane. He proposes a six
month grace period to bring public rights-of-way into compliance. There are
still some issues to address including who will remove the materials in the
rights-of-way? Does an engineer have to certify the pervious pavement? There
was discussion about what materials would be allowed in the rights-of-way and
how much coverage is allowed. Alderman Allen suggested that a certain amount
can be impervious, and the balance of the area should be gravel. Alderman Davis
expressed concern that paving would increase stormwater issues, and Mayor Pro-
tem Mosteller added that impervious, and sometimes even pervious coverage can
damage trees. There was a recommendation to give staff discretion to make
determinations. Ms. Therrien commented that discretion gets us into trouble.
Mr. Henley said that there should be three people needed to approve an
encroachment permit. There was discussion about vehicles that are parked in the
rights-of-ways, and also how many intersections are blocked because of the
vegetation planted right at the roads.
   4.   The next item on the agenda was the discussion about the Mayor’s term
and the City Charter. Attorney Brady Herman explained that there are specific
processes spelled out in the statutes of how to make those changes. A
resolution must be adopted that states the intent to make the changes and set a
public hearing. The Board can approve the changes, but the public has the right
to petition; or the changes can be voted on by the public in a referendum.
Aldermen Alt asked why they would adopt a resolution without stating what
changes are being proposed. Alderman Davis said she felt the charter was too
sacred to be changed by only six people. Alderman Davis suggested a committee
be created to focus on what changes would be best. Mayor Hatem stated that the
form of government would not be changed, and that government should not be at
the convenience of the elected officials. Several Board members agreed that
there are so many ongoing projects, maybe this can wait. Mayor Hatem reminded
the Board that this was not the first time they had discussed the topic.
   5.   Next was the review of the Regular meeting agenda on March 9, 2023.
Ellie Pittenger, the Electrical Superintendent, explained that it has been
years since a complete rate study has been done. The cost is $27,000. Mr.
Pittenger could only find one company who could do the study, Utility Financial
Solutions. The las full study was done prior to 2009. There is plenty of money
in the electric fund to pay for the study.
Heather Hemphill explained that Chris Creed, with Olsen and Associates, needs
direction as soon as possible about which areas to include in the survey. It
was the staff’s recommendation to include all six sections in the survey.
Eventually, the City can decide which sections to take the recommended actions
and repairs. There is an opportunity for the property owners of section six to
partner with the City to do the repairs in their area.
Melanie Trexler, Finance Director, explained the audit contract needed to be
amended because of the time it took to complete. There were no questions from
the Board.
There was some discussion about the wastewater rates and possible increases due
to the cost of the wastewater treatment plant expansion. He said he wants to
increase the amount that the City contributes to Brunswick Family Assistance,
to be able to help more lower-income residents.
F) Board Comments and Questions:
Alderman Allen said that it was a great meeting. Alderman Carroll, Alt, and
Lombardi all thanked Alderman Allen for suggesting the second monthly meetings.
G)
Mayor Hatem said that it was an excellent meeting. He thanked City staff and
the Board for attending the meeting.
H) Adjourn
Alderman Allen made a motion to adjourn the meeting, which was seconded by
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller. All ayes. Motion carried. Mayor Hatem adjourned the
meeting at 12:21 p.m.

SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
BOARD OF ALDERMEN
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
COMMUNITY BUILDING
MARCH 28, 2023
 
PRESENT: Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller, Aldermen John
Allen, Robert Carroll, Lowe Davis, Tom Lombardi, and Rich Alt
STAFF PRESENT:
Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, Assistant City Manager/City Clerk
Travis Henley, Development Services Director
ChyAnn Ketchum, Communications/PIO
OTHERS PRESENT:
Tish Hatem, Jeanne Brown Bush, Sue Hodgin, Jason Robbins, Fred Fiss, Dick
Sloan, and several other interested citizens.
 
A) Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special meeting to order at 1:32 p.m.
B) Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
C) Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)
Alderman Davis made a motion to approve the agenda. Alderman Lombardi seconded
the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. Mayor Hatem made opening remarks about
the critical housing shortage. He also commented that the City does not support
losing municipal power over planning. Mayor Hatem explained that he planned to
deliver a Resolution in person to Raleigh the next day. He also stated that he
had spoken with the Mayor of Shallotte, and they will be taking the same
action.
E) Agenda
Travis Henley, the Director of Development Services approached the podium to
speak to the Board about the proposed legislation being considered. He said
there were six bills to discuss.
House Bill 252 proposes that owners of multijurisdictional properties can
decide which regulations to follow. These would typically be the County’s or
the municipality’s ETJ. This is problematic because there might be incongruent
uses between the two jurisdictions. Alderman Alt asked if a developer could buy
a parcel across the line and then have the whole property could be removed from
our control. Mr. Henley confirmed that was correct.
Senate Bill 290 has to do with Short-term Vacation Rentals. The Bill allows
local governments to enforce a maximum occupancy provisions within rental
properties. There is a statutory cap of four people per bedroom, and real
estate brokers must verify the number of bedrooms and bathrooms.
House Bill 332/Senate Bill 275 establishes a process to streamline commercial
and multifamily building plan reviews. There would be a (21) day “shot-clock”
for the initial review. If comments are made, there is an additional (15) days
allowed. But, if a third party reviews the plans and approves, the City only
has (3) days to review and approve the plans. The applicant can use any of the
Department of Insurance certified plan reviewers, or a professional engineer or
architect. But the bill does not explain the process for when inspections fail.
House Bill 294 is the Housing Choice Incentive. This program allocates $30
million in available grant funding for communities to establish and promote
multifamily, “middle housing,” and accessory dwelling units. To be eligible for
the grant, there must be at least (5) zoning districts where multifamily
housing is allowed. There is a minimum of (15) units per acre. Of all the
criteria, the municipality must meet four of the seven. Applicants are allowed
one grant every (5) years. Municipal participation is optional.
House Bill 409/Senate Bill 374 concerns accessory dwelling units. At least one
accessory dwelling unit must be allowed. Accessory dwelling units must have
less square footage than the primary structure, but there is no maximum.
Accessory dwelling units are not subject to owner occupancy requirements,
parking requirements, and cannot be tied to a conditional or special use
permit. The City cannot charge fees that would be greater than they would be
for the single-family dwelling unit. Home-owner associations are still allowed
to regulate and enforce their accessory dwelling unit standards. Setbacks can
be (5) feet or whatever is customary to other properties in the area. These
standards apply to nonconforming lots, too.
Senate Bill 317 addresses the workforce housing crisis. For these projects, the
properties must be at least (10) acres. At least 20% of the lots shall be
improved with one and two-story dwellings and conveyed as workforce housing
improved lots. Workforce housing can occur in most all zoning districts. Local
governments can still regulate residential building codes, minimum housing
codes, and subdivision regulations. Only Federal floodplain regulations can be
applied. There is a (45) day shot-clock to review plans, and after (60) days,
if no decision has been made, approval is automatically granted. The
municipality may not require a connection to the public utility operated by the
local government. The municipality cannot deny an application to serve the
project. No dimensional standards can be enforced. There are already enough co-
sponsors that this bill would pass today.
F)
Mayor Hatem stated the meeting was very helpful. The slides will be available
to the public soon. He added that he does not see the wisdom in stripping the
local governments of their power.
G)
Alderman Allen said that the proposed bills are absurd, and he hopes the
municipalities are able to fight them. Alderman Carroll commented that he can’t
believe that this is the type of things they have to fight in Southport.
Alderman Alt stated that this has to be a full-court press with the other
Mayors in the area; we have to get the COG involved. Alderman Davis said that
the proposed bills being considered; and she encouraged the Board to consider
adopting a resolution in opposition. She also asked the public to contact our
legislators. It was suggested that the public contact Senator Rabon,
Representative Charlie Miller, and Representative Frank Iler. Alderman Davis
made a motion for staff to draft a resolution, approve the resolution and
deliver it to the State. Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. All ayes
Motioned carried.
H) Adjourn
Alderman Allen made a motion to adjourn the meeting, which was seconded by
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller. All ayes. Motion carried. Mayor Hatem adjourned the
meeting at 12:21 p.m.

SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
BOARD OF ALDERMEN AND PLANNING BOARD JOINT SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
COMMUNITY BUILDING
223 E. BAY STREET
MARCH 30, 2023
 
PRESENT: Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller, Aldermen John
Allen, Robert Carroll, Lowe Davis, Tom Lombardi, and Rich Alt

Scott Jones, Dick Sloan, Chris Jones
STAFF PRESENT:
Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, Assistant City Manager/City Clerk
Travis Henley, Development Services Director
Maureen Meehan, City Planner
Randy Jones, Community Relations Director
ChyAnn Ketchum, Communications
OTHERS PRESENT:
Brady Herman, City Attorney      Tish Hatem
Jeanne Brown Busch         Jason Robbins
Several other concerned citizens
 
A) Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special workshop to order at 6:03 p.m. He thanked the
Board of Aldermen and the Planning Board for attending. He also thanked City
staff and those watching from home.
B) Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
C) Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion to approve the agenda. Alderman Allen
seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. Mayor Hatem stated that the City
Attorney prepared the material for this workshop to benefit the Aldermen and
the Planning Board. Mayor Hatem thanked Planning Board Chair Sue Hodgin and the
Planning Board for working through the many developments. The City has two
talented Planners, a seasoned Planning Board, and two skilled Planning Board
liaisons.
E) Agenda
   1.   City Attorney Brady Herman introduced himself. It is said that it is a
municipal attorney’s job to educate and advise municipal boards in statutory
decision-making, advisory, and legislative capacities. The Brough Law Firm has
provided training for most of the Boards they represent.
Attorney Herman began by stating that North Carolina is a Dillon’s Rule state,
which means that governments only have the authority that is expressly given to
us. Chapter 160D brought all of the zoning statutes together. There are many
resources available. One of the best resources is the UNC School of Government.
Planning Boards are required by statute. They are mentioned primarily in 160D-
301, 160D-501, and 160D-604.
There are four types of local government land use decisions. The Board of
Aldermen makes legislative decisions which are typically things like rezonings
and text amendments. The Board of Adjustment hears quasi-judicial matters.
These decisions are discussed in a more formal hearing, similar to a court
hearing. The Board of Adjustment is the Judge and the jury. Administrative
decisions occur by applying objective facts to pre-determined standards in the
Unified Development Ordinance. These decisions are often zoning compliance
permits, building permits, and minor site plan approvals. Advisory decisions
are non-binding recommendations given by the City Board. This decision is a
recommendation the Planning Board provides to the Board of Aldermen. Mr. Herman
showed the Review Procedures Chart, which is part of the City’s UDO.
Attorney Herman stated that City Staff are the subject matter experts. Staff
speaks to the applicants and advises the applicant on how to help their project
confirm to the UDO. Staff also writes the reports and summaries for all the
Boards. The City’s UDO includes a statement that Technical Review Committee
meetings may occur at the discretion of the Zoning Administrator. Travis Henley
spoke up to say that he fully supports scheduling a “TRC” meeting whenever it
seems there might be one needed. He includes all required offices, agencies,
and departments. The Planning Board makes recommendations on rezoning and UDO
amendments and comprehensive plans. They also recommend major subdivisions and
preliminary plats and make administrative decisions on major site plan
applications. They may also prepare and recommend ordinance amendments to the
Board of Aldermen to align with the Land Use Plan. The Planning Board is not
statutorily required to hold public hearings, but they can at their discretion.
The Planning Board is given the authority to form smaller sub-committees to
further review projects and plans. The sub-committees may consist of no more
than three Planning Board members and should be used minimally.
The Board of Aldermen must adopt a written statement that addresses the
consistency of the proposed zoning decision with the City’s Land Use Plan.
Consistency Statements are not subject to judicial review. All members are
required to vote unless there is a conflict of interest. Dismissal and recusal
should occur at the beginning of the meeting or right before that item. There
are Rules of Conduct and ethical considerations for all Boards.
The Open Meetings Laws are far-reaching and address Board members discussing
City business with other members. There should be no group site visits unless
it is advertised. Any time the Board engages in City business, the
conversations are subject to the Open Meetings Laws. Mr. Herman advised the two
Boards to avoid private meetings to discuss business. The Public Records Laws
are more about content, not the form. Alderman Alt asked whether Board members
can ask developers to do things and conduct studies that the UDO does not
require. Attorney Herman said they could ask for those things, but the Board
should not hold it against the developer. Aesthetics are more of a preference
that an objective statement. In other words, the Board should not deny a permit
because they don’t like the siding of the building.
Mr. Herman fielded other questions about alternates and their participation.
Previously, Staff requested that Alternate members sit with some separation
between them and the full members to help clarify who is eligible to make
motions and vote. The Planning Board Chair stated that the Alternates are
members of the Planning Board, too, and she wants them to be able to comment.
Attorney Herman stated there was no harm in them participating, but the
Alternates sitting at one end of the tables would provide enough separation.
Chair Hodgin also asked for advice about responding to incorrect information
that gets published. City Manager Therrien offered to act as a buffer between
the Board and any media. Attorney Herman stated that was not his area of
expertise, but he would happily look into it further. There were no other
questions from the Planning Board.
F) Mayor’s Comments
   Mayor Hatem stated that it was an excellent meeting. He explained that it
was Doctor’s Day, so he was wearing a red carnation. He thanked all the doctors
for all they do.
G) Board Comments
   Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller thanked Attorney Herman and City Staff for arranging
the training.
Alderman Lombardi thanked everyone and wished Mayor Hatem a Happy Doctor’s Day.
Alderman Davis stated that she learned a lot and thanked Mr. Herman. Alderman
Alt suggested holding sessions like this more often. Alderman Carroll thanked
Staff and suggested that sessions like this be a part of onboarding for new
Board members. Alderman Allen said it was a great presentation.
H) Adjourn
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller motioned to adjourn the meeting, which Alderman Carroll
seconded. All ayes. Motion carried. Mayor Hatem adjourned the meeting at 7:29
p.m.

                     Joseph P. Hatem, MD, MPH.
                     Mayor, City of Southport

BOARD OF ALDERMEN

SPECIAL AGENDA REVIEW WORKSHOP
INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL

PRESENT: Mayor Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller, Aldermen Allen, Alt, Carroll,

A)   Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the meeting to order at 9:03 a.m.
B)   Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in reciting the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)   Approval of Agenda
Alderman Allen made a motion to approve the agenda with the addition of the
budget amendments. Alderman Lombardi seconded. All ayes. Motion carried.
E)   Agenda
   1.   City Manager Bonnie Therrien thanked Walter and David from First Tryon
Financial Advisors for joining us. She explained that the two advisors, Melanie
Trexler, Paul Billow (Bond Counsel), Assistant City Manager Dorrie Dutton, and
herself had recently had a meeting with the Local Government Commission (LGC).
The purpose of the meeting was to discuss funding the additional $27 million
that is needed to pay for the Mulberry Branch Wastewater Treatment Plant
Expansion. Originally, County Manager Steve Stone wanted the Board of Aldermen
to establish an agreed upon maximum debt level. But now it seems that the LGC
will not allow the City to take on any more debt. Even if the County funds the
project and the City reimburses them, the LGC will not approve the debt.
Instead, the LGC encourages the City and County to move forward with the Merger
Feasibility Study and merge the water and sewer systems. The City will likely
have to upgrade some of the system before the County will accept the system.
Additionally, the County was uncertain of the City’s desire to merge systems.
The County asked the City Board of Aldermen to adopt a resolution that stated
their intention. The City was awarded a low interest loan for wastewater
rehabilitation. That will allow the City to start identifying weak areas in the
system and make repairs and improvements. Mayor Hatem stated that the Board was
definitely interested in merging utilities, and this was something they had
started working on in 2017. There were some Board comments about favoring the
merger. The Financial Advisors asked if they should re-work the plan? David
Cheatwood said they would take out the numbers and add the new $8.5 million.
Mr. Cheatwood stated that the LGC was almost cryptic will the amount of
information they were providing.
Alderman Alt asked if there was a timeline for when the merger feasibility
study would be complete. City Manager Therrien said she would prepare a
Resolution and add it to the April 13, 2023 agenda.
Alderman Allen said that as humans, the uncertainty was unfortunate, but he is
trying to find the good news in this. Mayor Hatem said he is optimistic that
the merger is best for the City. Alderman Carroll stated he supports the merger
but is unsure about the additional $8.5 million loan without having a set plan
for it. Alderman Allen added that the plan would be laid out with the merger
feasibility study.
Ms. Therrien reiterated that she will write a resolution for the next meeting
that includes support for the merger, accepting the $8.5 million, and working
with the financial advisors. Before any funding is released, there must be an
engineering plan in place. In the meantime, the City Manager said she would
check with Wooten Engineering to see if they could approximate how far the $18
million will take the City on repairs and replacements. Once we merge, the
County will accept the debt.
   2.   Melanie Trexler approached the podium to review the Budget Amendments
proposed for the next Board meeting. The first one was a transfer because solid
waste account had gone over budget by $45,000. She proposed that $20,000 be
transferred from the Board’s budget, and $25,000 would be transferred from the
Buildings and Grounds budget. There was another transfer between Administration
and Finance just to clean things up. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked what cause
the overage in the solid waste budget. Ms. Trexler explained that there was a
lot of extra collections made including during festivals and other larger scale
commercial dumpster pickups.
The next budget amendment was to re-close out a project ordinance. There were
additional payables at the end, and the Auditor suggested re-closing it to make
sure they are covered. There was a budget amendment for the Fire Department to
appropriate revenues for expenditures. Ms. Dutton stated the Taylor Field
project budget amendment was to transfer funds back into the Part-F line that
were originally used to cover engineering costs. Part-F grant funds cannot be
used for engineering costs. There should be a balance in the PART-F fund line
item.
   3.   Ellie Pittenger, the City’s electrical superintendent, stated that he
and the City Manager had been researching possible grants that are available
for installing electric car charging stations. A Level 3 charger would be
similar to what you might see at a Walmart. It puts a larger burden on the
sponsors’ electrical system. A Level 2 charging station would allow two
vehicles to park for 2-4 hours. That provides a good amount of charge, and
there is no heating of the wires. There is a place that sems feasible on E.
Nash Street. Mr. Pittenger suggested installing one there and finding another
place to install one. Another place might be near the water tower, on the
grassy areas. To have two chargers it costs about $9590, and then is about $285
a year. The machines accept credit cards, so the City would get a small amount
of revenue back. Alderman Alt suggested that an ordinance be adopted stating
that cars can only park there while they are charging. He also expressed some
concern about the chargers draining the City’s electrical system. Mr. Pittenger
agreed and suggested that load management devices be installed on the chargers.
City Manager Therrien stated that this project was not on their upcoming
Regular meeting agenda, it was merely to gauge the interest of the Board before
pursuing grants.
   4.   Chief Coring explained that he had a request from the churches to have
an officer present at some of their events. Usually, vendors pay for that
service. City Manager Therrien said the City can’t afford to not charge for the
extra service. City Staff is proposing: $40/day (for-profit organizations);
$30/day (non-profits); $21.50/hour for vehicles; $25/day for vehicles (non-
profits). The Town of Leland uses an app that helps keep all the extra events,
times, payments organized. Officers and staff would get notifications about
opportunities in the area and could accept the extra work without getting Chief
Coring or Major Burke involved.
There was some discussion about how the Sheriff’s office handles requests.
Chief Coring stated that the County was going to use the same app they
described but tabled it for the time being. And the County charges $35
regardless of the group. Another good thing about the company and app, is that
they are covered with liability insurance, and the officers would still be
covered by the City.
   5.   City Attorney Brady Herman explained the Social Media Policy was
important for this Board, as well as future Boards. He added that the proposed
policy does a good job of balancing the 1st amendment rights and the high
standard of being a public official. The policy does not apply to any personal
account, only professional accounts that are tailored to their public
positions. Alderman Davis stated that on principal she is opposed to have a
policy. She added that no matter how noble it may be, it violates rights. She
will oppose it if it comes to a vote.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said she felt it was important to set standards.
Alderman Davis asked who decides what is inappropriate? And, when would the
Board stop the public from speaking?
Alderman Allen said that was ridiculous. The public is not the same as elected
officials.
Creating a social media policy has been discussed for years; even if it is just
used as a training tool. Mayor Hatem explained that the policy would not be on
their agenda for several months; but the voice of the people has never been
limited by the Board. Changes in technology and social media area driving the
social media policy.
Mayor Hatem stated there would be a quick break; and the meeting would resume
at 11:00 a.m.
   6.   Travis Henley, the Director of Development Services addressed the Board
about the proposed amendment to Chapter 9 in the Code of Ordinances pertaining
to noise violations. The proposed changes are to help the police, code
enforcement and others make decisions when it comes to noise. There are certain
noises that are strictly prohibited. Alderman Carroll asked about loud
generators, and whether it could be required to provide a casing around them.
Alderman Alt stated that encasing generators causes too much heat and creates
dangerous gases. There was some discussion about establishments hosting live
music. Alderman Alt mentioned the ordinance that stated sound would be in
violation if audible 100 feet away from its source. He said people should use
common sense. Alderman Allen agreed that he would like to see Chapter 9.93
removed, because everything is audible at 100 feet. He asked if using decibels
would be feasible. Major Burke explained that using decibels requires more
technical equipment and training. Major Burke recommended not extending the
distance out more than 500-600 feet. The amendment is a work in progress and
staff would bring it back again before it comes to a vote.
   7.   Mayor Hatem stated that all cemeteries are sacred, including the
cemeteries in Southport. He added that the City needs to have competitive wages
to have staff to maintain the cemeteries. The City should replace street signs,
mow, and weed eat. He suggested that the Beautification Committee be included
in this goal of allowing our cemeteries to age gracefully. He added that he
would like to form a committee and appoint two liaisons. All meetings will be
posted. He asked Alderman Davis and Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller to serve as the
liaisons. The Board directed staff to publish notices of the meetings. Alderman
Lombardi asked if he could also participate.
   8.   Assistant City Manager Dutton reviewed the proposed amendments to the
Boards/Committees/Commissions ordinances. The purpose of the amendments is to
clarify term lengths, the application process, interviews and also when terms
expire. There were some comments and revision requests form the Board. The
Board asked to remove it from the upcoming agenda until revisions were made and
the Board had the opportunity to review it again.
   9.   Next, the Board reviewed the agenda for the April 13, 2023 meeting.
There were no questions on the Consent agenda. The City Manager informed the
Board that eight bid packets were received for the space needs study. The Staff
group interviewed four firms, and they all recommend selecting Moseley
Architects. The Board will be asked to select them at the April Board meeting.
Development Services Director, Travis Henley, reviewed the plats that were on
the agenda.
There were some questions about permit-choice and tree removal ordinances. The
Board asked if the Oakton project had clear-cut the trees, and why? Mr. Henley
said that sometimes the grading work necessitates clear cutting. The Board
wanted someone to say that it is necessary. City Engineer, Tom Zilinek, added
that he has been reviewing this project. Alderman Alt asked Mr. Zilinek to go
back out to the site and make sure that the neighboring properties are not
being flooded. Alderman Allen wanted to verify the width of Ingress, to ensure
that it was as small as possible, and to retain as many trees as possible. Mr.
Henley explained that in order to meet the 100-year stormwater protection
requirements, grading is the best way to prevent the neighbors’ properties from
being flooded. The Oakton plan meets the requirements of the UDO, and the Board
must approve it if it meets the requirements.
Travis Henley described Lookout Point as splitting one lot into two lots. There
was no questions.
The proposed Highland Park is an older project and is subject to the older
versions of the ordinances.
Next, there was some discussion about alleyway abandonment. Mr. Henley
explained that after several committee meetings, the Planning Board was unable
to make a recommendation. Alderman Alt suggested that eventually, the City look
at all the alleyways to determine a reasonable plan and use. Alleyway
abandonment is not an urgent matter and there are far too many other ongoing
projects.
The next item on the agenda was the selection of a contractor for the Kingsley
Park repair. Ms. Hemphill recommends contracting with McPherson Marine. They
are local and have done a lot of work for the City.
Alderman Alt and City Manager Bonnie Therrien explained the request for a
build-out analysis for the City. Alderman Alt added that without knowing how
many vacant lots are remaining in Southport, how can the Board make decisions
about future development? Ms. Therrien added that the City needs a
comprehensive plan and a build out study. The comprehensive plan is more
important, but it will take up to two years to complete. In the meantime, the
build out study can be completed. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said she preferred
doing the comprehensive plan because it prioritizes goals. She also said she
thought that City staff at one time had done a count of vacant lots. Alderman
Alt said the information collected in the build-out study could also be used in
the comprehensive plan.
The City Manager and Finance Department explained the proposed credit card
policy, the proposed limits on cards, and the new credit card company. There
was also some discussion about charging fees when using a credit card to make
utility payments.
Finally, City Manager Bonnie Therrien explained that City staff needed
direction regarding the traffic pattern in the Yacht Basin. Alderman Allen
suggested reversing the traffic but keeping it one-way. Fire Chief Drew said
that will cause more problems when it floods. The recommendation from City
staff is to take it back to two-way traffic. Ms. Therrien said that a decision
must be made at the following Board meeting, it cannot be tabled again.
F)
Mayor Hatem said that it had been a great meeting.
G)
No one on the Board of Aldermen had additional comments or questions.
H)
Alderman Allen motioned to adjourn the meeting. Alderman Lombardi seconded the
motion. All ayes. Motion carried. Mayor Hatem adjourned the meeting at 1:29
p.m.

                     Joseph P. Hatem, MD, MPH.

APRIL 13, 2023
REGULAR MEETING MINUTES
Board of Aldermen Regular Meeting Minutes
April 13, 2023
223 E. Bay Street
Southport Community Building
6:00 p.m.
 
Present:    Mayor Hatem, Mayor Pro tem Karen Mosteller, Aldermen Thomas
Lombardi, Rich Alt, Lowe Davis, Robert Carroll, and John Allen
Staff Present:
   Bonnie Therrien, Interim City Manager
   Dorothy Dutton, City Clerk
   Randy Jones, Communications/Tourism Director
   ChyAnn Ketchum, Communications and Public Information Officer
   Charles Drew, Fire Chief
   Ralph Treadway, Battalion Chief
   Todd Coring, Police Chief
   Melanie Trexler, Finance Director
   Kelly Garrido, Police Officer
   Brandon Stevens, Deputy Finance Officer
   Paul Gross, Interim Finance Officer
   Brady Herman, City Attorney
Others Present: Jim Powell, Will Hewett, Sue Hodgin, Eliot Duke with the State
Port Pilot, Marjorie Jones, Jenna Fontaine, Jeanne Brown Busch, Maria and Paul
Swenson, Tracy Beaulieu, Andrew Boyd, and Josh Bennett with Moseley Architects
Meetings are open to the public. Complete audio/video is available on the
City's website or can be requested from the City Clerk's office.
A.)
   Mayor Hatem called the meeting to order at 6:01 p.m. He welcomed everyone to
the meeting.
B.)
   Mayor Hatem announced that Reverend Alderman Lowe Davis would provide the
invocation.
C.)
   Mayor Hatem led the pledge of allegiance.
D.)
   Mayor Hatem announced that Southport was the first Board to send a
resolution in opposition to the recently proposed bills including HB 317 . He
personally delivered the Resolution to Senator Rabon and Representative Miller.
He asked Ms. Dutton to call on the individuals who signed up for public
comment.
Jody Wilmoth, a resident of Southport, explained that he was frustrated about
the cemeteries. There are rules that dictate what can be done on the property
and what cannot. The Board is who sets the rules, and City staff follows the
rules and director of the Board and Management. He said that staff is not
allowed to cut grass around a headstone. It seems the Board is allowing one
person dictate what the City does with the cemeteries.
Tracey Beaulieu, resident of 206 W. Nash Street, stated that she hoped the
Yacht Basin would be a pedestrian, bicycle and golf cart road. Then, she went
on to discuss the rights-of-ways in the City. She understands that access is
important, but she has done a lot of work on her property to make it look good.
She asked if the City was going to make people cut trees down? Will the City
make more parking? She suggested that City staff and the Board think about the
character of the City.
Andrew Boyd, from 828 N. Caswell Ave., explained there is a 4-inch drop off
between the sidewalk and the road on Howe Street. He stated that it is
dangerous. In the March 7, 2023, Code Enforcement report mentioned an A-frame
“sandwich board” sign. He hasn’t been able to locate that section in the UDO.
But he has seen at least three businesses use A-frame signs and leave them out
overnight. Everyone should follow the same rules. But back in the January
report, the Code Enforcement officer’s report is unacceptable, and practically
called Mr. Boyd a liar. Mr. Boyd said he realizes that all the departments want
more staff in the upcoming budget, but he asked the Board to sharpen their
pencils and try to focus on what things are really important. He also asked why
the utilities are increasing, when there is so much development in the area.
Jenna Fontaine, a resident of Rivermist, said she was most concerned with
pedestrian safety. She prefers the way the Yacht Basin is currently, but it
needs improved signage. She also suggested that instead of taking the traffic
through the residential areas, why can’t it be routed back to Moore Street.
There could be signs that route people back that way, and towards the ferry.
Ginny Prunty, resident of 1509 Dutchman Creek Rd, stated that she is part of
the No High Density Southport (NHDS) group. She thanked the Board for the
opportunity to speak on behalf of NHDS and appreciates the Board’s efforts to
oppose the current bills being considered. She said that NHDS has been working
hard to educate the public about how harmful the bills would be to Southport.
They have also called and continue to call the state leaders to oppose the
bills. It seems if approved, the bills would be a dream for developers and
realtors. She urged the public and Board to pay close attention to how the
bills are written, they can be deceiving. HB 675, if approved, would eliminate
ETJs. ETJs were created about WWII to help manage all the diverse land uses.
NHDS was told that Resolutions from small communities won’t make a difference,
but it really has. The news stations have picked up the story and the State
leaders have said their phones are ringing off the hook. She urged the City to
keep drawing attention to the bills.
Pat Kirkman, a resident at 119 Park Avenue, stated she would be remiss if she
didn’t say she was hopeful that there has finally been efforts made regarding
the cemeteries.
Maria Swenson, resident of 107 N. Atlantic Avenue, passed out pictures to the
Board, showing two large vehicles parked in opposite directions across Yacht
Basin Drive. She further stated that the City is causing the business owners to
lose money by detouring visitors and allowing only one-way traffic. Some
drivers get frustrated and come back to visit the restaurants and
establishments in the Yacht Basin. She said that the citizens and business
owners have “made” the Yacht Basin, and that is why she is confused why no one
will listen to the business owners. She asked the Board to listen to them, and
that a vote is made.
Craig Blanks, resident at 319 W. Bay Street, explained that he manages six
pieces of property in the Yacht Basin. He is down there between 80-100 hours a
week. The current traffic pattern is not working, we need to put it back the
way it was before the pandemic. The Yacht Basin needs more lighting,
particularly the intersection of Lord and Bay Streets.
Paul Swenson, resident of 107 N. Atlantic Avenue, explained that there are
eight other businesses in the Yacht Basin that would be damaged if the traffic
is reversed. He added that if he were Potter’s, he would be upset. Mr. Swenson
went on to explain there are three types of tides: 1. One high tide where no
water gets into the street; 2. One when the whole street in inundated with
flood water up Bay and Yacht Basin Drive; and 3. One when the water comes in by
Fishy Fishy, moves towards the Mullet and Flava’s and then stops. Then he said
that on top of all that, the waterline in the Yacht Basin has been repaired for
the 4th time in a year.
Juantana Frink, a resident on Lord Street, wanted to address alleyway
abandonment. She is asking the Board to deny the request. She mentioned that
good things come out of the alleys. Her mother in law, who is now 89 years old,
used the alley to carry ice, but they are also nice for school-aged children to
play safely.
Adam Steadman, a resident on Dutchman Creek Road, wanted to address the
upcoming budget. He stressed the importance of adjusting the ad valorem tax
rate to reflect the new valuations. The valuation has been significant. He was
told by the Brunswick County Tax Department, that the average increase in
Southport was 44%. He asked that the Board keep the taxpayers in mind. Ms.
Dutton read a statement that was submitted by Fred Fiss, a resident on Atlantic
Avenue.
Mayor Hatem read the ethics statement.
E.) Approval of Agenda
Alderman Carroll made a motion to approve the agenda after removing 4.) Oakton
Subdivision, 10.) Amendments to Chapter 2 and Chapter 13 and adding a change
order for Engineering services to the agenda. Alderman Davis seconded the
motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
F.) Special Recognition
   1.   Police Chief Todd Coring and Major Burke said they were there to
recognize an officer that was selected by her peers as Officer of the Year. The
department is very proud of her. Police Officer, Kelly Garrido is a veteran;
she served as a Police Officer in Wilmington, and lives in the City. Chief
Coring and Major Burke presented her with a plaque.
   2.   Mayor Hatem read the proclamation for Arbor Day. Scott Len, the Chair
of the Forestry Committee came forward to accept the proclamation. Mr. Len
reminded everyone to attend the Arbor Day presentation at Taylor Field.
G.) Approval of Consent Agenda-
Mayor Hatem summarized the items on the Consent Agenda.
   1.   Budget Amendment #3: Howe Street Project
   2.   Budget Amendment #4: Taylor Field Project
   3.    Resolution Amending a Closed Project Ordinance: Howe Street Project
   4.   Approval of the Budget Reconciliation Transfer
   5.   Amendment to Article 6: Filming Ordinance
   6.   Special Meeting Minutes February 27, 2023
   7.   Special Board Meeting Minutes March 1, 2023
   8.   Regular Agenda Review Meeting Minutes March 3, 2023
   9.   Regular Board of Aldermen Meeting Minutes March 9, 2023
   10.   Special Joint Meeting Minutes March 28, 2023
   11.   Special Joint Meeting Minutes March 30, 2023
Alderman Lombardi made a motion to approve the Consent Agenda. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
H.) Agenda
   1.   Mr. Jim Powell provided an update on the Bald Head Island
Transportation. He said that the whole transportation system has become
political. Mr. Mitchell’s Estate cannot be closed until the ferry system sale
is complete. The Village of Bald Head Island has the right of first refusal and
have refused it twice. But the Village seems to be holding the process up. Mr.
Powell stated that he would be going to court over the situation. And it seems
that a company in Raleigh might be purchasing the ferry system for $68 million
but would hire the authority to run the operations.
   2.   City Manager, Bonnie Therrien explained that the City requested bids
for a Police Department/City Hall space needs study. There is $50,000 allocated
towards the study. The City received eight bids and interviewed four firms.
Unanimously, the selection committee recommends selecting Moseley Architects.
John Bennett from Moseley was present if there were any questions. Ms. Therrien
added that it wasn’t all about their history, Moseley’s group seems easy to
work with. Alderman Alt made a recommendation to contract with Moseley
Architects for the Police and City Hall space needs study. Alderman Carroll and
Mayor Pro- tem Mosteller seconded. All ayes. Motion carried. 
   3.   City Manager, Bonnie Therrien reviewed the status of the Wastewater
Treatment Plant project. There is a gap between what the City was approved to
borrow, and the actual cost based on the bid packets that were received.
Brunswick County asked the Board of Aldermen to decide how much debt they were
willing to accept. City Staff was working with Financial Advisors to explore
revenue bonds. But recently, City Staff and the First Tryon Financial Advisors
met virtually with the Local Government Commission (LGC) to discuss levels of
debt. While they were very vague, they implied that the City would not be
approved to accept any more debt than what was already approved ($30,000). The
LGC suggested we finish the Merger Feasibility Study with Brunswick County and
encourage the County to accept our infrastructure. It was recommended that the
City adopt a Resolution in support of the merger of utilities and also gives
authorization to City Staff to go to the LGC for approval of the $8.5 million
loan for infrastructure. Mayor Hatem read the Resolution out aloud. Alderman
Davis motioned to adopt the Resolution, as presented. Alderman Lombardi
seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. Ms. Therrien added that the
County would be working with us to figure out the difference in rates.
   4.   The City Manager added that Brent Lockamy with Brunswick County reached
out to explain that the engineers of the wastewater treatment plant need more
money to cover the rebid, and oversight of the project. The County will pay the
fees first, but the City will have to reimburse. The engineers had to re-write
the bid package. It is a lot of money. Alderman Allen asked where it would be
funded from? Ms. Therrien said it would be covered by our State Revolving Loan
that we already have. We just can’t access the money until after a contractor
is selected. Alderman Allen approved the increase in payment to the engineers
for the wastewater treatment plant. Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. All
ayes. Motion carried.
   5.   Mo Meehan, City Planner, described the Lookout Point Subdivision to the
Board. The owners are requesting to divide the property from one parcel into
two parcels. The Preliminary plat was approved in January 2022. The property is
zoned R-10 and has a private Right of Way. The Final Plat is in accordance with
the preliminary plat and all standards of the UDO. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller
motioned to approve the final plat. Alderman Allen seconded. All ayes. Motion
carried. 
   6.   City Manager Bonnie Therrien explained the next item was the final plot
for Highland Park. There are nineteen single-family lots. The preliminary plat
was approved in 2020 under a previous ordinance. The final plot complies with
all standards. A performance bond will be allowed for the sidewalks, and the
plat will not be signed and recorded without the City first receiving the bond.
There was some discussion about the wastewater infrastructure in the
subdivision. The sewer that serves these nineteen homes will be transferred
from the developer to the Homeowners Association. Jason Robbins addressed the
Board to explain that the responsibility for maintenance and repair of the
sewer lines will be a part of the covenants of the subdivision. Alderman Davis
motioned to approve the Highland Park final plat project once the performance
bond for the sidewalks is submitted and the covenants for the subdivision
include the maintenance/repair of the wastewater infrastructure for
subdivision. Alderman Allen seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. 
   7.   City Planner, Mo Meehan described the request for partial alleyway
abandonment. The Planning Board subcommittee met three times to review the idea
but were not able to make a recommendation. If the Board of Aldermen was
interested, City Staff could compose a Resolution of Intent to Abandon the
alleyway for their consideration at a future meeting. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller
made a motion to not abandon the alleyway. Alderman Alt added that alleyways
have more importance that the movement of ice to homes; they are part of the
culture here in Southport. Alderman Davis thanked Ms. Frink for educating the
Board of the significance of alleyways. Alderman Davis seconded the motion to
not abandon the alleyway. All ayes. Motion carried.
   8.   Assistant City Manager Dorothy Dutton explained that the City was
awarded FEMA funds to repair Kingsley Park. Although the Parks and Recreation
Director was not able to attend the Board meeting, she still requests that the
Board accept her recommendation to award the project to McPherson Marine. Mayor
Pro-tem Mosteller motioned to approve the selection of McPherson Marine to make
the repairs to Kingsley Park. Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. All ayes.
Motion carried. 
   9.   Alderman Alt explained that he thinks it would be helpful for the City
to hire the Council of Governments to do a build-out study for the City.
Alderman Alt made a motion to contract with the CFCOG to complete the build-out
study. Alderman Carroll seconded the motion. Alderman Davis suggested the Board
wait a month or two to see what happens with the proposed legislation. Alderman
Carroll said the state could have more bills like this next year. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller said that it is just raw data, so it couldn’t hurt anything. All ayes
except for Alderman Davis. Motion carried by majority.
   10.   Brandon Stevens, the Deputy Finance Officer explained the new credit
card policy, and the new credit card company. Each Department Head will have a
card and can check their own balance. There was some discussion about what
staff uses the cards for. The proposed company is First National Bank, and the
City will actually earn some money back. Alderman Davis motioned to approve the
new credit card company and policy. Alderman Carroll seconded the motion. All
ayes. Motion carried.
   11.   Alderman Carroll stated that he would like to hear a presentation from
City Staff about the Yacht Basin traffic pattern. Ms. Therrien said that public
safety is her #1 priority. She explained that Chief Coring, Chief Drew, Tom
Stanley, and Tom Zilinek went to the Yacht Basin to assess the situation. They
recommended it go back to two-way traffic. No matter what the decision is,
Staff is prepared to start working on it the next day by adding signage,
stripping, etc. General Statutes establish the governing board as the traffic
authority, and so it is the Aldermen’s decision. Chief Drew explained that he
suggested two-way because of the tidal flooding. With a lot of traffic, the
Yacht Basin traffic makes for tight traveling, but it has been that way for
years. He said he grew up in Southport and only remembers two incidents in the
Yacht Basin. There were some questions from the Board about the businesses in
the Yacht Basin. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller mentioned all the special studies and
considerations that have been made in the area, and said she is in favor of
keeping the traffic one-way. She suggested re-stripping and relocating a
wayfinding sign. Alderman Alt added that the City needs to do a better job of
maintaining the Yacht Basin and there are not enough votes to make it two-way
traffic at the moment.
City Manager Therrien declared that she had never seen a Board so fearful of
going against Staff recommendation. She encouraged the Board not to ever worry
about going against Staff.
Mayor Hatem reiterated that it is the Board’s job to make decisions. They
should listen to the information presented and use their wisdom. Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller motioned to leave the traffic in the Yacht Basin one-way, but to add
some additional signage and stripping. Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion.
In favor was Alderman Lombardi, Alderman Allen, Alderman Alt, and Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller. Opposed was Alderman Davis and Alderman Carroll. Motion carried by
majority.
   12.   Alderman Allen explained there were three vacancies on the Planning

retired attorney from Manassas, VA, is recommended for the City alternate

City Manager Bonnie Therrien thanked the Fire, Police and Community Relations
Departments for a successful weekend. She read through a list of the employees

Wilson, NC for the ElectriCities meeting.

and John Smith Cemetery.

Mayor Hatem reported that the ABC Board met the night before. Sales are up 10%.
There is a meeting planned so that new Board members can meet the staff of the
ABC store.

Mayor Hatem announced the Southport Unity Committee event was the previous
Saturday. One of the kids he knew from Elementary School had their kids there!
The Unity Committee has a festival at Caviness Park this upcoming Saturday.
Budget workshops are scheduled for April 21st and 24th. He also wanted to
announce that it is World Autism Awareness Month. Mayor Hatem thanked the Board
and Staff.
L.) Staff Reports
All staff reports were included in the Board packet.
M.) Board Comments
Alderman Allen thanked the Mayor and other Board members for their leadership
in getting information out to the public about the possible legislation. He
added that the State isn’t really concerned about what local Board’s think, but
they will listen to the voters.
Alderman Alt added that citizens have a gazillion votes. They are the ones that
have great sway with the legislators. He heard that the state was overwhelmed
by the number of callers opposing the bills. He also stated that recently, he
met with the local Habitat for Humanity Director. The cost of land in Southport
is very high. He said we may have to work with Brunswick County to promote
workforce housing near Southport.
Alderman Davis said there is an anecdote that says voters have short memories.
That is not true. She encouraged everyone to read the article in the State Port
Pilot about the runaway pig.
Alderman Lombardi said he was glad the state was inundated with calls from
Southport about the bills.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller said the also wanted the public to be aware of some
other bills-SB667, and SB675. She encouraged the Board and citizens to read
about these and how they would impact Southport.
Mayor Hatem said he will continue to work with the regional Mayors to promote
local authority.
N.) Adjourn

SPECIAL BUDGET WORKSHOP
BOARD OF ALDERMEN
SPECIAL BUDGET WORKSHOP
INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL
113 W. MOORE STREET
APRIL 21, 2023
 
PRESENT: Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller, Aldermen John
Allen, Robert Carroll, Lowe Davis, Tom Lombardi, and Rich Alt
STAFF PRESENT:
Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, Assistant City Manager/City Clerk
Patti Fortuna, Human Resources Director
ChyAnn Ketchum, Communications/PIO
Melanie Trexler, Finance Director
Brandon Stevens, Deputy Finance Officer
Paul Gross, Interim Finance Director
Bob Jarvis, City Engineer
OTHERS PRESENT:
Chad Huff with Allegacy Benefits Solution, Tish Hatem, and a couple of other
interested citizens.
 
A) Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the special workshop to order at 9:01 a.m. He thanked the
City staff for all the hard work in getting everything ready to start budget
planning.
B) Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
C) Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)
Alderman Allen made a motion to approve the agenda. Alderman Lombardi seconded
the motion. All ayes. Motion carried. Mayor Hatem made opening remarks about
the budget being the monetary reflection of the City. He said the Board wants
to provide quality service to the citizens, consider the revaluations by
Brunswick County, think “green” for Alderman Davis, and be mindful of the
health and safety of the citizens and the employees.
E) Agenda
   1.   Mayor Hatem asked Mr. Chad Huff to come to the podium for his
presentation on the employee benefits. Mr. Huff provided a comparison of how
the City of Southport stacks up to other municipalities, and we are above
average. The demographics and type of insurance claims the City employees have
had over the last year dictates what the rates will be. He also negotiated for
a lower renewal percentage. The City provides medical, a health savings plan,
dental, vision, short-term disability, voluntary long-term disability, basic
life and accidental death coverage, and the employee assistance program. Mr.
Huff mentioned that some companies might look like they are giving us a
discount, but it would only be for the first year of switching to that company.
Afterwards, the rates would likely be much higher, so it is his recommendation
to stay with Medcost through the NCLM.
There was some discussion about offering partial coverage to offset the cost of
a spouse’s or child’s coverage. The Board asked staff to write up a total
compensation statement that shows the salary and the cost of all the benefits
provided. Mr. Huff also mentioned that sometimes, dependents are still eligible
for Obamacare coverage. There will be an open enrollment period for new
employees, and current employees who want to make changes to their plan.
   2.   Melanie Trexler, Finance Director, reviewed the fund balance page
towards the back of the budget packet. She thanked the Department Heads for
maintaining their budgets. She said in her eight years, the City has weathered
five big storms and six City Managers. The City staff has grown from forty
people to ninety, and 179 volunteers! The City is in a really good position
moving forward, at 61% fund balance at the end of 2022. She mentioned the fund
balance prediction sheet and said she thinks the fund balance will be around $4
million at the end of calendar year 2023. Bonnie Therrien introduced the newest
City Engineer, Bob Jarvis. Mr. Jarvis will be focusing on the Capital
Improvement Plan and overseeing the Parks and Recreation projects.
The City Manager explained that one penny on the tax rate is equal to
$142,445.00. The Local Government Commission recommends keeping the fund
balance at no less than 30%.
   3.   Chief Coring addressed the Board to update them on the Police
Department and the proposed budget. He said there are (16) sworn officers. All
calls get dispatched through the Brunswick County dispatch center. He mentioned
their mission statement that references integrity, professionalism, and
service. Chief Coring reviewed their programs including Safe Sanctuary, We-
Care program, citizen ride alongs, golf cart registrations, and shop with a
cop. The Police Department is fully staffed, but they don’t want to be a
stepping stone for officers. It can be hard to retain officers because the
department is small. Salaries are more comparable now. During the day, there
are five officers on duty and two officers working overnight. Equipment
training for the officers has increased to every other month. Officers now have
access to a wellness tool to help with sleeping, PTSD, stress and more. The
department is working on accreditation with the NCLM. When one officer in the
US acts poorly, in truly affects officers throughout the nation. The City
Manager said that she was pleased by the diversity of the Southport Police
Department. Chief Coring mentioned the request for two new vehicles. They cost
about $45,000 each, and then it is about $15,000 to upfit them with the safety
features, decals, etc. There has to be a prisoner compartment to protect the
officer and other individuals.
Alderman Davis asked if being accredited would open the City up for more grant
opportunities, and Chief Coring said that it would, more than likely. Ms.
Therrien added that the location of the Police Department might cause problems
for the accreditation process. Chief Coring said that his view of the Police
Department is that they are guardians and citizens. He wants the department to
be approachable, and part of the fabric of the community. Mayor Hatem thanked
Chief Coring and the Police Department for serving the community and being
there when they are needed. Chief Coring said that he is most proud of the
women and men who serve. He introduced Detective Burgess to the Board and said
that he is a rising star in the department.
Mayor Hatem dismissed the meeting for a fifteen minute break.
   4.   Public Services Director, Tom Stanley and City Engineer Tom Zilinek,
approached the podium. He was going to review the Buildings and Grounds budget
first. He first mentioned that the Northwoods Cemetery needs to be surveyed.
The department is also requesting a building/property assessment of all the
City’s buildings. They are requesting $150,000 for that, but they think it will
end up being less. There was some discussion about cemetery maintenance, and
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked if there should be a line item for the new
cemetery committee. Mr. Stanley said that labor is included in that department
already, and City staff isn’t authorized to do much more than routine
landscaping. City Manager Therrien added that the ordinance does not allow us
to touch or repair the headstones. Mr. Stanley said that the City was in the
process of accepting bids for cemetery maintenance.
Mr. Stanley mentioned that the Parks and Recreation Department was requesting
to move two Public Services staff members to Parks and Recreation to manage the
parks. In his opinion, it will take more than two workers to maintain
everything in that department. He asked when the line would be drawn. If he
loses two employees, is Public Services going to be reprimanded for not getting
all their work done. Alderman Alt asked if an assessment had been done of how
long it will take to manage the parks. Alderman Allen suggested to wait and
have the discussion when Heather Hemphill, the Parks and Recreation Director,
can discuss. The Parks and Recreation Master Plan that was adopted, recommends
a staff of 4-5 people to manage the parks, but Ms. Hemphill thought that two
would be a good start.
Mr. Stanley said that if it rains, all the staff does is mow grass. Alderman
Lombardi recommended that Parks and Recreation hires their own employee,
instead of taking one from the Public Services department. Tom Stanley said he
will accommodate whatever the Board decides. The Forestry Committee line got
moved to the Buildings and Ground budget.
Tom Stanley directed the Board to the Garage Department. He said there are no
requests for anything major, just a mobile compressor that costs about $4800.
The difference in salaries from last year to now is because he decided not to
hire another person.
Next, was the review of the Street Department. Mr. Stanley, with the guidance
of Tom Zilinek, is requesting more departmental supplies, as there is a
potential for hot asphalt instead of cold patching. The department is
requesting two more employees to help with proactive maintenance. A “patching”
crew can work on areas as large as 10 x 20, and there are plenty of areas that
could use those types of repairs. One capital item being requested is a new
dump truck, a single axle to replace the 1995 model.
Alderman Lombardi asked if there has been any thought about filling some of the
cracks. Tom Zilinek said that he would explore that subject.
Tom Stanley mentioned that there are Powell Bill funds that can be used for
road repairs. Alderman Allen asked whether the Powell Bill funds could be used
to purchase the dump truck. Staff will research and let the Board know.
Ellie Pittenger, the Electrical Superintendent, spoke to the Board next about
the budget for the Electrical department. There is still a need for a second
point of delivery for service. He is still waiting for grant updates for the
electrical car charging stations. And the electrical underground work is still
moving forward. Last year, staff ordered supplies early, so that work could
progress without any hold-ups. Alderman Carroll asked if the $1.6 million was
still enough to budget for the conversion to underground, and Mr. Pittenger
said that it was. Approximately 75% of the electrical service in Southport is
underground. Mr. Pittenger said that he plans to retire sometime in the middle
of the year in 2024. He would like to budget to hire someone in January 2024,
so that he can train them before he retires.
Mr. Pittenger also mentioned that the existing substation cannot be expanded
because of the footprint. There is not enough room to add the new transformers
while the existing transformers are there. But you cannot disconnect the
existing transformers until the new ones are installed and connected. The
second point of delivery will involve land acquisition. It would be much better
to build a substation close to existing infrastructure and just move the
transmission lines out from there. There was a brief discussion about possible
locations.
Tom Stanley reviewed the proposed budget for the Water and Sewer Department. He
said that the City will be increasing the water reserve by 50,000 gallons.
There is a high demand for water meters, but he would like to order more so
there is a surplus. Meters would likely need to be replaced every ten years.
The meters the City needs are on backorder. One of the pump stations needs a
new generator, and it needs to be raised above the ground. Natural gas lines
are going down Atlantic Avenue. That will allow the City to transfer some of
the lift stations to gas, and the generators can kick on during load management
times. Mayor Hatem thanked Tom Stanley and Public Services for everything they
do for the City of Southport. Mr. Pittenger addressed the Board again to inform
them the wholesale energy rates were increasing 3.9% on April 2024. Mayor Hatem
recessed for lunch at 12:20 p.m. The Board hosted a luncheon in gratitude for
Melanie Trexler. Ms. Trexler worked for the City for eight years and was
leaving the area and moving to the Chapel Hill area.
Mayor Hatem called the meeting back to order at 12:54 p.m. He said that this
was Ms. Trexler’s last meeting, and he read a proclamation for her.
   5.   Randy Jones, the Community Relations and Communication Director
reviewed their proposed budget. He said that this year had been one of
transitions. Allayna Dail has taken over as the administrator for the 4th of
July Festival. ChyAnn Ketchum just reached her ten month of employment with the
City. Mr. Jones said he couldn’t do it with out them. He added that the
department couldn’t function without the volunteers. Alderman Lombardi said
that the Beautification Committee wouldn’t be able to accomplish as much
without Randy.
Mr. Jones explained that recently, a part time position was created to help
with the responsibilities of filming all the meetings. Eventually, later this
upcoming fiscal year, he would like to move it to full time. All the revenue
from the Community Building goes back to the Capital Fund.
Mayor Hatem thanked Mr. Jones and his staff for all they do.
   6.   Kate Marshall, Animal Protective Services Director reviewed the
proposed APS budget with the Board. She would like to increase the part-time
staff to cover two weekends. She predicts that the “kitten season” will start
soon. Ms. Marshall got her alligator handing certificate last year.
   7.   Ms. Therrien said the Board needed to schedule at least two other
meetings and host the public hearing on the proposed budget. There is another
budget meeting on April 24th, and the Board scheduled a meeting for Monday, May
1, 2023 at the Community Building.
F)
Mayor Hatem thanked City Staff, Department heads, and the Board for such an
incredible meeting.
G) There were no comments from the Board.
H) Adjourn
Alderman Lombardi made a motion to adjourn the meeting, which was seconded by
Alderman Allen. All ayes. Motion carried. Mayor Hatem adjourned the meeting at
1:22 p.m.
