Agenda
Emergency Operating Procedure (David McIntyre, Brunswick County)
Short-Term Rentals Presentation and Discussion (T. Henley and T. Jones)
Review of July 13, 2023 Board of Aldermen Agenda
Emergency Operations Procedure
   Mr. David McIntyre, the Deputy Director of Emergency Management for
Brunswick County, gave a     presentation on the complete overwrite of the
emergency operations and procedure plan for all of     Brunswick County.
Included in the updates are four levels of activation depending on the scale of
the    event. A county liaison has been added to the plan to be in direct
contact with the city manager to    coordinate information between the city and
the county, which will help communication flow better with    one point of
contact. The plan will be reevaluated and updated every five years. Alderman
Alt clarified    that all FEMA assistance and reimbursement requests would fall
under the center for documentation box.    Mr. McIntyre confirmed that the
Documentation Unit’s responsibilities are to assist with all    documentation,
receipts, contracts, reps, etc. Alderman Alt asked if the county’s finance
officers would    be in charge of their FEMA submittal plan. Mr. McIntyre said
yes.
Short-Term Rentals Presentation
   Development Services Director Henley explained that everything in the UDO
regarding short-term rental and homestays is being enforced, with the exception
of registration requirements. The text amendment is being presented to the
Planning Board at their next meeting. The primary regulation is how the use of
the STR is permitted. Mr. Henley said the city would still have legal
nonconformities if they were established under the 2021 ordinance. Alderman
Carroll questioned if there is a known vacation rental that was not part of the
original permitting process and what will be done about it. Mr. Henley said
that enforcement would be a challenge, but some recommendations would be to use
word of mouth, direct observation, checking vacation rental websites, room
occupancy tax records, or seeing frequent car rotation. Mr. Henley said that
once unpermitted vacation rentals are identified, it would be treated as a
zoning violation, a notice would be sent to the owner of violation by code
enforcement, and if necessary, a court order would issue an injunction.
Alderman Davis asked how the public could see the master list of vacation
rentals so that citizens can be aware of which ones have been permitted. Mr.
Henley said that he could work on getting the master list available to the
public and that the finance department is getting a handout on the rules and
who to contact regarding STRs to put in the utility bills. There was more
discussion on the enforcement and the process for violations. Mr. Henley said
that the process for violations is written in the UDO but may need additional
language with more teeth. There was more discussion on how to manage
enforcement. Mr. Henley said that hiring enforcement just for vacation rentals
would be very expensive. Alderman Allen would like to look more into
outsourcing for assistance.
Agenda Review
Public Hearing: Conditional Rezoning 
There was discussion on whether there would be a vote and if there would be
interaction with the public comments. Mayor Hatem said there would not be a
vote, and there could potentially be more workshops if needed. He said there
would be interaction with the public from the Board and Staff.
Maritime Museum Concession Agreement.
Mr. Tom Hale, Chairman of the Board of Directors with the Museum. He gave a
brief recap on the history of the museum and the agreement that they have had
for the past ten years. He said the current agreement will expire on May 31,
2024. Alderman Alt questioned who would be responsible for the maintenance of
the building. Mr. Wayne Berry responded that the “Friends of the Maritime
Museum” are responsible for the maintenance of the building, and this is why
the “Friends” are part of the concession agreement. Mr. Berry said that the
City only maintains the insurance on the building but not the contents.
Alderman Davis asked for clarification on which building(s) they would be
maintaining. Mr. Berry said the two buildings where they occur, the original
museum and the officers’ quarters that, have now been combined. Mr. Hale noted
that in the concession agreement, they had recommended some minor edits with
regard to what the state requirements are, not the city. He said the “Friends”
have paid a lot for the operating expenses, and he said they are asking as a
non-profit of NC that the state cover the utility bills, landscaping, and
contracting.
WK Dickson Contract Amendment. 
Alderman Alt questioned the length of time it would take to fix the three pump
stations. He said it appears to be about 2.5 years, and he believes that is
exceedingly long. Assistant Manager/ Clerk Dutton said that she would talk to
City engineer, Tom Zilinek to see if a shorter time period would be possible.
In a prior conversation, Mr. Zilinek explained to her that the problem was
actually getting the repair parts from the manufacturers. Mr. Zilinek will be
attending the Board Meeting.
Financial Policies:
Mr. Gross, Interim Finance Director, went over the water and sewer rates on
split parcels of land. He explained there are approximately thirty parcels of
land in the city limits that are split with the ETJ. Sixteen of these parcels
have been developed. He said there is no policy on how to process these sixteen
homes for billing purposes. He explained that some parcels are paying 40%
inside city rate and 60% outside rate. There are four that are only paying the
outside city rate. After consulting with the city attorney, it was decided that
there needs to be a policy on how to define who is getting the lower rate
versus the higher rate. It was suggested that a policy specifically defining
the cut-off was a parcel of land is at least 25% in the city limits, they will
get the inside water and sewer rates as well as debris and recyclable pickup.
Mr. Gross said those that are paying the 25% inside rate could request
annexation. Alderman Carroll suggested to try and get these customers annexed
into the city limits. Mr. Gross said that could be looked into, but there he
was unsure how that would affect their property tax. Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller
questioned if they were in the 25% threshold, would they be allowed to vote?
Mr. Gross said he would look into the answer.
Mr. Gross continued with a proposed Powell Bill policy and said that it was
written 99% verbatim off the Powell Bill Website. Some additions include what
are the responsibilities of the staff in Southport. He said the policy would be
very specific on how the Powell bill money can be used. It also provides a
deadline for the Development Services Department to meet. Also, for the Finance
Department to meet expenditure report deadlines.
Wilmington Metro Planning vs. Cape Fear vs. Grand Strand:
Mr. Henley explained that the city is in the Cape Fear Rural Planning
Organization (RPO). There are pros and cons to RPO, GSATS and MPO’s. Alderman
Allen questioned if cities/towns were leaning more towards going with Grand
Strand. Mr. Henley said it depends on the location. It was the consensus of the
Board to notify each planning organization to let them know that the city is
interested in their provisions. The Board would like more information on what
would be the best option for Southport.
Noise Ordinance:  
Mr. Henley noted that the only change since the last meeting in June was that
there was a section added for refuse pickup. This states that certain noises
for refuse pickup will be prohibited prior to 6 AM. Alderman Davis asked about
landscaping tools that can be a nuisance. Mr. Henley said that there is a
provision in the ordinance that would allow this type of work to be performed
during certain hours. Alderman Davis also has concerns about outdoor music,
such as the Haven, that are a nuisance to adjacent residents. Mr. Henley
explained that there are sections that pertain to the distance of the noise and
also how it is perceived. Mr. Henley said that the Police could be called to
see if the noise violates any of those provisions in the Code of Ordinances.
There was discussion on ways to address the issue, such as contacting the owner
of the business to see if there could be an agreement on managing the noise or
requesting a buffer that would direct the music forward away from the
residents.
Right of Ways:
Mayor Hatem stated that he believes in the cooperative use of the right of way.
He said people had maintained them with shrubs and trees over decades. He said
that there comes a point where if there is something unsafe, a hazard, or if
the city needs to do work, then people will need to understand that it will be
removed. He recommended putting a hard stop on all private usage of the right
of ways moving forward. Mr. Henley said the surfacing of the parking spaces
will remain, as stated in the UDO. The other issue would be grandfathered in
the existing use. There are three options (1) no grandfathering; (2)
grandfathering to a point that the city would have to move it and once it is
removed, it cannot be put back; (3) grandfathered in and can be kept until the
city has to remove it and then it could be put back. There was a lot of
discussion on how to manage. It was the consensus of the Board to have all
hardened structures above grade to be removed and allow the vegetation to
remain unless it had to be removed for hazards or work. This could start the
process of managing the right of ways. There will need to be more discussion
before a decision is made. And the Board would like to host a public meeting/
s to get more public input before deciding.
Request for Public Hearing for ZTA Sign Illumination and ZMA( MF to R-10 ) for
August 10th was discussed.

H)   Agenda
   1.
   Public Hearing: Conditional Zoning A Motion was made to open the Public
Hearing for the proposed Conditional Zoning Text Amendment by Aldermen Carroll,
which was seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   Development Services Director Henley gave a presentation and an overview of
the proposed amendment.
Ray Martino; 6065 Sullivan Ridge Rd. Recommended providing better communication
to the public. He said he does not favor Conditional Zoning and feels more
could be done by tightening up the UDO. He questioned how this would benefit
the City. He asked if this was an easier and more convenient way to process
rezoning. Mr. Henley explained that it was not an easier process because there
is a lot more review and overall, more work for staff.
Alderman Alt questioned the difference between CZ and a PUD with a development
agreement. Mr. Henley said effectively that there is no difference. He said the
PUD process is set up like conditional zoning. Ultimately he said the
difference between PUD and CZ is that with CZ, the applicant can ask for things
to be considered, but it does not guarantee anything could be approved.
Alderman Alt clarified that the developer could still apply for a PUD. Mr.
Henley said that was correct.
Karen Rife; 5980 Dutchman Creek Rd. asked for an explanation of the difference
between legislative and administrative decisions. Mr. Henley explained that a
legislative decision is a policy-level decision where the Board is the ultimate
decision maker. Still, along with the Planning Board, they have much more
discretion to ask for things to be considered during a conditional rezoning.
Whereas, in an administrative process, as long as the application checks all
the boxes of the UDO, then it must be approved. She asked if the builder is
approved for CZ and then sells the property and if the new owners want to
change something, they will have to go through the process again to get
approved since the property is now recorded as conditional zoned. Mr. Henley
said that is true. She asked if PUD and CZ are basically the same and will the
PUD process go away. She questions that if CZ is a more reviewed process than
PUD, why would a developer choose to apply?
Mr. Henley said that it would be up to the developer to decide how they want to
apply. From the planning perspective keeping PUD in place would be good so that
it can be referenced in other developments.
Tracy O’Bryant; Cottage Creek Rd, said that she has been following all the
meetings and all of the comments. She said clearly that the public is not in
favor of conditional zoning. She feels it gives too much discretion and power
to the Board. She would like to see the standards be updated and eliminate the
loopholes for the developers. She urged the Board to vote against the amendment
for CZ.
Lora Sharkey; 432 Cades Trail, thanked Director Henley, Mr. MacLeod, and Staff
for presenting the proposed amendment, answering questions, and explaining the
process of CZ. She said that when CZ was first approved in the business
district, she was excited because the city could get specific conditions on
places of concern with development. She favors CZ in the residential district
and says it could be a positive tool for the city to create better outcomes for
the community.
Stephen Carpenter, a resident of Surf City said he has a long-standing
relationship with the community and was a former planner in a nearby county. He
said that CZ allows for flexibility but also could lead to vagueness for the
developer and the staff. He said that this type of zoning is either subjective
or objective, and who will make that decision? His recommendation was not to
permit CZ in residential districts and follow the ordinance as it is.
   Alderman Allen said that the term “vague” has been mentioned. He asked
Director Henley to clarify if that is how the process works for conditional
zoning and to devise the conditions to put them into place beforehand. Director
Henley said the vagueness is intentional, and the conditions are in reference
to what is already required in the UDO and will allow provisions that will be
more suitable for the community but could be denied if the request is not in
agreement. Alderman Allen asked the City Attorney, Mr. Herman, if he could
address the legalities, especially in relation to spot zoning and contract
zoning. Mr. Herman said that contract zoning is usually applied to general
rezoning. He said that with conditional rezoning, some negotiating is involved
depending on the stage of the process. From a policy standpoint, he said that
when the board makes legislative decisions, the courts will typically uphold
those decisions because they won’t interfere with discretion. Alderman
Mosteller asked for clarification on setting precedents from one project to the
next. Director Henley said that he does not see conditional zoning as possible
to be selected as a precedent because of the strict review criteria, and public
input from each request will differ.
Rich Bandera; 409 N. Burrington Ave., has concerns that allowing conditional
zoning in the residential districts could potentially allow for an increase in
density and that staff could possibly make recommendations to the Board for
approval. He said that under the text of the proposed amendment, it has
language that says that during an election season, the Board of Aldermen may
not vote to rezone property beginning on the date of the municipal general
election until after the new board is sworn in. This would not allow an
application for conditional zoning to go forward until after the election. He
said he does not know exactly when the “election season” begins but thinks it
should wait to be decided. He also wanted to address why Sunset Beach and Oak
Island do not island CZ on the islands.
Mr. Macleod said Sunset Beach and Oak Island have a provision that doesn’t
allow applications for CZ on the island in the residential districts because
all the lots are platted, and the acreage threshold is void. Mayor Pro Tem
Mosteller asked if other zoning-related actions need to be addressed during an
election season. Mr. Macleod said that the Board does not have to have that
provision. He said it is common in places like Wilmington that have a lot of
applications, and they do not want that to interfere with their election
provisions. He said it would be up to the Board to decide if they wanted to use
this provision.
Ginny Prunty; 5906 Dutchman Creek Rd. submitted a comment that was read by the
Deputy Clerk. She would like to see the Comprehensive Land Use Plan and zoning
maps updated before considering CZ. She said she would like the Board to
reexamine zoning project priorities and vote no on the amendment.
Shirley Sullivan, a resident of Indigo Plantation, submitted a comment that was
read. She has concerns about the push for conditional zoning in residential
districts as it is being presented. She said the CAMA Core Land Use Plan and
Comprehensive Plan should be reviewed and updated for current statistics and
demographics before adding a flexible land tool. She would like the Board to
acknowledge the cons.
Jim Lightbourne, 316 W. West St., submitted a comment that was read. His
remarks focused on the contentious concern that CZ has the flexibility to
increase the number of residential dwellings on a property compared to what is
currently being allowed. He agreed with others to revise the Comprehensive
Plan, which may lead to more updates in the UDO, and then revisit the option
for CZ.
   Since there were no further comments or questions, a Motion was made to
close the Public Hearing for the proposed Conditional Zoning Amendment and the
motion was seconded by Alderman Carroll. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.

   4.    WK Dickson Contract Amendment
   City Engineer Mr. Zilinek is requesting authorization for the next phase of
WK Dickson’s sewer project. He said the first phase was for a survey and an
analysis of six lift stations has been completed. There is a recommendation
that three of them need improvement. They will require approval to amend this

Ninth Street, and Moore St. Alderman Alt confirmed that other repairs would

   5.    Financial Policies: 
      A. Policy on Taxes on Split Jurisdiction Properties: Mr. Gross, Interim
Finance Director, went over the water and sewer rates on split parcels of land.
He explained that approximately thirty parcels of land in the city limits are
split with the ETJ. Sixteen of these parcels have been developed. He said there
is no policy on processing these sixteen homes for billing purposes. He
explained that some parcels are paying 40% inside city rate and 60% outside
rate. There are four that are only paying the outside city rate. After
consulting with the city attorney, it was decided that there needs to be a
policy on defining who is getting the lower rate versus the higher rate. A
Motion was made to adopt the Taxes on Split Properties policy by Alderman
Carroll and was seconded by Alderman Lombardi. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
      B. Powell Bill Policy: Mr. Gross continued with a proposed Powell Bill
policy and said it was written 99% verbatim off the Powell Bill Website. Some
additions include what are the responsibilities of the staff in Southport. He
said the policy would be very specific on how the Powell bill money can be
used. It also provides a deadline for the Development Services Department to
meet. Also, for the Finance Department to meet expenditure report deadlines.
Alderman Carroll made a Motion to approve the Powell Bill Policy, which was
seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   6.   Wilmington Metro Planning vs. Cape Fear vs. Grand Strand:
   Director Henley gave a presentation on the transportation planning in NC and
explained the pros and cons of each organization. The City is currently a part
of the Rural Planning Organization (RPO). Alderman Allen asked what the
connection is between these types of Planning Organizations and in NCDOT. Mr.
Henley said that they work together and are effectively the same. Alderman
Allen clarifies that they are funded by the members and not NCDOT. Mr. Henley
said there is some funding from the NCDOT. He said the MPOs receive some
federal funding, but he does not think RPOs receive that funding. Alderman Alt
said that he just recently learned all about these types of organizations that
offer conferences to elected officials. He would be interested in having each
of them come and provide more information at a Board Workshop. It was the
consensus of the Board to invite all three transportation planning
organizations to a Board Workshop to gather more information. Alderman Allen
made a Motion to gather more information from each organization at a Board
Workshop and it was seconded by Alderman Alt.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.  
   7.    Noise Ordinance: 
   Director Henley reviewed the proposed amendments, including the specifics to
which these regulations apply. It stated that any noise clearly audible at a
distance of 500 feet from the property line of the property or location
originating the sound is prohibited. Following feedback from the Board at their
June 8, 2023 meeting, an additional subsection was added to address refuse
pickup operations, with the language providing for noise generated by refuse
pickup operations permissible after 6:00 am. Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller made a
Motion to approve the Noise Ordinance Amendment as presented and the motion was
seconded by Alderman Lombardi. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   8.    Right of Ways: 
   Director Henley gave a presentation on the options regarding enforcement of
right of ways. Staff requests that the Board identify its preferred directions
before beginning the public input process. He went over some options, including
allowable encroachments and grandfathering of existing encroachments. The
descriptions of these encroachments were presented in the agenda packet and on
the PowerPoint presentation.
   Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller made a statement as follows verbatim:
   “Thank you to Staff for bringing this conversation forward.”
   “I am grateful for our Planning Staff, their depth of expertise and
professionalism, and their commitment to our community. In part, the decisions
we make regarding our right of ways will determine how recognizable Southport
will remain going forward.
   On the home page, our city website says, “Welcome to Southport, Home of the
salubrious breezes.”
   In 1792, Joshua Potts platted our city with these 99 feet of road rights-of-
ways. What we know for sure is Mr. Potts laid the roads out perpendicular to
the river. It’s evident when you look at a map, our roads follow the curve of
the river. That’s why Atlantic Avenue and Howe Street are not parallel.
   From this, it seems plausible that since Mr. Potts believed the salubrious
breezes restored his failing health and saved his life, he may have platted our
99 feet rights-of-way to maximize the salubrious breezes for everyone.
   The openness created by these original 99 feet rights-of-way is unique and
very much a part of the design of our city’s old town area. These wide rights
of way were purposely platted and are an important historical reference. As a
community, we have taken steps to protect our historic character. The recent
creation of the Historic Preservation Commission is tangible evidence of our
community’s commitment to our past and our future. It is important to take
action that is consistent with our values and goals. These rights-of-way belong
to all the citizens of Southport and must be maintained.
   Drip by drip, the stone is washed away. The loss of these wide rights-of-way
would fundamentally change what we look like, and over time part of our
historic character will be lost.”
   There was a discussion on the options. Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller Motioned that
based on the Staff’s request for direction regarding clarification of the
right-of-way ordinance, to consider the following ordinance updates 16-8.
Option 1 and 16-10. Option 1 and the accompanying Appendix A: Right-of-Way.
Alderman Carroll seconded the motion.
   Unanimous Vote; Motion carried. 
   Additionally, Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller asked that staff continue the strict
pro-active enforcement of the existing ordinance that prohibits anything to be
placed within the rights-of-way beyond the horizontal plane.

   Alderman Lombardi announced that the Beautification Committee would not
schedule a clean-up for July and August. However, they will finish the
waterfront staining on July 15th.
   “We are getting ready to go into an election cycle. Please do not believe
everything you read or hear. For example, last week, there was a letter to the
editor in the paper with inaccurate information. Titled ‘It’s about trust’, the
letter stated that this board had sold the 400 acres without an appraisal, in a
private sale. Per the requirements of state statute, we discuss potential
contracts in closed session, however, to be clear, final action to sell city
property must be conducted in a public meeting. The 441 acres have not and will
not be sold without notice and being discussed in a public meeting.
   With regard to Short Street, in 2020, the City Manager stated that the
reversal of Short Street’s one-way traffic pattern had improved the safety for
pedestrians, bicyclists, and other non- motorists. Chief Coring agreed and
noted the importance of additional public awareness of the change.
   Regarding the Conditional Zoning comments, Oakton is not a PUD. Oakton is a
By Right R-10 subdivision which by law, unlike the Conditional Zoning process,
did not give this Board the authority to require changes to accommodate the
concerns voiced by neighboring citizens.
   Lastly, rest assured that every Board member sitting at this table values
the collaboration with staff. The new budget demonstrates our commitment and
recognition of the value of our professional City Staff. Please gather the
facts for yourself. And if you have questions or concerns about Board actions
or processes or decisions, please give me a call. All of the Board members
phone numbers can be found on the city website.
   Also, I have a couple of experiences that I would like to share.
   In the past few months, we have been building an accessory structure in the
backyard of our house. In other places I have lived, people always talk about
how hard it is to work with building permitting offices and inspectors. I am so
very proud of living in a community where our Planning and Inspections
Department is so professional, and staff is committed to the welfare and safety
of the public. Throughout the building process, our interactions with Tori
Deviney, the City Permitting administrator, and Kiley Barefoot, the City’s
building inspector, were first rate. Both Tori and Kiley took time to make sure
we understood every step of the process. Admittedly, no one likes to be told no
when they are trying to get their C.O. including me, however, not only was it
code, Kiley helped me understand the value of installing the vents that had
been overlooked. It is with gratitude that I recognize Tori and Kiley for their
service to our community.
   And finally, I would like to recognize Officer Kelly Garrido. A couple of
weeks ago I took my 16 ½ year old dog to Unleashed for a bath. Afterwards, I
put him in the car and turned around to see Mike Isenberg with his dog coming
out of the groomers…so we chatted, and then I tried to get into the car. Socks,
my old schnauzer mix had stepped on the interior lock and locked me out of the
car and of course my keys were in the car. We couldn’t find my spare key at
home so I called the Police Department to see if they had a tool that could
help. That’s when Officer Garrido saved the day. Within minutes of arriving,
Officer Garrido had the door unlocked and Socks was on his way home.
   So, Socks and I offer a ‘special thank you’ to Officer Garrido for her help.
And I share this as a small reminder of how grateful I am to live in this
community. “
   Mayor Hatem thanked the staff for their hard work and everyone for their
attendance and participation.

Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the meeting to order at 9:03 a.m. He said that it was a
robust agenda and thanked all those in attendance or watching from home.
Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in reciting the Pledge of Allegiance.
Approval of Agenda
Mayor Hatem explained that he wished to hold a separate town hall meeting for
the discussion about the homeless population. There are so many factors
involved. Some of the items are to be re-ordered on the agenda, so that some of
the presenters can leave.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion to approve the agenda as presented.
Alderman Lombardi seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
Agenda
Carlo Montagano, with Habitat for Humanity addressed the Board and public to
explain that Habitat for Humanity is a non-profit, a licensed construction
company, a mortgage lender and a retailer. Most of the people that they serve
are between 30-70% median income. They are working class people, but banks
won’s loan them money. Their mission is to build homes, communities, and hope.
They were able to build six homes last year. They are on track to build eight
homes this year. Coastal communities are always harder for them to build in
because of the cost of property. Habitat for Humanity is trending away from
single-family dwellings and considering townhomes. Mr. Montagano explained
there are lots of ways local governments can help them accomplish their
mission. The Cape Fear Housing Coalition can use more Brunswick County
representation. Some municipalities reimburse permitting fees once the
Certificate of Occupancy has been issued. Other municipalities waive System
Development Fees or donate land. Still others invest in infrastructure where
Habitat is likely to build. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked if Habitat had
considered rental units, and Mr. Montagano said that there has been some talk
about it but haven’t made a way forward yet.
The Homeless Population topic was moved up to be the next item. City Manager
Therrien explained that she and Chief Coring had been in discussions over the
last three weeks. There seems to be approximately five individuals in Southport
that are homeless. She reminded the public that instead of calling City Hall,
if they see anything troubling, they should call 911. Ms. Therrien invited Ms.
Sally Learned to speak to the Board. She is the Executive Director for the
Brunswick County Partnership for Housing. She said that homelessness was not
just a Southport problem, or a Brunswick County problem. Affordable Housing is
almost impossible to find anywhere in the state. The Brunswick County
Partnership for Housing has coordinated with several hotels in the area for
qualifying people to stay for the night. She said they recognize they are
helping people with a wide spectrum of needs. Some individuals need mental
health services. She encouraged the public to get involved; they always need
volunteers and financial assistance. Police Major Burke addressed the Board to
say that there are so many factors in each case including the person’s history.
But arresting these people and putting them into the Criminal Justice System
only compounds the issues. The more homelessness is criminalized, the more
isolated and dangerous people can be. Major Burke also encouraged people to
call 911.
Mike Kozlosky, the Executive Director from the Wilmington Metropolitan Planning
Organization addressed the public and the Board. He said that the WMPO is being
very deliberate about considering expanding their participating area. The WMPO
is considering both northern expansion and southern expansion. They were
established in 1978 and serve approximately 300, 000 people. There are twelve
staff members that work on either the Planning or Technical Review side. A lone
range transportation plan is required at least every (5) years and sets the
stage for prioritization of funding. He reviewed some of their projects that
have been successful.
Sam Boswell, the Director of the Cape Fear Rural Planning Organization spoke to
the Board next to describe the organization. He said there are (18) RPO’s
across the state. The CFRPO was formed in 2001. One of their larger projects is
the Comprehensive Transportation Plan, which plans out 30-35 years. Mayor Pro-
tem Mosteller asked if it was correct that Division 3 of NCDOT was receiving
$10 million dollars. Mr. Boswell confirmed and added that there was a lot of
planning with small dollars. The Southport project to build a sidewalk from the
hospital down to the ABC store was in their plans. For the RPO, funding is
split between six counties. There was discussion about who served on the RPO
Board. Mr. Travis Henley added that if a project is not part of an adopted
plan, it is not worth submitting for funding, because it doesn’t really
compete.
Mark Beauchamp and Rick Vander Maas were contracted by the City to complete an
Electric Rate Study. Mr. Beauchamp explained that the City is a very stable
utility. But it seems that the City is giving too much value for the load
management devices, particularly residential load management. It is hard to
predict five years out for electrical rates and infrastructure. The City’s
electrical department doesn’t have any debt and is very fiscally strong.
Without adjusting rates, and based on predicted population change, we have a
higher target operating income. The consultants recommend decreasing rates by
2% or keep them the same. Mayor Pro- tem Mosteller mentioned that we are trying
to transition everything underground, so she thinks that maintaining the rates
will allow the City to do that more easily. Alderman Carroll said he agreed,
but he would like more information about the load management device reductions.
Everyone’s benefit is the same, but we are valuing the benefit differently for
residential and commercial customers. Alderman Allen asked if the incentives
were lowered, would there be any benefit to participate? Mr. Beauchamp said
that he believes the program is important, but some changes should be
considered. Ms. Therrien asked if the City’s electric rates were too high? Mr.
Beauchamp said that from a national perspective, our rates are reasonable.
Alderman Davis read through the existing political sign ordinance and asked if
the Board was happy with the existing language. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller
explained that she liked the ordinance the way it is.
The Board discussed the agenda for the Regular August 10th Board meeting. Mayor
Pro-tem Mosteller asked to add the cemetery ordinance to the agenda, under
Consent agenda. The City Manager read through the list of items on the Consent
agenda. The Homeless Discussion was being removed and a separate meeting would
be scheduled. Alderman Carroll thanked staff particularly for the Bay Street
repair review and plans. He added that City staff is great, and the City is
very fortunate.
F.)
Mayor Hatem thanked City staff and all those in attendance.
Alderman Allen made a motion to adjourn the meeting, which was seconded by the
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller. All ayes. Motion carried. 
Mayor Hatem adjourned the meeting at 11:36 a.m.

   1. Public Hearing Text Amendment-Signage and Illumination.
   City Planner Meehan gave an overview of the proposed Amendment. She said the
applicant requested the following considerations to this Zoning Text Amendment
to provide for modifications to the City’s adopted sign regulations. The
request includes one of two (2) options: (1) Adding an OR where currently there
is an AND in Section 3.19.H.1.c
   (2) Add an additional section to the ordinance that specifically allows
backlit and halo lighting that meets all requirements of the UDO. After
consideration, the Planning Board voted to recommend adding an additional
section to the UDO. ‘Backlit and halo lighting that otherwise meet the
provisions of Section 3.19 of this ordinance are allowed.’
   There was a discussion on the types of lighting that are allowed under the
UDO. Planner Meehan said that currently, under the UDO, backlit signs and
internal lighting signs that are under 3,000 degrees Kelvin are allowed.
Alderman Alt questioned the signs that are currently in violation of the
lighting standards. Ms. Meehan said that most of those signs on Howe Street are
internally lit, which is currently allowed if under the 3,000-degree kelvin
standard. Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller noted that some were grandfathered into the
UDO before the sign ordinance was revised. She said that the Planning Board is
currently reviewing for updates on the sign ordinance.
   Public Comment:
   Mr. Bob Holben came to the podium and said he is not opposed to the Haven
halo sign. He asked for an explanation of the 3,000-degree Kelvin standard.
Mayor Pro Tem explained that it was not the temperature but the color of the
light, which was warm white.
   There were no further questions or comments. Mayor Hatem asked for a Motion
to close the Public Hearing. Alderman Carroll made a Motion to close the Public
Hearing, seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   2. Public Hearing: Map Amendment Rezoning 605 W. Brown Street. 
   Alderman Carroll made a Motion to open the Public Hearing, seconded by
Alderman Allen. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   Ms. Meehan gave an overview of the proposed amendment. She said the proposal
is a request to change a parcel of land from a Multi-Family District (MF) to a
Residential District (R-10). Both districts are residential and permit most of
the same uses. The difference is that there is an exception for nonconforming
lots of records located in the R-10 district, which grants rear and side yard
setback reductions proportionate to the size of the lot. She said that the
Planning Board did a review and recommended approval. Alderman Carroll asked
what the setbacks would be. Ms. Meehan said that with the allowed reduction, it
would become 25 ft front yard, 8 ft rear yard, and 4 ft for each side yard.
Public Comment: None
   A Motion to close the Public Hearing was made by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller and
seconded by Alderman Caroll. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
I)   Presentation and Update by Up Your Arts:
   Ms. Bonnie Bray and Mr. Bob Gentile gave an update on the proposed
reconstruction of the building. While funding for the $3.5 million
reconstruction will be secured and managed by the future Art Center board of
directors, Up Your Arts will fund the remaining two-thirds of the total
architectural services needed for design development and construction drawings
to fulfill the terms of the third MOU with the City of Southport. He said that
as we move forward, Up Your Arts is committed to transparency and
accountability in our partnership with the City of Southport and the various
community partners. The offers of support they have received, both financially
and pro bono, in a hands-on activity, point to a very successful project
outcome. The Board agreed that it was a great asset to the Community and will
bring many benefits to the City. The Board of Aldermen will be meeting with the
new Up Your Arts Board to go into further review. The Board thanked all the
members of the organization for their time and commitment.
J)    Agenda
   1.   W K Dickson Sewer Update Presentation and Contract Amendment:

project updates, process, and timeline. He said the Lift Station Rehabilitation
includes Draw Down Testing Hydraulic Modeling Prioritized Needs Conceptual

prioritize rehabilitation for 9th Street, Moore St, and Park Ave. Also, to
increase capacity by upgrading Park Ave Lift Station with a new Force Main to

   2.   Discussion and Board Vote: Conditional Zoning Text Amendment.
   Mayor Hatem stated that there would not be a vote at the meeting. There will
be a discussion, and the Board could determine how to proceed with the proposed
amendment.
         Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller’s comments:” In our Comprehensive Plan under
F. Plan for the Future, it states that the City of Southport must continuously
work at accomplishing plan implementation and maintaining an effective planning
program. And changes to Southport’s management of growth should occur.
          In contemporary planning, the most discussed concept is “smart
development.” In reality, this concept is not a new idea. It is simply the
blending of many existing ideas.
         Smart development supports the preservation of land and natural
resources. These benefits result from compact building forms, in-fill
development, and moderation in street and parking standards.
         Compact building patterns preserve land for city and neighborhood
parks as well as local woods and wetlands. Furthermore, compact development
shortens trips, lessening dependence on the automobile and therefore reducing
levels of energy consumption and air pollution.
         Finally, a compact development pattern supports more cost-effective
and efficient infrastructure.
         Our Comprehensive plan goes on to say inflexible standards,
regulations, and processes will discourage innovative approaches to development
and design.
         Again, the implementation of Smart Development practices is not new.
Our old town’s historic area, with our smaller lots, smaller setbacks, front
porches, and sidewalks that encourage neighborly interactions that build
community, is an organic example of many of the goals of smart growth planning.
Without updating the Conditional Zoning process, our current zoning does not
allow a residential builder the possibility to propose a project that is more
consistent with our character that could recreate modern streetscapes similar
to N. Atlantic or Caswell Avenues, with the diversity of housing…Big and Small.
         On the UDO page of the city website, it states that the City of
Southport Unified Development Ordinance Update was adopted in 2020. And among
other changes, the update includes, and I quote, “the inclusion of a
Conditional Zoning procedure to aid in consensus-built and public-supported
development outcomes.”
         Without this text amendment update, we do not have a potentially
collaborative upfront community input residential zoning process.
         That’s why I think it’s a mistake to kick the can down the road
linking the proposed Conditional Zoning text amendment update to the future
Comprehensive Plan project that could take as much as 2 years to complete.
         I support the staff’s recommendation to adopt this text amendment with
some minor changes.
         Out of respect for the work of the Planning Board, I make a motion to
send the proposed text amendment back to the Planning Board for review and
consideration of the following changes regarding the initial process steps,
consistent with the School of Government summary of Conditional Zoning
Procedure with a slight addition.
         Instead of optional, make a Pre-Application Conference with staff the
mandatory first step. This will allow staff to answer the applicants’ questions
prior to submitting the application and make suggestions to help facilitate the
Public Input meeting. Then the second step, prior to the submittal of the
application, would be the Public Input meeting. Having the Public Input meeting
before the Master Development Plan is officially submitted could make the
process more collaborative.
         Including the results of the Public Input meeting as part of the
initial application would allow upfront consideration of the Public Input,
allowing the applicant the opportunity to respond and incorporate community
input into the required Master Development plan before the application is
submitted.
         And gives our Planning Staff, from the beginning, the ability to
review the public input along with the submittal to understand how the public
input was taken into consideration in the proposed project. And then for staff
to do a technical review as part of the preparation for the public hearing and
Planning Board review”.
   The Board had much discussion on how Conditional Zoning would be different
from traditional zoning. Explanations were given on the benefits of CZ and the
ability to involve more public input and encourage the developers to engage
with the citizens to create a desirable development that would work best for
them and the community. It was clarified that the Board would always be able to
deny the project if it did not meet the conditions that the city would like to
see. It was said that traditional zoning and PUDs have a by-right approval if
the requirements from the UDO are met. However, Conditional Zoning can be
denied if the project does not meet the standards requested by the City.
Aldermen Alt and Davis, along with citizens from the public, would not like to
see the amendment approved at this time and do not see the benefits of CZ
currently.
   Mayor Hatem asked for clarification on the Motion from Mayor Pro Tem
Mosteller.
   A Motion was made by Alderman Mosteller to send the proposed text amendment
back to the Planning Board for review and consideration of the following
changes regarding the initial process steps, consistent with the School of
Government summary of Conditional Zoning Procedure with these slight additions:
      Instead of optional, make a Pre-Application Conference with staff the
mandatory first step. This will allow staff to answer the applicants’ questions
prior to submitting the application and make suggestions to help facilitate the
Public Input meeting. Then the second step, prior to the submittal of the
application, would be the Public Input meeting. Having the Public Input meeting
before the Master Development Plan is officially submitted could make the
process more collaborative.
   Including the results of the Public Input meeting as part of the initial
application would allow upfront consideration of the Public Input, allowing the
applicant the opportunity to respond and incorporate community input into the
required Master Development plan before the application is submitted.
         And gives the Planning Staff, from the beginning, the ability to
review the public input along with the submittal to understand how the public
input was taken into consideration in the proposed project. And then for staff
to do a technical review as part of the preparation for the public hearing and
Planning Board review. Alderman Allen seconded the Motion. Ayes: Mayor Pro Tem
Mosteller, Alderman Allen, and Alderman Carroll. Nays: Alderman Alt and
Alderman Davis. Motion Carried (3-2 )
   3.   Call for Public Hearing for Short-Term Vacation Rental Ordinance:

SEPTEMBER 5, 2023
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
Board of Aldermen
Special Meeting Minutes - Homelessness Forum
Special Community Building 223 E. Bay Street
September 5, 2023
6:00 P.M.
Present:
Mayor Joseph P. Hatem, Mayor Pro Tem
Karen Mosteller, Alderman
Rich Alt, Lowe Davis, Robert Carroll, and Tom Lombardi.
Absent:
   None
Staff Present:
Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, Assistant City Manager/ City Clerk
Todd Coring, Police Chief
Tony Burke, Police Major
Charles Drew, Fire Chief
Tom Stanley, Public Services Director
Randy Jones, Community Relations Director
ChyAnn Ketchum, Community Relations/PIO
Sydney Heil, Community Building Administrator
Mayor Joseph P. Hatem called the meeting to order at 2:01 P.M. and welcomed
everyone.
The Invocation was given by Reverend Alderman Lowe Davis.
The Pledge of Allegiance was led by Mayor Hatem.
A Motion was made by Aderman Allen to approve the Agenda and seconded by
Alderman Davis. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
Manager Therrien thanked Chief Coring and Major Burke for their thorough
research on the homelessness situation in the area. She said they learned a lot
of information and found resources that would be helpful. She said the current
Ordinance may need to be strengthened for further policies and procedures
regarding the issue.
Public Forum Comments:
Joanne Claire-Mayer, 710 N. Atlantic Ave., said bad things happen to good
people, and sometimes people need help. She has prepared care packs with
helpful items for the needs of the homeless. She would like to give it to the
Police Department to hand out to those who need it. Also, she questioned if
there were showers at the Fire Department. She said that if people can shower
and freshen up, it might help them be able to get a job.
Sally Spaulding, 310 E. Nash St.; she recalled seeing a ground-breaking
homeless village in the Star News called Eden Village. She said the village is
a permanent residence for low-income people who pay $300 for rent. She said
that 2% of the region's population is homeless, and many factors apply to these
situations. She encouraged providing assistance to them instead of pushing them
out.
Sue Marsh, 614 W. Brown St., said that there were comments at the last Board of
Aldermen meeting that suggested that the people who are homeless be arrested
and removed from the city. She said as Christians, we should support others who
are less fortunate instead of trying to arrest them.
Ronald Thompson, 115 Thompson Drive, said, “We must plan, and if we fail to
plan, then we plan to fail.” He said it is important to treat everyone humanely
and to include everyone and not exclude anyone. He said we must treat everyone
how we would like to be treated. Come together to find a solution.
Sally Learned, 4181 Cambridge Cove Circle, Unit 2, Brunswick County, Executive
Director for Brunswick Partnership for Housing, a non-profit organization that
serves unhoused individuals and families in the county. She said they have
properties at 250 E. 11th in Southport. She wanted to speak on the non-profit
entities in the community and how to give support to the city and local law
enforcement. Chief Coring has met with the Brunswick County Partnership for
housing, and the organization has agreed to come to Southport and help provide
resources and support to the homeless. She said there is an alarming amount of
national homelessness currently. She said that if there is a situation of
concern, she should call 911, have law enforcement address the needs, and
contact the proper crisis intervention.
Paul Whitmer said that he has lived in the area for 21 years, is with the
American Legion, and has been working with the homeless for the past ten years.
He is the treasurer for the Brunswick County Homeless Coalition, a group of
volunteers that reach out and help people stay in their houses. He said the
need for assistance is increasing and that there are groups willing to help put
something together for outreach and assistance.
Casey Poplaski, Brunswick Senior Resources, would like the community to know
that they are providing assistance for a safe space and assisting senior
citizens who are sleeping in their cars in their parking lots waiting for them
to serve lunch. A big part of their program is connecting with them to provide
more resources. She reiterated, as other spokesmen have stated, that there are
not many shelters available, especially in Brunswick County, and there is a
great need for more shelters.
Garrett Albertson, 5348 Glennfield Circle SE, one of the pastors at Trinity
United Methodist Church. He said that he has heard this discussed before, and
it could be possible for people to shelter some people in their own homes. He
said that he has a large house and feels compassion for the needs of people
with no place to go. He quotes scripture from the Apostle James that emphasizes
“ do, doing, done,” and at the end of the passage, reads, “What is true
religion is to give aid to the widowed and the orphaned.” He said his hope is
for us to open our hearts and provide for those less fortunate.
There were no further comments from the Public. Manager Therrien called Chief
Coring and Major Burke to the podium for additional information.
Chief Coring said that the Police Department is taking the situation seriously,
and it is something that is not new to Southport. Chief Coring noted that he
had encountered many homeless since his position as Chief and asked them what
brought them to Southport. He said many times they said they take the Ferry
over and enjoyed the breezes, the community, and the kindness of Southport. He
said that the Police Department is being creative in handling the situation,
and they are professional and courteous to all people. He said he is proud of
the men and women in the City’s Police Department who have been working on this
issue. Chief Coring thanked the resource programs representatives in attendance
and provided more information about other resources.
   Major Burke said that the resources are available, and we have to come
forward to look for solutions. He said the solution is more than just the
Mayor, The Board, and The Police. He said we need to keep the momentum and move
forward. Major Burke said there has been a lot of discussion on enforcement. He
said the city’s ordinance and policies have been in place and that they are
more of a preventative versus the conclusion of just writing tickets and taking
people to jail. He said that would not do a lot to solve the issue. He said
that as we move forward, they have made recommendations to the Board for
strengthening some of the ordinances that directly apply to the homeless issue.
Major Burke explained that there are two parts of the rewrite to issuing fines
and penalties. He said, for example, if you have a homeless person who has set
up camp in Franklin Square Park and the police get a call, the police will
respond and address the situation. and determine the issue and the underlying
problem is a homelessness issue. He said writing a $25 city citation will not
work because they do not have money. He said they would add that citation to
the repeat offenders, and the criminal response is trying to address is
justified to make an arrest on-site on view by the officer if it is necessary,
but the intent is treating the underlying problems and providing the
appropriate resources.
Manager Therrien, everyone for attending and providing comments. She said it
was a good discussion, and as a community, we need to work together to find
solutions. She said there are a lot of resources available to support people
who are in a time of need. She said that there were some people who were
interested in doing a community watch, and they could contact her or the Police
Department on how this may be done. She also said that the community should
contact their local representatives and talk to them because it is not just
Southport. It is a county issue that all should be working on.
Mayor Hatem said this was an excellent discussion, and he is proud of the
community and the people here with passion and heartfelt kindness. He said the
county needs to be involved to help find solutions and collectively find ways
to support the growing needs of the homeless.
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller made a Motion to enter into Closed Session per and
seconded by Alderman Lombardi.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.     
Alderman Carroll made a Motion to Adjourn, seconded by Alderman Allen.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
Adjournment: 9:51 p.m.

SEPTEMBER 8, 2023
AGENDA REVIEW MEETING MINUTES
BOARD OF ALDERMEN
AGENDA REVIEW MEETING MINUTES
INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL
SEPTEMBER 8, 2023
PRESENT:
Mayor Hatem, Mayor Pro-tem
Mosteller, Aldermen Allen, Alt, Davis, and Lombardi
ABSENT:
Alderman Carroll
STAFF PRESENT:
Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, Asst City Manager/Clerk
Tom Stanley, Public Services Director
Randy Jones, Community Relations Director
Sydney Heil, Community Bldg Admin
Heather Hemphill, Parks & Rec Director
Bob Jarvis, City Engineer
Tom Zilinek, City Engineer
Patti Fortuna, Human Resources Director
OTHERS PRESENT:
Tish Hatem, City Resident
Wes McLeod, Cape Fear Council of Governments
Pat Kirkman, City Resident
Jay Sharpe, Sharpe Patel PLLC
Rob Williamson, Evergreen Solutions
Mark Hoeweler, Grand Strand Area Transp. Study
Bill Fairley, City Resident    
Call to Order
Mayor Hatem called the meeting to order at 9:01 a.m.
Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Hatem led everyone in reciting the Pledge of Allegiance.
Approval of Agenda
Mayor Hatem gave a quick overview of the agenda.
Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller made a motion to approve the agenda. The motion was
seconded by Alderman Lombardi.
All ayes. Motion carried.
Agenda
   1.
    Mayor Hatem invited Mr. Wes McLeod to the front to review the Cape Fear
Council of Government’s Build Out Study. Mayor Hatem and Wes McLeod stated that
Brunswick County was the 7th fastest growing county in the nation. Mr. McLeod
continued by stating that Southport has almost doubled in population since
2000. The City averages about (7) new residents a month. The population is 60%
or more over the age of 55 years old. Southport would need approximately (800)
more residences to account for the potential growth. Mr. McLeod reviewed the
amount of available acreage. Only 70% of the available acreage would be
considered buildable, and the remaining 30% would be considered open space,
roadways, utilities, and stormwater. Alderman Allen stated that Conditional
Zoning, or conservation zoning would mandate a portion of the remaining
property be designated as workforce/affordable housing. Alderman Alt asked if
it would be possible to calculate the total number of possible units and their
affect on the water/wastewater system.
   2.
   Mr. Jay Sharpe, with the City’s Auditing firm Sharpe Patel PLLC, spoke to
the Board next. He was able to provide a brief explanation of the audit
process. He stressed the (5) Key Phrases: Pre-planning, Planning, Risk
Assessment, Fieldwork, and Wrap-up. The purpose of an audit is to give an
opinion on the financial statements of an organization.
   3.
   Ms. Fortuna introduced Mr. Rob Williamson with Evergreen Solutions, who was
about to conduct the Pay/Classification Study on the City of Southport. Mr.
Williamson stated that Southport has a great team and that a “do nothing”
attitude is not an option. Benefits are always welcomed, but the younger
generations are not as driven by traditional benefits. Companies are working a
(4) day work week or allowing remote work. When the organization is flexible,
productivity is higher and retention increases. Mr. Williamson reviewed the
list of other municipalities that they will consider when carrying out the
study.
   4.
   Mark Hoeweler, with the Grand Strand Area Transportation Study, and two of
his staff members, discussed the GSATS program and how they might be able to
assist Southport. The GSATS is able to help with transportation models,
development impacts, the administration of contracts, corridor studies, and
reviewing TIAs. If the City opted to join GSATS, we would be part of the
Greater Grand Strand Area including Horry County, SC, Ocean Isle Beach,
Shallotte, and Holden Beach. But if some of the other adjacent municipalities
do not opt to join GSATS, we would not be eligible, because the areas have to
be contiguous. Alderman Alt asked about how the funding would be allocated
because the pot of funding would remain the same, but it would be mean more
municipalities would be trying to have their projects funded. Until the urban
boundary is here at Southport, the City can stay with the RPO or join GSATS.
The Board decided to take the item off the September Regular agenda and move it
to the October Board meeting.
   5.
   An item from the Regular Agenda review was moved up for discussion next. Mr.
Bill Fairley addressed the Board. He said he received a letter from the City
about using land inside their property’s setback. He said if the City builds
what is proposed, the City would be saving its property at the expense of the
Fairley’s property. Erosion has been astonishing, and he suspects the problem
will return and intensify. He said that they would be happy to participate and
suggested that the proposed wall extends out farther. He said the City could
build a reasonable wall now or wait and build a larger one later. He added that
the issue is emergent.
   City Engineer Tom Zilinek said the same thing is happening downstream from
this area, regardless of the rocks being in place. The Board would have to
decide which approach would be used to repair the area on Bay Street that has
become a hazardous area.
   6.
   Bob Jarvis, one of the City’s engineers, explained the draft of the Six-Year
Capital Improvement Plan. A copy was provided to all of the Board members. Mr.
Jarvis reviewed the process and stated that he was mainly looking for feedback
on the format of the CIP plan for now. He asked the Board to provide comments
as needed.
   7.
   Heather Hemphill approached the Board and explained the proposed ordinance
amendments. The proposed changes include language specifically forbidding
camping in any of the City parks and City properties. The amendment also
establishes a more definitive penalty for offenses.
   Mayor Hatem announced that there would be a break for lunch at 12:23 p.m.
Alderman Lombardi and Alderman Allen had to leave early.
   8.
   Ms. Dutton reviewed the revisions to the proposed Right of Way amendment.
She explained that the draft ordinance incorporates the suggestions made at the
last Board meeting. At this point, City staff and the Board will set up a
couple of public meetings to explain the changes to the public and get feedback
before anything is adopted by the Board. It is not on the agenda for September
12th.
   9.
   Ms. Dutton explained the proposed Minimum Housing Ordinance and how it would
be another tool for City staff to use to help abate some structures that are
derelict, or in need of repairs.
   10.
   Randy Jones, Community Relations Director, explained that he had been asked
to work on replacement signs for many of the City’s buildings. He used an
existing sign to have some renderings done. There are several shapes to choose
from, but the color scheme is the exact colors taken from the City Seal. Using
all the same colors and theme helps with branding. Mr. Jones would work with
the Historic Preservation Commission to make sure the proposed signs are in
character with the historic areas of Southport.
   11.
   The Board reviewed the items on the agenda quickly. On the agenda was the
proposed contract for Mr. Paul Fisher. He attends the ElectriCities meetings
and works as a liaison between the City and ElectriCities. There was a question
about whether other municipalities provided financial compensation to
ElectriCities representatives. They opted to move some of the items to Consent
Agenda.
F.)
Mayor Hatem stated that the meeting was excellent. He thanked everyone for
attending, and those watching from home.
G.) 
Because there was not a quorum present, Mayor Hatem just adjourned the meeting
without asking for motions.
The meeting was dismissed at 1:31 p.m.

   4.   Merger Feasibility Study:
   Mr. David Malinauskas, Wooten Engineering Water Resources Practice Manager,
gave a presentation on the study. He explained that The Wooten Company examined
current sewer rates, capital project needs, and capacity needs. The Study
concluded that after evaluating four alternatives, two remain viable. The City
of Southport can continue to operate independently and pay for its pro-rated
upgrade of the Mulberry Branch WRF, or it can merge with Brunswick County and
benefit from a higher customer base and economies of scale cost savings.
   The Board discussed how merging with the county would be beneficial. Mr.
Malinauskas said some advantages would be that Southport would no longer be
solely financially responsible for repairing, operating, and maintaining its
sewer system. City customers would pay a negotiated rate as part of Brunswick
County's system, and the City would no longer pay a bulk wholesale rate to the
County. This new rate is expected to be approximately 60% of the current
customer rates. In summary, Mr. Malinauskas concluded that, in perspective, it
would be more cost-effective to merge with the county.
    5.    Amendment to Interlocal Agreement with the County-Sewer Expansion: 
   Mayor Hatem summarized the current agreement to date. The County needs a
revised Interlocal Agreement with the City that lists the terms moving forward
with the payment of the County Sewer Plant expansion. Manager Therrien said
that bids went out twice, and the 47 bids were opened recently and certified by
the county engineer. She the bids last for 90 days, and as of November 7th, a
decision must be made before the process has to start over. She said that it is
imperative that the county goes to the local LGC and be allowed to issue the
revenue bonds, and the LGC will not entertain until they see the merger
feasibility study. Manager Therrien said this amendment would be in place until
a merger feasibility study is negotiated. Aaron Smith, Director of Fiscal
Operation for Brunswick County, was present to answer questions. Mayor Pro Tem
Mosteller asked for clarification on the classification of different rates. Mr.
Smith said that as of the 2020 agreement, the City was in retail, commercial
customer rate to get where the plant could be built, and then the City would
become a full participant in the system. He said once there is full
participation in the system, the City would pay the participant rates. He said
if a merger took place, there would no longer be residential customers, and all
that goes away. The county would be taking care of all the City’s customers.
   Alderman Allen made a Motion to approve in concept the First Amendment to
the Interlocal Agreement with the County-Sewer Expansion with the provision of
the wastewater treatment services subject to final negotiations and revisions
by Staff, the City Attorney, and the City Bond Council and to forward the
recommendation for the approval to the Brunswick County Commissioners and
second by Alderman Lombardi. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.

1.   Presentation and Update of the NC 211 Construction:
   Mr. Josh Pratt from NCDOT gave a presentation on the NC 211 construction
project. Alderman Davis expressed concerns about the traffic flow going in the
opposite direction from their turnouts. Mr. Pratt explained that drivers must
turn right and then make a U-turn, which was designed to reduce accidents and
fatalities. Mr. Law clarified that no additional traffic lights were planned.
Alderman Davis asked why four lanes were going into two lanes, and Mr. Law
explained that the concept is that traffic will be moving around, with options
to turn onto different roads. Mr. Pratt mentioned that traffic studies were
done for the project.
   Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller provided some background on the project. The
engineers worked with the City to end the expansion at the intersection of Howe
St. and Robert Ruark to preserve trees. They also will bury power lines at no
cost to the city and design sidewalks for 80% of the price and other features
that would benefit the City.
   Alderman Alt mentioned that in Leland, there are specific traffic lights set
up to facilitate U-turns, which prevents traffic from backing up when drivers
need to make a U-turn. He questioned why the state wouldn't consider
implementing similar measures to ensure smoother traffic flow for U-turn
makers. Mr. Law, the project engineer, said this would be a reduced conflict
traffic situation and that he could speak to the design team and come back with
answers for specific locations on designated U-turn lanes.
   Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller noted that the last public meeting was in October
2017, and the project design was completed. All design work has been on their
website since 2018. The project was initially set to begin in 2018 but was
delayed due to Hurricane Florence and other factors.
2.   Easement Agreement with Atlantic Telephone Membership Corporation
   Manager Therrien provided an overview of the proposed agreement. She
mentioned that Focus Broadband is seeking to purchase a property in Southport
to enhance the City's internet services. Although there are four sites that
they are interested in, all of them are located in residential areas. She
suggested that the location on River Road, where there is a City Lift Station,
would be more suitable. Public Services Director and City Engineer Zilinek
visited the site to assess if a shared easement would be possible. They agreed
that the construction could be carried out without affecting the lift station.
The City Attorney reviewed the draft of the permanent easement agreement that
was provided to the Board. She said that instead of purchasing the easement for
around $4,300, Broadband is willing to put down $10,000 towards WiFi in
Downtown and the Parks. Manager Therrien recommended the agreement and thought
it would benefit the City.
         Mr. Chirs Ward from Focus Broadband was available to respond to any
inquiries. Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller asked if the installation would be entirely
underground. Mr. Ward confirmed that all the facilities were underground, and
they were collaborating with Brunswick Electric to install them up to the Hwy
211 widening project. Alderman Davis asked if the entire City would have access
to Focus Broadband. Mr. Ward said they intend to serve every portion of
Southport at some point. If the agreement is approved, installing the fiber
optics will eventually give access to the entire City. Alderman Alt asked if
this would interfere with connecting with other WiFi connections. Mr. Ward said
that it would not. Alderman Alt asked what the timeline would be for the
project. Mr. Ward said he did not know and would get back to him.
         Alderman Allen Made a Motion to grant acceptance of a deed for a
permanent easement on the City-owned parcel #2210002707 as outlined in the
attached Easement Agreement, which has been reviewed by the City Attorney and,
in exchange, accept the $10,000 towards the partial installation of WiFi in the
downtown area and the City parks and seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
         Alderman Carroll sought clarification regarding the $10,000 allocated
for the WiFi installation and its total cost. In response, Manager Therrien
said that the estimated cost for the entire project was $20,000. She suggested
that the installation could be done in phases, and the remaining cost could be
included in the next budget.
