4.   Regional Planning Organization Selection
   Mayor Hatem said the City has been presented with two options regarding
joining a regional planning organization responsible for transportation study
and development. The first option is the Grand Strand Area Transportation Study
Group (GSATS), and the second is continuing to work with the Regional Planning
Group the City is currently affiliated with through the Cape Fear Council of
Governments. Initially, the City was also suggested to consider joining the
Wilmington Metro Planning Organization, but they have decided not to expand
their membership. These organizations can help with transportation funding
applications, as well as planning studies for future projects and technical
reviews.
   It was the consensus of the Board to continue with the Cape Fear Regional
Planning Group. Alderman Alt made a Motion to have the City of Southport join
with the Cape Fear RPO for the City’s future planning needs and opportunities
for transportation funding, seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous
Vote; Motion Carried. 
5.   Short-term Vacation Rental Ordinance-Board Decision
   City Planner Meehan said the proposed amendment aims to remove references to
the already- unenforced annual registration requirement in multiple sections of
the Ordinance relating to Short Term Vacation Rentals and Homestays.
Specifically, the request is to amend Section 2.6. I 'Annual Zoning Permit for
Homestays and Short-Term Vacation Rentals,' Section 3.6.G 'Homestay,' Section
3.8.II 'Short- Term Vacation Rentals,' and Article 8 'Definitions. ‘This
amendment is intended to bring the Unified Development Ordinance into full
compliance with recent judicial decisions.
   Alderman Carroll expressed concerns about enforcing an ordinance related to
short-term rentals. He cited examples of non-compliant properties on rental
websites. To enforce regulations, Manager Therrien said they must constantly
monitor rental websites. Planner Meehan said that Code Enforcement had already
sent letters to non-compliant properties, and the penalty was around $25.
Alderman Allen added that the cost of violations increases with non-compliance,
and Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller mentioned a daily violation fee. The Board would
like to gather more information on software, violation fees, and other ways to
manage non-compliant rentals.
   Alderman Carroll made a Motion to approve the Land Use Consistency Statement
to remain consistent with current General Statutes and the Zoning Text
Amendment regarding short-term vacation Rentals and Homestays as presented and
seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller.  Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
9.   Political Signs (moved to agenda item 6).
   Alderman Davis has expressed concerns about the current regulations in the
UDO that govern political signs. The current regulation limits the number of
political signs to one per property, which Alderman Davis believes is unjust
and violates the First Amendment. After consulting with several constitutional
attorneys and organizations, she has confirmed that this regulation could be a
potential violation of the Constitution. Alderman Davis cited a Supreme Court
decision to support her argument. She urges that the Constitution be upheld and
that this regulation not be enforced until it is revised in the UDO.
   During the meeting, the City Attorney, Mr. Brady Herman, joined via
conference call to answer inquiries regarding the Ordinance. Upon reviewing it,
he believed that the Ordinance was not unconstitutional but was excessively
restrictive and needed to be addressed. He suggested that the revision of the
sign Ordinance, including political signs, should be postponed until after the
election and the start of the new year. He also added that if only one sign is
allowed, it could be deemed too restrictive by a court. Furthermore, he
proposed not enforcing the political sign Ordinance until the Planning Board
drafts and recommends a revised version for adoption approval from the
Aldermen. However, Alderman Davis respectfully disagreed.
   The Board discussed reviewing the revisions of the sign Ordinance but
decided to vote on not enforcing the use of multiple signs on private personal
property. Manager Therrien asked Mr. Herman if it was legal not to enforce a
part of the Ordinance with a Board vote, to which he replied that it was the
best temporary solution to rectify the situation.
   Alderman Carroll made a Motion to direct City Staff not to enforce the
portion of the political sign ordinance related to the number of signs on
private personal property and not in the right-of-way, seconded by Mayor Pro
Tem Mosteller. Aye: Alderman Carroll, Allen, Alt, Lombardi and Mosteller. Nay:
Alderman Davis. Motion Carried (5-1)
6.   Forensic Audit
   Alderman Alt proposed a plan to improve the policies and procedures related
to financial oversight. Mayor Pro Tem expressed her disagreement with spending
$10,000 on the forensic audit and suggested that the professional staff should
handle it instead. Alderman Alt clarified that the issue was not with the
project itself but rather the process of how the money is being utilized. He
suggested verifying that the money was being used correctly. Mayor Pro Tem
Mosteller recommended reviewing the finance director's report first. Alderman
Allen explained that a forensic audit is an examination to find illegal
financial records and activities. He mentioned that if there is no evidence of
financial misfeasance, then there is no need for a forensic audit. Alderman
Lombardi questioned the staff's capability to manage the project, and Manager
Therrien confirmed that the staff was capable. She expressed her belief that
there may have been mistakes in the Taylor's Field project. Alderman Davis
asked when the Howe Street project was completed, and Alderman Lombardi replied
that it was around 2018. Alderman Davis suggested asking the finance director
to conduct a financial audit on these projects to pinpoint any mistakes.
Manager Therrien explained that the finance director had only been in the
position for three weeks and was still learning the program. Manager Therrien
said that it would be difficult to take the Finance Director off of everything
he is doing now with the budget season approaching to specifically devote time
to the finances of these projects.
   Mayor Hatem stressed the importance of monitoring the projects and ensuring
that the staff had the necessary support and resources.
   Alderman Alt proposed a motion to allocate $10,350 for a forensic audit of
the Howe St., Bay Street, and Taylor Field projects. However, there was no
second motion, and it was denied.
   Robert made a motion to direct the staff to research the subject further and
come back to the board with recommendations. Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller seconded
the motion.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
7.   Creek Committee
    Alderman Alt requested the City Manager to take necessary measures
regarding public health warnings based on creek readings at Cottage, Bonnett’s,
and Price’s Creek. He proposed forming a workgroup comprising City staff,
County Public Health officials, and State water quality experts. This group
would be responsible for giving monthly updates to the Board of Aldermen. The
purpose behind this is to authorize the city manager to allow signs warning the
public about high bacteria levels. Mayor Pro Tem suggested reviewing all
policies, while Alderman Allen inquired whether the county and state had been
consulted.
   Manager Therrien informed the Board that she had reached out to both the
county and state officials. They provided some levels that are required to
trigger warnings, but it depends on the type of water and other factors. She
also informed the Board that the Staff is working with a lab in Colorado to
conduct a test. The County reverts to the State on such matters. Alderman Allen
further inquired about the composition of the committee. Alderman Alt clarified
that the intention was to have a policy that would allow testing and come back
to the Manager with a recommendation to move forward.
   The Board's consensus was to ask the city manager to appoint a group or
person to look into the situation and put signs up if needed. The Board members
also expressed a desire to converse with health departments to determine if
there's a need for warning signs.
   Alderman Alt made a Motion to allow the City Manager to decide who should be
on the Creek Committee, set up procedures for monitoring the Creeks for
bacteria, and take appropriate actions if needed. The Motion was seconded by
Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion carried.
8.   Affordable Housing
   Recently, Mayor Hatem met with neighboring mayors to discuss the issue of
affordable housing. Each municipality expressed concern about the lack of
workforce housing and possible solutions to address it. The Mayor emphasized
that a collaborative effort with county officials is necessary to find a viable
solution.
   In this regard, Alderman Alt has requested the City Manager to form a
workgroup comprising City staff, Brunswick County Habitat for Humanity, and
other non-profit organizations. The workgroup will provide the Board of
Aldermen with a list of options for both economic and non-economic incentives
that the City can adopt to promote workforce housing initiatives.
   Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller announced that a new Development Services Director
will soon be joining. Once the Director and the Planner arrive, they will
evaluate the planning process for affordable housing. Alderman Carroll
acknowledged that the issue is essential and appreciates the effort. However,
due to the average lot cost of around $30,000 in Southport, it would be
challenging to execute any plans for affordable housing in the area. Therefore,
he suggested looking into alternative options in Brunswick County, where
affordable lots are available. Alderman Carroll favors affordable housing and
supports the need to work with other entities with the resources to
accommodate.
   Mayor Hatem announced an upcoming meeting for the mayors seeking help from

County, the seventh fastest-growing county in the nation. Manager Therrien
suggested the Board send a letter to the County to generate support and
collaborate on a solution.
    Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller made a Motion to instruct either the Mayor or the
City Manager to reach out to all available resources, including county and
state officials, Habitat for Humanity, and other relevant organizations, to
work on creating affordable housing for the future. Alderman Lombardi seconded
the motion, and it was unanimously approved. The aim is to start the housing
projects as soon as possible. Second by Alderman Lombardi. Unanimous Vote;
Motion Carried.

H)   1. Presentation and Update of the NC 211 Construction: 
 
         Mr. Josh Pratt from NCDOT gave a presentation on the NC 211
construction project. Alderman Davis expressed concerns about the traffic flow
going in the opposite direction from their turnouts. Mr. Pratt explained that
drivers must turn right and then make a U-turn, which was designed to reduce
accidents and fatalities. Mr. Law clarified that no additional traffic lights
were planned. Alderman Davis asked why four lanes were going into two lanes,
and Mr. Law explained that the concept is that traffic will be moving around,
with options to turn onto different roads. Mr. Pratt mentioned that traffic
studies were done for the project.
 
         Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller provided some background on the project. The
engineers worked with the City to end the expansion at the intersection of Howe
St. and Robert Ruark to preserve trees. They also will bury power lines at no
cost to the city and design sidewalks for 80% of the price and other features
that would benefit the City.
 
         Alderman Alt mentioned that in Leland, there are specific traffic
lights set up to facilitate U-turns, which prevents traffic from backing up
when drivers need to make a U-turn. He questioned why the state wouldn't
consider implementing similar measures to ensure smoother traffic flow for U-
turn makers. Mr. Law, the project engineer, said this would be a reduced
conflict traffic situation and that he could speak to the design team and come
back with answers for specific locations on designated U-turn lanes.
 
         Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller noted that the last public meeting was in
October 2017, and the project design was completed. All design work has been on
their website since 2018. The project was initially set to begin in 2018 but
was delayed due to Hurricane Florence and other factors.
 
2.   Easement Agreement with Atlantic Telephone Membership Corporation
   
         Manager Therrien provided an overview of the proposed agreement. She
mentioned that Focus Broadband is seeking to purchase a property in Southport
to enhance the City's internet services. Although there are four sites that
they are interested in, all of them are located in residential areas. She
suggested that the location on River Road, where there is a City Lift Station,
would be more suitable. Public Services Director and City Engineer Zilinek
visited the site to assess if a shared easement would be possible. They agreed
that the construction could be carried out without affecting the lift station.
The City Attorney reviewed the draft of the permanent easement agreement that
was provided to the Board. She said that instead of purchasing the easement for
around $4,300, Broadband is willing to put down $10,000 towards WiFi in
Downtown and the Parks. Manager Therrien recommended the agreement and thought
it would benefit the City.
 
         Mr. Chirs Ward from Focus Broadband was available to respond to any
inquiries. Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller asked if the installation would be entirely
underground. Mr. Ward confirmed that all the facilities were underground, and
they were collaborating with Brunswick Electric to install them up to the Hwy
211 widening project. Alderman Davis asked if the entire City would have access
to Focus Broadband. Mr. Ward said they intend to serve every portion of
Southport at some point. If the agreement is approved, installing the fiber
optics will eventually give access to the entire City. Alderman Alt asked if
this would interfere with connecting with other WiFi connections. Mr. Ward said
that it would not. Alderman Alt asked what the timeline would be for the
project. Mr. Ward said he did not know and would get back to him.
 
         Alderman Allen Made a Motion to grant acceptance of a deed for a
permanent easement on the City-owned parcel #2210002707 as outlined in the
attached Easement Agreement, which has been reviewed by the City Attorney and,
in exchange, accept the $10,000 towards the partial installation of WiFi in the
downtown area and the City parks and seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
 
         Alderman Carroll sought clarification regarding the $10,000 allocated
for the WiFi installation and its total cost. In response, Manager Therrien
said that the estimated cost for the entire project was $20,000. She suggested
that the installation could be done in phases, and the remaining cost could be
included in the next budget.
 
3.   Building Assessment Consultant Selection
 
         Mayor Hatem provided an overview of the City's Building Assessment. He
emphasized the importance of regular maintenance for municipal buildings.
 
         Public Services Director Tom Stanley said the city had sent requests

part is that their price falls below the budgeted amount, leaving some funds
available in case any repairs are needed. The team is ready to begin the work

4.   Regional Planning Organization Selection
 
         Mayor Hatem said the City has been presented with two options
regarding joining a regional planning organization responsible for
transportation study and development. The first option is the Grand Strand Area
Transportation Study Group (GSATS), and the second is continuing to work with
the Regional Planning Group the City is currently affiliated with through the
Cape Fear Council of Governments. Initially, the City was also suggested to
consider joining the Wilmington Metro Planning Organization, but they have
decided not to expand their membership. These organizations can help with
transportation funding applications, as well as planning studies for future
projects and technical reviews.    
 
         It was the consensus of the Board to continue with the Cape Fear
Regional Planning Group. Alderman Alt made a Motion to have the City of
Southport join with the Cape Fear RPO for the City’s future planning needs and
opportunities for transportation funding, seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried. 
 
5.   Short-term Vacation Rental Ordinance-Board Decision
 
         City Planner Meehan said the proposed amendment aims to remove
references to the already- unenforced annual registration requirement in
multiple sections of the Ordinance relating to Short Term Vacation Rentals and
Homestays. Specifically, the request is to amend Section 2.6. I 'Annual Zoning
Permit for Homestays and Short-Term Vacation Rentals,' Section 3.6.G
'Homestay,' Section 3.8.II 'Short- Term Vacation Rentals,' and Article 8
'Definitions. ‘This amendment is intended to bring the Unified Development
Ordinance into full compliance with recent judicial decisions.
 
         Alderman Carroll expressed concerns about enforcing an ordinance
related to short-term rentals. He cited examples of non-compliant properties on
rental websites. To enforce regulations, Manager Therrien said they must
constantly monitor rental websites. Planner Meehan said that Code Enforcement
had already sent letters to non-compliant properties, and the penalty was
around $25. Alderman Allen added that the cost of violations increases with
non-compliance, and Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller mentioned a daily violation fee.
The Board would like to gather more information on software, violation fees,
and other ways to manage non-compliant rentals.
 
         Alderman Carroll made a Motion to approve the Land Use Consistency
Statement to remain consistent with current General Statutes and the Zoning
Text Amendment regarding short-term vacation Rentals and Homestays as presented
and seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller.  Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
 
9.   Political Signs (moved to agenda item 6).
 
          Alderman Davis has expressed concerns about the current regulations
in the UDO that govern political signs. The current regulation limits the
number of political signs to one per property, which Alderman Davis believes is
unjust and violates the First Amendment. After consulting with several
constitutional attorneys and organizations, she has confirmed that this
regulation could be a potential violation of the Constitution. Alderman Davis
cited a Supreme Court decision to support her argument. She urges that the
Constitution be upheld and that this regulation not be enforced until it is
revised in the UDO.
 
         During the meeting, the City Attorney, Mr. Brady Herman, joined via
conference call to answer inquiries regarding the Ordinance. Upon reviewing it,
he believed that the Ordinance was not unconstitutional but was excessively
restrictive and needed to be addressed. He suggested that the revision of the
sign Ordinance, including political signs, should be postponed until after the
election and the start of the new year. He also added that if only one sign is
allowed, it could be deemed too restrictive by a court. Furthermore, he
proposed not enforcing the political sign Ordinance until the Planning Board
drafts and recommends a revised version for adoption approval from the
Aldermen. However, Alderman Davis respectfully disagreed.
 
         The Board discussed reviewing the revisions of the sign Ordinance but
decided to vote on not enforcing the use of multiple signs on private personal
property. Manager Therrien asked Mr. Herman if it was legal not to enforce a
part of the Ordinance with a Board vote, to which he replied that it was the
best temporary solution to rectify the situation.
 
         Alderman Carroll made a Motion to direct City Staff not to enforce the
portion of the political sign ordinance related to the number of signs on
private personal property and not in the right-of-way, seconded by Mayor Pro
Tem Mosteller. Aye: Alderman Carroll, Allen, Alt, Lombardi and Mosteller. Nay:
Alderman Davis. Motion Carried (5-1)
 
6.   Forensic Audit
 
         Alderman Alt proposed a plan to improve the policies and procedures
related to financial oversight. Mayor Pro Tem expressed her disagreement with
spending $10,000 on the forensic audit and suggested that the professional
staff should handle it instead. Alderman Alt clarified that the issue was not
with the project itself but rather the process of how the money is being
utilized. He suggested verifying that the money was being used correctly. Mayor
Pro Tem Mosteller recommended reviewing the finance director's report first.
Alderman Allen explained that a forensic audit is an examination to find
illegal financial records and activities. He mentioned that if there is no
evidence of financial misfeasance, then there is no need for a forensic audit.
Alderman Lombardi questioned the staff's capability to manage the project, and
Manager Therrien confirmed that the staff was capable. She expressed her belief
that there may have been mistakes in the Taylor's Field project. Alderman Davis
asked when the Howe Street project was completed, and Alderman Lombardi replied
that it was around 2018. Alderman Davis suggested asking the finance director
to conduct a financial audit on these projects to pinpoint any mistakes.
Manager Therrien explained that the finance director had only been in the
position for three weeks and was still learning the program. Manager Therrien
said that it would be difficult to take the Finance Director off of everything
he is doing now with the budget season approaching to specifically devote time
to the finances of these projects.
.         
         Mayor Hatem stressed the importance of monitoring the projects and
ensuring that the staff had the necessary support and resources.
 
         Alderman Alt proposed a motion to allocate $10,350 for a forensic
audit of the Howe St., Bay Street, and Taylor Field projects. However, there
was no second motion, and it was denied.
 
         Robert made a motion to direct the staff to research the subject
further and come back to the board with recommendations. Mayor Pro Tem
Mosteller seconded the motion.
   Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
 
7.   Creek Committee
 
          Alderman Alt requested the City Manager to take necessary measures
regarding public health warnings based on creek readings at Cottage, Bonnett’s,
and Price’s Creek. He proposed forming a workgroup comprising City staff,
County Public Health officials, and State water quality experts. This group
would be responsible for giving monthly updates to the Board of Aldermen. The
purpose behind this is to authorize the city manager to allow signs warning the
public about high bacteria levels. Mayor Pro Tem suggested reviewing all
policies, while Alderman Allen inquired whether the county and state had been
consulted.
 
         Manager Therrien informed the Board that she had reached out to both
the county and state officials. They provided some levels that are required to
trigger warnings, but it depends on the type of water and other factors. She
also informed the Board that the Staff is working with a lab in Colorado to
conduct a test. The County reverts to the State on such matters. Alderman Allen
further inquired about the composition of the committee. Alderman Alt clarified
that the intention was to have a policy that would allow testing and come back
to the Manager with a recommendation to move forward.
 
         The Board's consensus was to ask the city manager to appoint a group
or person to look into the situation and put signs up if needed. The Board
members also expressed a desire to converse with health departments to
determine if there's a need for warning signs.
 
         Alderman Alt made a Motion to allow the City Manager to decide who
should be on the Creek Committee, set up procedures for monitoring the Creeks
for bacteria, and take appropriate actions if needed. The Motion was seconded
by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion carried.
 
 
 
 
 
8.   Affordable Housing
 
         Recently, Mayor Hatem met with neighboring mayors to discuss the issue
of affordable housing. Each municipality expressed concern about the lack of
workforce housing and possible solutions to address it. The Mayor emphasized
that a collaborative effort with county officials is necessary to find a viable
solution.
 
         In this regard, Alderman Alt has requested the City Manager to form a
workgroup comprising City staff, Brunswick County Habitat for Humanity, and
other non-profit organizations. The workgroup will provide the Board of
Aldermen with a list of options for both economic and non-economic incentives
that the City can adopt to promote workforce housing initiatives.
 
         Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller announced that a new Development Services
Director will soon be joining. Once the Director and the Planner arrive, they
will evaluate the planning process for affordable housing. Alderman Carroll
acknowledged that the issue is essential and appreciates the effort. However,
due to the average lot cost of around $30,000 in Southport, it would be
challenging to execute any plans for affordable housing in the area. Therefore,
he suggested looking into alternative options in Brunswick County, where
affordable lots are available. Alderman Carroll favors affordable housing and
supports the need to work with other entities with the resources to
accommodate.
 
         Mayor Hatem announced an upcoming meeting for the mayors seeking help
from the County Commissioners and NC State Officials. They aim to collaborate
to provide incentives for affordable housing for the workforce in Brunswick
County, the seventh fastest-growing county in the nation. Manager Therrien
suggested the Board send a letter to the County to generate support and
collaborate on a solution.

E.   Agenda: Shoreline Stabilization
   Mayor Hatem made a comment regarding the Shoreline Stabilization project. He
highlighted that this was not the final meeting and provided a brief history of
the project. The project has received better engineers, better qualifications,
and new funding.
   Tom Jarvis, the project lead, gave an overview of the project. The Olsen
Group has been appointed as the engineers of the project. Chris Reed provided
an update on Olsen's progress, and the city attorney has been consulted on the
design concepts. Greg Finch from the Data Group Land Management Group was also
present.
   Mr. Reed gave a PowerPoint presentation, which was divided into three areas.
He discussed the sand section on the west and the private wall with the living
shoreline. He also talked about the site conditions and considerations, such as
the federal navigation channels, detailed hydrographic survey in 2023, and
cultural resources investigation in 2023. All these factors will be reviewed in
the regulatory planning process.
   Previously discussed project goals were also reviewed, and the pre-Hazel
Shoreline Condition of 1954 was presented. The project approach involves
developing the project scope based on the current conditions. Alternative
options are then created while keeping in mind the goals and constraints of the
city. Existing shoreline protection is also taken into account during the
development of these options.
   Previous alternatives that were proposed are also considered. Option one
involves creating a sandy beach, which is the most expensive. Alderman Alt
asked about the feasibility and cost of this option, and Mr. Reed said that
they would need to do further research.
   Option t involves the creation of a revetment in the center portion. Rich
suggested using larger rocks on top, but Chris disagreed and said that the
stones were too small and needed to be laid down on a bigger rock. Alderman
Davis asked about the appropriate size of the rocks, and Mr. Reed explained
that the rocks at the revetment needed to be oversized. Alderman Alt mentioned
that it was only a temporary solution, and he would look for a more permanent
one. Alderman Carroll inquired about the rock in front of the Garrison. Mr.
Reed provided some examples to help clarify. It's worth noting that the
revetment does not have a beach with rocks. Living shoreline in Southport
erodes with ships and structures in front so that grass can exist.
   The area in question consists of a sandy beach with breakwaters. The
shoreline has sand in the east and a revetment in the middle, while the east
side has a living shore. The project involves riparian rights, which must be
considered during the regulatory process. The priority areas have been
identified, and a solution needs to be chosen quickly due to the limited time
and funding available before 2026. Mr. Reed believes that obtaining permits
will take about a year, and a revetment would be the easier option to permit.
Decisions can be made faster if the revetment is chosen. However, Chris also
thinks that the cost of revetment would exceed the amount already allotted by
the city. Mr. Reed suggests obtaining a permit for the entire project or in
pieces.
   The state has been planning a project involving design and planning for
almost 30 years. The next step in the process will take 2-3 years. The most
significant challenge will be to select a plan and cost comparison,
particularly for the west portion. The living shoreline is not optimal. Mr.
Reed suggested responding to the current conditions, while Rich recommended
adding sand to the beach. The legal issue, however, is who owns the beach.
Alderman Lombardi inquired about the permit duration, which is five years for
CAMA and CORE, that do not overlap. Mr. Finch expressed concern about the
sand's impact on the yacht basin. Alderman Alt explained that the CORE and the
commercial aspect play a significant role in this. He also asked if the project
generates new sand, to which Mr. Finch replied that there is no sand coming to
Southport. During the meeting, it was discussed that the sand on the beach
comes from erosion. The board wanted to make some decisions regarding the
beach. Mr. Jarvis explained what they wanted to do to get things moving for
November. They needed direction from the board and input on phasing.
   Alderman Alt suggested using rip rap, starting downstream and moving up the
shore. Mr. Finch was unfamiliar with the term, but Alderman Alt explained that
it meant placing stones along the shore. Mr. Reed suggested that if they were
dealing with the beach, they should consider using other options. Alderman Alt
said that three options were more stable. He asked if they could do one at the
west before time runs out. Mr. Finch said that options one and three present
riparian issues, which means they involve the rights of property owners. He
said that everyone would benefit, but the law is unique on these issues. The
legal advice has been provided in the packet, but they needed more legal
counsel. Mr. Jarvis suggested prioritizing the east end of the west and giving
directions on which to start.
   Alderman Alt recommended a three-segment plan and suggested starting with
option two to obtain the necessary permit. He also advised considering the cost
of that particular section. On the other hand, Mr. Jarvis suggested analyzing
everything in depth before determining the cost. Alderman Alt pointed out that
the revetment would be less expensive. Alderman Davis enquired about the plan
and the materials that will be used. Mr. Reed responded that he had not
reviewed the exact plans yet and that there may be several options to consider.
Mr. Jarvis suggested that they prioritize urgent repairs and add any additional
necessary enhancements to the beach. As there is a time constraint, they must
start with completing the east end first. Riparian rights and property rights
need to be confirmed, which can be done through CAMA. Homeowners will still
have access to their docks despite the repairs. During the meeting, a
recommendation was made to start with the hardest part of the project, which
would require obtaining difficult-to-get permits. The suggestion was to begin
with the breakwaters and sand, which might be more expensive but would help
secure the necessary permits. There was also a discussion about riparian
rights, and it was explained that property owners start at the mean high land.
However, there was a risk that the property owners might lose the rights to
riparian access. It was suggested that the project team explore the possibility
of granting easements for those rights.
    The Board discussed the wooden wall and unanimously agreed it needed to be
constructed as soon as possible. However, there was some disagreement about the
height of the wall, and it was decided that more conversation was necessary on
the topic. Alderman Alt asked what would happen if one homeowner did not agree
to grant riparian rights. Mr. Creed was uncertain and suggested seeking legal
counsel to explore the matter further. Mayor Hatem asked the previously
established steering committee if they wanted to discuss the issue. Mr. Paul
Fisher asked about the scope, suggesting it should cover east to west. Manager
Therrien emphasized that a decision needs to be made, and Mr. Fisher added that
the entire area needs to be considered. Mr. Jarvis suggested evaluating from
the yacht basin area to Bonnets Creek and asked if the scope covers the whole
city. Mr. Jarvis said they would look into the future. Mayor Hatem suggested
considering the future to go into the scope.
   Mr. Tommy Harrelson, 202 W. Bay St, Mr. Paul Fisher, 101 River Dr., BJ
Gorman, 406 W. Brunswick St., and Frank Marchetti, 1523 Shephard Rd., were on
the steering committee. Mr. Harrelson thanked them for their efforts and
suggested it could be done sooner. He expressed that he was not blaming anyone
for the delay and appreciated that something was being done. Mr. Harrelson also
mentioned that they were told they could not use sand from the river to
replenish the beach and suggested using beach nourishment instead.
      Parks and Recreation Director Hemphill gave an update on the repair of
the street on East Bay. One section is eroding and compromising. Ms. Tara
McPherson with CAMA mentioned that there was an exception, and they did not
have to go through the permit process. She said they want to extend it, but it
does provide an exemption. Ms. Hemphill suggested joining the revetment and
then extending it and added that there was a portion that does not need a
permit. Ms. Hemphill replied that it would not affect the design. Mayor Hatem
was asked about Mr. Fisher’s question regarding dredging. Mr. Creed explained
that the process is expensive and requires dredging millions of yards of
material within a small space, making it even more costly. Mayor Pro Tem
Mosteller requested an opinion on the best approach and what factors should be
considered. Mr. Reed responded that option one was great, but the middle
section was the most critical factor to consider. He added that the living
shoreline to the west was the least problematic for now. The next step was to
determine the direction to take and then move on to the study phase. Bob Jarvis
suggested that the most important sections to look into were section one and
section two, which the Mayor agreed were the most vulnerable. Alderman Allen
concurred with Mr. Jarvis’s suggestion. Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller noted that the
legal aspect is a critical part of the project and should be addressed
immediately.
F.   Public Comments
   Deputy Clerk Tanya Shannon read a comment from Brian Stevens, a resident of
503 Cades Trail, expressing his concern about the absence of a paddle board and
kayak launch at the waterfront. In response, Mr. Jarvis stated that it was too
early in the process to know about a secondary launch. Alderman Allen suggested
that access to these activities could be provided at the beach side of Caswell
and Bay Streets. He also pointed out that there is already a launch available
at the Morningstar Marina, which he believes is preferable to use. Manager
Therrien assured the Board that she would provide a full report on the Kayak
Launch during the next regular meeting.

OCTOBER 30, 2023
Special Meeting Minutes
BOARD OF ALDERMEN
INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL
SPECIAL CALLED MEETING
113 W. MOORE STREET
COMMUNITY BUILDING
October 30, 2023
PRESENT:
Mayor Joseph P. Hatem
Mayor Pro-tem Karen Mosteller, Alderman Lowe Davis, Alderman Tom Lombardi,
Alderman Rich Alt, Alderman Robert Carroll, and Alderman John Allen joined via
phone.
STAFF PRESENT:
Assistant City Manager/City Clerk Dorothy Dutton, Electrical Superintendent
Ellie Pittenger, Public Services Director Tom Stanley,
OTHERS PRESENT:
Paul Fisher, Roy Jones, Jason Thigpen, Brandon Rummage, Dan Werdel
Mayor Hatem called the meeting to order at 10:00 a.m.
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
Mayor Hatem led everyone in the pledge of allegiance.
Alderman Carroll made a motion to approve the agenda that Alderman Lombardi
seconded. All ayes. Motion carried.
Mayor Hatem welcomed everyone to the meeting. He said that the purpose of the
meeting was to review the benefits and relationship Southport has with
ElectriCities and the North Carolina Eastern Municipal Power (NCEMPA). He
introduced Mr. Paul Fisher, who has served as a Commissioner on the NCEMPA for
many years. Mr. Fisher asked the CEO of ElectriCities, Roy Jones, to begin the
presentation. Mr. Jones said the plan was to start at a national level and move
down to the municipal level. He thanked the Board for having them and
introduced Dan Werdel, the Supervisor of Production. He explained three types
of electric utilities: Public Power Utilities, Rural Electric Cooperatives, and
Investor-Owned Utilities. He reviewed how each type is different. A public
power utility serves one out of seven customers. The City of Fayetteville is
the largest public power utility in North Carolina.
Alderman Alt asked some questions about the supply chain and where transformers
are made. Mr. Roy Jones stated that most are made in the US, but there has been
so much growth after the Coronavirus pandemic that there has been a
manufacturing shortage. Many manufacturers do not want to expand because now
they have work guaranteed for the next few years.
Mr. Jones and Mr. Werdel went through a timeline of electric service from the
Electric Act of 1965 to 1984, when ElectriCities was incorporated, and in 2015,
when the NCEMPA sold its electric generation assets to Duke Energy Progress.
Now, each municipality has a seat on the ElectriCities Board.
Jason Thigpen, Manager of Power Supply Operations with NCEMPA, addresses the
Board of Aldermen next. He said, "The interconnected grid for electricity is
one of the greatest inventions of all time." He explained that one hour of use
at the highest peak is equivalent to 63% of the bill. Alderman Alt asked how
they determine the peak hour. Mr. Jones said they have over ten years of
history to help predict. They consider the most extreme temperatures and time
of day when the most use occurs, and the entire system is considered, so the
peaks are not just for one municipality. A total of 800 people in Southport
participate in load management.
One facet to consider is the time of use rate, which might save more money
overall. Mr. Thigpen confirmed that the City could use both load management and
time of use rates. Mr. Jones said the two- way meters are already installed;
they must coordinate with Brunswick Electric. There was some discussion about
battery systems that can be used during peak hours so that there is more
savings. Mayor Pro-tem Mosteller asked if all communities have this system and
how much that battery would cost. Mr. Jones stated they would help the City do
a cost analysis for the battery system versus the generator.
Alderman Carroll asked if there was a limit to how much solar a customer could
install in Southport, and Mr. Ellie Pittenger said that the City's program was
mirrored after the BEMC program, which was a 10kW max. Mr. Jones said there was
a difference between home generators and back-feeding the system. Mr. Werdel
said that, as a whole, the populations is heading towards a 21% renewable
future. There was some discussion about the systems being more active at night
because of the electric vehicles charging. There was some question about
whether the City is installing the correct infrastructure for the future. Mr.
Paul Fisher explained that BEMC monitors future infrastructure with their
engineers to help determine what might be needed. Solar capacity has increased
by 80% since 2013 because of creature comforts and necessities. Wholesale power
costs have declined since 2015. Next, there where discussions about strategic
planning, priorities, and the Billing history with the City of Southport.
All the electrical providers in the area share designated peaks. Wholesale
power costs have declined since 2015. NCEMPA absorbed small increases, so rates
didn't increase for their customers.
Mr. Paul Fisher thanked Mr. Jones and his team for coming to speak with the
Board of Aldermen. He encouraged more people to attend the meetings in Wilson,
NC.
Mayor Hatem thanked Mr. Fisher for thirty years of service and said the
information was wonderful. He also thanked Mr. Ellie Pittenger. Mayor Pro-tem
Karen Mosteller wanted to emphasize that ElectriCities is a real partner to the
City.
Alderman Carroll made a motion to adjourn the meeting, which Alderman Lombardi
seconded. All ayes. Motion carried.

H.   Presentations:
   1.    Final Presentation-Build Out Study
   Mr. Wes MacLeod, Services Director of the Cape Fear Council of Governments,
presented the Build Out Study. Population has doubled in the past 20 years,
with an increase of 70,000 people since 2000 in Brunswick County. The median
age demographic is 56. Southport has a median age of 63, and Sunset Beach is
the eldest at 68. Ages 20-34 make up only about 7%. Southport is projected to
gain five people monthly for the next five years. During summer, seasonal
residents and visitors populate close to 10,000. 1,700 acres are developed, and
2,220 are undeveloped, mainly on the outskirts of the City and dedicated to
single-family development: no questions or comments. Mr. Macleod thanked the
Board.
   2.   Short-Term Rental Vacations Presentation
   Ms. Meehan, Ms. Dutton, and Ms. Jones reviewed some updates on the process
for enforcement, purchasing software, and the collection of taxes. Ms. Meehan
explained that the procedure and process for registration and enforcement are
up to date. Ms. Jones said that the City is currently levied at 3% of gross
receipts on occupancy tax. She said approximately 50 individual properties are
reporting. She said it is a challenge to determine the exact locations of these
rental properties because they are paid in a lump sum with no detailed report
or if the rental is registered and in conformity. There could be many potential
undocumented and unpaid fees.
   Ms. Dutton explained two software programs that would monitor compliance,
such as sending enforcement letters and increasing efficiency by adding
evidence to enforce communications. Of the two options reviewed, the staff
review recommended Granicus Software as a more formidable tool for Southport
for an annual cost proposal of $9,840.
   Ms. Dutton confirmed that the software has a high success rate and increases
tax revenue. If approved, it can be implemented immediately and is billed
annually. It was agreed to revisit this matter in December for a final
decision.

   3.   Yacht Basin Dredging Contract Extension (Jamie Pratt, TI Coastal)
   TI Coastal has been assisting the City with surveying, permitting, and other
services related to dredging the USACE channel and adjacent areas to the
Southport Yacht Basin. They have completed hydrographic surveys, taken sediment
samples, coordinated with the Audubon Society, and engaged in discussions with
the USACE. Upcoming work includes applying for project funding, performing a
shellfish survey, creating long-term use plans, finalizing dredging plans and
cost estimates, and continuing follow-up with permitting agencies. The biggest
problem currently is finding a disposal site for the spoils. He said the first
site was not suitable, and now they are looking at the 2nd Bridge going to Oak
Island with an available pond source. The contract will allow them to continue
to coordinate permitting. The state will match every dollar the City spends on
dredging with $3.00. The expenditures will be less with the grants. Alderman
Alt asked what is the approximate cost of the requested extension. Mr. Pratt
said $30k. Alderman Carroll confirmed that the entire cost for the dredging
construction will be roughly $2M, which includes transporting the spoils.
   Alderman Allen made a Motion to approve the Contract with TI Coastal
Services, authorize the City Manager to sign the contract for dredging the
Yacht Basin and continue with the state funding application and construction
for the Yacht Basin at a cost not to exceed $30,000 and second by Mayor Pro Tem
Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.

   7.   Budget Ordinance Amendment for Fire Mitigation Fee Schedule
   Chief Drew explained that the Fire Department could charge two types of
fees: Permit (Operation) Fees and Mitigation (Fire Response) Fees. The
Mitigation Rates offset the cost of emergency services outside of structural
fires. However, these Mitigation Rates have not been updated in the past nine
years. As a result, the Southport Fire Department recommends billing the
Mitigation (Fire Response) rates for those living outside the City limits. This
requires the adoption of a Budget Ordinance Amendment to add this section to
the existing fee schedule.
   The Mitigation (Fire Response) Rate will increase by 1.5% annually or based
on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index. Rate adjustments
will occur when the new budgets are adopted to keep the Fire Department's cost
recovery program in conformity with increasing operating expenses.
   Alderman Alt asked how the proposed fees compare to other areas. Chief Drew
said they're comparable. Alderman Alt was worried about inflation. Chief Drew
explained that car insurance usually pays for car accident fees, and they don't
pursue collections; if fees can't be delivered, they will be dropped. Manager
Therrien stated that the proposed fees will be brought to the budget workshops
for more detailed discussion.
   Alderman Carroll made a Motion to adopt the proposed budget amendment to the
FY 23- 24 year. And the Mitigation (Fire Response) fee schedule, as presented
and seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   8.   Parks and Recreation Ordinance Amendment
   Mayor Burke explained that a few grammatical errors have been corrected. He
said they regrouped the parks by including the Garrison Lawn in the ordinance,
which will have the same restrictions and guidelines as the waterfront park and
no closure. He said all the other parks have been regrouped and put together
and recommended closing them at 9 o’clock. He said that is consistent with
other closure times with additional facilities such as the public restrooms.
Major Burke also requested on behalf of Parks and Rec. Director Hemphill to
restrict metal detecting, digging, and disturbing grass lawns and vegetation on
the Garrison Lawn.
   Alderman Carroll made a Motion to approve the amendment to the City of
Southport Code of Ordinances Chapter 12: Parks and Recreation, as presented and
seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   9.    Community Building Deck Project – (Removed from the agenda)
   10.    Yaupon Drive Extension Paving Project
   Some concerned citizens informed Manager Therrien about a topic she was
unaware of. The issue pertained to a storm drainage system brought up in
previous board meetings but was never approved for implementation, possibly due
to its high cost. Alderman Alt asked about the difference between this road,
Hankinsville Rd., and the dirt road off Atlantic Ave. Mr. Stanley clarified
that Hankinsville Rd. is not a city road. There are three unimproved/unpaved
roads: Yaupon Extension Drive, a small block off Atlantic Ave. in between E.
11th Street and Stewart Ave., and a portion of W. 11th Street where the
pavement extends and ends around 9th Street, partly in the city limits but
considered an unimproved road.
   Alderman Alt asked what that price would look like if a gravel road would be
made compared to engineering the improvements. He said he asked because this
project is estimated at $58M, while there are 40 other projects to fund. He
wondered if the road could be graveled or filled with dirt to improve the road
temporarily and how significantly this would reduce the cost. Mr. Stanley said
these rough estimates do include the utilities. Mr. Stanley explains that any
water/sewer expansion would be the developer's responsibility to pay. Alderman
Carroll asked what the cost difference would be if it were graveled or filled.
Manager Therrien said she wanted to bring this to the attention of the Board
and then get a recommendation on how to move forward so that it can be reviewed
for the next budget and that there will need to be cost estimates on what
gravel or dirt cost difference would be. Alderman Carroll said he feels like
this is a safety issue and something should be done. Mr. Stanley said he
estimates that filling and grading would cost roughly $300,000-$400,000 without
storm drainage, utilities, and paving.
   Alderman Davis asked about the official designation of Yaupon Drive as a
City road. Mr. Stanley checked the records but found no evidence of its
dedication. However, it is listed on the Powell Bill Road directory. Alderman
Davis expressed concern that this could set a bad precedent since other
privately owned roads are in poor condition, and taxpayers are upset. Mayor Pro
Tem Mosteller agreed and called for an evaluation to be carried out to provide
confirmed estimates on alternatives. Attorney Herman stated that if Yaupon
Drive is a city road, it must meet the city's standards.   It was the consensus
of the Board to research the history of Yaupon Drive Extension and determine if
it is a city road.
   11.   Contract for Parking Study-Walker Consultants

Parking Study. Their revised proposal and narrowed scope meet the budget of
$50,000. The study will assess current parking and identify issues. Then,
recommendations will be made to add traditional parking or parking structures.
The Board can pick the revised or original proposal. Voting for the original
proposal of $75,000 will need an amendment from the Capital Project account.
   Alderman Allen made a Motion to Approve the revised contract with Walker
Consultants for the Parking Study at $50,000 so that work can begin in
coordination with the Comprehensive Plan work and authorize the City Manager to
execute the contract seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mosteller. Unanimous Vote;
Motion Carried.

I)   Board Nominations
   1.   Alderman Davis explained that she has heard about potential candidates
from many people over the last few days. She has given it a lot of thought. She
has someone in mind who is a registered voter and a resident of Ward 2. She is
nominating Frank Lai. He has owned a nearby property for forty-plus years. He
is well-informed about Southport and current issues. He was a top executive at
Goodyear. He has a strong background in community service. Alderman Kelley
seconded the motion.
Alderman Mosteller offered the following comments:
The School of Government recognizes in accordance with State Statute, “there
are no specific rules about who must be appointed or how they are selected.
Although there is no legal requirement, some cities decide to appoint the next
highest vote-getter in the most recent election.”
We are in the unusual position of filling an alderman seat by Board
appointment. Our charter does not specify a procedure.
The last time this happened was when Chief Coring stepped off the Board to
become our Police Chief, the Board appointed the next highest vote getter on
the ballot to fill his seat until the next election.
While we determine the outcomes of elections by the candidates that receive the
highest vote counts; it is important to acknowledge the community support for
other candidates.
Based on the total number of votes cast in the election, almost 40% of the
people who voted in this election cast a ballot for Ms. Bray.
Congratulations to newly elected Alderman Kelley. Approx. 46% of the
participants voted for Ms. Kelley.
Quite honestly, I would rather support the appointment of a new Board member
who had the support of 700 voters, almost 40% of all the ballots that were
cast. And only about 6% less than the second highest vote getter in Ward 2.
Rather than picking someone that has not participated in a public process,
supporting a candidate who demonstrated her commitment by standing up and
volunteering to serve the community, a candidate who took part in the League of
Women Voters debate, a candidate who has recently invested months of her time
to learn more about her community seems more representative.
It helps that Ms. Bray has already been serving as a volunteer in our community
for many years. Ms. Bray was a member first then served as Chair of the
Beautification Committee; she served on the Up Your Arts Board for several
years and is serving on the Historic Preservation Commission. Except for
sitting on this Board, I would wager that Ms. Bray has committed more volunteer
hours for the benefit of our community than those of us here at this table.
Alderman Carroll asked Mr. Lai to come to the podium. Alderman Carroll asked
questions about trees, what organizations he has been involved in, and growth.
Mr. Lai described his experience with finance and budgeting. Alderman Carroll
commented how the nomination of Mr. Lai seemed orchestrated. Alderman Mosteller
explained that the School of Government does not establish a procedure for
filling a vacant seat. It is important to recognize the will of the people. She
would rather support a new Board member who stood up and volunteered to serve.
Bonnie Bray has already been volunteering in the community for years. She has
probably donated more volunteer hours than some people already at the table.
There was a call for a vote. Alderman Kelley, Alderman Spencer, and Alderman
Davis vote aye. Alderman Carroll and Alderman Mosteller voted against
it—majority rules. Mr. Frank Lai was appointed to serve on the Board of
Aldermen. The Honorable Judge Jason Disbrow performed the Oath of Office for
Frank Lai.

J)   Special Presentations
   1.   City Manager Bonnie Therrien introduced Mr. Everett Jones, an arborist
who assessed Franklin Square Park. Mr. Jones went through his presentation.
Overall, he said there are (22) trees in the park that need a Level 3
assessment to look for extensive decay within the stems and root systems. The
assessment will determine if the trees are worth saving or saving. Soil care
throughout the park is needed. Trees need nutrients and extra care. He
recommended adding more mulch, fresh wood chips, and some organic matter. The
Level 3 assessment uses sonic waves to measure the tree's health. He estimated
$20-25 000 would be needed each subsequent year to protect the trees. There are
also (4) trees that need to be removed. Mr. Jones also recommended planting
more native species. Mr. Jones said the $15,000 for the Level 3 assessment
excludes tree removal, pruning, or other mitigation. There was some discussion
about the damaging effects of compaction. There was also some discussion about
how much damage was being caused by the activities in the park. Mr. Jones said
that the events were causing damage to the trees. If the City takes no action
to improve the park now, more trees will likely die. He suggested putting up
physical barriers to protect the trees. Alderman Kelley asked Alderman Davis
about the Forestry Committee and their annual tree planting program. Alderman
Davis said they would be interested, but it would also depend on the timing.
Alderman Carroll motioned to approve the appropriation of $15,000 for the Level
3 assessment. Alderman Mosteller seconded the motion. All ayes.

the amendment to the audit contract, which Alderman Lai seconded—all ayes.
Motion carried.
   7.   The next item discussed was the Comprehensive Plan Steering Committee.
Previously, there was an approved motion to appoint the Planning Board as the
steering committee, but originally, there was a desire to have more public
input.
Alderman Mosteller provided the following comments:
I do not understand why Mayor Alt has put this on the agenda again. The Board
has previously voted 5 to 1 to designate the Planning Board to act as the
Steering Committee for the Comprehensive Plan Update.
The original agenda item summary that was submitted to the Board of Aldermen
included the following guidance from City Staff and I quote, “The Steering
Committee is an advisory group that provides guidance on priorities,
strategies, and generally helps keep the project moving forward. In the Unified
Development Ordinance, several responsibilities of the Planning Board are
identified, including amending, and revising a comprehensive and coordinated
plan for the area’s physical, social, and economic development.
The Planning Board is already dedicated to a similar purpose. The Planning
Board can use their regular meetings to review and consider material for the
Comprehensive Plan. For these reasons, City Staff recommends the Board of
Aldermen appoint the Planning Board as the official Steering Committee for the
Comprehensive Plan.”
The department head comments stated, “I feel that the Planning Board already
reviews projects and ordinances and makes recommendations for the betterment of
Southport. The Planning Board is well respected and will serve well as the
Steering Committee.”
Staff went on to say, “The Comprehensive Plan process will also include several
meetings with local stakeholders that will bring their own perspective.
Also, our parking study consultants will work closely with Stewart Inc. to
share information and ask questions. This will hopefully save some time and
resources.”
Just to put a fine point on it, reading from Stewart’s printed material in our
packet.
The project design is structured in three phases that include multiple:
Staff meetings
Stakeholder Group Meetings
Steering Committee Meetings
Community Visioning Workshops including a walking tour
Board of Aldermen Meetings
To quote from Stewart’s Southport project description, “This plan update will
be developed through integrating public engagement and best planning practices
while also being refined by local priorities and prospectives.”
Mayor Pro-tem Kelley recommended using members of all the current committees to
serve as the steering committee. Alderman Carroll agreed with Alderman Davis to
postpone this topic and decision until the December 20th meeting.
M)   Committee Reports
There was a brief update on the Historic Preservation Commission. The ABC Board
has adopted an Employee Policy and will hire an Assistant Store Manager. They
have also implemented a lottery to get the more sought-after items.
N)   Manager's Report
City Manager Therrien congratulated several employees for work anniversaries.
The Bay Street project should be completed soon and back open at the beginning
of next week. She wished everyone Happy Holidays.
O)   Board Comments
Alderman Lai said he looks forward to working with the Board. There are a lot
of good people in Southport. Alderman Spencer said he had received a petition
from some folks on Fodale asking for help with speeding. Mayor Pro-tem Kelley
thanked everyone for their votes and their confidence in her. She said she is
looking forward to learning as much as possible. Alderman Davis wished a Merry
Christmas to all and to all a good night! Alderman Carroll welcomed the new
Board members. He looks forward to serving alongside them. He hopes they can
continue doing the right thing for the citizens of Southport. And he wished
everyone a Merry Christmas. Alderman Mosteller wished everyone a good night.
P)    Mayor Alt thanked everyone for attending and wished everyone Happy
Holidays!
A motion was made by Alderman Spencer and a second by Alderman Carroll; the

   1.   Introduction of the new Center for the Creative Arts Board (formerly Up

   2.   Boundless Playgrounds:
   Parks and Rec. Director Hemphill presented the plan for the all-inclusive
playground concept. She said it has been in planning for about 5-6 years. It is
part of the PARTF grant and Phase 2 Taylor Field Project. The Boundless
Playground removes any barrier based on abilities. The park will be named the
"Taylor Field of Dreams" and is intended to capture the history of the maritime
museum. The City has fronted $2,000 to partner with Unlimited Play, which helps
design and plan boundless playgrounds. Manager Therrien estimated the cost to
be around $750,000, but grants have already been applied, and donations from
non-profits and surrounding communities typically show generous support.
Alderman Mosteller asked where the park will be constructed, specifically at
Taylor Field. Ms. Hemphill said it would be in the center of the park. Ms.
Hemphill thanked the Board for considering "The Taylor Field of Dreams and its
partnership with Unlimited Playgrounds.
H.    Agenda
   1.   Discussion and Decision Regarding the System Development Fee Rates.
   At a public hearing on December 14, City Engineer Mr. Zilinek presented a
system development fee study, which the Board accepted. The decision to set the
fee for the coming year was postponed due to a question raised by the Board.
After seeking legal opinion, Mr. Zilinek confirmed that the fees could be
increased in the future but cannot exceed the maximum listed in the SDF study.
A new study must be conducted at least once every five years.
   The Board discussed whether to base the fees on commercial rates that can be
calculated based on the number of seats or by using the meter rate based on the
amount of usage. Alderman Davis questioned where these funds go. Ms. Therrien
said the sewer fund must be used for capital improvements to the system. The
fees collected would be kept until the merger with the county. A special
meeting will be held in January to discuss the sewer merger. Options are
available to spend the money collected so that the county takes less and the
customers benefit from the full worth of the fund balance.   
   Alderman Carroll made a motion to Update the Rates according to the new
study and apply residential rates by use but commercial rates by meter size,
seconded by Alderman Davis. Before the vote, there was more discussion.
   Alderman Mosteller discussed the meter rates versus the calculation fees.
She said there should be some consideration for what those impacts are. She
noted that new rates are calculated based on future expenses and costs. Knowing
that a merger will occur, making a short-term decision doesn't seem helpful.
Alderman Mosteller said she would like to have more discussion on using the
meter rate method for commercial rates. She would prefer to keep the rates and
revisit them in 6 months. Mayor Pro Tem Kelley agreed. She said that she would
like to see the comparison for commercial businesses based on calculations or
usage fees. Mr. Zilinek gave an example of a 40-seat restaurant; using the
current structure, the system development fee would be $77,232. He said that
the meter-based fee would be if they have a three-quarter-inch meter, it would
be $15,847, and for a one-inch meter, it would be $39,617. Mayor Pro Tem Kelley
asked what it would be for other businesses, and Mr. Zilinek said he only did
the restaurant calculations. Alderman Carroll suggested evaluating the UDO to
see if there could be modifications to whether a person who purchased a
property with an existing tap would have to pay another system development fee.
Mr. Zilinek said that a rate has to be set by December 31, but it could be
later when the rate goes into effect.
   Alderman Mosteller explained that if a flat rate is charged for a meter
size, it would apply to a restaurant with 40 seats or 200 seats. She added
that, in all likelihood, a 200- seat restaurant would require more capacity
than a 40-seat restaurant, and therefore, meter fees for commercial purposes
would be questionable. Alderman Carroll said the motion could be amended to
remove meter size, go by usage, and have more discussions, including the merger
with Brunswick County.
   Alderman Carroll amended the motion to update the rates according to the new
study and use the usage method for residential and commercial and second by
Alderman Davis. Aye: Alderman Mosteller, Carroll, and Davis. Nay: Mayor Pro Tem
Kelley, Alderman Spencer, and Lai. 3-3, Mayor Alt breaks the tie with a Nay
Vote. Motion Denied 3-4.
   Mr. Zilinek reminded the Board that a rate still needed to be set. Mayor Pro
Tem Kelly made a motion to leave the rates as they currently are pending the
January meeting that would provide more information regarding the merger with
the county seconded by Alderman Spencer. Aye; Mayor Pro Tem Kelley, Alderman
Spencer, Lai, and Mosteller. Nay: Alderman Carroll and Davis. Motion Carried 4-
2.
   2.   Request for Waiver of Penalties
   David Wayne Smith of Wayne Smith & Son said they are building a custom home
for Bill and Sally Demidovich at 683 Carolina Bay Ct in Indigo Plantation. They
believed they'd submitted all needed applications and only removed trees from
specific areas around the footprint. They offered to plant new trees to offset
the removed ones. Wayne Smith & Son is a small, family-owned business with
years of experience. He thanked the Board for considering waiving the fees.
   Former city building inspector Mr. Wayne Strickland spoke in favor of Mr.
Smith, stating he has always followed the rules. Mr. Strickland also mentioned
many people had difficulty using the permit portal, making it hard to complete
the process without consulting the building inspector. He believed the fine was
disproportionate to the Ordinance's intent and the penalty for clearing the
lot, which he had done, was unusual.   
   Alderman Carroll feels that this is not the contractor's problem. It is the
property owner's problem. He reiterated a similar situation with unpermitted
tree removal; the fees were not removed, and the people paid less than the
Ordinance required penalty.
   Alderman Caroll made a motion to enforce the penalty of $46,583.29, seconded
by Alderman Davis. Before a vote was taken, there was a discussion.
   Mayor Pro Tem Kelley appreciated the City's tree ordinance and suggested
adjusting the penalty fee for the cleared area instead of the entire lot.
Alderman Carroll believes it is the responsibility of the property owners,
contractors, or builders to research the Ordinance and follow the guidelines.
Alderman Davis said removing trees without a permit undermines the tree
protection ordinance. Mr. Smith's wife presented a topography showing 119 live
oaks on the property.
   Alderman Mosteller appreciated that there are several members of the Board
from the POA for Indigo Plantation. Still, the POA does not enforce the City's
Ordinance, and the POA or ARB was unaware of the City's tree ordinance adopted
in 2018 and required with the building permit. Alderman Mosteller stated that
the point of having rules and regulations is if they are not enforced. Alderman
Davis agreed and said that if allowances and waivers keep getting approved, it
will undermine the Ordinance. Alderman Mosteller asked Manager Therrien about
the 9th Street project where there was a lot and many trees were cut without a
tree permit, and the fine was $11,910 and asked if there was a resolution and
what the status was. Manager Therrien said she would review the records and
provide the status. Mayor Alt stated that there is a difference in the cases.
One case has a topography showing what trees were there, whereas the others did
not apply for permits. Alderman Caroll stated that it is apparent that there
are many steps in the process of applying for a building permit where questions
are asked about trees and obtaining a tree permit. Alderman Carroll asked to
whom the fine was levied. Manager Therrien said to the property owner.
   The motion was repeated: Alderman Caroll made a motion to enforce the
penalty fees of $46,583.29, seconded by Alderman Davis. Aye: Alderman Davis,
Carroll, and Mosteller. Nay: Mayor Pro Tem Kelley, Aldermen Spencer, and Lai.
3-3 Mayor Alt broke the tie with a Nay: 3-4 Motion denied. Mayor Alt said he
believed the fine was too high and entertained another motion.
   Mayor Pro Tem Kelley made a motion to look at the square footage of the
cleared space of the lot, add the remediation plan that was put forth, and use
the calculations that are currently in the tree ordinance to come up with a
modified amount for the fine for the property and seconded by Alderman Lai.
   It was noted that four trees were removed from the ROW, which must also be
calculated fine.
   Mayor Pro Tem Kelley amended the motion that the fine be based on the 25% of
the clearing of the lot, including the mitigation that was already put forth
and what the penalties for the four removed public trees in the right-of-way
will be and seconded by Alderman Lai. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   Alderman Spencer questioned what would be the total amount for the fine
would be now. Manager Therrien stated that the motion could be tabled until a
calculation for the penalty could completed or voted on and then determined the
fee and brought back to the Board in January. Alderman Carroll recommended that
it be determined that as much as 25% of the lot was cut and given city staff
direction on how much to charge for the fines moving forward.
   Mayor Alt stated that Manager Therrien will have the city staff recalculate
the new fine and report it to the Board.

   Return    2:22 p.m.
   3.   Minimum Housing Ordinance and Discussion
   Manager Therrien stated that there was a discussion on many options and
solutions at the Public Hearing. After meeting with Attorney Herman, they
determined that there has to be a legal process to give the property owners due
process and protect their civil rights. She explained that typically, the City
will request that the owners demolish and remove the structure, and if they do
not respond or comply, the City will be allowed to remove it after a court
process. The City would pay the removal expenses, and then a lien would be
placed on the property, so if the property is sold, the City would get the
money back. She said this is something that the City needs so these abandoned
houses can be removed.
   Mayor Pro Tem Kelley noted that some of the language in the proposed
Ordinance is questionable. She recommended the following changes: 1) Any
reference to screens in and out should be removed; 2) Any reference to mandated
garbage disposal at a sink or incinerator should be removed; remove required
off- street parking; and Mayor Hatem's name should be to Mayor Alt. Alderman
Spencer recommends taking out the interior condition of the house. Mayor Pro
Tem Kelley said that is included in the proposed Ordinance.
   Mayor Pro Tem Kelley motioned to approve the Minimum Housing Ordinance as
presented with the amendments mentioned earlier and seconded by Alderman Lai.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   4.   Shoreline Stabilization Contract
   Mr. Bob Jarvis, the City Engineer, provided a brief explanation of the issue
of shoreline erosion. Olsen Associates completed an initial planning and design
phase, which has been approved. Developing a phasing scheme is necessary due to
the current funding for the proposed improvements' design, permitting, and
construction. Funding for the project was provided through a $5M grant from the
State Emergency Response and Disaster Relief Fund. The grant will expire on
June 30, 2026. Approximately $70k has been spent on the project since Olsen
commenced their work in January 2023. Mr. Jarvis recommended that the City
enter the next phase of Olsen Associates' contract for ongoing engineering and
enable the project to be completed within the funding timeframe. It is expected
to take approximately 150 days. The City Attorney has reviewed the proposed
Task Order.   
   Alderman Mosteller made a motion to authorize the Contract with Olsen
Associates to continue the work for design development, coordination, and
permitting for dredging the Shoreline Stabilization Project second by Alderman
Lai. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   5.   Discussion of Municipally Owned Alleyways
   Alderman Mosteller proposed a policy allowing citizens to restore and
maintain their alleyways for rear access to their property. The Planning Staff
will review and help create a policy. Alleyways are crucial assets to the
character and walkability of older neighborhoods. Some community members are
asking about debris and tree removal. Alderman Mosteller wants a policy
implemented soon and does not believe this is an encroachment issue.
   During the discussion, ensuring that individuals who receive permits to
clear paths and trees do not attempt to claim city property as their own, such
as by erecting fences, was brought up. Alderman Mosteller clarified that such
an action would be considered an encroachment and noted that a policy is
already in place to address it.
   Alderman Mosteller made a motion to allow the Planning Department Staff to

their alleyways for rear access and walkability, second by Alderman Lai.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
