January 5, 2024
REGULAR MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN Regular Meeting Minutes
January 5, 2024   Indian Trail Meeting Hall
SOUTHPORT, N.C.   9:00 A.M.
 
Present:   Mayor Rich Alt, Mayor Pro Tem Rebecca Kelley, Aldermen Lowe Davis,
Robert Carroll, Marc Spencer, Karen Mosteller and Frank Lai
Staff Present:
      Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
      Dorothy Dutton, Assistant Manager/ City Clerk
      ChyAnn Ketchum, Community Relations/PIO
A) Mayor Rich Alt called the meeting to order at 9:00 a.m. and welcomed
everyone.
B) Alderman Lowe Davis gave the Invocation.
C) The Pledge of Allegiance was led by Mayor Alt.
D) Public Comment:
None
E) Approval of the Agenda
A motion was made by Alderman Lai and seconded by Mayor Pro tem Kelley to
approve the agenda. All ayes; motioned carried.
F)  Presentations
   1. Mayor Alt introduced the representatives, Dave Smith, and Johnathan
Layton from HICAPS. They were hired to inspect all of the City owned
properties, provide an assessment on the condition, and also make
recommendations to help maintain them. The final report provides an executive
summary for each building, property descriptions, and a review for safety and
fire protection. HICAPS rated each building as good, fair, and poor. And they
provided an estimate of the cost of repairs. The representatives said that the
report will help plan the Capital Improvement Plan for the next ten years. They
also assigned different levels of urgency to the recommendations-immediate,
short-term, or over-term.
In many cases, there were gutters and downspouts missing, which caused damages
to the structures. The old City Hall building has mold, water infiltration, and
all major trades have issues. The building still needs a complete structural
inspection, and hazardous materials abatement. The urgent costs are estimated
at $3.94 million. Abatement of mold will likely cost $150,000. Alderman Carroll
stated that it wouldn’t do any good to remove mold and asbestos but leave it
unconditioned.
Mr. Smith and Mr. Layton reviewed each building and their findings. For many
buildings, there was overgrown vegetation, ADA improvements and gutters needed.
Overall, the total estimated costs are $5,014,375. Mayor Alt stated that the
old City Hall building might not all be considered urgent, because no one is
currently using it. The HICAPS team added that they are happy to re-estimate
projects as needed.
City Manager Bonnie Therrien thanked them for the report and added that the
report is so important for future planning.
   2. Mr. Hugh Fosbury approached the podium to explain the proposed 4 th of
July Festival agreement with the City of Southport. Ms. Lucinda Arnold and
Trisha Howarth, from the festival committee were also in attendance. Mr.
Fosbury explained that the proposed agreement was the same as the previous, but
the deadline date is October 1 st . The agreement will roll over automatically
unless someone requests a change. The 4 th of July Festival Board meets monthly
on the third Tuesday. Mayor Alt asked for a copy of the original declaration
and the original charter with the committee’s regulations. Alderman Marc
Spencer asked if it would be possible for the City to have a voting position
within the festival board. Ms. Fosbury stated that the City is listed as the
lead sponsor in all the community information. Alderman Davis asked for a list
of all the current 4 th of July Board and Committee, so she can thank them .
Alderman Carroll made a motion to accept the revised agreement. Alderman
Mosteller seconded the motion. Alderman Carroll amended his motion to state
that the City be listed as the title sponsor and authorize the City Manager to
sign the agreement. All ayes. Motion carried.  
   3. Ellie Pittenger, the Electrical Superintendent for the City, introduced
Ms. Deborah Fish, with Brunswick Electric. Ms. Fish said that BEMC had just
finished a project-the Cape Fear Drive conversion to underground. She showed
some pictures of before and after. They also finished the conversion of River
Drive. She added that the entire system will be underground within the next ten
years. She reviewed the NC211 project, some subdivisions, and also the next
projects that are planned. They have been ordering supplies ahead of the
projects because of material shortages and delays. Sometimes it takes up to
(60) weeks to get the supplies in, so they are asked for a PO for the project
they want to do next year. Once the materials have arrived, they will do a PO
for labor. BEMC wants to finish up the 2023/2024 work plan and then start on
the E. Moore Street conversion. After that, they will remove all the poles down
Howe Street, and install the decorative exterior lighting per the City’s
policy.
They would like the Board to approve a PO for $900,000 for materials. There was
some discussion about where the three-phase services are located, and also who
is responsible for the expense of moving electrical service underground.
Ms. Fish explained that Dosher Memorial Hospital’s electrical is completely
underground now. They are working on a loop system that will allow most
locations on while there is an outage. There was some discussion about
accommodating the 4 th of July Banners. Alderman Carroll made a motion to
approve taking $150,000 from the electrical fund to amend the BEMC plan to
include Lord Street. Alderman Spencer seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion
carried .
4. Chief Drew addressed the Board of Aldermen about an amendment to Chapter 7
of the Code of Ordinances regarding Fire Protection. He explained that because
the City provides yard debris collection, there should not be anything left for
residents to burn. The Fire Department is recommending the use of gas-burning
fire pits that do not emit smoke or ash. Fire pits have become a widely used
feature at many residences. Chief Drew stated that cooking outside and food
preparation is allowed. There was some discussion about amending the ordinance
later to include smokeless wood, or other fire pits as long as they are in a
controlled environment. Alderman Kelley made a motion to adopt the amendment as
presented, and Alderman Mosteller seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion
carried.
G. Agenda
1. City Manager Therrien explained the current Yaupon Drive Extension
situation. Tom Stanley and Tom Zilinek did a lot of research on the street but
determined that it is only a “paper road” and the City is not receiving any
Powell Bill funding for its maintenance. There is no evidence that the City
ever took ownership of the road. City Engineer Tom Zilinek estimates that it
would cost $1.5 million to fully improve the road. City Manager Therrien said
the City has no obligation to improve it, but it is a public safety issue.
Mayor Alt suggested that the property owners fix the road. And Mayor Pro-tem
Kelley added that if the cost is divided between the property owners, it is
approximately $15,000 per owner. She said that it would be setting a bad
precedent if the City paid for the improvements. The other Board members agreed
that it would set a bad precedent. Alderman Mosteller said she hoped the lots
sold for a reduced amount so that the residents can afford to gravel it.
Alderman Carroll said he would like to learn how Boiling Spring Lakes handles
all their gravel roads. Alderman Davis made a motion that the City does not
fund the road improvements for Yaupon Drive Extension. Alderman Spencer
seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
   2. Assistant City Manager Dorrie Dutton, and City Planner Mo Meehan reviewed
the possible options for managing the short-term rentals in Southport. Alderman
Kelley had met with City staff and recommended that staff works with the
residents and property owners that are currently operating short-term vacation
rentals. Staff can ask for their help in identifying rental properties that are
not compliant with the current ordinance standards. Ms. Dutton and Ms. Meehan
recommended that the City contract with Granicus for at least one year to help
identify the short-term vacation rentals and get the City on the right path
moving forward. Additionally, City staff would be releasing more information to
the City’s website and hosting community meetings to explain the ordinance and
how it will be enforced. Alderman Mosteller made a motion to contract with
Granicus. Alderman Davis seconded the motion. There was more discussion about
other options. Alderman Spencer and Mayor Pro-tem Kelley voted no to the
motion. Aldermen Davis, Mosteller, Lai, and Carroll voted aye. Majority rules.
Motion carried. Alderman Spencer added that he thinks limiting short-term
vacation rentals is a kind of illegal property taking.
   3. Chief Coring and Major Burke addressed the Board regarding the recent
petition to reduce the speed limit on N. Fodale Avenue. Chief Coring said that
the Police Department had placed a sign message board and had placed patrol
cars in the area to capture the speed of passing vehicles. The average speed
captured was 31 miles per hour. They explained that all patrol officers are
running radar if they are out, and they don’t have to be stationary. But once a
driver sees an officer, they start spreading the word. Major Burke said they
were relocating the equipment to the other side of Fodale. Alderman Davis asked
is reducing the speed limit would be helpful, but Major Burke said that we are
looking for voluntary compliance, so he didn’t think a reduction in the speed

Stewart because they are being used as cut-throughs. We need to educate the
public. Alderman Carroll added that we live in an area where a Board member can
make a request and staff is able to jump on it quickly. He said it was
wonderful. There was some discussion about re-routing the traffic to and from
the ferry. And Alderman Spencer asked Ms Therrien to arrange for the NCDOT to
come back to speak to the Board about re-directing traffic. City Manager
Therrien said the Police would be back to present the findings from the other
side of the road.

January 10, 2024
Water/Sewer Merger Special Meeting Minutes
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN Water/Sewer Merger Special Meeting Minutes
January 10, 2024  Indian Trail Meeting Hall, 113 W. Moore St.
SOUTHPORT, N.C.   9:00 A.M.
 
Board Present:   Mayor Rich Alt, Mayor Pro Tem Rebecca Kelley, Alderman Karen
Mosteller, Robert Carroll, Marc Spencer, Frank Lai
Absent:   Lowe Davis
Staff Present:
   Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
   Tanya Shannon, Deputy Clerk
   Lance Flint, Finance Director
   Teresa Jones, Tax Collector
   Brandon Stevens, Deputy Finance Director
   Tom Zilinek, City Engineer
   Tom Stanley, Public Services Director
   ChyAnn Ketchum, Communications Director
A.   Mayor Alt called the meeting to order at 9:00 A.M.
B.   Alderman Spencer gave the Invocation.
C.   The Pledge of Allegiance was led by Mayor Alt.
D.   Alderman Carroll Made a Motion to approve the Agenda, and second By
Alderman Lai.  
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
E.   Agenda
1.   Manager Therrien reviewed the issues that must be resolved before a
merger. Such include annexation loss, use of fund balances, whether to merge
water or not, staffing levels, and other services provided to the residents.
2.   The Board discussed hiring a special attorney to assist with the potential
water merger with the County. Mr. Mac McCarley, an experienced attorney with
expertise in mergers, joined the Board via conference call and discussed the
success of a previous merger with Shallotte. He expressed his interest in being
considered for the job. It was noted that a merger could take anywhere from 3
to 8 months to finalize. Ms. Therrien informed the Board that the cost of the
attorney would be $495 per hour and that the fees would be paid from the water
and sewer fund.   
   Alderman Carroll made a motion to appoint Mr. McCarley as the City Attorney
for negotiating and developing legal documents with the County for the merger.
The motion also included granting authorization to the City Manager, Therrien,
to oversee the agreement and to sign any correspondence. Alderman Spencer
seconded the motion. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
3.   Finance Director Lance Flint provided a financial overview of the fund
balance and the use of funds and grants with a PowerPoint presentation for the
Water/Sewer Merger Financial Analysis. Mr. Flint explained there will be
significant savings for utility customers by merging. Each customer's savings
depend on numerous factors, including the services used, the size of the water
meter, and location within or outside of city limits. The Water & Sewer fund is
funding City services that will continue post-merger. These costs will transfer
to the General Fund and require new revenue sources to fund. The Water-Sewer
Fund balance contains net assets valued at $27 million, including $12.4 million
in cash. Decisions on which assets to retain and convey must be made, and
opportunities to use cash now should be explored. The City has several capital
projects in development with funding that involves incurring debt. The funding
identified for the Wastewater Treatment expansion that was voided is not
sufficient to cover the current cost estimate. Incurring debt to complete these
projects can be avoided with a merger. Funding that is specific to the City may
not be transferable to the County.
   The Board talked about the potential spending of the General Fund and the
allocation of funds for various capital projects. Manager Therrien mentioned
that the City and County Staff will meet to discuss the different projects and
decide which entity is responsible for completing each project. There was a
question about determining the use of funds, and it is unclear what the
County's bottom line is. If the City proposes five projects, but the County
disagrees, why not discuss the necessary projects until an agreed-upon amount
is determined? Manager Therrien replied that she would like to get an idea from
the Board on exactly what projects would be considered.
   Break- 10:34 a.m.
   Return-10:44 a.m.
4.   Tax Collector Teresa Jones and Public Services Director Tom Stanley
discussed the merger's potential effects on their respective departments. Ms.
Jones noted that a complete merger would impact three full-time and two part-
time positions. If only the sewer department is merged, staffing levels must
remain unchanged. However, if a complete merger is approved, the Utility
Billing Specialist position can be eliminated, with the Customer Service
Representative and Utility Department Supervisor taking over the remaining
duties.
5.   Mr. Stanley explained that while there are currently eight positions in
the water and sewer division, these employees are responsible for much more
than just water and sewer tasks. He was asked how many positions would become
unnecessary if the county took over the water. Mr. Stanley replied with two
positions. But these positions could be negotiated with the County to hire
them. He said it's important to remember that two projects could affect the
future manpower needs of Public Services: the Building Assessment Survey, which
revealed a need for additional maintenance of City-owned buildings, and the
Storm Water Mapping & Planning Project, which will include a Capital
Improvement Plan. This plan will likely include projects or improvements that
City Staff may perform in addition to contracted work.
6.   a) Should Water be Merged with the County?
   Alderman Carroll motioned to merge City Water with the County, seconded by
Alderman Mosteller. Unanimous Vote, Motion Carried.
   Mayor Pro Tem Kelley pointed out the need to discuss the revenue and
compensation structure for the city staff affected by the merger. Various
sources of revenue, including ad-valorem taxes, were discussed. Manager
Therrien said this issue will be addressed during the budget meetings. Alderman
Mosteller noted that it appears as a loss of revenue but also noted that the
rates are decreasing.
b) Reallocate $1.263 Million of ARPA Funds out of Water/Sewer to a General Fund
project. Resurfacing of Roads? Shoreline Stabilization?
   Mayor Alt requested clarification on separate funds, which are not part of
the $12 million budget. Finance Director Flint confirmed that the separate
funds were not included in the $12 million. Mayor Alt emphasized that the money
was not allocated to the sewer fund, which is now being removed. Mr. Flint
clarified that the funds were not in the sewer fund but were designated for
expanding the voided wastewater treatment facility. These funds can be
transferred to the general fund and must be utilized for the stated purpose by
Federal regulations by 2026. The Board agreed to discuss the allocation of
these funds during the Budget Meetings.   
   Alderman Carroll motioned to reallocate the $1.263 million ARPA funds of the
Water/Sewer Fund to the General Fund. The decision regarding the use of these
funds will be made later in the year 2024. Mayor Pro Tem Kelley seconded the
motion.  Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
c)   Positions to Keep with the City and Those to Go to the County.
   The Board agreed to table this discussion for further review.
d)    Use of Fund Balance:
1.     Set aside funds to pave roads after sewer projects.
   There was a discussion about the paving of roads. It was concluded that the
city needs to identify the roads that require repairs after the sewer work is
completed. The responsibility for repairing the roads damaged during the City's
repair work would fall on the City, whereas the County would be responsible for
repairing roads damaged by their work. The decision regarding who will repair
the roads will be made after negotiations.
2.    Subsidize lower rates so customers are paying County rates.   
      Alderman Carroll made a Motion to instruct City Staff to determine what
the new rate would be less the additional $1.6 Million that is being added to
the Fund Balance from the Sewer Fund Balance every year and implement those new
rates seconded by Alderman Lai and Mayor Pro Tem Kelley.  Unanimous Vote;
Motion Carried.
3.   Use some funding to offset loans.
   Manager Therrien stated that there will be more discussion about offsetting
loans once there is more information about the rates.
4.   Collection of fees  
   Manager Therrien raised concerns about collecting fees and how they would be
collected. She asked if there would be a substation for fee collection or if
customers would have to go to the County Complex to make the payments. The
Board agreed to table the discussion and revisit it later.
e)    Mayor Comments:
Mayor Alt thanked everyone for attending and the Board for having a good
discussion and wished everyone to go out and enjoy the beautiful day.
f)    Board Comments:
The Board appreciated the Staff for all their hard work.
   There was no further discussion. Alderman Carroll made a Motion to adjourn,
seconded by Alderman Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
Adjourn- 12:04 p.m.

Mayor, Rich Alt             Deputy Clerk, Tanya Shannon

G.   Public Hearings
1.   Mayor Alt opened the Public Hearing for Text Amendment-Section 3.9.B.5
Setback Exceptions and Encroachments.
   The proposed amendment includes heating and air conditioning units in the
encroachment provisions. It aims to accommodate smaller lot widths within
cluster subdivisions and nonconforming R-10 lots throughout the city. Since
October 2022, the UDO has enforced the 30" standard to reduce equipment
encroachments, but staff must often address the issue. Nonconforming lots not
located in subdivisions may have a 4’ side setback, allowing units to have no
setbacks.
Public Hearing Comments:
1)    Dean & Rachelle Warnecke, 311 Firefly Lane, submitted a comment, and the
Deputy Clerk read the statement. They live in the Prices’ Creek subdivision and
are writing to support the proposed amendment. They believe the amendment would
provide an equitable solution for future homes for both the homeowners and the
City. They said this is especially true for smaller lots like theirs, with only
a six-foot side easement.
2)    Brian Kimball, 786 Skipjack Circle, submitted a comment read by the
Deputy Clerk. He said the proposed text has raised valid concerns regarding the
enforcement of setback regulations and the impact on property owners. He said
it is crucial to amend the UDO to ensure consistent application of regulations.
Fair treatment of property owners, regardless of their property type, is
essential to maintaining a just and equitable community.
No further comments were made. Mayor Alt closed the public hearing.
2.   Mayor Alt opened the Public Hearing for Text Amendment-Section 3.12.B.2
Driveways.
      Ms. Meehan provided an overview of the Amendment the Board of Adjustment
requested on September 24, 2023. The Board granted a variance for a single-
family dwelling unit driveway that did not meet the setback and lot width
provisions found in Section 3.12. The variance was approved for the setback
reduction, but the Board required the applicant to conform to the less than 50%
lot frontage for the driveway. The driveway provisions in the UDO were
discussed, and it was advised that more variances of this nature would be
forthcoming. During the meeting, the board discussed the driveway provisions in
the UDO and anticipated more variances. The consensus of the Board of
Adjustment was that this section of the ordinance should not apply to single-
family or two-family dwelling units and that a text amendment should be
submitted to the Planning Board.
      The Planning Board recommended approval of the zoning text amendment
allowing driveway setbacks for single- and two-family dwelling units to be
changed from 10’ to 2’ from the side lot line.
   There were no comments. Mayor Alt closed the Public Hearing.
H.   Agenda
1.   Discussion and Decision Zoning Map Amendment of a Tract of Land on
Jabbertown Road submitted by Gandy, LLC for JC Rentals, LLC.
      The request is to change a portion of a parcel of land located at 558
Jabbertown Road from Light Industrial (LI) to Mobile Home (MH). The property is
adjacent to the Cottages at Prices Creek and Harbor Ridge mobile home park and
is currently zoned MH. The future land use map designates the MH portion of the
property as medium-density residential and the LI portion as low-density
residential. The Planning Board recommended approval of the proposed zoning map
amendment to the Board of Aldermen.
      Alderman Mosteller pointed out that the proposed zoning change would
permit the construction of up to two units on a 5,000-square-foot lot without
any requirements for open space. While she appreciates the owner's intention of
developing small housing structures on the lot, and some adjacent property
owners also believe it would be a better option than light industrial use, she
disapproves of rezoning based solely on the promises of the property owner. The
proposed district has different allowable uses, not just for small single-
family homes. Alderman Mosteller suggests that conditional zoning could be a
helpful tool in situations like this, enabling the community to consider such
projects that could prove beneficial. In conclusion, she believes it would be a
mistake to approve the rezoning based on assumptions of what will be
constructed rather than what is allowed.
      Mayor Alt asked about the potential uses that would be allowed if a
proposed zoning amendment was approved. Ms. Meehan replied that the following
types of dwellings and land uses would be permitted: Single-Family (SF), Multi-
Family (MF), Triplex, Quadruplex Dwellings, Family Care Homes, Manufactured
Homes, Manufactured Home Parks, Mixed Uses, and Modular Homes.
      Mayor Alt explained that for a development project to move forward with a
potential conditional zoning option, a developer must be the one to initiate
the process and sign a development agreement. Ms. Meehan confirmed this
statement and noted that due to the property's size, it would have to undergo a
Major Subdivision review process before any development could occur. She
explained that as part of this process, the developer would need to submit a
proposed development plan outlining the subdivision of lots, infrastructure,
utilities, size of lots, intended uses, and ingress/egress. Mayor Alt also
pointed out that if the rezoning is approved and the developer decides to
pursue a different plan, it will be considered a by-right use.
      Mayor Pro Tem Kelley asked if the developer could request a PUD instead.
Ms. Meehan said it could not because it is in the ETJ, and there must be at
least 25 acres to do a PUD in the ETJ. Mayor Pro Tem Kelly asked if the
developer had met with the adjacent property owners since the last meeting. Mr.
Adrew Laing, 6217 Pebble Shore, came to the podium and said they had met with
the Prices Creek Board and would prefer the property rezoned to Mobile Home
instead of Light Industrial. He said they favor the project but understand that
this discussion strictly concerns zoning.
      Mayor Pro Tem Kelley asked if there were alternative options for the
development project, and Ms. Meehan replied that there were none available at
the moment.
   Alderman Davis made a Motion to DENY the Land Use Consistency Statement,
citing inconsistency with Policy 2.3 of the Land Use Plan and the proposed
Zoning Map Amendment from LI to MH as presented. Seconded by Alderman
Mosteller. Aye: Alderman Davis, Mosteller, Lai, and Carroll. Naye: Mayor Pro
Tem Kelley and Alderman Spencer.  Motion Carried 4-2.

Ordinance or hold a Public Input Meeting to discuss penalties and enforcement.

and should be protected. Developers need to apply for removal to keep track of

5.    Discussion of Sunny Point Property
   Alderman Mosteller began the discussion with these statements requested
verbatim.
   By way of background…
   “In 2020, for the purpose of conservation, the Board of Aldermen voted
unanimously to begin discussions with the NC Wildlife Resources Commission for
the sale of the 441-acre Southport tract that’s part of White Springs Natural
Heritage Area.
   With action by the Board of Aldermen, the NC Wildlife Resources Commission
then received the endorsement of Wildlife’s Land Acquisition Committee allowing
their staff to pursue funding opportunities to purchase Southport’s portion of
the White Springs Natural Heritage Area.
   Why has the NC Wildlife Resources Commission continued to pursue the
purchase of the Southport parcel?
   In efforts to secure the rare wildlife habitat, the NC Wildlife Resources
Commission has previously purchased two parcels of land that are part of the
White Springs Natural Heritage Area adjacent to the Southport property. NC
Wildlife acknowledges the Southport tract of this Heritage Natural Area
contains some of the most important habitat of any of the tracts conserved in
and around MOTSU.
   There is a high concentration of wildlife “Species of Greatest Conservation
Need” or “priority species” as identified by the North Carolina Wildlife Action
Plan that occur on the tract. Species of Greatest Conservation Need (priority
species) are defined as, “species that are currently rare or have been
designated as at-risk of extinction. Many of the priority wildlife species that
rely on the habitat of the Southport tract are in significant population
decline in our state. NC Wildlife Resources Commission is best suited to manage
the tract appropriately in order to sustain high quality habitat for these
priority species, and staff are already managing the adjacent NC Wildlife
Resources Commission owned property successfully. Expanding ownership to
include the Southport tract will enhance proper management and provide habitat
connectivity for these species.
   In 2021, NC Wildlife received a NC Land and Water Fund Grant award that
would provide partial funds to purchase the Southport tract.
   Since that time, NC Wildlife has continued to work on the funding plan and
has received a second grant with the hope of protecting in perpetuity the
land’s significant wildlife habitat conservation value.
   This land is of the highest natural significance rating as documented by the
NC Natural Heritage Program. Recognized by the state as a Significant Natural
Heritage Area, this tract of land, known as the White Springs Natural Heritage
Area, is also identified in the Southport Comprehensive Plan. Our comprehensive
plan names our community values, guides our land use policies and decisions,
and provides the underpinning for our Unified Development Ordinance.
   Noted in our comprehensive plan, fragile areas include coastal wetlands,
complex natural areas, areas sustaining remnant species and prime wildlife
habitats.
   Policy 2.21 states: “Southport supports the protection and preservation of
its environmentally sensitive areas and fragile areas.
   Policy 2.19 plainly states that, “…residential, commercial, and industrial
development should not be supported in Natural Heritage Areas…”
   On page 54 in our Comprehensive Plan, it states… “The North Carolina Natural
Heritage Program identifies significant natural heritage areas within North
Carolina of which three are located in the City of Southport.” Map 8 in our
Comprehensive Plan depicts these Significant Natural Heritage Areas which
includes the Southport - White Springs Natural Heritage Area.
   On page 133 it states, “On the future land use map, there are some areas
that are considered least suitable for development…in most cases, they are
considered least suitable because it is a park or other Protected Land or
Significant Natural Heritage Area.”
   On page 28, it states that a land use plan is intended to accomplish four
primary objectives…one of which says a land use plan is intended … “To preserve
wildlife habitat and wetlands necessary to support threated and federally
protected species.”
   NC endangered and threated species on this land include the Carolina Gopher
Frog, the Ornate Chorus Frog, the Eastern Chicken Turtle and five other
amphibian and reptile priority species are known to occur on the tract and a
further 19 priority amphibian and reptile species are likely to occur on the
tract but have not yet been surveyed. Only 7 populations of the Gopher Frog
remain in North Carolina out of over 32 populations documented historically.
And the Southport Tract has 1 of the 7 populations that are left. What we need
to understand is these animals breed in the pond and spend the rest of their
time in the uplands. Traveling 1 to 2 miles to their summer burrow year after
year. In their words, NC Wildlife Resources wishes to proactively conserve
these rare species, which are declining rapidly due to habitat loss from human
impacts, to prevent their populations from going extinct in our state.
   Finally, this land is zoned Open Space and the Comprehensive Plan names the
appropriate and inappropriate uses in Open Space District Zoning. Page 148
   “Appropriate uses would be… City Parks and Recreation, additional City
facilities that help preserve and protect the natural environment, cultural
heritage, and areas that are environmentally sensitive and fragile.”
   “Inappropriate uses would be multi-family developments, residential and non-
residential uses, and industrial operations.”
   In the Unified Development Ordinance, that we refer to as the UDO, Open
Space District is defined as, “Areas of special public interest that should be
placed in a zone protected from any development other than improvements or uses
undertaken by the City of Southport.”
   Southport’s UDO does not list mining as an allowable use in any zone. I
referenced New Hanover’s UDO to understand which zoning district would
typically allow mining. Mining is listed as an industrial use. Mining is
inconsistent with the Open Space District intended uses in both the
Comprehensive Plan and our UDO.
   Uses undertaken by the city should be consistent with the Comprehensive Plan
and the UDO. Again, inappropriate uses in Open Space District includes non-
residential uses and industrial operations.
∙   What are our values? … Southport’s Comprehensive Plan recognizes the need
to protect Natural Heritage Areas.
∙   Industrialization of this site would be inconsistent with the policies and
appropriate Open Space uses in our Comprehensive Plan.
∙   In the table of permitted uses in the UDO? the allowed uses in Open Space
District do not include commercial or industrial uses.
∙   The City’s Real Estate Appraisal for the Southport-White Springs Natural
Heritage Area tract identified the highest and best uses as Conservation,
Recreation, and Timber.
   Reading from the NC Wildlife Resources Commission Land Acquisition Form
filled out by a staff Biologist, it states, and I quote, “The largest pond on
the Southport tract was the only pond where any gopher frog egg masses were
found in the last five years of surveys of all the ponds in this area. As such
mining, wells, solar facilities, or other hydrology altering activity on the
tract could lead to the extirpation of this entire gopher frog population.”
Which means gone.
   At the end of the day, the Southport tract is part of the “White Springs
Natural Heritage Area” and is of the highest natural significance rating as
documented by the NC Natural Heritage Program. I want to repeat this statement
and a few comments by NC Wildlife… NC Wildlife Resources Commission wishes to
proactively conserve these rare species, which are declining rapidly due to
habitat loss from human impacts, to prevent their populations from going
extinct in our state. NC Wildlife Resources is best suited to manage the tract
appropriately in order to sustain high quality habitat for these priority
species, and staff are already managing the adjacent NC Wildlife Resources
owned property successfully. Expanding ownership to the Southport tract will
enhance proper management and provide habitat connectivity for these species.
   Southport’s Comprehensive Plan and Unified Development Ordinance support the
sale of this significant Natural Heritage Area to NC Wildlife Resources to
protect the property’s significant conservation value in perpetuity. “
   “I would like to invite NC Wildlife Resources Biologist Jeff Hall to the
podium for additional comments and to answer any questions of my fellow board
members.”
       Alderman Spencer inquired about the location of the essential pond for
gopher frogs' habitat. Mr. Jeff Hall, who was present at the meeting, clarified
that the City-owned side of the property has the most suitable ponds needed for
the habitats. However, Alderman Spencer pointed out that the area had
previously been dirt-mined. Mr. Hall acknowledged that the main pond, which is
essential for habitation, is located a little further away from the mined area.
He added that although gopher frogs are in the pond located in the mined area,
they are not thriving because the environment is not conducive to conservation.
In response to Mayor Pro Tem Kelley's question, Mr. Hall confirmed that the
pond where the gopher frogs were doing best is a naturally occurring pond.
Alderman Carroll stated that the Board needs to decide whether to continue
conserving the property or explore alternative options like payment to the city
for mining. Alderman Carroll expressed his support for allowing mining for
profit. However, he also acknowledged that this could threaten the gopher frog
population. Mr. Hall agreed that mining activities would not be sustainable for
the gopher frog's habitat. Mayor Alt said there are many unknown questions.
With the water/sewer merger with the county, it is unsure if the county will
include this property as a sewer asset. If so, there may be no need for
discussion on the matter. He advised the City Manager to continue talks with
the County to determine if they will want the funds associated with the
property. The Mayor also suggested having the Polote Corporation for mining
sand discuss with Wildlife Conservation to see if an agreement for protection
and utilization can be made and then return to the Board. Alderman Mosteller
disagreed and said she did not believe the Wildlife Commission wanted to
purchase the property to work something out with Polote. Manager Therrien said
that the state had made an offer for the property, which she said was a little
less than the city's appraisal. She said she had talked with the city’s
appraiser, who said it was a viable appraisal. Alderman Carroll asked if the
City owned the mineral rights. Ms. Therrien said that she would find out. The
discussion continued, focusing on determining the county's interest in the
property included in the water/sewer merger. The Board also discussed finding
out the amount of sand that was previously mined and for how much, as well as
getting an acceptable offer from NC Wildlife for a potential sale.
Additionally, they discussed exploring the possibility of Polote Mining working
with Wildlife Preservation to determine if any agreements can be worked out.
6.    Request to Hire a Realtor to Represent the City
       A proposal has been put forward by Alderman Davis to hire a professional
realtor who would represent the City when buying, leasing, or selling
properties. The aim is to have an experienced representative who can assist
with the City's growing needs. The City has been actively searching for
available properties to meet these needs. Alderman Davis believes hiring a
realtor to locate properties, negotiate deals, and handle legal procedures is
essential, just as the City hires legal services for other needs. She believes
that the city would be well-served by a professional realtor, and it would also
relieve the burden on the city manager. Alderman Davis suggests that the best
way to proceed is to go outside the local network and seek recommendations and
credentials from the Cape Fear Board of Realtors. She recommends that the Board
provide direction to the City Manager, who would then give direction to the
Realtor and report back to the Board.
      Alderman Davis motioned for the City to retain a real estate agent for
services as needed and to give the City Manager authority to search beyond the
city limits for the realtor. Second by Alderman Mosteller. Aye: Alderman Davis,
Mosteller, Carroll, Kelley, and Lai. Naye: Alderman Spencer. Motion Carried 5-1
7.   Real Estate Negotiation Process
      Alderman Davis has suggested that the Board should inform the public
about the name, location, and intended use of any property they consider
purchasing before entering a closed session. She believes that making the
public ask for this information is unfair. If the Board is going to discuss
buying property, they should disclose this information to the public. Alderman
Carroll agreed that the Board should be transparent but believes sharing
information about the property they want to buy upfront may affect
negotiations. Alderman Mosteller said that the Board will disclose all the
information about the property and its purpose during a viable negotiation.
Then, it will be reviewed publicly before a decision is made. Alderman Davis
disagreed and said that the public should know everything upfront. Mayor Pro
Tem Kelley believes that the public should be informed if the property is of
significant interest and worthy of potential purchase. Manager Therrien said
that sometimes sellers want to remain private, so they can't always reveal the
information about the property they want to buy, and sellers may back away from
a possible sale.
      Alderman Davis made a Motion to disclose to the public the purpose of
purchasing the real estate, parcel ID, address, and owner's name before
entering a Closed Session. There was no second. Motion died.
I.   Committee Reports
      Mayor Alt provided a brief update on the ABC Board. He mentioned that

      Alderman Mosteller presented her final report to the Parks and Recreation

JANUARY 17, 2024
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
JANUARY 17, 2024  INDIAN TRAIL MEETING HALL
SOUTHPORT, N.C.   9:00 a.m.
 
PRESENT: Mayor Alt, Mayor Pro-tem Kelley, Aldermen Mosteller, Lai, Davis,
Carroll and Spencer
STAFF PRESENT:
Bonnie Therrien, City Manager
Dorothy Dutton, Asst City Manager/Clerk
ChyAnn Ketchum, Public Information Officer   
OTHERS PRESENT:
Bob Liepa, State Port Pilot    
A)   Call to Order
Mayor Alt called the meeting to order at 9:00 a.m.
B)   Invocation
Alderman Lowe Davis provided the invocation.
C)   Pledge of Allegiance
Mayor Alt led everyone in reciting the Pledge of Allegiance.
D)   Approval of Agenda
Aldermen Lai made a motion to approve the agenda. The motion was seconded by
Mayor Pro-tem Kelley. All ayes. Motion carried.
E)   Agenda
City Manager Bonnie Therrien welcomed the Board and said that she was happy to
hold the orientation for the Board because local government is a passion of
hers. She added that she feels very strongly about the Council-Manager form of
government.
F)    Description of Board Binders
She asked Assistant City Manager Dorrie Dutton to review the items that were in
their City binders.
G)    Structure of Government
Ms. Therrien then began her presentation on the role of the Mayor, Mayor Pro-
tem and Aldermen, and the City Charter. She shared a story from her past when
she worked with an eleven-member Board who hated each other set the town
backwards. Ms. Therrien read through the guidelines that make a Board
successful, including respect and honesty. Any one Alderman cannot commit the
City to any position without a vote or consent by the entire Board. She said
that the Mayor the City Manager should be the one who corresponds with the
media. Members of the Board should not be involved with the City employees and
their duties.
Alderman Carroll asked how they get any new managers to continue with the
current policies and practices. Ms. Therrien said that priority setting and
giving goals to the Manager when there is a change. She also added that there
is no reason why a Manager would leave if the Board is a good Board. Ms.
Therrien said that there is a manager’s Code of Ethics through the
International City/County Managers Association (ICMA). The Assistant City
Manager acts as the eyes and ears for the Manager, and acts as an extension of
the Manager.
Assistant City Manager/City Clerk Dorrie Dutton explained the role and
responsibility of the City Clerk.
   Ms. Therrien said that Staff resources are extremely limited, and they
should focus on the direction given by the entire Board. The Board should not
be involved with consultants, negotiations, applicants, or other government
entities as individuals. She asked the Board to please let her know about any
personnel complaints right away so she can address them. She cannot affect the
culture of the organization unless she knows about them. She urged the citizens
and social media to direct all questions to her. Ms. Therrien then distributed
a little quiz for the Board with questions about different responsibilities.
There was some discussion about the role of the City Attorney. Mayor Alt asked
if the Board members had liability insurance to cover themselves and the City
if they did something foolish. Ms. Dutton said she would reach out to the NCLM
for clarification.
   Ms. Therrien continued reviewing the Rules of Procedure and reminded the
Board that there was now a subcommittee to help review the existing document
and make suggestions. She explained that Chief Charles Drew is the Emergency
Incident Commander, and they work together to notify the Board of any
emergencies.
   Ms. Therrien urged the Board to ask questions and voice concerns before the
Board meetings. City staff is here to make the Board look good. Alderman
Carroll agreed but also stated that he doesn’t want to limit discussion at the
meetings. There was discussion about the Conflict of Interest and Ethics
policies. Any conflict of interest should be put in writing for the Board of
Alderman and should be announced at the Board meetings. The current Conflict of
Interest policy allows the Board member to remain present but cannot
participate. And Alderman Davis added that if you consider whether some is
ethical or in conflict, then consider it as a newspaper headline. If you
wouldn’t want it in the news, you probably shouldn’t do it. And Ms. Therrien
said that the Board should obey all the laws and rules of the City, that the
Board does not have any special privileges.
H.    Guidelines for the Board
There was a ten minute recess before the next part of orientation. Once
resumed, Assistant City Manager Dorrie Dutton presented information to the
Board about the different types of Board meetings: Regular, Special, Emergency,
and Closed. She reviewed the type of notices that are required for each type of
meeting. Ms. Dutton then explained the different types of notice that are
required for public hearings, budget adoption, zoning amendments, and
annexations. She explained the remote participation policy, open meetings law
and the different between administrative, and legislative decisions. Ms. Dutton
also explained the NC Public Records Law and what is exempt. A public record
has more to do with content than the device or method of exchange. This means
that a personal cellular phone can still contain public records if work items
are being discussed. Lastly, Ms. Dutton explained that travel and training
policy for the Board.
I)    Date for Next Orientation Session
   The Board discussed possible dates for the second part of orientation. They
finally agreed on February 12, 2024, at 9:00 a.m.
Mayor Alt added that he was looking for consensus about a topic that has been
in the news. He would like to ask the City Manager to write something about the
increase in insurance rates that has been announced. He asked if the Board had
any heartache about it, and they did not. While the Mayor is out of town, Ms.
Therrien will compose a letter to the legislators opposing the increase.
J. Adjourn
   Mayor Alt thanked everyone for attending and said there was a lot of good
information. Alderman Spencer made a motion to adjourn. Alderman Lai seconded
the motion. All ayes Motion carried. Mayor Alt adjourned the meeting at 11:02
a.m.

SOUTHPORT, N.C.

Mr. Terry Duff, a resident of Bethel Road, said he was speaking on behalf of

E)   Agenda
1. The first item was consideration of an IT Contract with a firm called
Katalyst. Assistant City Manager Dorrie Dutton explained the reason for the
item. The current IT consultant has worked for the City for about twenty years.
The City has never requested proposals from other companies. The City received
two proposals from companies, interviewed both and are making the
recommendation to contract with Katalyst. Dylan Warner and Luke Johnson, from
Katalyst were able to explain the proposal and answer some questions. A motion
was made by Alderman Lai to approve contracting with Katalyst for managed
services. Mayor Pro-tem Kelley seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
There was further discussion about any site visits that would be needed, which
would range in cost based on the personnel that assisted.
2. Mr. Sam Boswell, a transportation planner with the Cape Fear Council of
Governments, reviewed the Brunswick County Comprehensive Transportation Plan.
Comprehensive Transportation Plans used to be referred to as thoroughfare
plans. The report is (50) pages, with a (300) page appendix. There is a
steering committee that attends meetings and conducts outreach throughout the
region. The municipalities that are included formally adopt the plan, and the
NCDOT adopts the plan. In this proposed plan, there are (166) project
recommendations. Some of the projects include modernization, parking ideas for
costal communities, and bicycle and pedestrian plans. A comprehensive
transportation plan usually gets completed every five to six years. Mayor Alt
said he felt there was a disconnect from what staff was doing and what the
Board was aware of. He said that staff and the elected officials would have to
work together moving forward. Alderman Mosteller said that she had attended a
few meetings, and the Board is always invited. She suggested the City should
look into updating the transportation plan. NCDOT scores projects every two
years. Alderman Frank Lai motioned to adopt the Comprehensive Transportation
Plan. Alderman Spencer seconded the motion. All ayes. Motion carried.
3. Allayna Dail, the Interim Community Relations Director reviewed the
financial aspect of the 4th of July Festival. She said the City ended up
contributing approximately $78,000 last year. The Festival Committee spent
about $142,000. Alderman Kelley said that it was a huge feather in the City’s
cap to keep the festival going, and staff does a great job.
4. Dorrie Dutton, Assistant City Manager, did a brief presentation on the
right-of-way encroachments in the City. She provided several options for moving
forward, including not enforcing them at all, allowing the existing
encroachments to stay, and giving the residents a period of time to remove all
the encroachments. Alderman Kelley made a motion to ask the City Manager to set
up Public Meetings for further discussion. Alderman Spencer seconded. All ayes.
Motion carried.
5. Finance Director Lance Flint explained that the Investment Policy creates
compliance with the general statutes. He said that all the City funds make 5%
or more interest. There are three CD’s that have been rolling over every six
months. Mr. Flint added that the City was already abiding by the rules, we just
didn’t have a written policy. Alderman Mosteller made a motion adopt the
Investment Policy as presented. Alderman Spencer seconded. All ayes. Motion
carried.
6. Police Chief Coring, and Major Burke reviewed the findings of the traffic

7. Bonnie Therrien, City Manager stated that there were several outstanding
issues regarding the utility merger with Brunswick County. Does the City want
to reduce the rates now? What amount of staffing will be kept? Should some
roads be paved with the funds we currently have? She stated that the City is
able to use general fund, despite a common misconception. Finance Director
Lance Flint explained that there are some differences in the ways the City
bills customers and the way the County bills customers. If the City changes the
base rate, that will equate to a savings of $550 a year per account. He said
there are two options. Option 1 would mean a reduction of rates and targeting
no further growth by the City. That would be an automatic savings of $46 a
month. Option 2 entails getting closer to the County rates by reducing the base
and consumption rates. That would be a $62 reduction per month for City
customers. But this option requires the use of about $1million of fund balance.
Mayor Pro-tem Kelley motioned to move forward with Option 2. Alderman Lai
seconded. All ayes. Motion carried.

All ayes. Motion carried.  
Next, there was discussion about transferring $1.2million from the water/sewer

2.   Discussion of Sunny Point Property (Alderman Carroll)
Alderman Carroll gave an overview of the discussion at the last meeting. He
explained that the Pelote Corporation and the North Carolina Wildlife
Commission are interested in the property at Sunny Point, and the Board
questioned if both organizations could find an agreeable term for both to
utilize the property for each purpose without interfering with their
objectives. Alderman Carroll said that recently, Brunswick County has become
interested in the property for infiltration ponds as well as they were not
previously. The North Carolina Wildlife Commission submitted a letter to the
city stating they would not be interested in purchasing the property to be
shared by Polote Corporation or any company for the excavation of soils.
Therefore, Alderman Carroll stated that the best option is for the City to sell
the property to the NC Wildlife Commission.
Alderman Carroll made a Motion to instruct Mayor Alt to execute the agreement
between the City of Southport and the State of North Carolina Wildlife
Commission for the purchase of approximately 441 acres, less approximately 10
acres, to be retained by the City in the amount of $660,000. The Motion
included the opportunity for each party to make minor corrections to grammar,
language, etc., second by Alderman Mosteller. (no vote)
There was a discussion on the property's use and sale and the expressed
interest from Brunswick County. The land has been appraised and is considered
best used for wildlife conservation, as it was funded by the Clean Water
Management Trust Fund to protect the environment and wildlife. It was advised
by counsel to put the sale on hold until there can be more discussion on
whether the county is interested in utilizing it for negotiations and
agreements with the merger.
Alderman Davis made an amended motion to table a decision until the matter is
resolved with the county and what their interest is, and the negotiations are
completed. Then, the decision is made on whether the property could be sold to
NC Wildlife. (no second)
There was a discussion about the possibility of selling the property to
individual buyers. Some attendees also brought this up during the public
comments section. It was suggested that other conservationists might be
interested in buying the property individually. Alderman Mosteller proposed
that a time frame should be set for deciding. She also pointed out that waiting
for the completion of negotiations with the county merger could take several
weeks or even months.
Alderman Carroll and Davis rescinded their Motions. Alderman Carroll made a new
motion to table a decision until the March regular meeting, then pending
getting additional information and answers to questions about other specifics,
move forward with instructing the Mayor to execute the option agreement and the
State of North Carolina Wildlife for the purchase of approximately 441 acres,
less the approximate 10 acres to be retained by the city in the amount of
$660,000, and include the opportunity for each party to make minor corrections
to grammar, language, etc. Alderman Davis seconded the motion. Aye: Alderman
Carroll, Mosteller, Davis, and Lai. Nay: Mayor Pro Tem Kelley and Alderman
Spencer. Motion Carried 4-2.

3.   Discussion and Decision: Text Amendment-Section 3.9.B.5 Setback Exceptions
and Encroachments. (M. Meehan).
City Planner Meehan explained on November 16, 2023, the Planning Board decided
to recommend denial of the Unified Development Ordinance Amendment to Section
3.9.B Setback Exceptions and Encroachments to the Board of Aldermen. The
amendment proposed allowing HVAC generators and similar equipment to encroach
up to 48 inches into a required setback. However, the staff presented an
alternative, allowing for a 42-inch encroachment but not more than 24 inches
from the property line. The justification for this text amendment is to
accommodate smaller lot widths within cluster subdivisions and nonconforming R-
10 lots throughout the city. Nonconforming lots not located in subdivisions may
often have a 4’ side setback; therefore, the units would be allowed to have no
setbacks.
During the discussion, the need for the UDO to specify the impacts on
nonconforming lots with a 4' minimum side setback was raised. Alderman Lai
asked what would happen if the text amendment were denied and the exceptions
were not allowed. He wanted to know where the equipment would be installed. In
response, Ms. Meehan stated that the equipment would have to be installed
either in the front or rear yard. It would have to be placed where it can meet
the existing encroachment of 30' or change the design of the house and reduce
its size. Fire Chief Drew was then asked if maneuvering through 24" of space
with equipment would pose a fire safety hazard. Chief Drew replied that 24"
would be a tight fit for emergency access.
It was proposed to amend the text, and the recommendation was made to send it
back to the Planning Board for review. The primary focus of this amendment
would be on non-conforming lots, which seem to have the most trouble meeting
the setback requirements. However, it was also mentioned that homeowners could
apply for a variance if they had no other options. Mr. Cameron Smith, the
applicant, was called to the podium to clarify if the issue was mainly with
conforming lots. Mr. Smith said he has seen the biggest problem with the 5-6 ft
setbacks, mostly in PUDs. He then explained that it made sense from a building
standpoint and did not always work to put the equipment behind the house since
a generator needs an energy/gas source and cannot be placed anywhere.
A Motion was made by Alderman Davis to deny the Land Use Consistency Statement,
citing inconsistency with Policy 2.14 and 7.22 of the Land Use Plan and the
Zoning Text Amendment for setback encroachments as presented and second by
Alderman Mosteller. (no vote)
There was a discussion, and Alderman Mosteller clarified that she was in favor
of allowing the mechanicals in an R-10 environment with a 4’ encroachment. She
recommended sending the proposed amendment back to the Planning Board to
address language for non-conforming lots.
A vote was taken on the Motion. Aye, Alderman Davis. Nay: Alderman Kelley,
Spencer, Mosteller, Lai, and Carroll. Motion failed. 1-5
Alderman Davis made a Motion to send the Text Amendment-Section 3.9.B.5 Setback
Exceptions and Encroachments back to the Planning Board for more clarification
and review, second by Alderman Mosteller. Aye: Alderman Davis, Lai, Kelley, and
Mosteller. Nay: Alderman Spencer and Carroll. Motion carried 4-2. 
4.   Discussion and Decision: Text Amendment- Section 3.12.B.2 Driveways. (M.
Meehan)
Ms. Meehan reported that they approved a recommendation to the Board of
Aldermen during the Planning Board meeting on November 16, 2023. The
recommendation was in favor of a Unified Development Ordinance Amendment to
Section 3.12.B.4 Driveways. This amendment would decrease the driveway setback
for single and two-family dwelling units from 10’ to 2’ from the side lot
lines. Additionally, the staff has asked for the 50’ distance between two
driveways entering the same lot to only apply to nonresidential uses.
Alderman Carroll made a Motion to approve the Land Use Consistency Statement,
citing consistency with Policy 2.14 and 7.22 of the Land Use Plan and the
Zoning Text Amendment for driveways as presented. Mayor Pro Tem Kelley
seconded. (no vote)
In discussion, Alderman Davis stated that the text amendment applies to every
property owner in the city. She said that anyone disadvantaged by the situation
and feels they need only a 2ft setback, etc., can go to the Board of Adjustment
and apply for a variance. Mayor Pro Tem Kelley said that the 2ft setback came
to the Aldermen because it was requested by the Board of Adjustments because
they have seen it often enough to recommend a sweeping change instead of
consistently getting requests for variances. She feels that this is a case that
the Aldermen should certainly consider.
Alderman Carroll rescinded his motion.
Alderman Spencer made a motion to separate the proposed amendments and adopt
the Consistency Statement for approval of Policy 2.14 Section 3.12.B.4
e) No nonresidential driveway 
(nearest edge) shall be located within 10 feet of a side lot property line except in the case of a shared driveway 
(single curb/access point) utilized by two (2) or more lots. Residential
driveways shall not be located within two (2) feet of side lot property lines.
And second by Mayor Pro Tem Kelley. Aye: Alderman Spencer, Kelley, Lai,
Mosteller, and Carroll. Nay: Alderman Davis . Motion Carried 5-1.
Alderman Spencer made a Motion to send Policy 7.22 Section 3.12.B.4.a) Two (2)
nonresidential driveways entering the same street from a single lot shall be
permitted only if the minimum distance between the closest edges of the
driveways equals or exceeds 50 feet. Back to the Planning Board for further
review. Second by Mayor Pro Tem Kelley. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.

7.   Conditional Zoning Update and Discussion. (M. Meehan)
Ms. Meehan presented updates recommended by the Board of Aldermen at the
Planning Board's meeting on December 21, 2023. The updated language now
mandates a pre-application meeting instead of making it optional. It also
changes the timing of the public input meeting from after the application
submittal to before the submittal. It reiterates the requirement to incorporate
public input in the applicant-submitted meeting report. During their meeting on
May 18th, 2023, the Planning and Zoning Board voted to recommend the approval
of the Zoning Text Amendment. The Board's motion to recommend the approval
included two modifications: minimum open space provision within Conditional
Rezoning proposals and the inclusion of regulated trees within required
materials in a Conditional Rezoning application.
Alderman Mosteller made comments supporting the Zoning Text Amendment for
Conditional Zoning. She noted that the only downfall is that the process takes
more time to allot for more public engagement. She incentivized the concept of
smart development and the blending of mixed uses requiring less infrastructure.
Smart development supports the preservation of land and natural resources. She
does not agree with waiting until after the Comprehensive Land Use Plan project
has been completed and supports the recommendation to adopt the amendment by
the Planning Board, Staff, and the City Manager.
Mayor Alt stated that a development agreement could achieve similar goals as
suggested by Conditional Zoning until the Comprehensive Land Use Plan has been
updated and completed. Alderman Mosteller disagreed and said that a development
agreement can’t rewrite zoning. Mayor Alt said that the Comprehensive Plan is
to provide direction on how the city would like to look and feel in the future.
He feels that the community would like to have input on the comprehensive plan
before making amendments to the process of how new development will be
accomplished.
Alderman Davis motioned to deny the proposed Zoning Text Amendment and finds it
inconsistent with the 2014 CAMA Core Land Use Plan second by Mayor Pro Tem
Kelly. Aye, Alderman Davis, Kelley, Lai, and Spencer. Nay: Alderman Mosteller
and Carroll.
Motion Carried. 4-2.
Before moving into a closed session, Alderman Carroll motioned to discuss item
10 on the agenda, seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Kelley. Unanimous Vote; Motion
Carried.

O.   Closed Session
   Mayor Alt stated the purpose of the Closed Session per N.C.G.S. 143-318.11
(a)(3) To consult with an attorney employed or retained by the public body in
order to preserve the attorney-client privilege between the attorney and the
public body, which privilege is hereby acknowledged. General policy matters may
not be discussed in a closed session, and nothing herein shall be construed to
permit a public body to close a meeting that otherwise would be open merely
because an attorney employed or retained by the public body is a participant.
The public body may consider and give instructions to an attorney concerning
the handling or settlement of a claim, judicial action, mediation, arbitration,
or administrative procedure. If the public body has approved or considered a
settlement, other than a malpractice settlement by or on behalf of a hospital,
in closed session, the terms of that settlement shall be reported to the public
body and entered into its minutes as soon as possible within a reasonable time
after the settlement is concluded.

9.   Clarification and Details from the Meeting with East-West Partners.
(Alderman Carroll)
Alderman Carroll requested that an open discussion about recent events be
included on the agenda. He believes it is crucial for the board and the
community to come together and learn from what has happened. By doing so, they
can collaboratively work towards advancing Southport in a transparent,
cooperative, and harmonious manner. He outlined some key facts and dates
pertaining to Project Indigo. He questioned the transparency and city resources
used to meet with attorneys from both parties without the direction of the
entire board. Mayor Pro Tem Kelley said she was asked to sit it at a meeting,
and there were no negotiations. Alderman Mosteller noted that the code of
ethics was adopted to promote and strengthen the faith and confidence of the
citizens and their governing board. She said, “Our ethics say that we don’t act
without authorization from the board, so I just want us to understand that, for
me, there’s a question of ethics.” Mayor Alt said there was no wrongdoing, and
no negotiating was conducted.
Mayor Alt read the legal opinion from Mr. Terrell regarding the state's open
meetings law and the city's code of ethics. Mr. Terrell stated that the open
meetings law was not violated as a majority of the board was not present during
the meeting. Furthermore, he found no clear requirement or prohibition of the
city's code of ethics. According to him, it is common for members of the
elected body of every major North Carolina municipality to meet with staff,
developers, property owners, citizen groups, and adjacent neighbors outside of
the public hearing process. Therefore, Mr. Terrell suggested that the board
should consider meeting and communicating regularly with the development team,
just as it does with citizens opposed to the potential development of the site.
He also mentioned that although there are no laws or policies requiring board
members to share with each other when they learn or have heard from interested
parties, it is often a good practice to do so.
   Alderman Davis concluded that through this conversation, she had heard
nothing about facts being concealed. Alderman Lai stated, “We’ve got one
mission and one mission only, and that’s to take care of the citizens in the
City of Southport, and we’ve got to work together collaboratively to do that.
That is our job. Our only job.”
Mayor Alt requested a motion to adjourn after no further discussion. A motion
was made by Alderman Spencer and seconded by Alderman Carroll. Unanimous Vote;
Motion Carried.
Adjournment —10:50 p.m.

      Mayor, Richard Alt             Deputy Clerk, Tanya Shannon
