February 28, 2024
Special Public Workshop Meeting Minutes
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN Special Public Workshop Meeting Minutes
February 28, 2024 223 E. Bay Street
SOUTHPORT, N.C.   5:00 P.M.
 
Present:    Mayor Rich Alt, Alderman Karen Mosteller, Lowe Davis, Robert
Carroll, Frank Lai, and Marc Spencer.
Absent:   Mayor Pro Tem Rebecca Kelley
Staff:   Manager Bonnie Therrien, Assistant City Manager/Clerk Dorrie Dutton,
and Mo Meehan, City Planner
 
A.    Mayor Rich Alt called the meeting to order at 5:00 P.M.
B.    Alderman Reverend Davis gave the Invocation.
C.    Mayor Alt led the Pledge of Allegiance.
D.   Mayor Pro Tem Kelley made a motion to approve the agenda, which was
seconded by Alderman Davis. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.  
E.   Right-of-Way Presentation (D. Dutton and M. Meehan) 
   Ms. Meehan and Ms. Dutton discussed encroachments into the right-of-ways and
enforcement tools. Encroachments are prevalent in the city, mainly in the
historic core and non-conforming lots in R-10. Only new driveways, walkways,
parking for non-conforming lots, and overflow parking, if graveled, are
permitted. The UDO prohibits placing any structure or substance above the
ground on public streets, sidewalks, or other right-of-ways.
F.   Public Comments and Questions   
1.   Ms. Susan Delaney, who lives in the historic district at 304 W. West St.,
requested that the Board revise the policies in the UDO to allow property
owners to landscape around their properties and replace any items removed by
the city in the right-of-way. She has invested a lot of money in landscaping
and had the power lines buried around her house to prevent any damage. She
replaced the sidewalk to avoid tripping hazards and highlighted that property
owners have invested time and money to beautify the city.
2.   Mr. Angelo Collins, who lives at 1107 N. Caswell, has raised concerns
about the alleyways. He recently requested a permit to remove some trees from
behind his house to access his garage but was informed that there were
complications with issuing a permit for tree removal since the trees were
partially in the alleyway. Mr. Collins has taken the initiative to clean up the
area behind his house and is willing to remove the small gumball trees at his
own expense. Although he understands that alleyways are city property, he would
like the board to consider the properties that abut them and allow homeowners
to make improvements.
3.   Bob Holben, who resides at 114 W. Moore St., expressed concern about the
potential long-term parking issue in the city and believes that encroaching
into the right-of-ways has become the motive for taking action on such
encroachments. He acknowledged the incredible efforts of individual property
owners in the historic district in maintaining the charm of their homes,
preserving the trees, and landscaping. He emphasized that these efforts have
added to the unique and special character of Southport. Mr. Holben also noted
that the property owners understand their responsibility to remove any items
that obstruct the city's property. He acknowledged that if the city plans to
build a new sidewalk, parking spaces, or bury utility lines, it would be a good
thing, but preventing neighbors from beautifying the city at their expense
seems misguided. He argued that the barren right-of-ways are not charming, and
it is the property owner's efforts that make them so. He acknowledged that the
property owner's efforts are removable, if need be, but it should only be for
the right reason and not just to take over and assume the right-of-way. Mr.
Holben asked the Board to move forward with option four, which was considered
at the meeting on February 5th.
4. Do not amortize right-of-way encroachments; allow existing or new
encroachments until access is needed by the City or they cause a hazard.
a) The property owner can return the landscaping encroachments to the City at
no expense.
4.   Mr. Fred Fiss, a resident of 216 N. Atlantic Ave., believes enforcing the
right-of-way encroachments in the city is essential. He believes that safety
should always come first and that maintaining the city's property rights is the
responsibility of its citizens. Mr. Fiss finds it offensive when citizens fence
in the right-of-way, and he has noticed several examples of this around the
city, including 416 E. Bay St. In 2018, a fence and large boulders were placed
in the right-of-way at this location, which he believes could be hazardous to
pedestrians. He thinks people who must move into the right-of-way for passing
traffic could trip on the heavy landscaping and large rocks. Mr. Fiss filed an
official complaint with the city's code enforcement, but nothing was done in
2020 and 2021. The area that is fenced in is owned by a real estate broker, and
it infringes on valuable city property that could be used for additional
parking for Kingsley Park and potential sidewalks in the future. Therefore, he
requests that the city enforce violations of right-of-way encroachments, not
only for safety concerns but also for city property rights.
5.   Bob Gardner, who resides at 108 N. Caswell, has requested that the Board
be practical in enforcing right-of-ways. He believes it has been a common
practice for residents with non-conforming lots or those in the historic
district to enhance the right-of-way at their own expense for many years. He
agrees with the others that if the city requires utility access to these right-
of-ways, the landscape will have to be removed and replaced by the resident
with their money. Mr. Gardner believes that many people spend considerable time
and money on improving the right-of-way, which adds to the city's charm.
Although he understands parking is a significant issue, he points out that
certain areas have curbing that does not allow people to park in the right-of-
way.
6.   Kathy Cabral, 308 W. West St., echoed the prior speakers and agreed that
beautifying the right-of-ways has improved the city. She replaced the uneven
and hazardous sidewalk, buried utility lines, and planted a mature live oak to
replace a dead one. She implored the Board to allow the continuation of
improving and maintaining the right-of-way unless it is creating a safety
hazard.
7.    Hugh Fosbury, who resides at 120 W. Moore St., stated that property
owners know that the city owns the property, and that the city always has its
rights. However, some people misuse encroachment by using boulders and other
such things. He further explained that he put gravel on his side yard's right-
of-way (ROW) to prevent people from getting stuck in the mud while parking
there. Soon after, other residents added gravel to maintain uniformity and
improve the area's look. The residents paid for this themselves. He believes
that the city should not unnecessarily remove the ROW's beautification and
should allow the residents to maintain and replace the landscape if needed.
8.   Linda Pukenas, 119 N. Lord St., agreed with all the comments regarding the
right of way (ROWs). She said the residents take pride in maintaining the ROWs
in front of their homes and keeping them landscaped. She argued that if
homeowners were not allowed to maintain the ROWs, then the city should be
prepared to take on more of this responsibility and consider the cost. Ms.
Fosbury added that they all understand that the ROWs are city property and can
be removed if needed for city work but can be replaced by the owners if they
choose.
9.    Paul Swenson, who resides at 107 N. Atlantic Ave., stated that he has no
personal interest in the matter but believes that individuals who maintain the
lawn, plant trees, and use suitable quality pavers in the ROW contribute
positively to the area's aesthetics. However, he disapproves of people who
obstruct the right-of-ways (ROWs) in front of their homes during significant
holiday weekends to prevent others from parking. He suggested that during such
events, the public should be allowed to park in the city ROWs.
10.   Maria Horton, who lives at 414 N. Burrington Ave., expressed her
appreciation for the people who take pride in maintaining the right of way in
front of their homes, as it adds to the city's charm. She believes that
abandoning this practice is not conducive to the character of the city that
everyone loves. She also has a property with an abandoned alleyway with two
very large trees, and she wonders if the city will allow these trees to be
removed or if they will start maintaining the alleyways soon.
11.   Amy Patterson, who resides at 102 W. Nash St., expressed her concern that
if the right-of-way encroachment issue becomes enforced, it will lead to the
ROWs looking unkept and overgrown, just like they did many years ago. She
mentioned that she has never stopped people from parking in the ROW in front of
her property, but she takes care of it and keeps it clean. According to her,
these ROWs are situated in the heart of the city, where many people walk
around, and it would be a shame for the city to prevent people from
contributing to making it beautiful.   
   There were no further comments, and Mayor Alt thanked everyone for
attending. He announced the next meeting for further discussion will be on
March 11th at 6 pm.
G.    Mayor’s Comments
   Mayor Alt talked about parking issues in the city and how sometimes people
block the right-of-way with flags and tape. He suggested enforcing the city
code to stop this practice, or maybe the city could sell some right-of-way to
homeowners. However, this idea needs further discussion to determine if it's
feasible. The issue of staff versus residents maintaining the right-of-ways was
discussed. Structures and stone walls can block parking access, which must be
addressed. Mayor Alt noted that another solution may be to sell part of the
ROW, but this must be discussed and reviewed thoroughly. A meeting will be held
to discuss alleyways; some had permission to do what they wanted while others
did not. The Board will discuss addressing the abandoned alleyways at the next
meeting, and community feedback will be considered.
H.   Board Comments
   Alderman Mosteller expressed her opposition to selling city property,
particularly the right-of-ways, which she considers a significant part of the
city's heritage. She clarified that she does not favor hardened structures
(rocks, boulders, fences, etc.) in the ROW but believes the discussion of hard
structures and landscapes should be separate. She also emphasized the need for
rules and guidelines to be implemented, as there is a lot of diversity in each
situation. While she appreciates that people maintain the ROWs in front of
their property, she said someone might encroach the ROW with something less
appealing. She emphasized the importance of having an extensive conversation on
this matter.
   Alderman Carroll expressed his gratitude to the community for their efforts
to beautify the city, particularly in certain areas. However, he is against the
idea of taking possession of the right-of-way and blocking it from public
access. He acknowledges that some rules were not enforced when they should have
been, but he believes now is the time to follow the ordinance. He suggested
that certain concessions could be made in the ordinance to specify what is
allowed (such as landscape) in the ROW and make amendments rather than not
enforce.
   Alderman Davis questioned what would be done about enforcing right-of-ways,
especially for those blocking public parking for access to some city parks. She
said the owners know the ordinance but will not comply. She said that from a
legal standpoint, the city has to be cautious about selective enforcement. She
said there needs to be a way to amend the ordinance to deal with the different
issues that are inclusive to each property, as well as to achieve the overall
goal of improving the city right-of-way and not prohibiting public access to
public property.
   Mayor Pro Tem Kelley expressed her support for making amendments to the
current ordinance rather than enforcing it as it is. She believes that some
potential issues need to be addressed one-on-one. In response to Mr. Swenson's
comments about people blocking the right-of-way off from public parking on city
property during festivals and big holidays, the residents who maintain these
right-of-ways who say they understand the city may need to access them for
various reasons should also know that the public should also be allowed to park
on the right-of-ways if needed.
    Alderman Spencer expressed gratitude towards everyone for their comments on
the issue. He also presented an alternative perspective regarding the changes
that were being discussed. As a person born and raised in Southport, he has
seen many changes and understood that sometimes changes are not always
beneficial for everyone. He pointed out that the citizens of Southport have
diverse interests and preferences, and therefore, a 'one size fits all'
solution may not be suitable for everyone. He observed that many people are
moving to Southport and attempting to change and regulate the city. The issue
is complex due to the state setbacks on Moore Street, Howe Street, and Leonard
Street, which means different laws apply to various locations. He noted that
the alleyways had been neglected and require attention. He also suspects that
many other things have not been adequately addressed and must be dealt with.
   Alderman Lai thanked everyone for their valuable comments and their concern
for the city's beautification. He agreed that fences, boulders, and other
complex structures should be prevented as they obstruct the parking of vehicles
on public property, which is unjust and needs to be addressed. Parking in
Southport is a significant issue, so he suggested that using the city right-of-
way should not be limited to only property owners. He also encouraged more
discussion to find a fair and just solution that would be best for all the
citizens.
   One last comment was permitted by Ms. Karen Cobb, who resides at 107 N. Lord
St., raised a concern regarding the parking issue in the area. While she
welcomes visitors, she believes the residents should be prioritized. Limited
parking on her street often results in people parking on the right-of-way,
leaving residents with nowhere to park their cars. She requested the Board to
consider the taxpayers' needs before the tourists.
There were no further questions or comments. Mayor Alt requested a Motion to
adjourn. So, it was moved by Alderman Carroll and seconded by Alderman Spencer.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
Adjournment — 6:20 p.m.

February 29, 2024
Special Meeting Minutes
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN Special Meeting Minutes
February 29, 2024 Indian Trail Meeting Hall, 113 W. Moore St.
SOUTHPORT, N.C.   6:00 P.M.
 
Present:    Mayor Rich Alt, Alderman Karen Mosteller, Lowe Davis, Robert
Carroll, Frank Lai, and Marc Spencer.    
Absent:   Rebecca Kelley
Staff:   Manager Bonnie Therrien, Assistant City Manager/Clerk Dorrie Dutton,
Deputy Clerk Tanya Shannon, Communications/PIO Director ChyAnn Ketchum, Heather
Hemphill. Parks and Rec. Director, Police Chief Todd Coring, Finance Director
Lance Flint, Public Services Director Tom Stanley, and City Engineers Tom
Zilinek and Bob Jarvis.
 
A.    Mayor Rich Alt called the meeting to order at 8:30 A.M.
B.    Alderman Reverend Davis gave the Invocation.
C.    Mayor Alt led the Pledge of Allegiance.
D.   Alderman Spencer made a motion to approve the agenda, which was seconded
by Alderman Carroll. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.  
E.    Agenda
   1.   Budget Goal Setting for FY 2024-2025 (Ann White, NCLM)
   Manager Therrien emphasized the importance of setting short-term, medium-
term, and long-term goals for the budget. She introduced Ms. Anne White, a
municipal operations consultant with the League of Municipalities.
   Ms. White expressed her gratitude to the Board for inviting her and
presented some ideas for establishing the budget goal, both individually and as
a group. Ms. White sent out an assignment to the Board to bring back and
discuss each member's goals.
   Mayor Alt expressed interest in reviewing the discretionary funds. Since
most of the budget is allocated to areas with limited flexibility, one of his
objectives is to assess the total amount of funds available for discretionary
spending. To start the review process, he has requested an estimate of the
amount of money available for discretionary spending. He reviewed some key
components. 1) He believes Parks and Recreation should not be separated.
However, he suggested hiring a park supervisor with experience in trees and
landscaping or an outside company to routinely come to do concept landscaping
such as fertilizing, trimming, etc. 2) He would like to start the budget
process of how to protect and restore the old City Courthouse. 3) He explained
that with roughly $5 million in funds dedicated to the Shoreline Stabilization
project that must be used by 2026, there needs to be a plan for using the money
this year. He said that $5M will not be enough to complete the project, but it
can be done in phases and how much each phase will cost. 4) He would like to
address the alleyways and the cost of cleaning them up and making them
accessible for cyclists and pedestrians. 5) The cost of road paving and how
much to set aside each year for paving. 6) He discussed the RPO Greenway
Project, and although most funds will come from the State, there needs to be a
discussion about whether there needs to be a contribution or matching funds.
   Alderman Carroll shared his thoughts on the current short-term goal, stating
that the biggest challenge at the moment is the sewer merger with the county.
This merger will significantly reduce revenue, impacting on some of the staff’s
salaries. Consequently, he believes that the upcoming year will be a lean one.
Therefore, he suggests that there should be more emphasis on employee
recruitment and retention to tackle this challenge effectively. He would like
to see an asset maintenance plan and goals and funds to protect and maintain
all real property. He would like to see funding for the all-inclusive park in
addition to a private funding partnership. Improve the monetization of tourism
and keep revenue in Southport, not just during peak season but also from weekly
shoppers and diners.
Alderman Davis expressed her desire to see improvements in storm drainage. She
noted that while maintenance work is being done on the existing storm drains,
more of them are needed. According to her, heavy rainfall causes extensive
flooding and ponding in yards and streets, which is not just limited to storms.
Therefore, she suggests expanding the storm drainage system to improve drainage
and prevent flooding, especially in areas with new development. Alderman Davis
also raised concerns about parking issues and suggested the possibility of
using eminent domain to acquire the open area at the yacht basin. She
emphasized that the area is zoned residential and any new construction in the
vicinity could compromise the vistas, which would undermine the CAMA Land Use
Plan. She suggested that the space could be used for free or paid parking for
events and other purposes, making it a viable investment that would be worth
the cost. She would like to appropriate for real estate. She said a lot of the
buildings are crowded, and some are underused. She would like a good, solid
plan that can be agreed on for the best use of public buildings. Perhaps
purchase, sell, or preserve them. She would like to budget for electric vehicle
plug-ins for EVs. She would like to create a connector from Lowe White Park and
Taylor Field leading up to Kingsley Park. She would like to acquire land
between these parks to ensure smooth connectivity. The ultimate aim is to
create an uninterrupted pathway for people to commute between these parks.
Alderman Mosteller discussed her plans for budget planning in the short and
long term. Her objectives include developing a budget document that meets the
criteria for the Government Finance Officer Award of Distinguished Budget
Presentation and creating a 5-year budget structure. She believes these
initiatives are crucial for effective planning in the future. During the
discussion, she also mentioned reviewing the status of the building inspections
department fees and determining which staff and facilities can be attributed to
these funds. She also expressed her eagerness to review the analysis of the
staff pay study and move forward with it. Additionally, she hopes to provide
more training initiatives for staff and committee members. In the short term,
Alderman Mosteller aims to relocate the Police Department to provide more space
for city hall. She also stated that the yacht-basin dredging is a high priority
on the list. Advance in the Shoreline Stabilization project and determine how
to proceed with grant funds and additional funds needed. In the long term, she
aims to repair roads and sidewalks, install traffic calming devices, and update
the transportation plan for a future goal. She wants to look at the aesthetics
of city facilities, including signs, etc. Another important short-term goal is
to fill the planning department's open positions. She is also considering
establishing an Entry Corridor Commission to protect the corridor, which is a
main point for the city, and discussing managing impervious coverage to deal
with stormwater drainage.
Alderman Spencer suggested that tourism could be used more effectively to
generate revenue. He explained that while businesses benefit from the influx of
travelers to the city daily, weekly, or monthly, the cost of maintaining the
necessary infrastructure should not fall solely on the residents. He proposed
that visitors contribute to the cost of maintaining the infrastructure to share
the burden. He would devise a long-term solution to generate more revenue from
tourism effectively. He noted that due to the water and sewer merger, the city
would suffer a significant loss of income. As a result, most of the city's
revenue will come from taxes. He emphasized that setting goals and planning for
the future is crucial, but the amount of money required to achieve these goals
is yet to be determined. Alderman Spencer aims to enhance staff skills and
leverage technology to streamline operations. He recommended bringing interns
in to learn and bring in new ideas, evaluating and maintaining city buildings
and facilities, needing the funds to protect Franklin Square Park, and
renovating buildings for better use. The Shoreline Stabilization Project is of
utmost importance, and it is essential to set a goal on how to proceed with the
allocated funds before the year ends. It is necessary to redirect ferry traffic
from neighborhood side streets that cause road damage and incur expenses. The
State should be more involved in the repair of their roads. It is crucial to
ensure that if the ROWs (Right of Way) are restricted, the city maintains them.
The Police Department could be relocated to the old Fire Station to save money
on purchasing a new one. Budgeting for connectivity with the parks is
necessary. Look for resources to pay for sidewalks to take pedestrians to
Walmart and other businesses.
Alderman Lai expressed his agreement with everyone that tourism plays a vital
role in Southport's economy. He emphasized that the city needs to explore
various options to generate revenue through tourism. Shoreline stabilization is
also a significant priority, and the city must decide quickly on how to fund
and phase out the project. The city facilities require repairs and renovation,
and a Board Chamber would be a valuable asset. Alderman Lai recommended
investing in staff training and providing competitive salaries to attract and
retain the best talent. Relocating the Police Department is essential, and
creating more space for staff at City Hall is well-needed. The primary
objective is to establish a plan to generate more revenue through grants, paid
parking, and other means.
There was discussion on medium and long-term goals for generating more revenue.
It was mentioned that a slight increase in sales tax would be a tremendous
help, but it would have to be lobbied for and approved by legislators.
Manager Therrien expressed her concerns about the city's financial situation.
She mentioned that she has never seen a state restricting municipalities from
raising funds and that the city needs to work with other towns to ban this
restriction. Manager Therrien explained that in other states where she has
worked, there are options to raise funds, which would have to go to a
referendum for a public vote. With the CIP presentation coming up, she
emphasized that the improvements cannot be funded through tax revenue alone.
She was surprised to learn that the city does not have a bond rating, which
could be a viable option to complete big projects. In her opinion, grant money
alone will not be enough to cover the expenses.
Ms. White has compiled a list of all the goals and ensured that none
overlapped. She reviewed each goal and provided some valuable suggestions. She
has also recommended collaborating with the departments responsible for
specific areas of improvement. Additionally, she has expressed her willingness
to work with the city manager and finance director to review the goals in
greater detail. Ms. White expressed her gratitude to everyone who participated
and was enthusiastic about supporting the team in achieving these goals.
Everyone thanked Ms. White and the Staff for leading the direction in the next
budget cycle.
There was no further business. Mayor Alt requested a Motion to adjourn. So
moved by Alderman Carroll and seconded by Alderman Lai.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried. —11:08 A.M.

1.   Franklin Square Park Tree Assessment (Everett Jones, Bartlett Tree
Services)
Mr. Jones assessed the trees and reported that the majority of them have a low-
risk rating, which is impressive. However, he conducted a thorough evaluation
of 22 Oaks and discussed several options to mitigate the risks associated with
these trees.
Alderman Mosteller asked about the possibility of reopening the park once the
liability risks had been reduced. Manager Therrien consulted with the risk
agent and was informed that it would be safe to reopen the park once the
recommended trees and limbs were removed. The discussion then moved toward the
final report, and it was requested that $50,000 be allocated from the City's
Building and Grounds Budget to address the immediate issues outlined. Mr. Jones
stated that tree removal would begin in the blue area on the site plan, and
once the risk manager approves, the park can reopen. However, Mr. Jones
stressed that no mechanical equipment should be allowed in the park; this
includes vehicles, lawnmowers, weedwhackers, stakes, tents, trailers, etc.
However, pedestrian traffic should remain allowable once the park is deemed
safe, and all trees should have mulch surrounding them for root protection.
Alderman Carroll questioned whether the $50,000 was only for the blue area
(where the four sisters are) behind the city gym or for the entire park.
Manager Therrien clarified that it was for the 22 trees that needed attention.
Alderman Carroll questioned whether this would open the whole park, and Manager
Therrien responded that it would depend on the risk manager’s decision. Manager
Therrien also reiterated that the $50,000 was just an estimate and that an RFQ
would have to be sent out.
Alderman Davis Made a Motion to allocate $50,000 from the City’s Public
Services’ Building and Grounds account to address the immediate issues of tree
work in Franklin Square Park as identified by Mr. Jones and Bartlett Tree
Experts and to proceed with the provided option two which states “If you elect
not to remove the trees, the risk of trunk failure will remain low for live
oaks #3, #24, and #25. Pruning to reduce the relative size of the crown on each
tree may result in an estimated residual risk of low branch or crown failure.
These four trees should have root collar excavations performed if they are to
remain on site.” Alderman Carroll seconded . Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
2.    Proposed Ordinance Changes and Budget Requests (Friends of Franklin

Finally, the group requested the establishment of a separate Parks and
Recreation division to manage Franklin Square Park. They hope to be included in

The Board has recognized the need for more attention to preserve Franklin

Alderman Davis proposed a Motion to direct the City Manager to issue a Request

3.   Job Study and Classification Plan (P. Fortuna and Rob Williamson,
Evergreen Solutions)
   Ms. Fortuna introduced Mr. Willianson, who gave a PowerPoint presentation on
the study and the process. Mr. Williamson stated the study aimed to create a
fair and competitive pay plan.
   The Board discussed the plan and whether it included the cost of living, job
performance, or benefits. Mr. Williamson clarified that the plan did not
include any of these factors. Manager Therrien mentioned that cost of living
and job performance evaluations are handled separately. Mr. Williamson
suggested two options - above midpoint parity and below midpoint parity.
Midpoint Parity – places employees into new pay ranges based on relationship to
midpoint. If above the midpoint, move employees based on years in the current
classification. If below midpoint, move employees based on tenure. A chart was
provided for more clarification. Everyone agreed that retention of good
employees is valuable, and compensation should be fair and competitive.
However, it was the consensus of the Board to seek more clarification of pay
grades and the process for implementing these grades. The Board agreed to get
more information and discuss the options in the budget work sessions.

engagement.
4.   Resurfacing Roads (T. Zilinek City Engineer)
Mr. Zilinek presented a PowerPoint on the Paving Program for the Future of
Southport. He explained that the city currently has no long-term resurfacing
program in place. As a result, many of the city's streets have not resurfaced
for years, and most of the pavement has exceeded its useful life, showing signs
of failure. Unfortunately, the amount of Powell Bill funds the city receives
annually is insufficient to fund a proper resurfacing program. Without a
dedicated investment in a resurfacing program, the city's streets will
deteriorate, worsening driving conditions.
Annual Funding Received:
·   The city receives about $150,000 annually from the State in Powell Bill
Funds.
·   Resurfacing all city-maintained streets using only Powell Bill funds will
take about 66 years.
·   The average pavement life is 20 to 30 years.
What is needed:
·   Resurfacing all city-maintained streets over ten years will require $10
million or $1 million per year on average.
·   Recommended front loading and doing more in the first couple of years, then
reducing in subsequent years.
·   Recommendation is $2M, $1.5M, $1.5M, $1M, $1M, $0.75M, $0.75M, $0.5M,
$0.5M, $0.5M.
·   Recommended spreading throughout the City yearly and not concentrating on
one specific area. This way, an entire area will not need to be resurfaced
simultaneously in the future.
There were concerns regarding the finalization of the sewer merger,
particularly when the county began working on the sewer lines. It was unclear
who would be responsible for repaving the roads. Mayor Alt mentioned that $1.1
million had been set aside for road repairs after installing the sewer pipes,
which was part of the discussion with the county. He said the county would own
the sewer system by 2028, while the city would own the roads. This raised the
question of who would repair the roads if they were dug up to install new sewer
pipes. Mr. Zilinek recommended that the city repair the streets when the time
comes because the city would have control of the standards and specifications.
The county would handle trenching and road resurfacing, but the city would be
responsible for paving. Mayor Alt pointed out that inflation could cause the
cost to exceed the earmarked $1.1 million. He suggested considering an
appropriation for any extra funds needed. Mr. Zilinek noted that these numbers
are today's and did not act out future costs. Alderman Carroll questioned if
the appropriated funds were in a CD. Manager Therrien said she was unsure but
would consult with the Finance Director. It was decided to continue discussions
at a later date without further questions.
5.   Discussion of Alleyways (D. Dutton)
Alderman Davis raised a concern about whether the alleyway discussion should be

March 5, 2024
SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN Special Meeting Minutes
March 5, 2024     Community Building, 223 E. Bay St.
SOUTHPORT, N.C.   10:00 A.M.
 
Present:    Mayor Rich Alt, Mayor Pro Tem Rebecca Kelley, Alderman Karen
Mosteller, Lowe Davis, Robert Carroll, Frank Lai, and Mark Spencer.
Absent:   None
Staff:   Manager Bonnie Therrien, City Clerk Sara Thomas, Deputy Clerk Tanya
Shannon, ChyAnn Ketchum POI/Communications Director, and Lance Flint Finance
Director.
A.    Mayor Rich Alt called the meeting to order at 10:01 A.M.
B.    Alderman Spencer gave the Invocation.
C.    Mayor Alt led the Pledge of Allegiance.
D.   Mayor Alt asked for an amendment to the agenda to include a discussion on
Legislative Proposals. Alderman Davis made a motion to approve the amendment to
the agenda, and Alderman Mosteller seconded it. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
   Alderman Mosteller made a Motion to approve the agenda as amended and
seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Kelley. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.  
E.    Agenda
1.    UDO Changes and Process
   An Ad Hoc committee was formed to review the process and criteria for
requesting an amendment to the UDO and other procedures. The committee
consisted of Mayor Alt, Alderman Lai, and Carroll. During their discussions,
Mayor Alt raised the issue of how changes to the UDO are initiated and the
collaboration between Staff, the Planning Board, and the Board of Aldermen. The
discussion focused on the current process, which involves a proposed amendment
or revision initially raised by Staff, another applicant, or the Aldermen. It
is then sent to the Planning Board for a thorough review and recommendation,
after which the Aldermen decide. Alderman Davis suggested an Aldermen workshop
to discuss matters related to the UDO. She proposed that the Board discuss
topics requiring changes and then send them to the Staff and the Planning Board
for review.
The Board agreed to move forward with the UDO amendment process as it currently
stands. Additionally, they will schedule a workshop to discuss potential
amendments raised by board members or concerned citizens. The Board will
compile a list of issues that have arisen and may pose conflicts with the UDO,
which they will then provide to the City Manager and discuss in the workshop.
The consensus of the Board was to have an annual workshop to discuss UDO-
related issues.
Mayor Alt pointed out that the UDO specifies a 90-day timeline for review and
recommendation by the Planning Board. This timeline can be extended if
requested and granted. However, as it is not currently written in the UDO, he
proposes adding language explicitly stating that an extension is permittable.
It was brought up that the Board conducts an annual review of the Ethics
Policies at the start of each new year. Alderman Carroll suggested that this
review could be combined with the upcoming UDO workshop and include a
discussion on the Code of Ordinances. Manager Therrien suggested having a
weekend retreat to discuss the UDO, Ethics, and Ordinances. The Board agreed to
provide the City Manager with their concerns regarding these subjects and
provide the Board with some options for scheduling workshops.
2.   Public Comments for Rules and Procedures
   Alderman Carroll and the Ad Committee proposed limitations on public
comments, including a three-minute limit per person, a one-hour public comment
period, and concluding Board meetings by 10 PM unless the Board votes to extend
the meeting. However, Mayor Alt reconsidered the time limit proposal, believing
it's not in the city's best interest to restrict the length of public comment
and that every person who sign-ups should get a chance to speak. The Committee
also recommended that anyone who wishes to comment must sign up.
   Alderman Davis is passionate about giving citizens time to be heard. She
compared perception to reality by analyzing the length of public comments and
meetings from previous long sessions.
   The Board discussed the appropriate length of time for individual speakers
to comment. They concluded that a three-minute limit was reasonable. However,
Alderman Davis expressed disagreement with putting a time limit on individual
speakers. Alderman Spencer reminded everyone that there are two regular
Aldermen Meetings a month, and the public can speak at one or both meetings.
Additionally, they can submit comments and handouts and send emails or make
phone calls to members of the Board to address their concerns. Alderman Spencer
suggested that the consent agenda should include items that do not require
lengthy discussions. He also recommended that the meeting be limited to four
hours instead of stating 10 PM unless it is voted to extend. This is because
there are morning meetings as well.
   Mayor Alt announced that the Ad hoc Committee has reviewed all the
suggestions regarding the public comment period in meetings, including those
from the School of Government and neighboring jurisdictions that align with
these proposals. He also mentioned that further discussions would take place,
and a decision on the next steps would be made during the upcoming meetings.
3.    Role of Board Liaisons
   Mayor Alt presented an overview of the Ad Hoc Committees' discussion on the
role of liaisons and how to report information from Advisory Board Meetings to
the Board. The committee discussed the idea of providing each liaison with a
template or worksheet to fill out regarding the key points of the meetings. The
liaisons would then be required to submit the completed template to the Manager
and the entire Board within seven days of the subjective meetings.   
   The roles of Liaisons were evaluated depending on the Committee, Commission,
or Board. In some cases, Liaisons are not allowed to participate in
conversations at specific meetings, such as the Planning Board or Board of
Adjustment Meetings. However, there have been instances where the Liaison has
participated in technical review committee meetings. Mayor Alt suggested that
specific rules of engagement be established for those allowed to speak from the
Aldermen, such as a member of the Board of Aldermen who is present, The
Liaisons, or no one at all.
The Board agreed that the Liaison would use a template provided to share a
brief summary of the meetings. The summary should include the agenda, highlight
key concerns, and provide an overview of important points for each Board
member. However, there was a debate on whether the Liaisons or another Board
member would be allowed to speak during the meetings. No consensus was reached
on this matter.
4.     Policy on Public Contributions to Public Projects
   The Board has agreed to establish a policy for submitting and managing
donations. It was decided that the City Manager and the Finance Director would
bring policies and procedures to the Board for submitting and managing the
funds.
Alderman Lai clarified that if a contribution is made to the city, the donor
may want to know how and where the money is being spent. Therefore, the
objective is to create a policy that ensures donors feel confident that their
donations are being used appropriately. Additionally, there was a question
about whether cash would be accepted for contributions. Without records, there
could be potential complications.
If the public-private partnership agreement is established, the City will be
responsible for keeping records of the funds. There was a question about
including contributions and fundraisers such as DSI and the 4th of July in the
policy. The Board will continue to have more discussions at a later date.   
Break 11:48 A.M.
Return 11:52 A.M.
5.    Legislative Proposals 
   Mayor Alt provided each board with five legislative proposals previously
discussed and drafted by Manager Therrien for review, which need to be
submitted to the legislators in Raleigh as soon as possible.
LEGISLATIVE PROPOSALS
CITY OF SOUTHPORT – 2024-25
 
1)   Propose a legislative proposal so that Southport can keep the fines from
parking tickets, much like Oak Island.
Mayor Alt has discussed the current state of parking ticket fines, explaining
that they currently go to a literary fund or outside of the city. He mentioned
that Oak Island was able to keep $1.2 million in fines within their town and
asked how they were able to do so. They responded that the town had requested
the state legislator to ask that those fines remain in their town. Mayor Alt
stated that there had been some initial discussions on the topic, and it seems
to be a straightforward process. It was the consensus of the Board to move
forward with petitioning the State Legislators to permit the fines from parking
tickets to remain in the Southport Jurisdiction.
2)   Create legislation that allows Southport to increase the accommodations
tax from 3% to 5%. The current 3% would be assigned to the General Fund to
support Community Relations and the Visitors Center, but the additional 2%
would be solely designated for the City’s Capital Improvement Fund for
infrastructure upgrades and repairs. Southport has facilities that attract
tourists and non-residents and generate economic benefits for regional and
local commercial entities. The ever-increasing volume of visitors far outweighs
the impact of Southport’s residents on the city road, sidewalks, parks, and
buildings.
An additional 2% would help provide funding for the services, facilities, and
infrastructure needed to successfully maintain Southport as an economic engine
of the region.
The Board agreed to recuse Mayor Pro Tem Kelley from this discussion as she
requested due to a potential conflict of interest.
Alderman Mosteller explained how the particular process works and the benefits
it offers. She suggested that the city could request the State to allow for an
increase in rates that would enable them to maintain the infrastructure using
funds generated from tourism and the accommodations tax. The Consensus of the
Board was to move forward with sending this to the Legislators for request and
to allow Mayor Alt to collaborate with other mayors to inquire how this has
benefited their city/town.
3)   Allow Southport to put a sales tax for meals and beverages in a November
referendum to see if the voters would approve this. This would assist with the
rising infrastructure costs of the visitors and tourists and their impact on
the City.
4)   Alderman Davis mentioned that approval from the State is required before
adding an item to the agenda for a referendum. Manager Therrien confirmed that
the State's approval is necessary. Alderman Mosteller proposed changing the
term "sales tax" to "prepared meals tax," and Alderman Davis suggested
including "served beverage" in the language. The Board agreed that the City
Manager and Staff should finalize the correct language for the request and send
it to the Legislators.
5)   $1,000,000 for the Taylor Field Inclusive Playground v/s
6)   $900,000 (which, according to Chief Drew, may have been reduced to
$600,000) for the Fire Department radio replacement program, as the radios will
be obsolete in July of 2025. Because we have to order the replacement radios
ahead of time in order to have them ready for July 2025, funding is required
this year.
The Board must prioritize between the Taylor Field Inclusive Program and the
Fire Department radio replacement program.
The consensus of the Board was that funding for the Fire Department was a high
priority in proceeding with the request for the Fire Department radio
replacement program because if it is not done by July 2026, the radios will be
turned off. Mayor Alt stated that it would not be known if the money would come
before June at the end of the budget cycle, and then the city would have to
come up with the money. Alderman Carroll suggested creating a plan B in the
budget discussion in case of the worst scenario.
Mayor Alt requested a motion to adjourn the meeting since there were no further
questions or comments. Mayor Pro Tem Kelley made a motion to adjourn, which was
seconded by Alderman Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried . —12:11 p.m.

Special Right-of-Way Workshop
 
BOARD OF ALDERMEN Meeting Minutes: Special Right-of-Way Workshop
March 11, 2024    Community Building, 223 E. Bay St.
SOUTHPORT, N.C.   6:00 P.M.
 
Present:    Mayor Rich Alt, Mayor Pro Tem Rebecca Kelley, Alderman Karen
Mosteller, Lowe Davis, Robert Carroll, Frank Lai, and Mark Spencer.
Absent:   None
Staff:   Dorothy Dutton, Assistant City Manager; ChyAnn Ketchum, POI/
Communications Director; Police Chief Todd Coring; and Heather Hemphill, Parks
and Recreation Director.
A.    Mayor Rich Alt called the meeting to order at 6:00 P.M.
B.    Reverend Alderman Davis gave the Invocation.
C.    Mayor Alt led the Pledge of Allegiance.
D.   Mayor Pro Tem Kelley made a motion to approve the Agenda seconded by
Alderman Davis. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.  
E.   Right of Way Presentation
Ms. Dutton gave a presentation on enforcement options and provided an update.
She explained that currently, according to Section 16-8 of the UDO, right-of-
ways must remain unobstructed to allow for the passage of people and vehicles.
Additionally, she clarified that alleyways should also be considered as right-
of-ways.
She went over some options for moving forward:
1.   Option: Enforce the ROW Ordinance as it is written:
   a.   All existing encroachments must be removed by a certain deadline; Or.
   b.   All existing encroachments can remain until a time the City needs
access to the area, and then they will be removed and cannot be put back;
   c.   No new encroachments would be allowed.
2.   Option: Property owners are allowed to landscape and plant vegetation in
the City’s ROW, but there cannot be any hardscapes (pavers, fountains,
decorative rocks, etc.)
3.   Option: Property owners can create parking spaces only in the ROW areas.
(how many spaces will be allowed (1-2?) (will they be reserved for the owners?)
what materials will be allowed?
4.   Option: Do not amortize ROW encroachments. Allow existing or new
encroachments until access is needed by the city or they cause a hazard.
   a.   The property owner can put the landscaping encroachments back at no
expense to the city.
5.   Allow landscaping around existing trees for protection against parking,
but do not allow other encroachments.
Alderman Carroll questioned the year the alleyways were closed by deed. Ms.
Dutton said that, according to her information, one was in the early 90s, but
she would look into the others. Alderman Davis questioned whether any money was
exchanged with these closures. Ms. Dutton said she would look into that.
Mayor Alt mentioned that several questions need to be addressed regarding the
alleyways. Some alleyways were legally closed, while others were encroached
upon, and there are still some that are uncertain. He suggested collecting more
information and deliberating on the subject once some questions were resolved.
Alderman Carroll brought up the issue of Wilmington lines running across
sidewalks for EV charging. He suggested having a discussion on how to handle
this situation in the event that a smaller lot without off-street parking needs
to be charged. Mayor Alt emphasized the need for city maps to be provided to
understand the situation better. Alderman Davis raised concerns about a
historical home built before zoning was established, which is located in 1/3 of
the ROW. She questioned whether the city knows precisely where the ROWs are
located. She requested a map showing the exact location of ROWs and whether
they extend into the owners' property. Alderman Mosteller noted that homeowners
typically complete a survey of their property. Alderman Davis stressed the
importance of determining exactly where the ROWs are, as sometimes property
owners may not have a survey. It was the consensus of the Board to discuss the
alleyways in more detail when more information becomes available.
F.   Public Comment
1.   Bob Holben,114 W. Moore St., expressed his disagreement with the three-
minute time limit for public comments. He appreciates the hard work done by the
Board and understands that important matters need to be discussed, but he would
like the Board to consider allowing the public to speak without any time
restrictions.
Mr. Holben discussed the ROWs and suggested that the city should clarify that
no changes are planned for areas with concrete sidewalks or hard curbs.
Property owners should be allowed to add and maintain the ROW in front of their
properties at their own risk. Regarding gravel parking areas, the city
recommends a maximum of 1-2 parking spots, but Mr. Holben questioned its
rationale. He cited the Lord St. residents' example, who have graveled both
sides of the street and made parking available. He questioned if there was a
prioritized list of sidewalk projects and if there would be a connectivity plan
to connect Lowe White, Taylor Field, and Kingsley Parks.
2.   Kathy Cabral, 308 W. West St., submitted comments read by Ms. Dutton. She
requested consideration for language in the UDO for ROWs that would permit
planting improvements and parking slots in the ROW if the property owner
chooses to do so at their expense. She said it is understood that it is city
property, and if the city has to remove landscape, etc., to work, then the
homeowners would be responsible for replacing anything removed. She feels like
the improvements made to the ROW by the residents add to the city's beauty and
charm.
3.   Pat Kirkman, 119 Park Ave., expressed her views on the ongoing discussion
regarding the right-of-ways (ROWs) and hoped that some decisions would be made
soon. She acknowledged that beautifying the historic district and downtown area
are the most discussed topics because they are in the city's heart. However,
she also requested the Board to remember the rest of the city and consider them
as well. She pointed out that some residents on her street have graveled their
whole yard and encroached upon some of the ROW. She hopes that the Board will
make clear and decisive decisions that will benefit the entire city.
Alderman Mosteller motioned to close public comment, seconded by Mayor Pro Tem
Kelley. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.  
G.    Mayor’s Comments
Mayor Alt stated that there are many ongoing projects and policy reviews. He
acknowledged the community's frustration with wanting action sooner and
encouraged them to continue providing feedback. He said the Board is working on
the budget for FY24-25, and planning requires time. Mayor Alt highlighted
persistent issues with ROWs and the need to improve the UDO. Parking is a
significant concern that affects ROWs. The Board is committed to serving the
city's needs and best interests.
H.   Board Comments
   Alderman Lai stated that the Board has a lot of work to balance, especially
during festivals when parking becomes a major issue due to tourism. He believes
ROWs should be considered for parking without unnecessary restrictions. The
goal is to achieve the best outcome for the city and its residents.
   Alderman Spencer addressed concerns about the city's regulations on ROWs.
The regulations aim to recover and protect city assets. Parking is already a
significant issue downtown, and there are concerns about work vehicles,
landscaping equipment, and boats left in ROWs in other areas of the city.
Enforcing ROW obstruction regulations is difficult in the long term, and people
may take over property that does not belong to them. Alderman Spencer suggested
discussing the materials being put in ROWs and leaving space for parking by
placing them at ground level.
Mayor Pro Tem Kelley made several suggestions to consider. She proposed
separating the discussion of alleyways and right-of-ways as two distinct
issues. She also would like more discussion on expanding the conversation
beyond downtown and addressing the issue of parking spaces for homeowners in
the historic district during construction. Additionally, she emphasized the
need for a separate discussion to evaluate the historic overlay in comparison
to the rest of the city.
Alderman Davis mentioned that there are a few places in the city where the
Right of Way (ROW) almost reaches the front door of a house, and homeowners
have surrounded it with landscaping, sidewalks, and mailboxes. She acknowledges
that it is a complex issue and that taking action to address it will be
challenging. She emphasized that the city needs a comprehensive master map.
Alderman Carroll stated that the city had established ordinances for managing
ROW-related issues, but they were not enforced for a long time. He addressed
the limitations of parking pads, which could lead to unattractive concrete
slabs on people's lawns. He cautioned that stormwater drainage could be an
issue that needs to be addressed alongside other concerns.
Alderman Mosteller is concerned about safety due to the limited use of the
right-of-ways (ROWs). Her street is only 18ft wide, and accessing the ROW is
the only way to stop or pull off the road. Homes are situated near businesses,
churches, parks, and pedestrians, and the network of sidewalks is inconsistent.
Cyclists and golf carts on the narrow roads limit options for emergency vehicle
access during a crisis. Fences and hardscapes prevent emergency vehicles from
utilizing the ROWs. Therefore, she believes that these wide ROWs provide less
obstruction of vision, which equals more safety. From her standpoint, she does
not favor grandfathering in fences and hardscapes for safety reasons.
Ms. Dutton provided important information after discussing it with the city
planners before closing the meeting. She mentioned that the width of a driveway
cannot exceed 50% of the total lot width. She further noted that if any changes
are made to the structure's footprint or the right-of-way (ROW) measurements, a
new survey is required. For older lots, staff refers to the plotted maps from
the 1900s to ensure consistency. Mayor Alt confirmed that a map containing all
ROWs can now be created from the available data. Ms. Dutton agreed to proceed
with the process of generating this map.
There were no further questions or concerns. Mayor Alt requested a motion to
adjourn. So moved by Alderman Carroll and seconded by Alderman Spencer.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
Adjournment— 6:53 p.m.

G.   Presentations 
1.   Capital Improvement Plan
The City Engineer, Mr. Bob Jarvis, presented the second year of a six-year
Capital Improvement Program (CIP), which includes projects costing over
$100,000. The CIP is regularly updated, prioritized, and priced by staff. It
serves as a dynamic guidance document for annual budgets and long-term
financing needs. The multi-use program aims to collaborate more and receive
bond ratings and grants.
   The Board consensus was to break down the plan into what will need to be
appropriated for the projects depending on which type of funding will be
necessary, such as discretionary funding and non-discretionary funding. Mr.
Jarvis said he would happily break it down and delineate between the funding
and the sources.
2.   Audio/Visual Options and Discussion
   Communications/PIO Director ChyAnn Ketchum presented on the audio/visual
concerns and options for meetings. Some of the issues discussed included
difficulties viewing content on the VIBE board, problems incorporating remote
two-way participation with video, and challenges configuring the microphone
system, camera system, and screen presentation for viewing at the Indian Trail
Meeting Hall.
To address these concerns, several solutions were proposed. One option was to
replace the VIBE at the Community Building, which would cost between $7,000 and
$10,000. Another proposal was to bring the SCB VIBE board and mount it so both
the audience and the Board could view presentations at the Indian Trail Meeting
Hall at no cost. Upgrading the microphone, camera, and live-streaming system
was also suggested at around $40,000.
Alderman Carroll asked about moving the Community Building's equipment to the
Indian Trail Meeting Hall and installing new equipment at the Community
Building. Ms. Ketchum explained that the current system at the Community
Building was hard-wired, making it difficult to move the equipment. However,
she offered to explore the feasibility of the move.
The Board discussed prioritizing upgrading the projection screen and audio/
visual systems. It was suggested that a consultant be hired for cost-effective
solutions. Alderman Lai proposed an improvement where visual monitors can be
matched with the agenda item and page number for easy access. Alderman Spencer
proposed building chambers for the Board to offer a permanent solution. Mayor
Pro Tem Kelley suggested buying a large TV screen over the fireplace with a
mini split to aid visuals and inquiring about incorporating Zoom as part of the
meetings. Ms. Ketchum offered to research the feasibility. Alderman Carroll
questioned whether it was a top priority compared to other pressing projects.
Mayor Alt said that this is the preface for more discussion during the budget
workshops and also to discuss options for a permanent Board Chamber.
H.   Agenda
1.   Real Estate Services

2.   Authorization to Purchase Materials for Electrical Underground Project
Mr. Ellie Pittenger, the Electrical Superintendent, emphasized the importance
of timely ordering of materials for the upcoming East Moore Street underground
project. He explained that this is crucial to ensure that the project stays on
schedule and prices remain stable, thus avoiding any availability delays and
rapidly increasing costs of electrical construction materials. To proceed with
the project without any further delay, Mr. Pittenger requested approval for a
transfer of $860,000 from the Electrical Fund Balance to the budget line item.
This will enable BEMC to start work on the East Moore underground project.
Alderman Spencer asked about the start date for the project. Mr. Pittenger
explained that the labor portion is scheduled for the next budget year, which
is after July. He added that he is seeking approval on this budget to ensure
the materials can be ordered and ready in advance so there will be no delay
when the project is ready to begin.
Alderman Mosteller raised a concern regarding the underground project's
funding. She mentioned that $1.5 million has already been invested in the
project over the last few years and questioned if the newly requested amount of
$860,000 was in anticipation of additional costs. In response, Mr. Pittenger
explained that $1.6 million had been allocated in each budget cycle. He stated
that they aim to complete the project with a total budget of $1.84 Million.
Alderman Spencer made a motion to approve the money transfer from the Fund
Balance of the Electrical Account to Line Item # 30-93-7210-5900. Second by
Alderman Davis.
Alderman Mosteller expressed concerns regarding approving a purchase for the
following year's budget. In response, Mayor Alt explained that a similar
process had been followed in the past. He also pointed out that purchasing the
required materials beforehand would be proactive while they were still
available and before their prices increased. This would help avoid delays
during the project's initiation, which had happened previously.
Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
3.   Recycling/Yard Debris Collections, Neighbors to Neighbors
Finance Director Mr. Flint gave an overview of the discussion. He explained
that after the Water-Sewer Merger, the City will no longer have a mechanism to
collect fees directly for residential recycling and yard debris collection via
utility bills. The City will need to either identify an alternative method for
billing for the services or discontinue them as a City service.
Mayor Alt would like to confirm that the county is properly recycling. Mayor
Pro Tem Kelley said that in previous discussions, there was talk about asking
BEMC to add recycling/yard debris collections to their billing statements and
collect on behalf of the city. Mr. Flint said that with the water/sewer merger,
Brunswick County has agreed to collect for the services on behalf of the city
for a charge of around 10 cents per bill that would be charged back to the
customers.
Mayor Pro Tem Kelley motioned to allow Brunswick County to bill and collect
recycling and yard debris service fees on behalf of the city, which was
seconded by Alderman Carroll. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
Neighbors for Neighbors Program Discussion
Mr. Flint discussed the Neighbors for Neighbors program and asked for the
city's involvement in assisting low-income residents with water and sewer
bills. To apply for the program, residents can contact Brunswick Family
Assistance (BFA). Currently, 28 eligible senior residents receive a $40 credit
on their bills, while 10 non-seniors also qualify. The city receives a check
from BFA to cover their water/sewer bills.
The budget for the program in the Water-Sewer fund for FY24 is $13,650, with
the city paying about $1,200 per month (28 accounts) for participating seniors.
However, the budget is likely to be exceeded in FY24. The Board Donations
account budget also included $18,000 for the N4N program in FY24, but nothing
has been spent from this amount in FY24 or FY23. BFA sends payment to the City
from its own funds for participating non-seniors, around $400 (10 accounts)
each month, which is then applied as payments to the participant accounts.
During budget discussions, Mr. Flint requested the Board's decision on
allocating General Funds to BFA and whether the city should continue to
participate in the program after the water/sewer merger.
4.   Discussion and Consideration of Property for Lease
Manager Therrien explained that the city has an opportunity to lease space at
1669 N. Howe Street for a 5-year term. The building was previously a bank and
would provide additional space for the Police Department and allow City Hall to
expand. The monthly lease agreement is $5,520.83 plus utilities.
Alderman Mosteller motioned to authorize the City Manager to sign the lease
agreement with Admiral Holdings LLC for a five-year lease at 1669 North Howe
Street, as outlined on the attached lease, to be used for the Police Department
Headquarters. Alderman Caroll seconded.
Mayor Pro Tem Kelley noted that the building, formerly a bank, already includes
a vault, which is one of the reasons this space was selected: it would be used
to secure evidence in the Police Department.
Alderman Davis asked about the monthly rent of $5,520.83 plus utilities and the
expected annual increase after one year. Ms. Therrien confirmed a $130 yearly
increase for the next five years. Alderman Mosteller noted that the city has
been searching for this space to relocate the Police Department for over two
years.
Alderman Spencer said the current solution to the problem is only temporary.
This is because the city had previously decided not to allocate any funds for
the old City Hall/Courthouse. Although the Department has other buildings that
can be used, these buildings are also not suitable. While there is a need for a
space for the Police Department and City Hall, this solution is only short-
term, and long-term solutions need to be discussed further.
Aye, Alderman Mosteller, Carroll, Spencer, Lai, and Kelley. Nay; Alderman
Davis. Motion carried 5-1.
5.   Public/Private Donation Policy
Manager Therrien proposed a Public/Private Donation Policy. This policy would
establish a clear process for handling donations toward City projects or
events. As per this policy, all donations would be made through the City, and
the Finance Department would maintain written records and provide receipts. The
Rules and Procedures Committee drafted the policy, which was referenced by the
School of Government.
Alderman Mosteller expressed her support for a policy but suggested that the
Finance Director should review and create a new policy that can address
different types of public contributions for various events and projects.
Private partnerships often involve unique contractual agreements. She inquired
whether the policy aimed to establish a special revenue fund instead of a line
item. This would help in distinguishing and managing multiple projects and
events.
Mayor Alt has emphasized the need for a clear process and an accounting system
for all funds donated to the City. This process will ensure that there is a
proper record of the contributors, the amount of money donated, the project or
event for which the funds are intended, and when and how the funds were spent.
Mr. Flint explained that the intention is to carry out basic accounting
practices. He mentioned that donations are generally recorded under the
miscellaneous donations line item in the general fund. Over time, these funds
tend to merge with one another, making it difficult to keep track of them. To
make the cash handling process more efficient, he suggested that there should
be a separate line item in the system for each project or event, where
donations can be allocated. He emphasized the need for a unique fund code in
the accounting system so that each project or event can have its own fund. This
way, all donations can be tracked and managed effectively.
The discussion focused on how contributions are perceived and communicated. It
was agreed that a policy should govern the receipt and accounting of donations.
Alderman Mosteller made a motion to ask the Staff to review the language used
in the draft policy for Public/Private Donations to the City. The purpose of
the review is to improve the clarity of the language used in the policy to
distinguish procedures for different types of contributions and sources. The
goal is to establish a process that ensures transparency and accountability in
the handling of donations. Seconded by Alderman Lai. Unanimous Vote; Motion
Carried.

F.   Special Presentations
1. Shoreline Stabilization Project Update (Bob, Jarvis, City Engineer, and C.
Creed, Olsen Engineers).
   Mr. Jarvis provided a brief summary of the project. Then, Mr. Creed updated
everyone on the progress made so far and discussed future plans. He explained
that the Cape Fear River shoreline had been continually eroding due to wind,
ships, tides and currents, storm surges, and rising sea levels. He said they
are continuing to explore several options and are considering a phased project.
The project goals are to provide reliable protection to upland infrastructure,
improve recreational access and use, restore the beaches and dune/marsh
habitat, plan for future sea level rise, plan for larger and more frequent
boat/ship traffic, minimize the need for future maintenance and work with
funding limit and time constraints of the $5M grant that will expire on June
30, 2026.
   The Board discussed concerns regarding storm surge and flooding. While Mr.
Creed acknowledged that revetments would help, they won't guarantee the
prevention of flooding under certain conditions. Mr. Creed said that they want
to select the most efficient materials for the design to create better
stabilization.
   Mr. Creed explored different options for the project, which involved
stabilizing four individual segments. These areas were divided into four parts,
with Area One starting from the west end of Bay Street and Area Four commencing
from the east of the city pier. According to Mr. Creed, the most crucial areas
were One and Two. He reviewed two options, A and B, which addressed each area
separately in phases.
   There were some concerns regarding the property adjacent to the project
areas. Have they been adequately informed, and is there any pushback? Ms.
Therrien stated that one property has pushed back but not appealed. Mr. Jarvis
confirmed that the City Attorney had already been consulted about the riparian
rights and had been informed of the updates. He also reiterated that once the
Board decides how to proceed, the City Attorney will advise the city on the
best course of action.
After reaching a consensus, the Board decided to act on areas one and two that
require the most urgent stabilization.
Mayor-Pro Tem Kelley motioned to authorize Mr. Chris Creed, P.E. from Olsen
Associates, LLC, to move forward with Option B for areas One and Two. This
option involves detached breakwaters and sand fill. However, further
discussions regarding areas three and four will continue at a later date.
Second by Alderman Spencer. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried.
Break—Call back to order 10:57 am.
Due to a time-sensitive matter, Mayor Alt requested a Closed Session at the end
of the meeting per NCGS 143-318.11. A Motion was made by Alderman Spencer to
add a Closed Session to the Agenda, and second by Alderman Carroll. Unanimous
Vote; Motion Carried.

Purchase of a Fire Engine and Ambulance, to the top of the agenda for

   Alderman Spencer made a motion to approve the amended agenda, seconded by
Alderman Mosteller. Unanimous Vote; Motion Carried. 
5.   Financing and Terms for Purchase of a Fire Engine and Ambulance.
   Fire Chief Drew is seeking final approval for a Capital Project for Fire and
EMS. He has been working on writing specifications for a new rescue and service
truck. The Chief explained the purpose and use of each truck in rescue
situations. He said this vehicle would also serve as a command service and
could replace some other vehicles. Chief Drew also shared that if the truck is
ordered before 5/1, there will be a 2% savings, and if it is ordered and paid
upfront, there will be a savings of $200,000. Additionally, if the fire truck
and ambulance are ordered together, there will be a further discount.
   Alderman Lai asked about the fire truck repair costs. Chief Drew reported
$40k spent in the past year, and the aging ambulance is also incurring
expenses. Mayor Alt suggested adding a penalty clause if the goods are not
received by the deadline to ensure NC purchase process standards for fire
departments.    
Alderman Mosteller asked about the financing for an ambulance, and Chief Drew
confirmed that it would come from the general fund. Payments for the ambulance
won't begin until 2025-2026. The fire truck will be financed through collected
fire fees.

225 HDR Walker Rescue Service Fire Engine Apparatus at a price of $1.2 million.

Institutes. This purchase will be funded from the City Budget. Second by

E .    Budget Presentation
Manager Therrien and Assistant City Manager Dutton presented the proposed FY24-
25 budget highlights. They explained changes, revenue sources, fund balances,
proposed capital lists, and potential additional revenue sources.
A one-cent tax increase has been proposed to fund capital projects totaling
$145,000. Due to the merger, the Board has allocated $1.2 million from the
Water/Sewer Fund to offset General Fund salaries. However, other expenses
totaling an estimated $379,000 still need to be transferred from the Water/
Sewer to the General Fund. This year's General Fund allocation to the Fire/
Rescue Department is $161,010. The proposed budget also includes $162,584 set
aside for Salary Study Adjustments and a 3.5% Cost of Living Increase for
Employees. Additionally, there is a new 6-year Capital Improvement Plan with
ongoing and recommended projects. Ms. Dutton reviewed the General, Electrical,
Powell Bill, and Capital Funds.
Ms. Therrien discussed the proposed capital list to be funded through the
capital fund, with total revenues of $1,808,625. Some of the proposed projects
include a new police facility, road improvements, a new recreation center, and
shoreline stabilization. Possible revenue sources, such as business
registration fees, animal taxes, stormwater management services, special
assessments, and motor vehicle license tax, were also mentioned. During the
discussion, the condition of certain city facilities and associated repair,
usage, and revenue costs were addressed. Ms. Therrien emphasized that the Board
must determine the intended use of the buildings before making any decisions.
F.   Agenda
2.   Police Department and Animal Protective Services
Chief Coring outlined the department's structure and mission, emphasizing
integrity, professionalism, and service. He updated call statistics, noting a
slight increase. Major Burke discussed finalizing the move to a new facility,
staff training, community engagement, agency operation, and improving the
department's response to community issues. Major Burke highlighted upcoming
goals, including maintaining accreditation, developing new community engagement
programs, and enhancing APS/Police Operations.
Major Burke explained that two requests in the proposed budget are a shift
differential for officers on night shifts and a career development program for
new officers, including a step program for salary increases as they progress in
their training.
Mayor Alt asked about paying for the cadets' Basic Law Enforcement Training
(BLET). Major Burke explained that cadets are usually compensated for training,
and their schedules are adjusted to accommodate it. If the city sponsors the
cadets, the training cost would be around $300, with the Federal Law
Enforcement Training program covering the rest (around $1,500).
Alderman Mosteller questioned Chief Coring about the part-time APS assistant,
and she did not see that in the budget. Major Burke said it was designated
under APS salary and allocated explicitly for on-call services. Alderman
Mosteller also mentioned a concern with ‘farming’ out the APS Officer with
Development Services. She believes it does not support Community Values as the
APS has many duties and responsibilities, including a 28-page Animal Welfare
Ordinance to follow. She said this had been tried before and did not work.
Manager Therrien explained that after reviewing calls with the Police
Department and the Animal Protective Services, it was found that the number of
calls for the Police outweighed the calls for APS. As a result, she recommended
that the APS Officer, who has experience with zoning, assist the Development
Services Department. She stated that the numbers do not justify the need for a
full-time APS Officer and would like the officer to take on additional
responsibilities to remain full-time instead of part-time. Alderman Mosteller
mentioned that there is a lot more involved than just calls and that there is
also a significant amount of community service involved, similar to policing.
Ms. Therrien requested the Board also look into staffing Police and Fire for
significant events. She asked the Board to consider whether to charge fees for
these services for events; she said this would be a policy decision. Chief
Coring noted that an option for some events could be for Off Duty Management
(ODM) for officers to be paid by the event organizers versus paid overtime.
Alderman Mosteller asked if the budget included the kennel and temporary
holding facility next to the River Road Animal Hospital. Chief Coring confirmed
that it is included in the budget and the APS office on Rhett Street for
operational services.
3.   Development Services Budget Overview
Ms. Dutton explained that the Development Services comprises two divisions:
Planning and Code Enforcement and Building Inspections and Permitting. All
revenue generated by Building Inspections and Permitting must be spent with the
Department and their expenses. Estimated revenues for FY24-25 are $800,000.
The Planning and Code Enforcement department brings in about $30,000 annually
but does not generate enough revenue to cover all its expenses. The Rate
Committee will review proposed changes to Planning/Zoning fees, as some are
below average. Approximately half of the Director of Development Services
position is funded by the Inspections/Permitting Division, and there is a
vacancy for the Director of Development Services.
There was a discussion about evaluating the current fees in the development
services department. The goal was to have the Rate Committee recommend
adjustments to increase fees currently priced too low to generate enough
revenue to fund all staff salaries and make necessary adjustments to cover any
shortfalls.
4.   Community Relations and Community Building Budget Presentation
Ms. Dail provided an overview of the primary funding sources for the Community
Relations Department, including revenue from occupancy tax collection and
renting out the Southport Community Building for events. The projected revenue
for the FY25-26 budget is as follows: $200,000 from Community Building Rental,
$210,000 from Local Occupancy tax, $15,000 from Tourism Special Events, and
$7,500 from Gift Shop Donations. Budget requests for FY 25-26 include
allocating funds ranging from $3,000 to $5,000 for the Beautification
Committee, $3,000 for the Cemetery Committee, and $10,000 for new lights on the
Holly Trees on Moore and Howe St.
Mayor Alt mentioned that an organization could rent Franklin Square Park and
pay the city a fee. The city would now collect funds from vendors. Ms. Dail
confirmed this change. Mayor Alt asked about the impact on the budget. Ms. Dail
explained that they are currently collecting all funds and expect higher
revenue in 2025. She noted that it was not reflected in the budget due to
uncertainty about future events. Mayor Alt inquired about the estimated revenue
if all scheduled events were to take place. Ms. Dail said she would provide
that information later. Mayor Alt and Alderman Spencer discussed the cost-
effectiveness and rental fees for events. Ms. Dail explained that this year's
fees remain unchanged at $30 for a weekly booth or $300 for a season.
Ms. Dail discussed the chair cushions for the community building. She said that
is a budget request for all the chairs for stadium-style events or meetings.
She noted the community building deck needs to be replaced. She said the
project is to replace the existing deck, but there has been some discussion
about the type of materials. She said that it appears that it would most likely
be replaced by wood.
There was a discussion about how funds are distributed from the ABC budget. A
certain amount is allocated for first responders and for the city schools. It
was noted that there has been a long tradition of allocating funds to the
school for various projects. Alderman Spencer suggested that the Board should
attend special events that promote growth and entrepreneurship as a group. He
recommended that the Board as a whole should present the school with the yearly
donation.
Finance Director Flint concluded the meeting by briefly explaining how to
interpret the budget sheets. He discussed allocating funds to the three major
departments and emphasized the importance of accurately representing fund
transfers rather than fragmenting the costs across different departments.
